I really really enjoyed this game. I would recommed buying it. The customization is great, the improvements in your city are fun and the end game is fairly satisfying.  As much as I love this game, there are several things that annoyed me.
First, the game is quite short, I was able to beat it in about 24 hours.  However, to offset this, the replayability (forgive my spelling) is quite high.  Going into this I was expecting a game like KOTOR, unfortunately, it misses that mark by a wide margin.
As great as it is to build your city and see it improve around you, from what I could tell this had little improvement in the end game, other than visual improvements.
There was not enough character development.  There were some dialog between characters, but it was not enough to make me really care about them, save for one or two.
The game is still quite buggy.  I was not able to complete all my missions because of various bugs that would hinder my progress, by not letting me complete the quest, or jumping around "quest points".  This vexed me greatly.
I would highly recommend this game, as long as you know what to expect and are getting into.  I will definately continue to play this and enjoy this game.

I am not usually a fan of RPG games, but I have been blown away by this game.
Gameplay is not overly complicated, there is excellent variety in the character specs, with the ability to combine any fighting style with any other, and the interactions between characters and NPCs is endless. Looks wise, this game is also a cut above. I am running with a GTX1070 and it is simply gorgeous. Single player is smooth and effortless, in my 153 hours of gameplay so far I have only experienced one single incident of crashes, which was following a patch, and quickly hotfixed by the devs later that day. Even multiplayer I have not experienced a single connection issue, which is highly impressive. The devs on this game seem to really listen to player feedback and act on issues quickly. The result of such a dedicated dev team is a close to perfect, polished and thoroughly enjoyable game.
The main story itself is captivating and very well done, however, the different character storylines are, for me, the stars of the show. Each characters story is well written, with good background without bombarding you with details. They are also endearing and comedic, even sometimes a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥ (Yes Lohse, I mean you!). There are so many different ways to follow the story and interact, combined with the variety in party member options, the option to go completely solo, and various difficulty modes, that this is a game with so much potential for repeat plays. There is also Gamemaster mode, which I am yet to try.
I cannot recommend this game highly enough, but, as a warning, you will sink 100 hours of your life into it without even realising it!

Hello!
I've played this game across multiple ports (Xbox 360, Xbox One, PC) I can honestly say that you won't be able to find a medieval skill based game like this anywhere to be honest--I've always wanted to play a game where you could play and fight like in the movies like Kingdom of Heaven, Gladiator, Braveheart, etc. and I finally found one. I won't front though, despite the game's uniqueness, this game is a bit rough around the edges; I'll list some pros and some cons:
Pros:
-This game pretty much allows you to choose whatever medieval weapon suits you and charge into the fray, swinging it around decapitating foes on the battlefield.
-Its got a bit of a silly element to it (the laughing and taunting emotes are ridiculously funny).
-This game's melee combat system allows much more leeway than other games (Skyrim and Mount & Blade: Warband for example) allowing you to play how you want and come up with your own techniques that will allow you to prevail on the battlefield.
Cons:
-I won't lie when I say that the community is a bit cancerous due to this game being heavily skill based. Try to stick with friends when you play this game, it can be kind of rough out here in Agatha. Stay out of the way of the higher ranks and players involved in clans and you'll be ok.
-This con is very very subjective: There has been a massive technique vs. exploit debate going on since this game's inception. Truth be told, there will be playstyles used that you may or may not agree with as being legit and a natural part of the game. I won't get into too much detail.
-The learning curve can be quite frustrating.
-There is player customization, but for 80% of it you'll need to open up your steam wallet.
Basically I'm not going to sit here and say don't waste your breath or your money on this game, because it is an interesting and--sometimes addictive game to say the least. This game is definately worth a try. (At least until Mordhau comes along XD)

Fair Strike is ancient, and it shows. Limited resolution, too many buttons, lack of full support for gamepad, it adds up to a somewhat frustrating flying experience when you just want to blow **** up.
One would have hoped that whoever made it run on modern platforms (it does run fine on Win7x64) would have bothered to create a decent mapping for gamepad, but no luck here. Game doesn't want to map a lot of commands, and have no way of figuring on which control is which. For example, let's say you want to map the two triggers to shoot... nope, can't do that. Those are ANALOG controls. ARGH! Okay, map to "rudder" (left right turns). Go into the game... It's REVERSED! I hit left and I turn RIGHT! had to go into options/controls and turn on "INVERTED". Do this for EVERY analog control. Oh, and it doesn't support the digital pad.
I guess I could have opened up XPADDER and tried to remap some more commands, but I'm too tired fighting with the game rather than playing it.
Being an ancient game even on older machine frame rate is silky smooth. And graphics are decent. Sound is okay.
The main problem is the game doesn't quite seem to make of itself. Being a "Strike" series member, Fair Strike is trying to invoke some old shooters like Desert Strike, Jungle Strike, and so on, but those are isometric and semi-3D shooters. This is a full 3D arcade-y flight sim.  It'd be the difference between original River Raid and Lock-On. There's even a "simulation controls" (with full cyclic and collective controls) if you find the arcade controls (almost like hovercraft) too limiting.
If you want a fun helo shooter, go play Thunderwolves instead. This game is a bit too old and quirky to be enjoyable nowadays.

Fair Strike is an arcade combat helicopter flight simulator.
Originally released way back in 2004 and supporting a maximum resolution of 1280 x 960 at 32 bit depth.  The game does however work and plays smoothly on the core i7 and NVIDIA GT 770 under windows 7 64-bit.
Looking past the obviously dated graphics, the gameplay is fun.  The default controls took a little time to get used to, but are functional and for the most part usable.  Be prepared to master using a wireless X-box controller in tandem with the mouse and keyboard.  There are 7 pages of default control keys / settings to memorise and the game is not playable without getting these under your thumb so to speak.
The missions are fairly straight forward with main missions and side missions to be completed and bonus objectives and achievements.
There are Steam trading cards and Steam achievements to be earned and the game is both fun to play and challenging.  Be warned that the default game setting is Hard.  There are two other settings available, Normal and Easy.
There are a variety of weapons and ordinance, and a few iconic Russian military helicopters which have been reasonably well modelled.
This game stands up fairly well with other similar games available at the time of it's original release such as the Apache Longbow series.
While not a state of the art flight simulator, this game is far from being a pure arcade game.  It would fall somewhere in between the two.  Best description would a combat flight simulator with arcade elements.
The missions are fun to play, but are a little over-the-top fantasy with a solid melodramatic touch.  All the drug cartells in the world have united into this super criminal organisation which is stronger that the military organisations of the world's combined military super powers.  This does however provide lots of cannon fodder and bombing targets so lots of stuff to shoot and blow up!
A competent game that will provide several hours of fun at a budget price.

It contains enough content to hold you over, and when the map add-ons go on sale, get those.  It of course is a different setting, but the mechanics are the same. I once remember walking into a random cave in the middle of nowhere and ended up fighting a nest of spiders, followed by a giant Tarantula...all around, it's not the best game in the world, but if you like a steep learning curve and a game that's challenging, but also rewarding, try it out....It's free...play it, or delete it. I love/hate this game.  I've been on the fence about it for a long time, and really don't know what to say here, and -really- wish that Steam had a "In between" other than yes or no.  I recommend you research this game before you buy it.  Determine if it's right for you.  I will say, the servers aren't as lively as they used to be, though the "free expansion" (which was just a really big update with an extra biome) pumped some blood into it's veins.
You can build, you can fight, you can let your giant (or very, very tiny)♥♥♥♥♥♥♥flop in the wind.  Or boobs.  This game contains full nudity, dismemberment, slavery of innocent NPC's (mostly innocent), and the occassional giant god of destruction that can crap all over your base and hard work.  There is costly counter measures, but this is a survival game:  We all know that means that if you're starting out you're gonna have a hell of a time getting a good foot hold in any long-standing server.
It has a lot of stuff I adore about it.  The building is fun, and a little better than titular games like Ark.  Making a "city" for you and your friends requires a grind, however, material gathering in a game like this is always the burden of building---it can take forever to get crap so you can put up some walls and plop down some archers to defend stuff.  Customize your town, color outfits (Of which there is a variety), give NPC's those outfits even, and try not to die in your sleep.  Mods are available in plentiful amounts on the workshop, however---they can easily break with each update, which gets tiresome.  Rather than allowing you to start the game and disable the mods while in said game, it will crash consistantly until you remove the problematic ones from your steam subscriptions---THERE'S GOT TO BE A BETTER WAY TO DO THIS, POPCAP.
Ahem.
As for the other negatives:  Population.  Servers seem pretty empty.  I'm assuming that's a little less worse now that the update is here, but... I wouldn't be suprised if they dwindled back down.
Combat.  Hoooboy.  Combat.  So, it looks good in the videos, but... it's a lag-tastic dance of stupidity.  Lag-jousting was a real issue... till to counter that they -removed- the ability to run and hold a weapon.  Meaning, rather than fix the performance issue, they disable a previous "Feature" (which is a -STANDARD- in combat games) and even touted it as a new part of the combat system.  Lazy!  I'd rather see fixes and additions than them removing things for the sake of stopping the lag jousting.  It comes off as a rock-paper-scissors scenario still of dodging/blocking with strikes and heavy strikes.  Don't know if until lag/network issues are fixed if this will ever feel right... especially when fighting NPC's.  Nothing says fun like a teleporting hyena chewing on your bits.
So what makes this a "negative" review from me? The straw that breaks the camel's back on this is something that's prevelant in survival games:  The fact I can't just straight up host locally without having a ridiculous tether that's impossible to get around if I want to play with just a handful of friends.  If you want to do that, you'll have to drag your buddies about with a leash like they are a child that's had way too much sugar that has a very lazy parent.  ...It bothers me so bad many games do this.  I don't want to buy or rent a server just to enjoy a game with a few friends because there's no discernable setting other than possibly fishing through config files to set that dumb thing to 1000000 or something.  And even better?  They have expressed they don't want to change that!  Read as:  They don't want to make it functional.
So, long story short.  It's fun.  It has problems, and... I hate the problems.  I suggest checking it out via videos or... whatever before you buy it.  Not gonna be for everyone.  If you want adventure and action, it's here, but not something that's very fast-paced or even as well thought out as other games.

Beautifully drawn, puzzle-heavy, cartoonish adventure game with sympathetic cast, intriguing story and quite unique mythos.
The gameplay is standard point'n'clicking: You can either inspect (a magnifying glass), pick up (a hand), or interact (gears) with hotspots. Left-clicking brings up a "radial menu" with the inspect option on left and either interact or pick up option on right. This seems a bit clunky and wasteful considering right-clicking serves no purpose. You open the inventory by moving the cursor to the lower end of the screen and use items via the radial menu or dragging'n'dropping.
Graphics of the milieus in this game are top-notch. For some reason the developer decided to put less effort into character art, and they generally look like they were drawn in MS Paint. After the initial shock this didn't bother me personally, but as someone rightfully pointed out it makes the characters seem a bit disconnected from the surroundings. Animation is satisfactory.
Sound is good, and the naivety of the protagonist is quite cutely presented by the voice actor. Rest of the cast is up to par as well. There was one character in the game whose voice I couldn't bear, but it sort of suited him anyhow. Music is mostly ambient and forgettable.
The story and atmosphere are moody. Don't let the cute exterior fool you, there are some dark elements in the story and characters. Some of it felt borderline psychotic and rather morbid, which I enjoyed. Predictably, attempts at humor are made, but I only found myself chuckling a few times, so it was mostly a miss in my case. Dialogue was for most part pretty standard stuff compared to other point'n'click adventures, at times good, and on a few occasions a bit too lengthy. The world is imaginative and the game has a lot of personality, and the characters were generally likeable and/or relatable on some level. Writing felt a bit rushed toward the end, but I felt the story came to a closure.
Puzzles are of varying quality. They mostly felt logical, and some of them were quite clever, but sometimes I felt like things were set up badly and I needed to do things in some arbitrary order or fashion to achieve the end result although I had already figured out a/the logic. There is a help system if you get stuck.
The game spans five chapters and progression happens within constraints of a handful of [scrollable] screens at a time, restricting problem-solving to a rather narrow area and assets. This means less exploration and more fiddling with objects and talking to characters.
Technically, the game had one small annoyance: Sometimes when you'd interact with an object or trigger an event there is a noticeable pause before the character responds, similar to how older games used to stall for a few seconds to load an audio file from CD-ROM. It is annoying enough to warrant a mention here, but doesn't come close to affecting my opinion of the game on the whole.
The main complaint - as often is the case with these games - is that I wish the game was lengthier. I could have gone on for full 10 chapters at a slightly slower tempo or (preferably) with a more branching storyline. In any case, if there ever is a sequel I will definitely be getting it to see what more is going on in Asposia.

If survival FPS is what you are looking for then look no further. I started the series with Shadow of Chernobyl, which I highly recommend to play first. Even though the two stories arent strictly linked, the game and atmosphere feels alot more developed once you play through SoC.
If you decide to jump into Call of Pripyat anyways then once you get past the steep learning curve youll find yourself in a pretty large world without much indication of what to do. Basically all you need to know is that everything is out to kill you and unless youre 10+ hours into the game, everything will kill you without even giving you a chance. Hitting that F5 button is a must every 2 minutes because you can and you will die every 2 minutes in your first playthrough. Getting money to buy better gear is a must and doing the side missions just happen as you go along. Once you find yourself being able to kill bandits and small fry mutants, then you are in a position to actually start the main story and continue the game as intended.
Pros of this game is that the atmosphere in this is unmatched by any game ive played since its release up to the time of this review. The gun physics is amazing as the bullets are physical objects and shooting just doesnt get any more satisfying than this, that I can garuantee. The survival elements of this game are really harsh at first but once you get mid range equipment, you should be able to get a reasonable income for items and such to keep you going. End game is mainly about exploring and the survival elements are very minimal as youre probably pretty rich by then and the stores always have enough supply.
Cons are that even though the game is open world with alot of varying activities, I have to say that to me the main story felt no different than doing a very long series of side missions. Theres also the fact that once you reach a certain point in the game, the atmosphere changes from survival to just completing missions and loses alot of its immersion (IMO).
On the plus side again though there is a HUGE amount of mods available for this game and trying them out gives you a new experience every time.

I'm embarrassed to have almost 100 hours of playtime in this game show up on my Steam, given how much I hate it. My excuse is I was aiming to play as much as I could of it to figure out why the hell people enjoy it so much, and I still have no ♥♥♥♥ing clue. I played the main quest, all of the DLC quests, a bunch of side quests including some guild stuff and did quite a bit of exploring.
This game is beyond boring.
- Literally 5 voice actors.
- Zero effort for any sort of facial animation (or any other body animation for that matter). It's frighteningly awkward talking to people and having the camera just zoom up as close as possible to their face.
- No outcome or punishment for anything. "Oh, you can kill people, join a guild, rob a merchant, be any class you want, go to jail...." ....so what? What's the end goal? Nothing, there is rarely any reward for anything you choose to do.
- Casting spells is brutal. Choosing them too. The whole UI is pretty terrible.
- The story is awful. Or at least, it could be interesting, but even the good voice actors seem to fall asleep by it given their performances. The best quests were the funny ones that didn't take themselves seriously, such as this one you do for Sheogorath where you trick this one village and some others in the Shivering Isles expansion.
- A mind-numbingly easy levelling system.
- Very poor variety in enemy encounters. (Most of them just run up and attack you and don't do anything unique or challenging.)
The biggest redeeming thing this game has though is the world is actually pretty nice to lose yourself in. It's fun to just walk around, discover an old cave or ruin, kill everything inside it, get some loot and keep going on your way. I can appreciate that. One problem is, there are literally 4 types of environments in this game. Hills/forest (which covers 95% of the map), the Oblivion gates (which all look identical), caves (again, all depressingly brown and identical) and ruins (very similar to caves, but nicer, especially the Ayleid ones). So everything becomes really boring, really fast.
The only other thing that I can say is appreciated is the availability of mods. While I only played with a couple, it's nice to know that the developers are so open about that kind of stuff.
In the end, I'd give this game a 2.5/10. I think it's pretty terrible game that is massively overhyped. One day I'll play Skyrim and see if it's any better, but from what I've seen, I highly doubt it.

Oblivion is the first step the TES series took away from it's classic, dice-roll-centric CRPG roots, and more into the action-RPG direction of tactile, weighty combat and a bigger focus on experiencing the story, rather than forging it. The result is a much deeper feeling of the character being unique and personal to the player, as well as far greater enjoyment from the multitude of battles that you inevitably face. However, it also results in a big cutback on the depth and meaningful choices to be made, especially due to the transition to full voice-acting.
Nevertheless, that does not deter from the series' strong point - exploring the vast world and the secrets hidden within. Secrets that are usually accompanied by interesting and unusual quests, which are arguably the entry's strongest quality. Especially the Shivering Isles quests. You might hear some people say that it's worth getting the game for the Shivering Isles expansion alone, and that wouldn't be much of an exaggeration.

Before the flood of hate: I'M JOKING. TL;DR - this title has a shiny wrapper, but the contents are fairly bare bones.
But seriously,
is a fairly straight forward beat'em up with a mildly interesting mob mechanic.
is a beat'em up because it is mostly spam clicking, rinse-and-repeat. You drag your mob around the map to kill all the enemies and move on to the next level. This is where the game falls short, IMO. On the other hand the mob mechanic is cool, and works well, but I would have liked to have seen more done with it. Some people complain about the controls but I think they are responsive enough. I used a controller and it was good.
I felt it to be fairly easy - almost too easy, in fact. The bosses required no strategy through my whole run. I never ran low on people, either.
Oh, also, I hear some people on the forums talking about this being a roguelike/lite - c'mon guys this is hardly rogue-ish. Yeah, I mean you do have one life - that much is true - but that is where any comparison at all ends. There are mild metagame unlocks, but nothing like I would have hoped for. I just wanted to put that out there for those in the know, who may be disapointed if that is what they are looking for. I kind of was, to be honest.
As the game progresses, in order to increase difficulty the game forces you to manuever your mob through traps and such. I get why this is how it is, but I don't particularly enjoy that stuff.
More layers of complexity. There are only a handful of items, and they all feel fairly meh. The end-of-level 'upgrade' options are ok, but they could expand greatly on them.
+Obviously the artstyle is cool.
+The mob control ability is novel, and is implemented well here.
+The frantic nature of the game is a double-edged sword; on one hand its really cool to watch and be a part of the fury, but on the other hand it can be difficult to tell what is going on a lot of the times.
+I like the unlockable characters, although there are not near enough of them.
-Not enough complexity or depth to the game play. This is the deal breaker for me; it plays like a standard old-school beat'em up.
-While the music is high quality, the actual music choice is questionable. It doesn't all fit in the 'Greek' theme or even 'mythology' theme, or really any single theme. Sometimes that can work, and sometimes it doesn't, like maybe here. Like, what is that music being played at the upgrade table?
-Really, I don't think there is much replay value after you finish the game, which I won't likely do. I will probably get bored and move on before then. The devs posted somewhere that they expect people to get 8-10 hours out of a full game.
I'm not saying you won't have fun for the measly eleven bucks, but I think you can likely do better. I also don't think a majority of owners will see 10 hours out if it, if that means anything to you.

Essentially a cross between 'The Oregon Trail', 'FTL', and a dice and card game, Orion Trail is a fun, easy to play game of making decisions. Parody of existing science fiction tropes and series is constant, making the game a more light-hearted tale of survival - or horrible death - in space. Orion Trail plays as a series of decisions, the outcome of which is determined by what amounts to the roll of electric dice the odds of which are affected by the stats of crew, ship, and circumstance.
The decisions the player makes affect the stats that the random component works upon, and results in turn affect not only those same stats, but the resources that define the mission as a whole: crew, food, fuel, bravado, and science. The goal of any game is to survive a trip through a region of the universe. Each path has many alternate routes within it, each possessed of differing levels of danger and problems to solve. The game is different every time, making each adventure unique.
Orion Trail could best be described as a digital board game, though it does draw on early edutainment software for inspiration as well. The entire process of gameplay is decision based - there is no 'action' as such beyond player choice. Although humorous, the choices can have serious consequences. Survival is not guaranteed. The first galaxy is relatively tame, later missions become quite challenging indeed.
It is clear a lot of love went into Orion Trail, and the developers add more content to it from time to time as well.

Lets face it, this game is amazing. Its a true paradox grand strategy game compete with all the bells and whistles, and lets you do everything from manage your peasant army to determining how to best 'deal' with your imbecile dull son to then trying to find enough moneey to try and build that new fort you've been salivating over. I'll mention straight away that this game currently has several bugs and technical issues, but they get fixed at an impressive rate.
The most impressive feature of Expeditions: Viking: The detailed viking world brought alive. Religion, rituals, runes, other cultural and social habits - it's all there.
"It's all there" seems to be true for game mechanics too. RPG, tactical combat, trade, resource management and more. And while that provides lots of opportunity to frolic, the problem is that the game is trying a bit too much of everything. Sadly the part that managed to convince me the least, is the tactical combat. Not that it is "bad", it's just done better in other games.
Story development on the other hand is excellent. You choices matter, the characters are very believable and there are many twists to experience.
My final verdict: I can absolutely recommend this game. Maybe I would have invested more development in combat, than in other features. But this way you still have a RPG with a decent combat system, offering a very rich experience in general. It's good and particularly unique enough, to deserve a spot in your library.

To sum up my 24 hour experience, I had a lot of fun with Expeditions: Viking. Unfortunately, I experienced a small but noticeable variety of glitches. I'll try to offer some constructive criticism.
Good:
-Excellent story and pretty good writing.
-Highly reactive conversations, events and interactions. Wide variety of actions and consequences.
-Character progression supports a wide variety of builds, even if conversations seem to heavily favor characters with high perception and sense attributes.
-Pretty large amount of content. It took me a ful 24 hours to beat the main story plus a sizable but not comprehensive amount of the side content.
-In my limited academic understanding, the setting seems fairly historically accurate.
-Good overall graphics quality (played on ultra; can't speak for lower settings)
-Satisfying tactical combat combat; feels punchy.
-Good animation work relative to the game's scale
-Commendable sound fx work
-User interface was fairly intuitive despite its complexity
-Surprisingly addictive camping, resource management and basebuilding metagame.
-Interesting companion npcs; they even tried to give a little bit of life to the ones you create yourself by including their input in certain conversations and events.
-Massive thumbs-up to the developers, who seem very active in the Steam community and more than willing to answer peoples' questions in the game's discussion section and help them fix their problems.
Might need some work (Many of these are nitpicky, others are simple suggestions):
-The music, although it was very good and appropriate to the setting more often than not, became repetitive and grating over time in my opinion.
-I experienced some pretty long loading times. I would recommend using an SSD if at all possible.
-"Load game" menu was pretty uninformative at times, which was a pretty big problem for me at one point in the game, but not everyone will run into this issue.
-Cover system is infuriating at times. Line of sight for archers is finicky. This is especially true if there is a difference in terrain elevation between you and the enemy. My recommendation here is to either make the line of sight slightly more balanced in the player's favor, or make it so than archers can use "ranging shot" (a skill which allows you to temporarily force the enemy out of cover) more than just once per combat session. I lost track of how many times I wasted the one and only use of this move only to find that the enemy was still somehow out of the archer's LOS.
-Cannot access inventory or skills menu during combat
-Cannot pause/access the main menu during enemy turns
-A lot of time is spent running from one part of the map to the other
-Can only enter the campaign map through in-game locations, usually at the far corners of the map.
-I would have appreciated a way to pass the time apart from roaming around the campaign map and camping. This would have helped the player in getting all of the homstead upgrades without unnecessarily subjecting themselves to random encounters or burning through their resources while camping.
-I experienced many glitches during my playthrough, one of which was gamebreaking and caused some progress loss, and two of which almost were. On a few occasions, the game started a combat session, but there were no enemies to fight (presumably because I had already fought them). Sometimes, I found my entire hird hilariously stacked in a random corner of a map. Other times, there was an error in the dialogue box when someone's name was supposed to be mentioned. Once, a character who wasn't anywhere around entered the map for a split second, said something, then disappeared. Lastly, a corpse once got caught on the terrain, caused a stack overflow, and froze the game for about a half minute.
-Difficulty can spike at times in a strange way. For the vast majority of the game, the enemy units seem to be constrained to the same sets of rules as the player is, but I can think of at least 2 times they were obviously not. Once I witnessed an enemy healer running around like a madman healing multiple units even though, as far as I know, the player's healers can only heal one person per turn. On another occasion an enemy archer used a powerful ranged AOE ability four times (I count these things) even though the player's characters can only use it twice per combat session. This may be annoying to some people; for others I'm sure it won't make much of a difference. My gripe with it was that in a strategy-oriented combat system, this infrequent inconsistency can render certain strategic choices much less viable, with no way of knowing in advance. Despite my lack of brevity, this wasn't a huge deal. I'm just trying to be thorough.
I know I gave a lot of criticism here, but I would wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who is interested in the setting or at least enjoys story-driven RPGs with tactical turn-based combat. I look forward to seeing what these developers come up with in the future.

This little low-fi indie game is an awesome throwback to 90s arena shooters. Pick up your dagger and face the endless horde of flying skulls, creepy spiders and giant centipedes! But be careful;
Every run is timed, with your score added to the global leaderboard. Replays of your or top player's best run can be viewed at any time, allowing you to take a break and learn some mad strats.
Gameplay is simple, but with some lightly hidden mechanics like strafe jumping and rocket jumping. Hold down left mouse to shoot a constant stream of daggers, or simply click to unleash a flak cannon style blast. This is not a hitscan game, so you'll need to lead your shots ahead of moving enemies or watch as your shots miss by a wide margin.
Despite appearances, this game operates on timed scripted spawns that are always the same except for the locations they appear. This basically means you are always learning with every death, without having to worry about totally random enemy waves.
Devil Daggers and DOOM 4 mark a cool trend in 2016 to bring back the old style of shooters, but with their own unique modern twist. If you want a short jolt of action and excitement, get this game - it's damn good.

Oh boy does this game have a difficult learning curve. While positioning your squads or vehicles you'll definitely worry more about the AI doing wonky things that get them killed or do other facepalm-worthy moments as pathing can be terrible sometimes.
The game is impressive in world detail, effects, and lighting. You can manually control (in third person) the AI and do the aiming/shooting yourself. The destructible environments make battles a blast to experience, win or lose. Tank battles are incredibly fun and you can lose a tank or two in the blink of an eye if positioned incorrectly, rolling up towards a hidden AT gun or facing a much more powerful tank. Tank guns have AT, HE, and various other round types to deal with specific threats.
I'm terrible at this game, to be honest and find more fun scripting large battles in the game's powerful editor which is, in my opinion, one of the best out there in the market. The sky's the limit when it comes to your imagination and the ridiculous amount of custom mods and maps in the workshop expand the game's longevity exponentially. So, consider this an alternative to enjoying your money's worth if you find the game too difficult or too much of a drag to play competitively.
===
Pros:
(+) Decent graphics that still hold up to this day
(+) Fully destructible environments
(+) Detailed hit mechanics for realistic and detailed tank battles
(+) A huge variety of WW2 guns, vehicles, tanks and soldiers of various nations
(+) G.E.M.2 Editor for building your own maps, orchestrating your own battles and the ability to seamlessly transition from editor mode to gaming mode back and forth. You can even place more units during an ongoing battle.
(+) Workshop mods and custom maps.
===
Cons:
(-) Overall difficult gameplay: Damage values are realistic and soldiers each have their own inventory and ammunition to consume. As for vehicles, they have limited fuel and ammo as well. When playing missions involving a lot of units, it becomes a cluster♥♥♥♥ of micromanagement hell
(-) Outdated animations: The game still uses old animations from previous Men of War games
(-) Bad voice acting and soldiers sometimes say random unrelated things ("Quite unexpected", "Very suspicious!")
(-) Outdated Engine: Large battles and detailed city maps will gradually cause lag no matter how powerful your PC is.
(-) Wonky AI: Sometimes the AI responds to your commands to the letter, and sometimes they have a mind of their own. Remember to toggle the "Hold Fire" and "Hold Position" commands to ensure their complete obedience.
====
7/10
====

Conan Exiles is an incredible open world game, that have a giant number of diferent creatures and environments. I got really impressed at the level of detail related to collecting resources, a balanced amount that match with reality, and the effects when you hit something destructible. But, this is an early access game that still have a lot to do and to fix..
Pros:
- A Giant map with a great amount of environments and creatures that match with it.
- A enormous amount of itens to learn and to use.
- The Slave system! It is hard as h*ll to get a descent slave with a sh*t armor, but it helps a lot with a good amount of possibilities to use your slave (those who had that profession before).

This game is outstanding! I bought it and liked it so much that I played an entire hour of it in one sitting and if you get/have the game you will know that that is quite remarkable. In the game, you are a person trapped in the abyss standing on a large circle platform with a powerful magical dagger that shoots red crystals. These red crystals are what kills the many types of demons thrown at you each with their oun traits. There are two main types of attacking abilites and a third, special one. Rapid fire, burst fire and homing missles (Special). There is a small leveling ststem that upgrades your weapon as you kill more enemies but resets when you die. This level system quenches the thirst for a progression system. The point is to survive as long as possible with the game becomming more challenging as you survive. It is not only the most anoying and difficult game I have ever played but also one of the most unique. Its lack of soundtrack and backsplash create an amazing and dark atmosphere which fits amazingly in this game. I reccoment this game for players looking for a challenge above and beyond what they are capable of. However the game has a very terrifying demon theme and is not reccomended for younger players at all.

- Amazing price for what it is

- FUN!
Con:

Overall, well morth the money and will be spending tons more time on it in the future. Hope this review helped.

Although the residents aren't the brightest (you could have fifteen showers down and the game will still tell you that there needs to be more showers just because the residents do other things than shower), it's more than a challenge to complete the achievements. The only ones that I'm missing are the ones related to the final scenario as personally it takes time to complete something to that degree.
When I play, I end up spending hours upon hours creating a single bunker. And whilst challenging to collect the ore to get more building materials, after a while it piles up and having stockpiles of building materials is very satisfying if I do say so myself.
The only cons that I would give this game is the few small bugs it has, with no update in sight. It was last updated in May whereas of writing this review it's August. Though I'm not quite sure what needs to be added, it could certainly do with having a few tweaks made before it's a 100% no brainer buy. Honestly, if you're a fan of something such as Bethesda's Fallout Shelter this is definitely something that you should try out at least once.

Played this game, then there was the "redux" thing with some changes.
In Shadow Warrior, you play as Lo Wang (yes, that's type of humor here - it's like the sort of puns you get from a cheesy Arnold movie except Ninja-themed, so if that'll ruin the game for you to begin with, let's get that out of the way). He is a a ninja that finds fortune cookies and wields a katana. He is so badass he can kill himself by punching a wall.
It's not right for me, really, to want to compare this game to stuff like Duke 3D and Doom because it's just not part of that era. It was released in 1997. Quake and Future Shock were already released, Goldeneye was being shown off and going through beta, and Half-Life was right around the corner, just a year later. However, it's a Build engine game, so I feel I should compare it to some degree, and with a positive statement: even though this game's tech was becoming obsolete, they managed to squeeze every drop out of it. Level design is a lot more interesting than much of what I've seen from the time, there's water transparency, bullet marks that stay...things like that. In a sense, it feels like the very end of that era of shooters - where the focus was less on the actual weapons and more on progressing through labyrinths, obtaining keycards (or just keys, or something else that does the same thing) so you can open a series of doors and finally finish the level.
It's also more challenging than the games I'd compare it to, in my opinion. Not just on a 'normal/hard difficulty is harder than this game's corresponding normal/hard difficulty' level but in a quirky sort of way. In example, the first level of many old shooters have you clear a series of rooms. You can just rush to the exit.
The first level of this game involves you driving a remote control car (from a remote location) to move a key to a spot where you can pick it up, all from a tiny little screen with a resolution of about 0x0 pixels. I'm not putting that down - that's hilariously awesome, it's just dated.
However, it's not so much more difficult than its peers if you go around just swinging the katana all about. I suppose that's what part of the main focus is, but your firearms give the enemies way more of a chance than your blade does.
It's basically fairly routine for its time though presented in a slightly older format, with elements that go beyond its format. In some weird way, this game may just have been simultaneously behind and ahead of its time.
One of the things I love about this game and many other 3D Realms games is that for no reason other than adding to the world, you can screw around with things like switches, buttons, ambient vehicles/objects...many, many things you can interact with, down to minute details such as staring into a mirror and having it trigger dialogue where Lo acknowledges he is looking into a mirror at himself. It's stuff that didn't really become commonplace until sprites were not being used to represent characters in FPS games anymore. This is a practice that the developer has not only maintained to this day, but that seems to rub off on developers they publish or license games for. I can think of something like Prey as a good example.
Finally, complaints (of which I don't have much of, as this is a fun game):
*The closest I can come to a HUD option that doesn't take up a ton of the screen is "brief", and that's not quite as descriptive as the full HUD setting. I did not see an option to resize it there - please inform me if there is one.
*Game has reloading. This is redundant because you cannot choose when to reload, leaving you with a magazine that might have like 10% of its ammo left. Should have just not had reloading.
*"Redux" version and yet a rudimentary auto-save system can't be implemented. Seriously? The ability to save whenever is fine in the vast majority of shooters, but it's best if you have both working in tandem with seperate reserved slots and if you're going to do a re-release of an old game like 16 years later, why not implement it?
So yeah, recommended.

I don't get why the scores for this games aren't higher. Sure, I wouldn't say it's on par with the likes of Secret of Monkey Island, but I think it is fun to play all the way through (not stretched out), great humor, fine music and graphics and the puzzles are not outright evil, and if you get stuck there's a nice incremental hint system, that can be used instead of switching back and forth between the game and a browser every once in a while for someone who plays the game more for story than figuring out every single puzzle.
I am a bit tired of the "humorous" sexism though (humour is a typical excuse for discrimination), mainly directed at Laura, not the least when you play as her. Many of the characters she interacts with objectify her, one insisting she must be a maid and unintelligent too and another one focused only on sexual interest. Robert doesn't respect her either. At one point in the game there's also a kiss between a woman and a man that happens that's basically sexual assault, and the kisser is even confronted with it, and her rejection was basically disregarded and he even says he doesn't regret doing it. Not cool, Headup Games & Studio Fizbin!
The other irritating problem I found was that the game crashed or got stuck on me every once in a while (maybe 7 times when I played through the entire game including all possible dialogue), but nothing that ruined the save, so it's not terrible. What does make this issue somewhat scary is that the game only creates a single save, so if it was hypothetically corrupted, there'd be no option but to start all over. I think a good solution for this problem - other than fixing the bugs - would be to create a save at the start of each chapter besides the current save which saves during a chapter too. This way one wouldn't have to start all over, and furthermore these saves will make getting all the achievements less of a pain.
Finally there's generally always two actions you can perform in the game, which for some reason are both mapped to a submenu when left-clicking, instead of mapping one to the left and right mouse button, which is a simple change that would definitely improve the UX in my opinion.
To sum up I definitely recommend this (mostly) very charming game!

Time to dispense some mob justice on Zeus & his pals as we get to lace up our sandals and head out on an
worth writing Homer about in -
.
Probably best described as a mob-handed, roguelite brawler you lead a group of disgruntled Greeks across the ancient world to the gates of Mount Olympus. Your goal - to destroy all the gods. But rather than taking the old Kratos, God of War approach you don't actually get you hands dirty. Instead you get your horde of fighters, slaves and citizens to do all the head bashing for you. Sending them chasing after your target reticle in something akin to a twin-stick rampage of destruction.
On the plus side of things its a lot of fun getting your mob to cut a swathe across the map, trampling any monsters and building underfoot. And Coffee Powered Machine have done a fantastic job of getting that satisfying gameplay loop - of finishing a run; unlocking a whole load of new heroes; and then starting all over again with a new group and whole new combination of buffs & perks.
That said I wasn't a big fan of how the mob controlled on keyboard & mouse. And apart from (obviously) the unique presentation of the world as these little tabletop dioramas some of the design choices didn't feel all too original. Also some of the bosses felt a little too easy to just straight up steam-roll. Whereas other were nigh on impossible to beat as the game would crash or bug out as soon as you get that last hit in.
That said, all in all, the sense of fun, replayability and the pure amount of destructive joy you can unleash probably outweighs any negatives the game may have. And Okhlos definitely worth checking out.

I’m gonna go ahead and recommend this game purely on the merit of its ambience and sound collages.
The game does not really have music. Instead, you slog onward through bleak and barren terrain to the sound of brooding industrial-style synth pads that sweep over your brain like radioactive drizzle. The game is extra challenging at the outset. You are left vunerable in terms of armor, and with lousy weapons to boot. Add mods and this thing becomes an unsurvivable beast! If you can live with a messy quest interface, a quirky storyline and other shortcomings, you’re in for a somewhat different and charismatic FPS gaming experience. That said, I’d replay the initial release
over this any day.
Shortcomings are more or less similar no matter which game in the series you play. Many of the mutants are a bit silly and irritating. Seriously, what is that Jabba the Hutt-ish lump with toothpick legs running around for? And side quests tend to get repetative. For example, those bandits you killed? Yup, they’ve respawned ten minutes later. After the fifth battle you just can’t be bothered and run right past. Also, loot (and thereby money) is too readily available. After playing for a certain amount of hours the economic tension in this game is almost completely broken. The same actually goes for food, health, radiation medicine, ammo, and so on. You easily wind up with a huge stash, and the challenge often becomes just how much to lug around as you complete quests.
However, if you want to swill vodka, camp around a bonfire at night while some Ukranian bandit in a ski mask plays acoustic guitar, and live by a steadily deteriorating rifle in a harsh radioactive biosphere…good hunting S.T.A.L.K.E.R!

I'm embarrassed to have almost 100 hours of playtime in this game show up on my Steam, given how much I hate it. My excuse is I was aiming to play as much as I could of it to figure out why the hell people enjoy it so much, and I still have no ♥♥♥♥ing clue. I played the main quest, all of the DLC quests, a bunch of side quests including some guild stuff and did quite a bit of exploring.
This game is beyond boring.
- Literally 5 voice actors.
- Zero effort for any sort of facial animation (or any other body animation for that matter). It's frighteningly awkward talking to people and having the camera just zoom up as close as possible to their face.
- No outcome or punishment for anything. "Oh, you can kill people, join a guild, rob a merchant, be any class you want, go to jail...." ....so what? What's the end goal? Nothing, there is rarely any reward for anything you choose to do.
- Casting spells is brutal. Choosing them too. The whole UI is pretty terrible.
- The story is awful. Or at least, it could be interesting, but even the good voice actors seem to fall asleep by it given their performances. The best quests were the funny ones that didn't take themselves seriously, such as this one you do for Sheogorath where you trick this one village and some others in the Shivering Isles expansion.
- A mind-numbingly easy levelling system.
- Very poor variety in enemy encounters. (Most of them just run up and attack you and don't do anything unique or challenging.)
The biggest redeeming thing this game has though is the world is actually pretty nice to lose yourself in. It's fun to just walk around, discover an old cave or ruin, kill everything inside it, get some loot and keep going on your way. I can appreciate that. One problem is, there are literally 4 types of environments in this game. Hills/forest (which covers 95% of the map), the Oblivion gates (which all look identical), caves (again, all depressingly brown and identical) and ruins (very similar to caves, but nicer, especially the Ayleid ones). Oblivion is the first step the TES series took away from it's classic, dice-roll-centric CRPG roots, and more into the action-RPG direction of tactile, weighty combat and a bigger focus on experiencing the story, rather than forging it. The result is a much deeper feeling of the character being unique and personal to the player, as well as far greater enjoyment from the multitude of battles that you inevitably face. However, it also results in a big cutback on the depth and meaningful choices to be made, especially due to the transition to full voice-acting.
Nevertheless, that does not deter from the series' strong point - exploring the vast world and the secrets hidden within. Secrets that are usually accompanied by interesting and unusual quests, which are arguably the entry's strongest quality. Especially the Shivering Isles quests. You might hear some people say that it's worth getting the game for the Shivering Isles expansion alone, and that wouldn't be much of an exaggeration.

This is indeed a pretty fun game when it comes down to its core gameplay.  I'm not sure about the price tag associated with this but will gladly gives this an enthusiastic thumbs up if can pick this game up for 10 bucks or less.
The best thing about this game is that it's very east to pick up and play.  There really isn't much to it other than running around and picking up citizens along the way to add to your mob and wreck every thing and every one that stands in your way.
It isn't all about just running around though.  There are times in which you have to defend against certain types of attacks an enemy makes and when to rally the mob together to avoid a trap or hazard.
The replay value comes when finishing a playthrough.  Unlocking more heroes and player characters makes things a bit more easier the next time around.
Each playthrough offers something a bit more different and unique than the last.  You will sometimes happen upon a dungeon where you will fight a new mini boss.  Or there will be a trapped hero to break out of jail and have him or her join your mob.
The composition of your mob matters.  Get more warriors for more attack. Get more slaves to pick more items up to use. This in addition to the heroes that may give bonuses to attack or add to the maximum mob number.
The greatest downfall of this game though is the lack of depth.  Most of the time you just run around and direct your mob wherever the enemies are and that's about it.
The composition of your mob is hard to see until you stop and either trade your guys or pause the game and look.
It's extremely hard to keep track of your guys and your heroes could die without your knowledge and thus whatever bonuses they had provided such as mob number or attack power is gone.
Overall this is a pretty fun game that will provide at least a few hours of gameplay.

Alright...before I go any further, this is a difficult game. Resources are incredibly scarce, enemies in the dark will soak up your ammo faster than a sponge in a bucket of♥♥♥♥♥♥ anomalies are literally EVERYWHERE, some missions send you on really cheap routes, you'll probably get lost and die of radiation poisoning every other twenty seconds after you load up again, you're almost always in the dark on what you need to do unless you're paying attention all the time, and you'll likely accidentally wander into an anomaly where the gravity is 300 times normal and get smashed into gibs before you can say "Game Over".
That said...I think this game is awesome.
Firstly, this has an ENORMOUS world--nevermind how the graphics pale in comparison of the new games people fawn over nowadays. I haven't even played it for THAT long, and I've gotten lost at least 5 times. Consideirng I've only had around 3 missions so far, that's impressive for the time this came out. In fact, it's still pretty cool now, though that may be a bit of a biased statement since I prefer wasteland to the fantasy-type landscape of Skyrim.
Secondly, it has pretty nice control. Nice and snappy. You can stab a STALKER and then spin 360 to take out his buddy with a Kalashnikov headshot with this thing. Unfortunately, no controller support. That's a bit of a letdown. However, there are some kind of odd control scheme choices in the default setting. "X" sprints, and caps lock swaps between walking and running. You're probably going to be holding down the X key 98% of the game, excluding the parts taking place in caves and firefights, as well as when you run out of stamina. Left ctrl crouches, though you have to hold it down to do it. And holding Shift while crouching sends you into prone. I just find that a bit weird, considering most control schemes games go with.
Third, the gameplay. It's one of those games where you spend more time goofing off in the "overworld" of sorts rather than just doing what you need to do when you need to do it. Hell, I haven't even gotten past the first story mission because I've been goofing off fighting Flesh pigs the entire time. You can only carry up to 60kg, though. Pick up so much as one more piece of bread, you can't move and you'll likely have your♥♥♥♥♥♥bitten off by a Blind Dog. However, most of the time--unless you;re a packrat like me--you'll likely just sell all your useless extra stuff without any trouble with not being able to move. Other than that, it's standard survival FPS fare--you can pick up ammo from corpses/containers, and you go out and stab the crap out of all the wildlife in sight.
Now, I have to warn you, for some this game is an aquired taste. You have to pay attention a lot of times since you can't enable subtitles (trust me, I tried). It's grueling at points, and can get incredibly cheap. No tutorial, no help, nothing. Figure out eveyrhting on your own, or possibly Google if you don't feel like taking Pripyat on like a mann (which is understandable; there are some rather cheap moves this game pulls on you sometimes). No one will tell you how to play the game in the actual game, which will likely end up biting you in the♥♥♥♥♥when you walk into a Whirligig and get torn apart by centrifugal force. Forget the Stalkers, loners, raiders and mutated animals--your greatest enemy in this game is anomalies. Anomalies are pretty much invisible unless you look for the distortion they emit, or if they're on water watch the ripples (though you can just throw bolts at everything, but that's not all that much fun, is it?). In one of the first side missions you can get (where you have to get an artifact for Beard, the hairy dude on the boat), you have to walk through a bunch of anomalies. There're a few on the boat that will insta-kill you if you get too close. So, if you're dumb like me, you'll probably end up running into a few your first time and wonder what just killed you. And these things are EVERYWHERE. Luckily, a lot of them are obvious and very easily avoidable--if you're paying attention. A few of them are very, VERY painfully obvious, but some are so discreet you'll be thinking, "Why did I just explode?" every time you walk into them.
As I said, this is something of an aquired taste for some people, but if you're into the survival-open world-FPS games like I am, then I definetely suggest it, along with the first game. They're very good if you're into this type of thing. There're a good handful of flaws in it, but it's still quite fun even to this day.

Looking like it came straight out of the LittleBigPlanet level creator, Woodle Tree Adventures is a cutesy platformer where you play as Woodle(?), a stump of wood who is concieved to bring water to "this thirsty world".
It's a collectathon platformer in which you collect water droplets (rumored to be tears of anyone who actually played through this game) and berries, the latter of which are scattered around in mass throughout the levels. There's about 6 levels in total and surprisingly no boss battles to speak of. As a result, the game and its levels feel kind of empty with little to no dialogue and largely immobile enemies.
The game is short and you will probably finish it in about half an hour if you're not collecting everything. Until I finished the game, I didn't realise you could use different attacks. When you collect enough berries, you attain a leaf. There's 3 leaves in total and each gives you a different attack ability. To attain these attacks, go behind your house. This will help because the main attack isn't all that good.
Now, the verdict, is it good or is it bad? There are too many lingering problems for this to be just a mediocre or even decent game, the main problem being the game's camera. It will screw you over in more ways than you can count despite it being pretty flexible (you can zoom as far or as close as you want) and is the factor that single handedly ruins the game for anyone playing. This, along with the checkpoint system will stop most people from playing. Due to the enemies killing you in one hit, you'll probably find yourself dying alot and the checkpoints do not help. They vary, sometimes putting you close to where you died or back at the very start of the level. Mostly, it's the latter.
The music is decent enough but clearly uninspired and doesn't even loop well. The snow level and the bonus water level (collect 600 berries) are the only levels which have good tracks that fit them. The levels are at least varied and they have a little bit of length to them but again, a boss would of been nice to break them up. I got this game for free so I can't really say I wasted my money on it, but the game is cheap and you can at least get trading cards and easy achievements from this thing. So, check it out if you want.
There's also a local multiplayer feature where your friend can play as a beaver. Great.

As a fan of classic CRPG, the last few years have been good. But Divinity: Original Sin 2 stands out even among other great games in the genre.
The game is dense with content and production values. There is plenty of dialogue and it feels like your choices (in the side quests at least) matter. I can't think of many other games that pull that off with fully voiced NPCs. And the voice actors are good!
Quests are generally interesting and there are often several way that you can complete them. The pacing and ratio between combat, puzzles and interaction feels just right. Some of the battles can get lengthy, but Larian has been careful to not throw too many fights at you. Most fights are tied to one or another quest, so it never feels like the fights are dragging on.
Each of the pre-made companion NPCs have their own personality, background and story quest. Their quests are among the more interesting ones and span most of the length of the game. I found it easy to get attached to them.
They have removed a lot of the busywork associated with the genre. You can respec your entire party anytime past Act 1. The inventory carrying capacity is ample, and you can send everything you can't carry to your storage. There are plenty of waypoint teleports, which load instantaneously. You also have access to Teleporter Pyramids that you can plop down anywhere.
That's not to say that the game is without issues.
* Quite a few of the side quests are (at the time of release) bugged, and you may not be able to complete some of them.
* There are also a few other bugs, not related to the quest progress.
* Unlike the side and companion quests, the main quest is very linear and a bit less interesting.
* The UI has several issues. The worst ones for me: 1. When choosing quest rewards, you can only see current gear of one party member. 2. You can not see properties of the item you want to craft until it's crafted (which led to me not crafting much).
* The gear scaling is a bit too steep for my taste. It wasn't a big issue while leveling, but at the end I leveled up quicker than I geared up, and had to go searching for gear because I felt underpowered.
* There is still some annoying busywork that they could have done away with. The health of characters isn't restored after combat, and you need to resurrect fallen comrades. You need to travel to a specific place to refill Source Points (the currency of the most powerful spells), which takes about 2 minutes with the use of Teleporter Pyramids. These things don't contribute anything and only slow the game down.
Despite these flaws, I would still strongly recommend D:OS2 to any CRPG fan. Larian has modernized the genre and turn based RPG combat, and made it approachable to newcomers without dumbing down.

This is a lot longer than I intended, so I’m going to put my TL;DR in the beginning. If you enjoy heavy dialogue and choice based RPG’s, and can overlook a few (admittedly large at times) flaws, this is a great buy and 100% worth the money.
Great RPG. Super fun if you like heavy dialogue dependent RPG's like Dragon age. I'm sad to say I'd give it an 8/10, because I really think it deserves a 10/10, but there are just too many bugs, exploits, and balance issues. The resolution is never right, and you have to change it for the computer instead of in game. A few quests bugged out and I couldn't finish them. The game crashed a handful of times, which was very annoying, but it auto saves often so I never really lost anything from that. You shouldn’t be able to arbitrage the markets in the game so easily and effectively. If you can find a merchant who gives you better than fair prices you suddenly have infinite resources, and this is quite easy to accomplish if you build markets in your home town. I also don't think we should be able to create our own followers because they're too strong. I felt like I cheated the game by having perfect weapons and perfectly spec'd units before the conclusion of chapter 1 on insane difficulty. Also, I don’t even know the names of any of my characters, because they were all just people I made to specialize in a specific task. They weren’t deep characters that I cared about, they were just separated by their roles and pictures in my eyes. I had 5 pictures dedicated to combat, and 5 dedicated to camping (when you pick up the monk you can have 11 characters instead of 10). Due to how easy it was to specialize everyone and min max everything from an early point, the entire game all my damage characters basically 1 shot everything, and my tanks were nearly impervious to damage. My campers more than effectively kept everyone healthy, fed, and equipped with maxed out equipment well before it should have been available to me. Obviously not everyone is going to take advantage of this to the extent I did, and I easily could have just not done it myself, but for some reason when I find an exploit I just can't not use it. Idk, I'm weird in that way. Furthermore, the Dane axe's final ability almost never works properly, so I just don't use it, and if I were to play again, I would never make another dedicated Dane axe user. Dual wielding an axe and a sword is better for damage, and the spear is a better 2 distance weapon. It’s just outclassed and doesn’t have a real use. Maybe if it’s final ability worked properly it would be okay since AOE is so rare, but as it is, it’s useless. My last complaint is that the ending came about too suddenly. When I was finishing second to last chapter (I won’t say how many to avoid any potential spoilers) I told my roommate I think I’m about halfway through the game, then I had like 3 more fights and it was over lol. I just felt like there was so much more room for.. well, more. There was basically no character development for the minor characters, so I didn’t feel anything at the end for the relevant character(s), except disappointment that the game was over. And I think that last statement is worth emphasizing, because despite its flaws, I was very sad to end it. I wrote a long list of things I didn’t like, but overall, my experience with the game was extremely positive. Again, if it weren’t for the flaws I listed, I think this would be one of my favorite games of all time. The fighting was fun, to fully min max you had to plan and think, the choices felt relevant, and the dialog never felt forced or exposition-y. It truly was a fantastic game, plagued by what I assume was too little time in development before release.

If you want my short answer, it's buy this game. The atmosphere, aesthetic, and storyline is absolutely engrossing and fascinating. Fans of point-and-click adventure and magical realism works like Twin Peaks will find a distinct pleasure in this game.
In greater detail, Kentucky Route Zero is a beautiful work that plays out in literary fashion, with chapters forming Acts that are released episodically. The mood of the game gracefully floats through moments of quiet beauty (a gas station at dusk), chilling dread (an abandoned mineshaft), and abstract humor (animals where they shouldn't be). Throughout the game, you're given choices in how a character will respond to something, though often times it feels as though the game is asking these questions directly to the player, with the character simply being a medium. The questions are like Rorschach tests, asking you to find a piece of yourself in the obscurity before you. The effect of this is a feeling that the story is starting to belong to you, and you may even contemplate the spiritual and existential thoughts presented in relation to your own life.
In terms of gameplay, so long as you can enjoy point-and-click games, you'll be right at home with the way Kentucky Route Zero. For those who are fans of good story, but more compelling gameplay, you may find yourself bored with it's simplicity, but that's the nature of this kind of beast. The game isn't concerned with challenging your ability to solve puzzles or press buttons quickly and correctly, it's here to tell a story, and so the gameplay is there enough to guide you along.
Aesthetically, both the UI and art style of this game are downright sublime. The world map and UI are minimalist and perfectly fitted to the game's spooky mood. I found myself frequently capturing screenshots of different scenes before me, followed by appreciating and figuring out what I'm looking at. The game takes place in the dead of night, conjuring up feelings one may get when driving down a dark, unfamiliar road with desolate gas stations and old houses illuminated by an amber glow of a single streetlight. Everything looks spooky and forboding, but you never feel threatened by an ominous presence, you simply feel in the midst of mystery and the supernatural.
If I had to criticize the game for any particular thing, it's that after you've purchased the game and played through the available acts, Acts One and Two, you're left wanting for a continuation for Act Three, but the developers have been fairly mum about when it'll ever release, so your experience will be left feeling incomplete along with everyone else still waiting. That said, Kentucky Route Zero in it's current form is still worth experiencing, and if you have anyone that have or would play it, you'll have plenty to discuss and appreciate even with it being as short as it currently is.
Once again, if you enjoy games that are focused almost entirely on story and atmosphere, and you enjoy stories and atmospheres that are spooky, existential, abstract, and deep, you will enjoy this game. It has certainly left an impression on me.

This game is very good. In particular, it'd be a great starting point if you're interested in cRPG's as it is more accessible than many I've played. While it's accessible it's also open ended and difficult (assuming you don't use the cheese strats available to you) with a lot of different ways quests can go and bleed into other quests/stories, etc. If I were to put it simply it'd be this: behaving based on what YOU would do in your character(s)'s situation is a more sensible approach than behaving based on what you expect the game expects you to behave in a scenario. You have motivation to stray from being the generic good guy that saves everyone and is often even more rewarding to be evil/selfish than to be a good guy (which I really like, as it doesn't feel fun to be punished for not acting like I would in real life).
As for combat, it's very engaging (despite some balance issues). Armor is a fundamental mechanic of combat as CC effects in this game are incredibly debilitating but physical and magical armor prevent corresponding physical and magical form of CC. While CC'ing stuff into oblivion is still a viable strategy, it's a lot harder to pull off than in DOS 1 which means you don't need a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of initiative to win anymore (although it's obviously very helpful - for example it's pretty easy to destroy a frontline warrior with low magic armor's magic armor and also stun/freeze them in a single 4 AP turn). The importance of armor also makes upgrading armor and not being too underleveled important, as you will very likely lose a fight regardless of tactics if the armor difference is too vast in their favor and you aren't a high enough level to do enough damage to break it in a reasonable timeframe.
By the way, as of writing this I'm 80 hours in and am at the beginning of act 3, which isn't that close to beating it. This game has a lot of substance (and it doesn't have anything to do with grinding as enemies don't respawn, if you had the concern)

Another thing is optimization. It's always a gamble in early access games, cause you never know how's it gonna run. I got a laptop with gtx 970m, and how suprised was I when I've set everything to ultra, and the game just ran smootly. No kidding, 60fps easily.
At the time of writing this, I only have played for 3 hours, and I can safely say that this blows Ark or Rust out of the water.
If you can't decide if to try this game, listen to my advice and give it a go. You won't regret it!

Oh boy does this game have a difficult learning curve. While positioning your squads or vehicles you'll definitely worry more about the AI doing wonky things that get them killed or do other facepalm-worthy moments as pathing can be terrible sometimes.
The game is impressive in world detail, effects, and lighting. You can manually control (in third person) the AI and do the aiming/shooting yourself. The destructible environments make battles a blast to experience, win or lose. Tank battles are incredibly fun and you can lose a tank or two in the blink of an eye if positioned incorrectly, rolling up towards a hidden AT gun or facing a much more powerful tank. Tank guns have AT, HE, and various other round types to deal with specific threats.
I'm terrible at this game, to be honest and find more fun scripting large battles in the game's powerful editor which is, in my opinion, one of the best out there in the market. The sky's the limit when it comes to your imagination and the ridiculous amount of custom mods and maps in the workshop expand the game's longevity exponentially. So, consider this an alternative to enjoying your money's worth if you find the game too difficult or too much of a drag to play competitively.
===
Pros:
(+) Decent graphics that still hold up to this day
(+) Fully destructible environments
(+) Detailed hit mechanics for realistic and detailed tank battles
(+) A huge variety of WW2 guns, vehicles, tanks and soldiers of various nations
(+) G.E.M.2 Editor for building your own maps, orchestrating your own battles and the ability to seamlessly transition from editor mode to gaming mode back and forth. You can even place more units during an ongoing battle.
(+) Workshop mods and custom maps.
===
Cons:
(-) Overall difficult gameplay: Damage values are realistic and soldiers each have their own inventory and ammunition to consume. As for vehicles, they have limited fuel and ammo as well. When playing missions involving a lot of units, it becomes a cluster♥♥♥♥ of micromanagement hell
(-) Outdated animations: The game still uses old animations from previous Men of War games
(-) Bad voice acting and soldiers sometimes say random unrelated things ("Quite unexpected", "Very suspicious!")
(-) Outdated Engine: Large battles and detailed city maps will gradually cause lag no matter how powerful your PC is.
(-) Wonky AI: Sometimes the AI responds to your commands to the letter, and sometimes they have a mind of their own. Remember to toggle the "Hold Fire" and "Hold Position" commands to ensure their complete obedience.

This goofy throwback to Oregon Trail style gameplay is both cleverly written and hilarious, and the game is oozing with charm.
You play a galactic explorer in the Kirk/Picard tradition. Your goal is to cross unknown space and live to tell the tale! Along the way, you will lose fuel, hull plating, food and redshirts - er, I mean valued crewmembers! Whose loss will be keenly felt. *cough*
One day you're dodging the Analog Collective, the next you're negotiating to use the wormhole bypass to escape a nasty space anomaly. Along the way, you'll use diplomacy, science, raw firepower, sensible tactics, and sheer bravado, all of which your bridge crew will have varying numbers of skill points in. They can go up and down, depending on how lucky/unlucky you are and the choices you make. Usually it's best to specialize in three, to maximize your choices, but you can start the game being a science wizard and a terrible shot, and end it the best shot on the frontier and a science dunce, depending on how your choices unfold.
The references are clear and obvious, not just to Trek and sci-fi in general, but to the Oregon Trail and the old school of gaming. If you haven't played the old school games, experience is not required to get the jokes (Space Dysentery is self-explanatory).
So, if you're looking for a witty Trail game in space, this is the one to go with. I've yet to see one better. It may take awhile to get the hang of it, but it's definitely worth the effort!

TL;DR
Fun elements but overall just frustrating and incomplete. You'll see every encounter in the first or second playthrough (and playthroughs are very short). I received a free copy of this game after playing it at PAX East.
Pros:
-Fun shoutouts to other sci-fi games/movies/shows, not just Star Trek and Oregon Trail.
-Some of the stories and encounters are entertaining.
-Seriously, these guys are on to something, and someone else is going to actually pull this off.
Cons:
-The stories and encounters repeat every game. You visit the same outposts and have the same "random" encounters. You'll see everything there is to see in your first or second time through.
-Winning is probably an accident. I gave the game a break after initially trying it and being frustrated, and my first two encounters I had critical fails despite having 10 success, 1 critical success, and only ONE critical fail spot both times.
-Success usually means staving off disaster for a few more turns, whereas fails can make sure you never have a chance. You don't start off with enough resources to even make it to the end, so every fail hits hard, and the successes don't make up for it.
-You start with some currency but never see it again unless you trade in crew/fuel/food/hull and exchange it for another. They need to add the ability to pick up currency and it would make space stations much more worthwhile, instead of making you choose which area to harm yourself in. Too often I run out of fuel and engage the SOS, but don't have any resources to trade--once I only had the option to trade my remaining hull and I did it because I guess it was better than starving, so my ship exploded.
This is a great classic game if you love classic FPSes. Worth the purchase.
