TL;DR summary (and don't mind my english):
- This game is skill based and items/clothes have no impact on the game play. You can jump in and be on equal footing with veteran players.
- This game has it's merits with outdated graphics and missing settings (Ctrl + S for volume slider)
- Available song list is fixed and new songs are added by the developer in upcoming patches. This version of Audition (there are different versions for different regions) has prominent artists like Diplo, Weeknd and Krewella to name some.
- This games biggest strength revolves around the community. People tend to know each other and playing with friends while enjoying the music is just great. THIS GAME BECOMES SO MUCH BETTER IF YOU TALK AND MAKE NEW FRIENDS. You gotta socialize to fully enjoy this game. That's the main reason why i kept coming back to this game after a 8 year long break.
Side note: I am playing osu! (or DDR) myself and both games are too different to be compared. The osu! and DDR related modes are just one of many game modes in Audition.
===================================================================
Audition Online is an online dance battle game with a variety of gamemodes which are (somewhat) comparable to DDR (Beat Up), Guitar Hero (Guitar Mode) and Taiko (Space Pang) and it's own "normal" mode.
In the normal mode, the main mode of this game, you need to hit the arrows on your keyboard according to the arrows on the screen and press Space/Ctrl when the beat ends. This requires a lot of skill i'd say - sense of rhythm by playing instruments can help a lot to get good at this mode.
The songlist covers slow BPM (beats per minutes) and fast BPM songs. Slow songs are good to practice your muscle memory/reading as a beginner. You can't add own songs to the game, the developer adds new songs in future patches (i believe the reason is due to copyright/license issues).
The music genre is K-Pop/Western charts with some prominent artists like Deorro, Chainsmokers, Krewella, Zeds Dead, Weeknd, Diplo and more.
The game itself runs with V-Sync on(FPS caps at the refresh rate of your monitor, for most people 60FPS). There are ways to disable V-Sync as an AMD/ATI and Nvidia graphic cards owner  (which i recommend, guides are available on the official Redbana forums). The graphics are outdated for it's time even though i don't mind/like the anime style.
There are two currencies ingame, ingame (Beats) and real cash (Banacash). Even though clothes are purchaseable by Beats the majority of  clothes are Banacash ones. Items or clothes have ZERO impact on the competitiveness of this game - it grants no advantage at all as it's purely cosmetic. Veterans with high levels do NOT have an advantage either besides being more experienced and skilled at the game. Theoretically you could hop into the game and beat veterans just by being more skilled.
One thing i would like to point out is how much more fun this game becomes when you make new friends and interact with the community. You can become Couples, get married, join a Family and fight with them in FAM battles.
The last time i played this game was about 8 years ago and i keep coming back. The game has it's merits (graphics are outdated, lack of settings) but if you love to listen to music, meet new people and become friends and thrive to become good at music-based games this game is definitely worth a try!

I bought this game on a total whim...mainly because it popped up in my suggested titles.  Boy am I glad that I did!  This game is not a flashy, graphics extravaganza (it's very, very dated).  However, I have found the gameplay to be fun, the story intriguing and the different strategies on all levels (from turn based tactical combat, to party creation and development, to constructing your settlement) to be so enjoyable that I barely notice the dated graphics.
Basically, you play the leader of a Viking clan.  Due to challenges and your clan's own weakness, you are forced to pursue your fortune (and survival) over in Britain.  To do this, you assemble a party who will accompany you, fight and (if you're unlucky or neglectful) die for you.  Throughout the campaign you will assist in the rise and fall of kings, or maybe even conquer Britain for yourself.  Whatever path you take, it is a rich experience that I have found myself getting lost in.  I found combat to be accessible, but also relatively deep with lots of interesting strategies and combinations that can be attempted and rewarding effects when a good strategy comes through (like dropping the Beserker Skakki before he could even take a swing at me).
In short, in the last couple years this game is probably the best entertainment for my dollar that I have bought (and I buy a lot of games).  I am finishing my first playthrough (there is quite a bit of good content) and I am already contemplating how I will do my next playthrough.
The cons are the dated graphics, a few glitches and crashes and the fact that the campaign itself can sometimes seem very linear.  You really do just sort of run from quest to quest without a lot of open world or sidequesting in between.  If the main story weren't so good, these issues would be game breaking, but I really haven't found that to be the case (and I am normally a huge advocate for open world games).
I highly, highly recommend this game.

enjoy this chicken stir fry recpie
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan

100% Orange Juice is an Anime Style Objective-based board game by Developer Orange_Juice starring characters from other titles such as QP Shooting - Dangerous!!, SUGURI, and Acceleration of SUGURI X-Edition HD.
The game itself is far from perfect, but is quirky and fun and doesn't take itself to seriously. The gameplays starts off like most board games where it's 4 players pitted against each other. You start off by picking your character and after you have chosen you go to a deck buildig screen, yes I said it a deck building screen. This is what I think really sets this game apart and makes it wonderful. As you play you gather stars and using those stars you can buy boster packs and unlock more cards to play with. Each card has it's own properties and categories ranging from Traps to Battle cards to Event cards and each one can save you.

After you have chosen the deck you want to play with the game finally begins. The main purpose is to complete all the objectives before your opponents. You start off by having to deliver 10 stars to one of the home bases and from there you pick your next objective which is either defeat 2 enemies or collect 20 stars. From there the objectives are the same, defeat enemies or collect stars, but grow more difficult with each level.  About halfway through the game a boss will show up and depending on what level you are playing on determines which boss you fight. The boss is three times as strong as any of the other enemies you fight on the enemy tiles and twice as strong as any of the players so defeating it is gonna take a while and you will probably die.
There is a lot to do in this game if you get bored of playing others online you can play campaign mode. There are also tons of stuff to unlock which will keep you playing for many many hours. Oh! did I mention that the games RNG in the dice rolls is outrageous and will probably frustrate the hell out of you, but in a good way (if there is one). Overall this is a really good board game despite the Anime-ness of it and if you can get past that you will definitely get your moneys worth.

THERE ARE FOUR LIGHTS!
Think of it as a choose your own adventure novel filled with nods to the sci fi genre.  Each point in space offers multiple ways of handling the situation.  Each way can result in 4 different narrative paths.  The situations repeat often.  Choosing different options and having the RNG spit out different results will keep repeating stories fresh.  I often found myself speeding through dialog I'd seen before until I branched into a new result.
You choose your crew who each have a few points toward 5 different attributes.  These attributes give you a better chance at getting a positive result in the RNG.  Focusing on 2 of the 5 attributes seems to work well.
There is some resource management.  It boils down to "Hey, we're low on fuel.  Let's choose the get fuel option."
The humor is stupendous.  The music and sound effects are charming.
If you're looking for a low brain power time waster, look no further.

Full disclosure, I backed Orion Trail on Kickstarter and if you play the game, you have a chance of running into me as one of the villians. If that is just too much bias for you, you might want to find something else to read!
Orion Trail is Star Trek meets the Oregon Trail game with a slight detour provided by Monty Python.  The premise is simple enough; select a crew from the choices given (each crew member has different skill sets) then set out across space to encounter a rather ecelctic mix and use your skills to adapt, improvise and overcome. Or die trying. The puns are non stop, the encounters are full of BEMs (I might be showing my age here)  and you roll the digital dice (called the improbability drive which might have been stolen from some English writeer) and take your result in true RNG fashion. If things work out well, you gain some fuel or food or crew, if not, well, you might lose out! Your odds of a favorable solution are based on the skills you have and how many points you have in the skill you choose to bet on.  Its fun, silly and at times, a little repetitious but for a small game done on a tight budget, it came out very well.
Is Orion Trail perfect? No. I find it to be too heavy on food and fuel optimization. I can usually keep my shields and crew up to snuff. Some of the fun might be too inside for many; many of the characters are based on Kickstarter backers. However, is Orion Trail good clean entertainment? I think so. I like how I can play a mission in a few minutes and either be lauded as a great captain or be shown the door and a view of my tombstone (space dysentry anyone?)  There are nods to several pop culture genres here. Have some fun, try the game and see if you have what it takes to be a Galaxy Force captain or just another tomb in space! Oh, and if you run into me, I seem to be an easy grader. I gambled on taking the test last time and got a B-. I would have given myself a C.

LIB is a neat little management game that plays like a less frenetic (and easier to grasp) Dwarf Fortress, though it is nowhere near as deep a dive as that cult game.
The titular bunker is your fiefdom under the earth, where you shepherd the remnants of humanity until the world above is safe. Your job is to keep a few dozen plates spinning until the timer runs out, carefully trying to guide your bunker society toward a sustainable balance. This is kept challenging thanks to a scarcity of resources and a crush of demands that ensure you have to stay on your toes (expand too fast and you won't be able to maintain what you have and risk attack from molemen, expand too slowly and your people will start to suffer from starvation and sickness). To accomplish this you're given a lot of control and there are a few different ways to tackle the problems, which is essentialy for a good management game (after all, no one wants to lose because of pure RNG).
Postiives:
1. Setting is pretty unique for the genre
2. Game is well balanced to provide continuing challenge
3. Has some replayability as you test and experiment
That said, the game has some shortcomings. The game can seem a little thin in places, especially compared to other management games which often offer more room types, objects and systems (the game especially lacks for traps and defenses, but I'm not sure they would really suit the type of game). There are little UI tweaks that would help (a bit of simplification - for example to build a bunker wall you must go into a menu, then clock a submenu, and then click on the wall, which would make sense if there was more than one type of wall to build, maybe hotkeys? - and making it easier to tell how things are going at a glance). I'm also worried about replayability, since once you've "solved" the game then it doesn't offer any other modes or challenges.
But overall it's a good little game in an underserved genre that deserves some attention.

This is about the best you're going to get when it comes to a retooling of the Oregon Trail game. I was a fan of that game way back when, and I love this even more. Honestly, it's the best of the crop of the games trying to ape it. And the balance, fun, and replayability is far better than Organ Trail.
Plus! It's a great parody for Sci-Fi fans. Especially Star Trek fans. There's a lot of in-jokes there that only they might get. Something to keep in mind. Definitely a bonus for Trek fans, but perhaps a detriment to those who aren't.
Also. You can be a bear. Your captain can be a chubby bear, and they're usually pretty great captains, too. Honestly, what more could you ask for?
If you're an older gamer (like me), you like sci-fi, and you're looking for a short game to pass the time or something like the Oregon Trail, this'll do you.
I admit, this isn't the highest praise. But it is fun, good at what it tries to do, and very much worth the money. This isn't Undertale or the Beginner's Guide, after all. It's like writing a review for Tetris. If you meet the prerequisites I've mentioned, then you're likely to have a really good time.
I recommend it. Quite a bit.

At the time of writing, this $40 game has $240 of DLC available.
Crusader Kings II is a great game - and I'm not using that word lightly, it's a GREAT game - but I can't recommend it.  I've put a lot of hours into this game (more than Steam has counted), but it's never been a fulfilling experience because of all the goddamed DLC.
Listen, I'm no enemy to DLC, if a developer makes more content for their game, I'll pay to play it.  But the way Paradox does it is straight up insidious.
"This new update adds North Africa to the game......but you can't play there unless you buy the Sword of Islam DLC"
"The newest update adds all of India to the vanilla map.......but you can't play there unless you buy the Rajas of India DLC"
"We just added the entire Asian continent to the game.......but you can't play there unless you buy the Horse Lords DLC"
DLC in this game isn't comparable to DLC in other games, it's not like it adds a weapon skin or an extra level.  Crusader Kings II DLC fundamentally changes the core gameplay of the game, and some things that have DRASTIC changes on how you play (such as the ability to have a standing army, form custom kingdoms, or even the existence of the Jewish religion) are hidden behind 4 years and $240 of DLC.
To put it simply, I have never felt like I was playing a finished game.  Every time I turn it on, there's an ad for yet another piece of DLC.  Once I finally save up enough to buy the next biggest DLC pack, another is announced.  It's just not fulfilling.
Until Paradox decides to wrap this game up like they've done with Europa Universalis IV and Hearts of Iron III, and put their energy to developing Crusader Kings III instead of squeezing more DLC money out of current players, I can't recommend it.

I highly recommend it for roleplayers as well.  I have lost so many hours of my life roleplaying in my head while playing.  Yes, there is an overwhelming amount of DLC. Between MODs and literally getting to choose the content you want to purchase and play, the options are almost endless.  I tend to play CK2 based on the type of mood I'm in.  If I'm in a bad mood, I will typically start as a King and just curbstomp the world.  If I'm looking for a long haul game, I'll start at the lowest in the food chain and roleplay my way up into independence, or I won't and I'll remain loyal to my liege, leading his armies to victory.

Uhhh, I guess having to buy all the DLC if you want the complete package.  However, I see DLC and bundles for CK2 go on sale ALL THE TIME.  It's a huge value.

Oh boy, this is going to be rough.
So Expeditions: Viking, is it a good game? Yes, but there are a few problems with its design that I feel need to be addressed. The switch from party select before battle to entering town is questionable at best. It makes sense when you want your character to be in the game, running around and doing stuff. But here is the problem, most RPG's don't have your character doing stuff for this reason. If you have a party of 12 for example, and select 6 people for battles, you essentially have two teams ready for battle (lets call them A-team and B-team). When someone from A-team gets wounded, you swap him for his replacement from B-team. But when you are locked in with 6 characters from the start of the town, how can you play multiple battles with getting your party grow weaker as time and wounds take their toll? How can you tailor you party to suit the battle? A defence battle is totally different from an assassin fight, which is different from running to the end zone. One small change can have huge echo effects to the rest of the game.
The switch from amount of ground moved in a day to fixed camping grounds was one I thought I would welcome.But this didn't work I feel. The daily movement points system works because that makes sense if you are marching around during the day and making camp in the night. You can even have the option to get half your movement points back at the cost of making your followers get the hungry and fatigued debuffs. However, if you need to repair some awesome equipment you just found, or heal your critical character, you need to leave the town, go to the nearest campsite, camp for 16 hours go back to the town, fight that battle, go Back to camping, do it all over again. But you cannot even do that for you see, you do not have agency over when battles happen to you. Now this may be more realistic, but I am of the mind that I come to games to escape realism for a while. Pretend to be something that I am not for a while.
I am sure there will be things that I said here that will not apply to you, the reader. And this game is good, The leveling is balenced, the characters are very believeable. This game on its own stands as a decent RPG. But compared to what their studio has done before, this feels like a game that tried something new to have it just blow up in their faces.

So i have finally finnished this game and i feel like it has potential unfortunatly it would seem that the dev team may have abandoned it and even announced a sequel, i really feel that my original post was a little bit harsh after playing the full game so i have given it a quick edit here and there and updated it and posted it below:
After first playing this game i felt like there graphics were quite nice but frankly if games were mental issues, this would be complete reality disassosciation paranoid skitzophrenic psychosis, honestly this game might be fun if you has serious brain injury or something that restricted you from thinking properly. but after playing it through i can honestly say thats more or less just the first level from what i can tell this game is about collecting "fairy tears" but you never see any trace of the fairys or why they are crying. your bag that you use to carry items (berries) grows as you pick up items (you also make a munching sound as you put them in your bag?) and can be quite annoying by the end of the level because more often than not the bag will be bigger than you and obstruct your view, the tears just hover behind you so you know how many you have (3 per level) and your main weapon is a leaf... seriously a friggen leaf... i mean you are a log for crying out loud wouldnt you at least use a stick or something. the game encourages you to collect more fruit to unlock better leaves to kill the enemies(?) with, which pretty much just increase the range with each new leaf. The game doesnt actually let you know whats an enemy or not you can only tell by hitting it with a leaf (thankfully this was only an issue in the first level) and watching to see if it dies as for the creatures they actually look quite messed up like whoever designed them did so after a cactus eating wander through the desert, thankfully however the game calms down after the very first level. If like me you managed to push past the first level this game can be rather fun, however it feels like a very early 3D game in the sense that the enemies dont actually attack you just die if they touch you, the puzzles are figuring out how to navigate the map and the maps are rather small. After playing the game to the very end i was left with 2 achievements to still unlock (Collect 1000/3000 Berries) and started grinding the hidden level at the end of the game to achieve these and quickly grew bored at 2000 berries.(though i will eventually complete the last one). This game CAN and WILL be fun if you approach it with a juvenile mind and without Bias from the ammount of hate people sling at it, just remember that enemies are more often than not going to stand still and watch you pass them and are more of an obstacle than anything else.
I guess it would be alright for a young child to play and the price is rather cheap ($3) but the gameplay is weak, the camera angles are dreadful and there is only 6 levels and 1 bonus level. As for unlocks there are 3 leaves that increase range as you unlock them and 1 Red Bandanna, however the bandanna does nothing (as confirmed by the dev) and just adds to the look of your Woodle.
All in all i can say the 2 hours i spent playing this game were not infact wasted as i thought they might be after playing the first level, its more of a nothing else to do game or something to play when you have very little time on your hands, i doubt i will keep playing it after i finnish the 3000 berry achievement. I give this game a very Generous 5/10 as it has the right idea's but the wrong execution, i would love to see this game expanded with boss levels and bigger maps however it looks like this will never happen. I for one wont say not to buy this game if you want to give it a whirl but there are 1000's of keys floating around just waiting to be collected and loved by someone.
(P.S. from the Author, i have reviewed this game ignoring the level of hate that it seems to gain and without a Bias, i feel that this game is infact worth completeing and not just writing off after the first level as the first level is by far the worst and the challenges become more challenging, for example there is a snow level where you slide around while climbing up obstacles and a beach level which you are climbing up a tower.)

Pretty decent, but could be better.
The controls aren't bad, but can be a tad clunky. The problem comes mainly from the camera handling. I would have preferred a "first person" view better, rather than zooming in and out of a specific square, as the current system is less accurate.
I liked that the game changed things up in every chapter with a new feature each time, though they didn't really do much. What I didn't like was that solving the puzzles involved quite a bit of guesswork if the level didn't use the cube shape, so you couldn't really solve them elegantly by using logic. Fortunately, the game mitigates this slightly by letting you make a mistake or two without instantly failing you.
Though the level customization is a bit restricted, it adds a bit of replayability in case you're done with the main game.
Overall, for its price, it is not a bad purchase at all. It's an adequate time killer if you're bored and regular Minesweeper isn't doing it for you anymore.

A superb test of skill in a minimalist arena. It can be enjoyed as a casual time-killer for 10-15 mins, or as a mountain to be ascended, second by second, to the top of the leaderboard simply to delight in your own skill.
For me, this is the essence of 90's arcade shooters. There is no superficial progression. No guaranteed rewards of special weapons or abilities, which give you power just because you put in time.
It's this unrelenting test of your own skill, the slow but satisfying ascent to mastery of subtle game mechanics, that got me hooked on video games when I was just a toddler. As I grew up, I was sad to see this type of design all but disappear.
For $5, do yourself a favor.

That's not a comment I make often, but if you enjoy a casual Minesweeper game (whether it's the original or more advanced variants such as the equally marvellous Hexcells series), then you'll enjoy this.
You're presented with shape masses made of cubes.  Some of those cubes contain explosive material (the 'mines') which you need to identify and pick off.  The same principles as Minesweeper apply: the number on the cube indicates how many mines are in adjacent cubes (and the contact can be cube faces, their edges or even just corner to corner), so if you unveil a cube with ZERO on it, every other cube that makes ANY kind of physical contact with that cube is safe to unveil.  The unique style of THIS game (besides its 3D) is that when you've identified where an explosive cube is located, you can remove it, after which all surrounding 'clue' cube numbers drop by one to reflect its removal, further helping you to solve the remainder of the puzzle.
It's both fun AND tricky at the same time.  Getting used to Minesweeper in a 3D space takes some adjustment, and I found the mouse controls a little clunky at first when trying to navigate around my mass of cubes.  This is a game that seems to have been designed for tablet8/phone first which might explain this to a degree, but once familiar with the various clicks and how to switch viewing angles easily) it became a joy to play.
Quite honestly, this is the best £0.71 fun I've had in ages.  Yep, that's right: an enjoyable game that costs less than most postage stamps, is the third of the price of a Starbucks coffee or McD burger.  Honestly, the devs should really consider a Hexcells indie price because it is worth that.

The good:  Very challenging and relatively simple to play.

Despite the fact that this game is almost all about luck and RNG, it is very hard for me to dislike this game. In fact, I really do like it! The characters are cute, the story is humorous and tongue in cheek, the gameplay is simple but fun, it's basically a standard tabletop board game with adorable anime characters. Even with the collectible card aspect I can definitely imagine this game being easily recreated in real life. I will admit that the final boss is likely cheating on her rolls, and the RNG will likely mess you up when you need it to help the most, but I've had a bizzare amount of luck with this game.
What amounts to "strategy" in this game is only choosing which cards to put in the deck, what directions to take, when to use cards, whether to fight the other players or not, and whether to defend or evade. Regardless, it works, it's pretty fun.
The characters are also quite cute and endearing. As far as I know they're all from games of the Bullet Hell genre. So far, the only character whose game has a Steam release is Suguri, but it appears that QP will be getting a game soon as well.
Multiplayer has a "drop in drop out" system which works well for the game type, but it works rather well. Even if a player wants to use the overpowered final boss character, she is toned down for the multiplayer mode.
...I feel like there's more I should say, but I really can't think of much else. If you like basic board games where you move via dice, you'll likely have fun with this.

100% Orange Juice is an Anime Style Objective-based board game by Developer Orange_Juice starring characters from other titles such as QP Shooting - Dangerous!!, SUGURI, and Acceleration of SUGURI X-Edition HD.
The game itself is far from perfect, but is quirky and fun and doesn't take itself to seriously. The gameplays starts off like most board games where it's 4 players pitted against each other. You start off by picking your character and after you have chosen you go to a deck buildig screen, yes I said it a deck building screen. This is what I think really sets this game apart and makes it wonderful. As you play you gather stars and using those stars you can buy boster packs and unlock more cards to play with. Each card has it's own properties and categories ranging from Traps to Battle cards to Event cards and each one can save you.

After you have chosen the deck you want to play with the game finally begins. The main purpose is to complete all the objectives before your opponents. You start off by having to deliver 10 stars to one of the home bases and from there you pick your next objective which is either defeat 2 enemies or collect 20 stars. From there the objectives are the same, defeat enemies or collect stars, but grow more difficult with each level.  About halfway through the game a boss will show up and depending on what level you are playing on determines which boss you fight. The boss is three times as strong as any of the other enemies you fight on the enemy tiles and twice as strong as any of the players so defeating it is gonna take a while and you will probably die.
There is a lot to do in this game if you get bored of playing others online you can play campaign mode. There are also tons of stuff to unlock which will keep you playing for many many hours. Oh! did I mention that the games RNG in the dice rolls is outrageous and will probably frustrate the hell out of you, but in a good way (if there is one). Overall this is a really good board game despite the Anime-ness of it and if you can get past that you will definitely get your moneys worth.

To get it out of the way first: This is an Early Access game. If you buy it you're a beta tester. You are not entitled to demands in order to make the devs work for your comfort. The last point actually applies to _any_ game, beta or not. You don't own the developing studio by buying a game the same way you don't own a fun park after paying for entry.
The quirks I so far encountered in Conan Exiles are very clearly due to systems in development. The core of the game though feels pretty good and has a lot of potential. I am no PvP player so I simply can't judge what's going on in that department, but the PvE side of the the game I like a lot. The way the world is build invites for exploration and there are a lot unique and interesting places. Even more so if you know a bit about Hyborian lore. After starting as a naked guy/gal in a wasteland you can craft your first clothes and basic tools very quickly and also by stuff gathered by hand. No punching trees here. House building is pretty easy and gives you lots of options and room for imagination even with the most basic tier. While progressing it's totally possible to just stay where you are, but it's absolutely worth it to go up north at some point. There are a few things you need which are only obtainable in certain areas, which can be annoying sometimes, but in the end you don't even need those very often.
I can't say I tried every aspect of the game so far, but even the basic mechanics and exploring, base building and even farming materials (there's no survival game without farming lots of stuff) is addictive and fun.
So is this just Ark without dinos and modern tech? No. It's not. I think the whole survival game thing turned into a genre rather than clones of another game, and Conan feels much different and, as I like the Hyborian Age a lot, also more immersive. It's in beta state, so there are things to be done of course, but I enjoy the game very much so far.

Also the inability to anything to change the gameplay besides stack the odds as best you can leaves me feeling very powerless to do much as a player other than click through the menus and hope for the best.  As it currently stands, I can't really recommend the game unless someone is looking to while away a couple of hours doing something else and listening to the nice soundtrack while clicking around the game and enjoying the very good pixel art.
If the gameplay was as good as the art and soundtrack, I'd easily give this game 10/10.  As it currently stands though, the gameplay is lacking and the dice rolls are too punishing to even let this be an enjoyable distraction.  The game is trying to be difficult like oregon trail, but it doesn't reward the player for doing anything right.  This means the only thing you can do as a player is min/max and hope for the best.  If that appeals to you, click away, but I need some more reward for spending time with the game and learning the system.  Therefore I can't recommend the game in it's current state.

This game embodies what every open world game should be, the ability to choose how much of the main story and which elements you want to follow. You could do a mix of main and side quests as I do on most of my playthroughs. Another option is to only pursue the main quest line, and then once that's finished, delve into the rest of the world. Or you could choose to ignore the main quest entirely and play 40+ hours of interesting side quests fleshing out the rich, beautiful world the characters inhabit and then come back to the main quest line only once you've explored the entire rest of the world.
I would also suggest looking into mods once you've played through the game a time or two as this could add hundreds of hours of gameplay, scenery, and characters that are as good or better than the quality of the original game.
(Although I'm new to this game on steam, I've played hundreds of hours on my original physical copy.)

This is a cute, all-ages-friendly, point and click adventure game. The main character leaves his home as the naive protagonist and must work his way up to becoming the hero, along with the help of his friend Laura and her pet pigeon.
This is one of those adventure games where it's got a few cute, unique elements, but also it's more like a comic book you can play through. The puzzles are set up in a usual adventure game style, where you have to find and combine some items to make them work.
I'll warn you that it's a bit dialog heavy. You have to talk to a lot of characters, so if you're not in the mood to sit through quite a bit of worldbuilding-through-chatting, I'd wait to play this game until you feel more patient.
It's not a revolutionary game, but it is fun. I'm happy to have it in my library. The only bad thing is there was one, single puzzle that was impossible for me to solve, because I had already tried that combination of things, but not at the right exact time. Regular adventure game frustrations, you know? It could really have been fixed, I think, but it doesn't ruin the entire game. The thing is, once you talk to someone and they give you all the information they can, or they have said all there is to say in a conversation, that button gets grayed out. You can click it again, but throughout the entire game the character would just repeat the same thing over if you did so. That caused a problem with one of the puzzles.
Other than that minor issue, I enjoyed playing this, I found the characters cute (if not a little cliche), and it had some lovely art and a nice world.

Reviewing the game is a bit difficult because it lends itself to two different theories on what playing it actually is.
If you consider the game to be about getting from point A to point B for each stage (which is true), then it's INSANELY difficult.  A sensible player would choose never to interact with ANYTHING, because doing anything except choosing the shortest path and refusing to do anything optional saps resources you can't afford to lose.  Trouble is, you don't have enough of those resources in the first place.  Not even close.  So you HAVE to gamble to win.  But this works out about as well as it would in real life: buying lottery tickets to make rent rarely ends well.  So the game is HARD.
On the other hand, a perfectly sensible take on what makes this a game is that you're watching the comic misadventures of a Star Trek homage/parody.  Viewed that way, watching endless abusive-but-funny terrible things happen to your crew is the whole point.  You want the♥♥♥♥♥♥to hit the fan just to see exactly how it'll splatter.  Casually sailing through all the levels would be silly and boring.
This makes for an odd mix.  You die constantly, which is... not ideal.  But if you get into the spirit of that, it's fun again.
It's hard to say if this is intentional or not, but the sweet spot is easily hit by rampant cheating using a memory editor.  You can usually find two of the resources in just two scans, and the other two aren't much harder, should they ever pose a real threat of running out.  Once you have the power to simply undo the game's savage punishments for exploring, you're free to relax and goof off.  Which, honestly, feels like exactly what the game was designed to be about in the first place.
It's also important to note that I'm reviewing an early version of this game.  There's already talk of updating it to be easier coming from the developers.  One way I'd personally like to see them do this is by opening up your character stats to casual mods in config files, like how the "Political Machine" games do it.  That way, players could have fun by tailoring difficulty to their own taste.  Want to make it easy to heroically breeze through all the scenarios?  Ramp up those stats!  Want to laugh at pathetic foibles?  Use, uh, well, just use the original settings.
In short, the game is fun!  And the references are solid!  But you should be prepared to cheat like you have never cheated before if the idea of constant, near-inevitable failure stresses you out.

This is one of Paradox's better games. It doesn't drown in its own complexity, and because of this, it doesn't suffer as much from the developer's usual weakness: explaining the game to the player.
Fortunately, Crusader Kings 2 is streamlined enough (by paradox standards) to be enjoyable without having to strain your eyes too much looking for the game beneath all the 'complexity'. The game is well designed and the UI makes all the swaths of information even pleasant to interact with.
I would only warn some potential buyers that this is a game focused on the characters. You don't play as the kingdoms or countries themselves, you play as a person who is trying to advance the power and prestige of their family. As the years pass you will take over your successor in your dynasty and continue playing until your dynasty falls from power completely or you're just done with the game. The biggest focus of the gameplay is manipulating people's opinion of you and of each other.

The one distinguishing feature that doesn't cut it for me is the community [again], but that's dependent on the players themselves. Maturity level can be really low if you meet the wrong crowd. Knight - You've got the armour to take the hits, punch out a lot of damage, but you're slow.
Vanguard - Medium stats for armour and speed. With your primary weapon, running for a short while can charge your weapon up to do a lunge attack which is pretty fun.
Man At Arms - Fast, little armour, and a real nuisance. Being able to swing your weapon faster and possibly making the opponent flinch, so you get the extra hits.
Archer - Don't. People that play archer should just turn the bow around and let go with the arrow nocked in it. You've got medium speed and zero armour. Practically a one shot for any Vanguard or Knight that can catch up.
All around a great game, beating people up, dueling, honor rules and killing that damn archer in the back line.

Pros:
1. much improved over expedition conquistador in many aspects. Especially the character building element. Some of the characters such as Ketille and Nefjia feel much more alive and their well-beings matter now.
2. Equipment becomes more sensible and varied. In EC, the equipment is nothing more than numbers, and now, equipment(salvages) and usable (good) equipments are not the same.
3. Many useful skills such as crafting and active skills such as hook to disable shield. This makes battle much more interesting and decisions in battle matter more than sheer luck and brute force.
4. Decisions affected outcome. Like games such as Dragon age, Mass Effect and Witcher series, the different outcomes that are based on your decision is one of the most attractive boon of this game. Though buggy in its present stage, EV does show promises and I am willing to wait.
Cons:
1. Bugs. Please fix this.
2. Too many (useless) members. In the game where you can bring no more than 6 (max so far) into battle, I find the logic behind allowing so many other heroes (and making recruiting them compulsory) a rather buffling game mechanism. What are they used for other than slaves in camps? Furthermore, none of these user generated characters offer interesting personal stories to the progression of the main line. Even in EC, this setting is superfluous.
3. Minor things: such as building your homestead. An armourer gives you slavages while a smith gives you hides. It's a rather illogical setting and why am I not allowed to build both if I have the resources and time? Same applies to your longhouse.
4. You are supposed to be a viking who builds an army and (allegedly) conquers Britainia with an army of 1000 strong. Yet, you dun feel the immersion at all. Someone who (randomly and mindlessly) becomes your subordinate builds and controls this army while you serve as low level mercenary for the pictish or northumbrian king (or both). I have 10 heroes under my command and 40% of them are unemployed for 95% of the game time. Why not appoint one of them to the task? Let me have some say over the development of my army so at least I feel I am in command.
Despite the many shortcomings I see in this game, the appeal of this game still outshines its cons. If you are considering whether the buy is worth it, I assure you it's a bargain buy.

I will recommend this game but with some caveats. I only played single player solo, I did not play multi player on the server. First of all, this is a "survival" mmo, meaning there is thirst, hunger, and weather, as well as enemies to contend with. This is a grindy game. If you enjoy collecting virtual rocks and sticks, and cutting down virtual trees by the thousands (not an exaggeration) in order to progress to the better equipment and survive the challenges of this game, it's for you. But, they do include an Admin screen for the solo player to just get all of the things you could want if you are willing to "cheat". There are no quests, or any real story to the game. You are cut down off a cross by Conan himself and left to fend for yourself in a hostile world. That's the long and short of the plot. 99% of all the npcs you see in game will attack you on sight. You have some accomplishments to try to get to in your little journal, but there are no tutorials in game at all. I hope that they plan to add these things before release, but I have read that they do not plan to add any quests. The game world is large and interesting. You can build homes, and even castles or whole cities if you have the pateince. After 30 hours or so, mine ran out. I explored the world, killed some enemies, built a few structures and ... with no story or quests or any real goals of any kind, it just sort of went "meh" for me. That being said, the game world is HUGE and very interesting to explore. The fights are challenging if you don't cheat. However if you don't cheat, plan on spending hours and hours grinding to level up and unlock the ability to craft better gear, then hours and hours grinding to get the mats to make that better gear. It can be a nice time waster in that regard, but without a plot, story or even simple quests, it just kind of gets stale after a bit. Hopefully these things will be added by the devs, or by modders in the future.

In this game you are the Overseer or Warden in charge of commanding, building, and meeting the needs of the citizens of an underground bunker.  The overall goal is to reach "50 cycles" or 500 years to open the door to let your citizens return to the surface.
+ The way you build or command your citizens to build is absolutely fantastic in this game. (The game is very similar to Prison Archeitect in the way you build, but I found the way you build to be far more enjoyable and easier to understand)
+ Charming / Relaxing background music
+ I found the graphics / art style to be wonderful and accompanied the game quite well
+ The User-Interface was very simple and clean, typically building / managing sims are extremely cluttered but in this game the UI is simple while still giving you the control and information you need.
+ You feel a rush when things go wrong, on my first playthrough I let my population get to big, and then started running out of Oxygen so I built some air purifiers, but then realized I was low on power, but didn't have enough building materials for a water pump, and then after building a water pump I ran out of power and all of my people almost died lol.
+  The "challenges" when you start give a great pacing to the game and helps you learn the mechanics
- The "tutorial" or the text-logs that appear are a bit overwhelming at first. They do a good job at explaining the game, but I felt like there was just too much to read and remember and being overwhelmed is never a good thing. (it could have been presented in a different way, narrated, or presented in smaller chunks)
- The "camera angle" controls are not great. I really wanted to rotate and zoom in the camera to get a very close up shot at what my people were doing ro building, but you can hardly change the angle or position of the camera.
[Side Note: I'm not sure if this game was inspired by Fallout, but I absolutely love the idea, my favorite memory in Fallout 3 was being in the Vault and seeing how they operated and thought it would be so cool if I could have been the Warden]

The Good:
- The art design is delightfully nostalgic and colorful, evocative in the whimsical, retro ways I hoped it would be.

The Bad:

I realize that part of the fun is the risk and reward, but my preparations often seem to amount to a hill o' beans and that certainly was not fun.
I ended up quitting out of the game. The game has a lot of potential, but I, for one, would like to request more control of my fate.

Randomness, randomness and more randomness.  I felt while playing this game that I wasn't so much actually PLAYING the game as just sharing the Orion Trail experience, because from beginning to end, the game is basically pure luck.  You choose from random sets of crewmen presented to you, to give you certain stats, and that's about all you do to influence how the session goes.  I mean, you can pick your path in which systems to move towards, and whether or not to stop at certain things, I suppose, but it's not much of a choice, because in any given thing, you have no real control over your consequences.
There are no upgrades to purchase to make you more likely to succeed.  Your crew's stats can go up or down at a whim, as random events between nodes tick these abilities up or down with no input from you.  The time honored tradition of visiting tombstones from previous playthroughs on games like Oregon Trail is doable here, but even doing THIS can cause an utterly random stat raise or decrease.  Even what skills you use during a particular incident is entirely random most of the time;  You can push up and specialize in a particular stat only to be presented with an event that doesn't allow you to use that stat.  Even the -rewards or penalties- can be randomized in many events.
Perhaps in some games, all of this randomness wouldn't be a problem.  Orion Trail tries to allieviate things a bit with its quirky and outlandish dialogue, and it works for a time.  However, said dialogue runs out too quickly, frequently recycled every playthrough.  Given you need to play through the game multiple times to unlock the content... this is a rather serious thing.  Also not present is any sense of fairness.  On any given random event, no matter how good you are in the stat, you have the chance to critically fail, and the critical failure events are so harsh that just one of them can completely break your run, often completely exhausting a vital resource.  Critical successes, on the other hand, while certainly nice, do not give you things on quite the same scale.  Furthermore, it's almost impossible to recover from a critical failure because your rewards are often given randomly as well, and you can't just complete events that'll raise the thing the Critical Failure took from you, because the opportunities are just not given.
All and all, I'd go as far to say that the game is 100% Pure Luck in whether you succeed or not, and there's not enough dialogue in the game to make playing such a ludicrously random game worth your while.  Stick to FTL for your starship piloting dreams.

Prior to this being released on Steam, I played this game from 2007 to roughly 2013 on different servers as well (American, Korean, Sea, European). While I have had a generally negative experience with the people I've met on this game, that's not what this review is about. I grew up with Audition, and although I don't play it anymore I have a general love of rhythm games and this one would easily make it in my top few.
Like with most rhythm games, there is a learning curve and it's pretty steap. That's not to say you can't get better at it without trying, but it takes some time. From my experience I've found that people who have prior experience with rhythm games or those who play instruments have an easier time adapting to the game as it requires both of your hands and a very basic grasp of rhythm, but in such a way that you have to keep up with multiple things at once, i.e. flashing lights, a moving camera (that you can adjust), your character (because yes, it can be distracting), the beat, inputing notes, and the difficulty level increasing throughout a song repeatedly, etc. The game also rewards you for your endeavours by giving you fancy, shiny medals and icons that stay with your character for all eternity (but you can turn them off).
The game offers multiple modes to try, from things similar to guitar hero or things that have a mixture of DDR and ITG elements, to NPC battles, team battles, couple battles (yes, you can get married!), and much more. Likewise, there's a large song bank that is constantly being updated. When I played it was rare to see a popular song on the radio on the game, but from what I've heard the songs are a little different than before. But, that doesn't make it a bad game. It actually makes it better if you consider the fact there are a multitude of genres. I actually discovered many artists that I  otherwise would've never known of.
Previously, I stated I didn't have a great experience with the people I met on the game. I think that is standard of most games, if not all. However, despite this, I do have to say the mods on the online forums and the GMs are always trying to interact with others, be helpful, and available. They could be friendly or simple and to the point, but it didn't matter to me as they offered their services frequently and in a timely manner. My experiences stem from not only being a senior on the forums but also with my interactions with them in game.
Overall, it's not Osu, DDR, or ITG. But that's not to say it isn't worth giving a shot. And if you like games where you can have an actual avatar that you can decorate, then that's a plus because many other rhythm games don't offer that. Much less a garden where you can harvest points for your couple rating..

The Inner World is a 2D point-and-click adventure game and I have to say that I expected a bit more from it. There weren't any major flaws, but most things in the game felt very average.
The graphic style is probably the best thing about the game. The backgrounds are very detailed, but the same can't be said about the characters. The characters don't quite seem to fit in the world. But that's a very minor thing compared to the other issues the game has.
The main character, Robert, is an apprentice to a wind monk. He is quite naïve and goofy. The other character you get to play as is Laura, who is a thief. She seemed quite grumpy and had this "whatever" attitude. So they're not the most likable characters.
The game starts with some backstory of the world and events that lead to it's current state. After that Robert is seen polishing his master's amulet, which then gets stolen by pigeon called Peck. Peck escapes through a trash chute and Robert follows with the intention of catching Peck and getting the amulet back. The story then develops into a pretty normal point-and-click story about saving the world. After the first chapter I already knew what was going to happen in the end, because I'm pretty sure I've played game or watched a movie with a very similar plot. And it was really obvious how to story would go on after chapter 1.
The store page lists screamingly funny dialogues as a feature in the game, but I didn't find the dialogue funny. It was quite boring to be honest. Could be that the funny dialogue was lost in translation, since this is a German game and I played it in English. The dialogue certainly wasn't helped by the voice acting, which ranged from bad to decent. In the end there was this "emotional" part in the story and the voice acting seemed like the actors were just reading their lines out loud. There was no emotion whatsoever.
The puzzles in this game are also a mixed bag. Some were fairly easy to figure out while some were pretty illogical and basically required trying all possible items in order to solve them. Some items, that seemed fairly logical for solving the puzzles, didn't work and the item needed to solve the puzzle didn't always seem like they'd be a natural choice. The puzzles also required a bit of guessing. There is a hint system in the game, but it's optional and I didn't use it on my playthrough.
I had a couple of weird glitches where the character would just walk to where I pointed him/her and stop and not complete the action he/she was supposed to do. After waiting for a minute or so, the character would finally do what it was supposed to do. On a second playthrough I did to get all the achievements I missed the game also crashed to desktop twice.
To sum it up, The Inner World is an average point-and-click adventure with not much going for it. I beat the game in 5-6 hours, so it isn't very long. Some of the puzzles are quite frustrating and require some guesswork. The story wasn't anything special or new either to make me recommend the game. Unless you're a big fan of point-and-clicks, I don't recommend playing this one, since there are better point-and-clicks out there.

In this game, if you die you have to realize that it's YOUR fault. The drags, the rainbows, the different swing types make this game an absolutely astonishing masterpiece.
Usually you start by joining team death match, and enjoy brutally decapitating the opposing team's members, and you get ganked by 2 players. You decided that you want to go knight class and you want to level up the mace category. You run up behind someone and stab them, and then with 1 swing you kill multiple players.

Buy it now while there are still good players online (The game probably won't die until 2020). I am not usually a fan of RPG games, but I have been blown away by this game.
Gameplay is not overly complicated, there is excellent variety in the character specs, with the ability to combine any fighting style with any other, and the interactions between characters and NPCs is endless. Looks wise, this game is also a cut above. I am running with a GTX1070 and it is simply gorgeous. Single player is smooth and effortless, in my 153 hours of gameplay so far I have only experienced one single incident of crashes, which was following a patch, and quickly hotfixed by the devs later that day. Even multiplayer I have not experienced a single connection issue, which is highly impressive. The devs on this game seem to really listen to player feedback and act on issues quickly. The result of such a dedicated dev team is a close to perfect, polished and thoroughly enjoyable game.
The main story itself is captivating and very well done, however, the different character storylines are, for me, the stars of the show. Each characters story is well written, with good background without bombarding you with details. They are also endearing and comedic, even sometimes a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥ (Yes Lohse, I mean you!). There are so many different ways to follow the story and interact, combined with the variety in party member options, the option to go completely solo, and various difficulty modes, that this is a game with so much potential for repeat plays. There is also Gamemaster mode, which I am yet to try.
I cannot recommend this game highly enough, but, as a warning, you will sink 100 hours of your life into it without even realising it!

Devil Daggers is fast, snappy, frustrating, maddening, terrible, wonderful, and hellish.
The game is simple. Stay alive for as long as you possibly can while fighting off Hell's armies in a dim, dark, purgatorial arena, with nothing but your rapid-fire daggers and your (hopefully sharp) reaction times. Harkening back to late 90's games such as Quake, the movement system is extremely satisfying. Of course, you have standard movement with WASD and your mouselook, but once you get the general hang of the game, you can introduce bunny-hopping and dagger jumping into your repetoire. These systems reward you with speed and manueverability that can turn average, 'nothing special' runs into challenges to the world's top players. While not as snappy as one might like, its movement system just feels right at home here, and is immensely satisfying.
Truth be told, I'm not even that big of a fan of wave-based survival games. Sure, I've played and enjoyed games like Geometry Wars, (which, admittedly, is very similar to Devil Daggers IMO, just from an entirely different perspective,) but none of them have held my attention quite like Devil Daggers has. While a hefty portion of this addictive nature comes from the game just being fun as all hell, it's also partly due to the leaderboard system. Quite a few friends of mine picked up the game when it came out, and we slowly started ramping up our challenges to each other. Thirty second survival became seventy, seventy became one-twenty, and so-on and so-forth. I've swore up and down, I've shrieked like a small child upon near misses with skulls, and have had my feet tapping in anticipation beneath my desk, all because my best time was MILLISECONDS off my friend's best, and I was
close. Admittedly, they've all moved onto other games, and I finally hold the crown at 427 seconds. But... given that my record is about 70 seconds shy of the coveted Devil Dagger status, I can't just stop there, can I?
In addition to being one of the most fun games I've played this past year, it's an amazing looking and sounding game. I'm a complete fanatic for PSX-style graphics. The blocky style, abysmal render distance, primitive lighting systems and poor aliasing admittedly looks awful by today's standards, but it's incredibly charming to anyone who grew up with a Playstation One in their home. Devil Daggers effortlessly merges the look of a late-run PSX game with an aesthetic similar to Quake and a mid-90s Slayer album cover, and it always looks fantastic. At this point, with some research, I could probably write a scientific paper on why I love this visual style so, so much, but I'll keep that toned down for this.
If there's one aspect of Devil Daggers that absolutely must be talked about, it's the immaculate sound design. A satisfying sound is what makes the difference between a weapon being limp and forgettable, or powerful and an icon of an entire genre (see: the Super Shotgun from Doom II, or the AWP from any of Counter Strike's iterations.) Or, as another example, making the presentation of in-game reward boring and unfulfilling, or something that straight-up makes your day upon finding it. Sound is a big deal to me in just about every medium, but video game sound design, (especially in shooters,) is
. Devil Daggers sets a bar for what audio in video games should be.
Every crunch, splatter, and skitter has an unsettling bite to it that is distinct and clearly heard amidst the madness of the arena. Each enemy has a 'chatter' for when they are encroaching on your person, and getting dangerously close to ending your run for good. Enemy spawners have an ominous, low hum or a disgusting chitter to signify where they're coming from, or that yes, they are still there. Death rattles and screeches offer a triumphant, yet haunting finality to taking down a larger enemy. The sound of firing daggers grows from a machine-like drone to shrill screams of the damned with each upgrade you gain. And of course, above it all, Devil Daggers incorporates a positional 3D surround sound system, assisting the player in knowing where their next threat is without much difficulty. Everything is accounted for, it's satisfying, unsettling, and so, so good.
To make a send-up to 90's FPS games can be done by just about anyone with a Unity engine license. To make that same tribute by building your own engine, creating sound and art that is equally impressive and sinister, and designing one of the most immersive and entertaining arena shooters I've ever seen takes someone like Matt Bush, who did an incredible job with Devil Daggers as a whole.
At the end of the day, you can get either Devil Daggers or a nice burger for five US dollars. Both will cause heart issues. One is eternal.

*Updated for Act III, see bottom of the review*
Kentucky Route Zero is an indie episodic point and click adventure game, developed and published by Cardboard Computer. Revealed on Kickstarter back in 2011, the developer had to reach a goal of USD 6,500, but managed to raise USD 8,583. Kentucky Route Zero was planned for release in late 2011, but as with every single game development project ever, that never happened and eventually the game was instead split into 5 episodes with the first one released in January 2013 and the second in May.
The game’s story revolves around a secret highway in Kentucky and the mysterious folks who travel it. The player controls Conway, an antique furniture deliveryman, as he attempts to complete the final delivery for his financially troubled employer. Along the way he’ll meet dozens of strange characters and make a few new friends to help him overcome the obstacles in his path. Gameplay in Kentucky Route Zero is slow-paced, focusing on exploring new environments and talking with new people. Thankfully, “slow” doesn’t equal “boring”. The story is very well written, and although the player seems to have no way of affecting the outcome at all, it’s a pleasure to discover everything along the way.
The game has a simply, yet beautiful art style. Background and scene transitions are often brilliantly done, and it’s a shame not all the locations are visualized: Some of them are only described in text on the map screen. I’ve got a feeling the game could have been so much better with every location drawn in the Kentucky Route Zero style, even locations that are not responsible for driving the story forward. And driving is a key word in Kentucky Route Zero. You do spend some time “driving” around on the game map, making it a little disappointing when you reach a new location and it’s simply just described to you textually.
The music in the game is, like the visuals, great, but it suffers from the same problem: It’s just not enough music. Also, it’s a soundtrack that works very well with the game, but it’s not a soundtrack you’ll sit down and listen to, like the Machinarium soundtrack. The sound design, too, is a curious piece. I played the game with headphones on and it has serious volume problems at times, with some sound effects almost drowning out other sounds in a scene. This could of course be intentional, but I doubt it.
The replayability isn’t much to talk about. There are a lot of nice surprises, twists and turns the first time you play through, but since it’s hard to surprise the player twice when telling exactly the same story, Kentucky Route Zero is a game most people will play only once. And this brings us on the the subject of game cost. The game retails at a massive $24.99, which is rather pricy for this game. Yes, you will get 5 acts for that price, but I’ve already played through the first two acts and spent around two hours doing that. If we can use that as a pointer, you’ll get 5, maybe 6, hours of gameplay for $24.99, which isn’t impressive. It should be mentioned that you also get the soundtrack and a “private newsletter” included, but even though the soundtrack is very good, it does not justify the price. To put it in a way the internet generation understands: The price of this game is too damn high!
Kentucky Route Zero is not a bad game, far from it. But I’ve got a feeling it could have been so much better. Just a little more music and a few more visualized locations would have made wonders. Cardboard Computer has promised to release three more episodes, and unless they decide to pull a Valve on us all, those remaining episodes might very well change my overall impression of the game – for better or for worse. If that happens, I’ll come back here and let you know.
At the current price and with only two episodes released, I would not recommend Kentucky Route Zero, unless you are a die hard point-and-click adventure fan.
*Update for Act III*
Cardboard computer finally managed to release the third act (still out of five acts) of KRZ. I know this goes against popular opinion, but even with this third act, I can't recommend the game at the current price. Act III adds roughly 2 more hours of gameplay, and while it's a beautiful audiovisual experience that will tickle your brain where it fees good, I don't feel that I get my money's worth.
Wait for all five acts to be released, THEN go ahead and throw your money at Cardboard Computer. At the current release pace, this will be some time in 2016.

A lot of love went into creating this game, with it's nice artwork, and humour spread throughout which is why I originally backed this game on Kickstarter. However dispite the funny dialog and nice artwork I did not find the game enjoyable. The game plays out as a series events where you make decisions that all end with what is basically a slot machine, this results in a game where finishing a playthrough is based mostly on random chance.
Right from the outset the game inadvertently teaches players not to make decisions on what would you do, but rather pick the decision that will give the best odds at the next slot machine meaning the decision isn't really a decision at all, the choice is taken away from you. This also means some players stop caring about reading the dialog as they no longer have any real choice as to how the event will play out and the dialog is one of the strongest elements of the game.
With the latest patches winning a playthrough no longer feels like the grind through a random generator and now I can enjoy the humour and style of the game much more. It is and always will remain a simplified slot machine game in fancy clothing, so if the funny scripts and the winning and losing at slot machines are not something you enjoy then you'll probably want to give this game a miss.

Review as of 03/12/2016 -(3rd UPDATE)
---------------------------------
***As of 03/12/2016 there has been little said about patches or updates. Most topics on the community hub are a few days old too. Not a good sign.
**Almost 5 hours played and I seem to get bored after an hour or 2. I tried both what seems to be the easiest setting and "normal"; however I am not hitting that "lose yourself" in the gameplay mood I have with other strategy/sims. **Dev communication is on point -They released information for possible additions on 2/29/2016, however there are no set patch dates or any kind of ETA on when we could see more content. They had some bug fixes roll out but nothing game changing.
The game is enjoyable overall and I feel that with strong updates the game could become something great (and well worth $16 or more even)... just as it is now I would wait and see what the developers do within the coming weeks. Feels like a beta more than a release.
Pros:
>>Strong Survival/Strategy/Sim potential.
>>Game has a rough charm and systems that could work well if they were more polished/in-depth.
>>The multiple layers system allows for many possibilities when designing a bunk.
Cons:
>>Research can be completed almost too easily (especially if you have more than 1 scientist).
>>Bunk residents are generally annoying – They don’t seem to manage their jobs and personal affairs very well.
>>Older residents and children are completely useless in terms of gameplay (maybe add a classroom function for children(unlocks 1 additional random job choice or something) and add in some chore style jobs for elderly(teaching children, maybe only elderly can do research even)).
Tip if you buy:
>> Play on 1 or 2 speed (> or >>) ... Playing on 3 is fine but you will zip though the game pretty fast to cycle 50. **You don't have to end at 50 but it seems to be the soft end game goal.

For now I will vote “Negative” and update as I play throughout the month of March. I really WANT to like the game more and hopefully some updates will help.
TL:DR - Game seems like an Early Access rather than a released game. For an easy, norm, hard playthough stopping at 50 cycle you may get about 10-12 hours of gameplay out of it. Not horrible for $16.

I was never exposed to the original Oregan Trail, but learning from media and from my peers, I understand quite well what core mechanics are involved.
I quite enjoy the whimsical humour and the writing/sci-fi theme of Orion Trail. So do I much appreciate the art direction.
However, I am immediately put off by how much "chance" dominates your outcomes on the trail, disregarding your decisions.
In fact, my frustration with the RNG factor is so intense, I de-installed the game after several attempts.
It seems that the decisions I made in investing in specfic areas of expertise DID NOT MATTER AT ALL, because of the random number generater.
I'd much perfer a system similar to described;
Each mission for the moment have three possible solutions. Solutions involving expertise like "Science." or "Diplomacy".
To successfully complete the actions required of that solution, player must meet the skill "threshold".
Example.
My crew has the combined expertise in Science of 4 after initial crew member assembly.
Second mission of the trail, I am asked to gain access to an alien fuel source, blocked by an alien bio-matching vault panel lock.
Choosing my "science" expertise solution, which is to surgically transplant an alien tentacle to a crew's body to operate alien technology, requires a total roll of 6.
Before the roll, my expertise in Science GUARANTEE 4 points in the roll. So I only need a minimum roll of "2" to succeed.
This way, if I heavily invest in some expertise, I actually get rewarded by it. And can feel safer to make those choices.
Right now, the Odds of the Orion Trail is TOO heavily stacked against us. May the travelers rest in pieces.

I really want to like Vikings because Expeditions: Conquistador was a gem but holy mother this game, at least in its current form, is just an exercise in frustration. The trademark gameplay of Roleplaying <-> Combat <-> Survival is still intact here but there is an utter lack of polish in Vikings that ruins my time with the game every time I feel like I'm finally into it.
There is no reason for every single combat animation to be this slow and for archers to be so mind-numbingly overpowered. Just now the game forced me into a fight that took easily 40 minutes to finish only for a completely disconnected group of other enemies to show up and immediately start a second one—with even more units on the screen. It took me another 20 minutes to get even halfway through that fight and then the game just crashed. Needless to say I couldn't save during either combat encounter and the game didn't bother to auto-save inbetween them so that's that. It wasn't the first crash either.
If Vikings was really special I could see past the time-wasting animations. I could also see past the tedious barrel and crate looting that you need to do in every single village just to find a damn pig bladder. Unfortunately Vikings also lacks the roleplaying standards that defined the previous game. Conquistador explored a clash of cultures and gave the player so many ways of respecting or disrespecting the indigenous people he met. So far the only thing I've done in Vikings (and I'm over 20 hours in) is choose an ally and then fight his enemies for him, or choose no allies and fight everyone. No good character building, no good side-stories, just combat mission after combat mission.
I appreciate that you can at any point betray your alliances and start working with someone else—a lot of other modern RPGs don't even allow such consequence-heavy decisions. The combat is simply not enjoyable and polished enough for the amount of fighting Vikings throws at you though.
My recommendation is to follow the patch notes and come back in a few months.

The Inner World combines a beautiful and intriguing graphical style with some wonderfully off the wall design, such as a world built on the inside of a sphere, not the outside like ours. This is all backed with a melodic and inquisitive musical score that binds it all together (I could happily listen to the opening menu music for quite some time). The human-like inhabitants all have stripey arms, legs and nose, apart from the main character Robert, who seems different from everyone else with his flute nose.
The adventure starts with Robert going on a quick errand to rescue a necklace stolen by a pesky pigeon but he quickly finds himself being sucked into an adventure to discover the many secrets of the Inner World; which is a lot as he's never left the castle before!
Through his journey you meet a wealth of very original characters and combined with the delightfully naive Robert lead to some great writing with a nice dry sense of humour. The voice acting and translation in itself is superb considering that the game was written in German and any slip ups are almost unnoticeable.
The mandatory puzzles are also top class, encouraging you to explore and use that point-n-click crazy logic to allow you to progress. Many of these give Robert and the other characters a great opportunity to make you smile, particularly Laura the female lead. There is also a robust hint system for those that find this kind of game a bit too much of a challenge so you never feel held back from enjoying the story.
Completed this in 7 or 8 hours or so but enjoyed every second. A wonderful world with great characters to fall in love with.

As modern point and click adventure games go, this one is fairly decent. It's not a mind-blowing experience by any means, but it's definitely not bad either. You play as a guy named Robert who finds himself thrust into a quest to save the world (naturally). Robert is a very naive and unassuming sort of fella, so a lot of the plot and humor centers around his clueless innocence. The story and dialogue is fairly good for the most part, in turns charming, funny and dark. The voice acting is hit or miss, though - mostly it is decent, but a few lines here and there are inexplicably bad (wrong pronunciations, improper emphasis of words, etc). Mechanically, the game also has its ups and downs. Being a point and click game, you would think that the pointing and clicking would be spot-on, but that's not always the case. Sometimes you can't click on things that you should be able to click (though it usually fixes itself in a second or two). Additionally, half of the achievements don't seem to be working properly. However, the developers have started to release patches to fix some of these problems, so a lot of these things may not be issues in the future. Regardless, none of these faults are deal breakers by any means, anyways.
The puzzles are fairly standard in adventure game terms. You basically just go around talking to people, picking up objects, and using those objects (or combinations thereof) to solve puzzles and progress further. Thankfully, none of the solutions are overly ridiculous or unintuitive (as is the case with many adventure games), though you will need to really think some stuff through from time to time. Apparently there is also a help system in place if you need it (which I didn't even realize until after finishing the game), so you probably won't ever get stuck for long, if you even get stuck at all. The game is divided into 5 chapters, each of which consists of a self-contained series of puzzles that take place on 3 or 4 "screens". Playtime is probably around 7-8 hours or so, give or take. So keep that in mind in terms of how much you are willing to pay. All in all, the game is pretty good. As I said earlier, it is nothing mind-blowing for the genre, but it's a nice experience while it lasts. Probably the worst thing I could say about it (aside from the minor glitches noted above) is that the pacing is very slow. The dialogue in particular seems like it takes foreeeeeeeever sometimes, especially with a main character who is so low-key and slow. The pace may test your patience at times. But if you don't mind that and are into classic adventure games, this is probably worth a look at some point. I would probably recommend waiting for a sale, though, unless you are hardcore into adventure games and need something new to play now.
