I enjoy the world building. For instance, I was going through on a beach and I cam across some alligators. Well, one of these alligators started teleporting around which I thought was pretty odd.
After killing them I looted the one that was teleporting around and he had teleportation gloves on him which I thought was kind of cool because they allowed one of my characters to teleport. So, I equipped that and keep moving down the beach and just a little bit further along there was a corpse. looting that corpse gave me a journal and one of the entries talked about being able to teleport. Obviously this alligator ate part of this guy (I guess his hands), got his gloves inside of him and now could teleport.
That's really neat. That's cool. I loved that level of world building, it really makes it believable. it makes stuff makes sense and it's unique and that's what's really important. You can build a world that's believable and boring. This one is exciting and I love that.
Onto combat. So fighting these guys can be really difficult but in a good way. It's just the right level at least for me on normal. I think it's right there where it's the perfect level of needing strategy, trying different methods, save scumming if needed but enjoying when you finally beat them.
Also the elemental combos as I mentioned earlier are fantastic. You can create an oil spill and then another character can catch it on fire. That's wonderful. Of course, that being said there’s a lot of friendly fire. I'm not very good at it yet but I do enjoy it. I think it's a great combat system.
Lastly, questing. it's very loose and very believable and I think that's great. The quest giver is not standing there waiting to tell you about how they need you to kill something and then once you talk to them that enemy spawns. Instead you could find that enemy and its spawn and kill it before you even talk to the person and then because you've killed it that might be a good thing or a bad thing. Perhaps they wanted you to loot something and you already sold it or perhaps they needed you to talk to it first. The point is is that the game doesn't necessarily wait for you to move it forward in that sense you can explore at your own pace.
You can skip quests or you can not. There is an overarching story arc that will have to be followed but outside of that what you do is what you want to do and I think that's great.
All that being said, not all of this I have enjoyed. Now some of this is mildly nitpicking but but hear me out on some of this. First of all there are unlikable characters. What I mean by that is (and mostly I'm talking about Fane and the Red Prince here) - they just look down on you. They’re constantly talking down to you. They might be funny and they might have some good quips and that's great but otherwise they think they're better than you and I don't personally enjoy being talked down to in a game, at least not by the people I'm supposedly partying with.
Also a lot of them do the kind of nuanced tropes that we've seen time and time again in fantasy. Really they kind of remind me of like beginner D&D characters. Like your first idea you had. Many of them are from royalty but are either an illegitimate son or lost their kingdom or they're the last of their kind but they're searching for answers - or you know all that kind of stuff has been done to death. They are nuanced and believable but it's not exactly origina.
Additionally while playing the game you can accidentally steal stuff quite easily. You don't have to be in sneaking mode to steal. If you accidently click when you're trying to move and there happens to be a stick that somebody owns you will try to pick up that stick which will automatically attempt a theft. If seen you've now lost reputation and people are upset at you leading to you getting in trouble since you've committed a crime. It's annoying and not exactly intuitive nore is it enjoyable.
Another issue is the inventory. I feel like the developers haven't decided on what they want. You have an unlimited inventory space so you can carry as many things as you want. There is no 60 panel limit or anything like that. You're not playing inventory tetris like you do in Resident Evil or something like that however, there is a weight system, think Skyrim, Oblivion, that sort of stuff. So you have a limited inventory system but you don't, it depends on how you look at it. Additionally the weight system is so preposterous that you can carry multiple barrels of water in your inventory, making it unbelievable. Either way I'm not sure why they bothered with that as it seems kind of tacked on and unneeded.
The gameplay can also be cheated. It's pretty easy to cheese this game in a very obvious way that I'm surprised they didn't really think about. This mainly involves inventory tricks and dialogue tricks. If somebody is in a dialogue for instance,:you start a fight that starts with a dialogue, only one person can converse with them. That means while they're stuck in the conversation you can control your other characters and just move around the battlefield and set up where you want so that you can then swap to the main person that's talking go through that and start the battle at an advantage. With the inventory stuff you can have barrels of ooze that are in your inventory that give you permanent poison arrows or poison potions or you know, whatever. It's pretty obvious and I'm not sure how it wasn't caught in Q&A; or maybe they think that kind of gamifying freedom is nice but I don't particularly enjoy having it there because once I see it I struggle to not use it.
Also, I am afraid to say that while this does support mods, installing mods removes the ability to get achievements. I understand some people are really particular about achievements but there are programs out there to where you can unlock achievements with no effort so they are cheated anyway. At that point why make it to where I can't have a mod that allows me to run a bit faster so I can backtrack quicker and still get achievements?
As you can see those cons are fairly minor quips. Overall, the world-building, the combat and the questing, all of that as a majority of the game, all of that is very well done. I have enjoyed my time with it. I think it's great fun and I can't wait to spend another hour and then find out I've spent five.
Hope for the rest of the game:
I do hope that the companions become more nuanced - more believable and kind of stray from that kind of beginner D&D character idea as a defining character trait and instead become their own people. I look forward to the overall story arc becoming apparent. At least on the starting island it's very much in the background it's mentioned kind of right after the ship and then you're just doing your own thing but there's no major stakes at play that are readily apparent or that you know you're going towards some goals somewhere.
Also the combat hasn't actually been that varied -  the combat is solid and it's well done and they obviously have their ideas together but I want to fight a polymorph. I want somebody to turn my party into a chicken and me have to deal with that. I have no idea how I would deal with that! I want to fight large enemies, not just humanoids and stuff that are maybe smaller or animals. Maybe a dragon or some multi-part boss, that'd be cool. I also want to see more interesting scenario driven battlefields. So far, as soon as you come across an enemy if it's a battle then the battle starts. I want to see kind of like the gladiator fight where the layout is very strategic in that it's kind of pre-made or more scripted at least in the battlefield. You can do some fun stuff with that especially with the different status effects and environmental effects.

This game is fantastic. I purchased it in pre-release but decided to wait to play it until the full release last month. I've already put in 64 hours playing through with a friend and we just started the last act.
My rating: 9.5/10
Pros:
-Ton of content, long and interesting story
-Only one playthrough so far but feels like there are a lot of viable and interesting build options.
-All dialog is fully voice acted, and there is a TON of dialog. The voice acting is of good quality.
-Up to four player co-op
-Very few bugs. In 64 hours I've had it crash once, and had some weird behavior after reloading a save once.
-Great support - only out for 6 weeks and already a ton of fixes and updates to enhance the experience and fix bugs that users have encountered.
-Huge number of different ways to complete quests.
Cons:
-The pitch of "players can split off and do their own thing" sounded gimmicky and dumb when they announced it and it still feels that way to me now. Yes you can technically do that in many cases - but the fights are balanced for a full squad so while you can technically do it, almost nobody is going to actually do it - especially if your goal is to complete the game.
-I dislilke how the dialog system is configured. When you have to persuade someone in a conversation it's based on your stats (one option for strength, one for intelligence etc.) what this means is that instead of picking the option that you think actually makes sense given the context of the conversation, you end up feeling forced to just pick the option that aligns with your highest stat. I understand that logically this makes sense because those options are tied to that stat, for example "[strength] put your hand on your sword and threaten" vs. "[intelligence] if you work with me you'll benefit as well!" but the huge downside to this is that it takes you out of the "role playing" exprience and you can't just give the answer that you think applies best to the situation or aligns best when your personality if you actually want to have a chance to succeed in the persuasion.

Devil Daggers is fast, snappy, frustrating, maddening, terrible, wonderful, and hellish.
The game is simple. Stay alive for as long as you possibly can while fighting off Hell's armies in a dim, dark, purgatorial arena, with nothing but your rapid-fire daggers and your (hopefully sharp) reaction times. Harkening back to late 90's games such as Quake, the movement system is extremely satisfying. Of course, you have standard movement with WASD and your mouselook, but once you get the general hang of the game, you can introduce bunny-hopping and dagger jumping into your repetoire. These systems reward you with speed and manueverability that can turn average, 'nothing special' runs into challenges to the world's top players. While not as snappy as one might like, its movement system just feels right at home here, and is immensely satisfying.
Truth be told, I'm not even that big of a fan of wave-based survival games. Sure, I've played and enjoyed games like Geometry Wars, (which, admittedly, is very similar to Devil Daggers IMO, just from an entirely different perspective,) but none of them have held my attention quite like Devil Daggers has. While a hefty portion of this addictive nature comes from the game just being fun as all hell, it's also partly due to the leaderboard system. Quite a few friends of mine picked up the game when it came out, and we slowly started ramping up our challenges to each other. Thirty second survival became seventy, seventy became one-twenty, and so-on and so-forth. I've swore up and down, I've shrieked like a small child upon near misses with skulls, and have had my feet tapping in anticipation beneath my desk, all because my best time was MILLISECONDS off my friend's best, and I was
close. Admittedly, they've all moved onto other games, and I finally hold the crown at 427 seconds. But... given that my record is about 70 seconds shy of the coveted Devil Dagger status, I can't just stop there, can I?
In addition to being one of the most fun games I've played this past year, it's an amazing looking and sounding game. I'm a complete fanatic for PSX-style graphics. The blocky style, abysmal render distance, primitive lighting systems and poor aliasing admittedly looks awful by today's standards, but it's incredibly charming to anyone who grew up with a Playstation One in their home. Devil Daggers effortlessly merges the look of a late-run PSX game with an aesthetic similar to Quake and a mid-90s Slayer album cover, and it always looks fantastic. At this point, with some research, I could probably write a scientific paper on why I love this visual style so, so much, but I'll keep that toned down for this.
If there's one aspect of Devil Daggers that absolutely must be talked about, it's the immaculate sound design. A satisfying sound is what makes the difference between a weapon being limp and forgettable, or powerful and an icon of an entire genre (see: the Super Shotgun from Doom II, or the AWP from any of Counter Strike's iterations.) Or, as another example, making the presentation of in-game reward boring and unfulfilling, or something that straight-up makes your day upon finding it. Sound is a big deal to me in just about every medium, but video game sound design, (especially in shooters,) is
. Devil Daggers sets a bar for what audio in video games should be.
Every crunch, splatter, and skitter has an unsettling bite to it that is distinct and clearly heard amidst the madness of the arena. Each enemy has a 'chatter' for when they are encroaching on your person, and getting dangerously close to ending your run for good. Enemy spawners have an ominous, low hum or a disgusting chitter to signify where they're coming from, or that yes, they are still there. Death rattles and screeches offer a triumphant, yet haunting finality to taking down a larger enemy. The sound of firing daggers grows from a machine-like drone to shrill screams of the damned with each upgrade you gain. And of course, above it all, Devil Daggers incorporates a positional 3D surround sound system, assisting the player in knowing where their next threat is without much difficulty. Everything is accounted for, it's satisfying, unsettling, and so, so good.
To make a send-up to 90's FPS games can be done by just about anyone with a Unity engine license. To make that same tribute by building your own engine, creating sound and art that is equally impressive and sinister, and designing one of the most immersive and entertaining arena shooters I've ever seen takes someone like Matt Bush, who did an incredible job with Devil Daggers as a whole.
At the end of the day, you can get either Devil Daggers or a nice burger for five US dollars. Both will cause heart issues. One is eternal.

FATE: Undiscovered Realms Review – Raymond KT
Summary: Venture into new lands, armed with your wits, weapons, and faithful pet by your side. Explore ancient dungeons, slay terrifying monsters, and uncover riches as you journey through these Undiscovered Realms. [WildTangent]
Undiscovered Realms is a continuation of the single-player story from the original Fate (there's still no multiplayer). After a long campaign against the forces of evil, your hero returns to the town of Grove. Forget about any celebrations with beautiful elf maidens and grog, though. A mysterious stranger soon arrives and cons you into opening portals into two new realms, a wooded world called Druantia and an icy kingdom named Typhon. The cowled weirdo then reveals himself as some kind of evil wizard and takes off, leaving you to head through these gates as well to stop his dastardly machinations.
Not a lot of imagination went into setting up your adventures into these new lands, but they get the job done. Game structure here is also pretty similar to the original Fate and is based around hubs leading to towns and the dungeons. Your hero (either a brand-new one or an import of your character from the first game) starts off in the Temple of Fate hub, which features gates to Druantia and Typhon. From there, you choose a town to enter and wind up in a secondary hub populated by a motley crew of monsters who assign quests, sell goods, heal injuries, enchant items, and so forth. Once you do business here, you head off down the nearby steps to slay monsters and solve problems in pretty much limitless randomized dungeon levels.
Résumé: Aventurez-vous dans de nouvelles terres, armé de votre sagesse, de vos armes et de votre animal de compagnie fidèle à vos côtés. Explorez les donjons anciens, tuez des monstres terrifiants et découvrez des richesses au fur et à mesure que vous traversez ces royaumes inconnus. [WildTangent]
Undiscovered Realms est une continuation de l'histoire d'un joueur du destin original (il n'y a toujours pas de multijoueur). Après une longue campagne contre les forces du mal, votre héros retourne dans la ville de Grove. Oubliez les célébrations avec les jeunes filles maures et les grog. Un étranger mystérieux arrive bientôt et vous empêche d'ouvrir des portails en deux nouveaux royaumes, un monde boisé appelé Druantia et un royaume glacial appelé Typhon. Le bouffon de charrue se révèle alors comme une sorte de sorcier maléfique et enlève, vous laissant tomber à travers ces portes aussi pour arrêter ses machinations drasardly.
Pas beaucoup d'imagination a été de mettre en place vos aventures dans ces nouveaux pays, mais ils ont fait le travail. La structure du jeu est également similaire à celle du destin original et repose sur des hubs menant aux villes et aux donjons. Votre héros (soit un tout neuf ou une importation de votre personnage depuis le premier jeu) commence dans le hub Temple of Fate, qui comporte des portes vers Druantia et Typhon. De là, vous choisissez une ville pour entrer et vous débrouiller dans un centre secondaire peuplé d'un généreux équipage de monstres qui attribue des quêtes, vendez des biens, guéris des blessures, enchantez des objets, etc. Une fois que vous faites affaires ici, vous vous diriger vers le bas des étapes à venir pour tuer des monstres et résoudre des problèmes dans des niveaux de donjon aléatoires à peu près illimités.

This game is a lot like the original Oregon Trail - which it should be, since it's a space adventure based on it - only without the hunting.  Sorry, folks, that was a stretch goal that wasn't met.  Some people have complained that there's no skill involved, that it all comes down to a roll of the die.  This is broadly true, but aside from that sadly missing hunting game, Oregon Trail and the more recent "OMG anything is better with zombies" Organ Trail are pretty much the same way.
Will you ford the river or try to float across?  Sneak through the horde of zombies or go through guns blazing?  Rely upon your attack rating and set phasers to "shave" or go with tactics and put on encounter suits to avoid the allergy problems from these furry trading aliens?  In each situation you know something about which will be more likely to succeed, but can ultimately fail based on luck... it's just that Oregon Trail is more open about that fact.
Despite the lack of hunting, I still think this is a good game.  You can't just min/max as another reviewer said because you won't always get the crew you want (you get a random assortment of three candidates for each slot), you may not have your impressive attack rating as an option each encounter, and going full-on diplomacy will leave you hurting when a bravado or science crisis hits.  You instead need to try to balance your various skills, knowing that going high on a couple of things will make those challenges more likely to succeed but that it will leave other stats weak.  And while a roll of the dice may not be an extremely exciting way to play a game, what you do have here is excellent writing.
Whether you're trying to escape being digested in the "Oh the huge manatee" event, finding that your shields can't hold against savings of this magnitude when a Megamart ship flies up or playing 'pop goes the warp weasel' when you chased the little pests into your airlock, there is a lot that's worth reading and a few chuckles involved.  Perhaps it won't be your favorite game to return to forever, but it's certainly worth playing for a few hours in my opinion.  And with more content slated to be added up through and past the official release, there should be plenty to do for $10.

I love this game. I've been an MMO person for a long time and then in Wildstar I got hooked on building. I guess these types of games just became a natural progression from there. I tried Citadel first and was quite put off by how unfinished it is (it was my first early access). A friend played this and convinced me to give it a go. I have no idea what all the bad reviews are about (minus people B&M the PVP system).
We went on a PVE server. Honestly, the game can be challenging enough without having people come up and gank you, destroy your house and more. Why you'd do PvP in this is beyond me. The first thing the community will tell you is this: are you going to die, you are going to lose all your things. And it's true. The critters try to kill you, the NPC exile's try to kill, the damn weather tries to kill you. And through it all,  you farm,  you craft and you build your first house. And then your second...and probably a third. Maybe some shanties for safe havens in areas you grind a lot.
There is some sort of story. Obviously this game is still eary access and so that part is very much in development. But there are secret recipes to learn, lore to uncover and its much more comprehensive that I would have imagined to even start. There's group content, and soloable content. The game is still developing and bits and pieces are still falling in place.
The crafting is pretty well thought of in my opinion, and there's every type. The introduction of thrulls (slaves) adds an extra element I haven't seen in games and gives you something extra to farm.
The building works mostly well. The floors/walls/ceilings/roofs are all on a snap system, which can be really annoying if you're not used to it. It still has a few bugs and quirks, but again, they're fixing it. I do hope we get more decor pieces to fill the monstrosities I like to build, but all in time I hope.  Everything is climable. Even other people's houses (sometimes to your own detriment if they have attack thrulls).
Each zone has it's own unique weather, which may also try to kill you, ala sand storms in the desert. In the desert you can overheat (thus needing to drink more water) and even get heatstroke (and gradually die). The frozen area freezes you and can give you frost bite and...kill you. Wear the right gear to the right zone, take the right food and drink (because you can starve and die of dehydration).
You can level either by fighting and killing mobs (some people say this is the quickest) or by farming mats and crafting/building. I didn't really notice that big of a difference in either method. Overall, if you like to grind, build and fight for your survival, this is a pretty awesome game. The graphics are the best I've seen these games, and it's continually improving.
Do you want to end a friendship? Do you want to get beaten by your brother? Do you want Workshop support while doing all of them? If you said yes to all questions, this game is for you.

I played this game for 28 minutes. Enough time for two run-throughs. Time-wise, that was exactly what I was looking for in a game like this. I loved Organ Trail, even though I've only played it for 7 hours or so. I really enjoyed that game and was looking for something similar. This game was not it.
The problem with this game is it feels like soul-less RNG. There are no interesting decisions. Even picking your crew, you need to specialize to get the highest number possible in one category or another, meaning choosing a captain with a skill of 3, and a crew member with a skill of 2, with as much overlap in the same skill as possible, is a no-brainer. Combat basically amounts to rolling a die. Nothing you do can manipulate those odds. Planet exploration is the only interesting part of the game, but just barely. It amounts to a simple "press your luck" decision game. You can choose the path your spaceship takes, like sometimes... but the only decision there is to go to which resource you need most. And if the resource on both ends of the branch is the same, is that really much of a decision? You have no idea what sort of RNG event is going to happen or affect it in any way, so yeah... boring. By contrast, Organ Trail had lots of action-RPG events where you get rewarded for skillful gameplay and are constantly making decisions that affect your success.
In the end, this game plays itself. You're just there to watch and click buttons when necessary. No strategy. No tactics. Nothing. Really wanted to like this game. Didn't.

This is the first Kickstarter project I have ever contributed to as well as the first Early Access Game I have ever bought. I recommended it before, but now that it seems it is out of Early Access, I just can't recommend it anymore. It feels way too random. There just doesn't seem to be enough game here. You pick you captain and your officers, and you even get to rename them if you want. But the rest of the game is choosing which path to take and which stat (Attack, Science, Diplomacy, Bravado, etc.) that you are going to use to tackle the random events that crop up. After that it's all dice-rolling where the RNG feels like it, more often that not, works against you. And even now that Achievements have been activated, it doesn't really feel like any sort of actual achievement to get them. It seems like, if you just have enough playthroughs of the game, you'll get all of the achievements and nothing about your choices and skill will change that.
As for what I like about the game, there is the concept, which is basically "Oregon Trail In Space." I also like the visual style of the game; I am generally tired of all the indie games these days with their retro-pixelated graphics, but in this game I think it adds real charm.
People have referred to FTL when talking about this game, but the graphics and the sense of humor bring to my mind the old Space Quest series by the Two Guys from Andromeda. Also, there is so much depth of gameplay in FTL that it makes this game seem like a computerized Choose Your Own Adventure book.
I can honestly say that I have had more fun playing an implementation of the original Oregon Trail on my crappy 5 year old phone than I have had with this game. It's too bad because I had high hopes for Orion Trail.

Textual Summary:
I really wish there was a "conflicted" mode on steam, because this game is great!
It's ascetic is pleasing, it's systems are simple but well executed and it has enough content to keep you playing for quite a few hours (see mine above). But it has two major flaws i find so big, that it drags the rest of the experience down with it.
Lets break it down.
Graphically the game isn't insane or amazing. The stylized graphics are mostly nice to look at in pastel coloring, but the low-poly citizens are not great with animations that are sub par. The various icons and UI though are spot on - no confusion at all and convey all they need at a glance.
Sound wise the game there is nothing remarkable about it, which often means that sound is okay....which is the case here as well. Sounds do the job and the options menu for
sounds is phenomenal.
Performance is fine, FPS sticks above 100 at all times on my system (GTX780) and can be capped if you so desire, though i've noticed no screen tearing to speak of.
But...it's a sim game, and those thrive on two things: Progressions and pacing, and here the flaws come in.
Progression wise the games goal is to last 50 "cycles", but the game doesn't allow progression to that point. By cycle 20, you are done with all your building / research options.
You can put the game on, mostly, auto-play and walk away until you win. This also ties into the Ore & Mining system with finite resources that you will run out of and be
unable to progress forward in your settlement.
While i'm sure the idea here is to force decisions on you, it makes for a sub par sim experience as you simply stop being able to do... anything.
Which ties into pacing.
The game throws you in, and lets you start rapidly building your bunker, you have to manage a dozen needs and requirements and juggle available materials everywhere.
The game shines at this point where you are forced to pick between a variety of food or a better leisure environment, or more babies or etc... pretty good.
but as soon as you stabilize around cycle 5... there is no further decision making, everything turns linear and only boils down to "how long before i run out of mining resources".
So i'm conflicted... the game starts great and has all the tools it needs... but then falls flat on it's face at the midway point.
Its got the EXTRA seal of approval.

I've played through the game 3 times now, working on my 4th. It is more challenging than one might expect from the demo and there are a lot of elements to keep an eye on and manage. I do wish there was more uniqueness to random events, and more enemies but I believe those will be coming with future updates. As of now, your dwellers get injured, sick, old and useless, young and useless, and can be killed by Molemen, the only direct enemy of the game. Your people also get significantly slower at completing objectives if you let certain necessities slack, food, air, water, and so forth. I'm finding it highly replayable. Each launch of the game you get a different starter bunker plus some uniqueness to what foods you start out with. I'm really looking forward to what this game will have to offer content wise with a few more updates.
The 'breeding' system is also rather interesting as in your peeps don't have babies but you can program in the kind of children you want in incubators, and any combination of job skills but at higher research point costs (which is the currency of the game).
Tips for a player just starting.
Get Researching Pronto
Get A Refinery Pronto and soon after a escavator on a ore deposit
Get a Kitchen/Sit n' Eat Place Pronto (you start with some food).
Next get Beds, showers, toliets and start to work on some Food Production.
Keep an eye on your critical resources like water/power/air and ensure you never get to critical points on these as it can be hard to fix them in time.

Life in Bunker is a strategy simulation game similar to the likes of Banished and Planetbase with a hint of Prison Architect thrown into the pot. LiB puts you in the role of Warden of a bunker right after the somewhat ambiguous events that have forced you underground (there is a little intro cutscene but it’s not clear what it actually shows). Starting with only the bare minimum you’ll need to quickly begin expansions in your bunker in order to meet the needs of your starting group of ten inhabitants. Your bunker’s habitants will of course need the basics such as oxygen, food and water but they’ll also need entertainment and ways of exercising in the bunker so they can stay happy and healthy. Meeting their needs is no easy feat though, you’ll often find yourself dangerously close to catastrophe!
Full Disclosure: A review copy was provided by the developers.
LiB’s low poly graphics look good and fit the game well, even on the game’s lowest graphics settings (though I’m not convinced that there is actually a difference between the different graphic presets, I certainly can’t tell if there is). The UI is well designed for the game and easy to navigate, particularly the building menus.
The aim of the game is to keep your bunker going for 50 cycles (500 years) at which point the massive bunker door will unlock and you’re humans can return to the surface, this is the game’s win condition. However, you don’t have to leave at this point and you can continue playing for as long as you like though the devs have said in the forums that they plan to add a proper endless mode to the game at some point soon. 50 cycles is the equivalent of around four generations which means that you’ll need a steady flow of new humans so that once your first ten inhabitants become too old to work you’re not left with a gaping hole in your work force. Luckily for you there’s an incubator which you can use to ‘grow’ humans, when they’re born they’ll be children but one cycle later they’ll be old enough to work. Every human has certain jobs that they are capable of doing and these are randomly chosen. However, you can spend research points to ensure that the babies will be capable of a specific job, more on research later.
The meat and potatoes of the game is designing and building your bunker. You’ll have to get your workers to clear the dirt and rock away so that you can use the game’s simple building system to set up everything your humans could ever need. All you have to do is mark what you want removed and your workers will get busy, the same applies to building, you simply decide where you want something and it’ll be built as soon as your workers are available. There are upgrades to improve the speed of destroying and building things too and these are unlocked using research points. Research points are earned by having a scientist at a research station (it’s worth mentioning you can have as many as you like) and they’ll earn you points over time which can then be spent on unlocking new objects or upgrading current ones/the capabilities of your workers. Sounds pretty easy so far, the real challenge comes from effectively managing your resources and planning ahead. You do start off with plenty of building materials and food but your supplies will be quickly depleted and so it’s incredibly important to set up ways of getting more of these very early on. While food is obviously very important, it’s actually a lot easier to run out of building materials just when you need them most. Life support objects require a huge amount of building materials and if you run out just when you need more life support you’re going to be well and truly stuffed, hence planning ahead for such situations is important. Anyway, you can get more building materials by using ore converters which will take the ore you mine from deposits and convert them into building materials. This is quite a slow process but thankfully the speed of the mining machine and the converter can be upgraded.
While the first level of your bunker is quite small and has few resources (unless you set the map size to large) you can expand your bunker vertically, not just horizontally. With four levels for you to work with you actually end up with a huge amount of space and, honestly, it’s rather daunting. That’s not to say it’s a bad thing, it most certainly isn’t, but expanding into a new level is pretty challenging and requires a lot of stored resources. Not only will you need a lift to the new level (requiring a lot of building materials), you’ll also need a power, oxygen and water supply for the level as you can’t build cables and pipes vertically and the lift is sealed so your oxygen won’t make it down either. Once you’re down on the level you will have a little bit of oxygen to work with but you’ll need to get those suppliers set up quickly if you want your workers to actually work and not just asphyxiate.
LiB may be focused on the building side of things but that doesn’t mean there’s not an element of danger in the game. As well as the obvious problems associated with running out of food or water, you’re also faced with cave-ins and molemen. I haven’t actually seen a human get killed or injured during a cave-in but I’d guess that if debris falls on top of them it won’t do them much good. Cave-ins can be prevented by building floors as when you build floors your workers also build ceilings which will prevent dirt and rocks from falling on you. Molemen appear to be mutated humans that have mole-like qualities. They’ll sometimes dig up into your bunker and start attacking your inhabitants, even kill them if they become overpowered by the molemen. Thankfully these pesky little so-and-so’s can also be stopped by building floors on top of the dirt floor as this will prevent them from digging up into your bunker. Your inhabitants can also get ill but as long as you have enough infirmaries to handle all of them (infirmaries are also staffed by scientists) these illnesses shouldn’t be too much cause for concern. Then again, there will sometimes be outbreaks of illness and disease which will put serious pressure on your infirmaries and not dealing with these outbreaks effectively can be fatal.
My main gripe with the game is how the AI works. Even if a bunch of stuff breaks down, putting the entire bunker at risk, the engineers will just carry on with their life until it’s their time to work. When there’s no food the cooks won’t bother cooking more until it’s their time to work etc. For the most part, this isn’t really an issue, but when these situations do arise it’s a huge problem and I’ve had this kind of thing lead to what is effectively a complete failure of the bunker, it’s pretty damn frustrating. The other problem with the AI, while less pressing, is more frequent, your inhabitants will often leave a job without finishing it. Seeing a worker walk from one side of the bunker to the other just to do 20% of a job is again, rather frustrating.
Life in Bunker is an enjoyable strategy simulation game that adds a new and interesting scenario to the city/colony building genre. Whether you’re incredibly good at these kinds of games or, like myself, you’re not too good at keeping fictional humans alive, you’re going to have fun with this game.

Awesomenauts is a combination of 2D platform/side-scroller with a MOBA (3v3), which creates an interesting combination that turns out as a very enjoyable experience for people who are fond of both genres. Like most 2D platforms,  the main mechanics are simple and it's very intuitive, which makes it easy to learn the basics of the game. It's also similar to 2D platforms in how fast-paced it is, and how much it values reaction times.  However, it also has some of the depth of MOBAs; there are several characters to choose (16 so far and counting), each one with 2 unique abilities and a different set of possible upgrades to choose for your builds and item routes. This combination results in a game that's simple yet fast and competitive.
In regards to some specific contents of the game:
The developers are active on this game, they produced 15 characters and 4 maps for the base game, plus microtransactions for skins (which doesn't have any impact on the gameplay itself). They'll be releasing an expansion now (currently on beta/early-access) and expand the game from that point on, so if you want to get access to all present and future features (which so far we know are extra characters, maps, spectator mode and custom-setting games), you'll want to buy both the base game and expansion, which is actually really cheap if you buy it on Steam sales or related stuff.
The balance of the game is not top-notch but it's pretty good regardless. New players might feel some characters are OP and whatnot, but once you get used to them you'll realise all of them are pretty much playable and none is "game-breaking".
There's a big "luck" factor in the game. Players are not forced to play a full game and teams aren't required to be full to start and continue games (which means you can find yourself alone with 2 bots in your team vs 3 human players, although this doesn't happen often). Players are allowed to leave a game (although they'll be punished by losing ranking points), this happens very frequently, specially on losing teams, which can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥for both teams (losing teams with bots frequently have no chance of winning, on the other side, you can be on a winning team and new players will join the game and make a comeback).  You don't know the map you'll be playing either, which is a problem because some characters have a bigger advantage on certain maps. You don't know what characters the enemy picked either. There's no separated queue for premades and solo players, which is also annoying for a lot of people.
The game netcode is p2p (so, no servers), this is annoying for a lot of players because you won't experience "input lag" (any actions you'll perform will be instantaneous in your screen), but you will experience a delay in actions of other players (basically you'll see that other enemies will hit you even when it looked like you were out of their attack/skill range). This means that you'll need to deduce the enemy intentions beforehand and estimate the true range of abilities and attacks on your screen based on the player's ping.
Finding full matches is not a problem, and there's a decent amount of players online at most hours, so don't worry about buying a dead game (at least not yet!). There are a lot of players who'll want to play with you and it's easy to make "queue buddies".
The pool of characters is not as huge as in LoL or DoTA, but all characters have clear differences and they're all fun to play. Character synergy and team-comps are very important and sometimes if you don't pick your character properly you'll find yourself with a team that is incompetent in teamfights or pushing.
All in all, I think awesomenauts is a great concept and a very enjoyable game, specially for it's price. It's far from being a masterpiece because of it's issues, but despite that, it's a great experience and you'll have lots of fun playing it, specially if you play with friends.

Do you want a game like Skyrim, but worse in every possible way? Do you want to waste time bribing every person in an entire world, for little reward? Are you a fan of bugs, no controller support, and random CTD instances?
Then come, play TESIV: Oblivion.
Seriously, without mods, this game is one of the least aesthetic adventure games I've played in a more than a decade(Read, dreadfully ugly. Like Fallout: NV ugly.). Even with mods, it crashes. It even crashes when you try to quit playing.
With mods, and mod managers, and help from the modding community, and many hours of set-up time. It's a fun game with a lot of interesting characters, quests, and things to find.
So, the steps to enjoy playing this game go:
1. Download game.
2. Spend hours figuring out how to mod it.
3. Test stability of mods
4. Play game.
5. Mod some more.
6. Finally, enjoy the game, until you feel like playing Skyrim. Then, go play Skyrim.
Or you could just save your money, and just play Skyrim. It's not like they didn't take some bits from this game, and reuse it in Skyrim anyway. Your choice. I recommend it for the story, and eventual enjoyment you can get from it after modding. If you aren't interested in modding. Play something else.

It's an evil, cruel world out there, and "Woodle Tree Adventures" opened my eyes to the reality of it all. You are born into a life of crime. From the day you are born, you are running around collecting debts owed to the family, being fruit, of course. If they can't pay up, then their tears will suffice. Sometimes you have to use force, because sometimes they fight back. Your only weapon is a leaf, but I swear I have yet to see a leaf capable of so much pain and destruction in all my years as this one, and I've seen a lot of leaves, my house has windows. All it takes is one fell swoop and any retaliator or rebel is vanquished. Sometimes innocent lives are lost as well, caught in the crossfire, however some live to complain and tell the tale and must be taken care of later. Their deaths are most tragic and graphic; they fall backwards as a sign of submission, then right after they give a little "squee" they burst into white flakes, completely vanishing from existance. Families will forever be torn apart, populations drastically affected by the murders, but you remain unphased. This is what you were meant to do, and you do it with a smile. I value the time I've spent playing "Woodle Tree Adventures", as it has shown me a side of this world that I would have never seen outside of my bubble. It not only immerses us in the hard life of crime, but has an underlying message of love for one's family and how far people or small tree creatures will go to do what is best for the family.

Well, despite the fact I have 101.9 hours playing this game on Steam, I am a veteran that played it almost 2-3 years, when it became F2P (yes, this game was once paid), stopped for a period of 5 years, and came back to play again. So my review will have lots of comparisons with the former years I've played.
Long story short: Actual state of the game is almost --dead--. No other word to define it. Few players (barely 60-70), counting with the newer players that come slowly in numbers. The peak number of players, I suppose, never reached 200 or maybe 250. You will understand that this number is important when you know the HUGE extension of map.
I will now point the most important details that will explain my veredict:
1. Features and Gameplay
Fallen Earth implements very nice features, specially in terms of crafting and item reuse in crafting, that means, sometimes you need a specific craftable item to craft a better one. So, you won't waste a ton of items just to grind th hell of your crafting skill and throw away all♥♥♥♥♥♥you built to the air as it wasn't important. It was (when there was a handful of players around), now it is NOT anymore.
Gameplay is still kinda robotic, with some need for grinding. Yeah, it is not a freaking grind, because there are plenty of missions, and most of them, are related OR with the linear storyline, or with a sidestory that reflects one specific situation, like, the reason of a decaying state of a city, per example. So you don't need to kill thousands of mutants to just earn levels. Just do the missions.
The need of teamwork only is vital on the last level (55) when you reach a region called Alpha County, where the mobs are very difficult to beat alone, specially if you're a full crafter. On some middle-level bosses there is also one need of teamwork, but mainly, after you reach 55. And it has no meaning because the missions in Aplha County give mostly chips (ingame money), experience (that you won't need as you've reached the cap) and, a few of those missions, faction reputation. So, in a basis, no one does those missions because there is no need to do so.
2. Missions
As I've said, the missions are quite well made, and have some history behind (some of them). But indeed they're very straightforward (kill x wolves, collect y materials, destroy z element). There are no puzzles, nothing that could difficult the conclusion of a mission except for one or another boss that has a big pool of health and so you need some friends to finish it. Apart from that, easy missions, nothing spectacular, nothing puzzling. Just normal missions that follows one sidestory or the main storyline.
The only exception are the Defense Towns, where there is a mission to maintain one player-built town (it has 4 in total in game) and, from time to time, a big raid distributed in various waves appear to storm this city. The mission asks you and the other players to defend the town and counter this raid. Remember teamwork? If you don't have it, you lose the city, the city that you and other players built, and can rebuild again if lose. Why that? What's the advantage? Resource nodes around the town, plenty of them appears depending on which buildings were constructed. Trust me, it worths.
3. Crafting
Here is the jewel of the game, and I really thumbs up for this. The game has a complex crafting system, where you have a wide range of melee weapons (hammers, pickaxes, slesgehammers and even a big bar with a 40kg weight), ranged weapons (pistols, revolvers, rifles, shotguns, rocket launchers), various armors and clothes, food and drink, buildings (generally temporary, except from Defense Town buildings), vehicles parts and vehicles assemble, live mounts (horses and wolves), medicine items, poisons, grenades, bombs. The variety is damn extensive, and everything has its purpose: help you against the dangers of the Wastes (including other players). Full crafters have some fun unlocking complex recipes and distribute the products for your clanmates or the open market (Auction house), and this is one thing Fallen Earth still maintains on a positive stats.
4. PvP
The PvP on this game has a freaking damn potential, because it is firmed in one thing: the Faction Wheel. First things first: on a determined level, you need to choose a faction. There are six, i won't go into details, but if you choose one, you start to build some reputation with the faction (throught certain missions) you chose mainly, and with two other factions on a lower basis. On the other side, the other three becomes your enemies (your reputation with them diminshes on the same amount you earn for your faction and allies).
Inside the huge territory of FE, there are PvP areas with outposts or keeps, where a faction that takes control of that keep, rules the area, and has some benefits, including special resource nodes and the option to lay down harvesters (resource drillers). When the game had a big amount of active players (5 years ago), the fight for power was so imense AND insane, that keeps and fortresses normally were conquered and reconquered within one or two hours (counting that it has 45 minutes of immunity after it is capped).
The actual state of PvP is ♥♥♥♥♥♥, because there are not enough players to maintain an all-out war or a domination war over the PvP areas. You even find one or other flag caps, but nothing near the PvP state of 5 years ago.
5. The company (Gamers First)
I could say a bunch of bad things about G1, because, there are mostly only bad things about them related to FE. Suffice to say, when G1 bought FE from Reloaded Productions/Icarus Studios and changed the business model to F2P, a massive number of players quit the game on the next weeks, they knew what exactly would happen with the game, even with the fact Reloaded team would keep working on the game changes and new expansions. G1's legacy in turn one succesful game in♥♥♥♥♥♥is long and bold. Just ask the players of APB: Reloaded how the game is now. FE isn't an exception: the only news we, FE players, see are the Subscribers Rewards every month, mostly. Fallen Earth became, for G1, another reasonable source of money from subs, veteran players who still manage to like the game despite the lack of improvement over the years (only one new map expansion, a few new vehicles and gear and a new PvE coop mode called The Dome, all this in 5 years ... FIVE YEARS!!!!). What I could say to G1?? Follow the example of Keen Software House and "Space Engineers" game title. One update every week, either bug fixings or new improvements, EVERY WEEK FOR BLESSED 1 and 1/2 YEARS!!
Conclusion
I'd say, if you want one good experience of free open world game, you can even try Fallen Earth. It is a nice experience. You can still get addicted, but BE SURE that the end game, from the day of that review, is frustrating. To be very honest, the word that resumes all my experience from 5 years ago and now is this:
. But well, I have friends on this game, so that's why I still play. And the game has some nice features (thanks to Icarus Studios) I do study to develop something similar, so that's why I play. But, after all, considering the whole product and its actual state, I do NOT recommend the game.

I love this game. I've been an MMO person for a long time and then in Wildstar I got hooked on building. I guess these types of games just became a natural progression from there. I tried Citadel first and was quite put off by how unfinished it is (it was my first early access). A friend played this and convinced me to give it a go. I have no idea what all the bad reviews are about (minus people B&M the PVP system).
We went on a PVE server. Honestly, the game can be challenging enough without having people come up and gank you, destroy your house and more. Why you'd do PvP in this is beyond me. The first thing the community will tell you is this: are you going to die, you are going to lose all your things. And it's true. The critters try to kill you, the NPC exile's try to kill, the damn weather tries to kill you. And through it all,  you farm,  you craft and you build your first house. And then your second...and probably a third. Maybe some shanties for safe havens in areas you grind a lot.
There is some sort of story. Obviously this game is still eary access and so that part is very much in development. But there are secret recipes to learn, lore to uncover and its much more comprehensive that I would have imagined to even start. There's group content, and soloable content. The game is still developing and bits and pieces are still falling in place.
The crafting is pretty well thought of in my opinion, and there's every type. The introduction of thrulls (slaves) adds an extra element I haven't seen in games and gives you something extra to farm.
The building works mostly well. The floors/walls/ceilings/roofs are all on a snap system, which can be really annoying if you're not used to it. It still has a few bugs and quirks, but again, they're fixing it. I do hope we get more decor pieces to fill the monstrosities I like to build, but all in time I hope.  Everything is climable. Even other people's houses (sometimes to your own detriment if they have attack thrulls).
Each zone has it's own unique weather, which may also try to kill you, ala sand storms in the desert. In the desert you can overheat (thus needing to drink more water) and even get heatstroke (and gradually die). The frozen area freezes you and can give you frost bite and...kill you. Wear the right gear to the right zone, take the right food and drink (because you can starve and die of dehydration).
You can level either by fighting and killing mobs (some people say this is the quickest) or by farming mats and crafting/building. I didn't really notice that big of a difference in either method. Overall, if you like to grind, build and fight for your survival, this is a pretty awesome game. The graphics are the best I've seen these games, and it's continually improving.

After all the 8-9 ish years I've played it, Audition Online  is a great game!  Years ago, at first when I tried it, it took a long time to get used to, but I cant stress this enough.Try to explore all the modes! I didnt do so hot in some modes but I really excel in others! The mode most similar to DDR is Beat Up and Block Beat! The most most similar to Guitar Hero/ Rockband is the Guitar Mode (of course)! If you would like to enhance your gameplay (with 8k,C9 and beat up for example), you will need a numpad.The game really varies more than the normal mode you see upon the tutorial (in my opinion it's outdated and could use an upgrade to go over all the other modes). .You can look at a glimpse of them with the video provided. You can see how to play modes in depth (just a mini guide) by pressing f12 in the game room.
Community: As far as the community goes , it's nice!  The age range is about ages 16-20.  In-game, most high levels would seem intimidating to approach at first, but they are willing to lend a helping hand if you need to (like myself xD) ! You see familiar faces if you stick around for a bit! There are times where the game would show more locked rooms than unlocked but it depends on the times you're on. I know most players are fluent in English (the most prominent) but a few circles do speak fluent Spanish,German, Viet and Portugese which I learned quite a bit for my language skills LOL. You can also join FAMs and play in FAM battles together which is nice .There are suspicions of people hacking but the hacking doesn't occur as often as it used to be with Nexon. A huge huge majority of the population has leveled up on their own without the usage of hacks and bots. Any that were caught doing so have been banned. If there are any suspicions of hacks it would be done privately and submitted in a ticket.
Music: If you're into different styles well be prepared because there are a lot of them. The genres do vary but expect to hear Korean and Spanish. And it's not really all one list for every mode you play. Some modes like ballroom will have its own set of songs and guitar mode will as well. I find that songs suitable to fit the types of modes is a well thought out process instead of sitcking to 1 list for everything.
Game Currency:  BEATS are rather difficult to acquire when you don't have a ring/garden to work with. You would have to depend on Battle Parties which are fun but they're time consuming before you can spend your beats in mall on the higher items.  Time it would take to get 1,000,000 beats in battle party would take about 30 min - an hour depending on the amount you choose. With a couple ring and doing garden, you can get around 2-3 million beats in a day without having to play any games. Another thing I like about it is you can get coupons for your CASH items at anytime using time box.
Tournaments: As far as tournaments go, most of them start but there are a few that dont due to the lack of players entering the tournament that day. The current number required for a tournament to start should be fixed. That's really my only issue I've had with the game.
There is a forum website :
that players can communicate on about the inner workings of the game if an error occurs,  BANA CASH from GM and player hosted events and a graphics/drawings to show your creative side!
TIP: To run Audition in windows mode, you'll have to download the original client for now or try downloading the Audition Xpatcher
and click run Audition. Its always been the alternative patch to the original one for a few years now. Surely its not through steam, but it will save you time having to redownload the original redbana site patcher until they make a windowed mode for steam.

I have no interest or knowledge about MOBAs like DOTA or LoL, but I decided to give Awesomenauts a shot because it's in 2D, has a colorful art style, and a catchy Saturday morning cartoon style introduction (which sadly has been taken out in the newest patch). Much to my surprise, the game play reminds me a lot of the greatest fighting game of all time ST more than anything else, because it demonstrates  the two concepts "playing to win" and "easy to play, hard to master" better than almost every other multiplayer game I've ever played. Awesomenauts rewards the smarter and more skilled players and teaches players to improve through harsh defeat like 90's games rather than coddle them with gimmicky comeback mechanics as many other modern games do. The core mechanics are simple and it's easy to start having fun immediately regardless of experience however, to excel in this game you must master the fundamental fighting game concepts like footsies, zoning, spacing, timing, matchup knowledge, yomi, baiting, etc. The roster is extremely varied with all sorts of unique abilities and upgrades, yet it remains one of the most balanced multiplayer games around, while a few characters are far more powerful than others, every character has their own unique insanely powerful tools so no character is weak orsese rely handicapped. Modern fighting games should take balance patching notes from Ronimo.
The only negatives I can think of is the community itself which seems to unfortunately consist of a large number of immature and selfish gamers who rage quit the very second a game is not going in their favor or those who taunt excessively all game. The amount of rage quitters in this game far outnumbers that of any other competitive community I've been a part of, I'd say the majority of the game I join have at least one player rage quit which isn't just running the fun of competition, but more importantly screws your teammates, because the is a team game needing cooperation to work.
In short, buy this game now if you like competitive games that force you to think on your feet while remaining accessible.

The Shadow Warrior Redux pack is more or less what this game has needed for a long time: A working Source Port. It was fairly difficult to get this game working with things like DosBox, and this comes as a blessing (Though SW may have been playable ith eDuke). For those familiar with Duke Nukem 3D, Shadow Warrior is more or less the same, but with a new comic target: Asian Movies and Pop Culture. This includes numerous references to John Woo movies, martial arts films, and making fun of "generic Asian accent". It's crude humor and it might come off as offensive or politically incorrect, but I think that simply strengthens the humor from a time when that kind of stuff was funny and people didn't get too riled up about it.
The action in the game is pretty good, starting you off with a kitana (sword) and a bad guy to slice and dice. Unlike a lot of FPS shooters that relied on 2D 'sprites' for animations, the enemies in this game have different animations for the different ways they can be dispatched. Slash them with a sword, and they'll fall into pieces. Shoot them and they fall, or shoo them in the throat and watch them choak on their own blood before falling down. And of course, explosives cause enemies to blow into lots of red chunks. The weapons are varied and entertaining, with special mention to the sword. You cana lso dual-wield Uzis ("Be proud, Mr. Woo!"), sticky bombs, bodily organs, and a nuke launcher to boot.
Level wise, there are some creative puzzles and a lot of effects that pushed the aging build engine too its limit. This includes vehicles that can be driven, turrets, boats, remote control cars, and a surplus of new kinds of traps. Many of the levels seem to be set in dojos or cities, and the enemy variety isn't massive. The game has old school boss opponents, but they aren't much to note. Levels are wide open and offer for plenty of exploration on the side to find hidden weapons and power-ups, and with the enemies that do exist, encounters are varied enough and can offer some fun shootouts (or blow-outs).
Get it if you're looking for some fun violence to partake in. I hear multiplayer is coming soon, probably once the glitches with DN3D's Megaton Edition MP issues are cranked out.

This is one of Paradox's better games. It doesn't drown in its own complexity, and because of this, it doesn't suffer as much from the developer's usual weakness: explaining the game to the player.
Fortunately, Crusader Kings 2 is streamlined enough (by paradox standards) to be enjoyable without having to strain your eyes too much looking for the game beneath all the 'complexity'. The game is well designed and the UI makes all the swaths of information even pleasant to interact with.
I would only warn some potential buyers that this is a game focused on the characters. You don't play as the kingdoms or countries themselves, you play as a person who is trying to advance the power and prestige of their family. As the years pass you will take over your successor in your dynasty and continue playing until your dynasty falls from power completely or you're just done with the game. The biggest focus of the gameplay is manipulating people's opinion of you and of each other.

If you're looking for a funny, entertaining, space homage to Oregon Trail, this is your game. It is punishing at times, with a heavy RNG component, but your strategy will make a difference, and it is a hell of a lot of fun to play.
------------------------

The random encounters are witty and full of sci-fi references, which I love. I normally hold back from early access games, but I am glad to be part of the growth and evolution of this one.
I will update this review as the game progresses. At this point, I'd say: if you want to be active part of the development, and like the style and the concept, this is a perfect time to join in. If having little play content and some balance issues bothers you, perhaps sit back, keep an eye on the forums, and see how things evolve.
Update 1: after the first game update, I can already tell that the game feels far more solid. There is more content, everything feels far more balanced, and some of the ideas discussed in the forums have been implemented. Things are looking really good!
Update 2: after the last two updates, the game has noticeably more content. It feels much deeper and more replayable, and the addition of longer missions and extra encounters also up the challenge and the need to play more strategically, rather than relying on luck. I'm very happy with all the additions so far!

I went into this game with apprehension. I had head good things and bad things. Some had said that it resembled the mobile game model I had come to hate over time, and others compared it to Destiny, a game which I had previously enjoyed. Upon starting the game, I came to realize that Warframe could not be simplified down to such basic descriptions. Warframe manages to be a free to play title that feels worthy of a $60 price tag. It just works. The movement system sets it apart from many of its competitors, and the progression system feels rewarding. You can play the game as you see fit. Are you a primarily solo player like myself? You can play solo. Do you prefer groups? You can do that too. From my limited time playing, I can say that the community is a friendly place. People seem nice, and the majority of the game is cooperative and not competitive which helps to facilitate a constructive atmosphere. Once you get a handle on the game's many systems, this game offers hundreds if not thousands of hours of enjoyment. The developers are constantly adding and tweaking the game to make the most enjoyable experience possible. I was surprised to see the almost daily hotfixes released. The best part of all of this is that you don't have to pay a cent for anything. Even the premium currency can be easily obtained by trading with other players, although if you enjoy the game as much as I have, you will be tempted to skip this step and just buy the currency to help support the devs.
The only parts of the experience that I feel could be improved would be the limited number of weapons and warframes that you can have without spending the premium currecy for inventory expansions, and the rather hands off approach to letting players in. New players will be hit with a bit of a sensory overload, especially in the market. But will a few days of practice, its easy to settle in and enjoy the game.
At the very least, the game is free. There's no reason not to try it and see what you think.

Good game, solid sneaky/shooty gameplay. You start out with basic weapons and armour, an objective (investigate the crash of a flight of army helicopters) and not much else. You will progress through a mix of upgrading your equipment (costs money and/or time) and completing missions which then unlocks more missions and other options.
You may consider playing Stalker: Shadow of Chernobyl first. CoP is bigger and more open and has a better interface. SoC is scarier and more atmospheric. It has a gentler introduction to the basic gameplay mechanics and the story of how the exclusion zone around the Chernobyl Power plant became much weirder and more dangerous than it is today.
You will have to collect many different artifacts from the dangerous anomalies that dot the landscape. You can then equip them to protect against specific dangers, but usually they also weakens you in some way, e.g. some emit radiation.
Tip: you can get much more for excess artifacts if you are patient and don't sell them to Owl, the trader up the stairs in the beached ship Skadovsk. Instead collect a good variety of artifacts and go to Beard, the bartender at the entrance of the ship. Beard will give you a choice of three artifacts to get for a customer. Choose one already in your possesion and you get a huge bonus.
Graphics wont blow you away, but the desolate marshy ukrainean landscape is well depicted. Some of the anomalies are really spooky, my favorite is the Oakpine, 4-5 trees that grow together into a dome over a small canyon.
Recommend you get the SoC Complete mod, this enhances Graphics, make the weather more varied and adds a cheat-menu. Breaks savegames unfortunately, so install it before your first game. Only use the cheat-menu to teleport.

It's a shallow platformer that's not very worthy to begin with before you add in floaty controls, unnecessary enemy knockback, jumps that require perfect placement or a large portion of the level must be replayed (only up to LEVEL 8, remember), backtracking through said tedious jumps because the coins you're required to collect are on 2 different paths, constantly changing objectives (one level you're collecting coins, the next they're just a bonus while you're defusing bombs, the next is just grab all chests), a bad HUD (health "bar" is a shrinking heart icon with no indicator of actual HP #'s and the timer is just a color-changing line), and pointless mechanics (losing your health just respawns you, why have timed levels, and the enemies are just roadblocks that respawn if jumped on).
When it gets down to it, Canyon Capers is just jumping, collecting different items in linear levels, and occasionally more jumping on "baddies" that get in your way. That's it. If that's what you enjoy, fire up some NES classics and play something from the good old days that's still good. Not this.

Oblivion graphics, animations, combat, magic, voice acting, random conversations, fx, etc. etc. are very old. Many things can be improved with mods, but getting all the old mods to work together can be frustrating in itself. Steam wasn't around when the game came out and that can be a hurdle when dealing with certain mods/tools as well.
Voice acting when dealing with certain KEY characters is great, but standard npc use the same voice types over and over. Lack of voice variation is the biggest issue that stands in the way of immersion, and sadly cannot be fixed with mods.
Dungeon design is generally repetitive to a fault, but town architecture is unique and there are good town mods that make them even better.
The main quest isn't compelling and it drags on for what seems like an eternity. However, side quests can be quite fun -- especially the Dark Brotherhood questline. I also found the individual mage guild quests to be rather inventive.
Spell fx are again, dated and poor, but there are a lot of good spells to use in this game. The alchemy system is fairly straight forward and I like it well enough.
If like older, open-world games, or are just a Bethesda game fan, you might try Morrowind instead. If you go for Oblivion, you will likely need to spend a couple days hunting down mods before you ever get to play. If you only like the newest, most cutting edge games, this game will just annoy you.
Wait for this game to go on sale, or go out and get it used on CD. The GOTY edition was $9 during Christmas.

I would definitely recommend this game. The only thing you have to know is that it's not a conventional game. It's more like a surreal interactive storytelling experience.
We start the game with the objective of delivering something (we don't know what) to someone (we don't know who). The only problem is that we are lost and that we need to find the "Zero". So basically, the desire line of the game is about finding a way. And we soon realize that the objective is not about the delivery anymore, but just about finding ways. And you have to agree to wander off with the people that you meet on the road in order to find your way again. And it gets very strange.
This game is interesting because of the advanced narrative, the master storytelling and the unique experience that it provides. It is beautiful visually, yet very simple. The soundtrack creates a warm and dreamy atmosphere.
You will definitely get caught in the universe of this game.
I'm not a hardcore gamer and when I play to a game, it's not about performance or achievements. It's about storytelling, visuals and characters. I like to be part of something different than my own reality. And this game is all about that, so I was very pleased.
I can't wait for the next episodes to come out!
PRO:
- We meet characters and we feel like we really share an adventure with them.
CON:
- Our choices never seem to have real consequences on the game, other than building our own perception of what we're doing (which I guess is the point of the game). So far, we have the feeling that we are progressing, but we don't know if it's towards a resolution, because the mystery only gets thicker. And I wonder how it will unfold. The risk with a surreal narrative is that an abstract adventure could lead to an abstract conclusion. But there is no need to speculate as the rest of the game is yet to be released!
And I am definitely hooked. 9/10

I've been a player of the game for about 8-9 years. (yes this game is that old(er) ) As I read a lot of the reviews below me, I've seen that many of the reviewers had come into the game with their mindset thinking that this was supposed to be DDR Online, or an OSU competitor. I can honestly tell you that this game is neither.
Audition Online is a heavy rhythm based online dancing game with heavy social aspects. Originally made in Korea, the game has very heavy K-pop culture references (fashion mall/ K pop dance moves), and many Korean songs. If you are annoyed by pop, electronic, or music that is in a foreign language, you most likely will pass on the game. There are enough English songs to pass for an American server, but a vast majority of songs are in Korean.
As said above, the Korean culture for the game is quite immense. The fashion mall (cash shop) is full of Korean Pop star references and clothing that would mostly make sense to the Kpop audience. The cash shop is completely optional. NOTHING in the cash shop will enhance your skills to the point of unfairness. There is a non-cash currency. (beats). These beats can be earned by playing with other players in the server. The selection of Beats items is quite small compared to the cash items, but there is enough to satisfy one's fashion sense to an extent.
The Gameplay for Audition is very different from DDR or OSU online. This is something that many new players fail to understand when they write the game off as a DDR clone. Players are given a combination of arrow keys that correspond to the 4 directional keys on the keyboard or the numpad, and must press those keys within the 4/4 metronome displayed, and then hit the space key once the bar reaches the 4/4 on the metronome. The metronome's speed is determined by each songs BPM. Often new players assume that they are really button mashing, but every arrow key combination is attached to a certain dance move. The fact is that this is just ONE of Audition's many different game modes.
Audition has roughly over 10 UNIQUE game modes, with about 15-20 different variations of certain game modes. Each mode has a different concept, a different way to play, and win. Some are team games, some are solo (story mode), and some are social modes (wedding, love party, club). I'd advise the DDR fans to start off with Beat Up mode which utilizes the players numpads using the keys (741/963) as the keys are tapped in direct relation to the rhythm, unlike "Normal Mode" where only key combinations are pressed followed by the space bar at each fourth beat.
The game has a VERY steep learning curve. If you are prone to quitting easily, or not interested in taking the time to learn the different modes, I'd not recommend the game to you.  The game is currently in need of new players and a revitalization in its community. However, if you'd like to try something different, make some new friends, and even improve your playing skills. Look for me in game at ~KentyGaga~ There's so much more that I can't even bother to explain so I look forward to hearing from you!

I've been playing Audition on and off since 2007 when it was released in NA. (The original Korean version is over 10 years old now!)
It hasn't aged well, and the lack of settings (in-game and out) is a pretty big issue which is unlikely to ever be addressed, unfortunately. You don't play Audition, Audition plays you! Oh, but if you're looking for the in-game volume settings, press ctrl + S when you're in game. Solves everything, right? No???
I don't want to make this too long winded, so in short:
- If you like rhythm games definitely do give it a try, there are a lot of modes so there's bound to be something for you
- The learning curve is steep and the in-game tutorial isn't great. It's frustrating, and you have to be prepared for that
- On a similar note, it's extremely difficult to master, so you're constantly able to challenge yourself (...and others)
- Do not play alone!! Audition is a social game, plus being a noob on your own is not fun and will probably make you quit
- Despite being free to play it does obviously have a cash shop, but you can play 99% of the game no problem without ever spending anything. Most of the benefits of the cash shop are only cosmetic. The rest won't matter to you unless you get really into the game
I'm not going to lie and say Audition is a perfect game because it most certainly is not. But if you enjoy rhythm games and you are looking for something new I do recommend trying it!
P.S. My IGN is Inazuma!

After a month of playing CE, my overall conclusion is that the game has great promise, but right now (after nine months of early access) it is NOWHERE NEAR READY for launch.
The game has great potential. Good survival mechanics, good building mechanics, a workable combat system, and a reasonably good evocation of R.E.Howard's sword-and-sorcerey fantasy world. The mod and private server options are very nice also.
However, it has many problems that SHOULD have been addressed in the last nine months of early access. These include:
- Almost useless chat: it's full of bugs and limitations, and can't be seen at all while crafting, building, or even while looking at your inventory. MMORPG players will scream in frustration.
- Frequent lock-ups and total machine crashes. You may have to turn off your entire PC, and restart it it, to recover.
- Animation in combat is badly borked. Animals will "flip" rotate toward you, like 1980s sprites, at various points in a battle. As a result, you can and will get killed by lag, or unpredictable enemy movement. Action combat gamers will scream in frustration.
- Various server side bugs, which can crash a server, have work-arounds that radically change the game. For example, dropping everything you carry on death will crash servers, so for months characters have dropped nothing on death. This might be good or bad, but compared to the original intent, it's definitely an unsolved bug.
I could go on and on. Worse, Funcom has had a lot of financial ups and downs in the last year. Given their problems, this game might NEVER get that much better. If you're on the fence, my advice is to wait until it exits Early Access and becomes a formal launch.
