While the game play and graphics are indeed "out-dated", I feel as if that's the beauty of Audition. All of the current ~popular~ games feel much too flashy at times, and Audition, for a lot of people, is a childhood game that brings back nostalgia, whether or not you've played it before. Usually good old-fashioned games like these die out and it's really disheartening to not be able to play again. I've been a on and off player since 2007 and I've noticed that a vast majority of those that "quit" usually make their way back to this game in some way or another.
Audition is comfortable yet challenging, and it's barely overwhelming despite the amount of time it takes to become decent at this game. Although more updates to the game regarding patches (songs, items, etc) would be nice, I believe the current graphics and modes are one of the positive aspects about Audition.

A Battle Brothers-lite historical tactical RPG. You must pick up the many broken pieces of your Viking clan left by your recently dead father by being as blood-thirsty or as peaceful as you like.  Strengthen bonds, build bridges, or scorch the earth before the building even begins. There are many ways to tackle many different scenarios. It all depends on how you build your character and your Hird (party). Each party member has personality traits that you must take under consideration when making decisions, and will gain or lose morale accordingly. Manage your home base and choose upgrades leaning towards either power or prosperity, and decide the fate of the many moving parts that make up your clan.
Battles are standard turn based rpg fare with a few twists to make it interesting. All characters have both movement and attack actions. Any character can go in any order and you can keep switching between them until they run out of attack and movement actions.  This allows for excellent battle strategy in creating flanks and exposing the enemy out into the open. However, the same applies to the enemy.
In battles, when one of your members hp reaches zero, they become incapacitated, and will no longer be able to act in combat (unless revived). Once a character becomes incapacitated they will recieve an injury that can only be healed by resting at one of the many camps on the overworld map. Each camp has different levels of security, food, and shelter, and some might even be occupied, requiring you to clear it out before you can use it.  When you camp, each member of your hird is required to take on 4 shifts in which they can either scout, guard, sleep, hunt, eat, craft items, or heal injuries.  All of these skills are available to both yourself and your party members and can and should be improved as you progress through the game.
The plot and set pieces are very well presented, and there are quite a few conversation options that can depend on the stats or skills you pick, resulting in a unique experience each time through the game.
Highly recommend.

Great Game!
Expeditions: Viking is an Party-based RPG, combat happens in turns - if you are looking for similar games think of Baldur's Gate, Pillars of Eternity, Tyranny or Divinity: Original Sin.
When the game starts, your main character has just been named Thegn (Viking tribe leader) of his Clan and is faced with many dangers and many enemies, trying to get rid of him and take over his clan and his village.
So you have to assemble a crew, build a longship and sail from denmark across the north sea to plunder england - or maybe craft an alliance with the Kings there?
The game manages to create the same atmosphere as the Vikings-TV series. Hard warriors, intrigues, plunder, betrayal old and new gods and combat, combat, combat.
Here is one of the few problems of the game: at the beginning, you will lose many fights. Exp. Vikings is not an easy game, it is demanding and you have to accept defeats in order to grow stronger. Your characters level up, get more skills, better equipment (all kinds of weapons, armor etc.) and after some hard hours of learning how to win, your party will finally be able to go on a big expeditions.
The number of skills could have been bigger, they could be more varied but still, combats are fun!
Also, there is a Meta-Game. You travel around a world map and can get and solve quests from and for NPCs in several places (like cities, woods etc.) on the map. There are also campsites, where you can send your party for hunting or let them craft new weapons (both done automatically).
So why is this not just an average game? Because Expeditions Viking manages to create a dense atmosphere with a old-school kind of presentation. Almost no voice overs, no cutscences but good dialogues, really great music and a fine artstyle.
Give it a chance, if you into games like Pillars, Wasteland, Baldur's Gate and so on - it is a true gem!

Woodle Tree Adventures is a fun little platformer with cute graphics and easy-to-learn gameplay mechanics. It is very simple to pick up and learn, and even a child can do it. You can even upgrade your weapon by "farming" the pickups, so you can farm the easiest ones to get to if you are having trouble and want to get an upgrade.
It's a big plus that you are given unlimited "lives" and even if you die or fall off, you don't lose any progress in the level (except going back a bit geographically). All enemies vanquished stay gone, you keep any pickups and fairy tears you got on that level, and you are not penalized other than a bit of forward progress. That's a great thing that ensures the game can challenge you without becoming frustrating or problematic.
So far, I've only played (and beaten) the first level, and it's been very fun. I'd compare it to a simpler Super Mario 64 with smoother graphics. The camera can be a bit awkward and you cannot rotate it (the game handles that automatically) but you can zoom in and out as you desire. If you like 3D platformers with simple controls and easy-to-understand mechanics, you'll probably like this game.
It even comes with Steam trading cards, so if you pick it up cheap on sale you can recoup part or most of your investment and basically play it for free.
Overall, this is a very fun game and even at full price is a very fair deal.

Just finished classic mode with a playthrough with my wife and this is getting voted in my top 5 games of all time, and certainly game of the year so far. Up there with Portal 2.
This is a return to classic gaming. I cannot stress this enough, it's what we have been missing. A story, an experience, something that made you feel something like the high feeling leaving the movies when you were a kid. It's done right, the creators knew what they were trying to achieve and they gave the player what they needed with love, care and attention to detail. It has the classic hallmarks of this, a well defined editor for community content, a support structure that emphasised community and contribution, all voice acted (and well) humour, some feeling, head scratching puzzles, beautiful scenery, deep storylines, valid and important choices that impact your game, but still a flexibility to play it the way you want to play, and a brave multiplayer element that we've craved for in this type of gaming.
Nothing is without fault, but what fault there is is a compromise in places, between challenge, depth and replayability and the ultimate design of the game. Some of the puzzles or quests involved being VERY careful with your eyes and mouse, one particular one was a book to open a door. The endgame was particularly uncompromising also, especially the difference in "decisions".
I'm yet to explore the GM mode, but I principally bought it for that and saw the storyline campaign as a minor attraction. That was an underestimation on my part. There will be great things coming from this engine, it is a winning formula.
I sigh slightly at those that found it overly difficult or tedious. In a world of instant gratification, this was a mature and brave retake on gaming. I mean that sincerely, we have challenging play at several levels. I feel sorry for those folk that can't persist through this to experience the game's delights. It took some doing to get the game to run at all, though there's information in the Discussions that can help you. Essentially, the game doesn't create its own (long, complex) configuration file, so you have to do it manually or the game will crash before it even gets started.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 scratched an itch I never knew I had. I've never play DnD for more than a couple sessions and never took in any interest in tabletop style RPGs, but after playing this, I will be keeping my eyes to the horizon.
TL;DR-Game is great with how it lets you approach different scenarios different ways and crafts its world.  I think its replayabilty is harmed but not broken by giving too much player freedom with builds.  Certain abilities feel imbalanced and by bring down the experience.  Coop doesn't necessarily meld well with certain non-combat systems in the game but is still a blast.
Imo, the Strength of Divinity lies in the way it allows you to tackle scenarios in your own manner.  I feel like that is a common pitch for videogames nowadays but Divinity has a real claim to this idea.  You can control up to four characters to make up a party and specialize them to what your team needs.  You might choose to do a combat heavy team (who wouldn't for their first run) and have combo amongsts your group that you can use to prep for a fight (have your fire mage light the ground on fire and then have your Summoner create a pet in it to grant them fire damage.) Or maybe you want to rely more on the social aspects of to beat the game.  You can pump a characters points into Persuasion and then heavily comb over the environment and NPCs for advice for how resolve manners in a more diplomatic manner.
The world feels very much alive with how many tiny little interconnected narratives can take place in a town.  It grants the player a lot of leverage in choosing what interests them the most from a collection of events going on around them.  NPCs will react to your race very often as well granting a lot of life to the game as you take in ambient information regarding the story and lore of the universe that Larian Studios as set off to create.
As for negatives, I feel that the character might level up too frequently ( or maybe there just needs to be great stat sinks in the Combat Abilities.) As it is now I feel that my characters are starting to 'max' out on their core are given room to expand into other Abilites.  This is cool because it allows you to mix Abilities of different schools but with such a surplus of points I feel like my characters are starting to overlap in utility.  Based on the levels of what I'm facing versus my own level, I can say with high confidence that I am not overleveled, this is just an issue of the currenty system maybe granting too much liberty to the player.  Having up to 4 characters means you explore much of the game's magic system in one playthrough if you are the least bit explorative with it.  *MINOR GAMEPLAY SPOILER START* Another thing that exasperates this issue is the free respecs you get not too far into the game.  While allowing freedom to the player in building their character is generally good, I think this went to far as now you can literally experience all you have access to not to mention their is always this slight nagging feeling in the back of your mind whenever you get an armor piece with a stat you need for a utility but don't need surpluss for.  For instance,  youwant Hydrosophist 1 so you can cast Rain but for nothing else.  Get Hydrosophist +1 from a new armor piece.  Now you point you have invested is wasted or you warp to the respec area and spend like 30 seconds fixing your build up.  Do it again if you replace that armor with something that doesn't have Hydro. It may not seem like much but with 4 characters constantly getting loot, the nuisance is bound to become apparent to many. *MINOR GAMEPLAY SPOILER END*
Another issue I have is balance.  Now I have not done a rigorous amount of testing, theory or otherwise, but I feel as though thieving and lucky charm stand tall compared to the other Civil abilites for the sheer value in money they generate and consequently how much more they will open up builds for characters since you can afford to buy all the skillbooks you could want.  In contrast, Persuasion can get you to bypass certain scenarios, but you are often robbed of exp when you do this and while maybe your aim is to never commit to combat, the persuasion doesn't always allow skirt around it due to the lack of transparency to the system.  Persuasion works in a Fallout style stat check.  For instance, you may want to convince someone to let you pass them.  The dialogue options may list [Finesse], [Wits], and [Memory].  From what I can tell, selecting an option will weigh your corresponding stat and persuasion.  The issue here is that your groups 'Persuader' might not be invested very much in the correct stats in order to succeed, and failing the check will cause you to enter combat meaning that even having 2 'Persuaders' of different stat allocation is not enough since they will all be engaged in combat.
As for balance in combat itself, Summoning is the standout to me in being too strong.  On papers sacrafice their own individual power so that they can invest in the creation of a Summon(s) for later turns.  These reason this feels imbalanced is two-fold.  1. If you ever suspect that a fight is about to start, say you see explicitly labeled enemies ahead of you or you are about to end dialogue on an aggressive note with one your other characters, your summoner can actually summon their Incarnate and jack them up with buffs before the fight has even started.  This frees up the summoner to focus on creating secondary things like buffs or direct damage while already having a powerful ally on the battlefield.  2. Summoning is not limited to a single element of damage.  This doesn't matter so much earlier on but later, certain enemies will be immune to certain damage types or even heal off of it.  Inversely, they can be ridiculously vulnerable to elements as well but due to certain skills that Summoner has access to, they can effectively always have the upper hand while a Pyrokinetic mage might just be useless in certain fights.
Lastly, coop is a mixed bag.  Being able to party up and work togethor or split apart and try to ruin each other but certain systems crack when you have two people playing.  For instance, if one player pickpockets an NPC, the NPC will eventually notice and ask the nearest player character if they can check their stuff.  This alone is not so bad because if the innocent player allows themself to be checked, everything will be alright.  The real issue is if the innocent player is finishing unique dialogue with another NPC; the NPC who was stolen from will interrupt the quest dialogue to do their check and the innocent player can no longer hear the dialogue as the NPC will just revert to their normal lines.  Another example is that when a quest is finished, the one who turns it in gets to choose and receive the quest rewards.  The others players do not even get to look at the choices and could've been the ones to do all the work.  The civil abilites also play against a coop session as well.  Lucky charm makes it so that whenever a container is looted, their a chance for extra loot but only on the first check of the container and only if it's done by the character with the stat.  This means that in a sense, the most efficient way to use this stat is to have ONE character look EVERYTHING.  Not bad if you're running the whole group but if you're cooping, it can really suck not getting to loot.  It's the same issue with Persuasion and talking to NPCs, you might lose out if you don't have your dedicated smooth-talker initiating every conversation.
Despite all the flaws I brought up, this is the most fun I've had playing a videogame in awhile.  I never though tabletop RPGs like this looked all that fun so if you don't currently, I insist you give this a go, play for just under 2 hours within 2 weeks of buying it and if you don't like it, just file a steam refund.  I'm certain there are many more out there who would be surprised by how much they enjoy this game.

Y'know, when all was said and done, Kentucky Route Zero managed to be my game of the year. I couldn't tell you exactly why. The game's trippy, mysterious. Gorgeous. I could stare at this game for hours, but, of course, the mystery drives me on--because this is a real mystery, not some generic 'who murdered whom?' It's far more than that. I want to know who Julian is, what significance the mine has, how the barn ended up in a museum, and why the museum's occupants... why does the museum have occupants? Kentucky Route Zero is a mystery, a real mystery. I want to know more--I must know more!
And yet... the more I know, the less I understand. This is less of a traditional point and click adventure game, and more of... well, some sort of adventure. There's one point in Chapter 2 where my mouth dropped open, though I was looking at nothing more than inky blackness and a 2D map sketched in white lines.
This game looks good, but it sounds even better. The experience is practically made by sound. Oh, sure, the strange figures that appear if you shut off the lights in the mine are frightening, but something about it is way more compelling when you've got those headphones plugged in. Immersing yourself in this game's aural landscape is like taking a bath. Soothing. Gentle. Calm.
And yet... something there is unsettling, always unsettling. This is a room with a Bureau in an old cathedral, an abandoned storage facility that used to be a church, a floor occupied entirely by bears. This is a game that unnerved me with a simple phrase and a sound effect. This game... this game... it's something you, and everyone you know, ought to try.
As games I tried in 2013 go, Kentucky Route Zero was moving, mysterious, engrossing, and over all too quickly. For now. The first two chapters have released, and the game will be updated with three more in the future. I can't wait.
I loved every second of it, and I'm sure you will too.

Not all modes are completely the same. All modes require a unique play style. Here are some of the top Modes you'll see in game:
These are seen as "Normal" modes. Since they can all be adjusted when you create the room as "Normal Mode." This is one of the original modes Audition has carried since it has been just a baby! You basically have to press all the arrow keys in the correct order (within the given time,) and press space/control at a perfect timing that matches the BPM/Tempo.
Widely known for its "DDR"-like appearance, don't be mistaken. Beat Up is one of the most complex modes (in my opinion.) Not only must you rely on timing, but arrows will fling at you in multiple directions, perfection is key! Not many will go down this path. But those that do, may soon find themselves becoming a master of rhythm.
Much like it's older sibling Beat Up, Beat Rush relies on perfect timing with its arrows. Beat Rush feels like a mixture of Normal and Beat Up. If you end up becoming interested in Beat Rush, most likely you'll become hypnotized by it's swirly bars and spinning circle.
This is probably seen as one of the "newer" modes, even though it's been out for quite some time. Guitar Mode probably stands out the most. Not only for its classy guitar-like style, but because you can actually use an Audition Guitar (connecting to the computer) to play with it. If only I could grasp my hands upon this beauty...
We have a "server" within the game for only Tournaments. Everyday at unique times, specific tournaments are held based on the Mode. You can compete with the best, and see how high you can climb the Tourney Ladder! There are also multiple Player-Hosted Events on the Redbana's Official Forums. Here you can join in some fun events, and even win prizes (sometimes just for participating!)
You don't always have to go full on competitive (unless you want to!). Some modes give you outfits, items, and prizes when completing a certain goal. Coin Collect, for example, gives you exclusive items that are not available in the Mall/Shop! You can also have a couple, have a wedding, and even tend a Garden!  The garden offers unique items as well, they can give you items that are not available elsewhere. Even if you're not interested in the Couple-Side of Audition, there's just so many ways to meet new friends. Either by joining a FAM (like a group/guild), chatting in the lobby, or just joining rooms to meet people with similar interests.
Sometimes the staff of the game get a bit busy, so songs/content may not be updated as quickly as we expected. However, they truly do care about the players. They do a lot of "behind the scenes" work that many of us may take for granted.
Songs may feel a bit repetitive, especially if you practice/play them occasionally.
Not joining a fam or meeting new friends frequently may make you feel bored/lonely. It may also make the game as a whole feel a bit strange. The constant spam of always hearing music may start to bother you. (If you honestly feel youself slipping into this, taking a break may not always be a bad thing!)
You may find yourself feeling "below the ranks." Sometimes you will be in rooms/games with players who have literally played for years. The competition can be insane. (However, try to get to know these players personally, most of the community are really friendly and understanding.)
One popular issue, that many players will bring up, is that the game lacks a bit of helpful options and settings. Most players who wish to change their resolution, optimization, and performance may have to manually adjust their video card settings. Luckily, the community on Redbana's Official Forums, under the Technical Support section will have Stickied posts with guides and tutorials explaining every step of the way:
~Wiffles~

Kentucky Route Zero has the best use of atmopshere I've ever seen in a game. While most of the time atmosphere in games is equated to "spoopy dark hallways", KY0 uses solid, washed out colors and wide camera angles to make its world seem desolate and distant.
This aesthetic lends a lot of emotional weight to the game's story about the mudane lives of people dealing with poverty. The writing is excellent, especially that of the dialogue. All of the conversation is very mellow, but hints very effectively at the unsaid ways the characters feel. The dialogue trees are also done excellently. They're not about checking off little variables and affecting the game later, they allow you to make little decisions about what kind of people the characters are. It's more like being a part of the storytelling than choosing a path.
Unlike many other "story-focused games", KY0 has a sense of brevity. The pacing is excellent, 3 hours went by faster than a couple minutes of RPG exposition. Nothing feels cliche and every line is well-thought out. I don't think I've ever seen a game be more poigniant.
This is usually where I'd say that you shouldn't get this is you're looking for a traditional game, but that's not true. You should at least try it, it's more than just a fun waste of time. The $25 price-point is a little steep, though. As of writing the game is on sale for $12.50, but that's only for a day and a half. Another thing to note is that KY0 has only has 2 of a planned 5 acts completed, and there's no guarantee the next 3 will maintain this level of quality. Still, I definately recommend it.

I don't write a lot of game reviews, but I really had to review this one. This is one of the best strategy games I have ever played, although it is not a game without its quirks and flaws, which may not appeal to everyone. Hopefully this review will help you decide if the game is going to be a big hit for you or a total flop.
The basic premise of Crusader Kings II is to give you a fairly well-oiled historical political/warfare strategy game, but rather than playing a nation or a culture like many games, in CK2 you play a royal dynasty trying to gain and maintain power. This means that CK2 is one of the least dry strategy games on the market; instead of endlessly bean-counting a swath of resources or spending all your time tweaking your settlements until they are perfect, you'll be spending time grooming/murdering your children to create the perfect heir while fighting off bitter relatives who want the big chair.
This game very much so has that "Game of Thrones" feel (and it's no surprise there's a quite god GoT mod out there for it), so if that appeals to you there is a very good chance you'll get a real kick out of this game, but as I've said, this is not a game that suits everyone's taste, so I'd like to cover a lot of what I feel are the "breaking points" for this game; the "love it or leave" it features that you will either learn to live with or which will turn you off completely.
While some sandbox games will give you a pretty open world, but also give you some obvious threads to follow if you aren't sure where to go, CK2 pretty much just dumps a giant playground in your lap and says "have at it!". This makes it somewhat hard to engage with at times if you aren't able to create your own entertainment. So, if you enjoy roleplaying a little in your videogames and telling epic stories then you might be really happy with this game, but if you are looking for straight-forward strategy you might want to look elsewhere.
CK2 is a game with a lot of moving parts but with very little indication of what all the parts are or do exactly, and almost no indication of how they fit together in many instances. This is not a game you can just dive into and pick up as you go very easily. Things like the subtleties between different types of claims to land can be frustrating and bewildering at times. Once things start to click the experience is very rewarding, as a lot of the design is actually quite clever and gives the player lots of interesting options, but if you're not willing to be patient and have a lot of dumb failure at the start you may not care for this game.
I am not going to try to justify the DLC scheme by any means, but I think the impact of this is somewhat overblown by some players. First of all, as with virtually everything on steam, if you're not happy with the price of the game just wait for a sale. I picked up the base game and a nice handful of DLC for under $30 at the steam sale and am very happy with the game I got at the price I paid for it. Yeah, if I'd paid $200 dollars for all the content at full price I probably would not have been so happy, but there's nothing stopping anyone from waiting for the sales. Then there's the nature of the DLC itself. Some people would claim it's not a "complete" game without some of it. I would not agree; the base game of CK2 is quite good. There are some nice features that come with the DLC, but I played my first 20 hours without and loved it, which lead to me deciding to buy some of the DLC.
Now, I could go on a rant about the nature of DLC and micropurchase culture in videogames, but I won't because it's not worth taking out my frustratings with the current state of videogames on this one, quite good, game. It sucks that paradox are going that route, but I'm not going to let it ruin my experience with the game and neither should you (if you otherwise think you would like the game). First off, as I've said, you don't need any of the DLC to have an enjoyable experience. Secondly, you don't need all the DLC unless you decide that you want it all. Each DLC adds a unique set of features that enhances some aspect of the game; some make new cultures/government types playable, others generally improve one part of the game (such as religion, or your council). Play the base game for awhile and decide what sounds fun, and then buy those DLCs, and don't buy the ones that don't sound fun, it's that simple. The purely cosmetic DLCs are really just there for the people who play this game so much that they'll notice/appreciate the difference if each culture has a unique set of units, for instance, so again, don't worry about those, you aren't missing out on much.
Last but not least...
This is interesting because it goes against the grain of a lot of games which get easier with additional expansions. Some people see this as a turn off, but personally it doesn't bother me. This is not a newly released game by any means; the devs know that at this point it makes more sense to appeal to hardcore players than to try bring in scores of new players. Personally I like the idea that the game is going to get harder as I buy more DLC and more patches come out, but this is not to everyone's taste.
If none of those things I just listed sound like a major bother to you, then there is a good chance you are going to enjoy this game. It is truly a fun and unique experience in a world of bland strategy games; I mean in what other game can you change your religion so you can marry a close relative and keep your kingdom from splitting in half?

I've only ever felt compelled to write 2 reviews on Steam. One for a game that brought nothing but utter disappointment and one for the polar opposite: 'Expeditions: Viking'
As far as I am concerned this game is a true gem and I hope it brings the developers some well deserved success.
------------------
Pros:
+Excellent story with what feels like truly meaningful choices
+Great atmosphere and excellent writing
+Fantastic history setting as a framework (while not limiting the developers artistic freedom. Meaning: don't expect a history lesson)
+Enjoyable turn-based combat (with some potential for better balancing though)
Cons:
-Some minor bugs (quest markers missing, tooltip glitches, etc.)
-Some major bugs. Now I have played through the full campaign (33.5h) and never once encountered a game breaking bug, but according to the forums (and the devs) there certainly are some.
-OP archers... I mean don't get me wrong, it felt great taking down hordes of enemies with my archers, but overall I feel one class shouldn't be responsible for 90% of the battlefield deaths :) Melee classes could either do with a boost or the archers with a nerf.
------------------
Now a number of other reviews make (negative) mention of the 'timer' and the fact that one cannot indefinitely roam around the world map before the game eventually ends. I for one can only say that I've explored most (if not all) of the content and had about a quarter of the timer left towards the end of the game. At no point did I feel rushed or constrained in what I can or cannot do.
I get that many people simply dislike the feeling of a clock ticking in the background and usually I'm one of those people. But in the case of 'Expeditions: Viking' I feel the developers have been very generous and the timer dind't affect my enjoyment of the game at all.
Could it be removed? Sure, I don't think it would majorly impact the game and people could roam around all they want. But this is the developers vision of the game and I for one don't mind their choice in the slightest.
------------------
TL;DR
Excellent game, 30h+ of pure entertainment for one playthrough, definitely a recommended purchase.

Even if I encountered many choke points, I definitely recommend the third opus of S.T.A.L.K.E.R.
One thing this game gets (almost) right, is to give more directions and explanations to the player in specific areas (while leaving others in complete dark or drown under a lengthy description). I really appreciated the feedback on your status. Plus, you don't start as with amnesia or as go-fetch guy for a faction. You are basically sent into the Zone to investigate the lost of helicopters, and while sticking to your duty, you end up accepting some missions in order to get resources, that would come handy to use the services of the mechanic guy.
Since most the overall gameplay is a mix of exploring, talking, retrieving and shooting ; your best friend is definitely the guy who can repair and upgrade your gear (who happen to deteriorate quite fast) and he's not cheap. Unfortunately, the "tools" missions are not located into the map, so it's better to check online walkthroughs and note the locations so you won't loose too much time and end up too weak for not finding them.
The one and only part that feels quite out of place (date?) is the dialog window. Even if some characters can give you precious information, it breaks the flow and too often you end up with the same answers.
All in all, the experience of being a "stalker" is quite nicely rendered, in a slightly more inviting way than the first two games. I don't think there is a better strategy to "win", except maybe upgrading your armor and helmet to death, and finding / sticking to one combination of gun x ammo in a specific type (pistol, shotgun, smg, rifle, etc) then upgrade it to suit your play style. Always travel light (between 25 / 30 kg) to run long distance with caffeine boost ; and you should be OK.

Having played this game through to completion once (my listed time on here is less than I've actually spent in-game. Started playing it with a friend), I can generally say this game is most certainly worth the asking price.
Pros:
- Story - The storyline is deep and engaging enough to keep you going, with hard choices all around right from the get-go. Everything you do might SEEM innocent enough, but there are consequences to a great many more of your actions than there are in most RPGs. Characters are all varied as well, and unique enough to be interesting while still fitting with the setting.
- Combat - Combat is generally varied and interesting, with a multitude of different weapon types and configurations. A lot of people complain about archers being OP, but they're only OP if they're used smartly, effectively being complete glass cannons that can be killed in one hit if you're not careful. However, shields do seem to work a LOT better for the enemy than they do for your party, but that might just be bad luck on my part.
- Environments - Environments really fit the atmosphere of the era and regions you'll be playing in. While the locales obviously aren't that varied due to being in the same general Northern European vicinity, they're generally large enough without being unwieldy.
- Customer Service - The customer service/support people have been entirely helpful and have been actively responding to players in the Steam support section and elsewhere. Jonas in particular is doing an excellent job of that, so thank you to him. Bug reporting is responsive, and fixes seem to come within days of being reported.
Cons:
- Bugs - This one's the obvious one. This game had a LOT of bugs when it first shipped, but given the amount of potential quest variables they have in this game, it was frankly to be expected. Patching has been rapid and thorough since release, though, so they've already patched most of the bugs I encountered in my first playthrough, and it's only been a week. This'll be a tiny issue a month after release, so give it a bit of time if you want to play the game without any bug issues.
- UI - While the UI is generally not bad, there are a lot of different design choices that make it a tad awkward to use. I still don't understand why the only thing in the "Codex" is your faction standing. "Codex" sounds like it should have a history of your undertakings during the game.
- Time limit - This is only a con for some, but there's a time limit for the main quest that can make exploration difficult to do at best. I'm still not sure I've explored the full map in my first playthrough because I didn't have enough time to check all the different routes on the campaign map.
Overall rating: 8/10
Highly recommended if you want a good tactical RPG, or even if you just like vikings.

Rated primarily from a solo play perspective (IE going into PvE and PvP servers alone). Early access review.
Pros:
- Good variety of building blocks to build some visually impressive structures and cities.
- Huge potential with the thrall system. Looking forward to the day when you see slave armies crashing into slave armies.
- Faithful to the source material.
- Regular updates, some of which added significant content to the game.
- Community quite friendly, even in PvP zones (The roving band of jerks in T3 gear appear to be the exceptions rather than the rule).
Cons:
- Game is far from finished with many promised features missing and many basic functions still rudimentary or bugged.
- Expensive for the content being provided.
- Ho-hum combat mechanics. Trading blows generally the most effective way to fight.
- Frequent server resets on official servers. Don't get too attached.
- Odd developer priorities (The Scourge has yet to reveal themselves, but we've got some sexy emotes now!)
- Brainless AI. PvP primarily the focal point for the game.
- Sparsely populated servers. Best to go in with friends or a community.
Interesting Bits:
- Battle-Eye included as part of the install package for the game.
- Turn the nudity on and play with the skin colors to see some interesting things happen with the default position of the "endowment" slider (spoiler, your high school perspective on such matters will likely play out before your eyes).
Would Suggest To: Survival game fanatics who also happen to be Conan fans. Survival game fans sick of servers overrun with trolls and over-geared predators and who are bringing a few friends/a server full of people for the ride. Minecraft players who considered tearing down structures with TNT and Creepers just as fun as building them up. Patient people. People with understanding SOs.
Would Alternatively Recommend: Minecraft (For the crafting enthusiasts), 7 Days to Die (for the crafting enthusiasts sick of the Minecraft asthetic and who don't mind playing another game that will likely never be finished). Subnautica (For the survival fan looking for a more robust single player experience).

If you're looking for a dandy good time with your friends, then 100% Orange Juice is a party game for you!  Consider this as one of your fun nights by playing a game that doesn't have anything to do with Breakfast, but mostly have something to do with anime-like characters in a Fortune Street-style game!  You go around, land on different types of squares while collecting stars.  If you land on a square and manage to fight against your opponent and won, not only you receive a win, but take away their stars.  You can draw stars by landing on one of the green squares, fight the enemy while landing on the red squares, receive bonus stars while landing on yellow squares, warp to a new spot while landing on the purple squares, and drop the amount of stars after landing on the blue squares.
They are some cards in your deck that will help you through victory towards the game so if you have one that's good, then use that as an advantage.
The down side are the repetitiveness, but the nifty soundtrack helps keep the mood going while playing.
Overall, 100% Orange Juice is a huge 100% recommendation to the party game fans out there!  If it's on sale again, buy it!  the game is super cheap, and it's $4.99 and it's worth your 5 dollars to burn!

Challenging players to advance without telling them exactly how to do it is taboo in any game, but perhaps even more acutely taboo in an MMO. Many players may find the game confusing at first, and for others the combat will not be lively or vigorous enough, but as with any MMO these aspects can be improved over time. What will certainly not change is the inherent difficulty infused into the game by holding players responsible for their actions. This game isn't for everyone, and that may be the most compelling reason to try it for yourself.

3D Realms and General Arcade work together to bring the classic Shadow Warrior and its two expansions to the modern era. Shadow Warrior is an epic first person shooter that combines puzzle solving, fast paced combat, and explosions everywhere.
Shadow Warrior is a crazy first person shooter that offers jokes, violence, and crazy level design. The game is rather simple in first person shooter standards, as an older game it doesn’t possess the features of newer games. The missions are typically small and require getting keys in order to unlock later parts of the mission. There are an abundance of weapons that include melee weapons and ranged weapons: Katana, Fists of Fury, Shurikens, Quad Barrel Riot Shotgun, Uzi, Rocket Launcher, Grenade Launcher, Sticky Mines, Rail Gun, Guardian Head, and Ripper Heart. With limited ammo, rising difficulties, and hundreds of enemies you will find yourself constantly switching between guns to fight off the hordes ahead. There a few bosses, but when they occur they offer a great fight that keeps you pressed and requires great tactics.
Shadow warrior revolves around the character Lo Wang and his adventure trying to defeat Master Zilla who slayed Lo Wangs old master. Lo Wang must now avenge the death of his former master by defeating Zilla. This involves going through all of his warriors and destroying his industry one by one. The game features twenty action packed levels which involve solving puzzles, finding secrets, and defeating enemies.
After many arduous hours I finally defeated the evil menace. Twin Dragon is an epic expansion that adds 16 fun packed levels onto the Shadow Warrior Campaign. The puzzles are a lot more extreme than in the original campaign and some levels I found so difficult I looked up guides to figure out where to use some of the keys I had found. Twin Dragon doesn't introduce more enemies, but rather makes rarer enemies more common. The game is packed full of Red and Grey Evil Ninjas, Serpent Gods, Guardians, and Sumos. This makes for a great addition to the series, although ti does lack some of the "secrets" that the first one has to offer.
Another epic expansion for Shadow Warrior. Wanton Destruction includes a whopping 12 whole leveles (2 secret levels) and new skins for some of the baddies. Although, released after Twin Dragon, Wanton Destruction follows the story the original Shadow Warrior as Lo Wang continues on his quest to defeat Zilla. The game introduces a whole variety of new tactics as it makes the ninjas stronger. Some of the levels are short and sweet while others are longer, but they are all very complex and require a lot of investigation. This fantastic addition is a great example of a great first person shooter puzzle game.
Shadow Warrior Classic Redux reintroduces Shadow Warrior and its two expansions Twin Dragon and Wanton Destruction (in that order). I never played the Shadow Warrior when it came out and thus I am completely new to this series. So I have no nostalgia that made me automatically like this game, but rather I just liked it because it was a good game. This brilliant series packs over 30 levels (not including secret levels) and will give you lots to do. People who can't play old games because they cannot get past the graphics or gameplay systems might not want to invest in this title. If you played the original and just want to rehash old memories then this is the game for you. If you just want a fun game with funny dialogue and guns blazing then this is the game for you.
Pros:
+Lots of guns and action with fast paced combat.
+There are secret levels (new games seem to avoid rewarding players).
+Many puzzles to solve without seeming to repeat themselves.
+The levels offer traps that keep you guessing your moves.
+There are many enemies that push you to the limit keeping you on your toes.
+Simple story that doesn't really require playing the game to figure out, but just keeps you going as you want to fight the bosses along the way.
+If you happen to feel some of the achievements are too hard you can easily use cheat codes and still get the achievements.
Cons:
-The game started glitching on the last 7 levels where when I saved the game crashed not saving the file.
-The mouse sensitivity is very difficult to manage and at some times can be very insensitive while at others seem hyper sensitive.
-Judging depth can be very difficult as it’s an older game without a modern physics engine.

Notice: my steam playtime does not represent total time spent in this game.
Men of War: Assault Squad 2 is a real time strategy "Blitzkrieg" type of game, where you get limited amount of troops to finish the mission. Since you do not have the ability to build a base like in most other strategies, Men of War provides some challenge at higher difficulty settings if you try to finish it quick.
The story is based on 2nd World War events where you try to fulfill different objectives to gain some advantage for your fighting side. The campaign is seperated by single missions that do not have any connection to each other, besides some story description. The story is supported by some details about the events that supposed to have occured during WW2. The gameplay consists of only managing your squads and units that you receive to finish the mission, alongside using some special functions like air or mortar strikes, that fulfill your weaponary.
The combat itself is simple but some missions require micro-management to use your units in most effective ways. There are some different types of equiptment that units can use, so adjusting to different objectives and situations helps with progression. If taken slowly, the game does not offer much challenge since you can always re-draw units, heal them up and re-capture strategically important positions or simply camp for more points to produce a real huge army that simply rolls over the enemy. At higher difficulties howerever, the amount of units the enemy throws at you gets challenging so you have to micro-manage your units even better to not let them die in vain.
The graphic and effects are far more enjoyable than in most Blitzkrieg games, especially compared to the older Men of War titles. The interface has been adjusted for the better aswell and you can modify some of the UI for better squad management. Most of the actions provided are still somewhat needless, but since you can simply move them out of the center of the UI, they do not disturb that much like in previous Men of War titles.
The whole progress of the game is still done by slowly fulfilling the objective inside single missions, but it feels satisfying in Assault Squad to finally move few meters on the map. The battles are packed with some action, the town and other surroundings do look destroyed and impacted by the fire fights, so the progress inside single missions feels good.
The audio gives a nice feedback during the battles where the biggest fire fights happen, where the heavy weapons and tanks are placed. The music provided a nice background sound without being too intrusive. The immersion during the missions was definetely on a high level in Assault Squad due to combination of visual feedback from the battles aswell audio feedback from the gun fights happening mostly on multiple places at same time.
Men of War: Assault Squad 2 is an enjoyable blitzkrieg type RTS game and will most likely gather your attention for at least few missions. It is quite fun to fight in each single mission since the environments do change a lot and you get to destroy some towns and farm along your WW2 progress. I would recommend higher difficulty settings for some challenge since else you roll over enemies rather quick.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.
~ForestWolf

Warframe is a really nice game, and it's free !
Graphics are really good, and could compete with some AAA, musics are actually nice, and some themes stand off and are great, you have a lot of weapons to play with, and each "frame" you can play have a different feeling. Icing on the cake, you have a huge selection of mods to tweak all your equipment to your liking. Also, it's a F2P, but you can skip completly the cash shop if you want, it's here either if you don't want to farm and want stuff ASAP, or you want some cosmetic stuff. After all the hours I spent on that game, the only time I used my wallet was because I wanted to, to support the devs.
Last point is the story. Warframe is about grinding, you farm materials to craft thing you will xp while farming for more materials to crafts other stuff.... but at some points, you will have quests to do, and these are really good. The game actually do not throw all the scenario quests at the start so you finish them in a couple of hours then go to an endless grind; instead you get the quests with your progression, and some of the best come after hours of play, to keep you hooked in the world of Warframe. They even managed to make one side mission more scary than any horror games released these past years.
One major downside for me is the grind needed, especially after the release of the Plains of Eidolon (or the Plains of Grindolon as some of us call it). Before the plains, farming was ok, could be a bit long depending on RNG, but still in the ok range, even for someone with a short window to play. Plains ask for so much grind (it's not even farm at that point) it can be discouraging.
Oh, and the team behind the game is really cool, they communicate a lot, and try to improve their game to keep it alive and enjoyable for eveyone
Would I recommend it : yes, definitively. Not everyone like third person shlooters (well, it's a shooter where you loot a lot... so Shlooter), but the game is well made, enjoyable, visually nice, and the story can surprise by its depth.

I've completed the story and a good chunk of the side quests after 40 some hours, and feel entirely satisfied with my experience. The story is a bit typical for a Viking game, but well written, paced well, and smartly executed. It's immersive, but some bugs can easily pull you out of the immersion. The music is wonderful, the little voice acting there is is spot on, and there's a decent amount of replayability in how you handle the narrative. All in all, this is currently the very best Viking-themed game on the market, and a fine RPG that can stand shoulder-to-shoulder with modern cRPGS like Pillars and Tyranny. I paid $20 for this, and have absolutely no buyer's remorse.

So what you craft will stay with you until the end - looting - pointless. I do believe this will be changed in the future like many other design flaws this game has.
As for good things:
The game itself is exactly what I love about gaming. You can take your own pace while exploring the late 8th century Denmark and what is today northern UK. The timer is present but it is not an issue, if you get a hold of how it works. There is enough time for EVERYTHING, but you shouldnt waste it.
The storyline, atmosphere and writing in general is excelent. I do not recall a single boring quest and most of them are non linear so you can finish them with different outcomes in different ways, much like the game itself. Do you want to be a peaceful trader/diplomat? Sure! Do you want to be dreaded and ruthles or honorable viking? You can! You can do all this and improve your homestead at the time.
The graphics and music is very good. I often find myself annoyed by ingame music but music in this game is spot on! The graphics are better than in most CPRGs out there.
Combat is turn based, if you know Expeditions: Conqustador, its more or less same but with much better animations and more abilities for your characters.
Companions are loveable. Each have their own personality and stick to it. Their relations to you are changing due to actions or dialogue options you take during the course of the game. Some are agressive and greedy, others are religious or peaceful. Many must be acounted for.
After huge disapointment with Torment: Tides of Numenera, this is the game that really caught me and didnt let me go.
When devs clear out the mess after the launch, which was, lets admit it, terrible. This game will really shine and I look forward and pray to Allfather for expansions and DLCs, I wont regret spending money on them.

Overview: 9/10.  A good, detailed game that you won't master quickly.  Like the best Paradox games, you can get going after 5 hours fairly well but then you're constantly learning and developing strategies and understanding new dynamics.
Pros:
- deep and very replayable
- different enough to EU3.  I was concerned it might be too similar however relationships matter externally and internally in CK2.  For example, when your ruler dies your armies can easily be halved due to the new ruler not having great relationships.  Not only that, but marry people without thinking and on death of your ruler, your realm could break up.  Rulers make a big difference both to you and also your enemies (e.g. when their old, strong military king dies, their armies might be reduced by half and his new military ability low, well what a time to strike that would be).
- works with Win 10 (some had compatibility issues - I didn't)
- good number of people still playing.
Cons:
- some balance issues - shattered retreat was awful so I play the version 2.4.5 and that's great - I think they've made this retreat optional now in later versions.  Another balance example is religious revolts in small realms is ridiculously overpowered.
- not a cheap game even 4-5 years after its release, but its depth makes this justifiable to me.  If you get into it, you won't be playing for just 20 hours.

If you want to make a game that's just about collecting things, that's fine. There are certainly quality games with simpler premises than that. But if you're not going to go deep on gameplay, you need to go hard on the polish and the feel. A coin collecting game in this day and age needs to be the most incredible, mind-blowing coin collector in the world to make it worth your time. And that makes a pretty good segue into the mess that is Canyon Capers.
You play Dino, a dopey little fellow with an Alfalfa part and the loudest shoes imaginable. He's here to plod across simple levels in search of gems, coins, chests, food, or all four. The first thing you will surely notice is how impossibly ugly this game is. I can't even try to be nice about it, because every level is a trainwreck of sprites and colors. For some reason nothing is rendered at the same resolution, so you might have a photo-realistic tiki mask sitting atop a 16-bit tuft of grass. Not even Dino and the hapless creatures you goomba-stomp (with a farting noise, no less) match. The colors are also rich and garish, clashing against each other and making it impossible to know what is foreground, background, passable, and solid.
Even if the game weren't hideous, the absolutely tepid gameplay would drive you away after only a handful of levels. Every stage is just about collecting things, with no gimmicks or bonus stages to break up the monotony. Sometimes it's one kind of treasure, sometimes it's all four, sometimes it's ticking time bombs, and sometimes it's all optional on the way to the exit. Without exception, you will always be collecting something before reaching the exit. There are no powerups to hasten your lazy stride or let you jump higher than your normal, awkward somersault. Stomping enemies doesn't even gain you anything besides points, because they respawn seconds later.
That reminds me of one of my favorite parts of Canyon Capers, getting constantly hit by strangely unavoidable enemies. Taking damage makes you invincible for a few seconds but also makes you pass through enemies, so you have to stay well away until it wears off. Dying just respawns you nearby, and can absolutely spawn you inside a monster to get hit. Slow enemies are often set in caves where the ceilings are too low to jump them. And even if you come to grips with your awful foes, levels are laid out with ideal paths that make backtracking to collect missed items extremely time-consuming.
There are additional characters to unlock with different passive abilities, but they're specific to one kind of treasure and you don't know what kind you're collecting until you start the level. It's such a simple thing, but emblematic of the shortcomings which riddle Canyon Capers. The game feels like someone's first experiment with GameMaker, slipshod designs and artless aesthetics and all. It's absolutely beyond me to imagine anyone deriving any sort of enjoyment from this game, between its horrifying graphics and infuriating levels.

I will give this game a guarded recommendation, because although I like it (so far) it seems like way too long between chapters.
Kentucky Route Zero is beautiful, surreal, moody, and atmospheric to the max.  More a story than a game, it's about exploration and thoughtful consideration of events as they unfold. Creepy moments serve to keep you interested, which is important because there are no puzzles, no conflict and only the barest thread of a narrative. That means it's not everybody's cup of tea.
The only tension is whether your decisions and dialogue choices have really made any difference. For example, I think one of my decisions caused my character to develop a limp when he otherwise might not have. Who knows, I'll have to play it again.
So to sum up: beautiful game/story, not for everyone, well worth the sale price, concerned how long between chapters.

A game has: levels, a story, characters, different environments, a sense of progession, etc. etc. Pac-Man had more than all of those than this game. Asteroids, too. It's about on par with Pong.
Does Devil Daggers play well? Sure it does. But it's much easier to make what is barely 1/10 of a level for most games balanced and smooth when that's all you have to worry about.

The FATE series is definitely starting to show its age now.  But if you’re a fan of classic dungeon crawlers or are interested in exploring the history of Diablo-clones, it’s well-worth checking out.
Among other things, it used to be a popular Diablo-clone in its day, attracted a dedicated modding community around it for a number of years.  Plus it might especially interest fans of the Torchlight series, because the different developers behind Diablo II and FATE are also the same people who eventually got together to co-found Runic Games and made Torchlight.
Not only was Torchlight directly influenced by Diablo II in that sense.  But it likewise inherited a lot of features from FATE.  Sure, you could point out that even long before FATE and Torchlight, dungeon crawlers such as Nethack had pets, too.  But FATE was really the first one to introduce pets into the gameplay in a Diablo-type game, and to give them features such as their own inventory interface, so they could carry some of your loot, and at the click of a button be sent to town to cash-it-in for you.  Plus it introduced some other new things to that gameplay too, such as being able to fish for loot at fishing holes scattered throughout the game.  That’s not to mention it also came up with how the user-interfaces look and work for all of those things.  Other than maybe give them a lick of paint and a tweak or two, Torchlight barely changed many of those things at all when it inherited them from FATE.
For better or worse, FATE also influenced Torchlight’s toon-like style.  That conspicuously didn’t come from Diablo II.  And it’s a design-choice which might put off some players at first.  But it can also make FATE a perfect game with which to introduce younger players to Diablo-clones if you have kids.  That certainly proved to be the case in my household when my kid was growing up.
Despite how child-friendly and lighthearted FATE might look on its surface, once you get into it, it’s also still quite an expertly made and solid Action-RPG deep-down.  In that respect it’s still a blast to play today, because that well-tuned gameplay it had beneath its surface as a Diablo-clone is still there in an ageless sort of way.
You also needn't worry about having to get the whole FATE series.  The sequels mostly just add some additional content and include previous content in them.  Otherwise they essentially play and feel the same.  I happen to prefer the first FATE game a bit for my own nostalgic reasons.  But you’re good to jump into the series wherever you want.
Anyway, the bottom-line is the FATE series might not be for everybody.  But I’d still heartily recommend it to any fans of classic dungeon crawlers and Diablo-clones, young or old.
(Note:  This review also replaces a previous review I did for the FATE series.  It was a mixed review just to alert buyers to an issue it used to have being unable to run under Windows 10 for some users, despite trying many popular workarounds to fix that.  But as near as I can tell, it no longer has that issue.  So that means I can finally give FATE its real due with my new review here.  Not only that, but on Steam it also has more resolution-options now than it used to.  So it’s not only fixed, but it’s also improved.  That’s another real plus.)

The final battle in this area (against underlevelled, back-from-the-dead characters) was underwhelming.
The fourth and final act is a return to form for battles. However source skills can be used to cheese a few. The quests in this area are buggy and there is a lack of guidance. Some characters disappeared and quests could not be completed. Puzzles rely too much on Wits and finding switches. One has a particularly obtuse solution with few if any hints.
The final battle is excellent if not a little confusing. Once you know who needs to be killed, it is much easier.
The ending is excellent and I can't wait for a third entry.

So, you are playing Shadow Warrior Classic redux? Well, if you are looking for a modern fps complete with COD style gameplay, you are in the wrong place. But... If you are looking for some Doom style, Dukem Nukem devil may care attitude 2d-that-wants-to-be-3d fps shooter goodness, complete with 90s cheese, you are in the right place.
Gameplay: Fly about at hyper speed as the "shadow warrior" with a arsenal of weapons and enemies that will kill you 95% of the time. You are going to have to learn to strafe, not to ever use the shurikens or gas bomb, and swap from uzis to sword fluidly in order to get ahead in this mad house. Just don't hesitate to run, because the game will love to try to kill you, again and again.
Story: You are Lo Wang, Shadow Warrior and old chinese man whom mistakes everything for "chinese secret" even as he fights the evil zombie ninja producing Zilla corparation from Japan. Are we here for the story? Hell no. But still, the bad chinese jokes will always get a giggle.
The Puzzles: Ah, old school FPS and thier puzzles... Well, the puzzles in Shadow Warrior are terrible. They can be to difficult, kill you for no rhyme and reason, and you know what? That is just fine. The gameplay makes up for it. Just save. Alot.
Enjoyment?: Without a doubt. Go ahead, kill some old school zombie ninjas with this crazy old man and hit on some anime girls while you are at it. It is alot of fun.
Final Notes: Save. Save often, and enjoy the little things, like the Slayers referance in stage 1. It's what makes it worth while.
Definitely an enjoyable competitive game to play with friends.

Expand is a game about perspective. Every puzzle seems designed around this core concept and it's done so masterfully over the course of 2 hours that you can tell this was a passion piece by the developers. For a game with no story and such minimalist ideals and aesthetic, Expand manages to be one of the most unique and impressive puzzle games I've played in my entire life. It's also easily the most hypnotic experience I've had playing video games. The motion of things as they retract and expand is so entrancing despite the simplicity in their appearance. The music is fantastic too. Honestly, I recommend this game to anyone and everyone, as long as you don't have motion sickness. I'm usually quite good with motion sickness, but this game is something else and made me want to take a break (even though it's only 2 hours). That's pretty much my only complaint. Oh also the Elude chapter was 10x more difficult than the other 3 (4?) chapters but it was more challenging than frustrating so I can live with it. Just a surprising difficulty spike.

To all the people complaining about the timer and giving a negative review because of it; I dont think thats fair! Yes there is a time limit of 1 month for making preparations for leaving Denmark. This is absolutely plenty of time! You only spend time travelling and camping when moving around the world map and 1 month is more than enough time to complete all the quests before you leave. There is absolutely no timer when you are in a zone so you can take all the time in the world to explore every inch of every zone and loot everything at your own pace if you like. The only real way to run out of time is if you camp way too much which would be exploitable as you can craft and scout for resources and being able to do so an unlimited amount of times would give you a huge unfair advantage and make the game way too easy. The timeline limit is also important as it makes your decision making matter more and is actually a crucial part of the story. The game is absolutely amazing so if youre scared off due to the people complaining about the timer, don't listen to them. You do encounter some random bugs sometimes but saving your game regularly you can just reload and avoid the major ones, which the devs have already fixed a lot of. They are rolling out huge amounts of fixes almost daily through beta branches which is why Im giving this a positive review as Im sure the game will be almost bugfree before long. You can tailor it completely to your playstyle which gives it huge replayability and I will definitely be playing through it many times to try different approaches and character builds. I definitely strongly recommend the game to any RPG fan!

Pros:
- The price, the price point for me atleast is very low for a game, and for me to get 30 + hours in it, defintely got every cent worth.
- The changes to your homestead and the changes in enviroment in the game is fantastic.

Ok I've waited to beat the game before reviewing (unlike some) and this review isn't about bugs because they can be and will be fixed overtime, this review is about the content itself.
Let's start off by saying I loved Expeditions Conquistador and the idea of marrying the mechanics to a more hands-on RPG style thrilled me to no end. We start out great, of course you know this is the first hours of the game so it's alot more polished and rounded out with decent content levels. Then we get our boat and sail across the sea, still going strong as we land on foreign shores. Still great, some great options here and it's fun actually being IN the game as opposed to some phantom spirit commander.
You spend a few more hours chunking through content and then suddenly it hits you like a wall. What seemed like engaging companion NPCs turn very dry and shallow, only the romanceable ones having in camp events to add to their personalities and even then only 2 or 3 at most then it's blank nothingness from there on out. Even the NPCs in Conquistador had more personality and their events were random and based on their traits! I mean hell not just your party in camp and traveling events are scarce, ALL events are scarce.
All those fun little things you could just trip over in Conquistador? Gone. The large highly detailed map? Gone. The feel of adventure and actually being on an expedition to a foreign land? Gone. Still combat is challenging and fun (although the enemy goes first too often for my taste), the plot has strength that is wasted in the final act and upgrading your village does little more than just increase some stats and maybe give you some negligable resources here and there.
The music is SUPERB but does little to help obviously rushed and anti-climactic final battles. There is very little reasons to choose Northumbria over the Picts or just conquering both (seriously screw those judgey genocidal Christians who keep calling me a savage heathen barbarian while they slaughter everyone). I won't go into anymore direct spoilers than that but from the 30-50% marker and then on feels rushed.
For it's price I'd say it's a worthy diversion but honestly unless they start adding to it it's very rough gem that feels more like it belongs in early access. If I could give a thumbs sideways I would because it has alot of promise, a fascinating premise and concept but just poor execution in the second half.
All in all I hope Logic Artists reads the criticisms aimed at not the bugs like most of the reviews, but the content and gets onto polishing the real stuff.

After all the time I've played this game, I have to say the developers have the right mindset for futhering their product and keeping the community happy. There are microtransactions, but I wouldn't consider this game "Pay-to-Win", I'd call it "Pay-to-win-faster" since you can collect/build/acquire almost every item in the game just by putting in the time, albeit a lot of time. The game is set up to be primarily PvE(Player versus Environment) in my opinion due to the fact that modding and upgrading your equipment is almost free forming and can get unbalanced in some cases, but that's half the fun! Despite this there are PVP(Player versus Player) modes if that does interest you, I'm afraid I can't tell you what it's like since I haven't experienced it for myself.

Personally I liked the Viking backstory and RPG elements which reminded me of Bauldur's Gate. So if you liked Bauldur's Gate, you might like it this game. There is even a bit of base building which is really awesome. I don't dislike it, but I just can't recommend it because it feels somewhat unpolished due to design choices relating to the UI and breaks in immersion.
Characters suffer a malus like stats reduction for being hungry or intoxicated and frequently I only realized it while in a conversation with a skill check or at the beginning of a battle. These negative status effects do not seem to show up elsewhere like the character menu which seems like an odd design decision.
Characters reach maximum damage output quite early in the game based on skill point allocation so there is a lot less grinding to do compared to other titles but on the other hand it feels too easy.
Some loading screens simply took way too long for instance in Ribe which could have been prevented by splitting a large or densely scripted area into 2 or 3 parts.
Finally the protagonist and other custom housecarls are not voiced unlike named companions, and the contrast is quite stark during battle.
So if you can get past some of these flaws, go ahead and have a blast. It's a good 20-30 hours of fun for one playthrough and you will probably want another go at it with another character build sometime in the future.

This is a really epic game with a cool storyline that I found it easy to get into. It is an open sandbox game, so you can do whatever you want, and don't have to follow the main story if that isn't your cup of tea.
The base game is now very dated visually, but there are a lot of mods to improve the graphical quality if you care about that sort of thing. Modding is one of the best bits of this game - there are tons of the things and they are pretty easy to find online. I would personally recommend the DarNified UI, which massively improves the usability of the GUI and HUD, the Qarl's Texture Pack, which massively improves the visuals, and the mod which colours the in-game map (I don't recall it's name). If you find that your inventory is always full and it's really annoying, there's also a carrying capacity mod that allows you to adjust how much you can carry.
Overall I would rate this game 9/10.

is a beautiful game. It's stunning in all aspects—visually, poetically, thematically—and it explores many important, often poignant, themes of loss, debt, grief, as well as curiosity, perseverance, and adaptation.
At its crux, Kentucky Route Zero (KRZ) is about people. It's about people with stories (nonetheless fictional, or mostly fictional)—stories that provide human connection and emotion-based interaction, and that engage the listener/player. The game description [given at the top of the page] does its job in beginning to encapsulate the game's many complex themes and overtones, and ends on a note which implores players to discover, learn, and explore.
"It is important for me in thinking about working on a video game that it be about being alive right now," says developer Jake Elliot. Even with only three acts completed out of five total [as of April 2016], the game and its story so far accomplish this in full. KRZ is not about prescribed dialogue or stories, but about the human connections and moments found in players' experiences with these stories. It is the sum of these individual moments that serves to create an experience that is authentic, haunting, and real.

First of all, let me say I am an avid gamer.  I have played everything from Rust, 7 Days to Die, Galactic Empyreon, and so much more.  The reviews for this game are not really fair to me and I am not sure why they are so bad.  I have really enjoyed playing this game from the get go.  It has been a very enjoyable experience.  I am a die hard survival and crafting lover and I also love multiplayer pvp games.  I have noticed a small amount of lag and an rare server crash but the game boots up fast for me so not a huge deal.  I have only played this for one weekend so remember I am speaking from the view of a person who is an experienced gamer but who has limited time in the game.
Maybe in the beginning, it may have hads some issues, and I did not buy in at that time.  I do find some bugs every day and report them, small ones that are really not a big deal.  But I notice updates constantly which means they are working hard to fix them.  This game is Ark-esque in a way, but smooth and easy to play for me.  I wish it would support apple at some point but for now I am glad I can play it with my windows machine.  I do have an older windows desktop with an semi new graphics card and an updated solid state drive.  All in all not too bad, smooth running with a small amount of lag here or there.  But you will know when it's lag.  It usually does not play laggy at all, so when you get some it's evident it is lag.
Perhaps because it is a new game, there is not as much pvp, but I did not experience many other players yet, and no pvp.  However the players online seemed like a great community so far and not a lot of loudmouth jerks.  I joined a role playing server and am having a blast.
The characters are pretty nice looking and fully customizable.  I was able to choose from a variety of characters, racial features, religious beliefs or none if I didn't want that.  I felt pretty satisfied with my ravishing savage woman and my husband's savage man was sexy as all get out.  The characters are beautiful and attractive.
The world is gorgeous.  The details are just beautiful.  The spawn time is fast and you don't have to run far to find some good starting materials.  There are lots of animals and beasts to kill.  It's really beautiful and the landscape and houses look awesome!
I can tell the level of effort has been put into this game.  The fighting is great, battling tons of monsters, the mechanics of fighting work very well, is smooth and not difficult or buggy.  There are lots of things to kill and lots of variety which feels great.  You can also make your kills into trophies if you happen to score a head so you can display your kills on the wall of your castle.  I did notice that while fighting my clan members weapon injured me so we had to be careful of one another and how we fought.
The armor is nice looking, well placed and doesn't have any peek through so it looks very nice.  So far I have noticed several different sets of armor that you can work your way up through which is customizable in color with dyes, but I hope to see even more customizable armor that might be faction or religion related maybe with special capabilities depending on what it is made of.
Leveling up has lots of great perks, though I think we should get more points, over all when playing a server that has increased points, a person who does not have a lot of time can level up in a weekend and enjoy their crafting and builing and if you love building your castle there is a lot of freedom to customize your castle or build smaller shacks for fighting here or there, there is lots of fun to be had.  Granted you will be having to work hard to get some of your materials, bashing tons of nasty poison spitting spiders or battling large rhinos and other unusual creatures to get materials or travel to far away lands to get a decent amount of iron.
Overall, for having played just a few days I am pretty excited and I had a good time playing, almost as much as Ark, 7 Days to Die or Rust with some small bugs and minor issues.  But I certainly feel this game has an unfair bad rap as it is really enjoyable and does not deserve the reviews it had.  I am glad I bought it and as my husband said, it's his new favorite for now!
I think it was well worth the money I put into it!  And I plan on playing the crap out of it.  So if you like sandboxes and crafting, fighting and running all over the place fighting creatures, mythical or realistic, this game is a good match for you.
