Introduction:
If you already know what this game is about feel free to skip the introduction. If not read on! Awesomenaut is a 2D Action Rpgish game (Or in other words a 2D MOBA game which is based on strategy) that can statify a competitive or casual gamer with certain circumstances for competitive gamers. It mainly focuses on team based play and it is quite in depth in that respect. Now for the good things about the game.
The Good:
Awesomenauts is a fun game with a satisfying amount of characters each with their own role. They're colorful and have a very nice art style not used much anymore. The game has variety with several maps to play on and many builds to make your character fit your play style. In the introduction I mentioned teamwork, now let me expand upon that. The teamwork in this game is very intriquet with player's varying playstyles, characters, builds, and several other variables. It is very rewarding if difficult at times and I've won rounds with a disadvantage just because of teamwork. Overall a good experience, but not without some drawbacks.
The Bad:
At certain updates of the game it has been terribly unbalanced with characters clearly better than others and certain builds and team compositions dominating. Some characters did way too much burst damage or sometimes had too much healing power. Even now there are some character and build items not even used or barely ever seen. Also some characters are just bland and gimmiky, I don't end up playing a good lot of them because of that. Along with some wonky hit boxes certain updates can make the game super frustrating, but don't give up on this game just yet.
Overall:
Despite all the bad I personally think the good out weighs it, also the fact that there isn't another game I can think of quite like this one. I wouldn't hesitate on buying this game if you plan on playing with friends. Balance doesn't mean much if you have a laugh with your friends and use some teamwork. If you're not playing this game with your friends AND you want to play it competitively I'd strongly reccomend you wait for the game to go on sale so you can get a friend a copy. In the end a solid if off balance kind of game, but if you like the concept and balance isn't your top priority pick it up!

Rather than gameplay, this is more or less a review on the games evolution.
Awesomenauts has come a long way from when I played my first game. I remember getting it in a Humble Bundle a few years ago. I picked it up and played it for maybe a couple hours and completely forgot about it. Several months later, my friends were playing it and asked if I wanted to join in. It had been so long I was surprised to see that I owned the game. Things felt Clunky (pun) and choppy but the idea was there and was being fleshed out. The devs were pretty open with the community, often having streams and beta testings. They also read forums for critisism, ideas, possible solutions to fixes and did their best to impliment them.
I played this game for roughly 3 years and it was a fun time. I've gone from about 14 Nauts to 26(?) or so and a few maps in between. There have been updates that drastically changed and improved gameplay. Before you were only allowed 3 skills per row that had to be picked before a match and hope they would counter the enemies. They later learned to impliment the entire tree for you to choose from but still only allowed you to pick from 3 skills in that row. This changed the meta quite a lot. No longer did you have to go in hoping your pre-selected skill set would synergize with your team, now you could build as you go with the team and adjust when you needed to.
Awesomenauts always had a rather small community which meant you'd often know the people you were playing against. This could be argued to be good or bad. There are a ton of great players, many of whom I'm still friends with even having not played the game in years. We'd always host out own tournaments in the community and a sizable portion would turn out and have fun. This was made easy by the devs inputing a record/replay system and the community really appreciated it.
I'm having trouble really expressing what I want which is ironic as I feel it's often easier with written word than spoken. I'd say Awesomenauts is that kid you met in elemntary school. You were basic aquintances. You'd play here and there during recess or sit together for lunch once in awhile. You'd go away for summer and come back for junior high and run into them again. You've both matured enough to see the difference in each other and are able to find more common ground. Years go by and you watch your friend go through enormous growth: grades, looks, skills etc. while you more or less stayed the same. It then becomes high school where your friend has stopped growing and you've started your own slow growth.
You still hang out but you begin to see that even though your friend grew "up" faster than you, they didn't pick up nearly enough information as you have. You hang out less and less, the relationship starts to dissolve. You see your friend get into questionable situations and while those ways might attract others, it deters you. College comes and you haven't spoken in a couple years. You've got a steady partner, your own apartment and paid cash for a sexy 1998 Honda Civic Hatchback 5 speed colored passionate red.
You have your old friends address and drive by one day to see how they've been. Their apartment complex isn't the worst; though, not near good either. There's no gate around the community so people come and go, many of them not being tenants. They ransack pool and playground area leaving trails of trash. You follow the tiny cracked street to your old friend's place. Several chairs and Folgers coffee canisters lay on the ground filled with nothing but cigarette butts and broken dreams. Their door is ajar and you find their welcome pad saying, "F2P." You peek inside and see quite the commotion. Enough people to make the fire marshal shut the area down due to safety violations. Trash spilled everywhere and a gut wretching stentch fills the air. No one notices you peek in until the door fully opens and hits a little bell.
"Ding!" One person turns around, it's your old friend. They get up, smiling, arms open wide. They go for the embrace, you go for the shake. You make small talk but you've been thinking of how to get out of here. They invite you to sit down and you decline. You say you have an appointment to make but just wanted to stop by. You exchange info and they shoot you a genuine smile and wave you off. The sigh of someone with too much on their shoulders escapes your lungs. You crumple the paper that has their info on it and toss it between your seats. You remember the old times - the good times.

I would absolutely recommend this game. Great plot, great combat, many opportunities to choose my own path, and even though I've encountered several bugs, the dev team has been polite, responsive, and working their asses off to fix everything.
Pros:
Plot--forge your clan from dusty, humble beginnings into the wealthiest, most powerful clan in Jutland. Great story arc, and many ways to do this. Lots of side quests if you're a completionist, fairly straightforward progress if you want to pursue the narrative quickly.
Combat--lots of different options for skill trees, encourages you to have several different classes in your "A" team, as each one is best at a different situation. Having an axe-wielder who can hook shields away from enemy bosses, leaving them exposed, is a must. And best of all, in my opinion, they fixed ranged characters. In Expeditions: Conquistador, I never, EVER used a ranged character, because loading up 6 melee guys with heavy armor dealt far more damage, far more reliably. I felt bad that my optimal strategy completely ignored a whole class of combatant. Not so in Expeditions: Viking. The archers are huge damage dealers, but it's tricky getting them into position, so in my opinion, not over or underpowered, but well balanced.
Choosing my own path--if I want to be a totally bloodthirsty, pillaging viking, the game lets me. If I want to be diplomatic and seek allies to strengthen my own clan, the game lets me do that, too. If I want to maximize building up my own village's buildings to gain power and wealth, the game lets me do that, too.
Cons/Wishlist:
Non-returnable areas: Once you leave Denmark, you can't ever get back to those locations, except for your home village. I would love to be able to access Ribe, Jelling, and other locations, to flesh out the Denmark experience. It seems a waste to put so many merchants in Ribe if you can only access them when you're poor in the intro campaign
Dane axes: the two-handed dane axe is not worth pursuing. It does less damage than duel-wielding axes, and the spear beats it as a range weapon, because a spear can extend to three spaces.
Plot: when in-game, it's never obvious what is possible, and what is not. My initial plan was to ally with the Picts and invade Northumbria with my army, so I would have a kingdom with allies to the north and rivals (Mercia) to the south. But this wasn't possible, as I could only invade BOTH the Picts and Saxons, or neither of them.
Character Development: I would LOVE there to be more dialogue and interaction with party members. I made romances with two characters, but there were no follow-up conversations or any impact on plot. Similarly, I wanted to ask Aife just what she was doing hanging around in my group, what's her back story, etc. There is so much possibility for world-building and role-playing in going in-depth with character backstories and dialogue interactions, like Dragon Age: Origins for just one example. A huge missed opportunity in my opinion, especially since so many hird members are put there by the game instead of just random recruits like in Expeditions: Conquistador.
The boat: what did it matter what tree I chose for the keel? I was never told that my prioritizing of speed (or cargo or intimidation) over the other two options had any effect whatsoever. Just a couple of random encounters/ ship boardings/ one-off raids thanks to the choice of keel would have made that choice feel important. As it is, looking back, I could have chosen anything and not known the difference.
Overall: A great experience, though of course it's a small studio and this is the first few days, so you have to be patient and send in bug reports. But for a small studio, they put out a great game, and I know they'll do everything they can to smooth out the wrinkles and make this seamless. I only hope they take suggestions from reviews in putting in more content and options, because as good as this game is, it can be even better.

You are most likely here for one of the following reasons:
1. You played this game back in the 90s and are interested in replacing your lost floppy disc with a digital copy.
2. You watched TotalBiscut's video on first-person shooters and wanted to give this a try.
3. You were looking for a retro game.
If you are here for any of the above reasons, I urge you to buy this game. Computers don't accept floppy discs anymore, the game has a refreshed interface, but still retains its pixelated glory, and it does have the sort of open-worldliness TotalBiscut was talking about.
If not, this game is a mid-90s first-person shooter. It will not baby you. Within three seconds of spawning on the first level, you will be forced into combat. It is not obvious where you are going. There's no Call of Duty-esque objective markers showing you the way. And finally, it is much more open-worlded. If you are unsure whether or not you should get it following this description, play the demo to get a feel for it, but I definitely recommend it.

I like the game, but people should know what they're getting into.  I wouldn't recommend that anyone without a tremendous amount of patience and forgiveness in their heart buy Expeditions Viking.
First of all, this is a strategy game, and narrative is part of the strategy.  There's no happy middle of road please everybody solution to a lot of the quests.  You're either cold or hot, willing to make compromises and suffer for them, or a full on classical villain.  Morally it comes down to shades of grey, but they're all dark.  For the record, I am totally fine with this, but I feel like people considering playing this game should know that they will come into situations where they realize they've messed up or chosen poorly.  Often that is revealed when a decision comes back to bite them in the♥♥♥♥♥several hours later, or a needed resource is just barely short of a specific number to achieve a certain goal.
Combat is brutal and cruel.  I can't imagine the save scumming involved in completing an insanity run in this game.  Certain characters in your party die in a single blow, and the AI is hyper competent, and generally far more resilient than even the player character.  I really can't tell if enemies scale, but it seemed to me that the majority of fights were way too difficult to beat in their first pass without proper preperation and strategy, and a few were far too easy.  Even a peasant with no armor and a visually low tier weapon can be a monstrous damage sponge capable of turning your badass viking warriors into a mushy paste on the battlefield.  Surviving some of the more attrition based fights can be more costly than saving from the beginning, as herbs and medicine are difficult to come by, and it takes 4-6 hours to get a second healer in your group unless you purchase that skill on your player character.  What that means is that if the healer gets injured, it stays injured, because for some reason they can't heal themselves.  Injuries also have a chance of becoming progressively worse as the game goes on, so I think this was just an example of poor design.
What I am less thrilled with, and the chief reason I am not giving this game my recommendation, is the number of quests that can be bugged.  I am actually giving up on a week long 15 hour playthrough because I got myself into a situation with a quest that doesn't have a solution.  This is not the first time this happened during my 15 hours, but the other quests I couldn't complete were usually minor side stuff.
In short, to sum up my opinion quickly, we have here a game with an interesting narrative and great characters in a fascinating setting, with sort of an overall bad, buggy, poorly designed game obscuring it.

Kentucky Route Zero is a strange game, and for many people - it most certainly won't strike the same chord that it does for some like myself.
KRZ is a click and point adventure through a dreary and ever-increasingly strange landscape that holds an ethereal mood in its depths.
It does not revolutionise gaming, nor does it jump out at you and grab your attention.
No, Kentucky Route Zero is different. It's different in a manner that continues to mystify you as you delve through its beautiful, lonely aesthetics; carrying on your simple journey through a night that perpetuates your solitude.
KRZ is a story that won't appeal to the conventional gamer or even the typical indie game fan. It requires an emotional aptitude to appreciate the environment that Cardboard Computer have brilliantly crafted. You won't find yourself loading up KRZ with an attitude of immediate adventure or conquest, for there is no regular high-riding emotion within the confines of Kentucky Route Zero's acts (currently waiting for Act IV). But, this is not needed. You find yourself immersed in the surroundings deeply, carrying the central character's journey truly as your own. The low mood of KRZ allows its emotive sections to soar effortlessly and truly touch you in a meaningful way that only builds into how brilliant the game is. All that exists within Kentucky Route Zero's ethereal confines solidifies its elegance in striking you with absurdity, loneliness, yearning and a great sense of understanding that very few games achieve, yet alone aim for.
Kentucky Route Zero isn't necessarily something that everyone will appreciate. It is a game meant for the early hours of the morning: to explore a world of night, where there is no fear, but a strange longing for the unknown and to explore its mystery. To finish what you have to do and conclude, to reconcile with yourself somewhere upon a long journey home that is Kentucky Route Zero.

Actual Review:Fate is a Hack & Slash in the same vein as Diablo 2,Titan Quest and Torchlight(this franchise began waaay before Torchlight and actually inspired a lot of mechanics for Torchlight.)
It's fairly simple to pick up,you make a character,pick gender,choose from a limited set of appearances and load up in the game.
It's exactly like the first Fate,all the systems and mechanics of the previous game are present in this installment,and while it adds some new things,like more unique items and items in general,more pet transformations and two outposts to chose from over the generic setting of Grove in the first game..i can't recommend this game,and i think that a big part of that is because i played Torchlight 2 before i played Fate.
Fate introduced a lot of cool systems that weren't done(as far as i know,don't take this for granted) such as the pet system and the ability to tell your pet to go to town and sell all your items you don't need(so handy!!),more freedom when it comes to class specialization,fishing for pet transformations and such things like that.
And thats kinda where my positives about the game end,since i played TL2 before Fate,it felt to me like i played a inferior version of Torchlight,everything that Fate does now is done muuuuch better in Torchlight 2,i personally found the music of Fate pretty good but became very old very quickly since the game has a very limited soundtrack,i disliked the art-style and the generic and basic feel of the combat. The story is a pretty boring one aswell,the narrator is abit wooden if you ask me,i quickly just ignored the story and focused on the game's mechanics instead.
When it comes to a very important part of an Hack & Slash,Fate just fails to entertain me with good and unique items,it's your typical 4% extra damage and +15 fire damage,nothing interesting,the game also has no active skills aside from magic,no melee or ranged skills that you can activate,no talents or very indepth specialization like you have in Diablo 2,all you do is increase Strength and put 2 points in Spear skill when you level up and that was fine in 2005 but in 2015 it's been done so much that quite frankly,i'm sick of it.
The combat is also pretty straightfoward,just hit the enemy with your sword,walk back as the enemy begins attacking then hit the enemy again,and because of the fact that the combat isn't very satisfying,it's tedious.And this becomes even more apparent in the abhorrent Hardcore mode which increases enemy damage and health to an unfair level while giving you nothing,and it locks to permadeath(which i'd be fine with if it weren't for the artifical and BS difficulty)
But,i have to stress that my experience is somewhat spoiled because of the fact i played Torchlight 2 before i played Fate,so if you never played TL2 or any Hack and Slash,Fate is actually a very good and basic choice to get into the genre,it's straightfoward and decent at what it does,it does have a helpful amount of tips in the loading menus,there are no complex systems like the charge system in Torchlight and there isn't a very big amount of strategy required to be good at the game.
So while i appreciate and respect what Fate meant for the Hack and Slash genre,and while it brings a loooot of good and sensible mechanics into the genre like pets and such,Torchlight 2 just does it so much better that i can't recommend it in this day and age.
And that's a shame because Fate is a pretty significant game when you see what it inspired and i had a decent time with,it just doesn't hold up against TL2 in any way shape or form.

Warframe has been around for a pretty long time now, and it has grown to be something interesting and unique. Being one of the only MMO Lootshooters on the market, and by far one of the most succesful ones, Warframe honours the genre in which it belongs by having an extraodinary amount of weapons and charachters, each possesing different traits,quirks and abilities which are essential for a succesful loot shooter. Furthermore, while a lot of people have voiced complaints about the amount of grind Warframe has, and how the game requires a lot of dedication in order to progress and get items, I personally think it has one of the best F2P buisness models on the market right now. The only real thing that the special currency can buy you, which is unobtainable otherwise, are the special cosmetic items, all the other items in the game can be obtained through (excessive) farming, trading, completing quests or just logging in; hell, even if you did want to skip the farming and wanted to instantly buy a weapon or a warframe, you'd have to pay an unreasonably high price, which further highlights the fact that spending platinum on anything but the most neccesery stuff is useless. Warframe is also at the top of my personal list for games with fluid and intuitive movement, possesing a variety of different parkour moves which all feel smooth and well animated. The gunplay is also very well done, altho since the game is a third person shooter, the gun feel isnt as aparent as in an FPS. While the game lack any actual story mode or a coherent questline, it still has rich lore which gets expanded every month or so. Overall, if you dont mind the grind, I'd say Warframe is a straight upgrade from Destiny 2, possesing better and more in-depth charachters, a bigger variety of guns (both in looks and in how they actulally feel) and a much, much better movement system that doesnt feel slow and clunky. If you're a fan of loot shooters, I think you should definataly give Warframe a try, and if you do, dont forget to ask a friend or two to start playing with you, the game gets better the more friends you have!

A timer in a turn-based RPG? What a refreshing design choice!
If you enjoy exploring and taking your time like you are used to in almost every game of this kind, this game is not for you. You might get a game over several hours in - your "punishment" for enjoying the game at your own pace.
If you are of the Call of Duty / Starcraft / MMO fandom who enjoys rushing, finding the fastest path to everything, and for whatever reason want to try out a turn-based RPG, by all means give it a go.
If you are not dissuaded by timers in RPGs, as a bonus, there are also a plethora of game-breaking bugs that may take weeks if not months to iron out. There are also balancing issues, and missing essential features, such as formations / deployment, which can make the outcome of a battle entirely dependent on luck.
Many of us have requested for the timer to be optional, but the devs are unwilling to do so. Apparently the timer is a critical indispensible feature of the game, despite not being mentioned anywhere on the store page.
So sadly I can not recommend Expeditions: Viking, despite this being of my favorite genre (and its predecessor being one of the my most beloved games) and historical subjects. I will still keep an eye out for future releases in this series. Hopefully the devs will showcase more flexibility in their design decisions.

100% Orange Juice is a very entertaining game, especially with friends.
The rules are simple enough; the player should only have to play a few rounds of the single player campaign to understand it.
Because the game relies heavily on dice rolls, the player should give up any illusions of control that they may have. Seriously, the easiest way to get mad in this game is to fully believe that you know *exactly* how the next few turns will play out. Crazy stuff happens that can't be accounted for.
There is a skill component, however. Picking cards carefully at the start of a match can improve your odds of winning. Remember that the cards you and your opponents select get combined into a single pile for the group to draw from. This means that it is best to choose cards that benefit you and only you.
As other reviewers have said, the mutiplayer really shines. The game is at its best when the madness is shared with friends!
One more thing I've really got to give 100% OJ credit for: The devs have done some great updates with the game and also frequently hold events for multiplayer games. The community is pretty lively!
So I totally recommend this game for the board game and random chance shenanigans.

Well, the problem is there is a HUGE amount of DLCs and after years from the publishing of the main game they're still developing new one. They're getting always more useless, DLC after DLC, while the price gets higher (some of the last costs half the main game...LOL).
As a loyal and old Paradox fan i get frustrated not only because they're obviously trying to get any cents out of my wallet, but mainly because after 4 (FOUR!) years I still can't enjoy the full game: whenever you start a new campaign (and a CK game can be pretty long and time consuming) they announce a new DLC with new features and new rules and you feel like you're playing an useless match and feel like abandoning it and wait for the new DLC. Problem is: when you get it, they have already announced a new one.
Also, every DLC comes with patches which totally change the rules of the game and you have to learn them again and again and again. It's like playing an early access game, but I've always hated those and I would have avoided it if I had known.
Basically they're policy with games lately has become: "let's publish an incomplete game and let's charge a lot with DLCs if they want to play its full version" and they're not the only company to do it, but when they finished the game they started to make useless DLCs (there's one of fantasy history in which aztecs invade Europe... which is not a great thing in a game of such historic realism) and to change the rules to worse just to justify new DLCs. They're literally to the point in which a great game is turning into a bad one.
Saddest thing for a loyal customer like me was the DLC to convert CK2 games into EU4 games to continue a campaign there. So I, a huge fan who bought all of your games, get rewarded for this by being forced to pay 10 euro just for a crappy converter if I want to "fuse" together the Paradox games I possess? Nice policy Paradox...
To give you an idea, today you need 165€ just to play the full game (without even considering the massive amount of graphic and soundtrack DLCs or the EU4 converter) and DLCs are still coming out. The game can be good but its not worth half of that price.
You better wait till they start working on CK3 and stop squeezing money out of this game. Then maybe they'll lower the price of a 4 years old game (prices are still the same even for the main game) and you can buy a cheap package with all the DLCs.
It's not worth a penny before that. You can trust someone who loved this and other Paradox games.

I don't understand why so many people are hating on this game.  Honestly, the steam community as of late seems to be getting more and more venomous and nitpicking EVERYTHING.  First off, the game is what? $26?  That's like the pay of working two to three hours.  It isn't a bank breaker by any means.
The amount of content is huge and you can get an entirely different experience each playthrough.
Everyone is saying there are bugs everywhere.  I have encountered three bugs in my playthrough and have played 30 hours.  Any new game will have bugs, that's just the nature of games.  They will patch it and fix them eventually and really, none of the ones I have experienced are even close to game breaking.
My one and only gripe would be load times.  I have the game installed on a SSD and still have loads screens of about 50 seconds.  Not a deal breaker for me as I am not entirely impatient but stull worth noting.
The character development and the writing for the game are phenomenal.  Other than The Witcher Trilogy and Mass Effect Trilogy (let's not talk about Andronema) it is the only game I have read every single word of dialogue while playing.
The combat is immersive and balanced (archers are, as some have said, kind of OP but as long as you use cover and keep your people with shields in front like, you know, a logical tactician would, they really aren't that OP...) However, if you have a good archer on your party with a good bow, you can easily eliminate two bad guys with one turn right off the bat... that to me seems a LITTLE broken.
Crafting matters and resource planning matters as well.
Yes, there is a timer for the game but it is a LONG timer and time doesn't pass while you are in an area, only between quests and while moving from one location to another.  It is also a significant timer to the entire purpose of the game which I won't get into now, but look up console commands and disable it if you don't like it.
Back to the playthroughs... you have SO MANY CHOICES in this game, even to the extent that you can choose whether to incapacitate each and every enermy you fight or kill them.  you could do a pacifist playthrough and be the first non-lethal, diplomatic Viking.  You can do a Bloodlust playthrough and just slaughter everyone.  And here's the best part:  Your quests are DRASTICALLY different depending on how you play.  It doesn't just "cookie cutter" your desicions into the same 25 quests, it really does tailor your playthrough around what you say and do.  This is probably the biggest plus for me, as I rarely find replay value in games, but already have my next three playthroughs planned out.
I have had a blast so far playing this game and my wife and I love discussing the historical accuracies and incongruencies as I play through.
This is probably one of my all time favorite games and I would definitely recommend it to anyone who likes rich stories and tactical RPGs.  Don't get turned off by negative reviews, remember the game DID just release and bugs are inevitable, but you can fix pretty much anything that goes wrong with a quick console command or a reload (just save often and you have nothing to fret.)
Have fun friends!

It took me a while, but I finally completed
last week.
Before commenting on the game at length, I should mention a few things:
This version of
is a partial remake of the original game, which has seen a few re-releases under different titles and with slightly different extra content (think side stories). It is also only one half of the story: the amount of new content, including animated character sprites, apparently made it necessary for the remaster to be released as two games. I recently learned that the second game will be released for the Vita in 2018, so hopefully that means we'll get a Steam release and needn't worry about investing time and money in an incomplete story.
is set in Japan during the late Edo era, a time of political and cultural upheaval for the country. The protagonist, Chizuru Yukimura, finds herself caught in the middle of it when she comes to Kyoto looking for her missing father. (Players of the game can change her first name if they wish; I will refer to the protagonist as Chizuru for my review.)
Because
is an
game—that is, a romance game with male love interests, a female protagonist, and a primarily female player demographic—the story is divided into routes by character. In addition to a common route wherein Chizuru remains romantically unattached, there are twelve character routes. In general, the game makes it easy to determine which choices are linked to which character(s). There's also a “romance up” indicator that appears when a choice made increases a character's affection for Chizuru. It can be turned off if desired. (Some choices won't display this indicator but may increase affection.)
Each character's route has a happy end, an unrequited love end, and a bad end. Once a route is cleared, it can be easily replayed by chapter from the main menu, with affection set to “high” or “low.” This feature makes it easy to get the less-than-happy ends, though one could stumble into one if a chosen character's affection level isn't high enough.
The bulk of my review, however, focuses on the quality of the game's writing, which varies wildly and tends to be worse where the story includes new material. I saw many typos, including punctuation errors, missing words and extra words, and sometimes incomplete sentences! I believe an update has fixed at least some of the incompleteness—I had to speed through portions of the game to re-register them as read after an update—but I'll have to replay a route or two to confirm my assertion. I remember Sannan's route looked especially sloppy.
The main problem plaguing
's English translation is an unfortunate misunderstanding of English grammar. I say this not to be rude; even as a native speaker I understand how confusing and irregular English grammar can be. I was just surprised since the translation of the original had far fewer issues, especially regarding tenses. (There seems to be confusion about when to use simple past versus past perfect.)
Other problems relate to word choice. Sometimes, when reading a bit of text, I saw words that I knew weren't used correctly, either because of homophone problems (the example I can remember is past and passed), or because of other mistaken definitions (unrelated to trouble with similar-sounding words). The last nit I have to pick regarding word choice just relates to text that was technically accurate, but a word used made it rather stiff and unnatural-sounding. For example, “I tried to run” flows better than “I attempted to run.”
It's difficult for me to summarize these issues in a review that's meant to be short (though I do have explanatory screenshots I intend to upload), especially since there are other minor quibbles I wish I had time to discuss. Those playing the game, however, should see what I mean. It's a damn shame, because
is full of beautiful art and music, and the characters are well acted. I'm sure if many dozens of literary-minded fans got together in a room, they could help correct these problems. I know I'd happily contribute.
Despite the flawed localization,
is a moving experience filled with endearing characters, and earns my recommendation. It may be classified as a romance game, but I believe there's something in it for everyone to enjoy. Anybody interested in reading a coming-of-age story mixed with elements of wartime drama, political change, and a dash of the supernatural should consider it.

Kentucky Route Zero is best described as an interactive visual novel, along the lines of Superbrothers: Sword & Sorcery EP.
There is a huge amount of talent being demonstrated here, and primarily for that reason I'm ultimately going to give this game the thumbs up.
Unlike related games such as the marginally more successful The Walking Dead, however, it left me with little real feeling of player agency.
Sure, there is some flexibility to move around and experience different absurdist vignettes between story-arc set pieces, however for the most part these don't pretend to influence the narrative progression in any observable way.
The game doesn't demonstrate any noticeable sense of self-awareness about this either, like in The Stanley Parable.
Ultimately, the best comparison I can draw is to meditative extended video-clips, such as Baraka and Powaqqatsi, in that this game is a thing that exists primarily to be watched and admired.
As a meditation to be watched and admired, this game succeeds admirably.
The block colour/silhouette style is gorgeous; the audio sparse and evocative; and the melancholy dialogue intelligent, mature and well written.
The setting is whimsical and dream-like, with absurdist elements, and the pacing and tone works well in the context.
I'm on the fence, however, about whether I think that Kentucky Route Zero is any good as a game.
As I would define a 'game', player agency seems to me a defining characteristic. Agency might be via micro-decisions, such as what to shoot in a linear FPS, stat progression trees and character customisation in an RPG, or varying strategic and tactical choices influenced by the randomness of procedural generation. It is the perception of player agency, even if only a perception, that adds a level of immersion that allows one to be drawn into a story and personally invest in it.
In Kentucky Route Zero, while the player moves various protagonists around the screen and clicks dialogue choices, these rarely have any noticeable influence on the story other than exposition.
I therefore find myself drawing comparisons with other, more established, non-interactive media, such as graphic novels, literature and film that are more reliant on narrative and where examples of mature, quality story lines are plentiful.
How, then, does this game compare to great film, great literature, or a great graphic novel? On that basis Kentucky Route Zero can reasonably claim to be good, I think, but not quite great.
Ultimately, if I want to be taken for a ride I actually get better immersion from letting a story wash over me while reading or watching a movie. At Kentucky Route Zero's pace, the interaction can tend to break immersion rather than enhances it.
It does seem to me, however, that there may be a tendency for those well aware of the woeful absence of genuinely intelligent, complex and mature themes in most games to be a tad overenthusiastic when they find a game that does take a decent stab at these, even if it fails on virtually every other measure by which we normally assess computer games (Rock Paper Shotgun 2013 GOTY, I'm looking at you).
Having said that, after now playing through Episode III, I feel compelled to add that for the first third of this installment the game genuinely transcends its limitations to become something truly sublime. It is therefore even more of a disappointment when the remaining two thirds of the same episode drops the ball a little on several levels. Nonetheless, there is certainly potential for masterpiece if the game's best form can be recaptured for the remaining episodes.
Having now played through Episode III after decent break from the release of Episode II, it is also worth adding that the game doesn't hold up at all well to extended pauses between episodes. The complexity and nuance of the characters and story, one of the game's big selling points, is also its biggest downfall as the minutiae is particularly hard to recall several months down the track. For this reason, I'd urge people to consider resisting the need for instant gratification and wait for the complete five episode experience.
Episode III is slightly longer than the first two episodes, possibly due to some repetitiveness. With two more episodes to go, one might estimate that a full meandering playthrough will likely take around 9 hours, which seems fair for a game of this type.

This is the first standalone expansion (the others are The Traitor Soul and The Cursed King) for the game Fate, released in 2005. This is a diablo-like action RPG with all the frills: random generated levels, lot of quests, different weapons, spells and so on.
While the gameplay is pretty solid, there are some problems: music is below average, levels are re-generated if you leave them, you are overwhelmed with junky items, inventory management is quite messy, it gets repetitive, experience points can't be reused forcing you to never change the skill path you choose at the beginning of the game.
I recommend buying Torchlight instead: it is the unofficial FATE 2 (the game director left the FATE team to build it): more polished, less buggy, better gameplay, more fun. :-)

I cannot recommend this game enough. Yes it is a point-and-click. Yes it is basically an interactive story book. No it isn't actually finished yet, but unless the devs somehow manage to completely drop the ball with the upcoming acts, I can't imagine the experience being soured.
Unlike most point-and-clicks, this game does not rely on obtuse puzzles or "look-and-find" mechanics to progress the player through the game. Instead it lets the character development and presentation propel the story. The art and camera movements are fantastic, allowing for some genuinely stunning moments. It's difficult to explain without seeing it in motion, but this may be the most beautiful game I've ever played.
Even if you don't like point-and-clicks, if you enjoy a good story and cinematic presentation please play this. I still can't stop thinking about it after finishing what the devs have already put out, and I can't wait to see how it all wraps up at the end.

I'm really suprised this game has a mixed rating, cause it's a very good one! It isn't for who are looking for high end graphics neither a game you don't even need to think to do an action for example. This game is focused on gameplay, interaction and etc... I really don't like RPG games for true. I rather game like Gta, driver, battlefield.  But somehow, this game made me be curious and i really decided to download it, give it a try and see what would happen. In the first minutes, you don't have any clue, you'll be lost and you won't have any idea of what you have to do, and this is the part where a lot of players give up to the game, because almost no one'll help you thought your adventures. You have to have patience, this is the best part of it. You will be discovering new stuffs, new things to collect, new NPC'S by yourself. The is game is fully of players in almost every part of the map. You have an unexplainable freedom to do whatever you want, and you can do the quest any time you wish. The main thing that made me like this game, is the fact you can have a bike, a car or a horse. there's a good number of vehicles, Atv's and etc.. You can repair your vehicles, paint them, you have to feed your horse, also, you have a garage where you can store or pick up your vehicles. You can trade your stuffs with players or sell them to some specific NPC'S.  You'll be playing GTA and dark souls at same time, cause this game is very hard to play.
Why it's a very good game:
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
*** YOU WON'T LOOSE ANY OF YOUR VEHICLES, ITENS OR WEAPONS IF YOU DIE AT ANY PLACE OF THE GAME. *******
- If you die, you won't need to walk hundred of kilometers to pick up you vehicle again or to continue the quests. There are some bases near of the quest you was trying to do before you die. Also, your vehicle will be at same place it was before.
- Wasn't made for who is looking for a good graphics game. Fallen Earth, is focused on gameplay, interaction with another players, with the enviroment and so on...
- Unexplainable freedom.
- It's a very hard game, you must have patience and sense of exploration, or you'll give up easily.
- You can play GTA and Dark Sould at same time, choosing if you want to be a casual player, or a high level monster killer.
- You can fight against other players, while defending or invading a base.
- You can craft a lot of stuff, since a simple clothes or even an expensive car.
- You can scavenge stuffs.
- You can do some quests that require a higher level, but of course, you'll die easily.
- Very good interaction.
- You have a lot of skills to improve. Also, you'll earn XP points, and you can spend it upgrading your skills.
There's a lot of things, but you need to play a lot of time to find out. This is just a 1000 square kilometers map!

What is bad in Expeditions : Viking?
1)Incredible amount of bugs. Death/Incapacition system not working properly. Tooltips showing wrong info (like talon skill). Cover system not working like it should.
2) Combat is clunky, slow and not that much tactical as everybody says. I still can't believe, they thought that making my whole party or WHOLE group of enemies move in one turn was a good idea. Basically, your either kill 2-3 enemies at the start of battle or lose 2-3 party members. Good luck finding fun on harder difficulties, when fighting group of enemies with 3 or more archers. Not to mention, you CAN'T move your party members before the fight starts, so say farewell to your archers/berserkers. Great way to use cover system, when I can't even hide my squishy members before encounter.
3) There is no feeling of character progess in this game. There are tons of skills that are just plain usless. Not to mention you can get all the good ones in the first 8 hours of gameplay.
4) No mini-map and no compass must be some kind of joke. Using normal MAP every 5 seconds was one of most frustrating thing I met in a long time. And you have to rotate camera all the time, because you can't click objects behind walls/hays etc.
5) Animations are really average. The way the wolfes move made me cry in pain.
6) Crafting system. At first I thought it was cool and engaging. After only 5 hours I found out it is incredible shallow and it is easy to make weapons that 2 shot all enemies. Not to mention unbalanced bows, that deal 100+ dmg.
On the other hand, the game has really good lore and interesting story. But they couldn't possibly ruin it, because it is somehow history based. I also loved the interactions and dialogs between my companions, although there aren't that many of them.
Overall : Stay away from this game in this state. Get it on some kind of sale in a month or two.

If you like this kind of unusual minimalist platforming games
you have a gamepad, you might like this. However, I don't think this will appeal to general audience.
I like the minimalist graphic style, the fluent transitions, the clever ideas in some levels, the music.
I hate the controls. Really, if something drags this game down, it's controls. I can't imagine anyone playing this with a keyboard, I'd guess it's almost impossible. I can imagine controlling this quite conveniently with a mouse, but that's not implemented. So, gamepad it is. But there are a few problems with it. First, the game requires you to be pixel perfect quite often, which is very hard to do with an analog stick. Second, the movement is done very poorly. Since you're a square, you very often get stuck by hitting an obstacle with one of your corners, just with a few pixels, and that usually means game over (next time developers should use a circle, seriously!). Even worse is that your movement speed is considerably lowered when you touch a wall and you move along it while "pushing" against the wall even just a little. With an analog stick, it's very hard to avoid this, and yet, again, it often means game over. The game controls have been a very frustrating experience overall.
There are some more hard edges. The main menu deserves a head desk meme. The game starts with just a black screen on my configuration and I had to manually tweak the config file to fix it. The game bugs out quite often during gameplay after you die (when transitioning back to the last checkpoint) and sometimes the only way to fix it is to exit the game and start it again, losing some progress and having to replay it all since level start (that is infuriating).
Levels vary quite a bit, which is nice. But there's not enough of them, and not enough different mechanics. Sometimes the checkpoints are quite far off, the time limit is too strict, or the level mechanic is very obscure. But overall, the level design is decent.
The game tries to feel meditative (using relaxing music), but it's rather difficult and stressful instead (which is not necessarily a bad thing).
Be aware that this is a 2-3 hour game.

EDIT patch 1.0.4
I do anticipate changing my recommendation to Yes once the dev's fix issues.  Trouble is, there are a lot of issues.  I loved E:Conquistador.  E:V clearly has the potential to be a much better game than E:C but right now I would not even consider it E:C's equal.  Putting bugs aside, my major complaints so far are as follows (in no particular order).
#Custom keybindings are still broken.  I know I said I wouldn't list bugs, but permit me this one exception.  Per 1.0.3, LA has fixed the visibility of the controls from both the main menu and the in-session menu, but custom bindings are still broken.  Per 1.0.4, LA has added numeric shortcuts for the hotbar slots (so at least the related loading screen is no longer a lie), but custom key bindings are STILL broken.  Let's talk about Combat bindings.  Every time a loading screen occurs, the Combat bindings are reset.  Doesn't matter if I changed them from the main menu or the in-session menu.  Doesn't matter if I restart the game.  Doesn't matter if I start a brand new campaign immediately after editing the bindings.  I repeat: ***every*** time a load screen of any kind occurs, the key bindings are reset.  ......There are *six* different files in the InputBindings folder for E:V and so far the only one that has been immune to this keybinding f--kery has been "default.txt" which just happens to contain the Exploration bindings.  LA, I say it for the third patch in a row, now: please get organized!!!  The user interface is a game's first impression on a gamer and right now your impression is abysmal.
#Disorienting camera jumping during combat.  E:C had a setting in its Gameplay submenu called "Camera Follows Enemy" (CFE for short).  By turning CFE *off*, the player could position the camera somewhere on the battlefiend and the camera would remain stationary.  This enabled easy observation of everything that was happening.  In E:V, the CFE setting does not exist anywhere in the menus for the player to disable, but it *is* active in the background by default.  Thus, the camera in E:V constantly jumps from enemy to enemy and from ally to ally.  To say it is disorienting and headache-inducing and limiting of situational awareness would all be gross understatements.  There are times when I have to actually look away from the screen during the enemy's turn because I just can't take the constant jumping - it makes me dizzy and nauseous.  LA, bring the CFE setting back into E:V so I can disable that nonsense!
#Camp interface is even less intuitive than E:C, much more complex, and has fewer or less comprehensive mouse-over explanations.  Furthermore, the timelapsed speedy background after clicking "Make Camp" is disorienting, unnecessary, contributes nothing to the functionality of camping, and breaks immersion rather than supporting it.
#Zero explanation for how to raise morale.  I've been using techniques that worked in E:C but so far no luck.
#Inexplicable morale reactions.  Eydis turned from -2 to -10 virtually overnight when I was stuck in camp for nearly a week tending to Ketill's repeat injuries.  (He kept getting injured during random events associated with camping.)
#After making numerous custom hirdmembers, I have managed to make a list of what appear to be the grand total of 14 personality traits.  However, there is still zero explanation of what expectations are incumbent with each trait so it is still virtually impossible to gauge what conversation/gameplay choices I should make to manage morale.
#Personality traits seem to be assigned randomly to custom-created hirdmembers.  I spend 10-15 minutes building an awesome member of my very own and then they come off the assembly line with a personality that is contrary to my hero's role play?!  Idiocy.  At least in E:C I could *choose* pre-built party members who had personality traits that complemented the way I intended to conduct that playthrough.  I appreciate the goodness of being allowed to create custom fighters, but random personalities are a far worse badness.
#No permission to evolve a party member's biological traits over time.  I'd love to give Asleifr more Endurance but not allowed!  Guess he's going to end up being replaced by a random-personality custom hirdmember...
#No ability to swap starting positions of teammates upon entering battle.  Could in E:C, can't in E:V (yet, I hope).  I'm sick and tired of having my archer (Ketill) and my support role hero (with low Endurance) start at the front of the party in easy melee range of the enemy.  During ambushes, when the enemy has initiative and therefore first strike, I usually lose one or the other person if not both.  The E:C starting position swap was a beautiful system, very innovative, very effective, very *helpful*, not overpowered, and very appropriate for intelligent in-canon agreed party arrangement (like dungeon crawlers have been doing for over a decade).  Even when I did not have the initiative in E:C, I could still at least swap my characters around so my tanks could take the hits while my squishy members retreated to cover.  ***Please*** bring this system back for E:V.
#Repairing gear, either at a blacksmith or by a suitably skilled hirdmember during camp, seems to be unreasonably expensive in terms of materials spent on the repair.  Rebalancing may be in order.
#Incessant barrel/crate looting.  I enjoy looting enemies.  I enjoy finding caches while roaming the wilderness.  I enjoy collecting resources that my scouts have found while camping.  I enjoy being presented with treasure chests.  What I do *NOT* enjoy is walking around a major city like Ribe, literally walking into people's back yards and rummaging through personal belongings, looting hundreds of containers that clearly belong to *somebody*, yet not a single person bats an eye until I dare to touch the tiny handful of containers that are marked for "Stealing".  Seriously, I feel like LA has condemned the player to be a bottom feeder of society, looting containers while no NPC citizen in their right mind would overlook such a trespass.  E:C gave the player everything they needed for crafting from looting blue chests during exploration and from the spoils of battle.  Yet, in E:V, I feel like I'm that poor homeless guy who walks up and down every suburb block on Recycle Day checking everyone's bins for soda cans and beer bottles so I can return them for a few bucks to buy a meal.

CONs:
- the crafting system. while fun, it's completely useless except for a few items that you can easily find elsewhere as well.

In Hakuoki, you get to play as Chizuru, a girl who is looking for her father in Kyoto. She ends up staying with the members of the Shinsengumi, a group feared by most of the townspeople.
The choices you make in the game will lead you towards a path where you can end up with 1 out of 12 guys total to romance.
One important thing to keep in mind is that the game ends halfway through the story. Up to that point, there's also not much "romance", but more of a buildup of the relationship. If you're just looking for romance, I would recommend you to wait for the second part or play either
(Nintendo 3DS) or
(Playstation 3).
The gameplay is like any visual-based novel, you read through the story and you get to make some choices every now and then. All the lines except the narrative and main character are voiced by good actors/actresses and the background music is also beautiful. There are some characters that may sound a bit louder than the others though (like Shinpachi) so keep that in mind.
It's really easy to immerse yourself, partly because of the stunning visuals but also because the story is a bit long and complex. Most of the events and characters in the game are historically correct and you can learn a lot of Japanese history this way. However, some parts are fairly linear and play out the same in a lot of the routes and it takes some time to really branch out into the unique parts for a specific character.
All characters have their own story and they are not copy-pastes of each other. You may dislike a route or two but I personally find most of them enjoyable. I will not dwell too much about the characters though because this topic can be very subjective.
The only bugs and errors I found were some minor spelling errors and the lips of the characters being out of synch when speaking. I also had to use my gamepad to change the resolution and to play it in fullscreen.
Hakuoki is personally one of my favorite visual novels. I played the 3DS version so I've already played through the full story, but the added parts and contexts of the story were done really well and I was very happy about that. I can't wait for the second part and I really hope it comes out soon.
I will end this by asking:
1. Do you like visual novels?
2. Do you like having a lot of route options?
3. Are you okay with the romances not being fully fleshed out yet?
4. Are you okay with playing half the story?
If yes on all of these, I'm sure you will find the game very enjoyable!

TL;DR: This game is the perfect RPG in my opinion. Some might not appreciate the tinkering required to fine tune inventory, crafting, skills, and abilities, while others will love the freedom you have to dabble in so many awesome, fleshed out systems.
To begin - the flexibility you are given is unmatched in any other game I have played. Aside from the fact that you have to play from the classic isometric CRPG perspective (something I enjoy in general, and particularly in this game due to its beautiful environment and engaging landscapes), you can approach this game however you want to. It's super challenging, but lends itself to a methodical approach to exploration and highly strategic combat. I absolutely love pulling off exciting move combos that I conjured out of my own creativity - and then relying on those combos as part of my strategy moving forward.
The story so far is a great classic fantasy style tale, with comedy, drama, and intrigue in equal measures. I absolutely love the characters, and it's one of the first games where I find myself fully engaged in the dialogue. I missed Fallout: New Vegas, but the way I've heard its dialogue options discussed reminds me of this game. Your choices are plentiful, feel like they matter, and influence how others respond to you.
I've sunk 29 hours into it faster than any other game I've ever played, and when I am not playing I am constantly thinking about it.
Some fair warnings about things that might not be your bag: The inventory/ability/skill management is a bit cumbersome, especially as you begin to make some progress, it can be a bit of a process to optimize your characters' gear, abilities, and skills into the most synergized party. I personally enjoy that stuff, as to me it feels a bit like a puzzle, and I honestly consider it an additional challenge to be thoroughly enjoyed. Some people might not like how hard the game is, but there are easier difficulty options and losing battles is part of the fun because you get to readjust your strategy and try again with a new approach.
In conclusion, I bought this game on a whim because I read some good reviews and a week later I think it's my favorite game ever,

On release, there was a major error that prevented people from playing it for the first day and a bit (depending on timezone). However, since then patches have been fairly speedy and solved all major problems.
In terms of story, if you've played previous Hakuouki games, this ends around the halfway point (just a bit after leaving Kyoto, when the major twist happens to most of the ROs). This is because they added 5 new routes (Sanan, Shinpachi, and two new entirely characters including Sakamoto Ryoma), in addition to adding several new scenes to both the common and individual routes. Personally, Sanan's route is one of my new favourites, up there right alongside Shinpachi and Harada, although I won't spoil it since I was fairly surprised by the direction his route took, given his roles in other people's routes in the other games.
Personally, I liked this game, both in its own right and as adding additional content to the series which had otherwise been (as far as I'm aware) fairly static in terms of the main game other than porting it to other platforms. It's a little disappointing that we can't play Edo Blossoms yet, but only because I can't wait to see how the new routes are resolved and what other new content is added to the original routes. Would totally recommend, especially with the story pack (although the stories are very short and only cover 4 routes, so I'd buy them if they go on sale again) since it adds some lovely additional stuff roughly around halfway through this game (although you have to play them in the menus so I'd recommend finishing the relevant route first before playing it).

Fallen Earth. A game based on around the Apocalypse in the year 2156. It's a cool concept and was definately in its own league when it was averaging in the thousands for players on daily login a few years ago.
"Is this game like Fallout?" No, they share the same genre. Nothing more. Fallen Earth tops Fallout when it comes to roleplaying and exploration. I've been playing this game for 6 years, I've still only achieved 25% of the achievements on Steam and still haven't found all the tourist spots.
"Is the game dead?" Compared to its prime? Yes. I'd prefer the term "quiet" there's still a large number of people playing Fallen Earth in areas all over the game world. If anything, it adds to the genre of it being a post apocalyptic game with players being few and far between.
This game is heavily based around crafting, as such the in game economy is subject to amazing highs and devastating lows. Inflation sets in, items you farmed for hours are worth nothing and that one item you kept hold of is worth a small fortune. Give or take a certain length of time it returns back to normal.
The controls in this game leave a lot to be desired, it doesn't compare to your up to date MMORPG currently on the market, but that is not where this game is a powerhouse. It's not in PvP either.
So what has this game got, that all other games on the market seem to lack? A social community. Fallen Earth was and is full of players who have roleplayed with one another and had a blast, those who have made clans numbering in the thousands for membership and those who organise fairs for everyone in the game to attend.
So should you play this game? Yes. Don't expect the game to blow you away. The game is what you make it and for me it is not only a game that has allowed me to meet so many good people but also blow me away whenever I come back to it.
The only way for us to get this game worked on again is to get enough players to come back so they will realised Fallen Earth should not be abandoned. The potential here is massive. Lets not waste it.

100% Orange Juice is a very entertaining game, especially with friends.
The rules are simple enough; the player should only have to play a few rounds of the single player campaign to understand it.
Because the game relies heavily on dice rolls, the player should give up any illusions of control that they may have. Seriously, the easiest way to get mad in this game is to fully believe that you know *exactly* how the next few turns will play out. Crazy stuff happens that can't be accounted for.
There is a skill component, however. Picking cards carefully at the start of a match can improve your odds of winning. Remember that the cards you and your opponents select get combined into a single pile for the group to draw from. This means that it is best to choose cards that benefit you and only you.
As other reviewers have said, the mutiplayer really shines. The game is at its best when the madness is shared with friends!
One more thing I've really got to give 100% OJ credit for: The devs have done some great updates with the game and also frequently hold events for multiplayer games. The community is pretty lively!
So I totally recommend this game for the board game and random chance shenanigans.

Clever little title.
A lot of indie games use abstract art styles to cache their lack of substance. You know the type, generic platformer in block graphic with floating text that attempt to appear more profound than they really are (I think I'm beginning to sound like a broken record here...).
Expand is different. The minimalism of the visuals and the music create their own little world and the clever gameplay keeps you hooked. I was reminded of the rhythm and  pattern recognition skills of good shmups. A game of patience and moderate trial-and-error with an almost perfect difficulty curve. The controls, simple as they may be, take a little to get used to because it's a different way of playing compared to other games:
Left and right determine the direction of your rotation around the center of the screen, up and down move you closer or further away from it - sounds simple enough, but I promise you, the constantly shifting and rotating levels filled with artful geometric patterns will mess with your head (in a good way) and the great level design will keep throwing you curve balls. You will be surprised what the developers came up with. This is one of the few cases where I'd love to see a sequel (or spiritual sequel), because I can imagine this concept being taken even further. A lot of people have praised the soundtrack and I liked it as well, but I didn't find it very memorable. It works perfectly in the context of the game though.

For those who are looking for something a little different it's worth your time, I played it for two hours straight although I just wanted to take a quick peek.

Expand is one of those "where do you start" type of games when discussing it. In a nutshell, Expand is a simple puzzle games where you play a cube traversing through several levels with thematic obstacles. Your movement is fluid, but also affected by the pull of the inner circle.
But that doesn't do the clear understanding and excellence the team behind the game have justice.
Expands puzzles are so obvious; so straighforward in design you wouldn't think the game could evolve anything past any of the other thousands of games that inhabit the genre. Slowly new mechanics are introduced, affecting the way your cube acts and the level itself. From what was a plain "avoid the read walls, get to the exit" now becomes "avoid the red walls, get to the exit. Oh and by the way everytime you move up or down the stage twists and distorts around you". What from the surface level looks like a elementary platformer quickly reveals itself as in intelligent labyrinth puzzle game.
The game is split into 4 main sections: Peril, Reach, Elude and Control. Each section is linked thematically to the title it's given. Peril involves a lot of mazes with insta-kill red walls. Elude consists of numerous fast paced levels where obstacles are hurled towards you. Each one feels unique, despite using a shared pool of mechanics.
Indiduality of the sections is further exaggurated by the phenomenal, dynamic sound design. Genre wise the soundtrack is mostly electronic ambient, but the total shifts between the tracks gives a real sense of distinction. Where one section is almost techno sounding, up beat and in your face, another will be a mellow, dreery post-rock-y ambient sound you'd expect off a 65daysofstatic album. Of course these tones also match the level they're assigned to. The Aphex Twin esque manic electronica plays during the hectic Elude stages, whilst the calm, moody drones inhabit stages like Control.
The sound design is just one aspect of the overall majestic presentation style the game oozes from start to finish. The art direction is apparent from still images, but in motion is where the brilliance of it all lies. As the labyrinth closes in on you while you make a dash for the exit you somehow find time to admire the scene happening around you. The fluid nature of every moveable object in this game (in other words, everything in this game) enhanced my enjoyment of both the visuals but the game itself. This combination of bold, minimal design and smooth, effortless animation quality creates an ease for new players to understand the game, but also a method of raising the skill ceiling for more advanced puzzles. If the movement was less fluid, or the artstyle more detailed, not only would the overall tone of the game would be lost, but the advantage of having clear and concise goals would be obscured.
The developer describes the game as "meditative" which I don't wholly agree with, especially when the final "5th" stage is taken into consideration. I found that the later levels, where the game really explores every mechanic, were more stressful than relaxing. I completely understand using the descriptor for stages like Reach, but the final 20 - 30 minutes is pure chaos, both gameplay and presentation wise. Time limits and creeping red obstacles combine with a booming, blockbuster worthy symphonic score. There are times during this period when I was genuinely getting annoyed, so I wouldn't go into the game expecting a purely relaxation puzzle game like Hexcells.
The game recommends using a controller and I don't disagree one bit. The fluid motion of your character works extremely well with the maneuverability of a joystick, and since that is the only input that matter in the entire game, I would heavily avoid against using anything but a controller.
I hang my head in shame that I let this game sit in my library for so long. I have no hesitation calling this game a masterpiece, and would only reserve recommendation for those without a controller. I urge everyone not to sleep on this like I did.

This is a great short game that doesn't overstay it's welcome. There's four "themed" wings built around 4 variations of the core "move around the circle" mechanic, and within each section a bunch of discrete subsections that introduce variations on that wing's take on the core mechanic. What's great is that none of these subsections last too long; right about when you've got a certain mechanic on lockdown, you're on to the next one. None of it is too hard, and you shouldn't get stuck on any section for long at all, which also leads to moving forward at a healthy clip. Plus, I think I said "oh, that's really clever" out loud more times per hour in this game than anything else in recent memory; the game does some very smart things within the constraints of the aesthetic and mechanics provided.
So the game stays feeling fresh, with basically *zero* padding. It may only last about 2 hours, but it's a great two hours. If you want a challenge, this is not the game for you. Don't expect Super Hexagon or  anything like that. But if you want a visually sharp but very relaxing take on a "radial puzzler," it's fantastic.

Overall Expeditions: Viking is an excellent game. The quests, the world and the character systems are amazing and it really makes you feel like you're commanding a group of vikings.
There are, however, some massively infuriating design decisions in this game:
1. You are unable to exert any control over your party members locations outside combat. This means once combat starts, your party will be scattered about willy-nilly and you will often end up with your squishiest characters in the middle of every single enemy around, because there is no way for you to move them.
This is especially enraging when you anticipate combat and sometimes even know you'll end up having to fight, but there's squat you can do about it. In an ambush setting it's obviously fine, but even then it would be nice if I were able to tell my archers to stick to the back line, instead of walking face first into any trouble that might be coming your way.
2. There is absolutely no ability to initiate combat outside dialogue options. This means that even if you see people who are obviously going to attack you, there is no way for you to engage them other than walking straight past them into their ambush.
3. You can not clear fatigue, hunger or injuries in a city. You can not sleep, nor eat nor visit a local healer to get your wounds fixed up. And as of writing this review, it also includes your home town. Yes, you are unable to sleep in your own bed.
Overall I don't regret buying this game, but I am not going to keep playing until they address these issues, that should be
game mechanics in an rpg game. And until then, I will not recommend the game.

Expand’s greatest deception is in giving the impression that its stark black and white and red color palette and plain geometric characters were born out of an inability to do anything more. Sandwiched between so many half-finished platformers and blocky top-down shooters, it is all too easy to cast Expand in with the lot as just another amateur, dismissible production. Expand is in turns far too subtle for its own good, as what screenshots fail to convey is the elegance and creativity that guides each screen and level of a game that in many ways closer approximates a digital dance.
It is tremendously hard to do justice to Expand in words, as its genius is in its animation, simple shapes modulating and deconstructing around a pink cube trying to find a way out. What Expand asks from you is superficially simple – get through the maze, perhaps pressing a button here and there, and find the pink rectangle at the end. This straightforward goal becomes immediately complicated, however, once it becomes clear that these mazes are not static labyrinths but moving creatures, every wall and obstacle reacting to your presence as they collectively move and transform around a giant circle.
In many ways Expand represents an extension of the ideas of Duet, a game similarly focused around spatial awareness and poetic movement. But where Duet asked the player to react – to obstacles and emotive lines of text that collectively fleshed out a pseudo-storyline – Expand wants you to lead. Rarely does Expand push you forward, instead requiring that you take the first step and adjust your movements as you learn how the level is going to respond to you being within it. The experience would be oddly intimate if it wasn’t so bitterly challenging, a decision which at times causes the game to lose the rhythm it tries so hard to maintain as you fail again and again.
Expand intentionally refrains from putting forth much more than its art and atmosphere, and this can at times cause the experience to feel exceptionally lonely and empty. But that same stripped down approach makes it that much easier to lose yourself in an experience purposefully designed to never break until it has shown you all it has. There is something to be appreciated in Expand’s insistence that we needn’t go looking for things which don’t exist, and instead appreciate it for what it presents before us: a curious and extensive interactive animation that is so restrained as to cause even small deviations to come as a surprise. The experience may lack a soul, but in the end you barely miss it.
