This game is, in a word, horrible. First of all, the storyline is just weird. Collecting water is not a very interesting quest. Also,  when a character is talking, you can't even skip the talking. It took forever just to get past the opening scene. The controls are also very weird, and the camera seems to be stubbornly insisting on staying in one spot. All in all, a boring game that is almost unplayable.

The setting: If you look away from the technical part of character builds and magic, the setting seems fairly authentic. This games' rendition of the Viking age will please all but the most picky of historians. To make the game function, there has to be  sacrifices made to give players variety and tactical options in terms of team (Hird) building.
Character creation & character related: Visually the options that are there are nice but, perhaps, a bit lacklustre for those who truly appreciate and value games that allow you to customize your avatar visually. I must emphasize that what's there looks great but the choices are quite few. I personally think that getting custom portraits to work will help a great deal. Visual changes when changing armor and helmets are just fantastic compared to similar games, this put a huge smile on my face as I truly value these details.
Stats and abilities are satisfactory, it allows for a strategic build and, obviously, some strategies work better than others. Like always, easier difficulty allows for less min-maxed builds but the system generally expects you to focus in the attribute (strength, agility etc.) department. Attributes then sets your character on a logical course for which abilities are suitable for you.
The recruitable (Hird) characters can get a bit tiresome to build, as they have as many choices that the player has. Luckily (or not) they come with different abilities already set so their build is largely already premade. You just have to pick which part of the build you want to emphasize. I'd be happy with a narrower scope on the Hird members but I can totally see plenty of reason to disagree with me on that.
Combat: The combat is turn based and focuses on team strategy. It's encouraged to use characters (builds) that complement each other as the combat is quite hard on normal settings (and above). It allows for careful planning but you'll also face hardship because your attacks can miss (obviously) and put you at a huge disadvantage when you're too bold. Some abilities are, pehaps, a bit stupid in terms of realism, though. I'm not particularly talking about magic, but the ability to sit down and fully fix your shield while being surrounded by enemies which even does not result in attacks of opportunity. It does serve an important role for tanks, but I wish they figured a better way to balance out the shield that didn't look and feel so stupid.
The story: I haven't completed it yet, and I want to keep this review spoiler free, so the only thing I'd like to say is that it looks really promising. It certainly isn't bad and I read enough books to shun a bad story.
Feminism: I must admit that there seems to me that there are some level of feminism/leftism in the game. It's not at a point where I simply discard the game, however, and I admit that I am very wary of that kind of crap in games of late. Why feminism/leftism? Well, there are parts of the dialogue that gives you the option to tell someone to toughen up or be overly understanding of man's lack of manlyhood, for example. The way those parts are written just smells a mile off. I obviously picked "the wrong" choice on purpose (toughen up) and the result was unsurprising. It's not entirely Siege of Dragonspear as the characters doesn't smell gender dysphoria a mile off but the game does offer homosexual romance options, which for some people is a good thing. I'm OK with it as long as I'm not being force fed leftist morale in every friggin encounter and thankfully Expeditions: Viking doesn't go that far. The game is also full of overly butch females who kick some serious butt, which most definitely isn't historically correct at all, but from a fantasy stand point it's OK. My personal opinion on the matter is that I don't think PK has any place in story telling but if it has to be there, this is a decent way to do it. Sex, gender and love doesn't seem to take precedence over the main story in any way and for the most part it seems tolerable.
Conclusion: It is a very pleasant gaming experience and fans of RPG and turn based strategy should really pick up this title. Those who played Expeditions: Conquistador will probably recognize a few similarities. I personally found it easier to get immersed in this game, but I also loved Conquistador in many ways. The game also reminds me a bit of Viking Conquest (M&B-Warband) but with the obvious differences in terms of gameplay. Viking games seems to have caught wind lately, and that's really good. Expeditions: Viking puts a huge smile on my face and it's really satisfying to roleplay a Viking. Compared to other viking games released last few years, this one has to be the best experience. I recommend it wholeheartedly!
PS. Probably not the most detailed review but I wanted it to be short and accessible.

'Kay. I'm gonna come right out and say this: Perhaps this isn't worth buying if you've already bought the game before, which, all things considered, is incredibly likely. It could be if you're interested in the new routes, but prepare to spend an incredibly short amount of time alone with whoever it is you're targeting as this is only the first half of the game, ending right at the route split. I don't think this is clarified anywhere and I was totally baffled by the "mixed" score when I first blindly bought this because I rush into things like an idiot and was focused entirely on SANAN ROUTE, but now I know! This is some MGS: Ground Zeroes♥♥♥♥♥♥right here, my dude. I'm still going to recommend this as it goes down way smoother than the original, but be warned that. Like. The rest of the story is very obviously missing. It ends abruptly right before things are getting interesting. EXTREMELY abruptly.
If you want the short version of my review, it's this: "Okay, cool! Nice. Where's the rest of it?"
Now for the long.
My memory is trash so please forgive me if my comparisons aren't right on the money, but I'm going to hold this up against my blearly, fragmented snapshots of my first encounter with this game.
Firstly, it's visually stunning at any resolution and the new soundtrack is great. (I particularly had a problem with the old title theme because it was the absolute most generic jidai-geki instrumental theme you could imagine. It makes sense, but gave me flashbacks to my grandma hogging our TV to watch samurai dramas.) It's slick and easier to listen to. I do have a problem with it, but this has more to do with audio mixing which I'll get to later.
Graphically, as I said, it's beautiful. The lip flaps can be distracting (and look a little off to me) but it's forgivable. The new text box is fantastic, the menus are fantastic, and if I had any complaint about them it'd be that the "warrior record" has such an insane amount of negative space that it's a little difficult to figure out what it even is at first glance. I get that the blossoming cherry-blossom tree in the background is an affection meter and can applaud the creativity, but... I feel like it could have been executed a little better.
The text seems like it's been heavily streamlined. The first time I played this game I had to stop every so often because it felt
dense for a VN, but this feels far lighter. It's still heavy on history, but there really is no way to take that out of the story. If you've already played you know what to expect. If you're a new player, to put it shortly, "you gon' learn." Literally. This could be a huge problem if you're mainly looking for fluff. Hakuoki is already notoriously light on fluffy moments--which are increased here--but this is still mainly a historical fantasy.
I'm going to be an oddball here and say that I like the new routes better than the original ones. I loved the original, but I wasn't really interested in any of the guys... except for inaccessable Sanan. Which is why I bought this to begin with! His focus here has just the right amount of cold, subdued menace I was expecting. Sanan, out of all of the new suitors, has the least amount of fluff which is interesting considering the global fluff increase this game underwent. (This is great for me, but if you're wanting to go in and melt Sanan's bitter heart then. Well... Sorry.)  Iba is your typical smiley caring childhood friend type who would never hurt a fly. IMO, the most interesting part of his route was the presence of Kanryusai Takeda, who is a shamelessly messy ♥♥♥♥♥ who lives for drama. He's so monumentally jealous and scheming that it accidentally made him charming in my eyes. Souma is your very own kouhai who SCREAMS CONSTANTLY and was pretty forgettable to me aside from that. He's cute and REALLY LOUD, but... that's really it. The strongest of the new routes for me was Ryouma Sakamoto's, he's really fun and a welcome departure from all the heavy "HONOR" stuff constantly happening, so I went ahead and played his route again instead of finishing Yamazaki's so I could form an appropriate opinion on it. (Uh...)
Anyhow: Now for my biggest problem with this game aside from the second half being conspicuously missing. THE AUDIO MIXING. The mixing is all over the place, usually the voices in a VN are normalized, but here they're... not. They are OBVIOUSLY not. Shinpachi in particular is so incredibly, ear-bleedingly loud for no reason that I had to turn his voice down a whole lot and he was STILL loud. Other voices, like Iba's and Kazama's, are very soft, so they have to be turned all the way up. But when they raise their voices, it's still too much! (Souma in particular is a ride from hell since he has both of these problems bad: Being very soft and very loud at the same time. His shouts in particular are so loud that they have obvious artifacting. It's... not great.) The music was drowning out a lot of the softer voices, so I turned it down as far as I could while still hearing it, but it was still too loud. I turned it down a little more then it was nearly inaudible! I spent a huge amount of time fiddling with the mixing of various voices, sound effects, and the music. I got to near comfortable levels with the voices and effects, but the music is just doomed to being a faint whisper. I can't get it to play at a reasonable volume.
All in all: If you're new to Hakuoki, don't want to buy a vita and don't mind waiting indefinitely for the second part to be localized, knock yourself out. This is a great rerelease in spite of all of its issues, but you definitely need to take them into account and carefully decide whether or not you're okay with them. Purchasing this game when it goes on sale is perhaps your best bet, to be perfectly honest!

The most unique thing about this game for me is its dual armor combat system about which I have mixed feelings. The armor definitely prevents chain crowd controls to be over-powered so that combat stays challenging throughout the whole game. However, since it is most efficient to strip only one of the two armor types, I feel that this system restricts party building variety sometimes. Like, it's awkward to have both magic and physical damage dealers in your party and you need to focus on only one of the two. Personally I prefer Pillars of Eternity style where the magic and physical damage types can be mixed together so that I can use my favorite spells together. Also, having played both magic and physical parties, I feel that physical damage parties in this game is much stronger than magical, due to the variety of weapon types, variety of stats (str/fin vs int) and just general easier position/damage dealing/skill usage, etc. Personally I am a mage-biased player so... But the pyro spells are pretty cool though.

I just wanted to leave a review since this is my first survival game. I wanted to start by saying the game does crash, but it's a rare thing. I maybe crash once every 1-3 days. 90% of the time you can get back in within a 1 minute and your character is standing a few feet forward from where you crashed. Certain servers crash too. When they do, they generally go down for about 5 minutes, than come back up. Sometimes you'll come back to find you died during the crash, your body will be somewhere along the path you where walking before the crash, could be 10 feet back could be 100. that is also a very rare thing to have happen. In game i've notice a few bugs, they are all very minimal things though. For example if your stamina runs out sometimes your character will continue doing the heavy breathing and blurred vision thing it does until you run out of stamina again. All the bugs i've notice are as minimal as that, and won't hurt your game play. If you come into the game with the mindset that this is an early access game, and your okay with the things listed above it is 100% worth giving it a try. The devs are constantly working on new things to add. I've had the game a little over two weeks, and twice they've added new things to the game. The game it's self is a little challenging to start off, but if you make your character on a good server, people are generally friendly and willing to help you out, and answer your questions. It took me awhile, but I now have an amazing base, good gear, and am having a great time playing. It is very grindy, and takes a long time to build high end structures, and gear. But it feels so satisfying putting in the work, and having it pay off. I would personally recommend starting on a pve server until you get the hang of the game. Pvp servers are very choatic, and you can loose everything at any time if you dont know what your doing. So in conclusion if you come in understanding you will have the occastional bug/crash, and understand the game takes time and patience. You will most likely have a great time. Hope this helped some people debating about trying the game out.

I truly want to like this game. It is a post-apocalyptic MMORPG, reminiscent of Mad Max but with a much greater technological and traditional science fiction slant. It is an FPS, with a proper akimbo system and a good variety of firearms. It has delightful melee weaponry in all the flavors one would expect and desire from such a game. The landmarks of classic MMORPG gameplay are all there: mobs, crafting, looting, harvesting, and all the economic factors that come with them. On paper, it is the MMORPG of my dreams, and years ago it was probably up to the task of meeting my dreams fabulously.
Unfortunately, it seems someone forgot about it. Development has stagnated almost completely, its team brutally eviscerated and scattered in the desert. It has aged as well as tropical fruit on the windowsill, no longer pleasing to the senses. The combat is flat, awkward, and crippled by latency issues. Performance is what you would typically expect from an MMORPG, but with some inexplicable stutters and framerate drops that you would not (given the level of visual flair and fidelity). There is an option for Advanced Post FX which is apparently vaseline on the viewport that destroys what little definition and detail the game actually has.
In essence, it has all the ingredients of a fantastic MMORPG and may very well have been one at some point in time, full of promise and ambition. It's such a shame that it has aged so poorly, received little in the way of meaningful updates in the past few years, and seems to embrace a trend of short-lived fascination for new players and long-term disappointment for veterans. It achieves the goal of feeling desolate and abandoned - as all wastelands should - but not in the way that makes a game something one looks forward to jumping into; instead, it feels like one that everyone is quite eager to jump out of, and justifiably so.

Devil Daggers is a superbly disturbing blend of Quake and FPS style Geometry Wars. The learning curve is steep, but fair and quite rewarding once mastered. Simply put, it's a game about survival against giant floating skulls, weird spiders, centipedes and all sort of great nightmarish entities. You have two attacks: a constant stream and a shotgun burst that can be upgraded upon picking up red gems. Simple enough premise, but the execution is where the game shines. The Quake-like controls are very quick to respond and work well with shotgun-attack jumping (a'la rocket boosting in a way) and movement akin to bunnyhopping. The game requires as much patience and management of enemies as it does technical skill to land the shots.
I like the simple premise with tantalizing skill ceiling, and for $5 it's a price that seems quite justified. The leaderboards are a great learning tool for those wishing to ascend its ranks. The aspect of being able to watch people's replays very quickly and see what strategies they employ is quite helpful and pretty entertaining as well.

Right from the get-go, it should be said that this is a different game from Stalker Shadow of Chernobyl. In Shadow of Chernobyl (SoC), the entire game had a sense of mystery about it, a kind of unanswered questions vibe. It was a question of surviving the endless horrors of the Zone, of loud rain and calamitous thunder at night, and of breathtaking sunrises in the morning, as one gazes out at the brooding wilderness. It also encompassed a sense of massive and epic scale, as the player struggles for mere survival while the Monolith elite jealously guard the entrance to the Sarcophagus while the Ukrainian Military pours in all their best fighters, special forces armed to the teeth and guarded from above by a fleet of Mi-24 Hinds, to force their way through. Unsettling screams and distant gunfire at night, beautiful blood-red sunrises in the barren hills near the Army Warehouses, the haunting soundtrack of Cordon filling one's ears as stalkers wander aimlessly through the irradiated meadows, vengeance, melancholy, fear, and grandeur. THAT is the essence of SoC. Call of Pripyat gives off a different atmosphere. From the moment the player spawns, as he gazes out over the beautifully rendered swamps of Zaton, one gets the sense of opportunity. The Zone has been tamed, and there's money to be made here. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it does somewhat lessen the more emotional experience of SoC. Soundtrack was good. Weapons were unique and fun each in their own way, with customization available for most (they weakened my dear Ots-14! Waaaaaaaaaaaaaah!). Armor was plentiful, with many choices to pick (although no Merc Suit or Skat 9M). It is a pity one could not join the Mercenaries under Hatchet (what a swell guy!). I also liked the very idea of working with a fellow whose trade is the bartering of information (a valuable commodity in a place such as this!). I enjoyed the fact that some of these missions helped give one a sense of the scope of the Mercenary activities in the Zone, for they are without a doubt the most secretive faction.  Apparently they have some influential friends/allies. On the downside, I did not enjoy the fact that each weapon needed to be repaired before selling- this made the game much more difficult, especially since one needed to buy certain items in order to progress in the game. On the whole a fantastic game- not quite SoC, but worthy in its' own right.

SpeedRunners - First Impressions
My Stats:
- 2 days played (free weekend)
- Completed story mode
- Tested most of the game features
- Played Online for 1 day
Note: Before getting started, let me clarify that this is less of a straight up "review" as I only spent a limited amount of time on the game. It is more of my initial impression of the overall game - so keep that in mind when considering the use of this review.
SpeedRunners, as the name implies, is a competitive speedrunning game that combines the fast reactions and track memorization skills usually tied to traditional racing games with the elements of a platform game. This combo creates a rather unique game experience compared to most other racers I've played. In a sense, you could describe SpeedRunners as the Love Child of N+ and Mario Kart. This is an undeniably accurate summation of SpeedRunners' gameplay.
Players jump, swing, boost, slide, and wall jump their way to victory using very simplistic and intuitive controls that reward players mastering their execution and discovering the fastest ways around the various courses. SpeedRunners takes a page directly out of the Mario Kart series by also implementing items that players can use to disrupt other players and defend themselves from such tactics. This introduces an element of luck to the game, though I would argue that this feels more like a "high luck and high skill" racer rather than one that outright dismisses any application of skill. As a result, you'll see a higher level player pull off consistent results despite an item system that actually requires smart thinking and precision timing to properly ultize. Some items such as the missle, shockwave, or golden hook can actually backfire - hitting you instead or propelling the opponent in front of you.
SpeedRunnners, while easy to understand, does have some subtle depth to its overall gameplay. Falling onto slopes, swinging from just the right distance, and building momentum to push yourself up wall clings are some of the "advanced techniques" that distinguish skilled players from casuals. This gives the player more incentive to master the stage layouts and spruce up their execution skills in order to play the game on a highly competitive level. And while there were a few things I looked up online during the free weekend trial period (i.e. game play techniques) there really wasn't anything too complicated to understand to the point that it felt like it needed any extra tutorials or guides to be effective. The result is an accessible competitive racing experience that still manages to reward skilled players.
SpeedRunners is a little lacking on the single player side. There is a Story Mode that honestly isn't anything special. It's a relatively basic story: the player controls the game's main character, SpeedRunner, who gets challenged by four different characters, each with four levels, over the course of the "story". Each fourth mission of each "story arc" is a 1-vs-1 race to the finish with that "arc's" antagonist. Upon defeating each racer, the player unlocks a small comic illustrating who the character they faced actually was and their motivation for taking on SpeedRunner. The fact that the player needs to unlock the enemy's motivation is lackluster at best, and aside from some pre-match banter, there really isn't any "story" to Story Mode at all.
Each race has literally nothing unique to it. It's nothing more than a race against bots with the villian of the "arc" being the smartest AI in the race. While Story Mode serves as a serviceable introduction to the game's stages, power ups, and characters, it ultimately feels like a glorified training session at best. If the player chooses to play the game on higher difficulties, the racers (mainly the antagonists) will showcase more advanced techniques as well as an increased speed advantage. Playing at an advanced level can serve as a challenge to the player therby boosting their skill level. The rewards for beating each chapter is unlocking that chapter's antagonist as well as additional colors for each difficulty ranking that's cleared. It's by no means terrible but there aren't any specific missions or anything that really adds to the overall Story Mode. You could literally start a match with bots at the highest difficulty to simulate the experience of Story Mode. In addition, characters are nothing more than window dressing as none of them actually have any distinct feeling to them which makes unlocking characters somewhat pointless seeing how each racer plays exactly like SpeedRunner.
Worthy of notable mention, is the method used to unlock game features and levels. Basically, the player levels up with experience gained in matches based on how they played, how many points they scored, and so on - this is okay for unlocking characters and skins, but stages and power ups are also hidden behind this system. Even access to rank matches must be unlocked. I guess it makes sense when getting the player accclimated enough to actually play the game online, but the equvalent to this would be like buying a new kart racer and having to beat Story Mode before even being allowed to play online. If I needed help adjusting to the controls, stages, and power ups, I'd just test them out in practice mode. This is even sillier considering that unlocking power ups gives you access to weapons that the AI already has access to at the start of the game. It just doesn't really make any sense to implement such a restrictive system that's only undone through pure grinding.
The last main feature aside from replay theater and multiplayer is the ability to build your own race tracks. I didn't really toy around with this feature that much during such the short trial period, but the game seems to know when something in the track doesn't work and players can build the track pixel by pixel rather than just pre-made objects strung together. It's definitely worth checking out for wannabe level designers.
When it comes to online play there are a few aspects to the online play that I find somewhat questionable. For example, spikes and lasers in ranked matchs cause death rather than just stunning the player. I experienced occasional lag spikes while playing and combining those with lethal spikes and lasers felt a little cheesy to say the least. While the overall online game play is okay, the game also seems to have trouble syncing certain actions between players. There were times my game communicated very cleary that I grabbed someone with a golden hook just for them to dodge the hook frames later. To elaborate, I would nornally attribute this to user error, but other players stated they too were experiencing glitches when I played with them which insinuates this isn't uncommon though not necessarily frequent. This can make some matches feel a little random, but you could say this about a lot of online games. When it comes to connectivity, SpeedRunners is execution and timing dependent, therefore a good connection is a little more important for this type of game.
The game's music, while not bad, is fairly limited. It's based mostly around trumpets and horns. In fact, if you've ever played Sly Cooper, the music in that game is a prime example of what SpeedRunners' soundtrack leans towards. I only really loved one of the tracks in the game while others were either good or passable. In addition, players can't actually choose music for a level and the tracks appear randomly at the start of a race. Not a big deal, but I would have liked to choose the music at least when playing offline.
Overall, SpeedRunners was an enjoyable experience for me during the free weekend. At $14.99, it is definitely worth a look.

This game is quite good for its age and hardware requirements. The open world maps are huge and designed using topographical satellite imaging data producing a varied, immersive environment spanning over a reported 1k+ kilometer area. Fallen Earth (FE) posseses the most expansive crafting systems I have ever seen allowing players the opportunity to create a vast array of items including the basics like armor, weapons and healing/food stuffs. If you've ever played a Moba you'll know that such games have a rather steep if rewarding learning curve.
Awesomenauts manages to mitigate that often frustrating learning period somewhat and makes the overall experience more enjoyable.
That said the game is no less competitive and is worth your time if you like the idea of a 2D platforming Moba style game.
The main weakness compared to traditional Mobas is the smaller number of both items, abilities and heroes (I stress the word 'compared').
However it makes up for it in the unique way it handles the former two.
Instead of buying items you buy your skills and upgrades.
The interesting thing here is that each ability can be upgraded in varying ways.
A character's attack for example can be modified to either deal splash damage or heal allies thus leading to two very different play styles with the same character.
In addition the platforming elements require a level of manuevering that is rare in it's competitors.
The only other clear strength this game has over other Mobas are the map varieties (of which I feel is still somewhat small regardless of their differences) in the sense that they all play differently enough that strategies are developed for specific ones.
DLC skins while nice feel overpriced (I admit I am guilty of buying one) and lag remains a large issue due to the 'skill shots' and platforming elements of such a game. Some games can get away with such things however a game that is so reliant on reflexes requires a better connection.
Bots are at best useless and at worst detrimental to your team as they often die to competent players easily enough, thus providing an almost laughably easy source of currency.
If you plan on getting the most out of Awesomnauts play with either a reliable internet connection or at the very least with friends.
Bottom like is that even if you dislike Mobas in general, Awesomenauts does things differently enough that even those who normally don't enjoy the genre might enjoy it, perhaps at a discount if nothing else.
Those that enjoy Mobas would feel that this is a casual but fantastic experience and will find that's it's a great way to introduce newcomers to the genre.
I'd reccomend this game rather strongly.

Shadow Warrior was one of the holy trinity of Build engine shooters, released in 1997. This meant that in the fast-moving world of FPS technology, the Asian-themed successor to Duke Nukem 3D looked pretty old hat on release, and for a long time has not been remembered all that well. However, it was genuinely a great game in its own right and almost matched matched Duke 3D itself. Besides the sexism and racism (corrected in the excellent recent remake) and being arguably a little too unforgiving, SW is a neglected classic shooter of the '90s, complete with the interactivity, hectic action, zany weapons and humour of Duke 3D.
This version comes with two (already free) expansions which are surprisingly high quality. Do beware of a map set on a moving plane which while very ahead of its time, does over-reach technically meaning its exit requires a lot of trial and error. Given the beautifully redone main theme, very slick menus and hi-res support, SW Classic Redux is a must for '90s shooter fans.

There are also items, such as night-vision goggles, to aid you. You'll need all the help you can get fighting the enemies in this game, because they can get rather difficult. If you're unsure about getting the game, at least try the free version on Steam. If you want more Lo Wang, get this instead.

I did think the AI was good for the other vehicles, I did find myself getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at them for cutting me off and there was a fair amount of unpredictability in their actions. And of course, the view was great throughout the game. I love the American Southwest landscapes.
On that note... this isn't really American Truck Simulator, this is American Southwest Truck Simulator. I was/still am severely disappointed that there are only 3 states to explore. I understand that a lot probably went into creating just those 3 states and that to do the entire country would probably be a huge feat, but 3 (very similar-looking) states do nothing in describing the US as a whole. Maybe I'm glad there are only 3 states because I would have sunk countless more hours into it if there were more. Another thing I was disappointed in was the lack of desert sky at night. I thought it was a joke and they were all UFOs but I caught one in my sight long enough to figure out it was a plane. I did find some rather irritating bugs but nothing detrimental (not being able to go through railroad tracks after a train goes by, etc.).
Overall, good game that has the potential to be great but is lacking many details/states.

The point is that this is a 2D-sprite fighting action packed piece of handsome that just throws insanely hard mazes at you. No puzzles, no story, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Just Pure action. Chivlary: Medieval Warfare is exactly what it says on the tin. It is pretty much Medieval Warfare!
Swords, Bows, Throwing Knives, Warhammers, Claymores, Polearms and much, much more. If you have played anything like Mount & Blade, then you will love the experience that this game provides in-terms of combat.
Your first layer of choices is your class and obviously, some classes are fast, some are strong, but most are restricted to certain weapon choices, however, even the weapons have various advantages as well: Like Reach, Speed and Damage.
This means you can be a bulky Knight who can take damage, while using a maul for maximum damage or maybe you want to be a fast unit, who can use staves/polearms to reach people from as far away as possible? Despite all it's choices, however, I do believe some weapons need to be unlocked/purchased.
There are two factions - Agatha Knights and The Mason Order.
Weirdly enough, black and red are my two favourite colours, but I still choose Agatha Knights.
"Thank you, Brother!"
Now, don't expect a load of content in this game, it is pretty much like most online PVP games; were you have rounds, kill other players, earn EXP and all that stuff, only it handles the "art of warfare" very nicely. Swings and blocks are required consisntently.
Despite the limited content, there are still mods, various game modes and I just keep coming back to play more Black Knight Mode (a mod that lets you lose limbs in combat, I highly recommend picking it up!)
The only thing I advise: You will find some pretty nice people, every now and then, who are worth adding and training with in duel mode. However, most of the times, the community can pretty toxic for absolutely no reason and in some duel servers you are going to find idiots who can't read server descriptions for♥♥♥♥♥♥and just straight-up kill you for no reason. So it's best not to let anything get to your head, just find a new game or play with your friends. Don't let it tempt you not to play this game.
I definitely recommend picking it up, even if it doesn't go on offer.
You can even get the "Deadliest Warriors" DLC (which should of been a part of the game, in my opinion, but I digress), which allows you play as a Samurai, Knight, Ninja, Pirate, Viking and Spartan characters.

The Steam store page has this word in the description "meditative". Meditative this game is CERTAINLY not.
I'm having very conflicting thoughts on this game. On the one hand, I'd highly recommend it for it's superb music, atmosphere, innovative platforming (because in essence, this is a platformer) but this game also fails on a basic level with it's frustrating controls (even on the controller which is "highly recommended") and sub-par level design.
I'll go through the positive stuff first. This game has a very innovative concept. It is a platformer yet not really. The levels are entirely driven by a circular structure with transitions being radial wipes that black out most of the level except the tiny white island you are on and then revealing the rest with another radial wipe. This method is quite effective at getting a few ‘wow’ moments and some of the levels are really unique to play with. The music is fantastic and quite soothing and I would probably buy the soundtrack to listen to later.
Now for the negatives. Whew.
Let’s start with the controls because they are what exacerbate everything else that’s wrong with the game. The levels being circular, the devs decided (stupidly I might add) that at the center, the square would move faster than at the edges. This means the distance you are away from the center affects your speed quite a bit. Early levels make use of this but the later levels are PURE HELL because of this, leaving me frustrated many times when I would miss an opening by millimeters purely because of how slow I would move on the outer edges. The square also has this extremely floaty feel and doesn’t do exactly what you tell it. This is compounded and becomes a nightmare once the red areas are introduced which are insta-gibs if you touch them. Making circular levels also means moving around the circle at a single radius i.e. always at the same distance from the center (which is required MANY times) which is incredibly frustrating because it is not easy to do and has actually made me curse quite a few times.
The level design is weak, lazy and makes average use of the original setting. Most of the levels can be simply boiled down to “get to the other side of a corridor with stuff that will crush or insta-kill you” and the others are weak maze levels. Simple concepts are stretched to breaking points with the same levels repeated multiple times and sometimes just longer versions of the same level for laughs. There are also numerous unfair deaths and going through the game without dying on the first try is impossible because there will be things about the level blocked off from view that you will not expect. To make matters worse, there are levels with most of the visuals blacked out leaving you to guess what would happen next. The “boss battles”, a time-sensitive speedrun of all the various types of levels you just went through but just slightly harder enough to make them more frustrating and to cap it off, dying anywhere will get you right to the start and you have to go through the whole process yet again. What I noticed is you will almost never die to the “boss” which is usually some red circular section of blocks chasing you but always from poor telegraphing of the levels themselves. The final nail in the coffin is the final 10 minutes of the game which are literally a revision of every single level you just faced albeit dumbed down. I really didn't want to go through memories of the levels though the game seems to think this should have elicited a response other than anger and disillusion.
A beautiful but ultimately frustrating experience, writing this review only made me realize how little I actually enjoyed the game. I don’t really recommend it for a “meditative experience” but if you’re one for challenging platformers and can handle the generous helpings of rage-quit it throws at you, by all means you are welcome to it. Maybe buy this on a sale or with a bundle as I did.

All in all, I find this game way more appeling than its more modern counter-part, Skyrim. In my opinion the guilds are a lot more immersive and in-depth as you work your way up the chain in a way that makes sense for that particular group; battling evil necromancers and getting recommendations for the arcane university, rather than Skyrim's cast a simple spell get into the arcane college. The main story is also pretty epic, as the invasion of the daedra draws near ever minute, you along with the local Blades need to take certain actions to stop this onslaught. Need a break from quests or need something else to do in the game? Well you can make your own adventures by clearing the local fort or dungeon, either by yourself or with a group of adept adventures behind your back. The only issues I came across dealt with the leveling up/character build mechanic. Cookie-cutter characters are hard to make as a wizard build has to be purely towards the most magicka to cast the higher tier spells; warrior builds and theif builds aren't as restricting, but are still a little rigid. Also at a certain point your character becomes "too good", as your attributes hit insane heights. You become really hard to kill, save for a room FILLED with top quality enemies or a named legendary enemy. I'll admit that the perk system of Skyrim is better, as it rewards using skills and allows for intresting characters to form. Would give this game around a 9.5/10. The DLC's are amazing btw!

You like the Norse theme, isometric turn based battle, RPG games in general?
You should sure try this one.
The game is no innovation in any field, but it is definitely made with a soul. It does have downsides, but is is quite personal whether they overweight the positive sides. For me they don't, and by a large degree. Here go things that I immediately remember thinking about the game, I'm not trying to give it a detailed look, mind that.
So the goods:
- Believable setting. It is not generic, it is a true-like story with events that actually have me read the text instead of scrolling down through blah blah to 'where do I need to go now?'
- The game does not make you play a morally good person by any means. I mean, I'm tired of games where making moral choices is also the most beneficial way to go. Where being good is pure good with no downsides. Here you have choices that will leave somebody unhappy anyway, and you can't please everybody. And by unhappy I mean things like a grieving mother of a sick kid, or an orphan killed because he wanted to eat. Feels like choices of a real man, and not of a Chosen One who can miraculously plant gardens of Eden wherever he goes.
- Generally fine mechanics of an RPG game. You have loot, inventory, damage, resistances, bows, all that stuff.
- No magic! Finally a game with no spells or mages, like that is a must. Some abilities that are needed gameplay-wise, but look like magic, are disguised best they can with a materialistic approach. So, we won't be fighting with fireballs, but that is good, because I can finally play in a realistic setting, and not another Diablo game with Norse flavor.
- Good battle system. Now I'd like to say that battle is quite easy, and you should play on insane for any challenge, and battle is missing some good things it could use, like formations, but in general I'm having fun with it.
Bads:
- There is some unpolished mechanics. Like you need to loot hundreds of boxes in a very tedious point-and-click manner. Or you can not camp in a city and need to go to a nearby forest for that.
- Now this one is controversial, but with me definitely a flaw. Half of warriors in the game are women. You are even forced to have females in your crew at first. I have no problem with female
warriors in other games, and devs can generally put in their games whatever they want, but this game has a strong claim at being realistic, which it in many aspects is. Coming across a game that (finally!) does not portray the Norsemen as half naked brutes in horned helmets, I would really want to have its setting as realistic as possible. And while I quite get it that catering to the audience who wants female warriors is more profitable then not, that fabulous intent to depict the society of the days gone in a true-like manner should have at least found reflection in a small tick in settings, that would put the girls out of the dangers of battle.
As a conclusion, I do enjoy the game as it is now. The flaws, whether they are going to be fixed or not, do not break its charm. I greatly appreciate the effort that the devs have put into it, and I hope it is not the last thing about medieval times we see from them.

First of all I want to say that this was my first time playing a Hakuoki Game,
so I can't really speak of that disappointment many experienced players speak of, since my own experience was a completely different one.
Someone mentioned that "there wasn't even a kiss scene" which is true as far as I am aware of (only played three different routes so far one main and two of the treasure box routes), however I kind of feel like reminding people to think of the time (or era) and place. It's not like today, where you're already smooching each other's faces and dropping your panties on the second date or something. Though, even today (as far as I know) Japan isn't all over that public affections thing, so that's something to keep in mind when playing a game like this one. You need to learn to appreciate the small things like the character of your choice choosing to hold hands with you or just standing closer to you than would be considerate "normal". That 'complaint' of many people was something I really wanted to get off of my chest here. However, like I mentioned before, this was my first time playing a Hakuoki game so I'm unable to say if the rage over there being too little romance in the game is justified or not.
For someone like me, who was new to the world of the Hakuoki Games, I can say that it's totally worth to buy the game. The plot is nice, the characters amazing and I found myself often lost in the game for hours without realizing it. Don't let yourself be discouraged by the whole "there's no romance so don't buy it" comments from actually buying this game. Since, the only two things I can really complain about myself is the fact that at some parts the voices quited down a bunch so I couldn't hear them over the music (when they were mostly murmuring to themselves, so maybe that's partly intentional?), but then there were voices like Shinpachi's at times when I felt like I needed to plug out at least one of my earphones to make sure I wouldn't take the risk of possibly going deaf from his next line. The second part is more of a personal thing than a real flaw of the game. The treasure box supposedly gave you more possible romances with more characters, but there were two characters I had a huge interest in for they could possibly have opened up two completely new paths or points of views to the game and situation the MC was in, but instead I found myself thinking that we were offered characters that only differ slightly from some others in personality even if the whole stories behind them are all interesting in itself.
Long story short, if you're new to the Hakuoki games and keep the time and place of the setting in mind in regards of the 'lacking' romance (seriously, I found myself wondering where said lack was after reading some reviews and then playing the game myself 'cause it's subtle, yes, but plenty) then go ahead and buy this and most likely enjoy it, asking yourself what all the negative reviews are about.
If you're an experienced player of the Hakuoki games then maybe you should stick to said negative reviews of those other experienced players and wait for the "full" game to come around or just.. buy this to support the idea of games like Hakuoki coming to Steam or Hakuoki and the people behind it anyway?
Either way, can't agree with the people who say to not buy this game
since instead of feeling frustrated I ended up looking forward to the next and how all the MC and I as a player experienced so far wil carry over into a new experience and story.

Conan exiles is all about survival. Everything from temperature to rabid animals, monsters and demons are out to get you. You have to build shelter, increase your stats and upgrade your gear before you can expect to explore very far. The world itself has just gotten bigger with the "Frozen North" update (a high lvl area you'll want to be at least lvl 30 to visit) and it's all quite stunning to behold. You definitely feel like you're in the world of Conan. Though the big guy himself makes no real appearance in-game, you have a few key npcs that will divulge lore, emotes and religions. On occasion you may run across some ghostly spectres who will give you clues to other goings on (and help you learn a few more emotes). And now there are 3 dungeons to explore (one on the south river, the other two up north) that can reward you with new item recipes if you can survive them.
With all that though the game can still feel a little empty at times since there are no real "quests" - its all sandbox for you to figure out as you go. Where the game really shines is PVP and base raiding. Siege weapons, throwable explosives and even god summoning allows you to do some major destruction to your foes and their forts.
It will take you time, there are occasional bugs and more content is upcoming, but if you dare to brave it - the game can be quite rewarding. Bringing real life friends into your guild makes it doubly so.

While it's definitely not a perfect game, I definitely still recommend it. The description does say it's the first of a two part series - something very apparent by the time you reach the end. It's clear it's not a complete story.
I feel the '80 hours of romance' is a huge overstatement on several fronts. Even though it is necessary to play through multiple times to really get the full story (and it can be fun to uncover all the different moments available based on the choices you make), there's a lot of repeating what you've already read.
The art is hontestly flat out *gorgeous* on all fronts, though. All sprites are well designed, including the side characters. CGs are also beautifully done.
The 'extras' in the cast do have a bit of no-eyes syndrome going on but the protagonist, at least, has a face when she appears in CGs so that's a definitely plus – and it makes the no-eyes extras more forgivable.
There are also a lot of really gorgeous backgrounds. A lot. Because the scenery changes quite a bit, there's a huge variety of different environments and a lot of small details that really add to the experience (such as showing a simple ceiling BG when the protagonist is lying in bed.) It feels like they went to a lot of lengths to ensure the game was visually appealing. The fight sequences are also well done, and are set up in a way that makes them more engaging than just looking at static sprites on static backgrounds.
The simple animations definitely enhance the experience. And the lip-synch animation is actually done much better than a lot of visual novels. So props there.
All the love interests I've played so far have distinct personalities. While some characters have similar traits, each one is still unique enough to stand out from the others, which is really nice in a game with so many potential love interests. I think the characters are interesting and, for the most part, likeable. Some characters have clear and interesting development as well, which makes the story fun to read.
The writing, from a technical standpoint, is well done. Things are written clearly, they're easily understandable, though there are a few typographical errors here and there.
But…as I mentioned above. '80 hours'? I just don't see it.
First of all, there's not much 'romance' to speak of - much less 80 hours of it. Most of this part of the story focuses on the political goings on around the protagonist so she actually spends comparatively little time with whatever specific love interest you're pursuing. What scenes she does have tend to be more on the platonic side - there are exceptions and some routes have more obvious hints at romance than others. These moments are often short and don't really go far beyond hints until the latter chapters of a few routes.
But  I just struggle to see how there's 80 hours of content at all, due to the sheer amount of re-reading previously read content. It seems extremely exaggerated at best (unless the 80 hours refers to parts one and two together. In which case, it seems misleading to list the complete amount what is only part of the story).
Personally, I find the story to be the weakest part of this visual novel. While the characters are interesting, fun, cute, and often intriguing…
They frequently get a bit lost in a story that's trying to juggle too many events, too many sub-plots and a too-huge time scale. Characterization and relationship development often suffer while the story tries to cram a huge amount of historical upheaval into a fairly condensed game experience.
To be safe, I'll put the rest below spoiler tags:
All these elements together cause the story to sometimes buckle under its own weight. I found myself really dissatisfied, at times, with how sluggish things were moving and at others I was frustrated because it felt like I was just skimming the surface of what could be a really detailed story.
All of that may seem like a serious gripe but this visual novel definitely has parts that are enjoyable. There are some fantastically lovable characters, and it's definitely a joy to just look at. Seriously. The art's
beautiful.
For those thinking of buying the game, I recommend waiting until it's on sale. Lovely as it is, I don't think the story content warrants the full price. Despite its length, it very much feels like a prologue or set up to a longer story. Which explains the skips through time and glossing over of certain story elements and the lack of development in some areas. It feels very much like it's just prepping you for what's to come.
All of that's fine, honestly. But I wouldn't personally pay full price for something that doesn't really read like a full game/story.

My favourite Otome game, bar none.  This game has beautiful art, an excellent soundtrack, and complex stories that are rich with true-to-history detail.  This is a game best enjoyed by those who enjoy a more true-to-life historical romance; be prepared for a "slow burn" type of approach with most of the romanceable guys.
**Very Important**:  This isn't a Voltage or D3 Labs style game, and this is only the FIRST HALF of the full story for each guy.  This means more reading and fewer modern "romance" elements, at least in Kyoto Winds, the localized version of Hakuoki Shinkai: Kaze no Shou (the game was released in 2 parts in Japan as well).  Barring the supernatural elements, this game stays relatively faithful to the feel and standards of the historical setting, which is 1864 Japan (i.e., Victorian times, from an English-world perspective).  The second half of the game, with the final route endings, is being localized and is likely coming out in the Spring of 2018.
If you read the reviews, you will see that what most people dislike is that the game ends halfway through the main story lines.  This was unavaoidable because this game has twice as many routes (romance interests) as the original and adds content even for the original characters.  If it is important to you to have complete routes from the get-go, I recommend playing the mobile version of the game (Android and iOS) or the PS3 version (still my favourite version, as it has so much fun extra content).  There are only half the routes, however.  Also, there is less overall story.
PROS:  One of the best otome games out there *if* you like historical drama and don't mind a slow burn romance style.  The romance is all there, just a little less overt than in a lot of current games, except for a couple of characters.
CONS:  As in Japan, this game is only the first half of each story, which many find dissatisfying.  We'd all like to play each route all the way through!

As a Kentuckian and a patron of the arts, Kentucky Route Zero has quickly become one of my favorite indy games. One part existentialist play, one part art piece, and one part point-and-click adventure, it's incredible how much this one game manages to pack in without being too much to handle. Every part of the game is in-depth and interesting from the conversations, the interactive "sets", and the characters themselves. The minimalist art design and the vague, often melancholy/mysterious dialogue compliment each other perfectly giving the game its signature feel which is really undescribable. Upon multiple playthroughs, one finds that the different conversation choices available can drastically change the experience and mood of the game; not from the technical standpoint but more the emotional experience of the player.
While not a fast or necessarily exciting game gameplay-wise, various types of interesting and fun gameplay are introduced early on and continue throughout the different acts of KRZ. Examples of these gameplay styles being the character-oriented gameplay, travel gameplay, and perhaps the most fascinating of all, traveling on the Zero. These gameplay styles tie into the story which is exciting in its complexity and immersiveness, new sub-plots are constantly introduced keeping the game fresh. The often loose ends of these sub-plots, mentioned briefly perhaps in a passing conversation, give the characters depth and mystery.
I find myself lost within the world of KRZ every time I play and am almost tempted to drive out on the highways featured within the game (highways I know well) to see if I can find the Zero and explore it myself.
10/10
The additional "mini games" free for download, Limits and Demonstrations and The Entertainment, are both equally as intriguing as KRZ itself. While very fast to play, they provide small pieces of possibly important exposition which can be found referenced within KRZ if the player pays attention. The blending of storytelling throughout various games/time periods is genius. Both of these free games contain the same gameplay mechanics of KRZ so they are easy to jump right into after playing the main game. Definitely worth downloading and playing if you have a few minutes and want to expand your knowledge of the KRZ universe.
The script for The Entertainment is available for purchase in paperback for a very low price. I bought it and love having a piece of the KRZ universe that I can hold in my hands and read. Really fascinating.

Kentucky Route Zero is a magical realism novel, written as a play, presented as a video game. Beautiful graphics combine with a terrifically atmospheric soundtrack that elevates this game from simple point-and-click adventure to an engrossing, artistically rendered narrative. Though I completed the first two acts in about an hour a piece, there's pleanty more to be explored, lending the game some extra replay value. Unfortunately, most of what you might miss on that first playthrough are set pieces that don't really seem to go anywhere—in Act I, for example, you can stop to watch two broken-looking men push a plane down the highway. These types of scenes are undoubtedly beautiful, and English majors like myself will delight in them, but ultimately they're just well-rendered vignettes. There's also replay value to be found in alternate dialogue choices, a nice element that gives you the illusion that you're directing the story or character development.  The fact that these are illusions only strengthens the game's narrative—there's a heavy focus on illusion, surrealism, and mystery here, and these odd scenarios, characters, and locations will leave you dying for more.

I just finished the game, and while the bugs are indeed prevalent I still recommend it.
Something about the turn based combat feels a bit off. I can't quite place it. Maybe it's how fast you can drop enemies and how archers are a bit too strong. Combat resolves bit too fast while also taking bit too long because the animations are too slow for my taste. Critical hits for example are impactful, but after first couple of times you don't want to watch a person stagger for a few seconds while you're unable to do any other commands or attacks for that duration.
I like that there's no to hit roll in melee combat, but status effects are insanely strong, often death sentences. So it feels like they replaced standard attack RNG with even worse instakill RNG.
For example, if you don't resist a stun with your resistance roll, you not only can't act next turn, but you lose all your damage reduction and can be hit with dagger skill deathblow that doubles damage. This means if enemies have a dagger user left to act after a successful stun, it's an instant kill even on a dude that normally has strongest armor in the game and maximum endurance stat.
I played on insane difficulty, but even counting out the damage modifiers that it causes, the instant kills are still there.
Both sides take their all turns at the same time, so considering how quickly people die, whichever side starts the combat has too massive advantage.
In spite of these problems, the game tells a good story, is overall enjoyable, and easily worth the price. Like many others have mentioned, if the bugs are fixed and combat is made a bit better, the game could be a masterpiece.

Summary
=======
An artistic circular maze and puzzle game. This is a game that focuses on art. It is abstract, short, simple and a tiny bit hard. More of an experience than a game.
Review
=====
The game starts off by highly recommending a controller. It's not only not required but I personally do not recommend it. The keyboard is much more precise than a controller will ever be. Unless your up for a challenge, just use the keyboard.
This is an abstract game were you control a cube through a circular clock like maze. You can die by either being squashed or by touching the red walls. There's not much to explain about the game. It is self explanatory.
This game requires dexterity and precision. Some levels are timed and often require you to handle the cube upside down. This is one of the major difficulties of the game but eventually you get used to it. The game focuses more on being an artistic experience than a difficult game and for that reason it is a short but lightly hard game.
There are two major flaws in this game. Some levels are very well designed and worth checking out but overall the graphics are very bland and repetitive. It is a major flaw of the game, it would benefit from much more variety. The music is nice when it is calm but very annoying when it is loud. Often I had to turn off the music to beat one level.
One minor flaw is that the difficulty and save points are inconsistent. Some levels are much harder than usual. Other times you have to do a lot of parts in one go. It's not that bad however, it is very feasable. It could have been much better balanced however.
Veridict
=====
Pros:
+ Some levels are very well designed
+ Simple to understand and finish
+ Overall it is a nice experience
Cons:
- Repetitive graphics
- Sometimes the music is annoying
- Very short
- Difficulty and save points sort of unbalanced
If you like artistic, abstract, simple, short and lighly hard games, this is a game for you.

100% Orange Juice is a game that when you look at it, seems very similar to Mario Party. In a sense, it is. You collect Stars and cards in order to help you progress through the game. You roll a dice and move around the board and land on a space that has various effects ranging from you to collecting stars or cards, to losing stars and fighting enemies. Now, that's where the similarities end really. 100% OJ is by far more rutheless than Mario Party. Maybe it's just my luck, but even on normal the cpus are brutal and out for blood. If you make one wrong move, or if the game decides it hates you then you can very well go from a blazing lead to being in dead last within the span of a few turns. Now, despite that, the game itself is a lot of fun. Sure, it's a board game with goals that range from collecting a certain amount of stars, knocking out a certain amount of people or a combination of the both.
The game has only 3 modes really, campaign, single matches and multiplayer. Now with any board game, playing with friends is what makes it really shine a bit more. You can play with up to three other friends, using whatever characters you unlocked, making a deck of x amount of cards and then you're put into a board, fighting or running for your life (depending on your play style and character as all characters have different stats.) in order to gain first prize. Now, with all three game modes you ear stars (which are this games currency to buy items from the store.) But only in multiplayer can you gain exp to level up and unlock new items to purchase and the sort, which the game has a decent amount of. Honestly, I suggest giving the demo a try to get a feel for the game, then convince some friends to get the game as well or find some people that would want to play. All in all, it's a fun game but can be frustrating.

Hakuoki plays in the Tokugawa period (Edo Period) and makes use of the names of the most famous Shinsengumi members, which have actually once really existed.
We’ll find ourselves also in the middle of the Shogunat conflict. The whole story is very close to the previously real-life events and it will lead you through a lot of knowledge of japan history. Of course there are many differences as well, but you will be surprised if you google the characters and when you discover how much these fictive characters have in common with the real ones.
Each route has its own personal background story, which will getting interesting, the further you come in the story. At a certain point (only in the next part) the routes will be completely individual and can not be longer compared with each other like in Kyoto Winds, where you are mostly following a common path. The romance is not really present in Kyoto Winds, it is more like a "Meet and great" and it's filled with much information and a lot of story telling. Also, it will give you the chance to get familiar and attached to all of them.
The romance interests are characterized by individuality. Each guy has his good and bad sites. Every bachelor has an own unique story and background.
The MC Chizuro Yukimura (The name is changeable) is in comparison to many other MC's not just a head full of air, plain or just devoting herself to everyone, she has her own mind. It is possible to identify yourself with her personality, her decisions, reactions and her thoughts so it’s not a difficult task to dive completely into her role, if you wish so.
The soundtrack is really beautiful always atmospheric and perfectly fitting into the situations.
Since I don’t want to mention too much from the upcoming love story, which is missing in this game, I just want to say: It will be really worth it. Hakuoki has so many happy, shocking, calm, heartwarming AND heartbreaking moments as well that I can hardly put it into words... so I really look forward to the more detailed romance scenes which will, hopefully, come up with the next part.
One negative thing I have to mention though: I don't think that this game is really 80 hours long... there is a lot of skipping if you're using "Skip Read" after you've played through 2-3 Routes. I don't really like it, that IF isn't honest at some points, that includes that they haven't mentioned the fact in the description, that this game is only the half story.
NOTE: They added it to the description now, but it wasn't mentioned at the release or the days after that.
Nevertheless: Hakuoki is for me one of the best and most enjoyable otomes that even exists and is characterized by an outstanding, well-written and stirring story, which you will think about, many decisions and great characters. Even the side characters are really likable.
I really can't wait for the next game!

Okay, so, I want to start off by saying that I’ve been a Hakuoki fan for a couple of years now. And it’s exactly because I
a fan that I can’t in good faith recommend what essentially amounts to half a game – and the half that
there isn’t even well put-together. Four chapters of a long, absolutely labyrinthine common route, a brief fifth chapter for each love interest, and a “final chapter” that amounts to a non-ending. Frankly, it sucks
My issue with this remake can be summed up pretty simply: it’s too ♥♥♥♥ing big for its own good. The game doesn’t need twelve bachelors, and a million issues of scope follow from there. The common route, which was plenty lengthy in the original, gains more content and branches, none of which it actually needs. It’s exhausting, even with the skip button, and the “Record of Service” feature doesn't really alleviate this. I was so tired by the time I finally,
hit the route-split I was just about ready to stop playing altogether.
On top of that, basically none of the new routes are intuitive to unlock. It’s pretty easy to work out how to romance any of the five original Shinsengumi boys, and only slightly tougher to romance Kazama, but beyond that I got very lost very quickly. I’m an experienced otome player, and I combed and re-combed the common route for a solid hour without finding any of the new content aside from a couple of CGs. There’s just too much there, and it often felt like I was stumbling around blind – and I’m sure it would’ve been even worse for a newcomer. Yes, I could use a walkthrough but, to put it bluntly, I shouldn’t feel like I have to just to get the basic level of engagement. And don’t even start me on the decision to split the game in half; sure, the Steam store description says it’s “the first in a two-part series”, but the only route I managed to get through cut off halfway. Needless to say, this left a really bad taste in my mouth.
It’s a shame, because the artwork is really gorgeous! And I’m interested in meeting the new bachelors! (Even if I think a couple of them are weird choices… did anyone actually ask for Sanan?) Except the game is so high on its own expanded-remake energy that it completely neglects to try and, you know, feel like anything other than a hedge maze. Words can’t do justice to how
I am by the whole experience – this didn’t make me want to buy part two, but it did make me want to go replay the original on PSP. At least that version knew about things like “narrative cohesion” and “closure” and “fun”.

The Land of Eyas is an addictive game that brings unique Physics-based concepts, beautiful artwork, and an intriguing plot line together to form pure gaming enjoyment.  You can get lost for hours playing the simple, yet still so complex and difficult, puzzle levels.  It uses a level hub that allows you to play and re-play levels in different orders so if you get stuck on one level you can always try another and come back later.  Each of these levels is a work of art in itself with the beautiful backdrops and the catchy background music.  However, the true glory of this game doesn't come from its pretty looks but rather its unique use of game Physics to enhance the puzzles.  The Land of Eyas uses a gravity-flipping center line to allow you to propel your character around the game board.  This allows levels with puzzles and solutions that your mind has never thought about before.  This creative concept gives a great feeling of satisfaction when you realize what you can jump off to slingshot yourself to the next goal.  The combination of the artwork, this cool gravity concept, and tight gameplay make this a must have game.  Not to mention the replayability that comes in because of the achievements and level times (Gotta get all perfect times!).  I definitely recommend owning this game and losing hours of your time to it.  You won't regret getting lost in The Land of Eyas!

I feel quite conflicted about Divinity Original Sin 2. On one hand I loved the story, the aesthetics and to a large extend the gameplay. I will remember my time with it quite fondly. However there were times that the game was just throwing things at me on and on again and this started to become so tiring that I just wanted for the damn thing to be over.
The aesthetics and the overall presentation of the game are excellent. It is exactly as I would think a modern top level/isometric RPG to look like. When other developers, like Obsidian, focus on recreating the graphics of games of old trying to score points on nostalgia, Larian moves the genre a little bit forward on the presentation side of the things. And they do it magnificently. The slight desaturation of the color palette in comparison to the first game was much needed as the vibrant colors of the DOS1 would feel slightly tacky at times. Sound, music and voice acting is also well executed and nicely integrated into the game. The use of a live orchestra this time also enlarges the soundscape of the music when it's needed.
The story is definitely not one with intricate complexities however is memorable and has some twists. Your companions' origin stories are also fleshed out and quite interesting. You actually care about them and want to know more about their backstory. In contrast in DOS1 there was no considerable backstory on your companions apart from maybe a quest or two. But on DOS2 the personal stories of the PCs involved are told over the whole progress of the game, which makes them feel more members of your team rather than hirelings. You can also play one of them if you are so inclined. It's a shame that there is no meaningful interaction among your companions though. One problem with the story is that drags the game for TOO DAMN LONG. There are heaps of content in the first two "acts" but after that the story loses momentum. During the last arc when you arrive on Arx there are only a handful of quests overall which is a shame because Arx is a big city and is beautifully presented. But there are few things to do apart from the main quest. It seems like a waste to me. It would be better to spread the content a little bit more evenly. For example I spend more that 2/3 of my gameplay time in the first two areas of the game. There is that much difference in content.
There are also issues with discoverability of the content. Quite a lot of quests are cryptic and you can only encounter them by pure chance. You have to literally comb every area inch by inch in order to find everything. This was a problem with DOS1 though but it's worse in DOS2 due to the much larger world. A lot of quests are also buggy and some of them won't close or their description in the journal is wrong. For instance
. There are all sorts of annoyances with the quests and the journal, but this was the issue with pre-EE DOS1. They will be fixed eventually but it is definitely irritating.
As far as the gameplay is concerned there are several things that are an improvement over the first game. First the tiered skill system is gone and all known skills are available as long as they are memorised, although dedicating an attribute exclusively for the number of spells that a PC can memorise seems like a waste since Memory serves no other purpose whatsoever. Fortunately only a modest investment is required. The rock-paper-scissors minigame is fortunately also gone as it was mostly a hindrance rather than a useful gameplay element.
I left the combat for the end. There are major changes in the combat in comparison to DOS1. Although the issue with the armor mechanic is probably discussed to death I can't say it is entirely bad, but it is not really great either. It makes the battles run a lot longer especially since in late game all your opponents have loads more armor and HP than you, at times an order of magnitude more than your team. And that's on Classic difficulty. I will admit it adds to the tactical aspect of the game but at times it feels tedious and I would are say even not fun. The levels of your characters (and correspondingly of the enemies) also have a HUGE impact on combat. If one of your adversaries is a level higher than your characters you are going to have a bad time. If more of them are you are going to be steamrolled. The same happens with your characters of course. At level 15 you can probably obliterate most level 14 enemies unless there is a dozen of them. The battles are also full of surprises and require you to have a knowledge of how they are gonna play out in beforehand. So now instead of save-scumming to land that sweet critical hit chance you reload because of a cheap trick used halfway through the combat. This is totally normal and welcome for some fights, as boss battles but in DOS2 it happens every other time. If every battle feels like a boss battle the appeal deteriorates rapidly and after a while I started feeling... tired.
All in all I enjoyed the game for most of the time, some aspects of it are a considerable improvement over the first game. However it would be shortsighted to ignore some of its more apparent flaws.

This game is a cute, little platforming game made by an Indie developer. Your goal is to recover lost memories of a... boy in a cat suit. Yeah, you've read that right. Recover parts of your memory as you go through a bunch of mind-streching levels, where each of them have a twist - there are two gravities! Make new friends and enemies among met creatures, uncover the story that goes along and, if you feel up to the challenge, speedrun your way through the puzzles!
As you can clearly see, a good game is not always a game with 20 hours long storyline, side quests, amazing '15 3D graphics with antyaliasing. Sometimes, less is more. This game might not reach the top on Steam, but it definitely should be seen by more people. It's perfect to sit back with a controller in hands, hot coffe on a table and relax for a bit. Unless you're an overachiever in here, then have a great fun speedrunning all those levels and getting 100% of achievements, as The Land of Eyas is perfect for it.

I've been playing Land of Eyas for a while, and have streamed it a buncha times in the past for good fun. Its a pretty solid patformer that uses the under-half of the game world as an inverse gravity field, which allows for puzzles that span large vertical spaces to make bigger and better puzzles. If you like the idea of ibb & obb but never have a second player, this game will do more than just scratch the gravity-inversion itch, but probably leave you wanting more!
Storywise the game makes sense - a kid in giant onesie has to feed glaze-encrusted donuts to a very depressed talking tree. They both have trouble remembering stuff, and I kinda wonder if that inverse gravity layer isn't actually too healthy to be around. Then things start to get nasty when the mechanical gears come out too - there's a red room with a conveyor belt that forces players to use profanity to win.
Seeing all the polish and quality build up and come to fruition has been quite satisfying, and I'm really glad to see the overall result come out so well. Great work, Happy Square!
