Lost with no memory of where he is or how he got there, lead Eyas – a boy in a cat suit – on a quest to get home. But how do you know which way to go when you can’t tell which is up and which is down?
That’s the introduction to this game. The Land of Eyas is essentially a puzzle platform game. I’ll be looking at it primarily from a casual gamer standpoint. Not that I’m actually a casual gamer, but when it comes to platform games, I might as well be.
Let’s start first with the nitty-gritty. This is the stuff that any action game and any platform game has to get right or it’s already a non-starter.
How’s the response? I played with a keyboard. I think platformers are best done with a control pad, but if a game has good keyboard response, chances are it has got good response period. Eyas had good response. I’m comparing this to the rather fussy issues I had when playing Rogue Legacy. I did find the jumping to be a bit “floaty” feeling. As opposed to the “hard” jump of the classic NES Super Mario Bros—if anyone has even played that in the last decade. The sprinting and jumping had the typical response time challenges that I see common in many platformers though, regardless of who is playing them, so I’d say it’s as it’s supposed to be. The type of platforming you’ll do in this game necessitates the type of jump physics that are in the game. Prepare for multiple retries. Thankfully, longer levels have check points.
How’s the performance? I had no frame rate drops on my mid-tier gaming PC. That said, I didn’t get to test on any of the levels that had spinning saw blades, etc. But even so, I’ve seen FPS drops in games on my PC that were less action oriented. So I call this a success as well.
Now that we’ve got the non-starters cleared, how is the game itself? Well, you’ll not find anything revolutionary here. It’s an action puzzle platform game. That’s what you’re going to get. You’re also going to get really beautiful artwork. And that’s what drew me to this game. The boy in the cat suit (Eyas) is cleverly reminiscent of the boy in the white pajamas from Where the Wild Things Are. It’s a savvy decision on the part of the art director. I instantly gravitate to it. The rest of the artwork is crisp, ornate, evocative, and disarming—which is good when your game is a puzzle game and likely to provoke frustration (that’s the nature of the beast). Anything to keep me wanting to look at the game is unequivocally good. I’d almost like to say that artwork is the third rail of platform games these days. Without artwork, what is your platformer bringing to the table that the platformers before it have not already? That Land of Eyas is unapologetically beautiful.
This leads me to the next important aspect of the game: its gimmick. The gimmick is that the force of gravity reverses at the midline of each level. Later levels shake this up further, but this is the core conceit. It looks like a water line. You cross it. Suddenly you find yourself falling up instead of down. It’s not bad as far as gimmicks go, but it’s nothing we haven’t seen before. Does it need to be? What is important is that it adds just enough flexibility to the game that it can present you with some unusual puzzles. So really, I shouldn’t call it a gimmick. That implies that it brings nothing to the table. But it does. It makes you have to look carefully at what’s on your screen to decipher the solution to each level. So really, it’s a game mechanic and it works in favor of the game. Hopefully enough that you find the puzzles in this game to be ones you haven’t seen before. For a casual gamer, I think it succeeds very well.
The story? Well, there’s not a lot of story to interest me initially. You’re a lost boy talking to a talking tree (yes, I meant to write it that way). You’re looking for “Mother” (Isaac anyone?). I won’t say that I was drawn in instantly or anything. Perhaps as you progress you’ll be more invested in the character(s). I wasn’t. But frankly, I don’t play games any more to read a story, certainly not platformers. Play this game for the puzzles. You won’t be disappointed.
Am I going to get 100’s of hours out of this game? No. It’s not a grand strategy game, is it? But what I will get is enjoyment for my time and a sense of accomplishment in nice bite-size brain packets. I need a nice low-stakes diversion from time to time and Eyas provides that. It even opens multiple levels to choose from so if you get stuck on one, you can solve another and give your brain a rest. This allows you to progress the game until you’re ready for a fresh look at that one level you couldn’t solve yesterday. Again, a very savvy development decision. It circumvents the banging-my-head-against-a-wall feeling many other linear platformers have.
Do I have any criticisms of the game? Is there anything I did not like? Yes. I did get frustrated at times by the deadliness of spikes. Rubbing the side of a crystal doesn’t strike me as an offense that should be punishable by death. I’m not play 1001 Spikes, after all. Yes, that’s a real game. The little “hop” you make at the apex of a moving block was inconsistently implemented and therefore annoying. When you’re riding the elevator block, you want to jump at its highest point. This is not possible though because you “hop” when it gets to that highest point… except in cases when you don’t. Which is it? I want consistency here (you can witness this in my gameplay videos if it isn’t clear). The blocks that you can pick up and carry were a great introduction, but there was a 1 pixel exploit I found where a block was essentially hanging in the air. Not sure I want to complain about that one though considering how hard it was to get that block up there in the first place. None of these things stopped me from enjoying the game, though. I’m a rather fickle gamer, also. So it’s a solid testimony to the game’s strengths that I didn’t give up on its weaknesses.
In the end, I easily recommend this game to someone who wants something fun to do with their brain on a Sunday afternoon.

I click to roll my die. I move. I click to roll for combat. I take damage. I'm attacked. I click to roll and die. I roll to revive. Another turn. I roll to revive. Another turn. I roll to revive. Another turn. I roll to revive. At some point, I'm back on my feet. A CPU player intercepts me. I'm knocked back down. "Maybe if I had some cards," I think. The CPU guys are dishing out damage that I can't hope to match. I'm stuck with my weenie deck and no where to go but last place time time and time again. I don't think it'd matter, though, because the dice hate me all the same.
After four games of 100% Luck-and-Grind, I've had my fill. Having to grind stars to buy cards just for the chance of getting something playable is one thing, but the constant abuse of the CPU opponents and terrible combat system completely kill any fun to be had here. This game is sadistic, even on "casual," and the CPU will completely kick you around as they all possess stacked decks and better rolls. It's absolutely infuriating. There's no interesting challenge here, nothing you can overcome with practice and skill. No, you just have to chain yourself to the game, left clicking through loss after loss, farming stars for cards until you can maybe stand a chance against the other AI players and enemies. It's Progress Quest passed off as a legitimate game.
It's too bad, too, because 100% Orange Juice looks nice and has a fair premise, but having to roll to breath takes all the fun out of living. I see people claiming it's fun in multi-player -- which I can see, but then, that goes for pretty much every game in existence -- but having to rely on other humans to overcome the cruel AI just to play what remains a luck heavy time waster isn't saying much. This is a game for anime nerds and RPG fans who think babysitting some enemy spawn point killing creatures for hours just for the chance of a rare drop makes for a great game. I know there's a lack of Japanese cute games on Steam, but we don't have to embrace crap just because there's so little from which to choose.

Once you get beyond the occasionally challenging enemies Shadow Warrior opens up to you as a very enjoyable FPS. Not one that surpasses Duke Nukem 3D mind you, but still a very worthy successor to it.

Having played about 50+hrs, I have beaten the game, played different kinds of characters, remade my choices and so forth.
Enjoyable elements:
Expeditions: Viking is the roleplaying game reminding me about Fallout 1 and 2 (the best titles of the series in my opinion), save your home! Desperation, time limit etc.
The real cake here is your options to upgrade the settlement you try to keep. The change in the village, the peoples reactions are giving the player satisfaction.
The roleplaying elements, choices you can make are interesting but still also limited in certain areas... Trading isn't so straightforward as one might like, you won't get to see much trading happening, if there was certain choices which allowed me to, it was not apparent in any way.
Story: The story is very good, interesting characters and variable conversation options has the chance of making you laugh. This is a good thing. Still, I  was left wanting for more. More content, more alternative gameplay outside the main quest which in my opinion is quite short.
Gameplay:
The numbercrunching tactician can find certain enjoyment but in the end, it is very straightforward which builds will work the best into making the optimal hird. If you really want the best, you will most likely make use of few story characters and build your own mercernaries. Still, that wont be nesseccary even on the hardest difficulty, the game is punishing but rewards clever play as well. You don't need the absolute best damage to win if you can outplay the AI, which isn't the hardest since it's quite limited. It's a casual rpg game for the adventurer who enjoys a short story., not a grand challenging game like Disgaea, if you want that - dont go here.
Now I have been quite positive yes? Yes?
Let's go into my negative points:
Short story campaign, few "real" options. quite linear in the end.
Limited rpg feeling, this game simply lack "that" which Fallout 1-2, Baldurs Gate etc had. No, magic isn't what I mean..
The worst negative point of all: GAMEBREAKING BUGS
So many in fact, I had to restart the game several times to make it playable. Resolution does not stay the same, you have to constantly go to options and change, check to make sure you are playing on the correct one, having the wrong one for your computer can make the game crash in several ways. Blackscreens occur frequently for some, for me it mainly happenes on 2 locations in the game.
DID I MENTION GAMEBREAKING BUGS?
I couldn't finish the game without cheats since at the last battle, enemy units made the game freeze forever, no matter what I did - so I cheated, still. I was so overpowering strong at that time, that I could finish of several enemy units per turn, so I did not feel any shame in cheating to pass the GAMEBREAKING BUGS.
I like this game alot and will most likely play again to explore what more it can offer, but I can't recommend this game as a FINISHED PRODUCT, since it clearly isn't. THIS GAME IS NOT A FINISHED PRODUCT in my opinion, it launched too early.
I hope the developers didn't shoot themselves in the knee for doing this. Games which lack the feeling of a finished product when released does not always continue to sell well, many players would give up a half-finished work like this and move on into somethine else, something finished. Never to return.
When the developers have finished the product, they will most likely be hard pressed to release a DLC along with hotfixes to keep the interest in the game and return customers who most likely demanded a refund from facing these bugs. Testing their own game is all well and important to do, it isn't always good to allow customers to beta-test since it doesn't always give off the feeling of a professional company. Maybe they need to hire a quality game tester to help them keep these kind of gamebraking bugs from suprising them in the future.. after launch.
I am positive though, hopefully their next title won't have the same issues at launch!

Quite honestly Warframe is a very good game. If i were to go into full detail about it, we would be here all day. In short however there are a few main points that i believe warrant attention from anyone planning on playing this game for the first time or who have played it years ago and are now just coming back to it.
First and foremost Warframe can be summed up as a whole in the phrase "F2P Done Right" very aptly. The world of Warframe has you plop down into the role of a "Tenno", a skillful warrior with a variety of abilities to wield as you see fit. The three starting "Warframes" (essentially classes for reference) are Mag, Volt and Excalibur, each having their own strengths and weaknesses from a field of energy that redirects bullets toward your enemies, to a protective shield that you can fire through for more damage, to finally a 360 degree flash of searing light that blinds enemies and opens them to "Finishers" (executions/sneak attacks basically).
Following this you continue to progress though the Star Map (Solar System, called Origin) learning more about the history of the system and yourself as well as fighting various factions that war for its resources and artifacts of an ancient civilization called the Orokin, (Factions being Grineer, Corpus and Infested), again with their own strengths and weaknesses that you will become aware of as you progress. Saying more onto the story would involve spoilers and as such, i will continue onto other points.
The world that D.E. (Digital Extremes) has created is quite honestly expansive and interesting in many ways, from a lore perspective for instance, alot of it isn't just handed to you via lore dumps but rather it is on the player to collect entries in what is refered to as the "Codex" as well as to take the time and read through the various subjects contained within.
Another point that is highly praise worthy is its combat mechanics. In short, there are very few games that have a fluidity in combat like Warframe does. When i first started playing i procceeded under the assumption that its movement was standard fair, it wasn't until i started jumping and sliding and eventually combining the two that this fluidity became very apparent, and it wasn't long before "bullet jumping" (a combination of sliding and jumping) was second nature and now the primary way of very quickly traveling the in game maps as well as engaging targets in melee combat.
Following this the game have many interesting core design concepts, such as a Mod system wherein you can increase various aspects of your weapons stat profile to create interesting combinations. This goes hand in hand with a new type of weapon (at the time of this review) called Zaws, essentially modular weapons that you can build for increased customization. Along side this is a variety of attachments, color schemes and variant armor/weapon models that you can mix and match in order to personalize your equipment; short of adding your own content into the game, which again can actually be done via TennoGen (Community Created Content)
An important note for all those interested should be that no money is "required" to play this game, you can grind out and obtain all weapons and frames in game from various source, including "Vaulted" (Items no longer obtainable at the current moment) via in game trading between players. Plat (IRL currency) isn't pushed on you either for the most part, and the decision to buy some is actually a choice, especially for those of us that do so to help D.E. continue to make their game, rather then shoved down your throat at every given opportunity and enforced via limiting player power that every other development team seems to like doing. All of this being in addition to in-game ways of obtaining Plat such as selling Prime Parts to other players, these parts coming from "Relics" which are easy to obtain.
Finally, it would be remise of me to not talk about the enviorments in which you play for the majority of the game. These enviorments are procedurely generated (with some minor exceptions) from "Tile Sets", meaning that while you will still see some of the same rooms, that how proceed through the level still feels varied enough. This comes along with the Tile Sets changing depending on which planet you are on and if you are fighting a specific enemy ("Infested")
In Summary, Warframe is quintessentially one of the best F2P games currently on the market and i would most definately recommend its to any and all that are interested by what i have said above. In my time (490 hours at the time of this review) playing the game, i can more assuredly say that i have not wasted a single moment of it, having had things to do at every point along the way. Thank you for reading, and if you do decided to play, good hunting Tenno.

OK. Let me start by saying that i liked this game a lot. If it weren't for the bugs i'd say this was one of the best all time and definately THE best value for money games i've ever played. That being said there are some issues.
Firstly the bugs. They are numerous and while they dont happen every minute they do happen often enough to cause annoyance once you've been playing for a while and have experienced a few. Now i know it's a new game and i hope these will be fixed in time, if so i think EV will go on to be a major winner for LA.
Secondly there are some really basic things missing that give the game an almost 'unfinished' feeling. The camera needs work, a little more info on some of the quests would be good, the quick bar set up needs an overhaul, the ability to attack  any target would be good. All these things are pretty basic.
OK, what i love about this game. Character generation/customization, outstanding. The combat simple is simple and aside from some bugs i hope they fix worked pretty well for me. As a veteran roleplayer i love to see a game where you can create a character and then develop them as the game progresses, this game does this in spades.
What i don't like about this game. The scope, its too narrow, this game has the potential to be so SO SO much more than it is. Unfortunately LA doesnt seem to be interested in making THAT game so for now i'll have to make do. The initial campaign map is too limited, the time limit is ludicrous and there is no give and take between yours and any other region. Now i have not been able to play the game through to the end yet so if that comes later i apologize.
In short if you have the patience to play through the bugs then yes get this game, if you dont wait a while or get it on sale. I don't think you'll be disappointed.

There's a fantastic game in there somewhere, but in its current state Expeditions: Viking is tough to recommend.
It's riddled with bugs, from frequent crashes and quests which break if you explore areas in a sequence other than the one intended, to enemy turns never ending and locations not becoming available when they're supposed to. I lost hours of progress on multiple ocassions as a result.
It also entirely lacks polish. There are random events which occur while you travel, but there seems to be only 2 or 3 of them for land and for sea, which means you'll be having characters drink from a lake with a rotting deer in it or spotting an abandoned fishing boat dozens of times by the end of the game.
Balance also seems to have been given little consideration, and archers are far and away the most powerful unit, for both you and the enemy. It's not uncommon to lose 2-3 of your units before you even get a turn if you're up against enemies with several archers in their ranks, and the inability to arrange your squad in combat means you'll often start with your healers and ranged units out front, and your melee in the back. What's really baffling is that this is a step backwards from Expeditions: Conquistador, which allowed you to arrange your squad prior to battle. Gone too is the trap setting system from that game, which allowed you to place obstacles and traps before a defensive battle. So while units have many more abilities than they used to and are far more customisable, the combat itself feels much more basic than the previous game.
Camping also takes a step back from Conquistador, with it feeling more like a chore than a core mechanic. While in Conquistador your explorations were limited by ever dwindling resources and camping was key to managing those, in Viking I was swimming in rations and meat for the entire game, and so camping became an arbitrary action to complete whenever the fatigue indicator popped up. No planning or strategy to it, just a menu you have to click through before continuing.
On the whole, a severe disappointment.

(Review code was supplied free of charge by the publishers. TL;DR at the bottom)
The Land of Eyas is a unique and mentally challenging puzzle-platformer developed by Happy Square Productions as a result of a successful Kickstarter campaign. You play as a boy, Eyas, who wakes up in a cat suit in a strange world with no memory and a talking tree who may be able to help him. The game acts as a support group for people like me because I finally feel like someone understands me. Until this game, I thought I was the only person who constantly wakes up in a cat suit, talks to a tree, has difficulty telling which way is up and which way is down, and forgets about what happened the night before. But that all changed with The Land of Eyas.
As I briefly alluded to before, the unique game mechanic you'll see in The Land of Eyas is the two dimensions that exist in every level. There's this wavy horizontal line that represents the center of gravity, and your character is always pulled to it. So when you fall below it, it pulls you up, and when you're above it, it pulls you down. You'll have to find ways to use this mechanic to your advantage in every level if you hope to make progress in your adventure. This, alongside other game mechanics like building blocks, makes the game require you to take a moment and plot your way to the end of the level. It's not the kind of platformer where you simply make your way onwards - no. The Land of Eyas is a platformer where you'll have to think hard in order to complete the level as you would to solve a math problem. Just as soon as you think that you've mastered the use of the gravity horizon the game will throw more mechanics at you like saw blades and building blocks. You'll constantly have to adapt to these new mechanics in order to continue achieving success.
As if the game wasn't hard enough there are challenges you'll have to complete if you wish to experience everything the game has to offer. Remember that talking tree I mentioned earlier? Well, some levels have seer stones within them that you have to return to the tree in order for him to discover the truth behind his lost memories. These seer stones are often challenging to get and require you to really go out of your way and think even harder than you would to simply complete the level. The levels also display "perfect" times in the top right corner that you may attempt to match or beat, but I don't see any indication that the completion of these challenges in particular will unlock any kind of content.
The soundtrack and sounds in general are also very nice. The music is often fast paced, rushing you onwards and driving you to make mistakes, and sometimes it is mysterious, serving as a reminder of the strange world you've found yourself in. As for the sounds, there's something oddly satisfying about the "thump" you hear when your character lands. Similarly, there's something oddly disturbing about the sound you hear when your character perishes. The music and sounds within are fitting and add to the game wonderfully.
The art style is rather unique and it feels like there is more than one art style throughout the game. You can tell by looking through the screenshots on the Store Page that there are a plethora of different color palletes and environmental themes used throughout the game. There are bright levels, dark levels, cloudy levels, earthy levels, industrial levels...you get the point. Eyas's design is memorable yet it's also a direct copy and paste job of my cat suit. Shameful (/s).
Weaknesses...I suppose it's a good thing that I have to think hard in order to come up with weaknesses. The story is
but ultimately I feel like it serves as a backdrop to the gameplay, rather than what urges you to push forward. I haven't completed the story, but at the same time I don't feel motivated whatsoever by it. I wish there were more NPCs to run into and speak with, but they are far and few between. I also wish the game could make me care more about the story in the first place. I really don't care how Eyas got to where he is to be honest, just as I don't really care how and why I wake up in a cat suit occasionally. The only thing motivating me is the challenge of completing all of the levels. I also think you should be able to zoom out whenever you'd like, instead of it doing it automatically at certain points within the level. Furthermore, I wish checkpoints were slightly more plentiful (or better positioned) in some levels, but that's probably just me.
I'm very, very picky when it comes to platformers. I hate the ones that provide an artifical amount of difficulty. I hate the ones where you constantly die and get teleported back to the beginning. That♥♥♥♥♥♥gives me motion sickness. But I like The Land of Eyas - I really do. It has a charm and uniqueness about it that I'm drawn to. I like the music in it and I like the freshness each level presents. I never feel like it's getting repetitive as some platformers tend to. I haven't completed the game yet but I certainly plan to, just because I want to see what other game mechanics will be thrown at me. I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys platformers. I see and appreciate the hard work that was put into this game and I wish the developer the best of luck.
The Land of Eyas is a charming, challenging game with a touch of mystery. It's unique gameplay and unique world come together to create a memorable experience. While the story falls short, you'll be encouraged to complete the game simply to overcome the challenges it presents.

Best advice I can get is to judge the game for yourself and not by the rating. I hesitated too, but have no regrets. This game has great depth. If you love to build, decorate, explore, enslave the local population, fight, and delve into interesting dungeons this is a game for you. If you like Ark or Fallout 4 building you will enjoy Conan Exiles for that aspect alone. Various armors and weapons that can get dyed and mixed up for your play style. Game has a survival aspect that is decent, but not too annoying like other games. In my experience, this game is best played on a privately owned public server. I enjoy the PvE RP servers I have found. The PvP is not my thing in this game because you are forced to build certain ways for defense rather than something that is more practical and realistic.
Next patch is releasing even more building pieces with the ability to equip your thralls and future plans for mounts, additional armors and weapons soon. Game has come a long way in just the couple months I have been playing. Devs are active and give weekly updates on what is going on and what their plans are. Highly recommend giving this game a chance. Come check out Linnah's Oasis RP-PvE server for plenty of help and players.

1st person shooter / post apocalyptic survival / action game. Atmospheric game with open world feel, that takes place after S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl and is the last game in series. Once again you are inside the zone, but this time action takes place in outskirts and eventually town of Pripyat itself. You start off as an army man sent to zone, after few military helicopters have crash landed for no clear reason. With help of scientists, random stalkers and different faction groups, you must get to the bottom of what really happened.
You have three big areas on map you can explore, though they are somewhat empty and lack detail. There are occasional anomalies, landmarks, structures and machinery that spark the interest in exploring them, but very often you tend to not find anything of great value as everything is looted long time ago. Areas are still filled with radiation, anomalies and horrors, similar to previous games, with some new creatures.
There are decent number of side missions available, ranging from escort and protection, artifact hunt, mutant slaying to fetching stuff, finding tools and helping scientists with... Science, etc. There are no faction outposts this time around, like in S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky, but stalkers, mutants and other faction NPCs very often patrol many areas of map. You start the game somewhat neutral to everyone. Because of that you can safely observe firefight between factions, and afterwards safely scavenge defeated enemies. I find it to be funny as well as profitable endeavor, though you have to keep eye on carry weight as too much weapons in your bag can make travel a real burden. But nothing is more profitable as artifacts, they are still the best source of income, and you should regularly check anomalies with artifact detector.
Similar to S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky, you also have gear and weapon modifications that you can acquire from expert technicians, though some will require you to find specific tools. There's a decent amount of armor, weapon and gear variation, almost everything can be repaired and modified with help of local technician to suit your needs. Some technicians can't operate without good quantities of Vodka, so make sure you carry few bottles of those not just for anti radiation purposes, but also technician food. Speaking of food, you have to eat regularly to keep yourself full of energy, and I'm not kidding. Occasional sleep wont hurt as well, as you can replenish your strength and pass the time if you don't like nighttime.
From my point of view, S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat is weakest in series, S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky being the most fun I've had and S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl following closely just because how atmospheric and unique it was back in the day. I'm sure mods will make this game much better, as I experienced plenty on S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl and loved them. But somehow this particular game, in it's original state is somewhat aged and not as appealing as S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky and S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl was, and I think it's due to splitting of core development team in process of making, or maybe it's my wild guess who knows.
Never the less, game provides good visuals, character design and story telling for the time it was released in. I'll call it a "letdown" sequel to S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl. Game lacks optimization and even on modern system will eat frames, even though it's not even close graphically to S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky. True stalker fans will love it, and if you like apocalyptic games, then give this a shot.

Balances a largely RNG-based system with enough player choice elements to make you feel like what you do matters.  You can choose which direction to take at forks, when to play the cards you've drawn from a deck that combines everyone's personal decks, and whether or not to pick fights with other characters, but whether any of it will actually work comes down to the way the dice roll.
Single player is fun enough, but it's really just a way to teach you how the game works and unlock enough characters and cards to prepare you for multiplayer.  But it's a boardgame, so single player shouldn't be the priority anyway.
Multiplayer is good at creating fun situations and only gives experienced players a small advantage, so it's easy for new players to win without needing to grind single player for cards.
The game is regularly updated and the devs clearly care about keeping the game alive, unfortunately a lot of new content is locked behind DLC and exclusives for buying other OJ games.  They keep things balanced enough that it's not pay to win, but it does impart a disadvantage and can make it feel like you're missing out when half the content is locked away unless you pay several times what the game says it costs.

Reviewing a game this popular, that has been out for a few years might be pointless, but here are my thoughts on SpeedRunners anyways:
If you don't already know, SpeedRunners is a racing game, in which you pick a character who you can customise with a boost trail and character skin (Unfortunately, character skins are just recolours for the most part, and you gotta pay $0.90 per boost skin) and then race around one from a plethora of maps (Workshop included)  in an elimination based  game mode, with up to three other people. Those who fall behind and go off-screen are out of the race, with the last runner standing, I mean running,  being the victor. You also have power-ups, traps and evironmentals to help you, and your oponents, along the way.
It is a unique mutliplayer experience. There's nothing quite like it out yet that has achieved a similar level of success or any notable attention, even 3 years after the game's first appearance on Steam. Rightfully so, as SpeedRunners is still very much alive, peaking at several thousands of players each day.
The game is masterfully presented, with the soundtrack perfectly matching it's aesthetic and theme.  It adds another layer of thrill to what's happening on-screen.
Even if it's a multiplayer centric experience, SpeedRunners bothers to include a Story Mode. While interesting, and having a cool little plot twist at the end, the lack of narrative prevents it from being something truly great and almost nothing more than a tutorial with a few lines of text before each level. This can, however, only be attributed as a minor flaw (albeit a big missed opportunity) and doesn't bog down the core of the game by any means.

Edited on the 5th of May:
Changed into a positive recommendation as the devs are clearly hard at work to fix whatever issues the game still has.
The biggest gamebreaking bugs seem to be fixed with the latest patch, leaving only small, mildly annoying ones here and there. As such I can now, in good conscience, advise people who like the genre, or pillaging in general, to give this game a go.
-----
Bought the game on a whim because the premise was interesting enough. And while I've been pleasantly surprised by it, after putting 18 hours into it, the cons are beginning to outweigh the pros.
On the bright side... the story is good, the setting is engaging and you have plenty of options for roleplay and customization.
The combat is decent, but there's definitely room for improvement.
Sadly, there's quite a few bugs with the game, from the mildly annoying ones to gamebreakers.
The mildly annoying ones revolve around frequent crashes upon leaving areas (but the game autosaves often and loads fast.. so ehh), obnoxiously loud BGM that cannot be muted (looking at you, York) and a quest here and there that seems to bug out and be unable to be finished.
The gamebreaking ones come with corrupted savegames that will cause your game to crash every single time you exit a given area, forcing me to prematurely start a new playthrough....which ended abruptly by another massive bug that caused all my savegames to disappear from the load screen, even though they still are in the game folder.
So... do I feel like I got my money's worth on this?
No. Despite having a great premise, it's unpolished, buggy and seems somewhat unbalanced when it comes to combat.
Maybe it'll be a worthwhile game after a few patches. But not right now.

This is an under-rated and under-played example of classic shooters. If you have a historical interest in the genre, you might want to pick it up. If you've played the newer one understand that this one has a very different feel and plays more like duke nukem; you're rewarded (by not losing health) for winning fights fast and efficiently, not by using each weapon once. Also like any classic shooter, there's a few things that aren't conveyed, so here's some tips:
You should press the use key on absolutely everything to find secret caches. And shoot gongs. Also punching training dummies gives you health. And the sword kills spawning ghosts instantly.
A word of warning: The game is like 3x as hard without autoaim, and the game is more satisfying with it on. The gun and movement mechanics were designed completely around the assumption that autoaim would be on and the user might not be using a mouse. Difficulty 2/4 without autoaim is harder than 4/4 difficulty with it on.

A classic FPS revisited and given a modern port. Not a bad thing in any way, Shadow Warrior, much like its developers other flagship title, is a real relic of its time. Stuck haphazardly in the transition between 2D and 3D it still lives up to be a solid shooter that really couldn't have come from or  been done at any other point.
The initial reliance on melee interaction is.. novel, but the weaponry you are presented with soon outweighs this. Enemy variety, map restrictions and even simple ammo limitations constantly force a change of hand to keep the player on their toes. I wouldn't personally say its as much of a must-play as Doom or Duke, but if youre a fan of either and want more of the same then this is really not a bad starting point.
I suppose my only real gripe is that the port itself is more than a little unhinged. It feels the need to crash at the end of every episode without fail, just every so often at each level and on more than a handful of occasions jut closing itself when exploding a group of enemies like the process itself was caught in the aftermath.
Fix these issues and the game is golden.

In Expeditions: Viking you start out as the young Thane of a danish hamlet. Your father has died and he's left quite the mess. In Denmark your more powerful neighbours look upon you as easy pickings and together with a few trusty followers you set out to prove them wrong.
First of all, this is the best Viking themed game ever! The mix of strategic RPG and carefully building your village really draws you in. The RPG system is deep and you have to manage your hirdsmen/women by taking into account their motivations and superstitions to avoid mutiny. In addition to a camping system where you need to balance sleep and food, with the needs of repair and camp safety. If you are mostly into action RPG's this might seem a little overwhelming, but the flexibility of the system is very rewarding when mastered.
The quests also are varied and will have you facing tough decisions with results that might not become apparent until later in the game. The fights in the early game are not to hard, so it can be looked upon as an extended tutorial. Some of the later ones will however test your ability as a commander.
My main beef with this game is that a lot of it consists runninng around maps scrounging for resources, every chest or barrel seems to have a few pieces of wood. It may be that this becomes superflous in the later game, but the early game consists of a lot of container clicking. Some of the voice acting is limited in variation, and at times feels a little off. But I love how the have used Danish actors to read the lines, so you get a proper Danish accent. Some of it is also quite funny.
All in all, if you are into Vikings and deep RPG's then I would definitely give this one a go.

Canyon Capers is a bit of a mystery to me. It's shockingly polished, with never a hitch during any of my timing playing, imbued with tons of excessive flourishes and admittedly impressive if ill-fitting effects thrown about the level. It's gaudy with it's jump animations just as much as the excessive respawn animations, full of sparkles and swirls that easily distract, and oddly real stock flames that add a sort of surreal touch to the otherwise pixel heavy world. Artistically it is very inconsistant, and with the equally odd choice of stock banjo music blaring over everything, it didn't take long for me to develop a headache. Your character "Dino" also has one of the most excessive healthbars in platformer history, as it takes an estimated 15 hits for you to actually die, which emphasized the baby's first mentality to my naive mind, so I figured spending a mindnumbing few hours waiting for the cards to drop wouldn't be too much to ask.
Of course, it was far too much to ask, for once the tutorial heavy intro levels passed, this game became an eldritch abomination of horrible design choices that would make Ed Wood cringe. Constantly respawning enemies, instant death traps, unforgiving time limits; all wrapped together with one of the most sluggish respawns I have ever witnessed. Just to make it all the more fun, when you die, the clock doesn't stop, so the game quickly becomes a charade of trial and error, and don't even get me started about the homing bats. Not being able to control the height of your jump or the direction in any notable way makes this a genuinely infuriating experience that forgoes all sense of dumb to become something truly abyssal. Combined with the false challenge it present in sheer amount of BS, and you've got yourself a heartbreakingly confused platformer with no sense of direction. The greatest shame of all is that there seems to be a lot of heart put into this, so I can only hope the developers lick their wounds and implement something truly decent. Maybe with a choice in window sizes as well.

The games does a great job at rewarding curiosity and there are great game elements set in place for you to do just that. Spells aren't just for combat use as they can be used to reach places not usual accessable by foot or can clear paths if certain things are blocking the way. The looting and envirnment requires some thought to be put in to recieve rewards such as a chest across a broken bridge or a cavern you cannot walk down but you can teleport down.
If you decide to warp up to a guard patrolled area you can do just that or you can wait until a quest brings you into that part of the map at a later time. It's great fun and it allows you to play at your own pace. I never have a plan in mind for a game session rather I explore and see if theres stuff to loot and new things to explore.
Overall highly recommened, bugs are there but what can you do with such a large game.

I've only played 13 hours at the time of writing this, but that time has flown by and that's split between just two sessions. The game is fun, makes you think about what you say and do (I made the party leader save 4 times throughout a conversation because I didn't want to say the wrong thing), but is calming. Even in heated combat, it's still a calm, very entertaining experience. Turn based strategies aren't my favorite, but the game does it very organically, flowing seamlessly from exploration into combat. Its combat system is akin to XCOM style turns and movement, but it still feels distinctly different.
The investment I feel in conversation with every NPC I speak to is amazing and the narrator does a great job at explaining the nuances of certain situations. The voice acting is impressive, from a talking rat to actually discussing things with my friend's character. I accidentally started roleplaying my character and actually thought about what he'd say, with his background. This is the first game I've played where it is this easy to step into the mindset of the thing I am controlling with a mouse and keyboard.
The inability to switch a character between singleplayer and multiplayer originally frustrated me, but now I wouldn't have it any other way. Sharing the story and discussing decisions has made it that much better. The person and I have decided not to play the game except for together during the session we have running.
PROS
I can distract someone with conversation while my buddy robs them blind: 10/10 criminal capability.
I get to wear a bucket helmet: 10/10 armor items.
Decided to turn a bunch of water into poison. A candle lit it on fire and killed me: 9/10 combat consequences.
CONS
A crab insulted me: 0/10 animal manners.
My friend threw an arena fight and let me win: 11/10 boxing level fight fixing.
(I have not found any actual cons yet at this point in time, but if I do they'll be thrown in there.)

Kentucky Route Zero is a beautiful, understated adventure game that should not be ignored. Throughout the first two chapters (those that are released now) there is a range of imagery that is hauntingly beautiful. Seriously, the art direction in KRZ is something that should be noted by game designers everywhere. Thinking back there are some vistas that still pull an emotional response out of me weeks after playing the game.
As for gameplay, the overly cumbersome adventure game machinations have thankfully been left out of KRZ. There are no ridiculous item-combining puzzles to slog through, and no detailed logbooks to track lengthy bait and switch quests. KRZ welcomes you in with its stunning atmosphere, and leaves you to your need to explore. The game subtly bends its lore to your will, through dialogue choices that rewrite certain details of the world you are exploring.
When all put together, there are only a few hours of gameplay in the package right now. I eagerly await coming chapters, but it may be steep for anyone who is unsure if the game sounds right for them. However, if you are a fan of adventure games, indie games that dare to do something different or just plain want to be enthralled by an experience, buy in now.

TLDR; Bugs are hair pullingly frustrating. Could have been a good game but unlikely to ever become that.
It's been an open secret among game designers that providing a working, mostly bugfree experience, isn't nearly as important as marketing, securing funding, making the release date and keeping up the revenue cycle. The industry has been moving in the direction of ignoring non-gamebreaking bugs since Ultima IX, and developers now work the idea that their games will be buggy into their design process. Instead game designers rely on the human tendancy to want to keep trying to play a game despite crashes and bugs as a way of keep their games afloat. It's the same human tendancy that keeps gambler playing slot machines. The economics of game design is such that trying to make anything else is delusional.
What game designers instead sell you is the dream of a game, and let your imagination do the rest. This is why lead developers of the industries most famous pieces of vaporware, like Fable's Peter Molyeux and No Man's Sky's Sean Murray still have jobs despite them frequently crossing the line between puffery and outright lying to fans. The psychology of the relationship between these kind of developers and their fans has more in common with a domestic violence relationship than it has to an artist/fan one. Fans just keep coming back based on lies despite a history of constant disappointment.
An honest review of these games should tell you that your buying isn't a finished polished product, it's the dream of what a buggy, horribly cludged together game could be if only it worked well. It leaves fans thinking thoughts like, "I just hope the next patch fixes all of these annoying bugs", in the same way DV leaves it's victims thinking, maybe they will really change this time.
Conan Exiles fits this pattern completely. If you buy Conan Exiles, what your buying is the idea of a fantasy game that has a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥size slider. Your buying the same dream that a person who buys lottery ticket, despite knowing that the odds of winning are only slightly higher if you buy one, is buying. If your expecting that someday you'll have a polished game, worthy of investing hours of gameplay into, secure in the knowledge that it doesn't have any gamebreaking bugs that will make you throw all your hard work away, you are making a grave mistake.

1st person shooter / post apocalyptic survival / action game. Atmospheric game with open world feel, that takes place after S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl and is the last game in series. Once again you are inside the zone, but this time action takes place in outskirts and eventually town of Pripyat itself. You start off as an army man sent to zone, after few military helicopters have crash landed for no clear reason. With help of scientists, random stalkers and different faction groups, you must get to the bottom of what really happened.
You have three big areas on map you can explore, though they are somewhat empty and lack detail. There are occasional anomalies, landmarks, structures and machinery that spark the interest in exploring them, but very often you tend to not find anything of great value as everything is looted long time ago. Areas are still filled with radiation, anomalies and horrors, similar to previous games, with some new creatures.
There are decent number of side missions available, ranging from escort and protection, artifact hunt, mutant slaying to fetching stuff, finding tools and helping scientists with... Science, etc. There are no faction outposts this time around, like in S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky, but stalkers, mutants and other faction NPCs very often patrol many areas of map. You start the game somewhat neutral to everyone. Because of that you can safely observe firefight between factions, and afterwards safely scavenge defeated enemies. I find it to be funny as well as profitable endeavor, though you have to keep eye on carry weight as too much weapons in your bag can make travel a real burden. But nothing is more profitable as artifacts, they are still the best source of income, and you should regularly check anomalies with artifact detector.
Similar to S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky, you also have gear and weapon modifications that you can acquire from expert technicians, though some will require you to find specific tools. There's a decent amount of armor, weapon and gear variation, almost everything can be repaired and modified with help of local technician to suit your needs. Some technicians can't operate without good quantities of Vodka, so make sure you carry few bottles of those not just for anti radiation purposes, but also technician food. Speaking of food, you have to eat regularly to keep yourself full of energy, and I'm not kidding. Occasional sleep wont hurt as well, as you can replenish your strength and pass the time if you don't like nighttime.
From my point of view, S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat is weakest in series, S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky being the most fun I've had and S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl following closely just because how atmospheric and unique it was back in the day. I'm sure mods will make this game much better, as I experienced plenty on S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl and loved them. But somehow this particular game, in it's original state is somewhat aged and not as appealing as S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky and S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl was, and I think it's due to splitting of core development team in process of making, or maybe it's my wild guess who knows.
Never the less, game provides good visuals, character design and story telling for the time it was released in. I'll call it a "letdown" sequel to S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl. Game lacks optimization and even on modern system will eat frames, even though it's not even close graphically to S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky. True stalker fans will love it, and if you like apocalyptic games, then give this a shot.

Crusader Kings II is a grand strategy game from Paradox Interactive, a company that focuses on strategy games. From my somewhat limited experience, I have had a lot of fun, predominantly in a multiplayer setting.
You can choose to play as a ruler of a nation, or city, or hamlet, depnding on how difficult you would like the game to be. There is no true objective to the game, but the fun is in making objectives for yourself. For example: "Maybe I will press my claim against this neighboring territory to become their ruler", or "I shall plot to assassinate the pope."
There is a sharp difficulty spike you will need to overcome because the tutorial can only help so much, however, once you figure out your bearings, you will learn to do things you did not think were possible four, five, even ten hours prior.
All in all, CKII is a staple for strategy enthusiasts, and a fun (albeit difficult to first pick up) experience for anyone.

Two years ago, I got CKII on special offer just for the hell of it, and I played it for about 4 hours. Now, I've logged about 800(Make that 900) hours on it. Well, When I played it for 4 hours...
I hated it. it was just so goddamn complicated, boring, I couldn't work out the systems, it was BORING. I only played it when I got bored, until one day, in september 2014, I was playing it out of boredom and I married someone. Her father died shortly after, and she inherited his duchy in norway. Then, my character died and his 15 year old son became head of one of the most powerfu, duchies in Norway. fast forward 100 years and We're kings of norway and england. fast forward 50 years anf we're counts of some rocks in Cornwall. then, we became kings in less than 25 years. And that's the magic of CKII. anything can happen. It's impossible to describe, do I'll split it into pros and cons.
Cons: a learning curve of 90 degrees and an absolutely disgusting tutorial system that teaches nothing
Pros: when you learn the game, It becomes a vibrant, sprawling mass of politics, marriage, religion and warfare, trying to get on top and stay there while everyone else tries to kill you, and desperately surviving. The game tells a story of events, families, murders and warfare. Oh, and incest... It's gritty and down to earth, showing the reality of medieval history in the ways history class never could, whilst giving a delightful account of the bedroom antics of rednecks and showing that one kid, one wife who likes guys a bit too much, one bad trait, one guy with that ♥♥♥♥ing trusting trait can completely screw up a plan that has been in progress for 100 years, only for you to turn events around and become king of Spain, when you actually meant to be king of Scotland.
In short, this game can be tlked about endlessly, but only understood and loved when it's bought, when you climb that pile of corpses that mainly consist of your brothers because ypu havent got Primogeniture succession/ Climbing the learning curve and play it. It's been my favourite game for the last two years and has won that title easily due to it's ability to be remarkably simple, yet so goddamn complex, you're always learning.

To be honest, wareframe isn't that big of a game, but hey, it's free have fun
if you want some more here's my advice:
1. Dont spend any money
Warframe is free, and almost anything can be bought with platinum, a form of currency you'll get sooner or later by trading. The things that can be bought with money are not weapons (tennogen and prime access, but those are just mostly cosmetic)
2. Level diversity and overall feel
Warframe hasn't had much level diversity for a long time, and the aesthetics are detailed, but kinda bland. The best levels (in my opinion) are lua tileset and the plains. Speaking of which, plains brought something of what warframe really needed: open world. When this update came out I was overhyped, but only, you can only have so much of the plains at your disposal (This may change in the future, however only if the developers decide to expand) As for the overall feel for the game, most of the time you're too busy rushing to grind, so there's very little room to actually feel at home in the game, at least until plains came out (good on you DE)
3. Story
Yeah the story can feel unique, but it feels like there's a lot missing to it. Pieces of the story are scattered throughout the galaxy, leaving you to find them, but I do find that the things fans want to know are left missing most of the time. Don't get me wrong, storylines like Ordis's and Alad V are some of my favorite, but there's still a lot i want to know about this game
4. Frames
With so many frames to choose from and all of their different uses, it's hard to get a real feel for just one frame, and so many of the others can be very hard to use because you've adapted to a single playstyle. Find the frame that suits you the most and fits to how you actually play
5. End game
End game is a hard learning curve in this game (I call it a curve when it's more of a cliff) first to mid level you fly through these tilesets having a blast, but then you get to endgame where you're swarmed by what seems like countless infested, grineer, or corpus that seem almost like they'll shrug off anything you can throw at them. Oh and they hit like a truck too. If you want my input, try to avoid end game.
In all honesty this game is kinda mediocre at the moment but has the potential to become something greater, but hey it's free, have fun with it. I give it a 7/10

Expeditions: Viking created by Logic Artists is one of my most priced possesions of games I collected among the recent years. The fact that I value this game highly shall however not hinder me to give a comparative review of it.
The setting is historically grounded in the early Viking era, this also means you should not expect fights against fantastic creatures like trolls for example.
This game shares mechanics with many other games around and on an honest remark while emulating them quite succesfully their expierence in game will always pale in front of the kings of each genre. The game delivers a RPG expierence with turn-based combat while the world is traversed in a thematically fitting (woven carpet!) map, allowing the player character freedom of movement only between locations of the map and in about 25 locations, where you can then move around your character like in old-school RPGs. Crafting and improving your homelocation is a thing.
The combat expierence is solid and engaging, however since it takes up almost half of the game time one could wish for a little more nuanced expierence. Opponents you fight have apart from animals access to the same skillset as your character and his party, even the bosses, which makes for a good balance in theory. And while the AI doesn't do a bad job it won't pose to much of a tactical challange for many. Character creation is basic in appearance and more focused on the character you want to become due to your skillset. Those skills tie in well with both combat expierences and the more RPG expierences. Character development is steady and never grindy.
The plot is interesting but hardly original and while the music is very good, you will hear the same pieces over and over again after some time.
So far this must all sound like a pretty mediocre game to you, but behold! What makes this game truely amazing is how the world itself is presented. This game contains a lot more information than initial encounters with NPC may present, or to put it more bluntly: things may not always be like they seem. Quests live from the ambiguity of the (initial) lack of information, because you have no clue which action is the right one to take. And even if it seems obvious, inquiring further may give events a completely different framing and hence spin. This game rewards you for digging deeper than just the information presented in the excellently written dialogue (and read you will a lot!). Writing and artistic skill will allow you to fill in lacking information and solve mysteries you will encounter during the game and the quest design reflects this with usually a myriad of differnetly nuanced outcomes.
And then there are of course the bigger decision throughout the game whose impact you will feel, I promise. But see for yourself, I strongly encourage you if you feel like reading between the lines and manoevering in a historical setting without all the information instantly presented to you is to your liking...
PS: a last tip, characters with higher SENSE or PERCEPTION get more out of the story

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion, despite being seven years old by this point, is a great game. On its own, some may condemn it for being buggy, the graphics being out of date, the game suffering from consolitis in the User Interface department, and having potato-faced characters, but the game's greatest redemption is the modding community. All of the things mentioned in the previous sentence are things that the modding community have fixed. All the bugs and inconsistencies left behind when the development team moved on to other projects and ceased updating Oblivion? There are the Unofficial Patches for that. Don't like the UI? Darnify it. Potato faces got you down? There are a number of mods to fix that. Without even getting into the retexture mods, you've got a number of patches and even legacy ENB Series support to beautify the game. That's not even delving into all of the content that mods can add.
The game is of course not without its flaws. The game can be a little bland when run vanilla, and despite Bethesda's best efforts, the game's 'balance' is horribly out of whack. Unless you know exactly what you are doing in building your character, and level your skills to min/max attribute gains, you are going to have a mediocre character in a world that is scaling to your leveling. Spellcasters in particular can get the short end of the stick, because without armor, they are incredibly squishy—even with shield spells an enchantments—and with armor, their spellwork is less effective. Either way, if you try to stay out of the heat of battle, when it comes to some of the larger scale battles in the game, you may end up with a lot of dead allies and a number of angry atronachs ready to tear you apart. The game is all about walking a very fine line.
Another issue that people may have with the game is the dialogue. There is only a small number of voice actors, like one for each race and sex for generic NPCs, and only a few specific NPCs get unique voices. In the long run, it means that you are guaranteed to hear a voice actor having a conversation with himself at least once or twice. Likewise, the Radiant AI, which attempts to run NPC dialogue in passing leads to some real gems. "Hello." "I have nothing more to say to you." "Goodbye." "See you." This exact string is one I have personally encountered. It's a bit humorous to hear the first couple of times, but you can only listen to NPCs having disjointed discussions about mudcrabs before it begins to grate.
In spite of all of this, I maintain that Oblivion is a good game. There are so many things you can do in the game without any mods at all, that it's worth playing a couple of times.

The Land of Eyas is an incredibly charming puzzle platformer from developers Happy Square Productions and Rising Star Games. In fact, I'm particularly happy that RSG picked up this title - there are a lot of interesting titles in RSG's catalogue.
Platformers count amongst one of my most favourite game genres. I've absolutely adored games like
and
, and I definitely feel this game would fill a similar market to those looking for similar games.
You play as the titular character, Eyas, on a journey to find his home. Eyas is this incredibly cute boy in a cat suit, quite adorable. In fact, all of the art assets made here are impeccable - somewhat easy on the eyes, yet at the same time exuding a certain quality and charm to it.
They've been recently added.
The soundtrack is orchestrated brilliantly as well. Good use of various instruments and song selection for each level stage, with particularly more difficult levels being accompanied by slightly more frantic, yet never overpowering, songs.
As for the levels - they form the bread and butter of the game, and the level design is superb. A good amount of precision platforming and lateral thinking is required to solve the brunt of the levels - some require measured movement while others require well-placed jumps from specific locations. The somewhat unique gravity flipping mechanic comes into play a lot as, for example, you have to ascertain which level you have to jump off from the top side, in order to be able to land at the correct platform after you flip gravity.
I only really have one major gripe about this game, and it's somewhat personal, but - the platforming isn't precise enough for my liking. Unlike most platformers Eyas does not run at full speed whenever he moves, all the time - but instead he has to (somewhat more realistically, I'll admit at least) speed up from 0. I think others shouldn't have much of a problem with it though. It's just that I really demand a lot of precision when it comes to controls, and I often find it easy to move too much in one direction than I intended to.
Ultimately, I really like this platformer game and, again, feel that fans of the other two games I mentioned above would definitely take to this one as well.
In all honesty, for the amount of levels present in the game, I thought it would have been priced at $15. Which makes the $10 (without discount) price point rather appealing.

I found this game fun and addictive. The graphics are bright and colourful making the worlds in this game great for kids. The main character is a log... yes that's right a log, you play as a sentient log on a mission from his sentient tree father too bring water back to the world. The story is very simple to follow and seems very reminiscent of old school 90's platformer games (Like Super Mario 64) in which the main character (and the player for that matter) is given a simple plot device (e.g. save the princess) and the story is set up and the rest is up to the levels and gameplay.
The levels are very intresting each with there own unique style, there are six worlds in total to explore as you collect berries, fairy tears in order to heal the world and you chase down the complete set of 8 steam achivements. You can even team up with a friend to complete levels with the local two player co-op mode.
The soundtrack is quite charming and only adds to the overall enjoyment of the game, at times I even felt transported back to being a child and playing classic Nintendo platform games (Super Mario, Banjo Kazooie and Donkey Kong 64, to name but a few, came to mind.)
It's far from perfect, as the issues with the camera will show. As you are playing this game sometimes the camera will go a bit crazy and move to a point which will make it very hard to see your character, this happened to me on several occasions and made the levels harder to complete (not impossible just a bit harder.) As you can see from my total play time, (at the point of writing this it was 1.9 hrs) I has been quite a short game and even though the camera had its issues, I have still completed this game 100% with all the steam achivements unlocked.
In summary this game has some good moments that will spark nostalgic feelings in older gamers and spark new moments for younger gamers. The game is short so don't expect an epic story arc with hundreds of levels, but do expect fun gameplay, cheery music with bright colors and vibrance throughout. It may have its issues but this fun little game could keep you busy even if it is for a short while.

Generic, casual, simple platformer with no story. You start in the middle of the level and then jump around collecting the required items (and bonus items for extra score) and avoid (instead of kill) enemies. After collecting the items, a portal appears that you need to find and leave before time runs out. Score is somewhat important because you need to have enough stars (up to 3 given per level based on score) to unlock the next batch of 10 levels. For example, to unlock the 4th world you need 22 stars from 10 levels (which means you need to score at least eight 2-star levels and two 3-star levels).
There isn't much variety in levels or objectives- you always have to collect stuff and then exit before time runs out. Music and sound effects are silly but mediocre- I just muted the game and listened to something else while I played.
Controls are decent, and the only thing you can do is move and jump. After clearing all ten levels of a batch, you unlock a character to use. Each character has their own power, though so far they haven't been very game-changing. The starter character shows an arrow pointing towards the exit portal. The second shows arrows towards the last remaining gems on the map, the third has magnet-powers for coins, and the fourth ignores fireballs. There are enemies, but you can mostly ignore them. It takes a bunch of hits to kill you, so the main thing they do is slow you down and knock you off platforms. Falling into lava is insta-death, though you always respawn (though it means more wasted time).
There are definitely more complex and fun platformers around, but maybe this could be okay for someone who is looking for a basic collect-things platformer or as a brain-dead way to pass the time. Not for everyone, since there are many platformers out there.

Probably one of the most immersive and memorable games I've ever played. The music is atmospheric, the AI is immersive, the maps are big and all in all the game is very immersive and everything feels "alive". It looks pretty good (especially on the higher graphics qualities and/or with mods like AtmosFear), and above all else it's actually fun.
If you finish the game, I'd suggest you install MISERY. MISERY is even more immersive, and adds features such as vignettes for helmets (that change the more damaged your helmet gets), more armor and weapons, more items, and you have to eat and sleep to survive. Everything is more expensive, the AI is even sharper, weapons do more damage and I swear it seems like gear gets damaged a lot faster. It also enhances the graphics a little bit, adds three different classes, new starting locations for new games, and NPCs no longer have unlimited ammunition.
All in all, if you like FPS type open world sandbox games (or if you really like Fallout) this is a must play.

okay... at first this game gave me a small bad impression... but TBH... after i knew that it was the X360ce i was trying to use to support my controller as an Xbox controller... it ran fine...
Okay... how do i begin with this one... is made by a Country comrade... a Brazilian... and it was very cheap when i bought (arround R$2). but was it worth it?! Yes... and no...
Let's go to the Pros First:
-If there is one thing this game does right is the Metroidvania atmosphere. in some parts i was desperatly searching for the savepoints to refill the health, the same way i was on SOTN the first time i played it. for me, if a metroidvania can do this, it is because it succeeded in doing what it does.
-another thing it does right... but maybe... because i heard it recycles musics from other games, so it may not be the author credit... is the music. i gotta say, the Forest cave and the Ice castle themes surprisingly got me humming to it. i should be harsh because the guy is wining money on something that is not his own (the music as some people says here), but TBVH... i don't feel i should... i develop mods and games too, and if theres one thing i know, is that a person alone cannot develop everything from scratch. especially music and coding, if he is a game designer like myself. because it is only the first draft of the guy, i feel i should let this slip,and i believe you should too... but let this serve as a warning so he does not this again in the future when he gets a bigger team.
-The graphics may look a little... how can i say... Illustrator-ish... but that's fine by me... they are crisp and some effects got me surprised.
-The History... well... i cannot say much becuase i did not yet finished the game (i will put a more complete analysis once i do)... but basically... some crazy scientist named Gerry... wait a second.... *thinks about a friend of mine laughing like a madman in the background*... oh... i didn't knew you had a degree in biology... okay... anyway... so the crazy scientist named Gerry created a LOT of Bio-Monsters, and had a huge proving grounds where he could test and realize its experiments... one day however, and i dunno if it was he or was another person completely... so i'll say Someone for now... this Someone freed the monsters,wanting the humans to feel his/her wrath... so he released his primed creations in the wild, and the humans started to suffer as a result. Jerry however knowing that something like this could happen,created Sebastian, that, Tired of being on the C&A comercials(Bad Joke), has appeared on the laboratory,being freed by one of the drones of Jerry. The drone then is Destroyed by a Huge X-men Sentinel mixed with Mysterio from Spider Man, and then you gotta escape the lab,stop the monsters,including the huge sentinels, and discover the Misteryous Identity of Ashy, a guy that said to be with the humans, but want you to turn to their side... but... it is very suspicious what tey're doing... not to mention a little girl with a Knife that you know nothing about it, unless that she is too one of the experiences of Jerry.
-Gameplay.... well it is rough, i will not lie... but don't let the roughness get you away from the game... it is good for sure... could be better... but is good.
-Even tho this game was made with a off-the shelf tool, Specifically Construct 2, you can clearly see that it has a lot of originality. if anything i know that at this moment, 2017/10/4, i cannot do what he did on that tool... so, if anything, this should serve as an inspiration font,and a demo of what Construct 2 can and cannot do.
-R$ 2 for a game like this is a steal. easly worth it.even tho it can be better.
-and the Cons:
-okay... The worse problem the game has in my opnion is that the only controller supported by it, is the Xbox controller... and that it cannot rebind controls... wich left me with an odd configuration... yes i could get over it and adapt... but no game should have the jump button mapped to the Playstation Triangle button Equivalent... that's... not right...
-another thing that can get in front of your fun, is that... if you emulate another program, you should enconter massive lagging... so... don't use anything on the background with the game... the experience will be dreadfull if you do so.
-it crashed once on me while i loaded a save file. Not a big deal (i did not lose the progress and anything) but worth mentioning.
-The Ennemies doesn't act as you expect them to act if you played SOTN,Dawn of Sorrow or Metroid for example... sometimes they act too quickly and too wonky for my taste... but they all have cues to when they gonna attack. so it is NOT by any means unfair. is just... strange... their parterns are weird in my opnion. but i digress... this is just a minor nitpick
Score:
History: 8 (Is not the most original in the world. and it is not like it does not have cliches that you can see from a mile away. but it is VERY enjoyable. well done)
Gameplay: 8 (Could be done better. but it is satisfactory enough to keep you glued on the PC. wich in my book is a succes . very good)
Graphics: 8 (again could be better. but they did well their homework. some parts i was very impressed... some others... i was... meh... but good work nonetheless)
Music: Cannot give a Grade (i dunno what to put here... the Music is good but some say the guy did not compose it... since i dunno from where they came... i cannot consider giving it a positive or negative grade here. not that the music is bad,by the way, far from it. the music is Superb and very catchy.)
Fun Factor: 10 (on this, they nailed it right on the head. it feels like a true game from MetroidVania genre. Crafting, Leveling up, Exploring... even desperately searching for savepoints when things get rough... it hits every note right in this regard).
Extras: Extra 10 (the Sheer ammount of References of the Monster names and things in this game is astonishing. i mean... where else you can drop a Barrão For example XD... or Deal with a Bizoi. the monster names are Filled to the brim with Terms, and Popular Slangs and Jokes from the Brazilian Portuguese. granted other people that does not know about the language can miss the references... but it does not make them less funny XD)
Final Score: 7.7 /10. (a Surprisingly High 7.7 for a game of this caliber. i am even thinking on giving an 8 to it if it improves even more. it could score even better if somethings were done right... but this is a fun game. take my word for it, you gonna have fun. you just need to adjust yourself to the controls and the game wonkiness... but once you get past that... you'll get a good little fun gem. and for the developers, consider this game a Success for what it is.)

You step out into the brilliant sunlight after crawling out of a dark and damp dungeon. The world around you is a radiant green, and the trees and grass sway in the wind. Limestone ruins glimmer in the near distance, and a great stone city lies on the horizon. Then you stop and think that this beatifully rendered world was made over 8 years ago, when the Xbox 360 was a new thing, Google was just a web browser and a mail service, and iPods were not just unnetworked iPhones.
Then you walk into the city, you see strange, puffy faced people talking about mudcrabs, and greeting each other only to say they don't want to have a conversation, then go their separate ways for 30 seconds before repeating that conversation. Suddenly you're grounded. It's still a game from 2006.
This is pretty much what I could imagine any new player who is unfamiliar with TES IV: Oblivion experiencing. However, underneath the striking contrast between the successes and failures of its graphical design, lie a greatly engrossing RPG system and many ways to truly personalize every new experience in the game.
This is the middle child of the Elder Scrolls. Hard limits have been introduced into the game since Morrowind that prevent you from flying and becoming a demigod, and the whole world is always at the same level as you. It is less free than Morrowind, and more customizable than Skyrim. Sometimes the world feels static and bland due to this rigidity. Other times the great quests, cool rewards, and the experience of playing a class that you designed make you wish for bits of Oblivion in the other Elder Scrolls titles.
Ultimately, if you can handle sometimes goofy graphics and the occasional clunky control mechanic, Oblivion is a richly rewarding experience, and is truly the last mainstream RPG to include fully customizable class design, which in itself is a feature worthy of the price. Also, the landscapes and open world of Cyrodiil and the Shivering Isles set the bar for a whole generation of open world games. The AI design and living world are a precedent that few games, even today, set out to match. This is truly a legendary game, no matter what its detractors say.
Highly recommended.
