At first glance of gameplay, the game looks like a very simple movement puzzle flash game, but when you actually play it you'll see otherwise. This game uses a very interesting formula that I've never seen before, where movement is based on circular motion. It's difficult to put in words, but basically wherever you move, your square will rotate so that it stays perpendicular to the circle in the centre of the screen. White represents space you can move in, black is impassable, and red kills you on contact. That is literally the entirety of the game mechanics explained, but somehow they use this formula so well, and it feels like every level is a new, clever, innovative use of this simple formula. With such a simple formula you'd be surprised how much engaging play time this game delivers.
Also important is the soundtrack. The soundtrack is what elevates this title from being a good game, to a phenomenal game. The soundtrack has fantastic chill and ambient vibes, and sublime crescendoes for the finales of levels that leave you both excited and awestruck.
I only recommend this game if you care about, or can appreciate, quality soundtracks. That being said, if you do, it's a great experience that I would say is worth the money despite the relatively short playtime.

This game ranks up there for me with the likes of Dark Souls, Bloodborne, and Morrowind as a favorite game that I'll remember for years to come. Highly recommend.
- You get a real sense of progress through the game. Combat doesn't necessarily get easier, but as you level your party members up, get more skills, better gear, higher stats, you get a very rewarding look and feel of becoming more powerful and capable. I'm incredibly motivated to keep playing because my characters become more fun to play as I advance through the game
- The story is good, but what's far and away better is that the game offers you so many ways to approach scenarios (some are in your control, some are not based on who you entered dialogue with, in what order you encountered the scenario, items in your inventory, etc). This means there is no "right" approach, so I never felt bad with how a situation turned out because I know so many things will be different on subsequent playthroughs.
- The combat is rock solid, and as rewarding as killing a boss as Dark Souls is, Divinity 2 gives that same high when you come up with a battle strategy and adjust your tactics on the fly to see a plan realized
- Speaking of combat, enemies are varied and full of surprises so there's so much variety to the fights you encounter
- Graphically gorgeous, especially environments
- Fully voice acted with quality writing and acting
- The quest log is easily organized and concise, and there are no quest markers other than waypoints on the map if you've talked to the right characters for hints. It's not challenging to keep up with, and it encourages exploring the world and its lore
- The party is pretty spread out in the first act and it's a pain when you have to swap out a party member for another one with a racial bonus you need (Elven flesh eating, Undead lock picking, etc)
- Some perks seem infinitely more important than others (I'm looking at you, Pet Pal)
- Some utility skills also seem infinitely important to have (teleport), and they feel so necessary that I'll probably force at least one party member to have one in every playthrough
- I may edit this on my second playthrough, but with a 4 person party it's pretty tough to find early success in combat unless you're running a pretty traditional Rogue, Tank, Healer, Mage archetype, leaving the less traditional and possibly more interesting support and utility classes out of reach
If you like RPGs, DnD, and games that offer you legitimate challenges and matches those challenges with a variety of rewards, play this game. It's a once in a generation video game.

Call of Pripyat is the last game in the series which happens a few years after Shadow of Chernobyl.
You play as Major  Alexander Degtyarev, who is sent in to investigate the failure of this operation which the reasons why are extremely anti-climactic and the ending leaves you somewhat disappointed, in fact the story in this game is made to quite existent but it just ends up falling flat on its face onto a turd.
Call of Pripyat does add in a few new things: on the map areas are now highlighted with a bubble, the hunger system was brought back and emissions happen on a somewhat regular basis and you must take shelter and wait for them to be over. Call of Pripyat also improves a few things as well: now the gunplay is so much better than before, weapons jam a lot less than clear sky, and it only takes one bandage or med kit to stop you from bleeding out when clear sky it took a random amount of healing items.
Just like the previous games this is a strangely compelling game but it still comes with a few issues:
Everything weighs more in this game and you’ll be over the weight limit quite a lot in this game so you’ll be walking everywhere instead of running, when in the previous games you could carry two assault rifles, one sub machinegun, one handgun, one shotgun and a stack of ammo and healing items, when in Call of Pripyat I was over the limit on just having two assault rifles, one handgun, and a stack of ammo and healing items.
With gunfights it’s still very random on whether the enemies will hit you or not and how much damage they dish out to you.
And lastly this game does get quite boring at times since to begin with the mission objectives are really, really boring, since it’s usually go here examine object, and that the landscape is very baron and there’s quite a lack of enemies around.
This is a fairly good game and getting this comes down to whether you can be patient with it otherwise you’ll probably be too bored to play it.

STALKER: Call of Pripyat is a very fun game which is somewhere between Fallout, Metro, and DayZ. It has good atmosphere and is a lot of fun to play!
Pros:
- Atmosphere
- Weapons and customization system
- Arifact hunting system
- Open world; stick to the story or poke around and do whatever you want
- Plenty of side quests
- Challenging without being frustrating
- Mutants and enemies
- Factions and groups
- Remains engaging after hours of play
- Mods for lots of things
Cons:
- Graphics are a little old
- Tutorial nonexistent, expect plenty of internet searches
- Holstering system can be confusing at first
- If you don't have night vision at night you're in for it
- If you have a bad detector you will have a tough time getting artifacts
- learning curve can be rough
The cons however do not outweigh the pros, as the only significant negative point is the graphics. If you jack them up to DX11 and Ultra you will be okay, just do not expect to have your socks blown off. If, however, you cannot muster up the acceptance of sub-super graphics there are plenty of mods to give the world a better look.
The atmosphere in this game is great, the first time you have to enter somewhere dark (
) it feels like Metro 2033. Emissons add some urgency and anxiety to the experience as they come with little warning. Finding close shelter can be just as risky as trying to get to ideal shelter ASAP. There will be plenty of scares, fights, and victories. Enemies come in all shapes and sizes. Some roam, others hunt. Some are nocturnal and some are invisible. Not sure which is worse - being jumped at night by a dangerous hunter or being assaulted by invisible enemies. Until you have Nightvision and guns from Nimble I reccomend that you avoid the night. There are also zombies with guns. As if hordes of delerious men babbling in russian weren't bad enough, they all have guns - some of which are sufficently powerful to take you down quickly.
Trading is good, as are quests. Artifacts also provide unique benefits at the expense of radiation. I would reccomend finding an artifact that reduces radiation and holding on to it until you find a healing artifact. This allows you to permanetly equipt powerful artifacts. For instance, I wal lucky enough to find an artifact that takes away 4 radiation points and a healing artifacts that adds 6 health points at the expense of 3 radiation points. That means if I have both of them equiped I get healed for free (helpful because medkits are expensive in a pinch)
it takes away radiation. Although the selling price may be high one must weigh out the benefits of keeping artifacts for their benefits
selling them for ammunition, weapons, medkits, ect.
Overall, this is a great game that is worth every penny. The graphics aren't beautiful by todays standards and like every game it has its flaws, but the gameplay and atmosphere more than make up for it. I reccomend playing it on medium to high difficulty in order to really feel the experience as the extra challenge will just add to the feeling and attraction of the game. 10/10!
P.S. There are a few things to do in the beginning:
-Head to Skadovsk first
-
-Get tools from the area
-Also get the bigger and better AK from zombies
-Do the sidequests but hold off on the Chimera one until you are better equipped
-Stay away from the sewage treatment plant until you have a scoped rifle with AP rounds.
-Get a good shotgun. It comes in handy more than you'd think
-Once you are well equipped head to Yanov
-Find or buy a Veles detector. It will pay for itself quickly and makes artifact hunting much easier.
-Keep armor in good condition and Medkits in good supply
Have fun in the zone!

This is a fun MOBA game which isn't, for once, a DOTA clone. Rather, it is a 2D action platformer. Unlike the DOTA clones, teams are three players, and the games tend to go MUCH more quickly, resulting in much better pacing and much less frustration as you sit around and fight in a lost game. Instead, the game is designed such that it can end within five minutes if you are vastly overmatched, and even long games seldom last more than half an hour - and if a game DOES last a very long time, it is still in contention, not merely because your opponents can't land a knock-out blow. Indeed, letting the game go on too long is very dangerous for the opposition, as you can chew through all their defenses even from a disadvantageous position if they mess up.
The game is very fun and quite well balanced, and the aesthetic is nice too. Worthy of a buy if you want a fun MOBA.

Okay. I've played a little bit of this game, and will continue to play it, but I have to get this out here.
First of all, the vast majority of the game is phenomenal. It is an in-depth grand strategy game with slight role-play elements (certain events allow you to choose between character traits, which affect your ruler's stats). It is probably the most in-depth grand strategy game (maybe ignoring Paradox's other titles), and for the most part, is very fun.
...but... there is one game mechanic which makes this game nearly unplayable- factions. Factions are groups of vassals that band together to demand certain law changes within your realm- usually lower crown authority or elective succession. If you do not grant their demands, they will rebel. While in theory this is a very good mechanic, there are three major problems with it. Firstly, no matter how much your vassals like you, they will probably found and join factions. Secondly, the nobles are constantly- literally incessantly- making demands. Thirdly, usually half of your realm will back a particular faction. This means that every year or few years, you have to divert your entire army, and oft times even hire mercenaries, to defeat a rebellion from half of your realm. This gets very repetitive, boring, and frustrating. If you want to ensure that your realm will pass to one person who is in your dynasty, you will be facing constant rebellions. This is patently absurd and must be immediately removed from the game- or at least massively toned down- for it to be enjoyable.
One other small problem is that the game usually crashes two or three times when you try to launch it before it actually decides that it will launch. This is frustrating, but not game-breaking. Also, it might just be my particular computer- I don't really know for sure.
That said, factions are the only major problem I've seen with the game, and I will keep playing it, and even recommend it; but this is something that needs to be adressed by Paradox.

At the core, ATS is a relaxing, fun experience. If you just want to get into a truck and drive, this is a perfect "simulator/game" for you.
However, even in what would seem to be massive success with the Truck Simulator franchise, SCS seems to be coming up extremely short on the innovation and progression of the game.
The biggest issue is content. The base game simply does not have enough. First off, trucks. SCS seems to have only been able to secure a license with a single American truck manufacturer. That means, the only trucks in the game are made by Paccar. Kenworth, and Peterbilt. The saddest part is since these are both Paccar trucks, they are very similar with differences mostly being cosmetic. When it comes down to it, there are 4 trucks in the game. SCS said that more trucks were coming way back, but have been completely silent for quite a while about the trucks. I seriously doubt that any more are coming.
Now, area. I understand the challenges of modeling maps and areas, but the TS series isn't exactly a revolution in map detail, given that they're only mapping linear corridors, really. The lack of area mapped so far is... disappointing. Instead of exceeding expectations, SCS has actually come up very short. Again, putting everything new behind DLC is one thing, but new areas aren't even available as DLC!
Next to the core mechanics of the simulator. Let's face it, this is essentially a reskin of ETS2. If you're happy with the "business side" of running a trucking company to basically hiring drivers, leveling them up, and having enough garage spots and trucks for them compelling, then this will be satisfying. Because that's really all this game is beyond you driving your own truck. You can't own and manage your own trailers, you don't build contracts with certain shippers. There's so, so, so much more that can be done on the "company management" side of the game.
Finally, to the business of "simulating trucking". There's some very basic aspects modeled beside driving the truck itself. Yes, the game calls it "truck simulator". Not "trucking simulator", and that's a good reason. Most of the aspects like weigh stations, fueling, sleeping, aren't really modeled in detail. It seems logical to model the dynamic of having a sleeper cab or not determine where you could rest. That's simply not here.
So, this game is a good experience for just relaxing and putting some miles in. It's just not very deep and SCS seems OK with that. There's probably opportunity here for someone else to come in and make something better, since there's clearly a market and SCS seems willing to rest on their laurels and slowly crank out DLCs to keep their business running rather than innovating and putting in new features.
I'm gonna mark this as don't recommend simply because the game has some negatives and they need to be seen so expectations are properly set. As I said before, this game is great to pick up and relax and drive a bit, but don't expect much beyond the driving itself.

I really wanted to like this game. It has a lot going for it. Interesting (and well-researched) historical period. Attractive game design. Beautiful music. Turn-based hexagon battles (for true old-school connoisseurs like myself). Original RPG set-up that is different from the tired formula. What's not to like? Yes, the stories are true, game in its current state is extremely buggy - broken quests, CTDs, corrupted save files (after the hot fix). These are, however, temporary things that, I am sure, developers will soon address (although a question remains how they could release such a half-baked product). What worries me a lot more are some gameplay issues that are "as intended", which, together, come very close to ruining the experience for me:
-- Awkward camera angle that you can't adjust. It is almost directly above you, meaning that you are staring at roofs and heads most of the time. Adjusting it by even 5-10% would have made a huge difference. It's just odd looking at your party's heads most of the time. Thankfully, you can still rotate the camera, but since you can't also adjust the angle there are instances when you can't see certain items very well or at all.
-- No party formations. They just follow your main character in random order and you can't position them on the battlefield.  Not only that, you can't even decide when you begin a battle. That's right. You can't attack unless it's part of a scripted conversation/quest. Furthermore, whoever begins first (and there is no way to know that in advance) has a HUGE, disproporionate advantage. It's not uncommon for you to lose half of your party (especially if the other group is archers-heavy) before you even move because, unlike in many other RPGs, moves don't alternate between parties (i.e. everyone in the first group must move before the second group gets ANY chance to retaliate). I have no idea why the option to position your troups was removed from the game. It was in Expeditions Conquistador years ago. That almost makes any advance planning/strategy impossible.
-- Overpowered healers and archers. Thankfully, there is no proper "magic" in this game as it tries to remain relatively historic (apart from the completely unnecessary 50:50 ratio of male and female fighters, just like Conquistador), but healers come very close to that. Especially on harder settings it can become nearly impossible to defeat an opponent if his group has several healers as they all but negate any damage that you do. On a related note, archers are just way too powerful in my opinion. Not game-breaking powerful, but still completely unbalanced.
-- Looting and explorations are sub-par. You can highlight allegedly "lootable" after-the-battle dead bodies or barrels and other containers scattered around the map, but many of them are just empty. No idea if that's "as intended", but I see little value in highlighting containers with nothing in them or bodies with no loot. On the the topic of loot, it's also quite odd that many fights don't drop ANY loot, not even their old weapons. Furthermore, some encounters (at camping sites) won't even let you loot after the battle as you are immediately taken to the next screen after victory. No idea why it was done like this.
I haven't given up on the game and will continue playing it in the hope that developers will, at the very least, fix the broken quests that make the game unplayable, but all in all I cannot honestly recommend it yet.

I got Expand as part of a Humble Bundle, knowing nothing about it besides the trailer. So I decided to play it the other day on a whim and was pleasantly surprised by the weird, abstract world that awaited.
For such a simple concept and visual style, Expand manages to do quite a lot. Most areas of the game (yes, there is actually a hub world leading to five distinct areas) focuses on one mechanic and explores a wide breath of possibilities with it. The game itself only lasts 2-3 hours, but it constantly adds new unique puzzles to keep things engaging and never really gets stale.
The best part of this game has to be, in my opinion, the soundtrack. It shifts with the situation you're in, almost seeming to narrate the journey of your little square through the abstract maze. It gives a sense of meaning and weight to the otherwise silent and storyless adventure. And in some areas, the shifting environment directly syncs with the music, making for surprisingly cool moments.
Seriously, it's well worth picking up the soundtrack with this one.
The challenges you have to get through are certainly all passable, and the relatively frequent use of checkpoints usually limits the amount of memorization needed.
There was only one small part which seemed even slightly unfair:

It's basically Euro Truck Simulator 2, but in the US.

Sound design is mediocre, and I'm not saying this just to insult. Here is my feedback.
Firstly, when looking at proper sound design you need six things to be in shape.
-Panning: sound direction between left and right output.
-Balance: Prioritiztion of sound, what needs to be heard. Usually dialogue in top priority
-Equalization: Managing your frequencies. Bass-treble Low-High.
-Dynamics: When things are loud or soft and when they need to be loud or soft
-Levels: Technical standpoint of the waves output level. In this games case it is too much, the sound clips often
-Dimensions: Reverb, Delay. This directly correlates to atmosphere in parrallel with everything above
Footsteps: They are very dry, and their volume should be lowered slightly. They need a touch of reverb in order to give them that metalic room vibe and overall this should help in atmosphere.
Atmosphere: From what I've heard, there is none. A consistant deep bass drone tone is not going to give you any form of atmosphere especially with how random and inappropriate its placement is. I never feel like I am in the rooms that I am actually in. This is as simple as going into a room with the desired sound, recording the silence of the room, then placing that sound file to play in the corresponding rooms of the game
Door Sounds: Clipping... Lower the output level of the sound or use a better soundwave. P.s. Doors make sounds when they finish closing or opening, one electronic sound wont make the cut.
Pistol: Sounds cartoonish, like a stock sound even. I suggest making its pitch higher and shortening the decay so the sound doesnt play so long. Or jsu tuse a different sound altogether.
Flamethrower: sounds good.
Now for the Game Design aspect.
Questiosn to ask yourself when making a game.
"Why is this fun?" If you cannot answer this question quickly, then odds are you aren't making a fun game. This game gave me the same vibe as a previous game I had worked with "Space Beast Terror Fright" and that game was adrenaline filled and action packed and kept you on your toes. This felt like a slower, less interesting version.
Movement: I actually really like the movement in this game, the character feels like they have weight, walking feels good, aiming feels good. Character leans in a minimal fashion, and in general I feel like a person, not a video game character.
Enemies: enemies walking in a straight line is not interesting unless the gameplay is built around it. These little bugs should be on walls, jumping, scurrying, quick abript movements. not slowly walking towards you.
WHAT I WANT TO SEE
I see this game uses the same assets and such from a previosu title you made. That title has mixed results, and makign a game that looks the same will also leave you with mixed results. The visuals dont look improved, the sounds are reused, and It's not somethign people will look at and say "I want more of that"
I would rather see what more you guys can do, as I see potential in how you make your games. there is definitely some knowhow going on but it needs more work and application.
My advice, don't stop making games.

So, Conan Exiles.
Funcoms latest flop so to speak, or well. Flop would perhaps be a bit of an overstatement, or is it?
It's not been out for too long and it's in early access so problems are a given I guess you could say.
Let's cut to the chase however, there's no beating around the bush with this game, so lets take the positive things first.
-For the engine it's running on, it looks great, fantastic even, it has a lot of cool idea's, most of which are extremely poorly implemented but cool nonetheless, I bet that when it's done, which I assume is going to take just about as long as it took for the DEV team behind ARK to get that game in a playable state, this game will be fantastic.
I like the game, the building in particular is fun and enjoyable, a bit or slightly annoying at times but there's always a workaround for those kinks to get around them.
My major issue with the game isn't the features it has, but the features that were promised but are missing from the game, not there or simply just fictional as in, they're in the DEV's head and not in the game, as that's what it feels like.
Their blogs are all about how they're going to implement new things, I even read the part about adding Necromancy to the game, great, that sounds amazing, and then I start thinking; Necromancy, that's, oh.. That's about re-animating creatures, how's that even going to work, animation wise at the very least?
-Let's review an example: The first creature you meet, is a Batdemon who's animation are similar to that of Quake, not quake 2 or 3, but the OLD Quake from -96, or better yet, let's review the other ones from when you get to your first water source, Shalebacks and Gnomes, actually lets just add everything you meet to the list.
It's like every single creature only has four movement patterns, Left, Right, Forward and Backward and they rotate through them instantly, making them look like an In-Animate object, then looking back at the video and the 'hellhound' looking things they fight there, I had the impression that the creatures you meet will at least look like they're turning when they're ment to, but no. I would be just as scared of a Moving Foundation as I am of a Dragon(in this game) that came at me, because animation wise, the animals are just as lifeless, they're sounds are great, their animations?. Not so much.
That's one HUGE gripe I have with the game, and then there's the missing lore, we we're told about untold lore and a story to explore, well it's hard to explore any lore when the ONLY working Ancient Stone Tablet and few lore bits you meet in the first 3minutes of playing the game, which sums up to 2 Notes and 1 Ancient Stone Tablet, everything else is missing lore, tablets don't have any sound which I assume based on the first one it's supposed to have.
With those flaws in the game, I honestly can't recommend the game to anyone AT THIS POINT, once said things have been fixed, by all means, do get it.
If the things I mentioned are of no concern to you then get the game, there's a lot more bugs, glitches and problems with it which I didn't mention, but those are the two deal breakers for me, I do have my own server and we do play it and will continue to, just to follow the progress of it, but between Ark and this, ark will be the main game in terms of survival and overall finish, but that game has also had a long time to get where it is.
If you still want to try the game, buy it at a discount and not it's current price because it's simply not worth it.
This is MY opinion and wether you agree or not is of no concern of mine, just wanted to share my thoughts in hope that I reach out to those of you that have similar views of games released in the 21s century.

First off, this game is hard as♥♥♥♥♥♥ If the concept of obtaining progression only after putting lots of time into dying repeatedly doesn't appeal to you, then simply don't buy it.
For everybody else, this game is an absolute masterpiece in high-intensity cluster♥♥♥♥ery. It's made to make you feel helpless, and the only thing that keeps you going is the excrutiating desire to prove those floating skulls wrong.
Graphics are intentionally dated, and you can see the quality underneath all of the pixelation. It's meant to feel like you're playing an arcade cabinet, and it does so very successfully. As a result, I'm inclined to give the look of the game a 10/10, as the art style appeals to me, and it fits the mood of the game. If all of the game's mechanics were placed into unreal engine on ultra settings, it simply wouldn't be the same game, and for that reason I appreciate the decision of the devs to use the charm of pixelated graphics.
Sound design is incredible. I have no words to describe the emotions the cacophony of sounds invokes in me. My first few attempts were filled with confusion, and the sound design is almost entirely to blame for that, which is a good thing. When the way a game sounds affects how well you can play, you know you're in for a treat. 10/10.
Gameplay is smooth, if only a little undefined. The perspective that's afforded to players makes you feel like you have presence on the stage, which is very much needed once the clock ticks past the 90 second mark for the first time. Knowing where you are on the stage comes very naturally, so I give it an A+ in that regard. Of course, the gameplay isn't without its issues, but the issues I take with it are very subjective and personal to me. I suggest playing the game to get a clear view on how it feels under your mouse and keyboard. 8.5/10
Conclusion: The game probably won't♥♥♥♥♥♥you off until you've died for the 50th time, and even then you will realize it was completely your fault, and not the games. Only until you reach world record status, which an extremely select few have, will you see a very clear line drawn in terms of fairness.
This game isn't just for people who enjoy the FPS genre, as it's a lot more than that. The omission of a targetting reticle makes the experience a lot more smooth, and the learning curve is steep. Because of this, I'd honestly recommend Devil Daggers the type of gamer that enjoys something like Dark Souls, where punishment is constant but player-perserverance is rewarded greatly.
With the three aspects of the game I scored, my average comes out to a 9.5, but keep in mind that this game isn't for everyone. Even though I've got a short amount of time played, I'm in the top five thousand globally with a current survival time of 179 seconds. Not everyone is going to catch on in less than two hours. And even though I've achieved this time, I'm still compelled to get even better, eventually obtaining that 0.1% achievement to showcase on my profile until the end of time. Because believe me, that achievement is going to STAY at 0.1% with how hard it is to get.

I really hated this game.
I bought it, downloaded it, launched it, and found myself plunged instantaneously into the Zone. I was alone. There was no tutorial, no introductory cutscene, no explanation, not even a basic explanation of how the game worked. I walked forward, and looked around. I was instantly shocked at the low FOV and uncomfortably "floaty" mouse control. This was not what I was used to - my most played FPS is Team Fortress 2, closely followed by Fallout 3. S.T.A.L.K.E.R. was something else - something new. I was excited. I continued walking and came across three people with guns walking in the other direction. "STOP WAVING THAT THING ABOUT" one of them bellowed, while sticking his assault rifle up my nose. I pressed "e" (because by now I'd explored the options menu and rebound some keys) to speak to him.
What was going on? That was a question that I'd ask myself a lot while playing this game. This guy told me absolutely nothing of interest, except that there was a base of some description a little further down the hill. By now I'd figured out what some of the HUD was for, and how to open my inventory. I then went to Skadovsk (although I didn't know what it was called then) and got yelled at to put my gun away again. So I opened my inventory and moved my rifle from its slot into my backpack. I would be doing this for a while until I discovered that I could just press "3" to holster my weapon. I then walked into the ship.
I didn't know what the hell I was doing. Where was I? What am I doing here? What do I do now? So I spoke to someone who told me there was a strange glow in the distance that he wanted me to check out. Fair enough, I thought. So I went where the map pointed me and found a ship. I walked onto the ship - and died instantly for (seemingly) no reason. (In actual fact I'd hit an anomaly, I just had no idea what anomalies were or what I was doing.)  Having not saved at any point, I started the game again.
When I got to Skadovsk for the second time, I couldn't find the guy I'd previously talked to, so I talked to Sultan instead. He wanted me to help kill some people. Once again, I thought "fair enough" and went with him. At midnight I boarded a boat and once again struggled to see what the ♥♥♥♥ was happening in the darkness. I think I killed someone. And I got some money. So then, being a Fallout veteran and this being an open world game, I decided to go exploring. I went about 100 metres and the game crashed. One thought ran through my mind: "♥♥♥♥ this". I quit the game and didn't come back for at least a month. I ♥♥♥♥ing hated this game. What I piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ I thought. I couldn't understand the 95% positive review score. This was after about 1 hour's play time. Eventually I was bored and I decided to boot the game again. After switching my lighting renderer from DX10 to DX11 (as the internet told me to) the game didn't crash (although it does crash a lot when trying to enter the "load game" screen). I then tried again. I got to Skadovsk. I talked to Sultan. I did the mission. I learned how to quicksave. From there, I continued (on the easiest difficulty because I'm a casual scrublord).
I then discovered why this game has so many positive reviews. Although the graphics are somewhat dated, the gameplay and atmosphere are second to none. I warmed to the game within another hour. Did some side missions, figured out where I was and what I was doing. I learned what anomalies are. I learned how to collect artifacts. And, ultimately, I learned that Google is my best friend. From this I can see that at least 90% of the negative reviews are either performance issues (there is admittedly a good deal of stuttering in this game) or they are people who, like me, just haven't given the game a chance. I see people in the negative reviews saying how awful the game is with 1.6 hours on record. And I know why. This game tells you absolutely nothing. You know a sum total of jack♥♥♥♥♥♥
Why am I dying instantly for no reason? "♥♥♥♥ you, figure it out!" Why do my bullets not work? "♥♥♥♥ you, git gud." What do these numbers and icons mean? "♥♥♥♥ you, use google!" This is a good thing when you've got into the game because it enhances the atmosphere and is more immersive. The downside is it scares away new players who are frustrated by how bad they are at the game. To people who are looking at buying this game: I say buy it and don't give up on it in the first hour. Google things you don't know and teach yourself about the game - this is hardcore FPS survival horror and it does not hold your hand. In actual fact, it amputates your hand, kicks you into the ground and spits on your face. And that's
the Misery mod! If you are strong enough to get past that, it is one of the most atmospheric and immersive games I've ever played. The gunplay is amazing, it feels realistic, and you truly feel like this could be happening and you could be there experiencing it. If you like FPS survival horror, look no further than the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series.

Picked this up largely on a whim, since its OST and visual design struck a chord with me, and everything about it has been above and beyond all expectations.
I went into it expecting a point-and-click with some nice art direction and relaxing ambient music. What I got was a enchanting piece of (semi-interactive) theatre filled with nuance and detail; a surreal world filled with intertwining stories and characters, each with something memorable to bring to the fore. Every time a new act has been released, it's been played at 2am with the lights off. I've just completely lost myself in it for a few hours at a time, and it's constantly been on my mind at some level since I first played it in 2013.
It's slow-paced and very much non-traditional - it doesn't feature much of the pixel-hunting and puzzle-solving you might expect from a typical adventure game - but the dialogue, worldbuilding, themes and atmosphere carry this game effortlessly. Even something as simple as the movement mechanics are constantly played with to make different sections of the story distinct. Exploration and uncovering the myriad secrets is heavily recommended.
Note that the final act has yet to be released, and if previous experience is any indication, it will be a long, long while before it is. However, said experience leaves me with no doubt that it will be worth the wait. If you do check it out, be sure to play the free "Interval" content the developers have also produced. They add much to the mood and lore of the game.

So Warframe. Now that I have 150+ hours in the game on steam I finally feel that I can give an honest opinion on the game. For the record, I'm not finished with the game and still plan to put hundreds of hours into it. I've had many accounts and have seen the game evolve from update 7 all the way to the current state
TLDR
Warframe is an epic space ninja game with a really fair free to play model. There is a complex weapon modding system where you can do many different builds and fit it to your playstyle. The game requires a lot of time, but if you like the grind and the gameplay mechanics you're in for a treat.
Introduction
It can be a little hard to get into the game because warframe is so complex, but it does a relatively good job of teaching you the basic mechanics and points you in the right direction of what to do next after the tutorial missions have ended. Also, warframe has one of the best communities in any game. You can be sure to make new friends and be helped by complete strangers just out of their kindness. You sadly don't see stuff like that often in other games.
Gameplay
The main thing you'll be doing in warframe is missions. There are many mission types like Survival, Extermination, Defence, Assassination etc. The basic idea of a mission always stays the same, but the map is randomly generated each time. The way you get around those maps is using the pretty excellent parkour system. Like many things, it has evolved a lot over the years. You can slide, walldash, bullet jump and more. It isn't perfect but still quite fun.
Modding
One of the deepest and most complicated systems in Warframe or so it seems. It isn't actually that hard when you know the basics. There are over 800 vastly different mods which all have levels, different stat boosts and more. You can really change up your frame or weapon by modding it. If you have any problems you can always ask in the general chat
F2P?
Some people jump into the Warframe and upon seeing that there is a cash shop instantly leave. It's actually really fair you can get everything but some cosmetics with credits(the regular currency in Warframe). The devs have put so much love into this game and If you like the game you can always give them your hard earned cash to help them make the game better also the prices of things seem fair. Btw you can get platinum(the premium currency) in-game by trading with other players. I still haven't spent a penny and I've never had problems with platinum and have had some to spare. Even if you buy a weapon, you have to level it and mod it and possibly forma it, which all takes time so I don't think it's worth to spend plat on the things you can earn in game
Story
The most surprising part of warframe (at least for me) is the story. It is sooo damn good. The later quests especially The Second Dream and The War Within are really well acted and the music is astonishing.  I haven't completed all the quests, but there is surely more greatness to come from Digital Extremes.
Replayability
One of the things that I like a lot about warframe is the fact that DE releases so much new content. You can come back every few months to find new awesome quests, events weapons, frames etc. The latest update "The Plains Of Eidolon" is one of the biggest yet. It made the jump to an open world. I haven't spent enough time in the plains to give my opinion on it.
Lastly, I want to point out to the newcomers that warframe is a very complex game. give it some time. You might not like it at first, but after 10 hours you should get a basic idea of the mechanics. There are also great beginners guides on youtube. When you start trading I suggest using warframe.market. Most people use it because the in-game trade chat can get really cluttered and it could be hard to find what you are looking for.
I would also recommend to look in the forums or the recruiting chat for a clan, because like most things, Warframe is more fun with other people. they are usually helpful and will give you an easier start in the game
Pros
+fun gameplay
+great story
+amazing community
+a deep modding system
+a fair f2p model
+tons of weapons and frames
+constantly evolving
+clans
Cons
-learning curve
-grind
-confusing early game

My initial review was positive - this was the only game I've waited for in the last 3-4 years and I thought that, with a few patches, it'd be the best cRPG of the year. After restarting the game 6 times due to bugs and completing a sizeable chunk of the game I have to say that, at least to me, it's this year's biggest disappointment.

Round-up: numerous bugs even after 4 different patches, imbalanced and flawed combat system, a step back from Conquistador in terms of player choices. The ultimate problem is that you cannot play like an actual viking in this viking game.

In-depth:
There's a lot to say. First of all, I loved pretty much everything in Conquistador: their approach to racism and different playstyles resulting from the ideology you chose for your character (through choosing your companions, allocating skill points and choosing) was astounding to me. For example, I decided to test how the game would react to me playing a racist piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥who solved all problems with violence and an occasional dose of sweet, sweet coercion on top of empty promises. As a result... I was drowning in money and blood of my enemies - I killedeveryone who opposed me as well asevery Indian I could. The best part was that the game never judged me. For every enemy killed, I got their loot, and for every betrayal, I got the correct benefits, without the game telling me whether I was right or wrong. There was emptiness where I expected backlash to be, and in that emptiness I confronted my conscience: if I wasn't challenging the game, then I was just... doing very bad things because... why? Was I a bad person? Being able to experience that cognitive dyssonance was amazing and I'm grateful for the experience.

So why did I just spent half a page talking about the prequel to this game? Because this game judges you from the start. It judges that you're a fool who's unable to read between the lines or follow hints, instead needing everything to be explicitly said out loud. It provides backstory to even the smallest characters, but those characters don't ask you the right questions and you're not given the right choices. Know how some people started ignoring quests in Witcher 3 because they all ended badly? This is even worse, because you need to finish them in order to progress.

Before illustrating my point through an example, let me give you a picture of who I role-played as: I played a viking leader - with strength almost rivalling Gunnar’s, good Endurance and exceptional Perception, I was an honourable brute who gladly resorted to violence, but was also a good leader and was skilled in diplomacy. Honour, my clansmen, and violence were the things I respected, carrying little for anything else. The example I’ll give comes from the first landing in Europe (I’m intentionally not using the prologue because I think it’s good for the most part). You land near a village. You need horses, so you go into the village and the first thing you do is… talk. Conveniently, Ketil understands the language to some degree. You can attack the villagers at this point, but my character is honourable, so we follow them to the chieftain. Conveniently, they also fetch a priest who understands my language. When I tell him I want geld, he says the village has nothing because it’s been raided by some highwayman and suggests that sorting out that problem will make villagers grateful and they may give us what we need. Somehow, the conversation ends up with me having the following choices: “Fine, we’ll show these villages that they have nothing to fear from us” and “The village is the weaker target.[Attack]” (the village isn’t the weaker target - there’s more of them and you get to kill 1 bandit before the fight even starts). A viking wouldn’t say either of those things. Let me try to remake that scene:
Good morrow, stranger! What brings you here? Your features are alien to us and you carry weapons, it’s quite scary!
Give geld or I give axe you your stomach.
Um… the village is very poor… no geld here, but there are some raiders to the northeast, if you helped then-
Raiders have geld?
N-not sure, but the villagers-
[You place your hand on the monk and easily pull him right in front of your face. He’s a lot shorter than you so his feet are dangling above the ground] We take from villagers and we take from raiders. Take weapons and raiders don’t fight. They resist, they die. No horses when we return and you all die. [You place him back on the same spot you picked him from and leave.]

The problem is that pretty much all characters are cardboard cutouts, safe caricatures used so that nobody gets offended, and when it comes to choices… there just aren’t enough. Usually you can kill one group or the other and that’s it. It’s simplistic and uninteresting.

Combat is also glitchy and just doesn’t work well. I played on Insane and nothing is balanced - there’s a quest where you can escort a group of refugees to the town and when you get to the bridge, 8 enemies spawn and get the first turn - you have a party of 5 who die in 2 hits. This, the uninspired abilities, and a complete lack of polish to the mechanics and even tooltips (if you want to see what a certain injury does, you have to be in combat, otherwise the game won’t easily tell you).

It’s a complete disappointment because I see flaws in the design itself rather than just bugs. Changing the engine and the scope of the game really didn’t work out for them.

As of now, this game has dropped significantly in steam ratings (89 -> 70% within a day). That's a damn shame. Because this  game truly has the potential to become a masterpiece of an RPG. The story, the historical authenticity, the sandbox, real choices having real impact on how the game unfolds... I could go on. However, there are two huge problems with this game in it's current state:
- People are correct in that this game is full of bugs. I personally haven't seen any performance issues or CTDs, but many quests are straight up broken - causing you to use console commands to progress. Right now, I'm stuck in Pictland because I'm greeted with a grey screen everytime I go inside a building in two of the main story quests.
- The fixed timeline game mechanic seems unnecessary, and if you don't notice it (the game fails to point it out besides hints in the dialog), you just die. Game over. Again, I had to use a console command to get past this wtf moment. This seems like suicide for replayability.
Even with these points, I'm going to recommend this game. It's a work of art. The devs have apologised for the bugs, and they are activley releasing patches every few hours.

Ehhh it’s alright. But honestly, aside from the artwork being gorgeous, this game really feels like a school project done by a team with that one kid who wants to go 1000% above and beyond the assignment guidelines.
From the sound and music, to the disjointed goals between levels, everything feels very raw. Canyon Capers is by no means an unfinished title, but the polish was done wrong. Through the first 6 levels I had 6 different objectives and between levels even items seemed inconsistent. It was as if one group member liked coins from Mario, one enjoyed gems from bejeweled and the third was a lover of Spelunky chests and enemies. Meanwhile, the overachieving fourth member was busy incorporating all 3 rather than bringing focus to the game.
The game is pretty, the controls are passable, but the sounds are obnoxious and the entire title feels very disjointed and incohesive. It’s not a pricey game, but I’m not sure I’d recommend Canyon Capers even for a few cents.

TL;DR: This game is the perfect RPG in my opinion. Some might not appreciate the tinkering required to fine tune inventory, crafting, skills, and abilities, while others will love the freedom you have to dabble in so many awesome, fleshed out systems.
To begin - the flexibility you are given is unmatched in any other game I have played. Aside from the fact that you have to play from the classic isometric CRPG perspective (something I enjoy in general, and particularly in this game due to its beautiful environment and engaging landscapes), you can approach this game however you want to. It's super challenging, but lends itself to a methodical approach to exploration and highly strategic combat. I absolutely love pulling off exciting move combos that I conjured out of my own creativity - and then relying on those combos as part of my strategy moving forward.
The story so far is a great classic fantasy style tale, with comedy, drama, and intrigue in equal measures. I absolutely love the characters, and it's one of the first games where I find myself fully engaged in the dialogue. I missed Fallout: New Vegas, but the way I've heard its dialogue options discussed reminds me of this game. Your choices are plentiful, feel like they matter, and influence how others respond to you.
I've sunk 29 hours into it faster than any other game I've ever played, and when I am not playing I am constantly thinking about it.
Some fair warnings about things that might not be your bag: The inventory/ability/skill management is a bit cumbersome, especially as you begin to make some progress, it can be a bit of a process to optimize your characters' gear, abilities, and skills into the most synergized party. I personally enjoy that stuff, as to me it feels a bit like a puzzle, and I honestly consider it an additional challenge to be thoroughly enjoyed. Some people might not like how hard the game is, but there are easier difficulty options and losing battles is part of the fun because you get to readjust your strategy and try again with a new approach.
In conclusion, I bought this game on a whim because I read some good reviews and a week later I think it's my favorite game ever,

I utterly adored Divinity 1 and played it through more than once. So I was calendar watching for the release of Divinity 2. But something about it just grates with me. I find it frustrating as much as anything else. I’m not saying I don’t enjoy it, but the moments of frustration come too frequently to make it likely I’ll replay it.
The lack of direction is fine, I don’t mind random exploring, except – the complete lack of logic to solve some of the puzzles unless you have stumbled on some clues is infuriating.
Like, you get into a tomb but can’t open the sarcophagus. There’s a pressure plate and 3 levers on the wall. If you happen to have gone first into the tomb with the clues, you’re good. If not, Save Trial and Error Reload - for a very long time, because there is no logic to the solution.
And even if you had come across the clues, chances are you’d not have taken them in. There are far too many books to read, which makes us skim through some of them, which is a mistake, because 3 hours down the line you may just need the clues in one of a hundred books you didn’t carefully read.
Some of the battles are unnecessarily long and tedious – a good example is the one in the Blackpits where you have what feels like a thousand bug things to take out. One after a-boring-nother.
There are too many skills – it feels padded out – just how many poison skills does one Geomancer need? Maybe Larian should have considered skill upgrades? When you have a character with Geo/Pyro/Summon who has like 60 skills, often you need to get half way through a long battle to know you have the wrong ones equipped for that particular scenario. Unneccessarily complex imho.
Bugs: okay, a few minor bugs are inevitable with a game like this – you know that when you buy it. But some are just too big to overlook. Tarquin – there’s a lot of Tarquin bug posts.
In my case he won’t leave the darned boat and go to the Graveyard and trigger his quest. I’ve gone to that graveyard so many times, but nope, he’s still hanging on the boat. I’ve already stumbled across the artifacts, lord only knows if I’ll ever get the chance to give them to him. And I read a lot where players say he won’t return to the boat – don’t know who’s better off lol.
I totally want to love this game, but am struggling to do so. I expect I’ll play it through to the bitter end, there’s enough to enjoy to keep me at it. But I will have sworn a lot, a very very lot, before I get there.
I'm not saying don't buy it - it's a lot of hours of fun as well as mind numbing vexation; I just feel I can't actually recommend it.

Similar to those flash games where you can't hit the walls with your mouse cursor, but with lots of clever twists and puzzles that make this game engaging and challenging.
Pros - The controls are a great example of doing exactly what you expect and feeling tight, I was pleasantly surprised that despite being in a circle which is an odd place to move about, I never felt like the block moved unexpectedly.
- The music lends to the game feeling at times very chill, and also exciting when you are close to finishing a level and desperately trying not to die.
- Cool death system, in some puzzles when you die, rather than simply respawning to the same spot, you will respawn in the same spot but at a different point in the circle, which gives a fresh perspective on the puzzle.
- The "expand" effect is hard to describe in writing, but moving outward toward the circles edge or inward sometimes gives this stretching effect, which is very cool and lends itself to some very clever puzzles.
- Similar to the last point, the puzzles in the game consistently had me thinking that they are very unique and clever.
Cons
- "Trial and Error" Like most puzzle games there were a few parts that were frustrating because it felt that in order to solve them you needed to have died multiple times, in order to memorize the layout of the puzzle and just grind through it.
- The checkpoint system felt inconsistent, sometimes being very close together and sometimes having to go back an entire room which felt tedious.
- Menus, I get the game has an aesthetic and all, put using the cube to change graphics options and resolutions took way too long with all the animations, and since I had just started the game it wasn't very intuitive how to even get to the options menu in the first place.
Overall I recommend it for the unique take on a "dont touch the walls" game.

First off, this game is hard as♥♥♥♥♥♥ If the concept of obtaining progression only after putting lots of time into dying repeatedly doesn't appeal to you, then simply don't buy it.
For everybody else, this game is an absolute masterpiece in high-intensity cluster♥♥♥♥ery. It's made to make you feel helpless, and the only thing that keeps you going is the excrutiating desire to prove those floating skulls wrong.
Graphics are intentionally dated, and you can see the quality underneath all of the pixelation. It's meant to feel like you're playing an arcade cabinet, and it does so very successfully. As a result, I'm inclined to give the look of the game a 10/10, as the art style appeals to me, and it fits the mood of the game. If all of the game's mechanics were placed into unreal engine on ultra settings, it simply wouldn't be the same game, and for that reason I appreciate the decision of the devs to use the charm of pixelated graphics.
Sound design is incredible. I have no words to describe the emotions the cacophony of sounds invokes in me. My first few attempts were filled with confusion, and the sound design is almost entirely to blame for that, which is a good thing. When the way a game sounds affects how well you can play, you know you're in for a treat. 10/10.
Gameplay is smooth, if only a little undefined. The perspective that's afforded to players makes you feel like you have presence on the stage, which is very much needed once the clock ticks past the 90 second mark for the first time. Knowing where you are on the stage comes very naturally, so I give it an A+ in that regard. Of course, the gameplay isn't without its issues, but the issues I take with it are very subjective and personal to me. I suggest playing the game to get a clear view on how it feels under your mouse and keyboard. 8.5/10
Conclusion: The game probably won't♥♥♥♥♥♥you off until you've died for the 50th time, and even then you will realize it was completely your fault, and not the games. Only until you reach world record status, which an extremely select few have, will you see a very clear line drawn in terms of fairness.
This game isn't just for people who enjoy the FPS genre, as it's a lot more than that. The omission of a targetting reticle makes the experience a lot more smooth, and the learning curve is steep. Because of this, I'd honestly recommend Devil Daggers the type of gamer that enjoys something like Dark Souls, where punishment is constant but player-perserverance is rewarded greatly.
With the three aspects of the game I scored, my average comes out to a 9.5, but keep in mind that this game isn't for everyone. Even though I've got a short amount of time played, I'm in the top five thousand globally with a current survival time of 179 seconds. Not everyone is going to catch on in less than two hours. And even though I've achieved this time, I'm still compelled to get even better, eventually obtaining that 0.1% achievement to showcase on my profile until the end of time. Because believe me, that achievement is going to STAY at 0.1% with how hard it is to get.

Unique game modes and maps, each with a defining feature that makes every round feel a little different.
Class customization is okay, with the ability to switch between different weapon types.
A lot of medieval weapons are featured and overall it makes a good game, however I do like to point a few things wrong with it.
-Most of the classes do very similar things, its not like there are different classes to fulfill separate roles.
You have the man at arms which is a light weight mobile class.
You have the Vanguard which is the two handed weapon user, which charges in the front of battle.
You have the knight which is a slow hard hitting tank.
All of these are damage dealers, and generally they fulfill the same role in battle, which diminishes the class being unique kind of ordeal.
Archers are pretty distinctive to the rest, but that still doesn't say much.
Most of this is recovered due to the fact that each class's customization, theoretically you could likely get maybe 50-80 different class setups?
-This community is THE worst community from what I have seen in almost any game possible, Dota 2/ CSGO/ League of Legends do not even compare to the amount of unnecessary toxicity I see in chat. At least this game is open to trash talk, but boundaries may be over stepped for those sensitive minded people, if you're not sensitive. Enjoy the game how it is, it's a lot of fun.
-Getting good may require glitching.
This is the biggest culprit for me, as many of the players who are good do not play the game how it was meant to be played.
I see a lot of people spinning in 360s only to get a jump finisher on you, while this is rare. It shows that in order to truly develop skill, you need to glitch.
I don't choose to, I prefer to play the game how it is. And I do have a lot of fun doing it, but it's unfortunate to hear that I would need to break the game in order to gain more potential. To me this is the biggest downer of the game itself, this won't be a big deal if you're a casual player though.
But in this game you feel like you are always taking apart of something, whether its freeing captive slaves, slaughtering filthy peasents, or dumping oil on those using the battering ram below. It's highly satisfying, and this is a great game. Sure you will run into exploiters or whiners in chat, but it doesn't take away from the core game itself.
At it's core this game is incredibly good, and playing a match with friends is exceptional.
I highly recommend this game, right now it's 90% off, and in all honesty I would wait for it to go on sale before you buy this game, I don't see myself spending 25 bucks on it, but this has certainly surpassed my expectations and offered a lot. I will likely continue playing this game for a little while, I expect to be able to pump at least 100 hours before I get bored.

Kentucky Route Zero is a lot like being home. The environments have a pseudo-surrealist/realist feel to them much like the of Twin Peaks if you are familiar to the popular cult show. It has a unique style that scratches an itch that few things can satisify. So, just on how well this game conveys tone and world building alone makes it recomendable.
It's a simple adventure game that follows the likes of Telltale's the walking dead, it isn't so much about puzzle solving but about the relationship of the characters and how much involvement you decide as a player to invest in the story. But instead, you don't just control the actions of one character you often switch to many different character's perspective and you get a sense of being not just a passive reader, a recipient, of a story but as a writer or an actor too. It's a nice feeling, because everyone is likable and there is a lot of heart and love in the backstories of the characters however simple they may seem. They're just good folk. You can tell the developers of this game have a passion for play writting style because a lot of the scenes come off as stage directions which give the exchanges a unique feel.
I feel we are on the brink of redefining what the term video games mean. Of course video games really well describes what the first iteration of games look like, things like pacman or space invaders where there are clearly expressed winstates and scoreboards. But, as the medium has matured we have gotten narrative focused games like Bioshock or even something like Metal of Honor/Call of Duty, where it is implied but not really that winining the game is by finishing all the narative content. And, now we are even in more obscure territory with things like Kentucky Route Zero or Dear Esther and Proteus, where the process of calling them 'games' seems almost silly. This could be the start of something, maybe a new medium, or a change of definition. In any case KR0 is a good example of the expanding definition of this genre of "non-games" that has suddenly gained popularity.

Okay. I've played a little bit of this game, and will continue to play it, but I have to get this out here.
First of all, the vast majority of the game is phenomenal. It is an in-depth grand strategy game with slight role-play elements (certain events allow you to choose between character traits, which affect your ruler's stats). It is probably the most in-depth grand strategy game (maybe ignoring Paradox's other titles), and for the most part, is very fun.
...but... there is one game mechanic which makes this game nearly unplayable- factions. Factions are groups of vassals that band together to demand certain law changes within your realm- usually lower crown authority or elective succession. If you do not grant their demands, they will rebel. While in theory this is a very good mechanic, there are three major problems with it. Firstly, no matter how much your vassals like you, they will probably found and join factions. Secondly, the nobles are constantly- literally incessantly- making demands. Thirdly, usually half of your realm will back a particular faction. This means that every year or few years, you have to divert your entire army, and oft times even hire mercenaries, to defeat a rebellion from half of your realm. This gets very repetitive, boring, and frustrating. If you want to ensure that your realm will pass to one person who is in your dynasty, you will be facing constant rebellions. This is patently absurd and must be immediately removed from the game- or at least massively toned down- for it to be enjoyable.
One other small problem is that the game usually crashes two or three times when you try to launch it before it actually decides that it will launch. This is frustrating, but not game-breaking. Also, it might just be my particular computer- I don't really know for sure.
That said, factions are the only major problem I've seen with the game, and I will keep playing it, and even recommend it; but this is something that needs to be adressed by Paradox.

Where to begin.
I was a young kid living in a run down shack with my widowed mother and my three younger siblings. She spent three years saving up money for a low-end laptop, which I can never thank her enough for. It meant and still means the world to me.
On this laptop, I managed to purchase Super Meat Boy, a classic game. I never thought I'd find a game better.
Until today.
To compare this game to Super Meat Boy would be fickle and pointless. The smooth leaps and gameplay demolish that of games like Mirror's Edge, and the impeccable free-roam world crushing anything that Skyrim could hope to offer.
Instead of Crysis 3, this game could easily be the game people look for to test their high-end graphics cards and processors etc., and even still, the game runs like a dream on any platform.
The incredulously satisfying collection of the mushrooms is matched only by the enlightening soundtrack which follows you as you pave your way through the exquisite level design, which flows so perfectly that the frame slide between the levels is completely unnoticable.
The challenging achievements are high up with what this game has to offer. It is obvious that when PinkySwear was forging this game in what must be quite the expensive developing lair that they wanted only the best for the players. The artwork in the achievement icons alone is beautifully hand-crafted, and the game even includes some comedic achievements for a well-rounded experience.
Despite the fact that there are no voice lines in the game (unless you play the free DLC, of course), the immersiveness of the game surrounds the player as if they were in the world themselves.
The only downside to the game is it's saddeningly short storyline, yet the beautifully tear jerking beginning, content and  ending make up for this entirely.
All in all, this game is possibly the most wondrous game ever created, and I hope that PinkySwear goes on to create other amazing works of art. 98.7/100

English Version:
Expedition: Viking is game from mixed genre. It tells about people from small settlement in Danemark, Skjen, following their story with elements of sandbox (you can choose whatever you want to do, but have to face consequences of that), turn-based tactical battle game ( in fights), aswell as resource management and survival game (encampments, developing your homestad).
There is tendency in reviews to blame this game due to it's bugs. Sure, it's bugged due to early stage of development, but developing studio is working hard on fixing it. Also, considering limited resources, which devs have, the bugs were unavoidable. The developers, as I've stated earlier, are working on bugfixing heavily and are honest and helpful towards players and potential customers. It doesn't mean that you aren't sometimes stuck due to gamebreaking bugs however.
I personally have to reinstall this game each time I close it, due to loading saves' freezing.
The story is dependent on your decisions in all means. You can choose if you're peaceful diplomat and trader or, in opposite, fearful raider burning everything to the ground and leaving only corpses behind. Later in game you can choose to side with one faction or their antagonists or became neutral. I don't want to spoiler anything, but both routes (and their mixes) are deepely written, meaning that you'll spend plenty of time just on one of them. My current playroute is my first and you can see, how much time it took me to just play half of it.
On history matters, everything is good designed - names, enviroment, people, weapons, culture and society. However I wouldn't personally recomend this game for intolerant people - you'll often find women warriors here and basically the game is gender neutral, as supposed to be. You can even find a homosexual love, as I've found in game files. On the other hand, each character and quest was made with hardwork, as I haven't noticed typical filling stuff like random monster encounters nor noname people saying "bring me x, kill y, and I will give you z". Each quest has also alternative endings, depending on your character skills and traits.
Grafics are decent even on lowest settings, but it's personal fillings, so won't tell much about that.
Summarizing, it's a good game, which I can honestly recommend. But not for everyone. If you want an AAA game without bugs or flaws, as well as partriarchary society game and don't want to read much, this game will disappoint you. However, if you like good story, can tolerate some flaws and bugs, can accept and tolerate "liberal" feeling on this game (as supposed due to creators living in liberal - in society means - country) with historical context, I can really recommend this game to you.
Polska wersja:
Expedition: Vikings jest grą łączącą różne typy gier. Opowiada o losach mieszkańców małej duńskiej wioski, Skjen, łącząc to z elementami gry otwartej (gdzie podejmujesz decyzje i ponosisz ich konsekwencje), turowej strategii bitewnej (w walkach) i strategii zarządzania zasobami i przetrwania (obozowiska, rozwój własnej osady).
Wśród recenzji jest tendencja do krytyki tej gry za jej błędy techniczne. Nie mogę zaprzeczyć, gra jest pełna błędów, jednak twórcy pracują nad ich usunięciem cały czas, a z uwagi na ograniczony budżet należało się liczyć z ich obecnością. Sami twórcy są wyjątkowo uczciwi i pomocni dla graczy i klientów, i jak napisałem wcześniej, cały czas czyszczą grę z błędów. Nie oznacza to jednak, że są one rzadkie. Osobiście muszę reinstalować grę za każdym razem po wyłączeniu, z uwagi na błąd z ładowaniem się zapisów.
Historia opiera się w całości na decyzjach gracza. To on decyduje, czy chce być dyplomatą i kupcem, czy przeciwnie - krwiożerczym łupieżcą, palącym wszystko do szczętu i pozostawiającym za sobą tylko trupy. W miarę rozwoju sytuacji dochodzisz do momentu, w którym możesz wybierać między zawarciem sojuszu to z jedną, to z drugą frakcją, jak i prowadzeniu działań na własną rękę. Odchodząc na bok od spoilerów, pozwolę sobie stwierdzić, że każda z tych dróg (lub ich mieszanek) jest dokładnie opisana, pozwalając na długotrwałą rozgrywkę. Możecie to zobaczyć po moim czasie gry, który został spędzony tylko na jednej rozgrywce, do tego ukończonej w połowie dopiero.
Historyczność gry jest dobrze opracowana - tak nazwy, środowisko, ludzie, broń, kultura i społeczeństwo. Nie polecałbym jednak tej gry dla konserwatystów obyczajowych - można tu znaleźć zarówno kobiety-wojowniczki, jak i nawet miłość homoseksualną. Z drugiej strony, każda postać, zadanie i jej historia jest dokładnie rozpisane i ma alternatywne ścieżki końcowe, zależne od umiejętności i cech postaci gracza. Nie znajdziesz tu też typowych zapychaczy w rodzaju losowo generowanych potworów czy nijakich ludzi mówiących "zabij to i to, przynieś to i to, a ja dam ci to i to".
Grafika jest w porządku nawet na najniższych ustawieniach, ale to odczucie osobiste, więc nie będę się nad tym długo rozpisywał.
Polskie tłumaczenie też jest dobrze napisane i zachowuje klimat rozgrywki.
Podsumowując, jest to dobra gra, którą mogę szczerze polecić. Ale nie każdemu. Jeśli szukasz wysokobudżetowego, wolnego od błędów dzieła typu AAA, a także oczekujesz, że wszystko będzie się toczyć wg "tradycyjnych reguł" i stereotypowego wyobrażenia Skandynawów i nie lubisz dużo czytać, obawiam się, że ta gra Cię rozczaruje. Jeśli jednak lubisz dobrą historię, zarówno w sensie literackim, jak i stricte historycznym, a także jesteś tolerancyjny, zarówno wobec wizji gry (która powstała w Danii, w społeczeństwie bardziej liberalnym obyczajowo niż w Polsce) jak i jej niedociągnięć, jestem pewny, że ta gra ci się spodoba.

<sigh> A negative review.  I picked this up as part of a Humble Bundle.  I didn't really have any expectations going in aside from it looked reminiscent of Super Hexagon but the blurb indicates it is 'meditative'.  I grabbed the controller as recommended and got to it.
You're goal is to navigate a series of progressively more difficult rooms to activate triggers and collect...something. The visual style is a stark black on white with red for danger and gray for buttons.  Navigation is oriented in reference to a central pivot point, and each 'room' is circular in design.
I did find some of the mechanics interesting, but the reason for my negative review is that it just wasn't fun.  With puzzle games, I get joy out of those 'Aha!' moments where the solution becomes clear, or a clever method presents itself.  I never felt that with expand.  Instead, I increasingly felt that I was looking forward to the game being over, which it is quite quickly.  There are 4 goal points followed by a final sequence, all achievable in a single sitting.

I'm not sure how to put this lightly, but... Canyon Capers feels like a flash game. Like, a poorly designed flash game at that. You run and jump, you pick up collectables, you reach the end of the level. That's it. I realize games like this were rather popular a while back, on sites like Newgrounds and in truly retro-style games on NES, but... There's a reason we've evolved beyond this crud. Games that try to pull off retro need to be able to do something satisfying, fun, or interesting, like Fez or VVVVVV. It compensates for the pixely and simple design. Mindlessly collecting♥♥♥♥♥♥isn't satisfying. Linear progression through jump puzzles isn't fun. Lifeless music and bland character models with no plot isn't interesting.
I usually play a game for two hours before deciding whether to shelf it or continue. I couldn't make it past half an hour. Avoid like the plague --and that goes for you too, fans of platformer and retro games. There's so much more out there that deserves your money.

When it comes to digital audio workstations, Ohm is a perfectly acceptable piece of software in the way that Fruity Loops (ahem, I mean, ~FL Studio~) is competent. In other words, if you know its limitations - and aren't expecting to be impressed past a certain degree - Ohm certainly will not fail to impress with the few core functions it has to offer.
Main perks? It's certainly more intuitive, and has a shorter learning curve than some of the heavy-hitting DAWs like ProTools. If you've ever been turned off by overwhelming arrays of synthesizer configurations and mixing boards (looking at you, Cubase), Ohm may be the program to start with. In addition, it's one of the only programs that features a live collaborative option. If you've ever attempted to integrate a project with a collaborator across multiple platforms, DAWs, or even DAW version numbers, you'll know what a MASSIVE pain in the♥♥♥♥♥it is to try to synchronize anything. This is what makes Ohm exceptional - and especially so because it's basically freeware.
TL;DR - Ohm is good for creating basic arrangements and experimenting with sounds, but if you're planning on doing any analog recording or serious mixing/mastering in the future, prepare to move over and invest in something with more soulpower, like third-party plugin compatibility. I've been using DAWs like Ohm for about five years, from everything from integration with live sets to full-suite mastering for commercials, and can say conculsively: Sure, Ohm is not as set-ready or reliable as Ableton Live, or mix- and recording-friendly as Apple's Logic Pro X... but it certainly does the job.

Devil Daggers is a first person shooter, rogue-lite, geometry wars -type game. The game is very simple and thus very easy understand - but mastering the game  takes alot of skill.
The game takes place in a hellish arena (very quake-esque) that spawns hordes of demons at you (in a pattern that is very slightly randomized) and your task is to kill anything that moves. The challenge of the game is to survive the demon horde as long as possible. This is easier said than done since you die from one hit (herein lie the rogue-lite elements). The game is very fast paced and very fun movement-wise - you can for instance perform something called a "dagger jump", which basically is a rocket jump, and it does seem like you gain some momentum by continously jumping (not sure though).
The music in the game is great (only plays in the menu). It brings back memories of Alone in The Dark and the old Resident Evil games. The sound design in general is actually very good. Everything really does sound hellish. The demons sound scary, the weapon sounds terrifying, the big spider skull enemy actually makes me uneasy. Different demons emit different sounds which makes it easier to telegrapgh where they are relative to your own position.
There are some issues woth the game though. The sound design is, as I just said, very good. Butt some sound effects blend in a little too much. There is a mechanic in the game where you have to collect red gems in order to upgrade your weapon. The game does not present how many gems you have collected (you need 10 for the first upgrade) and you have to count them yourself by listening to the little thump-like sound when they are picked up. However this sound effect is far from clear and it blends in with the background noise a little too easily.
Secondly the game lacks a proper options menu. The game would really benefit from some visual settings. Furthermore the games performance is rather iffy at times. I have an i5 4690k and an R9 280x and for some reason the game slows down a lot at times and at other times the game runs super smooth. It might very well be an isolated case.
Lastly the game only features one weapon (I'm not even sure what to call it). The weapon is upgradable, sure, but the upgrades don't really change all that much and it can get a little boring using the same gun over and over again.
I do recommend this game because I feel that I got my money worth and for 5 dollars you could do a hell of a lot worse.
