, The Sentient is a procedurally generated space-adventure focusing on micro-managing a crew through various sectors of space. Careful scheduling of tasks between crew members during their respective free-time and combat situations will ensure a successful exploration through this anomaly filled universe.
After witnessing the decaying moral and physical status of Earth’s inhabitants, an artificial intelligence has taken upon itself to discover a way to improve their quality of life. Tasked to oversee mankind’s space exploration agenda, the player controls the AI in an effort to bring as much research and knowledge as it can back to Earth via an orbital station known as The Ark.
The universe of The Sentient is comprised of multitudes of sectors, each with nodes or anomalies marking points of interest. Presented initially as a 3 x 3 grid, the successful investigation of each sector will yield additional adjacent sectors that may be explored. Earth, marking a sector of operations, is located at the center of the original 3 x 3 grid, and must be returned to in order to reconfigure the ship, consolidate and utilize research and recruit more crew members.
Within each sector is a handful of nodes/anomalies to investigate. Upon entering a sector with an FTL jump, all anomalies must be investigated before leaving the sector. The sectors and anomalies are all procedurally generated
– meaning that a re-load of a save point prior to visiting a particular anomaly may generate a new one. Some of the examples of an anomaly include: distress beacons, ship-ship contact, floating cargo, or traps/ambushes/exploitation attempts.
There are many ways to experience a game over in The Sentient, so an instantaneous/automatic save system helps alleviate the burden of premature death. Due to the procedural generation of anomalies upon investigation, along with the difficulties of extended/large scale combat, save scumming is definitely a common reoccurrence. Upon the destruction of the ship from a game over, the game provides the ability to create a new ship with the exact same configuration to hasten a new play through.
The journey begins with the creation and configuration of the space vessel of interest. The ship is comprised of various rooms each with unique functions, such as: the command room, cafeteria, engine room, bar, bathroom, etc. Within each room are various objects that must be placed in order to access the above functions. These include weapons/shield consoles, flight stick, bunk beds, vending machines, etc. Multiples of each object can configured to create a more personalized ship of the player’s choosing. Various crew members must operate particular objects in order to meet their respective needs or fulfill scheduled commands. Each object will also have a maximum durability that must be maintained with a crew mechanic in order to extend the life of the object.
There are two major types of crew members: flight crew and mechanics. The flight crew operate and perform almost every major task needed for the maintenance of the ship and for combat situations. The mechanics restore durability to objects or generators. Each crew member is unique, outfitted with a special set of Perks or Issues: lazy, commanding, hygienic etc. They can also level up with experience for an upgrade in stats.
One of the core mechanics defining The Sentient is with regards to crew micro-management. Each member will have a set of needs that must be fulfilled while performing mandatory tasks for continued space exploration. To aid in improving the efficiency of crew and ship management, it is imperative to strategize and plan assignments for each member using a shift schedule. A day is broken up into Morning, Midday, Afternoon, Evening and Combat shifts.
These Needs are represented by decaying bars indicating: hunger, energy, fun, morale and health levels. In order to maintain high levels for each need, it is important to take a break from ship-related tasks periodically. There is a crew management option that allows a member to disregard scheduled tasks if a Needs level reaches a minimum percentage.
Specific tasks can be pre-assigned to every crew member during each shift in order to help maintain command and vessel integrity. Some of the required tasks that can be assigned include: gathering of weapons/shield energy, fixing of generators/objects, control of the flight systems, etc.
Upon encountering a hostile anomaly, or instigating one, a battle will ensue. The success of a ship-ship battle requires the destruction of the enemy’s shields and subsequent hull. Scanners provide tangible health numbers that the AI controlled ship must deplete using battle canons and lasers. Throughout battle, the player’s shield and weapons energy will deplete in real time. This is because using the on-board weapons systems require a set amount of energy per shot; a cooldown prevents rapid spamming of the fire button. There is a very small energy recovery rate that will eventually provide another shot if all weapons energy is used. Assigning vital combat related tasks will determine the outcome of the battle, including the gathering of weapons/shield energy and energy storage use.
Various tasks/anomalies will reward the player with research points that will unlock permanent upgrades for the ship or its weapon systems. Some of these researched abilities will greatly affect the survivability of the vessel, including: increased damage, improved scanners, faster travel speed, etc.
Originally launched at the end of February this year, the developers of The Sentient have been very active and transparent regarding game updates and future work, as can be seen on the “Recent updates” section in the Store page. There are also many threads from the developers in the Discussions board requesting suggestions and information regarding encountered bugs. Also, almost every thread regarding player support is also presented with a developer response.

I just bought this game and had high hopes. I played a lot of ark and this game appeared too be going in the right direction but its the only game I've ever seen where you can't run with your weapon out. The game is already hard enough with how many hits an npc takes, weapon durability being terrible, leveling taking forever and no clear zone progression.

The state of the game is very Early Access but entirely playable. I’ve invested around three hours in my first play without finding anything too boring or repetitive and there are plenty of game mechanics in place to keep you busy. I think most of the base features are already implemented with most just needing fleshing out to feel a little more fuller and a few things added, tweaked and balanced.
The story of The Sentient is a fantastic one which follows an AI which, you guessed it, became a sentient being and changed the world as we knew it. The story is very well written and though there is only a relatively small snippet at the start it is impactful and the art that goes alongside it is really, really amazing. I would love to see a little more of the story added though honestly, in this style of game I’m not too sure where it would fit in.
The gameplay in The Sentient echoes FTL in many areas such as things like exploring sectors via nodes, random events, crew control and ship combat. But The Sentient seems to have extra features already even though it is still in Early Access form.
You start by being able to build the rooms on your ship where you want them. Each ship must have specific rooms but placement is up to you entirely. You also have the ability to choose which items go in a room, once again some are required, others will give you a room specific boost and some will contribute to your crews needs. The customization reminded me a lot of Theme Hospital and other games like that where you must utilize the space you are given to reap the best benefits and can choose what goes into what room. There are many different rooms you can build and they will either be needed for combat/navigation or to restore your crews needs when they aren’t on duty or in combat, but since combat can happen at almost any time the layout of your ship will be pretty important. Though you only have one ship at the start you are able to unlock more ships via the research tree and these will be stronger, allow for more weapons and have more building space.
Crew members are split into two groups, normal crew and mechanics and each has a different task. Your normal crew will do things like man the weapons and shield controls and fly your ship whereas the mechanics sole job is to keep equipment repaired. You can choose the crew you hire (but can only hire on earth) and your crew has their own stats alongside side perks and negative traits allowing you to pick the crew you think would be the best fit for the job. There are 4 parts to each day and your shipmates can all be assigned tasks to do across the various times in the day allowing for a little micromanagement.
As you travel and explore you encounter different randomized sectors. You can choose which you visit and how many you visit but seeing as you can only repair, hire and upgrade on Earth you’ll find yourself popping back and forth occasionally. Sectors can be scanned (if you upgrade your ship in the research tree) to reveal some features of each sector making it easier to choose which ones you want to explore as the game goes on. Since sectors are randomly generated the possibilities are endless and you can keep on playing and playing still finding new things but the sectors will get harder the furthur from earth you venture. Each sector will also have random events with rewards or consequences as an outcome so there is incentive to explore as much as possible.
You can upgrade features on your ship using research points you’ll find yourself coming across across out in the galaxy making your ship more powerful or unlocking more rooms. You can upgrade things mostly in whatever order you choose allowing you to focus on combat over defense or ignoring both to try to get a new ship if you want.
The soundtrack is short but very atmospheric, I just hope more tracks are added to it over time so it doesn’t feel too repetitive considering there is a lot you can explore.
The graphics are really clean pixel style giving the game an almost retro feel. What I think really deserves a shoutout though is the art you see during the story. It really is beautiful and seems like someone spent a lot of time on it and honestly it’s one of the main reasons i’d love to see more story added.
--- Ship customization
--- Randomized sectors with random events.
--- Crew traits and needs.
--- Crew schedule allowing for micromanagement.
--- Vast research tree.
--- Multiple ship types.
--- Simple yet intuitive combat.
--- Active and receptive developers.
--- Early Access bugs & glitches.
--- No time control hotkeys
--- Needs a little more content
As you can see, most of the cons are relating to things that will hopefully be fixed over the period it is in Early Access.
The Sentient is truly fantastic and though it’s still in Early Access it does a better job than many full release games on Steam. The development team are active and open to suggestions and regularly engage and reply to the community. The gameplay itself while a little buggy is fantastic and there are some brilliant features i’ve never seen before in the genre that work really well. The Sentient is a game with amazing potential and a must-have for any FTL fan out there. (I have clocked in 123 hours on FTL and it’s my fifth most played game.)

[. . .] Its premise is very strong: you take the exploration and RTS gameplay of
, and you add in deeper crew management and ship customization features. And this is exactly what
does, putting the player in control of a fleet of humans as they search the galaxy for the means to research, expand, and survive. [. . .]

The game lacks meaningful decision making and is very buggy right now.
Exploration: The optimal order to explore anomalies in is fairly obvious (just circle around and try to keep travel time to a minimum).
Combat: Your main job is to press 1 and 2 to fire your weapons. There is a little decision making involved here, because you have to decide whether you want to spent your precious weapon energy on the less effective gun or if you just shoot with one gun instead, but besides that there is not a lot going on. Your crew will just sit at their stations and there is no need to order them around (in fact, it would be a terrible idea to do so).
Loot: Very boring loot. You only get supplies and research points (which you can spend back on earth, if you make it w/o dying).
Reasearch: Probably the most meaningful decision to make are when deciding what to research. You have two trees (Controls and Weapons) and some of the technologies will alter your gameplay quite a bit (new weapons, new ship types etc.).
Ship design: You can change where which room is, how big they are and what is in there. This is vey important for the outcome of your mission but at the same time it is very obvious what a good design is and what not (especially on the starter ship). Also the interface is a little fiddely. If you are into designing 2d rooms, you might enjoy this part however.
Crew management: Hiring the right crew members is weird, since some of them are just plain better then others. They have a lot of different stats and perks though, which makes the system quite complex. When you did set up a schedule for them there is not much left to do when in space, though.

This is without a doubt one of the best RPGs I have ever played and after completing it I can honestly say it has secured its place among my top favorite games of all time.

When beginning the game you have the option of creating your own character or choosing from one of several premade characters, each with their own unique backstories and questlines. I highly recommend going this route as these characters and their quests are very well written and interesting. I found myself extremely invested in my main character (Lohse) and what would become of her and her companions. It's also really interesting witnessing the members of your party, each with their own motivations and biases, try to work together while also clashing as they look out for their own best interests. Each character is so well written and perfectly voice acted that it really helped make what is already such an immersive game feel even more alive. The dialogue is great, whether it be the main characters or random NPCs, it really feels like everyone has their own unique personality.
The gameplay is incredibly fun, and I really can't think of the last time I had such a hard time putting down a game. You are given a lot of freedom, leaving it entirely up to you how you choose to progress throughout the world. There are often numerous ways to complete one task, depending on just how creative or good/evil you want to be. To add to this, the choices you make actually have consequences, and sometimes the line between what is right and what is wrong might not be so clear. So you will sometimes find that a decision you made might come back to haunt you in one way or another. I loved this and it was really cool seeing how some of the choices I made previously came to have a much wider impact than I had originally imagined.
The turn-based combat system is really well done and there are lots of ways in which you can get creative and use the environment to your advantage. Each battle is well designed and interesting, with each type of enemy presenting their own unique strengths and weaknesses. You have to really put some thought into exactly how you design your group, providing for a nice amount of strategy both in and out of battle. If you find that you have messed up your build there is an option to respec, something which I think most of us can appreciate for its ability to save us a lot of wasted time.
It is also worth mentioning that there are quite a few options as far as difficulty. I did my first playthrough on Classic, which is the default difficulty, and found it to be perfect for me. There were a few fights which I struggled on, but anytime I faced such a roadblock I found that all I needed to achieve victory was to simply reevaluate my strategy. Personally I love just how rewarding of a feeling this can be, and I look forward to doing future playthrough on the harder difficulties. However if you're someone who is looking for less of a hassle, you will be happy to find that the lower difficulty, Explorer, will allow you to simply enjoy the ride without any frustration.
The quests are extremely fun and varied, some of which require solving puzzles, riddles, or getting a bit more creative with your abilities and items. One thing I really loved about the quest system is that it doesn't hold your hand, meaning that unlike some RPGs that basically give you a GPS tracker showing you exactly where you need to go, this game tends to just point you in a general direction and expect you to figure it out on your own. Now if this is offputting to you, please know I am speaking as someone with a truly awful sense of direction. I had a ton of fun with this and found that getting lost while trying to find where I needed to go to next provided for some of my favorite moments. Some of the random encounters you come across as you explore are the most surprising and rewarding experiences in the game.
The attention to detail is truly incredible and the world really feels so alive. Even areas that at first glance appear to be devoid of life might have something hidden. Especially with the pet pal ability, which allows you to talk to animals, or spirit vision which allows you to see/speak to ghosts, you'll find that if you look close enough there is no shortage of things to be seen or done. And to top this all off the soundtrack is incredible, providing the perfect music to accompany you on what is truly an epic journey.
The universe that Larian have built here is absolutely astounding and they managed to pack so much into this game that it's honestly a bit overwhelming at times. Between all of the characters and their questlines, the decisions you have to make throughout the game, and the sheer size of the world, it's truly impossible to take it all in on just one run. Speaking as someone who rarely plays games a second time, I'm already gearing up for my second trip into Divinity Original Sin 2 and imagine I'll be making even more eventually.
Now that I've ranted and raved about just how much I adore this game I must point out really the only negative thing I have to say about it, and that is just how buggy it can be. During the course of my 111 hour playthrough I ran into a number of bugs, ranging from mildly annoying to gamebreaking. The biggest one, of course, being the gamebreaking bug which made it impossible for me to enter into a room you need to use to begin the final quest. In order to get around this I had to get a bit creative and basically stack items until I could get one of my characters to glitch into said room, then allowing the rest of my party to teleport to me. While I am obviously pleased that I was able to get past this annoying bug, I can't help but be frustrated that such a problem would even exist in the first place. For as much as I love this game some of the bugs I faced really took away from my overall enjoyment and I truly hope Larian will patch them as soon as possible. Of course I'm sure there are those who played the game without facing bugs, but it doesn't change the fact that I was unfortunate enough to encounter them and that some of you might as well.
Overall I truly love this game and believe it deserves all of the praise it is getting. As I mentioned, my one and only complaint are some of the bugs I encountered. While frustrating, such issues can easily be fixed through a patch. And it does speak to just how captivating I found this game to be that I continued to press on despite these issues. There is absolutely no denying that this was a game crafted with a lot of love, and so I have complete faith that Larian will continue to be very active in it post release. If you're on the fence than I suggest you wait a bit to buy, but I imagine it won't take long for these issues to be fixed. For 45 Euro I managed to get one of the most amazing gaming experiences I have ever had and I encourage everyone who is interested to give it a try. This game is a masterpiece, plain and simple.

Where do I start with this game.
I suppose I'll start by saying that I almost never write reviews for games. I may have written one before this, and I likely never will again after this. But this, this perfect gem of RPG madness, needs as high a positive review percentage as possible, and I will do my part to ensure that.
Pros:
Stories, both main and side, that are engaging despite no cinematic camera style whatsoever, and are driven home by excellent narration and voice acting (good choice, Larian Studios). You will laugh, you will (maybe) cry, you will want to strangle that jerkwad villain who's too high level for you to actually take on at the moment. You will stare at your dialogue choices in a cold sweat, the music enhancing the tension as you rack your brain to decide which choice will sidestep lethal conflict, and which will make you relaod the last quick save. Yes, it's a bit cheap to be able to just undo major decisions if they don't go your way, but that's what the "one save" difficulty is for.
Combat that is both fun and challenging. Turn-based combat with a pinch of resource management (Action Points seems to be a good system for this game) makes for an excellent playing field for those who like strategy, while the skills and their visuals will have most cackling like madmen as their enemies burn to a crisp in a wall of fire or get turned into a lovely red paste, only to be risen again by the party necromancer. I won't say everything's perfectly balanced, but the enemies at least all have their strengths and weaknesses, and will punish you for ignoring them.
Story and combat are the two primary things that make up RPG's, and I'm not going to go through listing every good thing about every little mechanic, because I'm hungry and I want to eat sometime today. Sufficed to say, most of the things done by this game, are done right.
Cons:
The graphics, on occasion. Don't pay too much attention to the character models. Why no, it would not be physically possible, much less sensible, to hold a dagger like your rogue is doing currently. Why yes, that dwarf is gripping that two-handed sword by the blade. All-in-all, while it's better by far than many older top-down style RPG's graphics, it could use a bit of work. However, you will be spending much of your time with your camera up in the heavens, and as such won't notice these glaring mistakes.
Game-breaking bug(s?). To be fair, I'm sure they're working on these. I haven't kept up with the most recent patches. But, I do recall having a party member talk to an npc, and then become completely unable to interact with the world, besides dealing damage. Now, from a certain twisted perspective, this could have been considered a feature. It would have been entirely possible to go through the game, and wipe out every enemy with my new ghosted party member. But, that would have sucked the fun out of everything.
Lack of direction at points. As I played through the single-player campaign, I sometimes found myself asking, "what the heck am I supposed to do now?" And let me tell you, when you find yourself asking that, it's usually a good hour or two before you stuble across the answer. Reading the journal seemed to rarely help in those cases. Not that being lost in the world is such a terrible thing, as it often leads to discovering new and exciting things, but it can get frustrating if you're set on pushing through a certain quest/story.
Playing with a another player that doesn't understand D&D style combat. Help them. Teach them. But in the meantime, you have my condolences. You will die. They will die. A lot. The desire to reach through the screen to punch them may rise. But be patient: in time, you will have a reliable partner in crime to roflstomp voidwoken with.
Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys story-driven RPG's. If you're looking for a movie-in-a-game, it may not be for you, but otherwise, definitely give it a chance.

Devil Daggers is an odd game to discuss since it’s very ‘small’, but it can easily be described as a spooky first person shooter time attack game that is dirt cheap, but incredibly challenging. It’s a very deceptive game however, as the simple objective of staying alive for as long as possible is marred by specific rules used by the enemies that in theory are simple to read and avoid, but when put into play together go from zero to frighteningly threatening in no time at all. Add to that a leaderboard that demands player perfection to reach the top, and you have a small game that fills a -big- niche.
The name of the game is survival, and with every passing second the game grows more and more invested in murdering the crap out of you. At first you’ll simply get squid-like enemies that vomit a gaggle of minor skulls and a lone horned skull that tracks you much more intently when your back is turned, but before long the danger rockets up with enemies like ribbed-horned skulls that are -very- keen on biting your ankles and horrifying spiders that will produce offspring when they consume the valuable gems dropped by enemies, [just] to name a few of the obstacles the game will employ against you. Gems  dropped from specific enemies go towards powering up your dagger firing hand, and make no mistake, you -need- these upgrades if you want to survive beyond a minute. You at first have two methods of attack; a constant stream of daggers machine gun style or a shotgun blast that does great damage. The only issue is that the shotgun spray is random, which is a realistic representation, but having a run be ended by a minor skull because a stray round zips by its target grows incredibly frustrating after multiple attempts at a record run. With later upgrades your fire rate increases and you gain access to homing daggers that require constant charging through gem gathering - I know this not because I’ve accessed it, but because I’ve watched replays of others from the leaderboards who clearly have been playing old school shooters more than I have.
Speaking of, the replay system is a magnificent inclusion to the game, allowing you to download and watch runs from other players to see the how's and why's of leaderboard toppers, or compare your runs against friends via filters, allowing you to improve your game. Minus very brief hiccups in the playback from time to time, the replays are a verbatim recording of a player’s run right up their demise - You don’t ‘win’ Devil Daggers. You’re going to bite the dust eventually, which is evident  from how chaotic replays from the latest or recent top times get. Thanks to the study of replays and chatter on forums, subtleties like bunny-hopping and rocket-jumping have been picked up along with other nuances; always keep moving, let off on firing to gather gems quickly, prioritize certain targets, and so on. Knowing the tricks to Devil Daggers is one thing, pulling them off is something else entirely. Thankfully death can be -very- brief, as a tap of the R key at any time will reset the game into a new, fresh run for you to attempt.
You won’t be playing this game to relax and unwind thanks to the frightening enemy design and the deliciously disturbing sound design. The way the spiders flail and the crackling of their spindly limbs echoes nearby, pursuing skulls pant like horrid dogs when they’re an inch away from robbing your run. When the later minutes start rolling on not only are the constant waves of enemies overwhelming but the sounds that are going on are oppressive on the eardrums. I actually have to turn down my volume while playing, otherwise I begin to sweat and feel more stress than one should, never mind when I get to later times where my limbs begin to tighten and my heart rate leaps up. I can’t quite put my finger on why, but the Quake-style graphics only add that bit more to the appeal. While other games use pixel or ‘retro’ style graphics to cut graphical costs and merit visual appeal, Devil Daggers looks, feels and plays like it came right out of a time capsule as some sort of unreleased game, save for the modern leaderboards and replays.
Save for the at times hair-pulling unreliability of the shotgun, there really isn’t much extra that Devil Daggers could use, other than perhaps a practice mode to allow experimentation or careful studying of enemy movement without having to get killed and restart each time. The lightning quick restarts, the near seamless replay system, the floaty yet fully controllable movement and shooting, the sound design that will plague my nightmares in the most positive ways possible… As far as time attack games go, Devil Daggers is, for my money, the very best you can get. It’s also stupidly affordable at $5.49 (Canadian), so striving for leaderboard greatness will only hamper your blood pressure, not your wallet. I very much recommend the game, but I would warn those who suffer too greatly from stress-induced ailments should pass on the game for the sake of their health.

Not sure I can see this game ever getting old - it's one of those occasional ones that is only improved by sinking a bajillion hours. The depth offered by a game where you can play one campaign as a lowly Scottish count, the next as the Pope and the next as Genghis Khan or a Maharaja of India or the Abbasid Caliph speaks for itself really.
Yes, it's super hard to understand at first, but just get going in Ireland and the finer points of assassination and gavelkind will make sense to you in no time. The only other criticism I can think of is that - like other Paradox games - you need an active imagination because a lot of the graphical detail is a bit basic (though mods completely improve that) and action like battles and assassinations take place automatically, pretty much in your head. It's more than made up for in the level of detail offered, though.

Oblivion is a fantasy RPG set in the continent of Tamriel more specifically, the province Cyrodil. You start off (As expected with a TES game) as a prisoner in the Imperial prison for an unknown reason (You can fill this gap yourself I suppose). You escape this prison after Uriel Septim and his blades pass through your cell using a secret escape route. Long story short Uriel falls, the last surviving blade gets depressed and you leave on a grand adventure where you can pick daisies, be a pleasant person and shove an axe in someone's face. Yes it is a great thing to have the freedom to murder someone without it actually being real, it's also nice to suffer consequences like prison sentences, I mean how hard is it to have authority figures that don't try to kill you on sight for stealing an iced bun! Let's talk about the positives of this game (I'm trying my best to not be biased but nostalgia is a cruel ♥♥♥♥♥ isn't she?). It has moments that scared the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me. I once chanced upon a village south of Chorrol filled with villagers that disliked me to say the least (My quest senses were tingling, this was a few years ago of course but Hackdirt still has some effect on me). I decided to rest in the Moslin in whereupon a half naked Nord man attacked me with a club and tried to beat me to death. After the heart attack inducing event I ventured downstairs only to find the inn empty and the town seemingly deserted (I didn't know about the Church meetings and the such). The side quests were a fun little pickle in the game, they generally had some story to them and were a bit of fun such as the one where a Dunmir approaches you in the Imperial city and you're sent on some massive vampire hunt with a couple of twists in the middle. The soundtrack was lovely and I enjoyed the songs myself and the Main quest was quite fine in my opinion. Last positive is how beautiful the world looks, really made me want to explore. Now the negatives, the voice acting, oh dear god the voice acting. There are about 11 voices (excluding DLC) in the game, 9 for the individual races and 1 each for Uriel and Martin Septim (Sean Bean, always destined to die it seems). Seriously, why was there only 11 voice actors it makes no sense! (Don't get me wrong the voices were done quite well but when you only have 11 voices it get's easily annoying ad every character sounds the same). The dungeons and caves were a bit dull (Understandable it was only a team of about 8 for hundreds of dungeons). The combat felt as if I was swinging about a frilly but lethal feather, it's like a paper cut is the equivalent of a Nuclear bomb going off in Cyrodil or something. Overall, Oblivion is a fun to play, well done game and has earned its place not only in the TES series, but in my heart (Cheesiness is not a sin by the way, don't act out the holocaust for that last line).

Right...
Original Sin 2...
I am truly in the middle, despite the tag...It's a must title if you are, like me, an RPG freak. And that, surprisingly, in today's day and age is a saving grace(absurd, I know)! It doesn't make for a bad game in the end, too. It's a rather rough gem and its problem is that it is trying to achieve too much without having enough resources, and it shows. If you have no previous RPG experience, you will probably be overwhelmed by all the choices you can make. But in time you will learn to be more conservative...I am sure of it. But to sum it all up with words:
GREAT ACT 1.
RUSHED REST OF THE GAME.
I am not surprised at all that it has gotten all the hype.
You will have absolutely no second thoughts about the presentation of the game. I would never want anything more from an rpg, both graphically and from a musical perspective.
In addition, Act 1 has a very balanced, interesting, complex, varied and gripping design that draws the player in, and unveils a mature fantasy world, presented with depth, lore and lots of small stories that add to your own impression of the world rather than try and tell you that something or somebody is evil/good. Everything that you interact with makes the flavour of the game much more appealing and the main plot unveils itself rather smoothly. Act 1 is truly a masterpiece. I will trade my entire play through with those 150 + hours for half that with the quality of Act 1 Original Sin 2 Divinity!!!!! I have no regrets when i say that.
But to continue with my review:
Basically(spoilers), everything is good until Malady shows up. After that things start running around with a mind of their own. Well...in all honesty, Reaper's Coast did have some nice encounters, but those come through exploration of otherwise averagely handled semi-open world design. Some say that everything is good, that everything is depth, scope, choice and consequence, Baldur's Gate 2, Planescape, Neverwinter Nights, Witcher 3, yada, yada...
It's a mistake to compare games like that. And when talking about this game--not that bad(it's trying to pursue its own path), but it's not that good either(it doesn't do it that well, overall). Like I said, it just tries to be too many things at once. Developers had fallen into a trap. They should learn from this mistake and pursue a more balanced design.
Combat starts very nice, but later on becomes...I dunno...Wonky. All over the place. Or rather not...I definitely experienced more variation in the beginning, though. Also, I fear that as you progress with the game it becomes less tactical; sort of storm trooper magic medieval style rush simulator with too much easily accessible mobility skills. Height and distance mean almost nothing.
Oh...Two last but very important things. The antagonistic force is underwhelming...The baddies truly come across as an average 'meh'. Everything was fine when the game wasn't trying to FORCE you to choose. When you want to give choice to the people, you need to let them get informed. Original Sin 2 bypasses that idea in it's later half. It allows you to make your own observations during the beginning of the game, then you can role-play and decide based on those. That is an EXCRUCIATINGLY IMPORTANT PART OF AN RPG THAT WANTS TO GIVE CHOICE. By the end of the game that is morphed into info-dumps. The world has much less detail and you cannot make observations. The game is trying to make you choose through quick and sporadic conversations in the spirit of 'Take all of that info! You didn't know that until now! But now you know! So CHOOSE!.'

i have played chivalry since it was a mod for the HL2 engine and then bought the standalone game when it came out. on and off i have played it for a laugh and only recently started to play it regularily.
pro's:
-the soundeffects for this game are spot on. from decapitating an enemy to the roar of charging knights when your team   moves in cant be called anything other than epic. the soundtrack itself is also epic as is the offside "announcers" that comment on objective modes. oh yes and ingame voice commands. the only other game i ever played where the ingame voice commands are hilarious is killing floor.
-the swordplay can be fantastic. this for me is a pro and a con but more on that later.
you can have epic fight when finding the right players. the combat system feels great and if you dont mind learning all about "rainbows,waterfalls" and the likes you will have a great time.
-the goresystem feels great and many a smiles was put on my face when just about hitting an enemy right sending his/her head flying. love it!
-there are a ton of weapons and they do make an impact. you need to choose the right weapon for what you are facing. a sword against a heavy armored knight doesnt do as well as if you would use a blunt weapon and so on. the 4 classes in the game do make a difference.
the con's
-the swordplay, as mentioned earlier this is a 2 sided coin. the game allows for some very frustrating exploits and once you have hit level 15 there is no escaping them other than to reset your level...or learn them yourself.
in a game all about swordplay this can be very frustrating or fun depending on your point of view. i have made my peace with these and learning them myself right now as for me the game is still a blast. the learning curve for these is huge but if you stick with it you will get it right. there are also a good few tutorial videos out there for you to watch. overall i think these exploits take out the fun for most players unless you like punishment and go through a lengthy learning process to master them yourself. for me that is ok because i like the challenge but it might not be for you.
-skins are entirely cosmetic and dont add anything that would give you an edge over another player not having them. having said this...the prices are rediculous. you cannot get anything below 5 euros and these skins are not made by torn banner. so if you want to look cool in a shiny suit prepare to pay  quite a bit of money for items that are made by fans. (they do get a share though)
-the bigger part of the community is very very toxic. for me that is the biggest complaint when i play this game. after work i want to sit down, crack one open, and have a few decent duells but the constant ingame hate-spewing and arrogance will put you off very fast. the only thing you can do is to completely ignore it.
having said that iam playing on 4 servers i favorited and those are duell servers. there is alot of salt on those as well but also some friendly and very helpfull individuals who will help you out or just simply not look down on you.
overall i will recommend chivalry out of the pure reason it is good fun. if you dont mind the exploits or just wait for a sale go get chivalry. there are still a decent amount of servers (i live in europe) out there. this is particulary true if you have friends you can play with as this will be a blast.

Awesomenauts is a game suited for old school action platformer fans. While being a MOBA it isn't complex when it comes to character management. Sure, the roster is big enough to keep you entertained for a while but you will not find yourself reading extensive guides to help you choose from dozens of possible item combinations. This simplicity, while being seemingly off the genre status set by famous MOBAs nowadays, makes the game stand apart. Awesomenauts focuses a lot more on the heat of battle, the fast paced showdowns between teams, rather than the strategy vs. strategy dinamic. This doesn't mean strategy is left aside, but rather that you will spend a lot more of your time supressing the adrenaline induced trembling on your gamepad than talking to your teammates. Try this game if you want to test your action platforming skills against the world.

It's a short point and click game which suffers from disjointed storytelling.
When the game starts out you have no idea what you're supposed to do or even what the basic premise is. After five minutes of clicking and exposition I finally figured out that there's a guy about to visit his mother-in-law and he's asking a shopkeeper for advice about a present and how to approach the (unfriendly) mother-in-law.
Depending on what things you click on you get a different story. There are also different dialogue options and a few different endings, but which ending you get is essentially random. Completing the game takes less than five minutes and then you can try another pattern of choices.
But the whole story is pretty mundane. Even the "best" ending is rather underwhelming. Yes, the game is inexpensive but there's not much to it either.

There's the nugget of something interesting in here, but the game itself fails badly on execution. It's no big spoiler to mention that the game relies on a short, repeating loop of story. This can be and has been done well before in both games and movies, but here, it's a disaster. There simply isn't enough variation in either actions or dialogue to keep it engaging. It works the first handful of times because you can choose different conversations, but after that it's simply maddening repetition. There's no clear indication of what you need to do to "win", and in fact even after trying dozens of combinations, I had to look up a guide to find the exact chain of events to get the final ending. This ending had a somewhat surprising twist, but it was nowhere near enough to make up for the tedium of trying to get to it. I don't know that I could even recommend this game if it were free, just because the work/reward ratio is awful. Again, there's a piece of a story that could be good, but it was botched horribly.

This is one of my favorite RPGs of all time, probably third favorite behind Dark Souls and Morrowind. It totally blows Skyrim out of the water if you're capable of overlooking the visuals and slightly downgraded combat in comparison.
The best thing about this game is the questing. I'd say the game has the best quests of the TES series, between the Shivering isles DLC, Dark Brotherhood questline, hell, there weren't many quests I really hated, almost every guild felt great. Compared to Skyrim where you'd be told to go to a cave full of dragur to get some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ item and bring it back, Oblivion would RARELY repeat this formula. You'd occasionally need to explore a large tomb or a fort or cave, sometimes even a daeadra plane (Which is basically the equivalent of a randomly genned dungeon crawl for this game), but they'd usually do something special such as giving you a temporary companion or contain some unique NPCs/areas in the dungeon.
Now on the bad side, the scaling is one of Oblivion's most infamous problems in comparison to the other games. Personally I prefer Oblivion's method of giving high level armor to random bandits compared to Skyrim's method of making a superman bandit who has 20x the health and damage of every other one. It gets a little silly to see the best armor in the game on some random guys in a cave over and over, and it hurts the progression a bit.
The game is a still a TES game. Meaning the combat is♥♥♥♥♥and consists of you spamming your attacks over and over. On the plus side the combat is a step up from Morrowind where making visual contact will actually well, do damage. On the downside the skills are simplified and require little thought. You can still spam chug potions every 2 seconds in fights, so bringing good gear still simply dominates any strategy or build. And the story is hit or miss, personally I liked the main story just a little less than Morrowind's, and it felt eons beyond Skyrim. Whereas in Skyrim you are the Dragonborn and the world revolves around you, Oblivion sets you in the supporting role of the true hero, though you're still seen as a powerful being.
The visuals look alright if you're willing to mod the game, the bodies have some neckline issues (+1 for Skyrim fixing that at least) but the faces with OCO look decent and the world as always looks great. Personally I loved Oblivion's generic fantasy setting of forests and lava plains mixed with snowy mountains, compared to Skyrim's dead forests and snow. It feels much more alive.
If you can't overlook visuals or are an extreme Skyrim fanboy, you might not enjoy Oblivion, likewise if you were a hardcore Morrowind player and can't stand dumbing down you also might not enjoy Oblivion. But if you can look at it for what it is (A mix between the two games) then there's plenty of enjoyment to be found and is easily one of the best games of last gen.
I have hundreds of hours of playtime, though for whatever reason my overlay conflicts with several of my mods, so the playtime you see is mostly me experimenting with stuff in vanilla or forgetting to activate mods. There's still upwards of 100+ hours of content with the DLC.

Combat is basically shoot them, explosions go everywhere, and if you have better stats, you win.  The enemies have enough movement and action points that you really can't limit them much.  The only real tactic you can use to crush them is to run back to a choke point and have them trickle through.  Other than that, there's stuff like cheesing them with death fog or teleportation.  I suppose a lot of people will claim that is deep strategy.
Conversations boil down to 3 options; if there's more, it soon boils down to these after some flavor text:
1)Walk away
2)say something dumb (it's almost always something dumb) to get the quest to advance.  You really really don't want to say something so dumb, but it's that or skip the quest.
3)say something even dumber and either get more flavor text or fail the quest.
But it's a game.  Collect loot, shoot stuff, watch the story.

This game made me excited to play games again. I love it, 10/10. Okay, maybe not. Assigning a number score is ♥♥♥♥ing useless anyway. I will just be critical of this game and probably talk more about the things I dislike as opposed to the things I do, everyone has already gushed enough about this game. I think it is one the best RPGs of this generation, but it's not perfect.
Extremely open ended, with lots of possible ways to approach a given objective (encounter/quest etc.) which opens up a lot of possible playstyles/roleplay choices. This however, does introduce a lot of broken sh*t, the quest log being one glaring example and I have broken a few enounters by doing X when I should have done Y first
.
Characters are well written, although all the fantasy cliches are there, they are subversive to those tropes in places and each main character has a nicely rounded theme/character arc. Writing in general is nuanced and mature, serious in tone but not lacking in humour a la classic Larian. Main Quest has some interesting ideas and dynamics, but kinda falls apart by the end of act 3 imo

Combat is a little different from Original Sin 1 because of the inclusion of the Armour system. It prevents turn 1 CC deciding battles, and I think it makes you think a bit more tactically during the initial turns but overall I think the system needs some improvements as your mindset going into each battle remains mainly the same, and it also makes some builds pretty trash (tanks, phys/ele hybrids etc). I like saving throws in D&D, a hybrid system where, for example, armour values influenced saving throws would work better imo.
I am not a fan of the character development, way too much number creep (going to the next levels means each piece of gear is instantly outclassed), gear isn't really that intersting, just get some +stats and maybe a free non-unique skill. Vitality/armour/damage scale way too high and picking stats comes down picking whatever gives you the damage multipliers for your skills. Not really engaging or meaningful. Thankfully these points can be easily solved by using mods, but mods don't influence my opinion on the design philosophy of the base game.
Tactician mode is kinda busted, maybe I need to git gud, maybe my fun
do not abuse mechanics enough. Classic mode gets too easy, too quickly. Woe is me.
Overall though, this is on par with some of the best in the genre, and Larian should be commended for their ethical kickstarter/development process. The director has alluded to extra content in the future and has admitted to some flaws so thumbs up again.

Speedrunners is the modern day equivalent of what its players imagined on long car rides. Jumping and swinging from rooftop to rooftop, making incredible feats of strength and dexterity. Players of Speedrunners know this feeling all too well.
The core gameplay of speedrunners is running a 2D side scrolling footrace. Players will have to navigate a variety of maps, all of which have different styles. Certain maps can be tight corridors with lots of wall running, while other maps rely on grappling and swinging across wide open areas. Players must avoid various obstacles such as spikes, crates, walls and even lasers. Players also will have access to a variety of power ups ranging from magma balls to heat seeking grapple hooks. Players must be the last player on screen, by eliminating opponents by any means necessary in order to win. As players get eliminated, sudden death mode becomes a factor; the screen will start shrinking around the player in first, and if another player falls off the screen, they are eliminated.
There are 3 main game modes in speedrunners; story mode, practice mode and multiplayer. The story mode is essentially a playlist of maps with a main bad guy to beat/unlock. Practice mode and multiplayer are a basically the same thing, pick a player, pick a map; the only real difference is if the player feels like playing offline or online. Difficulties can be selected for AI before any match.
Speedrunners does a lot right:
* Addicting
* Fast paced
* Good variation of difficulty
* Fantastic map design
* Good sound/art design
* Balanced power ups
* Fantastic fun with friends
Speedrunners does a few things wrong:
* Short story
* Servers are almost dead
* Can be repetitive
* Can be difficult for players lacking hand/eye coordination
* Easy to drop from first to last
* The keyboard controls are strange
* Lacks substance and drive
Overall speed runners is a well made game, with very good designs and ideas. At the price of $16.99CND it is a bit expensive, but for fans of fast paced games or platformers, it's a must have. Pick it up on sale and play it with some friends.

Not sure I can see this game ever getting old - it's one of those occasional ones that is only improved by sinking a bajillion hours. The depth offered by a game where you can play one campaign as a lowly Scottish count, the next as the Pope and the next as Genghis Khan or a Maharaja of India or the Abbasid Caliph speaks for itself really.
Yes, it's super hard to understand at first, but just get going in Ireland and the finer points of assassination and gavelkind will make sense to you in no time. The only other criticism I can think of is that - like other Paradox games - you need an active imagination because a lot of the graphical detail is a bit basic (though mods completely improve that) and action like battles and assassinations take place automatically, pretty much in your head. It's more than made up for in the level of detail offered, though.
Basically, history nerds will love it, and everyone else who plays it will become a nerd then love it. Highly recommended.

Having driven real trucks alot in the past and being a fan of Giants Farming Sim games i thought this would be right up my street. Unfortunatly after a few hours of playing ATS I'm really bored of it.
Its lack luster in many ways, feels like a really old game and is really boarder line if this should actually be classed as a sim.
I had a go with 18 wheels of steel, years ago and i actually think that in many ways that is a better game.
The graphics, physics and sounds in the game suck.
It doesn't matter what truck you use to haul cargo of any description, its all got the same feel.  Apart from speeds decreasing when pulling up hills, the game gives you no sence of weight. I just did a job with a 370 bhp truck with a 10 speed transmission, hauling a 55 ton load. In real life the thing would have been crawling but in the game i was happily cruising at 65 mph. I was also supprised that i could also  take a tight bend at 80 mph with a trailer on without any drama.
The brakes are way to good even with them set to least effective and they don't seem to be effected by weight. You can come to a fairlyquick stop just by using the jake brakes even when hauling 55 ton
The only incentive to carry on is to earn money and points to buy more powerfull, cooler trucks but if the most basic ones happily deal with the heaviest loads then what is the point in specing a 700bhp truck? If anything, the better you do, the more boring the game becomes
You have the ability to buy your own truck and hire drivers but you can not buy a trailer? In real life a haulage firm has its own trailers which are loaded and unloaded at the start and end of the journey, they do not ALLWAYS simply pick someone elses trailer up and drop it somewhere else.
You can't get out of the cab to inspect where you are going or to interact with anything. When entering the yards it would have been nice to get out and go and report to an office as you would in real life.
There is no interaction with the loads, i.e, strapping down, moving the position etc.
Loads are collected and dropped off at some really random places. For example, why is there a full cable reel to be collected from the side of the road with the destination of a yard? Why does a transormer need hauling from one big yard to another but never to the end user.
Collection and delivery points are pretty much all just big lifeless yards, it would have been nice to take/collect loads to/from a more diverse range of places such as remote, hard to get to sites... quarries, construction sites, farms, etc.
There are no tricky to get to sites, its all just roll off the freeway and you are there. You pick up another load and then get straight back out onto the freeway.
The AI are quite good but the placed things such as tractors with plows on that are just randomly parked on the side of the road look stupid.
Theres no option to buy a used truck. If you were really starting a company from scratch you would buy an old truck and make do until you could afford a better one or upgrade it as you go.
The quick jobs are stupid, it would have been better to be employed by a company and then have the option to look for other jobs as you go.
The frieght market is really dull. In real life a company would bid for a job or sign a contract to haul for a company where as in this game, the price is the price and that is that.
The modding comunity doesn't seem to be all that behind the game. When compaired to Farming sim games, the amount of mods are really limited and most mods are just simple skins.
On the whole im really dissapointed in it. I think i will stick to Farming sim where you can download truck mods and in effect play this game but with so much more freedom.

The game started off as a harmless game with vaguely entertaining undertones.  Something to spend an hour , before moving on to other matters.
Little did I know what broiling, seething, endless amounts of hatred this game would inspire. The voice acting is grating and repetitive. It is easily ignored at first, but after a while you hear them say the exact same thing over and over again. There are limited choices you see, and each of them as meaningless as the last.
What item you choose in the shop means nothing. It just has a meaningless bit of trivia attached to it. One you will hear over and over again, as sometimes seemingly at random you will start outside of the store and instead of going in, the game chooses an item for you. You start knowing each item by heart and hating yourself for it.
The dialogue with the mother in law is equally meaningless. The only ending in the game which seems remotely entertaining is where she dies. None of the characters are remotely interesting or evoke the slightest bit of sympathy or engagement. The protagonist is a shiftless, whiny, useless man who his wife probably married to spite her mother. Understandable, as the mother is a shrill harpy whose voice slowly makes one wish for blunt cranial trauma. The best character is the shopkeeper, for he is only ineffectual instead of being an outright blight on humanity. To add injury to insult, I think I made the characters twice as interesting as they are in the actual game..
To make this game palatable, I would suggest the following.
1. If one is outside the store, allow one to simply skip to be within it. You already heard everything the flower shop guy had to say.
2. Always allow one to choose your item. That is the point yes?
3. Let people change perspective themselves.
4. Provide subtitles
5. Allow one to skip dialogue if it is the exact same. clicking through simply isn't fast enough.
In short, strive to not waste people's time with the game.
Although in hindsight a letter of apology for releasing the game would seem the better option.

Oblivion was the first Elder Scrolls game I got into, and man did I get into it. I had one character that had almost a hundred hours, and that's just one character. I can't even remember how many characters I've created and played only for the 20 or so hours it takes to get through two of the guild quest lines.
Just like Morrowind was impossible for me to get into because it was so dated, Oblivion may be impossible for some people to get into today. The biggest hook of a Scrolls game, at least for me, is the immersion factor. I love getting lost in the world, and it's hard to do that when the graphics no longer look as good as they did on release day and the next game in the series is already out and has made a lot of the mechanics more streamlined.
However, if you can get into it, you're in for a great time. The Dark Brotherhood quest line is the best thing in the game, and way better than anything in Skyrim. I personally enjoy the look and feel of Cryodiil more than the swamps of Morrowind or the snowy mountains of Skyrim, but this is all down to personal taste. Some people, even when Oblivion was new, thought Cyrodiil was too bland and too traditional of a fantasy world, with lots of grey castles and grassy plains.
Here is a list of things, in no particular order, that I enjoyed more about Oblivion than Skyrim:
1) In Oblivion, you could create your own spells. One of my favorite things to do was make a 1 damage, maximum radius fireball and shoot it at the sides of castles as if I were laying siege to them.
2) The little things. I'm of the opinion that Elder Scrolls is at its' best when it's NOT trying to be epic and grand. Some of the most memorable quests in Oblivion, for me, are the ones that have the lowest stakes. Lying in wait in a shop that has been repeatedly burgled in order to catch the thieves; investigating deaths along the gold road; falling asleep in a boat that was turned into an inn and waking up to find yourself out at sea, etc. I like to feel small in these games. I like to feel like I'm NOT the center of the universe, and that I'm just an adventurer going about my business while the rest of the world does its' own thing.
3) If you were planning on playing a pure mage, you HAD to get into the guild, and it took some work. The spells you could buy weren't good enough, you had to make your own, and only the university in the Imperial City had enchanting and spell-making altars. In Skyrim the only spells you can use are the ones you can buy, it takes two minutes to get into the guild, and you don't even get much from finishing it.
4) DLC. While Oblivion had its' fair share of DLC snafus (horse armor, *cough*) it released the grandaddy of all DLC—Shivering Isles. It is, arguably, better than the main game. The design of the world is absolutely stunning, the quest line offers the player choices at every turn, and it's just plain fun. They really fleshed this place out with lore, religious factions, politics, etc. A lot of thought went into a realm of existence that could've been brushed off as, “well everyone is crazy here so things don't have to make sense.”
5) Guilds. Guilds, guilds, guilds. While Skyrim may have had a better main quest than Oblivion's absolutely terrible one, the biggest deciding factor of a Scrolls game is the guild quests, and Oblivion did it better hands down. The Dark Brotherhood was better, the Fighters guild was better (and hilarious at times), the Mages guild was better, the Thieves guild was better (you sneak into the IMPERIAL CITY and steal an ACTUAL ELDER SCROLL. COME ON!). In Skyrim the progression from grub to faction leader felt way too fast, and people were treating you like a grub for far too long. The progression in Oblivion was more gradual. You gained ranks as you progressed, so instead of going from grub to leader you first went from grub to experienced amateur, and the dialogue reflected that.
It's been quite a while since I played Oblivion. After writing this review I'm starting to feel it pulling at me again. I honestly think I'll be revisiting this game every so often for the rest of my life. If that's not an indication of how addicting it can be, I don't what is.

This seems like a really fun game, though I sadly wouldn't know because I can never get into a game. The 5 minutes I managed to play I enjoyed, but the other 85 minutes I spent trying to get into a game where not worth it. The game I managed to play for 5 minutes only had 2 other players, which put me in a 2 vs 1, one of the players was a higher rank, therefore had better parts and easily killed me.
Whenever I tried to connect to a game with a decent amount of players (10+ / 16), the game would just fail to load, freezing and occasionally even crashing as I try to connect into the game. Since the game uses a P2P (peer to peer) connection, all it takes is a single person with a bad connection or high ping to cause problems for the full game. If this game is to take off, they need to implement servers (expensive, I know) or at least a matchmaking system, that links people in a close geographical location together. The current system has you simply join a game, based on no information other then the number of players and current map. This means you get players from all over in a single game, making pings often range from 30ms - 400ms, which i'm guessing is the cause of problems connecting to games.
One positive is there are a good range of parts to build your tank with and the payment model the devs decided on is honestly one of the best I've seen for a F2P game. Free players can access all content and it doesn't seem it would be a huge grind to unlock the parts. Personally I'd probably buy the basic version and then I feel I can achieve something by unlocking parts in the game, without having a limit to the number of parts I can store at once.

This game made me excited to play games again. I love it, 10/10. Okay, maybe not. Assigning a number score is ♥♥♥♥ing useless anyway. I will just be critical of this game and probably talk more about the things I dislike as opposed to the things I do, everyone has already gushed enough about this game. I think it is one the best RPGs of this generation, but it's not perfect.
Extremely open ended, with lots of possible ways to approach a given objective (encounter/quest etc.) which opens up a lot of possible playstyles/roleplay choices. This however, does introduce a lot of broken sh*t, the quest log being one glaring example and I have broken a few enounters by doing X when I should have done Y first
.
Characters are well written, although all the fantasy cliches are there, they are subversive to those tropes in places and each main character has a nicely rounded theme/character arc. Writing in general is nuanced and mature, serious in tone but not lacking in humour a la classic Larian. Main Quest has some interesting ideas and dynamics, but kinda falls apart by the end of act 3 imo

Combat is a little different from Original Sin 1 because of the inclusion of the Armour system. It prevents turn 1 CC deciding battles, and I think it makes you think a bit more tactically during the initial turns but overall I think the system needs some improvements as your mindset going into each battle remains mainly the same, and it also makes some builds pretty trash (tanks, phys/ele hybrids etc). I like saving throws in D&D, a hybrid system where, for example, armour values influenced saving throws would work better imo.
I am not a fan of the character development, way too much number creep (going to the next levels means each piece of gear is instantly outclassed), gear isn't really that intersting, just get some +stats and maybe a free non-unique skill. Vitality/armour/damage scale way too high and picking stats comes down picking whatever gives you the damage multipliers for your skills. Not really engaging or meaningful. Thankfully these points can be easily solved by using mods, but mods don't influence my opinion on the design philosophy of the base game.
Tactician mode is kinda busted, maybe I need to git gud, maybe my fun
do not abuse mechanics enough. Classic mode gets too easy, too quickly. Woe is me.
Overall though, this is on par with some of the best in the genre, and Larian should be commended for their ethical kickstarter/development process. The director has alluded to extra content in the future and has admitted to some flaws so thumbs up again.

Boiled down, this game is about running the same arena over and over for better times on the leaderboard. You probably already know if that's your thing, and if it isn't, avoid.
If it is however, Devil Daggers is recommended.
The important things to note are:
- This game is rock hard. Don't be surprised if you're stuck below the 40 second mark for a while.
- Nothing is explained in-game. While this adds some mystery and discovery elements, it also adds artifical difficulty. (Read the Gameplay Features section on its Steam page to get an idea of some of the core abilities available to you).
- There is enough RNG in the game to keep it from getting stale, but not so much that it distorts the rankings on the leaderboards. As a result, people's records feel fair.
- You can view in-game replays of other player's records. This will spoil whole sections of the game, but does demonstrate that these 600 second runs are in fact completely achievable.
The art and sound design is unique enough to give the game its own charms. In particular I'm very fond of the audio, a disturbing mix of the organic and synthetic.
Overall recommended, but can get repetitive if you weren't already keen on this style of play.

While I know I would like this game even if it didn't give me nostalgia for the PSX days, because it's a really well-constructed little arcade game, it has an appeal to me that goes beyond even nostalgia. The clacking, wailing, screeching horrors of this game sort of trigger something deep in the recesses of my lizard brain. I guess it seems to me sort of like a game from a pearl-clutching anti-gaming TV movie. Like what Joe Leiberman or Hillary Clinton thought all games were. It has such a dark, foreboding, violent quality to it and it's so addictive that it's like what normies used to think gamers played all the time, back when being a 'gamer' was something to be ridiculed and not hip and trendy. People often compare it to Quake, which I suppose isn't entirely unfair, although Quake never gave me anywhere near the adrenaline rush Devil Daggers does. The fact that I only bought it a few days ago and I've already spent almost three hours playing a game in which I have yet to last longer than two minutes in a single session certainly illustrates something about the grip it's got on me.
Beyond all that, it's ridiculously well-designed in pretty much every way. 'Retro' is a big thing in gaming recently, and I usually hate it, but I've never seen anyone do it precisely this way. It's interesting that the PSX is probably the biggest reference point for me in terms of the software-rendered visual style this game revels in, since at the time the PSX was big I didn't have one. I only bought one near the end of its life cycle. During the heyday of the PSX, I was gaming on a high-end PC with a 3D accelerator, and sneering at all my friends who only had consoles. Had this been an exclusive, as so often happened in those days, this would have been one of the ones that would slap that sneer off my face. This game wears its visual style well, and it's perfectly suited to the dull color palette of the game and its various nightmarish creatures.
The sound, as noted by many, is a thing of glory. It reminds me of games even older than the controversial games of my childhood, games I never got to see in an arcade, like Battlezone or Missile Command or Tempest with their thumps and drones and throbs. Tempest can probably even be viewed as a distant ancestor of this game in more than a few ways. I can just imagine Devil Daggers' nightmarish cracklings, grindings, and wails seething through mall arcades somewhere in the depths of the mid-90s. If someone ever cared to port this to a cabinet, it would be more than worth it.
Like the best arcade games, the gameplay itself is ridiculously simple to pick up and horrifically complex to even be competent at, much less master. The weapon you wield is powerful, but if you stop moving or lose focus for even a second, it can mean death. There are so many different intermixing strategies for dealing with the various monsters that have to be balanced and combined at all times to have any chance of success, you have to empty your mind before the onslaught begins. And I wish I hadn't accidentally read about the jewel power-ups, because I feel like I unintentionally cheated. Figuring out how that worked on my own would have caused me to get wrecked even more often than I did when initially starting, and I would have enjoyed coming to the conclusion organically.
I guess one of my only complaints about this game, and don't interpret this as a refusal to git gud, because I'm certainly working on it, is that echolocation, the ability to gauge the positions of things based on sound, plays a massive role in staying alive from moment to moment even beyond figuring out and managing the interlocking strategies required to deal with the different monsters. Not a huge problem, except that not everyone is equal in terms of the ability to echolocate, so some sort of map or at least proximity indicator apart from just sound or the monsters turning orange wouldn't have been a terrible option.
TL;DR it's great. If you like arcade games or are nostalgic for the kind of graphics on display or just the kind of guy or girl who wants to beat everyone's time and show us all how inferior we are, buy it. As someone mentioned in the discussion, if you played it in an arcade, your money would be gone in five minutes and you'd still walk out pumped up, covered in sweat, squinting at the light of the outside world, and smiling ear to ear. You may not do that irl ever again, if you live in Murrica at least, but this can get you somewhere close to that sublime euphoria.

The S.T.A.L.K.E.R series is known for great atmosphere and difficulty, and Call of Pripyat is not lacking for either.  The combination of abandoned ruins and encroaching nature makes for a haunting and desolate game world that you can get lost for hours in. The combat is very tense, as even one bullet can kill and the otherworldy nature of the Zone means a variety of unpredictable dangers, ranging from gravitational anomalies to invisible bloodsuckers. Fun assortment of Warsaw Pact gear and weapons to run around Chernobyl with as well.
Go with Ukrainian/Russian audio and English subs for the best experience, once vanilla and the next heavily modded. If possible, play the original (Shadow of Chernobyl) first. The mod community for Shadow of Chernobyl is absolutely ridiculous in size, and many characters and plot elements in Call of Pripyat will be poorly understood if you have not played the first game.

I have had a few instances where tanks get hung up on some obsticle and just sit there with the tracks running.  I issue a move command to realize that only 1 soldier of those that I selected actually received the command and he just gets mowed down by overwhelming enemy fire when i go back to check on the group I commanded to move.  I strongly dislike when i issue a command to attack a particular unit or position and since whatever unit I commanded is out of range, they all just stand there ignoring me until i manually select them (usually one at a time) and move them into range and then issue the command again.  The individual unit control mode is cool but elsewise completely useless.  The RPG style inventory system is interesting but a complete micromanaging pain. Speedrunners is a fantastic game. Fast paced, side-scrolling game, between four players local co-op and/or online multiplayer.
Only one will be the fastest and only the fastest wins.
I love this game, nothing is better than using a grapple hook to pull your best friend from pole position to a dead last, or having a fireball about to burn your spandex  to return to sender with a shockwave.
If you are the competitive type that loves racing, or you love getting one over on your closest friends, or loved ones over this is the game for you.
This game is all about winning, being the fastest you can be.
There a few different game modes single player
and multiplayer,  with multiplayer offering a great number of game options, maps and many many more community made maps.
The main aim of the game is to win, well being in pole position isn't always the safest place. Yourself and others can pick up and use items that can take you living in first to dead last. Don't fret you can always use your speed boost.
On multiplayer you get to choose from a playable character, although this is just cosmetic. I am sure you will find your favourite after unlocking a few different ones.
Story - Says it all
Multiplayer
Practice - says it all go at it alone or with bots.
The story mode has a difficulty and it well practice makes perfect. Takes some effort complete on hardest setting.
Supports both mouse and keyboard and controllers, as I mentioned before controller for me is the preferred input.
This game has some fun steam achievements. Which are no easy crate pick up for some, but in time they are all achievable if you are dedicated.
Speedrunners originally was a free online game under the name Speedrunner that you could play on your web browser, then took flight on Xbox 360 and later Steam.
I only found that in online game play with others who have high latency will have a large advantage over yourself and others in the same match.

A game that sucked on a random website, called Speedrunner, was given a sequal, one of the best, most simple games that I have ever played, Speedrunners. Speedrunners is very simple, and will put you in a good mood. It is very fun, and great for stress relief. I spent five dollars, during the sale, thinking I'd never play this game. I'm glad that I purchased it. I bought Just Cause 3, Assetto Corsa, and The Crew along with it, and I play Speedrunners by far the most of the three.
You can play from simple characters, like Speedrunner, or Hothead, or you can play a beloved TF2 character, oviously, The Scout. With those two, there are weird ones, like my personal favorite, Sherlock Bones. He is a detective dog, like Sherlock Holmes, but he is very dog like. You may call Sherlock Bones "cute".
Beginners enjoy walking and jumping in official levels, like S.S. Royale, or Powerplant. But as you advance past Expert league, you'll end up in faster, more skill based workshop levels, like Snowed in, or Ginetics. The only skill based official levels are Swift Peaks, Resort, and Casino. Out of ranked, you can play non-currated workshop levels such as Fun Fox Trampoline Palace, or XP square with Extra Powerups. Those are plain humorous maps. Eventually, you will know nearly everyone, and meet a lot of friends. From what I know, half the worldwide community is in my Home city, Dover, New Hampshire, where I know many people who play the game.
I would strongly reccomend Speedrunners, a fun, unstressful humorous game.
