It truly breaks my heart giving this game a negative review.
This game used to be my most favorite MMORPG, simply from its action-oriented and non-targetting combat style, w/ its good community (from what I saw). Don't be misjudged by my hours of playtime, I had to run it on Nexon as for some reason the steam version never worked for me.
So, what's so bad about it now?
For starters, the playerbase is basically dead. I predict a few more months or maybe some years, and the game will be completely dried out of players.
If you're new, wanting to play, you most likely won't come across anyone who will play w/ you as most are just lvl 90+, and have no interest in doing such little tasks for a person who will inevitably get bored and leave.
That brings me to my next point: The level cap.
Before, the level cap was 60-70, a good level cap for this game in my opinion. However, apparently from the time I was on hiatus until recently, they've changed the cap to 93 (I think)
So, instead of fun dungeon-crawling with random people or guild-mates, you're stuck basically grinding alone in a dead server to reach 93 and get some actual good stuff.
3-4 years ago, this game WAS MY LIFE. I would NOT stop gawking about it to friends, trying to get them to play, then them join and have a blast w/ me.
Now?
Now it's a dead place with hardly any chat in global andno one to dungeon crawl with (which, people to hang out with was one of the best parts, and grinding to such a level on your own would eventually wear you out). Just that, is enough to pull me away from this.
Now something for all those verteran players like me, that kinda set us off. Apparently, around september 2016 and before, you could switch your account to EYEDenity (Nexon had control over DN first, then it was switched to Eyedenity). HOWEVER, if you didn't transfer it between that deadline, all your content was erased. Yep. MEANING, If you have a lvl 70 character, with some REALLY good gear, and you payed REAL LIFE Money on the game, that was all for nothing, as it was erased on the transfer. Granted, I never spent a dime on it, but it aggitated me, trying to use my Nexon account, finding out it wont work, and having that ONE Character I spent hours upon hours to get to lvl 50 with a single friend, which the file had a lot of memories for me.
It's a sad tale, a wonderful game turned into.... this.
Sorry to say, but I can't recommend it :(.

Awesomenauts is a fun, fluid, and quirky 2D platforming MOBA. While the cartoony graphics can be an acquired taste and the game is easy to pick up, it still offers enough depth for those looking for a challenge. The classes are fairly basic, but mastering them in a team play setting will still take you hours upon hours.
With tens of thousands of people taking part in each season, the community is still active and you're almost guaranteed to find active games in your region. I've only really had issues during the odd hours in the mornings. The jump in, jump out way of joining games can offer some frustrations, especially if you face a pre-made team, but isn't generally any worse than the solo queuing in any other MOBA that I've tried. The game will also not match players from the two ends of the ladder.
For the more competitive players it is worth knowing that some of the available classes suffer from balancing issues, but the game is still being patched and improved by the developers.

It shatters my heart to write a negative review for Dragon Nest. I only have 60.4 hours on steam but I played Dragon Nest before it was on Steam for 1000+ hours. When I started playing, the level cap was 40 and there was only 4 classes. I was never particulary "good" at the game as I only made it to level cap once when the cap was 40. However, 3-4 years ago, this game was just a ♥♥♥♥ing blast. You could play on Abyss difficulty which made the endless grind feel more like a challenging but rewarding adventure. I was never a succesful player but I remember getting so excited over new gear I saved up for a long time by getting Goddess Tear Drops. But now with the level 93 cap, this game is just dead. The added classes are honestly incredible and really diversifies gameplay. The problem is the 1-93 grind is so painfully boring due to limitations on what difficulty you can play. If that wasn't enough, you'll have a hard time trying to find people to play with. It's really a shame because when the game was active, the mentor system worked so well in trying to help your friends get to your rank and really gave an incentive for playing with other people of all ranks. The Goddess Tear Drops and mentor system all still exist which is great. It's just the fundamental aspects of an MMO are compltely and utterly GONE. The market is dead. I mention this because the marketplace used to be PACKED by dozens of people on every server when this game was alive and well. The combat, which is so incredible it kept this game alive far past the time it probably should have actually died; has been made more boring as dungeons have suddenly gotten ridicously easy. I am begging, and I mean BEGGING for Dragon Nest to be shut down in favor of a Dragon Nest 2 with updated graphics, balances, a sensible level cap between 40-93, and less pay-to-win schemes. The arcade-like feel of Dragon Nest makes it unique compared to other MMOs even after so many years that have seen bold competitors enter the MMO market. If they brought Dragon Nest to the next generation with a second installment, everyday gamers would fall head over heals for it. But for now, please don't support the current version.

Unlike most visual novels, this VN has multiple routes with extremely varying dialogue and scenarios that occur. There's a large amount of visual content in the game, fans of sonico will recognize a lot of the outfit from official artworks. It stays very true to the sonico character as a jack of all trades style character. Your clothing and dialogue selection shapes which route, what clothing you unlock, Sonico's personality to an extent and which ending youll get. If you're a huge anime fan, or a fan of the Super Sonico character this game is a must buy.
Jessica Nigri is a surprisingly good voice actor for having so few roles, the benefit of this is when you hear her as Sonico you don't think of every other character she has read dialogue for (Looking at you, Johnny Yung Bosch).
If you like dating/companionship sim games then this game is a for sure buy. I'd compare it to the dating scenes in Conception 2.
If you are the type of person that once you see the credits once you lose interest in the game then you will not experience the content in this game to the fullest.
Where the game is lacking is the main FPS portions, after about 15 or so photoshoots the patterns of targets to hit become predictable and the 3 minute endurance of photo taking for each shoot can become tiresome if you're trying to obtain all the endings. There is a free mode where there is no timer or targets, you can add overlays to your setup and choose any pose you've unlocked (Lots of freedom here for the lewd).
This game has 18 endings.
If you read all the dialogue and listen to all the voice acting during any indidual playthough your total playtime per route will be around 2-3 hours.
If you skip all the dialogue and just focus on getting to the next photoshoot you can expect a bit over an hour of gameplay per run.
Pros:
Shape your waifu's future
Dress your waifu
Save lewds of your waifu directly from the game client
Lots to unlock
Many routes
Dual Audio
Can skip photoshoots you've already completed on subsiquent playthroughs
Cons:
FPS portions can drag on
FPS gameplay can be repetative
Some RNG in unlocking a few things
You need a guide to 100% this, some dialogue options are cryptic
True ending has a very specific path to take

The art style is neat but gets wasted in the three screens that come over and over again. So the art style gets boring very fast and very undeserved.
It is a shame to give this game a bad review seen what it could be, that it looks relatively good and that the premises gameplay and story wise are interesting. But as bad as the execution is, it is needed.
Get this game in case you feel lucky or very intrigued. There are people who seemed to enjoy it very much. And in case you won’t like it, you can always refund it.

Okay, so Gear Up is a tank building game. It's pretty self explanatory; build yourself a tank, shoot the bad guys, earn cash for a better tank, repeat. A concept seemingly hard to screw up, however Doctor Entertainment appears to have done just that.
Pros:
Cons:
Although the limited backpack space annoys me to no end (the fact that they offer you
extra backpack slot for joining their steam group making it twice as insulting), let's touch upon the lack of matchmaking for a second.
In a game like this, where buying parts with ingame currency determines how well your tank will fare, having the only way to actually get in game be through a lobby system is a big no. Let's look at a common scenario: You're starting up a game. At your starting level (with the default tank) it is VERY easy get matched into games with veterans, most of whom will have much better armor, guns and tires than you will. Bam, straight into a respawn timer. This is exactly what happened during my first gameplay (and likely what will happen during any new player's as well). An experienced player's tank can take multiple shots from a default tank before it dies, all while frollicking around the map literally one-shotting anything that moves with rockets and flamethrowers.
Did you catch that one part? "
one-shotting". Because that's actually a thing that can happen.
Gear Up could honestly be something great, but as of right now, the lack of matchmaking coupled with the limited amount of backpack space for free players makes it merely a pay-to-win Robocraft clone. I'm sure I speak for a lot of the community when I say I am thoroughly dissapointed in this game. I don't care how good the graphics look or how solid the controls are, if you can't play with a matchmaking system, all the Free-to-Play tags in the world won't make Gear Up worth my time.

Although this game is great alone. With mods it is waaaay more enjoyable. Arsenal with 60 new armos and 200 new weapons is great. Atmosphere 3 is usually included with all of the larger mods. But, Misery. Dear God, Misery. It scares people off because its incredibly difficult. It shouldn't though, it's extremely immersive, letting you live an actual life in the zone, doing what you want to do as a Loner Stalker. Misery is if anything, playable forever, there is so much micromanaging, as far as waking up in the morning, planning on observing a certain area, deciding to go in for the kill, and planning your raid, to cleaning your weapon, to setting up camp for the night and just putting food on the table, to watching your radiation and other needs, to planning a hunting trip to make reap a god kill and harvest the goods. I've been playing this game for a long time, I live for immesive realism games, ArmA, DayZ, Ranger Hardcore on Metro, Master difficulty on the vanilla S.T.A.L.K.E.R., never have I actually woken up in real life, got showered, breakfast, etc. And decided to plan out my ingame day over a real life cup of coffee on a Saturday morning. If you want something real, something that makes you feel like you have to earn it, all of these games, you play♥♥♥♥♥the main character, gunslinging, medkit addicted, bullet eating protagonist with a misson and everyone stepping out of your way for your story the world revolving around you. But not Misery, in Misery your just some everyday stalker, walking in eating your flesh (the ingame monster) bacon wrapped in brown papar to keep the grease from dripping (actual description, immersion is life) planning on going for that artifact today, or that camp, the rounds your taking for your gun, the equipment you'll need for that area, maybe a sleeping bag and a safe place, incase youre out ill nightfall or an emission happens all of the sudden. In order to be a badass gunslinging veteran stalker, you had to train yourself and learn to be a badass stalker, absolutely no handholding in the mod. Misery will make you feel like you're there, but its not for everybody, the mod is infamously difficult, harder than Dark Souls, harder than the original Ninja Gaiden (well maybe not THAT hard *cringes at Ninja Gaiden*), at any moment something could leap from the marshes or shadows, whether it be a enemy stalker bullet, or the claws of a bloodsucker, if you're not on your toes with some real friggin' reflexes, you will die. A lot of times, no matter how good you are, sometimes you just get unlucky and a stary bullet will nail your head ending your journey in the zone. If your a serious immersion freak, wondering how you would really do in the zone (with basic knowledge of weaponry and cooking and medicenes) Misery is for you. If you like things tough, but still want to be a bit on top of everything else, try Master difficulty with Arenal Overload. However, the game is enjoyable and incredible regardless, 10/10!

Oblivion was the first Elder Scrolls game I got into, and man did I get into it. I had one character that had almost a hundred hours, and that's just one character. I can't even remember how many characters I've created and played only for the 20 or so hours it takes to get through two of the guild quest lines.
Just like Morrowind was impossible for me to get into because it was so dated, Oblivion may be impossible for some people to get into today. The biggest hook of a Scrolls game, at least for me, is the immersion factor. I love getting lost in the world, and it's hard to do that when the graphics no longer look as good as they did on release day and the next game in the series is already out and has made a lot of the mechanics more streamlined.
However, if you can get into it, you're in for a great time. The Dark Brotherhood quest line is the best thing in the game, and way better than anything in Skyrim. I personally enjoy the look and feel of Cryodiil more than the swamps of Morrowind or the snowy mountains of Skyrim, but this is all down to personal taste. Some people, even when Oblivion was new, thought Cyrodiil was too bland and too traditional of a fantasy world, with lots of grey castles and grassy plains.
Here is a list of things, in no particular order, that I enjoyed more about Oblivion than Skyrim:
1) In Oblivion, you could create your own spells. One of my favorite things to do was make a 1 damage, maximum radius fireball and shoot it at the sides of castles as if I were laying siege to them.
2) The little things. I'm of the opinion that Elder Scrolls is at its' best when it's NOT trying to be epic and grand. Some of the most memorable quests in Oblivion, for me, are the ones that have the lowest stakes. Lying in wait in a shop that has been repeatedly burgled in order to catch the thieves; investigating deaths along the gold road; falling asleep in a boat that was turned into an inn and waking up to find yourself out at sea, etc. I like to feel small in these games. I like to feel like I'm NOT the center of the universe, and that I'm just an adventurer going about my business while the rest of the world does its' own thing.
3) If you were planning on playing a pure mage, you HAD to get into the guild, and it took some work. The spells you could buy weren't good enough, you had to make your own, and only the university in the Imperial City had enchanting and spell-making altars. In Skyrim the only spells you can use are the ones you can buy, it takes two minutes to get into the guild, and you don't even get much from finishing it.
4) DLC. While Oblivion had its' fair share of DLC snafus (horse armor, *cough*) it released the grandaddy of all DLC—Shivering Isles. It is, arguably, better than the main game. The design of the world is absolutely stunning, the quest line offers the player choices at every turn, and it's just plain fun. They really fleshed this place out with lore, religious factions, politics, etc. A lot of thought went into a realm of existence that could've been brushed off as, “well everyone is crazy here so things don't have to make sense.”
5) Guilds. Guilds, guilds, guilds. While Skyrim may have had a better main quest than Oblivion's absolutely terrible one, the biggest deciding factor of a Scrolls game is the guild quests, and Oblivion did it better hands down. The Dark Brotherhood was better, the Fighters guild was better (and hilarious at times), the Mages guild was better, the Thieves guild was better (you sneak into the IMPERIAL CITY and steal an ACTUAL ELDER SCROLL. COME ON!). In Skyrim the progression from grub to faction leader felt way too fast, and people were treating you like a grub for far too long. The progression in Oblivion was more gradual. You gained ranks as you progressed, so instead of going from grub to leader you first went from grub to experienced amateur, and the dialogue reflected that.
It's been quite a while since I played Oblivion. After writing this review I'm starting to feel it pulling at me again. I honestly think I'll be revisiting this game every so often for the rest of my life. If that's not an indication of how addicting it can be, I don't what is.

Good alternative to ark survival evolved, but still early alpha with very much lacking in optimizations (only playable on high-end systems). However, you can still play provided that all drivers are up-to-date and are capable of utilizing vulkan runtime libraries. The BattleEye application causes high disk usage, so I'd suggest tweaking your system to give most disk, memory, and cpu resources to the game. The game may lag for one of two reasons: internet lag or your system running out of free RAM. The game has some memory leaks and this is what I have done to fix them a bit:
Disable steam overlay
Set game launch option to: -malloc=system
Put game in low-end laptop mode; then, exit game; start game again and put in auto mode; and now gamerusersettings.ini can be changed without game overwritting it from the auto-mode algorithm --> set all scalability values to zero except for anti-aliasing to 1 and resolution to 90.609001 or 95.609001
gameusersettings.ini can be found in C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Conan Exiles\ConanSandbox\Saved\Config\WindowsNoEditor

Unlike most visual novels, this VN has multiple routes with extremely varying dialogue and scenarios that occur. There's a large amount of visual content in the game, fans of sonico will recognize a lot of the outfit from official artworks. It stays very true to the sonico character as a jack of all trades style character. Your clothing and dialogue selection shapes which route, what clothing you unlock, Sonico's personality to an extent and which ending youll get. If you're a huge anime fan, or a fan of the Super Sonico character this game is a must buy.
Jessica Nigri is a surprisingly good voice actor for having so few roles, the benefit of this is when you hear her as Sonico you don't think of every other character she has read dialogue for (Looking at you, Johnny Yung Bosch).
If you like dating/companionship sim games then this game is a for sure buy. I'd compare it to the dating scenes in Conception 2.
If you are the type of person that once you see the credits once you lose interest in the game then you will not experience the content in this game to the fullest.
Where the game is lacking is the main FPS portions, after about 15 or so photoshoots the patterns of targets to hit become predictable and the 3 minute endurance of photo taking for each shoot can become tiresome if you're trying to obtain all the endings. There is a free mode where there is no timer or targets, you can add overlays to your setup and choose any pose you've unlocked (Lots of freedom here for the lewd).
This game has 18 endings.
If you read all the dialogue and listen to all the voice acting during any indidual playthough your total playtime per route will be around 2-3 hours.
If you skip all the dialogue and just focus on getting to the next photoshoot you can expect a bit over an hour of gameplay per run.

Speedrunners is a fast-paced, competitive, racing game where players play as superheroes trying to outrun each other in 16 different official maps, in addition to thousands of user created levels. Speedrunners offers both online and local matches that can hold up to 4 players and different game modes that suits a wide range of skill levels, from practice mode for beginners and ranked mode for more experienced players. There is also a friendly tutorial for those who are new to the game, and all these game modes are designed to suit players as they improve. As there are only 16 official maps, Speedrunners has allowed us to use our creativity to submit workshop levels, which keeps the game interesting. Although I have been held back due to connectivity problems, I have enjoyed the challenges that the game offered me regardless.
The objective of the game is to outrun each other so that one player might fall off-screen and lose. In Speedrunners players race and outwit each other through a variety of obstacles, such as crates, lasers, and spikes, and power-ups, such as fireballs, ice rays, missiles, and grappling hooks, which has often caused close wins, amazing moments, and huge upsets. Additionally, the players can adjust the settings so that the game turns a whole new turn, with mechanics such as a “Lethal Spikes”, which causes players to drop as soon as they hit a spike, and srennurdeepS, which causes the map to be flipped. However, theses additions get boring after a while, and I recommend that, in the future, the developers could add more or change features and power-ups to shift the flow of the game.
In a universe where superheroes race each other to save people or capture criminals, the game design blends into this universe by using a cartoonish yet straightforward and sharp design. The variety of characters, the power-ups the players use, and the clear sound effects of explosions and ice beams all emphasize the theme of world.
I cannot lie, but the game has some amazing soundtracks, which also fits with the overall superhero theme and the fast pace of the game; however, as the soundtracks are repeated often during matches, the developers could add more soundtracks to keep the game interesting.
Speedrunners features tons of unlockable Heroes; each with their own personality and character. What’s more: they also have skins! Moreover, the community is allowed to submit trails, which gives the game even customization.
The best thing is, you can play this locally with your friends! In conclusion, Speedrunners is an innovative and friendly game that combines superheroes with racing and lets you improve at your own pace, but somewhat lacks in the aspect that could keep a game interesting. I would recommend this to everyone who enjoy fast-paced games and racing.

Do I recommend this game? Yes.
However, I do have some complaints.
I think Super Switch as a concept is really neat. It's a platforming game where you have to quickly switch parts of a level on or off. Traps, boosts, platforms, and walls must be switched avoid death. I have to admit the switching mechanic makes the game pretty hard compared to some platformers. You have to worry about where you're jumping as well as what needs to be switched on or off mid jump. Getting your mind into the rhythm of switching is tricky, and it's that trickiness which will cause most of your deaths.
The first thing you'll notice when you start playing is that SS seems a lot like Super Meat Boy. The small square character, rotating spikes, wall jumping, and quick restarts were all reminders of SMB, and that's okay. SS has it's own unique game play, and isn't a rip off of SMB, the games just share many similarities. Due to their similarities however I'm going to draw a lot of comparisons between SS and SMB as I go through this review.
Visuals:
SS has a minimalist art style, with a simple color palette and bare design aesthetic. It's an indie game so the art style makes sense, and I find that it fits the gameplay pretty well. Uncluttered levels let the player focus on the game, and the simple palette makes obstacles clearly visible. I do wish however with that zone 4 wasn't dark blue. The lighter colors of zones 2 and 3 are way better on the eyes than the color of zone 4, and I think a lighter blue would make zone 4 much more appealing. Overall not bad visuals.
Sound:
The sound of this game doesn't really fit the art style and level design. The soundtrack is reminiscent of SMB with its heavy electric guitar usage. But for a game with such a simple art style, the music clashes with the game's visual presentation, and I found that I enjoyed the game more when music was turned completely off. Sound effects are all where they need to be, and nothing stands out as particularly good or bad.
Gameplay:
Movement and switching are all handled well. Your character handles like a heavy Meat Boy, which takes a little getting used to, but after a few stages you feel comfortable with its movement. The controls are really easy to feel for, and the game does an adequate job of showing you how to properly play it in a way that lets you figure things out organically.
One thing that I found consistently annoying were the amount of times I would die on a rotating blade I thought I was clearly not in danger from. At first I thought the rotating blade hitboxes were messed up, but after some testing I found out that they were spot on. The problem actually stems from the way the blade is drawn to the screen. The blades have two frames of animation that they cycle through, and because the individual blades are spaced so far apart, those two constantly changing frames give the illusion that the blades are shorter than they actually are. I would strongly recommend that the developer make the rotating blades have more actual blades on them. Super Meat Boy does this really well, copy that.
The game consists of 40 stages across four zones (levels). There is some variety from zone to zone, but after a while many of the stages seem samey. The same four or five obstacles show up in nearly every zone, and for the 40 stages there are maybe 15-20 level I say are unique enough that they felt different. Another big problem the game has is its repetition of the same obstacle over and over chained together. The game seems to have the mentality of, "if the player can overcome an obstacle once they should prove it by doing it five more times right after this." It isn't fun jumping over a laser, switching to turn on a platform, and then jumping and immediately switching back to avoid a laser if I have to do it four times in a row with no variation. When you take out the repetition of obstacles in each stage you see that the stages themselves are really short, and with only 40 stages that means this game is lacking in content. I saw every stage in under 40 minutes after staring the game.
Despite these complaints I think this game is worth it. It was a fun platformer even if it was a little repetitive, and I think the $2 price tag fits it well. I don't regret my purchase, and I don't think you will either. It's a fun short game to plug up an afternoon. I give it a 5 out of 10.
Maybe if the game had some more unique stages, or some more unique gameplay mechanics I would have rated it higher. I would have easily payed $5 for 80 or so unique stages, but for the 40 stages we have I think the $2 price tag is fine. It's not a bad game, but it's not a particularly outstanding one either.

Things Woodle Tree Adventures does right:
-Cute Style and interesting character design
-Bright worlds with a decent enough amount of variety
-Those block guys who cry when you hit them
Things Woodle Tree Adventures could improve:
-Music is nice but get's repetitive quickly (would be nice to get some bouncier more energetic tracks)
-Killing enemies serves little purpose and doesn't feel satisfying (Most of them don't even try and hurt you and they make no noise while alive or dying. Also they all only take one hit even the big ones. An achievement similar to the 1'000 berries one could also remedy this nicely)
-Collecting berries after a while feels pointless (Could use an in level counter in one of the corners to show how many you've accumulated. Also berries really aren't used for much except for unlocking a couple levels and items)
-Exploration should be rewarded (A lot of times I'd find a secret little area and everytime I'd think it would be great if there was something here even if it was just an extra berry)
-Weapon upgrades don't feel very noticeable (Yes your projectile goes farther but all the creatures only take one hit to kill)
-Controls feel a little slippery and the world feels weightless making it hard to gauge where exactly you'll land when jumping. (Aside from a few clumps Woodle really has no effect on the enviroment)
-Could use more levels
-Boss fights wouldn't hurt
If I had to describe Woodle Tree Adventures in a word it'd be: complex. WTA is a short 3-D collect-a-thon platformer (reminiscent of Mario 64 and Banjo Kazooie) as much as it is a coming of age story. I won't get into the meat of the story but Woodle is sent on a life threatening quest to gather the fabled Fairy Tears and a crap ton of berries all while  trying to prove himself to his Father the Deku Tree. In this quest he encounters terrifying enemies such as Caterpillars, Candy Corn People and a couple really tall guys. There are 6 different levels rich in colour and interesting in design, as well as a few unlockable weapons (Although the don't differ much, I actually still have no idea what the headband does.) You can also bring a buddy along as a beaver to help you collect your berries. On the surface WTA is a cute platforming adventure you can waste a couple hours in, but at it's core WTA is a deep philosophical journey and a look at today's society as a whole. You collect berries monotonously as an allegory for everyday life, there are also underlying themes of surpassing your elders and whether giving up on your dreams to take up their mantle is the right choice.
In the end though there are a lot of things wrong with WTA and a lot of things right I have to give it a 6/10. I hope a Woodle Tree  Adventures 2 is in the works and if so the developer takes my criticisms to heart.

A Considerable Speck
by Robert Frost
A speck that would have been beneath my sight
On any but a paper sheet so white
Set off across what I had written there.
And I had idly poised my pen in air
To stop it with a period of ink
When something strange about it made me think,
This was no dust speck by my breathing blown,
But unmistakably a living mite
With inclinations it could call its own.
It paused as with suspicion of my pen,
And then came racing wildly on again
To where my manuscript was not yet dry;
Then paused again and either drank or smelt--
With loathing, for again it turned to fly.
Plainly with an intelligence I dealt.
It seemed too tiny to have room for feet,
Yet must have had a set of them complete
To express how much it didn't want to die.
It ran with terror and with cunning crept.
It faltered: I could see it hesitate;
Then in the middle of the open sheet
Cower down in desperation to accept
Whatever I accorded it of fate.
I have none of the tenderer-than-thou
Collectivistic regimenting love
With which the modern world is being swept.
But this poor microscopic item now!
Since it was nothing I knew evil of
I let it lie there till I hope it slept.
I have a mind myself and recognize
Mind when I meet with it in any guise
No one can know how glad I am to find
On any sheet the least display of mind.

The Shopkeeper sports a surreal tale where a man is looking for an antique object to try and impress his rich mother-in-law: you'll get to hear the story behind each object and see the consequences of your choice.
Sadly this interesting concept is ruined by shallow and repetitive gameplay and a story that simply isn't interesting.
-the hand drawn graphics are quite nice
-decently ambigue and surreal atmosphere
-fully voice acted
-trial and error gameplay gets boring fast
-extremely short, each game session lasts about 5 minutes (before you either get an ending or have to restart)
-characters lack depth
-voice acting is pretty awful due to the flat, emotionless tone all characters have
-the whole story simply fails to be engaging or interesting enough
Gameplay in The Shopkeeper sadly boils down to this, pick an object, see the effect it has on your mother-in-law when paired with your choices and either get an ending or find yourself teleported again in the shop as if nothing had happened. You're basically just trying different combinations until you find one that gets you an ending and that's all there is to it: you can see how it gets dull fast.
Sadly the story doesn't fare any better due to the characters having little background or depth: this means you'll find it quite hard to care what happens to the client or her mother-in-law since you'll never have a connection to them.
The Shopkeeper is sadly not good enough as a game or even an interactive story to recommend.

If you're looking for a review you're at the wrong place, but heres a receipe for spaghetti!
Step 1: Get Your Supplies
Before you can start making your spaghetti you will need to first get the proper supplies and materials. To make this spaghetti you will need:
a box of spaghetti
a jar of marinara sauce
1-2 pounds of ground beef or Italian sausage
two large pots, one for boiling the pasta and the other for making the sauce
serving untensils
salt
water
You can use as much meat as you want, really - but anywhere from 1-2 pounds per large jar of sauce should work out best. I tend to use 1 pound of meat nearly every time.
Step 2: Cooking the Meat + Get the Water Boiling
Before you start, fill up a large pot with water and add a handful of salt. Put it on the stove and turn it to high so it'll start boiling!
Next you will need to cook the of meat. Take all of the meat out of its container and set it all in a large pan, then put the pan on the stove and set the stove to medium.
After that you will need to break the meat into smaller pieces. When the meat is in small pieces you will then need to start flipping the meat and make sure it gets brown all-around and cooked thoroughly. The cooking should take approximately 10-15 minutes. When all of the meat is brown and cooked you can add in the sauce.
Step 3: Mixing in the Sauce
Next you will need to mix your marinara sauce with your cooked meat. Take your jar of marinara sauce and pour all of it on the cooked meat and then stir it all around until it is all blended together. Then turn the heat down to low and let it simmer while you cook the pasta.
Step 4: Cooking the Spaghetti
Once the water has come up to a boil, you can throw the spaghetti in. Typically it should cook within 7-11 minutes - just follow the time on the box!
Make sure to stir every couple minutes to keep it from sticking.
Depending on your timing, you can either strain the spaghetti and set it aside, or you can put it right into the sauce.
Step 5: Serving Your Spaghetti
You can do this in a lot of ways but I prefer mixing the noodles in the pan with the sauce. I use tongs to drain the noodles and place them in the sauce, and then put in a couple spoons of pasta water. Stir it all together really well - the pasta water coats all the noodles and lets the sauce stick more.
You can also put plain spaghetti on individual plates and spoon the sauce over top. Whatever works for you.
Top with cheese and enjoy!

This review is based on the NA-region server. Performance will mainly be the same but updated content can vary between the differing regions, KDN (Korea), SEA (South East Asia), NA (North America), and EU (European).
With my experience over the years, this game has gotten quite a lot easier (that's an understatement... :( ) then when i first started out. The combat system is enjoyable which very few games possess (non-target based). The storyline is enjoyable if you do take your time and don't spacebar through every dialogue option you see. Performance-wise and even developer-wise this game is terribly out of date. Even running modern hardware the game is optimized poorly. Having an ice-witch/adept in your party in later levels may literally NUKE your frames from an "acceptable 30 fps" to much lower.
Level progression is much easier than what it used to be, but to be efficient in this game's standard is to grind repeated dungeons on end. Dungeons and their hubs are instance based where you can run up to 4 people (including yourself) through a few minute dungeons. These used to be a bit harder a few years ago, but with the temporary 1-week costume you get from your level up boxes, it overpowers your character (until level 80 or so) where you can nearly 1 shot every boss or mob.
Endgame-content is....okay. There are 2 versions of the raids, normal difficulty and HC (Hardcore). Each normal version of Red dragon nest and ice dragon nest allow you to revive up to a max of 3-times. Hardcore only once. Besides getting legend-grade gear (RDN-L (Red dragon legendary level 80) or IDN-L (Ice dragon legendary level-90), you can only clear nests (besides minotaur nest at level 24) a limited number of times per week. The raids in this game which consist of 8-man parties only really shine in IDN (Ice Dragon Nest).  *Rune Dragon nest comes to North America later this year.*
Gearing up your character is much easier when levelling as you can just use the armor pieces you gain along the way to clear the newer dungeons you unlock. True end-game gear, mainly Genesis Accessories take months to unlock.
The Cash shop in this game is becoming much more P2W than it used to be. Despite the cosmetics and small pets you can get to help pick up items. The stats on the costumes are very OTT and should only be purchased if you plan on sticking with this game. There is a 200% experience scroll which you can buy, but it's completely optional of course. Currently released costumes can cost up to $30 USD, while some of the older costumes (which have less stats) cost less.
A plus side is that the developer, EyeDentity for NA, does give out DNP (Dragon nest point) coupons if you reach the level-cap, 93, which you can redeem for use in the cash shop.
In summation this games does have it's pros and cons (which is far too long for this review). There are a few questions which you should ask yourself?
Do you like non-target based combat?
Do you like to grind dungeons or do you want a variety?
Do you like a decent storyline?
Do you like to progressively gear throughout your time playing this game, or do you prefer a challenge to gear at the end?
Do you want to make multiple characters to help with your end-game progression or do you feel 1 character should be enough to gear up?
This game is a mixed bag for myself included. With possibly over 3k hrs + (including my non-steam client estimation). I wouldn't recommend this game if you HATE to grind. Sure the storyline is a nice distraction, but once you've finished with that, literally everything is a grind from efficient levelling to even how your quests go. If you want to try a good combat system, sure give it a shot, but do note that this game is very flawed. Take this review with a grain of salt and read other reviews of this game on the web as well to help with your judgment.
Thanks for reading and have a nice day :)

Summary: This is an great game in my opinion. The game is a mix of MOBA and platformer, and is incredibly easy to learn but hard to master. You only have two abilities per character which can be upgraded, as well as his or her attack and general items such as health and speed upgrades. The game unlocks different upgrades as you level up your solar level, which you grow as you win or lose, meaning you should stick around if you are losing because you will grow solar anyways. The game is a standard MOBA, but a 2D platformer.
Positives: Great art, very unique characters, well balanced for the most part, also great music.
Possible Negatives: Losing may be not very fun at times, but you should still stick through it. Matchmaking can sometimes pit you with very skilled opponents.

How short?
A man enters an antique shop to buy a present for his mother-in-law.  Then the man has a conversation about business and family with said mother-in-law.
That's it.  You've completed the game.
You then return to the beginning to play through it again, in case you have literally nothing else to do.  This wouldn't feel like such a punishment if, say, the animation and voice-over work were anything but horrible, or if the conversation led anywhere interesting.  Instead, the game succeeds only at being a decent simulation of rooting through garbage for a prize that isn't there.

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is not only one of the best RPGs I've ever played, but simply one of the best games I've ever played, period. While the game received major acclaim when it was first released, it is rather underappreciated nowadays with Skyrim having been released. People seem to only take a glance at it before calling it 'outdated', simply because of its 'outdated' graphics. This is total bogus, because 1: the graphics were actually great at the time of release, especially for such a massive game and 2: since when do graphics make a game anyway? In many ways, I prefer Oblivion to Skyrim. The world of Cyrodiil feels much more rich than Skyrim's does a lot of the time, the cities feel varied and are filled with awesome people, and the quests feel less contrived or boring, and more diverse and interesting. Don't get me wrong, I love Skyrim, but I'd recommend for more people who have avoided Oblivion to play it, and I'm 99.99% sure you won't regret it.

New UI suitable for larger screen resolution: DarNifiedUI
Upgraded graphics textures: Qarl's Texture Pack III
Patch for over 2500 bugs in the main game: Unofficial Oblivion Patch
And patches for the DLC: Unofficial DLC Patch, and Unofficial Shivering Isles Patch
These few mods make Oblivion look and feel like a modern game again.

I absolutely love this game and it will definitely have a place in my heart. However, that's not to say the game doesn't have problems. See, the concept and story are amazing. The whole time I was actually thinking it would be an amazing visual novel. But the way the campaign was constructed was just... lacking. It ended really abrubtly, it didn't evolve the characters enough, it didn't expand on ideas I wanted to know more about, and was all-in-all really underwhelming. I even beat it in just a couple hours. It was actually really easy as well. The most expansive campaign in the game is just a mod they incorporated into the game (which, by the way, is still pretty fun. But also suffers from a lot of the same problems I mentioned).
The combat in the game is probably what shines most. See, what you're supposed to do is fist fight/kick strategically based on what your opponent is doing. And when those moments occur, it is fun. But when you have the bunnykick (jump and kick their head while in the air), which does an absurd amount of damage - an insta-kill in some cases, it really defeats the purpose of the previously mentioned combat. HOWEVER. The game doesn't fail to 1) Make you feel awesome, and 2) Keep you on the edge of your seat. The combat is really exciting in most cases, and legitimately fun.
I said earlier that the campaign was really easy. However, there were some levels that stood out to me with how many times I had to play them to get it right. Some levels actually took a lot of retrying and rethinking of my strategy to beat. And the stealth missions were really fun too. But the problem was with how short the good levels were, and how little there were. The second campaign, a prequel called Lugaru 2 (Yeah it's the same name as the game Wolfire made a while ago with the same concept as Overgrowth. I never played that so i don't know how accurate Lugaru 2 is) was basically everything bad I mentioned about the main campaign times 2.

There is a small variety of levels and by the 10th game you've already seen most of what the game has to offer. To complete all storylines you are expected to win 40+ games against AI, which is incredibly boring and tedious, even at max speed.
Multiplayer: Lots of online play is required to acess extra items in the shop. Unlike the singleplayer experience, chatting with your opponents and collectively complaining is great stress relief and makes the matches much more bearable.
Updates: It is currently impossible to permanently 100% this game because they keep adding paid DLCs with new characters and new achievements. So far it was 6 in one year. If you're a completionist, I recommend staying away until they abandon this property.

1. The surrounding game world is very beautiful. Everything looks like in reality - mountains, rocks, waterfalls, forests, desert, snowy plains. And all this is just an early access.

Straight up - Conan Exiles is a lot better than a lot of the reviews would have you believe. Yes it's early access and yes there's varying degrees of performance issues, bugs, crashes and a whole lot more - but overall the game is in a good state and only improving as it proceeds through early access. Firstly, anyone whose played it for only an hour or two - i'd dismiss those reviews straight up. These low playtime reviews tend to focus on a few annoyances and ignore the rest of the game.
There's a lot of survival games out there, and arguably Rust, ARK and Conan Exiles are the three main ones at this point in time. I've not played Rust, but I've played a lot of ARK. ARK has always had the benefit of replability because of the dinosaurs - and despite coming a long way, you effectively need to play the game like a second job due to the ridiculously long tame times.
Conan on the other hand has really suffered from a lack of replability. Once you've built a base, explored the map a bit, there was really no reason to stick around. Much of this has changed with the recent Frozen North expansion. Not only does this introcuce another huge land area to explore, it's also brought in another two dungeons, lots of NPC camps - and probably the biggest allure - loot. The NPC's now actually have loot tables and drop all kinds of items where before they'd only drop very basic materials like stone and fibre. Straight away there's incentive to go and farm them.
In addition, the game has brought in a bunch of new building items, crafting systems and weapons & armour. In short, there's a crapload more to do which is precisely what this game needed at this point in time. The thralls (NPCs) are also considerably stronger now - particularly the higher level thralls, adding real challenge to the game. The wildlife is still pretty buggy and in lots of cases dont roam but spin around on the spot, but when you engage them, they're also a lot tougher. They havent had a first ai pass like thralls, but they are now super dangerous. Rhinos in particular used to be easy to kill by simply strafing around them - now they have this circular charge which will smash you up. Spiders are also far deadlier than before - and they were already ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s!
On the downside - there's bugs. The update has brought in crashes, certain design changes that are questionable (such as sprinting unwielding your weapons) and what not. But it's early access and it's being actively worked on.
Ultimately - i think Conan Exiles has the best potential of the survival games. Once the combat is souped up and further ai enhancements go in, mounts, magic, the settlement update and best of all - the purge, the game is going to be great. It has the best building system of all the survivals IMO where the building pieces build into the surrounding environment - unlike ARK's where you need to start on flat ground.
The game is certainly not for everyone - but it's also certainly nowhere near as bad as all the 1-2 hour ♥♥♥♥♥es will have you believe.

Don't bother playing this game if you don't have a group of friends do play against or once you can't play on low level servers anymore. There's no matchmaking which means you'll be pitted against level 50's, when you're a lowly level 15. Yeah, I've killed my share of high levels in fair fights, but most of the time they've perfected the weapon they're using and they flail around so it's impossible to hit them.
The biggest sticking point is how the models work. The Y axis is based on the model's hips. So, if you look up, you're spine is pretty much snapped in half. If you look down, you're forehead is now covered in dirt(or blood, most of the time). It's not so much how they are protrayed outside of combat, it's how they are used in combat. Most low levels don't do this, but people that are more experienced do. They abuse it to the point where they actually dodge arrows and weapons because of it. If you crouch, then look straight down, then your profile is very low. You can dodge swings and arrows like this. Using it to dodge arrows is accepted, actually. But when players fling themselves around and combine blocks with the character's model, it's frustrating to fight against.
Don't even get me started with the weapon's hit detection. FOV makes it super difficult to judge if your stab is going to hit or not. I've gotten killed because friendlies flail their weapons around, and they don't directly hit me, they overhead or stab and I just so happen to brush the weapon. Plus, once a swing or stab is initiated, anyone who is touched by the weapon takes damage. So, in effect, you can be killed because of someone bringing their weapon over their head to hit someone infront of them. This is used by level 50's. Or, rather, abused by them. They swing it over their head, turn around, and then you're dead, when the weapon wasn't even going towards you.
The matchmaking, or lack thereof, is terrible. Low level games are really fun, even against someone who is good, not perfect, at the game. But dueling and unranked matches are terrible to play with. Dueling is full of two kinds of people. You have the people who are trying out the game mode and put up a fair fight, or there's the people who devote almost all of their playtime to dueling. Which means if you're like me, who is rather basic in his fighting techniques, people who flail themselves around and abuse the damage model are infuriating to deal with.
Imagine you, buying this game for your first time. You get yourself into a low level game. You're more than likely going to die a lot more than you kill. But, that's understandable. You're new to the game, and it's okay to be pitted against people that are of similiar level and skillset to you. What is NOT okay is having to deal with the people that are level 50+. Experienced. Hardened. It's like trying to shoot a rabbit with a .12 gauge slug and expecting most of the rabbit to still be there.
And as always, there's the people who spawncamp with three or four guys with him, and absolutely wreck people. It's not fun to be on the recieving end.
Save your money. Buy something like Red Orchestra 2 or Rising Storm 2. They use the same engine and they're absolutely fantastic games.

This is in my opinion the second best Paradox title ever, just behind Victoria 2. That said, it is also quite different from other titles. Imagine this is a historicla Game of Thrones, and it is focused on dynasties taking power in various countries. The purpose is to accumulate as many powerful titles as possible, all the while keeping your vassals in check. The intrigue and family politics (strategic marriages and such) prove an amazing challenge. There have been some issues with some of the later DLC which have introduced some poorly thought through ideas, but Paradox is now working on making them optional, according to their latest updates.
One minus is the fact that the game tends to get easy once you get to have a large enough Empire. But that is not such a huge issue, as CK2 (like other Paradox games) allows you to switch countries upon loading a save. In CK2 you can just ditch your Emperor, and start anew as one of his vassals, trying to take over the Empire from inside. My normal game starts in 1066 (there are earlier start dates too, though I rarely use them) and includes a switch of characters around 1250-1300 before starting the scheming, plotting, conquest and alliances all over again. Just beautiful.

I had rather detailed review all written out, but I switched tabs and ended up losing it as a result, so I will keep it simple this time around. This game is not worth your time, do not play it, do not buy it even if it's on sell for less than 50 cents. It plays and feels like a cheap cellphone game, or even an unfinished prototype. In fact I believe that the game IS unfinished, because the enemy AI is mostly non-existent, the level design is atrocious and the animation is the bare minimal, with some of the enemies having maybe 2 or 3 frames of movement. The game has a lot of bugs and is very glitchy, I ended up using glitches to my advantage just to beat the terribly unbalanced final boss fight due to the game being obviously incomplete. I literally just hid behind the final boss and spammed him with the strongest weapon until he was defeated, that's it, game over I won.
The game has a whole one song that plays 90% of the time, it's a very generic rock song and it's set on an infinite loop, there may be a song that plays during the boss battles, I just can't remember and it was probably just as unmemorable as the fights themselves. The only good thing I can say about the game is that the backgrounds are pretty good, they're very detailed and really fit the overall tone of the levels. Someone obviously put a lot of work into them and it's a shame they were wasted on this game, I really hope the artist(s) moved onto a project that's more worthy of their talent. It's a shame really, becauuse this game could have been rather good, but for whatever reason it seems that the developers completely abandoned it and the publisher released it anyway.
Overall: The game took me about 4 hours to complete, that includes all attempts and when it lost my save data. It is not worth your time, the fact that it's normal price is $9.99 is laughable and I feel for those poor few who purchased the game at full price on a whim. So please heed my warning, back away and spend your money on something better.

Replayability: As of writing this review, Awesomenauts has stolen over 750 hours of my free time, and it is bound to rob me for many years to come. With the multiple match ups (meaning how good certain characters are against other certain characters, on a scale of equal player skill) no session has ever felt the same.
Arenas: I cannot compare it to the likes of DOTA or LoL, since I havent played either, but coming from someone whos played the likes of Powerstone 2 for the Dreamcast, I can tell you that this game offers a robust experience. The arenas are structured in such a way that allow you to go miles by taking an inch.
Characters: The prime beef. Ronimo takes a bit of slack when it comes to balancing certain character traits and abilities, half of which I would say are very much deserved, but at the end of the day using the character in a way that outplays your opponents strengths and capitalizes on there weaknesses will outrule any match up against you. You are bound to find a character, if not half the cast, to your liking~
Single Player: There is none. This game will not engage you if not played online. Future DLC will patch in alot of match customizablity, so I cant say much on how they will integrate it, but not including the Starstorm DLC, I would not reccomend this game to anyone who is timid of the online environment.
Art: The game is advertised to look and sound like a Saturday morning cartoon. The Musical Score matches this, with catchy rhythmic beats that loop in the background and character specific that play ala reward for killing sprees. The graphics, not so much. Dont get me wrong, the sprites are colorful (albiet small in relation to everything else on screen, but still packed with personality) and the levels looks gorgously bright and tell a story, but the only thing "Saturday Cartoon" about it is the intro video and character portraits. Still, you get what you get, and if youre a fan of the child friendly art style, you wont be disappointed.

With only 12% positive reviews (22.05.2015) it is a major incident I had played this game and you know what: it was great! Some of the main reasons people do no like this game are the following:
The game is not as simple as it seems: There are lots of situations where the perspective is shifting (from the shopkeeper to the customer and back); the short playtime of 3 minutes per visit is really fitting to represent the setting as a hopeless scenery for the customer; all the objects in the game contribute with their little background stories to the whole, involving macabre stories. And yes - there are no subtitles: but if you don't understand the whole conversation, it's not a big problem; wait 3 minutes and the story begins again ...
Well, what's the conclusion: If you like a small point and click visual novel with a nice art-style, deep and black humor writing, an indie game with well done voice acting, where you try to buy an old antique for your mother-in-law in order to let her sponsor your business, then it's worth a try.
Be prepared for a bad-tempered mother-in-law, a marked-by-life shopkeeper and a family tragedy with a surprising end (the right one!)!
Game has achievements (some are hidden), in order to get them, the playtime is around 1-2 hours; if you manage to figure out the right end at your first playthrough, you are done in 5 minutes!

An interesting game. While at first it seems like there is not much to this game, there really is. With each passing scene, new information is revealed that deepens the story line.
Clicking on objects in the game gives more information and it's up to the player to put  the puzzle together to move forward.
This game is good if you like to persist and you like puzzles that are not too obvious in a "hand holding" kind of way. The game isn't easy.
That said, it's NOT a bad game, as some have said. It's just conceptually a bit obtuse. It takes time to understand and get used to, and repetition does happen a LOT, so if you want a game that is more straightforward, perhaps pass on this title.
But I would recommend this game for people who like the point and click genre. It's simple, and repeatitive, but if you stick with it you can make your way through the story.   I CANT recommend it for anyone other than the point-and-click diehard fan.
One thing that I would improve is the voice acting. It's clear that the actors are reading, and it would be nice if the vocals were more polished.
Overall a nice little game. But I can't recommend it for any more than a couple of dollars and an hour of time. To like this game you must be a point-and-click fan. Not so sure how a general audience would find the game. But, it's a short experience that might be worth your time. It's cheap, so nothing lost if it doesn't work out.

Now this... This is excellent. I have to complain about the lack of base mechanics. There's only three forms of combat? Fists, swords, spears... Versus four types of enemies: Bunnies, Rats, Dog/wolf, and cats, luckily all with their own various versions. By base mechanic, I mean:
Jumping to ledges is fine and dandy, but gets mighty boring after a while. I'm decent at platforming, as much as the next 90's child, but that was just ridiculous. I do like, though, how the game walks you through things at a pace.
Level intensity was great, but the droning of >platform >kill enemy >platform some more< got real... Eh. The platform areas to fight on were small enough to give me a real big frighten though, definitely an A+. The overall designs for them were great, and i can't wait to see what the modders got in store for me.
Combat is extremely fast paced. I'm glad it's set up in a sort of physics-based way, though its... Kind of off to me. I dunno, just something about it felt less mechanical, and maybe I'm not sured to it. Or, maybe there really was something up. I don't know.
The character design really was out the window though, my goodness. If you planned to make a story-driven game with combat elements, at least.. You know, do a little research. My God, for a fantasy-ish styled game with anthro characters, someone did a real♥♥♥♥♥♥job of designing their outfits and characteristics. Their fingers don't even move! Animation errors? Plenty. Graphical errors? White squares at random. Coding and overall scripting? Feels fluid enough to name it honey. Do I feel anything at all for any of the characters I've met? Abso♥♥♥♥inlutely not.
Regardless of its few flaws, I have to seriously praise the game for being something definitely different. Anthro creatures beating the snot out of eachother to become a hero to all and known to none is really something else. Whoever Turner was in his past life (I assume assassin/murderer or soldier variant), it seemed like he was all there, and really just wanted some peace and effing quiet. If there was a continuation, I really hope you up your game and hire some voice actors for some cinematics. 8/10 game, for sure.

The Shopkeeper is a short point and click game with many similarities to a visual novel. The game is very brief, with a playthrough taking around 2 minutes. The full story is learned through multiple playthroughs, which could take about 30-45 minutes overall.
The gameplay in The Shopkeeper is minimal. You are immediately thrown into the story, without much idea what is going on. You can click on items to learn more about them, and also click on responses while you are talking to your Mother-in-law. After a round or two you will kind of get the gist of what you have to accomplish. There are about 4 total scenes, and you will not see every one on each playthrough. Once a round is over, you are thrown right back to the beginning of the story to start again. Eventually, you will achieve the desired result through your clicking and will see the ending.
The graphics look pleasing, but there was very little to create between the handful of scenes. The sound, voice acting in particular, is bordering on the line between grating and unbearable.  Lucky the game is short, because I probably would have had to turn it off just due to the voice acting alone in another few minutes.
I cannot recommend The Shopkeeper. Although it is already offered at a low price, current $3, it just doesn't seem worth it. I spent a rather unenjoyable 30 minutes with this game, and would advise you to avoid doing the same.

This is a very, very short choose-your-own-adventure story with multiple endings, but with one true ending that makes going through all the other endings to get to its true ending worthwhile.  It takes 2-5 minutes to play through it once, and you'll need to play through it over ten times to 100% this thing.
The strange and off-setting thing about this choose-your-own-adventure game is how character perspective changes on the fly.  It's very confusing at first, because you will enter this game thinking this story might be about a shopkeeper, and that you will be playing as the shopkeeper, and you briefly will, but the story is all about the customer, and it's the customer's destiny you control and take control of for the rest of the story.   Sometimes, the story begins with the customer, completely cutting out the shopkeeper, but when the story begins with the shopkeeper, the time you control him is very short--up until the customer has entered the shop.  These sorts of character perspective changes that happen on the fly can be unsettling and confusing when unexpected.  So, this is my warning and education to you.
Otherwise, it was okay.  Unique, unsettling, surprising... not bad... a chill and grim story.  That's about it.  I laughed at its' true ending, which is why I recommend this.

Oblivion is the sequal to the critically acclaimed TES 3 Morrowind, and predessessor to the well-known Skyrim (TES 5). This time it is set in Cyrodiil, the Imperial Province of lush forests, snowy mountain caps and dark swamps, all to be explored at will. There are nine major cities, Anvil, Kvatch, Skingrad, Chorral, Bravil, Leyawin, Bruma, Cheydinhal and the Imperial City, plus many other minor settlements, temples, farms etc.
Right at after character creation, you are taken by the Emporers guards on an escape from the palace dungeons, before he tasks you with delivering the Amulet of Kings and shutting closed the jaws of Oblivion. From then on you have the entire province to explore at your own will. You can join guilds such as the fighters guild, basically the legal vigilanties of Tamriel, the mages guild, who are basically the wizards of the empire, the thieves guild, which is an illegal guild of robbers and thieves, the dark brotherhood, who are the spiritual assassins who worship Sithis and the Night Mother, and the Arena, which is pretty self explanetory.
A good understanding of TES lore is recommended, and will always make the game feel more real. I recommend this series to bring you up to speed.
It will inform you on the many races, religions, provinces and more that exist on Nirn (It also explains what Nirn is). Or you could read the many ingame books as an alternative.
The only downsides I can think of is the chat system, which is a little outdated, and the stupid essential NPCs. Unforunatly they removed Morrowinds 'you can kill anyone, as long as you can deal with the consequences' system in favor of appeal to casual gamers. These don't damage the overall game too much, however.

Singleplayer: Too much randomness makes the experience not fun. The wildly unpredictable nature of the game means you have little to no control over the outcome. There is no room for strategy other than "collect stars/wins and get to a home". It takes multiple attempts (~1 hour) to beat any level. Supposedly the AI dice are rigged. There is a small variety of levels and by the 10th game you've already seen most of what the game has to offer. To complete all storylines you are expected to win 40+ games against AI, which is incredibly boring and tedious, even at max speed.
Multiplayer: Lots of online play is required to acess extra items in the shop. Unlike the singleplayer experience, chatting with your opponents and collectively complaining is great stress relief and makes the matches much more bearable.
Updates: It is currently impossible to permanently 100% this game because they keep adding paid DLCs with new characters and new achievements. So far it was 6 in one year. If you're a completionist, I recommend staying away until they abandon this property.

I’m gonna do something a bit differently from how I usually do in these reviews. Now, the paragraph up here that you’re currently reading is what I like to call the ‘hook’ of my review. You read an over-detailed and usually funny anecdote about the game I’m reviewing and then I give you the name and genre, both of which you already know considering you’re on the game’s steam page. After that redundancy I get into the meat of the game, and you probably stop reading about a paragraph or two in because I’m a maniac who consistently goes over the word limit on Steam and has to delete a chunk of his work to put it on the market. I’m gonna swap the format this time.
Warframe is a riveting and highly rewarding looter-shooter. It’s a well-oiled and meticulously crafted addiction machine designed to sap as much time out of your day as possible and then convince you to come back tomorrow. I’m going to be transparent; this game is a grind. There is no reason to play the game other than to play the game. The story is background noise and the lore is a neat addition, but you’re playing this game to shoot stuff and feel badass doing it. In-game rank is tied to mastery, which is gained by leveling items up to 30 and then probably throwing them away to try another new toy, encouraging players to try new things. The game is visually stunning and chock-full of things to do at all times. The customization options are rich, and the premium currency can be traded for and earned free of charge if you learn about the in-game economy. I have not spent a dime on platinum in this game, and you probably won’t have to either. In short, if you love the gameplay, you will love warframe. If you don’t like the gameplay, you didn’t exactly pay for the game so you’re guilt free if you stop playing. That’s all the info you’d look for in a review. Now, if you’ll stick with me for a bit longer, I’d like to tell you a story.
REVIEW
Warframe
GENRE
Action
The year is 2015, and the month is probably November, just as it is at the time of writing. By that time, I was a highschool sophomore. I was, and still am, a ruthless slacker, so I was playing some Warframe instead of doing my year-3 Spanish homework. I was relatively new to the game, so I was trying to get through Venus so I could farm the boss for Rhino warframe parts. I’m not quite sure if Venus was the second planet in the game like it is now, this was before the starmap got redesigned to make sense to a human being. Be that as it may, I was blazing a trail through Venus when I picked up a random player during an exterminate mission. He was a mastery rank below me and using Excalibur, the beginner frame that I’ve never chosen because he looks dumb and Mag is way cooler, I swear. We continued silently, as most players are wont to do when playing with randoms, until about halfway through the mission when he piped up.
Wouldn’t you know it, I was about to get my first real-world test on foreign language. While I did pass, today I couldn’t begin to tell you what he said aside from the rough translation: “Can you help me get through Venus?” Even when I first saw it, I immediately dismissed the query with a quick “No hablo espanol mas. Lo siento.” (“I don’t speak much Spanish. I’m sorry.”) Accepting my self-doubt, we continued onward until I took another look at his message towards the end of the mission, and, to my disbelief, realized that I not only understood it but could also respond in Spanish. So I did just that, essentially saying: “Oh wait, I DO understand what you said. Yes, I will help you through Venus.”
Thus began an hour-long journey with some random guy over the internet who didn't even speak the same language as me. Neither of us talked much aside from simple sentences, considering that’s about all I knew. Before we knew it though, we stood in front of Jackal, the robotic, quadruped boss of the Venus system. A grueling fight ensued as we beginners slowly figured out how to defeat the creature, eventually triumphing. Having fulfilled my word, we parted ways. “Goodbye, friend.” he said.
I spent the rest of the day farming for and building the Rhino warframe components with a dopey, self-fulfilled smile on my face. Not only had I proved to myself that I knew how to utilize Spanish on at least a basic level, I’d been helpful to someone. I went into school the next day with an epic tale to tell my friends, the one you’ve just read now, and the knowledge that when I got home I could start the agonizing 72 hour build for Rhino. When those three days had finished, I don't think I’d ever felt more accomplished in my gaming life for years. Equipping my new frame, I felt as if the game had truly began. Swiftly passing by the many months of gameplay that ensued, I was learning about Prime items when I noticed that two Prime frames were getting vaulted soon: Nova and Rhino. Thus began a rigorous week of grinding which ended, once again, in triumph. A day before being vaulted, Rhino Prime was mine. I got to play with my new toy three days later, and, in the coming weeks, maxed him out to level 30. Rhino would come to be a symbol for me of Warframe, being both a representation of the point where I truly began playing as well as where I stopped.
Just as sudden as a paragraph-break without a proper segue, I stopped playing Warframe and moved on. To give you a frame of reference to when I stopped, Inaros was the newest frame in the game, being that he was released maybe a week prior to my quitting. I had just gotten plenty of new games thanks to sales and all, so of course I had to play those. With 100 hours on record, the game sat unplayed and unthought of in my library until October of 2017. Fresh off of milking Nuclear Throne for all the fun it was worth, I was looking for another game to occupy my every waking hour. Remembering the fond memories of the quirky sci-fi shooter of old, I downloaded the game again. It was like a brand-new product. Plains of Eidolon had just been released and the amount of content added to the game since my leave was downright overwhelming. What’s Endo? What are Void Relics? Why are some people coming out of their warframes?
That was 100 hours ago. But what’s more important to this story is what happened just two days ago. I’d been meaning to learn about clans for a while now, as I’d been skimming the wiki and looking at all the stuff clan research labs could get you. So I went to the recruiting chat, and someone named The WeatherPony took me under his wing and showed me around his clan dojo. I got to look at just exactly what I was missing and, at the end of the tour, join the clan myself. I was astounded. Every single turn I took during this game, someone more experienced was there to help me steer if I needed it.
And then I remembered my old Spanish friend. I realized that, even back then, this game was about learning and teaching. You reach out for help, and several hands will reach back. You rely on others and they rely on you. You coexist. I think that’s beautiful -- this wonderful, unspoken synergy between players. Bonds like that transcend explanation. They transcend language itself.
If you’re still reading by now, which I would imagine you’re doing so while groaning at how wonderfully ‘poetic’ I’ve gotten, I encourage you wholeheartedly to try Warframe. It’s free, it’s fun, and it’s overflowing with content. You’ll be confused. Trying to figure out the game will be like trying to learn a foreign language. You’ll stumble over the basics while others excel. You’ll misunderstand so, so much and maybe never really get it. You’ll think about just giving up entirely and dropping it off your schedule. If that happens, I encourage you to ask for help; I’m sure one of the thousands of teachers will notice your raised hand. And when you sit back down in your seat and see someone else struggling with the same concepts, I encourage you to become the teacher. We’re in this together, Tenno.

SoniComi originally released for PC sometime in 2011. Eventually, the game had a slightly improved re-release came to PS3 in 2014.
The game itself is mostly a visual novel, with a couple of scenes for the Photography segments are in 3D. Also, the only character model in 3D is Sonico herself, with a wide assortment of outfit and color options for you to pick from. Obviously, you don't have access to the really good outfits until later in the game.
The visual novel sections are pretty standard, with the inclusion of backlogs. One thing you need to know however, is there's no "Save anywhere" option, like other visual novels. You are only given save points at the beginning of each chapter, and before the photography segments.
The Quick-Time Sections are just slightly different alterations of the visual novel section, where you have the option to interact with Sonico with a pre-selected action, and aim wherever you want. These actions can vary from patting her on the head, Grabbing her arm, Talking about a certain subject, and more. These segments of selection are also timed, so it is possible to not interact.
The Photography segments have similar controls to a first-person-shooter. you have free movement around an enclosed area around Sonico at your location, and you must take pictures of her from different angles at specific points. Time them all perfectly to start a combo, and a traditional point scoring system shows your results. The outfits you select for Sonico to wear for these segments will determine your ending.
Performance wise, on my beast of a machine (i7 4790K, 16gb Ram, GTX 1080), this game was a breeze to run. The game supports up to 1080p resolution, and can be played in windowed mode or fullscreen.
Ultimately, if you are a fan of virtual japanese idols (including Hatsune Miku), this game is right for you. If you're here for fanservice, it may not be worth the current asking price.
