Phew... What can I say? The only reason that I decided to write this review is because finishing this game left such a hole in my routine that I'm suffering from withdrawl, but let's get REALLY SPECIFIC as to why:
tl;dr  9/10 great game with complex strategy. Needs a few balance tweaks (and gui tweaks). Would benifit greatly from more skills and combat-related content (#ThatsWhatTheSteamWorkshopIsFor).
--- COMBAT ---
This is probably the main reason why this game is so fun. The combat is challenging and engaging throughout the game. I never felt like a particular obstacle was excessively easy nor did I find any fight completely insurmountable. Here are some specific points that best describe the pros and cons of the combat system.
-The Good: So many classes: There are about 10 different main classes if you go strictly by the skill books: Aerothurge, Necromancer, Geomancer, Pyro, Hydrosophist, Huntsman, Scoundrel, Warfare, Polymorph, and Summoning. Each of these pushes a certain character to prefer certain positions and circumstances in combat: The magical arts and huntsman generally prefer a range while Polymorph, Warfare, and Scoundrel are generally up close and personal. Mixing and matching these "classes" with each other does create quite a large array of possible setups for a given party, especially since all of your companions are completely customizeable (It is fair to note however, that there are combinations of these "classes" that do not mix well). One of this systems greatst benefits is that after act one you may respec your character an infinite amount of times, allowing you to explore all sorts of differnt builds without locking you to only a few possibilities.
- The Bad: So few skills: Each of these classes has a max of about 12 (non-source) skills that are available in total, this may seem like a lot if you mix classes, but keep in mind that the game can be 60+ hours long and many of the skills lose their efficacy longterm. Halfway through the game I had already learned about 80% of the skills I would use at the end, not including sideways moves or source skills.
- The Underpowered: Source skills: Why do I leave out the (very powerful) set of source skills? Well, source-skills depend on you being able to spend a resource called source-points, of which you can have a maximum of three. These skills are powerful and require that you use your Action points as well as source points to cast. Seems pretty good right? The problem lies in the fact  that you dont get a consistent way to replenish them until almost halfway through the game. Even then collecting enough source points to regularly, or even occasionally use them is a difficult and time consuming task that requires hunting down random pools on the ground or consuming corpses. There is one combat that, for just that combat, you are allowed to use source skills with no source cost; I have to say that finally breaking out some of the cool source skills that I had rarely used made that combat one of the most entertaining without becoming too easy, since the skills ALSO require high action point cost. The simplest rebalance would be making them easier to replenish.
-The Good: Positioning is key: The amount of strategy in this game is inspiring. I constantly found myself being thrashed if I just waltzed into a fight. After I would lose I would think to myself "Geez that's impossible!", but after restarting the battle with good positioning and finding advantages, the fights became much more manageable, without ever becoming easy. Height can seriously affect a battle: Everyone gets a bonus to damage when shooting ranged attacks from above ESPECIALLY the huntsmen (Ballistic shot with a height advantage is probably the most damaging single attack in the game). Not only that, height advantage ALSO gives major bonus to range making it easier to rain heals and hellfire from above. As you might expect, being at lower heights has the opposite effects. This gives the game a greater feeling of accomplishment when you successfully turn the tide by clever positioning.
-The Neutral: Always fire and poison: One of aspects of combat that is particularly present in this game are clouds and surfaces. I personally guarantee that you will never have a combat that does not include oil, poison, or fire surfaces in some way. They are a huge part of the strategy of the game. Break open an oil barrel in a small corridor to force the enemy melee combatants to risk getting burned to get to you, or punishing them for sticking around. There are a few different types of surfaces in the game: water, poison, blood, ice, shocked water/blood, oil, and fire. Many of them have gaseous counterparts like steam and smoke which can block vision, and all of these have a cursed version (much more hurt-y) and a blessed version (much more heal-y). As you could imagine there is a lot of variance, especially since they can cause different effects like knockdown (ice), stunned (shocked water/blood), and slowed (oil). The great diversity of surfaces  adds yet another layer of depth to the strategy in the game, but it comes at a cost: many of the simple fights can become monotonously similar. Water, shock, repeat. Oil, fire, repeat. These surfaces can become especially annoying since they are quite hard to remove, especially the cursed versions which usually can't be removed at all without spending a source point to bless it back to normal first (looking at you NECROFIRE). Oh and don't get attatched to keeping the fire from turning to necrofire, because it turns out that, apparently, every single enemy in the goddamn world has the curse spell which makes it unremovable again. Another gripe I have with the surfaces is the fact that all of them target an enemies magic defense. Perhaps they could have added a caltrops surface, or a sharp crystal surface that could target physical armor.
The Overpowered: Knockdowns anyone?: Statuses are one of the many ways in which divinity shows its diverse combat system and complex strategy, but problems arise when certain statuses are too powerful while simultaneously being easily accessible, and knocked down is exactly that. In a system where every enemy gets at least two attacks every turn (assuming that they aren't f&$#ing you with their other abilities), making units lose their actions is absolutely invaluable. Once enemies no longer have physical armor, they can be knocked down and will spend the entirety of their next turn getting up. There are so many early abilities that cause knockdown for just two action points, the same amount as a regular attack, and I found that the answer to a dangerous amount of difficult fights was to nuke the physical armor and stun-lock the tough characters with constant knockdowns. While reducing the physical armor is not as simple as I make it sound, it made enough of the fights feel similar enough to warrant a note about it. Keep in mind that there are better statuses than knocked down: Charmed causes them to fight for you for multiple turns, the difference is that charm is just difficult enough so that it is not overpowered (although it is strong).
-The Overpowered: Summoning: Incarnates are ♥♥♥♥ing disgustingly good. After you get to level 10 in summoning, your small summon becomes quite the big boy. After spending one turn summoning and infusing the incarnate it is almost guaranteed that this beast will do more damage than any of your characters could hope to do in one turn, while also posessing abilities to knockdown, taunt, and fire from a distance. Not to mention the fact he will have more magical and physical armor than you will have health in general. At the end of the game my Incarnate was regularly doing
damage when my thiefs crits could only manage
not to mention he had
physical and magic armor. Rebalance probably needed.

There is an end state to Devil Daggers, and it's precisely at the point where you'll look at your leaderboard score that hasn't changed in the past two weeks despite daily intense sessions of the game, and finally give into the despair. It's realizing there is nowhere else for you to go, and giving up.
Devil Daggers is a fight between you and some floating skulls in Hell. It looks like 1996-era Quake and it's meant to because that's how it wants to intimidate you. The soundscape of Devil Daggers involves skull noises, raspy laughter, high-pitched screaming, industrial humming, and spider tickling. Your job is to survive the hordes of skulls and to take their precious blood rubies - initially, they don't do anything, but if you grab ten of those things, you become a more powerful monster among the monsters, nuking skulls and creepy spider-skull monsters with greater ease. But just because you're a more powerful combatant doesn't mean it will get easier, because Devil Daggers will throw all sorts of♥♥♥♥♥♥at you, and it loves to make you squirm.
Your first few playthroughs will last approximately around 60 seconds. In order to 'beat' the game (read: get the sole achievement that says 'Devil Daggers'), you will need to last 500 seconds, or approximately 8 minutes and 20 seconds. This is not a goal you are likely to accomplish unless you are very, very good at first person shooters. I consider myself well-learned in the genre and I made it half a second away from three minutes (which puts me roughly in the top 10% of all players who have submitted a score). At the time of this review, only seven people have beaten this game out of the 27,000 players that have tried to conquer it so far. That does not make it a bad game, that makes us all weak people who can't stand up in the face of naked, unfiltered terror, and those seven people are our champions.
Devil Daggers is a game you're not likely to beat, but that doesn't mean you shouldn't count it out. After all, the narrative experience is not the only valid experience in video games. Sometimes crying in the face of seemingly insurmountable frustration is a valid experience, too.

As for the game itself, it has a lot of potential. There were a lot of Steam reviewers who said Conan Exiles is better than Ark Survival Evolved, but now having played both Ark Survival is a far more polished and amazing game than Conan Exiles. This is a great fast-paced third-person arena game. To top it all off they have an interchangable part system much simpler than, but comparable to robocraft. While you can't build your own robot from the ground up you do have parts and pieces that you can mix and match to suit your play-style.
As with any game that gives you the freedom to mix and match, you will try and fail miserably to make your war machine, and learn through viscious trials how to perfect your machine, learning by playing, and watching the tanks and gameplay styles of those around you.
Additionally, this game does its free to play marketing well. Instead of locking parts behind a paywall, they limit you to a certain amount of parts, and if you want to play with more parts beyond that you have the option of selling your old parts to exchange them. If you purchase basic, you get an unlimited size garage to hold all the parts you earn, and access to an increased variety of color schemes to change the cosmetic appeal of your tank.
This game is great for killing time, or for a quick adrenaline-filled series of battles, but don't expect the replayability of some classics like CoD at the moment, because the rank system hardly matters from what I've noticed, and if you ever burn out on the game there's nothing to reel you back in aside from the possibility of trying new part combinations.
Now the downsides of this game are really dependant on the type of gamer you are. This isn't a realistic game in any sense and it's whacky and crazy, but the tactics and strategy are very real. If you're not good at taking a vicious beating and learning from it this is also definitely not the game for you, as I myself had to play a good two to three hours before I got a handle on things and figured out a tank build that worked for me.
Overall, it's a great game for what it is. Definitely worth trying.

I liked Lugaru. So much so, that I think it's in my top 10 games of all time, despite being so short. Naturally I really wanted to like this one too. It's basically Lugaru 2 with great animations, physics and modern graphics, after all. However it's not only unfinished even after a decade of development, but it's just simply not as good as Lugaru, it's predecessor from 2005. It is really ruined not by it's unfinished state, but by bad design choices and a seeming lack of understanding of risk and reward and overall combat mechanics. Which is baffling, seeing how great and balanced those very mechanics were in Lugaru. It's almost like the original developer of Lugaru didn't have any voice in the desing of Overgrowth, and the new designers didn't learn anything from Lugaru.
In Lugaru the bunnykick was a high risk - high reward move. In Overgrowth there is almost no risk to it and it is so powerful that it doesn't actually make sense to use any other move in the game. The best way to fight is to not fight at all, and instead repeatedly jump over the enemies bunnykicking them. Also the dodge in the game is useless, since you can just jump away from attacks. Unlike in Lugaru, the enemy doesn't pull you back to the ground if you try to jump too close to them. Even if you get trapped in the middle of 4 armed enemies, you can just jump away as if nothing happened. Even if the jump wasn't stupidly overpowered, the dodge should still be integrated in to the block. Simply make it so that if you succesfully block an attack that cannot be blocked, Turner dodges instead, and not have dodge and block be 2 separate actions. That's just unnecessary complexity that doesn't add anything to the game.
Also for some reason succesfully blocking an attack no longer does a counter that can then be then countered again. Instead it just blocks, unless you hold the block key after the block. Why can't he just finish the move without the player having to hold the key? And the button-hold-counter isn't even a counter anymore, it's just a judo throw. Which doesn't make sense since countering a rather quick animation in a short time window is something you should be rewarded for. Instead of anticipating the enemy and utilizing counterattacks, often the best way to win a fight, apart from the bunnykick, is to just spam attack. If you have a knife, all you have to do is run backwards and hold attack and Turner will slash the pursuing enemy to death while they do nothing but run in knife range. In lugaru you couldn't attack enemies running behind you unless you stopped to meet them.
Wolf attacks cannot be blocked at all, so the only viable way to beat them now is to spam the new OP bunnykick on them, which removes any actual challenge from the toughest enemy in the game, as it does from everything else. Also legsweep, is almost useless now, and punches are so quick that it's almost impossible to react to them. Weapons almost never get disarmed with a counter attack, and instead most often get thrown away from the user only when he gets smashed to the gound. There are a plethora of mostly useless and a few overpowered attacks, instead of the few and all around useful and well balanced attacks in Lugaru.
There were a few positive changes made to the gameplay as well. Not enough to compensate for the bad and broken ones, but still. The increased stealth speed is nice. It bothered me in Lugaru how you had to be constantly rolling if you ever wanted to actually reach someone unnoticed. The removal of the need to be crouching in order to jump higher is also good, since it removes unnecessary complexity in the controls Most of the time in Lugaru I didn't even remember that I could have jumped higher if I crouched first. The longer grace period where you can still attempt a stealth take down after being noticed is a nice quality of life change. Increased enemy attentiveness makes stealth more interesting; Now if an enemy sees you, they actually tell their nearby friends and they all come at you, so you can't fish them out one by one as easily, which was the biggest cheese in Lugaru. Higher damage from hitting the ground is satisfying. It was stupid to drop someone from 20 meters high head first only to see them get up and run back to fight you. However I think they went just a bit overboard, especially with the damage you take you if you hit head first. You can literally die from being pushed to the ground and hitting your head in a sand dune. Also football kicking someone in the head when they are down is almost a guaranteed kill, which feels just slightly too powerful, that move being a very easy followup to sweeping someone off their feet. And it works against the player as well.
Separating block from crouch was a nice change. Having crouch and block bound in the same key worked in Lugaru's favor, since that way you could duck under a roundhouse kick and block a punch with the same key, and if you spammed block uncontrollably (crouching in front of the enemy), you could be kicked in the head with an unblockable low kick as a punishment. However had the rest of the combat been designed properly, I believe having a dedicated defend key is beneficial, since it's more intuitive than having multiple completely different actions bound to the same key. However as I mentioned, the dodge should be integrated to this new dedicated defend key. The new dodge isn't comparable to the old hanspring anyway, since it doesn't work as a repositioning move. Which it doesn't need to either, since jump is OP.
Even if the game actually gets updated to a state resembling a full game, which I don't believe will ever happen, unfortunately I don't believe these fundamental flaws in the design of the combat system will be addressed, and that's why I can't give this game a positive review. It feels like they have forgotten what made Lugaru good and why it worked so well. Maybe they should play that game again, and really ponder it.

I completed Dawn of War a couple of months back and have been starved for Warhammer 40K games and lore, reading wiki articles on the Emperor and Librarians, and checking out the various games that use the license. I picked Kill Team up for about 2 bucks on sale, despite seeing that it had "mixed" reviews. I don't think I've ever liked a game with a rating so low that it was qualified as "mixed," so I knew I was likely in for something awful, but I don't think the game is as poor as such a low Steam rating would imply.
This game is an isometric shoot-'em-up with a shockingly enjoyable melee system. There's no real skill involved in the melee, but it feels incredibly satisfying swining a power sword as a Librarian and watching Orkz and the goblin-looking ones go flying and screaming from my swings. It makes me feel like a less-studly version of Sauron from the opening of Fellowship of the Ring, and I am very content with that!
There are four different classes to choose from, with some being better in melee and others being better at ranged. Each class has its own special ability, and the ability recharges on a cooldown over time. It's a simple game, and the shooting was handled well enough, though I didn't find it as satisfying as the melee...which is actually the exact opposite of what I expected from this game, and it's a pleasant surprise, really, because I will always have fond memories of slashing Orkz and Tyranid with my Power sword.
Lore is pretty thin here, of course, and only the fellow radioing you your objectives says anything...well, except for a lot of Orkz screaming "Waaaagh!" of course. ;)  That said, I didn't mind it. I found the game to be pretty fun quite often, with some good challenge here and there. I thought I wouldn't use the temporary power-ups or that I wouldn't like them (becasue I normally don't enjoy temporary power-ups in games), but I really liked Kill Team's power ups. It was easy to remember what each one does, they're all useful in certain situations, and you can wait to pick them up when the time is right for the best damage output, healing, or invulnerability, etc.
I was quite eagerly awaiting the appearance of Tyranids because I had actually never fought any in any games before, as they seem to be a lot rarer in 40K games than Orkz and Chaos. Honestly, I thought the timing of their appearance was excellent, because I hadn't gotten bored of the Orkz yet, and I was very excited to see the Tyranids.
Unfortunately, that's also about the time the game went downhill for me. There is an enemy type called a "Termagant," which is a small-ish Tyranid that attacks using a gun that shoots green stuff. 2-3 of them appear at a time, spaced out, and with remarkable aim and fast firing. Four of them I was expecting showed up and killed me in under 3 seconds despite my best efforts and having almost full health. Checkpoints are sometimes poorly placed, and I became far too frustrated from playing the same lengthy section over to handle everything perfectly for about 2 minutes, then suddenly die within a couple of seconds from over-powered common enemies.
If not for the Termagants, it's entirely possible that I may have enjoyed this game, but I do not feel that they are properly balanced for this game. Both cautious and aggressive approaches result in my imminent demise every time. I'm hardly a great player, so if you're very skilled, I'm sure you will likely have no real problems, but for me, it turned something fun with a bit of challenge into an exercise in frustration that I just don't want to put up with any longer.
TL;DR: This game has some fun parts with a poorly balanced Tyranid unit that rained on my parade, turning a nice challenge into a bloodbath comprised of my Space Marine's blood. I found the game to be better than most reviews seem to have found it, but I cannot abide by this absurd difficulty spike caused by the Termagant enemies.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Note: MIGHT is currently in Early Access. The version reviewed was a mix of 0.4.0.83 (EA release) and 0.4.0.84 (latest).
MIGHT (what is with these all-caps game names lately!?) is an online-only team-based fantasy arena game played from a fixed-angle isometric-styled viewpoint.
MIGHT is multi-player only, pitting you and two teammates against three opponents in short, fast-paced battles to the death in a single small glade arena.
Graphics - MIGHT uses nice cel-shaded 3D models and clean, simple textures. They are relatively limited, though, with only two different colour variants of each class available for the player characters, and only a single small arena level available.
The interface looks smooth and stylish, but menus need some button response implemented to be able to determine when a button is clicked. The in-battle mouse pointer and target selection needs similar feedback.
Graphical options include the standard resolution, full screen, and vsync options, as well as a handful of other more advanced detail options and settings. I ran the game in 1920x1080 with everything set to 'ultra' on a five-year old gaming laptop without any issues, so it's unlikely any modern gaming PC will experience any difficulties.
There are a few small interface-related gaps and bugs, such as various placeholder tooltips still in places, some grammar errors, and a bug causing messages to overlap in the centre of screen, making them impossible to read. Also, the "Yes I'm ready" button on the main screen (used to enter a battle) sometimes doesn't work and drops back to the game create/join menu instead.
Sound - The first thing I noticed about the sound was the lovely music on the main screen. There seems to be one other music track in the game, played while selecting characters before a battle. There is no in-battle music.
Sound effects in the game proper (the arena battles) are okay, but nothing stood out as being excellent. The "Three, two, one, fight!" voiceover at the beginning of a battle is terrible and really doesn't fit the game.
Gameplay - Currently MIGHT provides the player with essentially no information on anything about the game. The main screen is a greyed-out image of the battlefield from an angle unachievable in game, with a news feed on the left and an unexplained HUD on the top. The game's title isn't even written anywhere except for in the news feed text!
Playing around with the menus reveals nothing about the game, but clicking on the big PLAY button in the centre of the HUD provides two options for playing the game: ranked 3v3 match or custom game. Unfortunately there are no options for the custom game (yet), so I can only assume it's the same as the ranked 3v3 match, but not ranked. In any case, the custom game lets you start a one-player game so you can at least sort of see what the game is about.
Each game of MIGHT places you in a team of three, allows you to select one of the character classes, and then drops you all in the single small battle arena, together with your three opponents. The goal is to eradicate the other team members.
Finding a game of MIGHT at the moment is a very time-consuming process. There are two servers offered: Americas / Europe and Asia / Oceania. Both are severely underpopulated, from what I can tell, but with no server stats available in game it's impossible to tell. In any case, I was unable to find a single game on the Asia / Oceania server, and only one on the Americas / Europe server. In over two hours of waiting, I managed to play MIGHT for less than 10 minutes.
At the moment there seems to be no way to select who you fight with or against, but perhaps if there are more games available you're able to choose. With no visible lobby, team selection, or chat system, this whole aspect seems rather lacking for a multiplayer-only game.
MIGHT includes seven character classes: druid, guardian, pyromancer, witch doctor, duelist, ravager, and hunter, with more apparently on the way. Each class has five abilities available, with the last and most powerful for each class requiring collection of 'resources', located in the centre of the arena on timed re-spawn. Unfortunately, though, I found that in my one game there was significant lag, making the ranged character class I'd chosen next to useless. I'd press one of my attack buttons/keys, only to have the game lag before actually firing off the attack, meaning that my target had moved well out the way before the attack would hit. This could be because I was playing on the more distant server, but in any case it seems that ranged characters are at a definite disadvantage in laggy situations.
Given that I've been unable to play any more actual games of MIGHT, at this point I'll just list a few more things I noticed about the game:
- no in-game tutorial, instructions, introduction, or single-player skirmish (e.g. against bots) making it much harder than it should be to understand tactics and practice
- no camera zoom, rotation, or angle change; the only camera controls are moving the mouse, which pans the camera slowly, or holding down mmb and dragging, which pans the camera quickly
- "Error: internal service error" when playing games sometimes
- no way to change in-game name (uses your Steam name)
- ranking system: looks like you start at Rank 20 and work your way down; information elsewhere describes an interesting quarterly league system, which sounds fun
- no server or player stats available in game; everything is a black box, making the wait even more frustrating
Pros:
+ lovely music on the main screen
+ reasonably nice cel-shaded graphics
+ the league system sounds good
Cons:
- Hard to find games; it's only just been released and there's no one around
- No tutorial and limited available in-game information (tooltips)
- No single-player support (e.g. bots) for learning and practice
- No server/player information available; just press 'Start' and wait, fingers crossed
- Game interface needs some work on visual response, tooltips, and grammar
- Significant lag makes some classes next to useless and the others not that much fun to play either
- Only one arena, and it's small
- Very repetitive; after a few short games you've seen all MIGHT as to offer
If the player base increases significantly and the developers continue working hard on the game, then MIGHT might be a bit of fun, if you can actually find a game. But from what I've seen at this point in time, that's not going to happen often. You may have luck following the developers' 'discord' feed and trying to organise play time using a third-party platform, but MIGHT itself doesn't provide any information on games at all.
I'd like to be able to recommend MIGHT, but in its current state I can't bring myself to do so. After more than two hours of play time I've only actually managed to play for less than 10 minutes, and that was too laggy to be enjoyable.

How to do a review for a game that you spent over 3000 hours playing?
Could it be objective? Hardly. But i will try at my best to keep it real as much as it is possible.
First off, this game is not old. Its ancient.
are, by todays standards, in world that saw titles such as Crysis, CoD:AW, Battlefield or Witcher series, laughable at best. It looks old, it ''plays'' old, but it has some of its charm for it.
? Interesting, starting parts are very cohesive, but later on its starts to be very watered down.
? That depends solely on player. There are multiple things you could do ingame (crafting, pvp, pve, farming, exploring, ect), and it works well on its part, but some features definately need to be worked on.
I could spend hours explaining each part separately, but generally, game has complex crafting system, pve is fun as far pve goes in other games (there are bosses, instances, dungeons, team raids, ect), farming and harvesting are nice way of getting materials in large quantities if you dont mind posibility of being attacked while doing so (depending on place where you farm/harvest).
Over the course of playing i met lot of interesting people. Some were nice, some were not, but all around, Fallen Earth has (or had) one of best comunities around in MMO's. There is always someone who will help out new player, give some usefull advice, share money, resources or items. There are also individuals who organise various community events.
One of biggest problems most post apocalyptic games have is that they are constantly being measured towards Fallout universe games. That is a problem, since most games do not measure up to Fallout.
Fallen Earth is one of games that comes very, very close to that. Not the same, but not too much diferent from it. Each of those games has its own pros and cons.
Sadly, at current time, it seems that G1 (company who owns FE) isnt too much interested in adding new things (although they do occasionally, but not to extent from before), but we always hope they will come to their senses and finish polishing the diamont that Fallen Earth is, and make it shine as it should.

The goal and controls aren't self-explanatory, and there's no tutorial. The only options in the "Options" menu are for resizing the screen, resuming the game, and exiting the game. I've played for over half an hour and the gameplay still doesn't make any sense--I can never know when to expect the game will go to what scene or what I'm supposed to do in a scene to make things progress in a new way. Every area has a time limit. Exploration seems to be discouraged because you have only seconds to look around any given screen before the default dialogue for that location starts. The game also restarts itself again and again without prompting when you get to the end, which is never clarified as being the end.
The "Notes" don't help you figure out how to get different endings--they're just flavor text from what I've seen--and this game could really use some kind of hint system so the player won't be forced to use trial and error just to learn the game mechanics. You can't control the movement of any of the characters. The very few offered dialogue prompts are in only one scene, and they're as unintuitive as any of the other mechanics. The only hints I can give as to the gameplay are that clicking on an object in the antique store and getting its long story can sometimes effect the dialogue you get when you return to the store, but not always; and that clicking on an object in the mother-in-law's office can occasionally give you a different ending scene if you pick the right dialogue path.
I've found none of the four characters to be likeable--the mother-in-law seems to have no positive dialogue paths that paint her as a likable person, the son-in-law is a failure and/or a jerk in every dialogue path he has, the gardener only has unkind things to say about someone he barely knows, and the antique shop owner doesn't have a lot of personality and is more of a storytelling device than a person--his only bit of backstory that I've found was from the gardener and the line had more personality than the antique dealer. The animations are jerky. The one true ending I've found had a cutscene that faded to black, played hard to interpret noises, went on to a scene that explained what happened, and ended with two scenes that didn't make any sense with the context.
The only positive thing I can think to say about this game is that the longer stories about the antiques are interesting, but good luck being able to trigger one. If you miss your chance at a long story you need to wait for the game to cycle through the mother-in-law area again; and, even then, you aren't guaranteed to end up back inside the antique shop. You could end up outside and have to wait for the game to play through again and hope you're not outside this time. Even if you do end up back in the shop after the mother-in-law scene they might talk about a different antique than the one you chose at first regardless of whether you got a long story.

An gorgeous, funny and enjoyable Breakout-style, with RPG-elements, game that does an awful lot right and will keep you entertained for hours.
There's a genre mixing group of games out there that take enjoyable arcade games and combine them with the story and depth of role-playing games. It's a type of game I feel has yet to find it's genre-defining entry, and while Dreamstones isn't quite there, it's definitely a major step in the right direction.
Firstly as a Breakout game it is as good as any, though it suffers from the same faults I find with other Breakout-style games, for example getting stuck on the final block can be frustrating, as can being put in a situation where the ball is impossible to reach, though anyone who has played a Breakout-esque game will be aware of these issues, issues that are fortunately often fixed by some of the spells and power-ups.
Both active and passive spells are equipped to your weapon, which in-turn determines how much damage your ball does when it hits certain enemies. Active powers are useful, giving you a chance to destroy more blocks, from a simple dagger being fired up to a spell that splits the ball and more, these are great for hitting those last few blocks and completing a level and you can have up to six of them equipped, unfortunately they share a cool-down so while the dagger only takes twenty seconds to recharge, some abilities can leave you waiting over a minute before you can use another. I feel the game would be more enjoyable, though easier, if each skill had separate cooldowns.
Passive abilities can cause you to have an extra life, receive more gold or do more damage, these too are equipped to your weapon, which means you have to decide what effects you want equipped before you start. Unfortunately this means some abilities, like receive 10% more gold are ones I feel I won't use unless I have spare slots. I believe it would have helped towards the feeling of progression if these were permanent upgrades once you had unlocked them.
Outside of the block-breaking meat of the game there's somewhat of a story and even town-building, if any part of the game needs more depth it's this, the buildings are well drawn and add to a Kingdom Score but little more than that, there's citizens to save but saving them doesn't unlock anything other than helping you get slightly closer to 100%. The story, characters and dialogue are genuinely entertaining and only left me wanting more.
The art-style is gorgeous, the music awesome and everything about the game has character, though it can be hard to tell exactly what the ball will hit as the background and foreground blend seamlessly, even so it's a good looking game and there's easily more than enough content to keep you playing for several hours.
There are a lot of levels and new mechanics are introduced regularly enough to keep the game fresh and the monsters and bosses make for rather unique and, most importantly, fun experience.
All in all fun and worthwhile gameplay makes for a title that has a few minor issues and could do with a little more depth in places but overall and fun game that is well worth the price of admission, with many hours of varied content and as entertaining as any similar game.
If you're looking for a Breakout-style game with a unique twist then Dreamstones is a must.

Normally, I wouldn't bother writing a review for a game I've barely played for a few minutes. "Devil Daggers" is the exception that confirms the rule.
You're some hapless damned soul and are, apparently, in Hell. A single gleaming dagger hovers in front of you, its Eldritch light the only source of clarity in the otherwise pitch-black environment. Pick it up, and the opaque expanse turns reddish, and infernal whispers start to fill the air. Soon enough, tentacled turrets that look like relatives of Nyarlathotep sprout out of the ground at the edges of the arena, and spit screaming skeleton heads at you. Some of them have horns and break off from the swarm in unpredictable patterns.
A sustained click unleashes a barrage of red magical daggers, a single click fires off a pseudo-shotgun blast.
Survive as long as you can, in the knowledge that bigger, scarier and tougher horrors await you. If you're tough enough, you'll have the opportunity to collect gems off of your fallen foes, to bolster the offensive power of your daggers.
You'll probably die 45 seconds in. Once you're dead, you can check out the leaderboards and chew on your resentment while watching replays of demigods trouncing the Hellspawn for ten minutes straight, dodging and weaving their way out of a maelstorm of pixellated horrors that makes the first Quake's monster designs feel tame in comparison.
Then, you're likely to hit "Retry", bolstered as you've been by the sight of DraQ laughing in the face of Hades' minions for what feels like an eternity. You'll obviously want to improve that leaderboard placement if you've got something of an ego. If not - like me - you'll be fine living in the realms of mediocrity otherwise known as the "I Survived For Less Than Two Minutes" Club.
Then you'll die. Then you'll try again. Then die. Then try again. Then die.
Whoops, four hours have potentially gone by. Maybe you should think about going to bed.

After reading through a lot of reviews and trying to filter out the ones that didn't understand what EA was, the game went on sale and I decided to try it out. My first day was with the release of the new snow area. As luck would have it, a new patch crippled some things in the game, such as keybindings and I had a CTD walking around the desert in my first 5m in the game. I closed up and waited till the next day to try again. Luckily the devs put out another patch (and maybe another after that) and my ills were corrected.
I've been playing around for a few days now and I've been enjoying the game quite a bit so far. I'm not much for PvP, so my time has been in PvE. It was simple enough to set up a local server, like with Ark and 7d2d. I've not experienced any other crashes and for the most part, gameplay is fairly solid. There are some obvious signs of the game being in EA. Crafting feels a bit odd at times, a little graphical glitch here and there and some creatures aggro in odd ways. For the most part though, this is a lot more fun than I thought it would be.
I enjoy crafting, a lit bit of building and picking fights with AI mobs and Conan fits that bill perfectly so far for me. Crafting feels a bit tedious at the moment, so it could go either way as development moves along. Some things feel unbalanced at times. Problem easily solved by changing some settings on the server to give a few more resources when collecting. As you level, you unlock new recipes. Some levels make you happy to get that new piece of armor or a bed. Some levels leave you wondering when the next level is coming.
I'm by no means a master builder in these kinds of games. After watching some youtubes on other people's creations, I don't think I'll ever publicize what I build. That said, you can do a lot more than the basics on look and feel. If you're into fancy layouts, other than the resource grind, you'll have plenty of fun with it.
Fights are a toss up. It's mostly spam click and hope their hp drops before yours. I'd like to see at least a little bit more strategy involved. It was still fun fighting. First time a gator and I tangled, I cursed the screen. When I was finally able to open the return punishment, there was a small feeling of victory. Being mostly solo, some of the upper level fights are bit frustrating, although there are a few settings on the server to play with that somewhat help.
On the negative side, there's a temperature system in play that takes a lot of enjoyment out of it for me. Walking around in some areas causes you have a heat stroke. Along with the need for food and water, I find myself having to either stop every little bit to satify my dwindling body or just avoiding some areas for the most part. From reading, this is a new system implemented, so it may get some needed attention in the future. I didn't care for the default food and water needs, so I scaled them down a little on the server. Other than extreme heat effects, it's kind of cool to need to pay attention to your body. Food spoils way too quick for my tastes (pun?), so I also scaled that back far as it would go.
Overall, I'm enjoying the game quite a bit. There are plenty of areas that I haven't explored yet, so I'll definitely get my money's worth given the amount of time I've already played. For an Early Access game, I'm very happy with the experience. As with all EA, I'm sure there will be some updates that I'll frown upon and some I'll enjoy. Make sure you understand what EA is before you jump in.

I might give this game another shot someday, but for now I've refunded it. Overgrowth seemed like a very good idea on paper, but had some poorly implemented features that made the overall experience more bad than good for me.
The thing I disliked the most (and the thing that other people end up praising) is the combat. It takes some getting used to, and you CAN get used to it eventually, but it's extremely unbalanced. The combat system is supposed to be "simple", with a dedicated attack button and various moves that can be performed by altering your movement and position in relation to an enemy. The problem is that, in its attempt at being organic and intuitive, the combat system lacks basic features in most other hand-to-hand combat games, such as the ability to choose when to lock-on/off to an enemy. In situations where you accidentally alert more than on person, a 5 on 1 fight is almost a guaranteed  loss for you since you have no way to
(key word there) simultaneously attack and defend from multiple directions at once. Alert more than 2 or 3 enemies at a time, you get swarmed and beaten to a pulp. Again, I might be missing something here, but after playing other games that handle the same thing much better (Dark Souls, Metal Gear Rising, Bayonetta, etc) it comes off as just bad design. I know those games have wildly different playstyles, so don't rag on me in the comments for that, but the point is that they give you the controls needed to properly approach a fight with multiple enemies. Overgrowth does not.
Barring combat, the controls actually feel very good. Movement is swift, responsive, and natural. The first few chapters of the storyline that I experienced were actually interesting, the graphics are decent, and the overall presentation and tone work pretty well. Also worth noting are the game's surprisingly fun stealth mechanics; sneaking around and slitting an enemy's throat before dragging their body out of view is satisfying, and if the game had been designed with more of a focus on stealth it might have been a lot better. It also probably would have been a lot better had it been designed as a platformer. But while these elements exist, Overgrowth was built as a brawler more than anything else. The core experience is not supposed to be the platforming or the stealth, but the fighting. If Overgrowth wants to be labeled as a fighting game, I will judge it as one. I think it falls flat on its face.
As you can see, lots of people do enjoy the game, and for fair reasons. Overgrowth is not OBJECTIVELY bad. I just don't like it, and I think I have a solid argument as to why. If you're looking to try it out, then go ahead. Just don't set your expectations too high.

This review is written in mind for those of you who are intrigued but put off by the DLC.
Crusader Kings isn't for everyone. Just because you like or even LOVE civilization 5 doesn't mean you'll like this game. I grew up with Civ 2-4 and found 5 to be dreary and I then found this game. The only real similarity is the historical role playing aspect.
This game has MUCH more appeal to history geeks, serious game of thrones nerds; fantasy and mideval hobbyists in general.
That said, you shouldn't invest too much money in this thing if its not going to fit you, so an intro run on the vanilla game will be fine to determine if you should invest in the game.
The community knows Ireland as "Tutorial Island." Pick an independent petty king in Ireland and use this guide to get yourself familiar
. The in game tutorial is a bit crap so be forwarned.
You might wonder WHY there's so much DLC? This is a nichey strategy game for history nerds. It has a pretty limited appeal, but its also fabulously deep and complicated. The devs have a passion for building these projects, and making the game better, deeper, more complicated and a better experience.
I've played this game over the last few years and its grown and become better with each patch. The DLC is what makes this possible. Its not so much a 100 dollar game as it is something that is constantly evolving and growing and changing, and in order to support that they came up with this DLC model. Its much more "pay what you feel" than it looks, the cosmetic dlc is split off so that you can save some money getting the base DLC if you want.
Here's a quick guide that you can use to help decide what DLC to get first
1) GENERAL GAMEPLAY DLC adds overall improvements and additions to the base game. Listed subjectively but fairly by value of essentialness.
CHARLEMAGNE adds a new start date (769 AD), a slew of new mechanics and improvemens, a custom duchy and kingdom tool, and an automatic chronicler for those of you who like to look back at your (mis)deeds. Also unlocks Zunists for play, who are a particular cult favorite of the community. This and Old Gods are generally regarded as must buy.
WAY OF LIFE unlocks new options to develop your ruler.
RULER DESIGNER does what it says on the tin. I don't feel like this is essential at all, but some people think its absolutely integral. ymmv
SONS OF ABRAHAM unlocks new ways to interact and utilize abrahamic faiths (Islam and Chritianity primarily) as well as unlocks the very rare Jewish rulers for play. I've really never found the college of cardinals to be particularily intuitive but others have tremendous amount of fun with anti-popes and heresy.
REAPER'S DUE makes death more interesting/funny. I have not played it but it has been a pretty big hit with the community, especially after all the negativity surrounding the Conclave patch. It doesn't seem to exactly add too much to the game beyond more narrative and roleplaying content so I place it here in terms of esentiality.
CONCLAVE is controversial to say the least. I have actually found the reception to be so venomous that I have not purchased it. However, much of the anger is actually about changes made in the free patch. The free patch mechanics did not bother me, in fact shattered retreat is preferrable to how it was originally.
SUNSET INVASION is silly ahistorical content that provides a horde invasion of Aztecs from the east. It is possibly the least essential DLC that there has ever been in the history of DLC.
2) NEW RULER TYPES DLC All of these have unique mechanics that are very different from catholic/orthodox rulers in vanilla. These are generally all very well recieved by the community. Buy them if you are interested in playing as these entities, but if you have no interest in being a Caliph then its probably not worth your money. The only one generally considered essential is OLD GODS. These are listed in order of release.
SWORD OF ISLAM unlocks Muslim rulers.
LEGACY OF ROME doesn't unlock anything technically but it does provide greater depth and flavor for Byzantium and the Orthodox rulers which is why I add it here instead of above. I like to play as an obscure orthodox kingdom called Georgia, and playing it with this DLC was far better than vanilla. Also adds retiunes which is a very helpful mechanic. Probably the second most essential of this group of DLC.
THE REPUBLIC unlocks merchant republics like Venice
THE OLD GODS unlocks pagans like the Vikings for play as well as zoroastrians, adds a new viking centric start date 867, adds further complexity to uprisings and revolts, and provides a new threat to your throne in the form of adventureres. This, with Charlemagne, are probably the first two dlc to buy.
RAJAS OF INDIA unlocks the continent of India, generally viewed to be the least essential of the unlockable rulers DLC
HORSELORDS unlocks nomads like the Mongols for play
3) COSMETIC AND MUSIC DLC - this stuff is basically purchase as you see fit. I think they split this off because it more directly goes to the artists, or guages the marketplace for it. I don't mind it as if this was something rolled into the DLC proper it'd cost more so its an itemized bill. Most of the time they provide bundles of the DLC and cosmetics. Further there's sales going on all the time, I have most of the cosmetic dlc, most of the rest of the dlc except for Reapers Due and Conclave, and I really haven't invested entirely that much in it. Just took advantage of bundles and steam sales.
Hopefully this will help those of you who are intimidated by the amount of DLC. Support independent gaming!

Well that was unexpected.
I'm not really a "car person." I have zero interest in trucks and never considered driving a big rig in real life (the prospect of maneuvering the things would stress the hell out of me). Driving games never appealed to me (this is the first driving game I've ever purchased and I've been a gamer for 30 years), so this was the last game I ever expected to like.
The only thing that gave me a glimmering that I might like something like this was trading in Elite: Dangerous, but even then I passed it over as it went on sale again and again (I mostly heard about Euro Truck Simulator 2, not ATS).
The only reason I picked it up is because I enjoy driving and I heard it was a pretty chill and relaxing game. I figured it might be good for when I just want to zone out or listen to music, podcasts, or audio books while playing something. It turns out to be a lot more fun than I expected.
It isn't tagged as an RPG but it has RPG elements - you gain levels and put points into skills that unlock more types of deliveries you can make (such as various hazardous materials and delicate goods), increase your income per job, and boost your fuel economy. Beyond that, you can buy a truck, upgrade it, buy garages, more trucks, and hire drivers to drive those trucks in your business. When you have drivers working for you, you can direct how they upgrade their skills.
Currently there are 4 trucks you can buy (Peterbilt 389 and 579, Kenworth W900 and T680). More are supposedly on the way (when licensing with manufacturers is worked out), but in the meanwhile more trucks are available from mods (there are a good number of mods available, quite a few more than are listed on Steam Workshop).
The base game world has 3 states - California, Nevada, and Arizona (free DLC). There are also mods that add to this (though I haven't tried them yet). A long delivery in the base game will be about 1000 miles. With a scale of 1:20, the last journey I did of that length (from Tucson to Redding) took 1h 5m to complete in real time driving the speed limit (kept the timer running when paused and planning where to rest and get gas, but didn't include the time to park, as that would vary more according to the player).
I thought that I would want longer trips and would still like more states for the option of going on longer journeys, but when making 800 to 1000 mile deliveries, I never thought to myself, "This feels too short."
Downsides:
I don't mind these, but others might - only 4 vehicles and 3 states.
Money seems too easy to come by - when you take out a loan, you can pay it off early without paying interest or penalties, and a single job can pay over $80,000 when you have all your skills upgraded. This can make money trivial later. To avoid this, I use a hard economy mod so that jobs pay about 1/10 that.
The AI of other drivers can be flakey and sometimes, while making turns, you can get boxed into a bad position with other cars. In real life, you could communicate with other drivers to go around but in the game they just sit honking at you. To get around this without collisions, you can save and reload (all cars around you vanish on loading a saved game) or use a console command to make cars vanish.
I use a 360 controller and found myself wanting two things. A steering indicator when in external view to show the position of your wheels when there is no lighting. The option for both the mouse and the controller to steer. The controller stick turns your steering wheel at a constant rate and there are times I wish that I could switch to the mouse to turn more quickly.
Overall, this game was a big surprise and can see myself sinking many more hours into it.

Despite what many reviews may say, this is actually a pretty solid game. Yes, game, not quite a simulator. It could be named Need For Speed: Trucks. Although the graphics are definitely not the greatest, they work. And, this game is for you if you are looking for a giant open world where you can drive in one direction for a few hours.
Pros
-A pretty large scale map (even bigger than the rescaled American Truck Simulator).
-Truck damage!
-Cop chases! (An easy way to get the cops in your rear view mirror is trying to run random people off the road) The cop AI is not too dumb, when you fail to stop they speed up and attempt to stop you by brake checking you from the front.
-Realistic road placement and good city density for the scale
-About 9-10 trucks, a good number for this type of game
-The awfully narrow angle camera CAN be zoomed out.
-A nice variety of AI cars, and you can even choose how much traffic you want.
-Lifelike AI; I forced a cop car to a different lane and the truck in that lane swerved to avoid the car.
-HILARIOUS crashes, I once sideswiped a cop car and it flew into the oncoming side of the freeway, never to be seen again.
Cons
-For those looking for a realistic game, Rig 'n' Roll has some room to improve
-When you are scraping against a guardrail, the spark particles are so big it looks like fire. Kind of cool actually but not realistic.
-Collision physics are a little wonky and funny at times but they still work (when rear ending a normal AI car, their behaviour makes them seem unrealistically light, and when sideswiping cars, it looks like they are lagging really badly as if they were real players and had a high ping)
-Cities have many intersections but only 1 or 2 main roads you can drive on.
-There could be a lot more detail for how big the game world is (twice as big as ATS but half the detail overall...)
If you like both truck simulators and Need For Speed, this game is a must buy. And if you're wondering why only have 1 hour on record, it's because I was so hyped after playing this for 1 hour I wanted to write a review and tell the world how amazing this game is.

Awesomenauts is a  2D Multiplayer Online Battle Arena, MOBA for short.  This game is available for €10, and offers you lots of fun for that price. You don't have to pay for anything else, except when you want to buy skins for the 15 awesomenauts. These skins are pure cosmetic, they won't give you an advantage in-game.
So, what is this game all about? Well, you play as one of the 15 available awesomenauts and you have to destroy the enemy base. Sounds easy right? Well, to do that you have to fight your way through turrets, robotic minions and of course the other team. At the start of the game you try to earn some 'Solar', the gold of Awesomenauts, and buy upgrades for your awesomenaut with it. And you try to kill enemies of course. Unlike MOBAs like Dota or LoL, this game doesn't feature items or a leveling system. Aeesomenauts also doesn't have a laning stage, which means you can be ganked every 30 seconds. After a while, one team will have more upgrades and more Solar than the other team and they will push to the other teams base. And then of course destroy it.
Verdict
--------
Awesomenauts offers a lot of fun, and in beautiful graphics. The game feature's Offline Training and allows you to practice with friends. It also offers ranked matches and 15 awesome awesomenauts.
Awesomenauts will keep you behind your computer for at least 75 hours. If you want to collect every upgrade and get Prestige 10, you will be playing Ronimo Games little game for at least 150 hours.

: A new XP-based system was implimented that grants passive HP and related buffs to players, creating a massive balancing issue between anyone with a significant gap in XP values. The game is nigh unplayable now, with the higher-ranked players having even more of an ability to crush the enemy team. Until this system is reworked or removed, I cannot recommend Awesomenauts unless you don't play online with other players, and either stick to LAN or playing with bots.
Awesomenauts is one of the first MOBA games that I actually enjoyed. Unlike many MOBAs, it features some fair humor and a funky, cartoony artstyle that's sure to please. Also unlike many MOBAs, Awesomenauts has a smaller character roster than one would expect for a game worthy of the title. However, I consider that to be a plus: too many characters and too much complexity make it hard to get into a game without lots of determination for learning all the ins-and-outs that the game has.
Awesomenauts allows you to jump in and jump out of servers whenever you like, featuring bots that take up empty player slots in online ranked matches; these slots can be filled by actual players at any point in a match, vastly improving--or deteriorating--your game. Battles can turn in a matter of moments, so you have to keep all your vulnerabilities in check. Awesomenauts also features local multiplayer, with multiple people using the same keyboard, different keyboards, controllers, and the like; you can even play online and bring your friends with you, both local and online, with the implimented lobby system.
The controls are simple and, if not to your tastes already, completely customizable. The default control selections are straightforward and easy to pick up. I noticed some bugs when mapping certain combinations of actions to the same/similar keys, but that certainly isn't a dealbreaker; just find some other key to bind.
If you've never played a MOBA before, Awesomenauts may seem different. However, its differences make it a fun and fresh game that takes a new spin on the MOBA framework. I recommend it to fans of lighter-hearted MOBAs and arcade-style gameplay.
The only real downside is similar to that which plagues other MOBA titles: the hyper-competitive nature of the players, who commonly abuse powerful tactics to always have the upper hand. No one really talks during games, making them feel less interesting. If you really want to get the most out of this game, play with friends, and don't bother with the DLC.

Sometimes, the indie-game-world produces amazing games. They can be minimal, they can be short, they can have bad voice-overs or bad music. A game just needs to be fun, or at the very least, entertaining in some way. "The Shopkeeper" fails in every possible way.

There are only 6 characters in the story. Two of them, will never interact with you. Clicking on items will sometimes give an explanation... and sometimes it won't.
...and... that's about it for gameplay. Oh, there is ONE dialog tree. Most of the time, the dialog doesn't change. You have to pick the correct item AND the correct dialog options in one run. Make a mistake? You must play through the entire sequence to start over.
The graphics are quaint, but poor. If all I'm going to see in a game are 5 screens, those screens should look amazing. Instead, we mostly have neutral tones of brown and gray.
This isn't a game, it's a story. A non-interactive story that provides choices but punishes you for making the incorrect decision. It just isn't fun. This is a really bad way to tell me a story.

OK lots of thumbs down and here's another but this game is not *just* junk, I believe it's "about something" in the way that most student short films are "about something" and it does contain thought provoking ideas and some sort of emotional payload. However, there is very little "content" here and many problems with the way the ideas have been implemented and packaged as a for-money videogame.
If you've seen the movie Groundhog Day, imagine a version of that which is 5 minutes long with only about 5 camera shots and instead of being about learning how to be a great human being, the story's about Bill Murray having to guess the correct gift-object to give to his crush out of a choice of maybe a dozen. (And spoilers, no happy ending.)
Or The Stanley Parable with 2% of the content.
Factor in some amateur voice acting, minimal animation, a short background ambient sound which fades out and back in at each repeat instead of looping seamlessly, forced repetition of conversations that even the developer tells us to skip and literally one puzzle to solve: which hotspot do you click on at which time and which of the possible paths do you take through a 3-level dialogue tree?
All of the "Achievements" can only be won by brute force random clicking, while the game tells you aloud that you suck and chose poorly every couple of minutes and punishes you with the exact same 3 choices and audio clips for the Nth time.
To make things worse, for me it seems buggy. The scene would change back to the start room and the customer would complain that an object I hadn't even clicked on was totally wrong for him. Then I'd get an Achievement.
Having "won" (after more than an hour) it seems the secret message is about *not wasting our precious time* but I feel this minigame does just that and for very little reward. Glad it came "free" in a Humble Bundle. There are many nice things in how it was made and I look forward to the creators' next, more fleshed-out project.

A helpful review
I previously wrote a gear up review stating that its a great game, and the usual blah blah everyone sees, I decided I'd try to be a bit more helpful as I've been seeing a few newbies to the game.
I'm going to do this in sections to help organize (I suck at writing out stuff)
Parts/G points
First off, parts are not your source of how good you are, yes there are some slightly unfair parts that can cause rage, but for the most part they are balanced. If i'm a bit bored, or there are a lot of new players abroad, I tend to go basic tank, and I still tend to rek some scrubs, because when compared to some other typical layouts the basic (scout) tank is pretty good. So don't always see someone using some big fancy gun and go "Wow, if I start using that, I'll be that good", cuz that ain't it sugar. Just practice with what you have and then try one new thing, don't always buy something just because you think it'll make you "better".
The people you meet
There are several types of people in this game that you will meet quite quickly, not all are as nice, or as helpful as I can be.
First, the "Basics" as I call them, people you know just started, either based on rank or the parts they have. Typically consisting of all scout but one part or two, and usually using a machine gun or heavy cannon, they are usually high health but really slow and don't know what they're doing (they pick some big heavy body thinking that it will keep them alive, heh, if only it were that easy).
There are the snipers, all shapes and sizes, from the flying ones that have just enough health to not get one hit by heavy snipers, the fast little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s with no health at all, or the spiders that get somewhere cheesy and pick off basics, they all can get very annoying, but luckly it only takes one or two hits with something higher damage to destroy them.
The Heavies, the big ones with like 300+ health and a lust for explosives and fast bullets, not fairly common, but they can ruin your day.
The Gunners, fast guys with around 100 health and a need for speed, along with a passion for machine guns, they tend to zoom in F*** S*** up and run off for health and ammo, they are the type to rely on weapons as their skill, and don't confuse them with harpooners and lazer'ers
Harpooner/lazer.. er
These type are pretty simmilar to the Gunners, except they actually have some decent skill, they tend to use the harpoon gun[s], or the vintage laser and assorted secondaries, which require pinpoint accuracy, and a steady freaking hand (with how fast they go, they need to account for their movment, your movment, obsticals, and gravity with the harpoons), and if they are as good as I make them out to be (and usually they are) they will kill you... again and again.
The Maps
Well there isn't much to say, there are several maps, some with optional night time, and most of them are pretty cut and clear, the open ones are fun for snipers and slower based combat, the duck and cover ones are better if you like quick kills and nasty 3+ person skirmishes, and the skate park ones are for some sick moves and rad jumps... bruh
You can pick three at a time when making a game and so long as someone is in the game it will keep cycling the three indefinitly, but there is no G coin/exp gain from just you in a match, even if you have a score, but someone leaves, you wont get any gain (sorry for you farming type)
Health, ammo, and power ups, oh my
The three aformentioned things are found everywhere on maps (almost redundanly so), and are pretty simple, health packs give you 25 health, ammo packs refill ALL ammo (every single gun and secondary, even if empty will totally refill), power ups have two effects, blue shields will reduce damage taken by 1.5X and visa versa with red rockets (yeah I have no clue where they pulled that idea from, damn swedes) will increase your damage by 1.5X, and if combind you get a fun purple...y glow
Weapons
Well, I figure you can guess what that means, there are several type, lets delve them
Bullet/laser GUN, run o' the mill machine guns, with a quick travel time and low to fair damage (this includes the description of the lasers that fire like a gun) and really good reload times
Snipers/laser BEAMS, instant travel time, fair to INSANE damage (up to 113 with the desecrator and 1.5X dmg) but nil on reload
Shotty/fire
Flame throwers, and the shotgun, oh god, what can I say, MASSIVE damage over short time, but no range, pick something fast nimble and good god make sure you can turn fast
Missle
The ole' standbye, whether lobbed or launched they do good damage, have a range of decent to F*** all short, but deals decent to insane damage, and has really good reload times for the damage
So wrap up anyone?

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Larian Studios strike again with massive cRPG game and if you love this genre - you have to play this one. It's pure game as it gets, no micro-transaction bullcrap, no day 1 dlc, nothing - just a brilliant game made with passion.
Obviously the game is not perfect, no game is and nothing is, but it's bloody good. You start the game you are not hand-held by anything, you figure you way thru and do your things your own way. You have plenty of option to choose from, starting from your own character - you have many playstyles to choose from: fighter, summoner, necromancer, archer, rogue assassin, mage of 4 different forces of nature, polymorphy and you combine those anyway you like to make a truly unique build and experience in gameplay. You can create your own character from scratch or play one of the 6 origin characters. The origin characters serve as fantastic companions to choose from as well, all of them being different and unique in personality and special abilities. All companions have a unique storyline to experience.
The quests, dialogue writing and exploration feel really good and thru your gameplay you'll be accompanied with brilliant music written this time by a new composer (Borislav Slavov) and it's up to par with original composer that worked for Larian for so many years, but sadly passed away soon after prequel of this game came out (rest in piece Kirill Pokrovsky). Unlike many other cRPG - this one is fully voice acted for all NPC and a narrator and it ads to immersion - believe me!
Combat is one of the best in cRPG games in my honest opinion. It's tactical turn-based combat, but it's not hexagon map based. Instead you only have range units that limit you how far you can move your character or how far you can reach with your skills and how big area you can cover - this way it feels more natural. Each turn your party characters get set amount of action points and there your tactics begin on how to use them - whether to strike some damage, crowd control enemies, buff you or your party member, or move your character to a new position. On top of that - you can combo elements for extra effects: fire + oil = massive explosions, etc. You can use environment to your advantage or it can be used by the enemy against you - so play smart, every decision matters and has consequences. You cannot ask for a better combat in cRPG.
Ofc there are few minor problems with the game - a minor bug here and there, but nothing impacting your experience a lot and story is not the best I've seen in genre, but it's solid enough to suck you in.
I didn't play 10/10 game yet (because it would have to be absolutely perfect in every way - that's how strict I am) but Divinity Original Sin 2 is close one. My 9/10 would be 10 for most reviewers out here.
If you are looking for fantastic adventure without being held by your hand - the game is for you. If your are looking for modern cRPG - Divinity Original Sin 2 should be your prime choice!
Personal GOTY of 2017

Fellow Fusion developer Windybeard has finished and released his third #MadeWithFusion title to Steam today. "Dreamstones" is self described as " an exciting combination of modern block breaker gameplay with action RPG statistics, collectible loot and world building", and it delivers that in spades.
Dreamstones starts you off with the challenge of helping restore the kingdom of Dreamweavers, hapless chaps who are suffering at the hands of the fairly evil Nightlings. All that remains is "Gentle Kenneth" whom implores you to aid his people in over 200 levels of brick breaking challenge.
During gameplay you will collect coins and stones which will aid you in rebuilding the Dreamweaver's kingdom, which in turn unlocks more powers and abilities to aid in your quest to flush out those nasty Nightlings.  Over 50 different skills and items are available to help you along.  This mechanic of unlocking blueprints and crafting new buildings that unlock new options is a great break and balance to the old brick breaking formula.
At the core of the game of course is actually breaking those bricks. Windybeard has done a great job crafting interesting levels that are expansive and create a sense of the world. Each board is populated with bricks disguised as environmental items like fences, bushes and other items. The goal is to remove ll the purple surly looking bricks from the board to proceed, but true to its RPG claim you can remain on the board and earn more coins or experience by completing as much as can. This means taking out and lingering monsters that remain or finding some hidden coins still laying about.
The player is given excellent control to direct the ball, down to initial positioning where to shoot the ball at level start to using a well written angle algorithm allowing you some determination of where the ball goes based on where on the paddle it hits.  Random drops also provide additional help in the form of bonuses like increased paddle size or a catch all one time save. All of these different aspects help keep the game fresh and continually interesting.
The only critical thing I can really say about Dreamstones is when in the world building area it seem the only way to get out of sub menus is with the Escape key. I spent a lot of time looking at the sub menu trying to find a exit button or the old X.  Overall Dreamstones is a extremely polished brick breaker with a TON of value embedded within for only $11.99 USD.

Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is one of those games where you can fully immerse yourself within it's environment and society. The world (called Cyrodiil)  has multiple regions of landscape, all giving you a taste of wildlife and roleplaying elements, like old, swampy caves or a great fort in the uplands of Colovia. Everywhere you go you can interact with the environment, from plants and mushrooms to animals and NPCs.
When you open the grate out of the sewer for the first time you realise the immense beauty of lake rumare, but thats the tip of the iceberg. You could if you wish, follow the main quest, and complete it how the developers thought it would be like. Or you can find your own path venture into an unknown cave, or explore the Imperial City's marketplace and see what it has to offer.
The game has oppertunities to be each class as you will, and a race to go along with it. You could be a High Elf Mage, the Arch-Mage of the Arcane University, or a Nordic Warrior, leader of the Fighters guild. There is a great range of quests to complete and level up your character. You may want to find certain items and loot dungeons to find them, while selling what else you find.
The Shivering Isle DLC, lets Sheogorath the Daedric Prince of Madness invite you to his realm, where everything is run a whole lot differently. The Knights of Nine DLC sends you on an epic quest, to defeat Umaril, who threatens Cyrodiil, while worshipping the Nine Divines. Depending on which pack you brought, one edition will come with four DLC houses, each with their own quest, and some other miscellaneous DLC.
So go explore Cyrodiil in all its glory. Be a Warrior, or a Thief, or a Mage or even all of them together! Thats the thing with Oblivion, its an inviting world at your fingertips that will never get old.
However they could patch up on the Havok Physics a bit.

TL;DR - Don't play the game for more than two or so hours in one sitting, combat is the core of game, if you're buying for story- don't - and it's a blast!
So I've had the game for several years and have played it across several computers. I've seen it get updates that completely broke the game for me by incompatibility with my graphics card and then there were updates that made the game smooth as butter. And I've played a lot of hours in this game so I can say, it feels great once you learn the combat mechanics! That being said, sometimes those mechanics don't completely work out, however that's in the minority of occasions.
Moving on to the big issue I see discussed in a lot of reviews, the story. I can't personally speak to it because my current gpu crashes whenever an overlay pops up in the game so I can't play the story. But I wouldn't say the game should be bought for the story, you should buy it for the intense brutal fights. Buy the game, throw it straight on expert difficulty and play the sandbox maps getting your butt handed to you, until you learn the mechanics and can win. That's the part of this game that is so satisfying. Seeing the enemies outsmart and out-fight you, until you can block, evade, and kick their butts. That's why this game is great.
But in the end, that's also it's biggest weakness. You'll get burnt out on the combat. Eventually it all feels the same and you get bored with the game. Which is why you shouldn't binge this game. Play it in short sessions so that you get the most out of it. It can be a great stress reliever that way. Say you're losing real bad in another game and are furious, you just throw on Overgrowth and beat up some rabbits and you feel great!
All and all, it's a flawed game at times, but can be a real blast.
