Overfall is played as a series of short hops between islands in a fantasy setting.  At each island, dialog choices and often combat occur, allowing the player to progress toward the overall goal of winning.  It features interesting turn-based combat on a small hex map and a wide variety of artful npc's to deal with.  Aside from combat, the game focuses on making choices that may impact race relations or in acquiring some basic resources.  And therein lies the strange problem with Overfall.
It would appear the writers do not understand basic principles of right and wrong.  It isn't that the game teaches rebellion or 'evil' or anything like that, because that requires a world view itself.  Surprisingly, they don't seem to understand the concept of making important or moral choices at all.  For example, there is an encounter where a group of dwarves asks for help retrieving their stolen ale.  Why was it stolen?  Because the thieves, quote, "are addicted to it, just like everyone else!"  Interesting choice of words.  Based on outcomes, the game clearly thinks that helping these drug dealers reclaim their addictive (and stolen) brews is the "good" thing to do.  It doesn't seem to understand the moral conundrum it creates in doing so.  In another instance, the game throws a guilt trip at the player for taking a runaway child home; the young child wants to remain a runaway, and the party-pooper player has insensitively returned him to his father!  I can only assume that none of these writers has any children in real life.
The image of non-humans is wildly inconsistent.  In some instances, orcs are portrayed as good people who (I suppose) are unfortunately monstrous in appearance.  In other cases, they speak like stereotypical cavemen and engage in kidnapping and murder.  The game doesn't seem to realize it is showcasing opposed stereotypes side-by-side.
There is a 'style guilde' written for the game's encounter editor, I assume in the hopes of preventing home-made tripe from being uploaded to the Workshop by players.  But the game's authors themselves break the standards of that guide,  not just a few times, but consistently.  It's really a shame.

Overfall is a combination of real time and turn based strategy with a couple of roguelite elements thrown inbetween. You travel the sea, visit various islands and fight a different aray of enemies (which costist mostly of humanoids of different classes), all because space vikings want to f*** up everything you know... or knew?
The story starts when the king decides he wants some bling and sents you to an alternate dimension in order to retrieve an ancient disc. This does not provide a challenge for a couple of great adventurers as yourself and you quickly return, only to discover 300 years have passed since you embarked. Not only that, the space vikings that reside in the other dimension aren't pleased with your little trip and start sending ship after ship after ship of warriors, which basicly means you're screwed... but not just yet.
Combat is focused mostly on different buffs and debuffs. It is played out in three phases. First comes the movement phase, then you can use different non-combat abilities and in the end, you can use an aray of combat skills. You have to plan ahead and know your characters, which gives the combat a nice, tactical feel to it.
The thing that I loved the most is the amount of option you get in most conversations. There are multiple things you can say and if you aren't carefull, you can quickly find yourself in battle with the previously friendly residents. Different classes sometimes get aditional options, which is also a wonderfull edition. It allows the game for stay fresh despite the fact conversations eventualy start to repeat themselves. But hey, it's impossible to have an infinite amount of new stuff to do.
The aestetic is certainly interesting and unique with a lot of lively colours. The soundtrack however, isn't anything special, at least I didn't think much of it. It does a decent job, however I didn't even remember it after not playing for a couple of days.
To sum it up: Overfall is a game which is definately worth a look. If you don't believe me, take a look at the steam rating. A must buy for everyone who likes the idea of roguelite games and one of the best games I've played this year.
Final rating: 8.6/10

I'd had my eye on this game for literally years, through development and early access, and I finally broke down and bought it on release.  The premise looked so promising and the game play seemed smooth and interesting.  I just wasn't interested until it was a finished product because it seemed there was so little to do.
The actual game play elements worked fairly well.  Platforming felt intuitive and I was able to navigate the environment without too many mishaps.  That being said, the controls are very context sensitive and that sometimes was as much of a hinderence as a help.  For example, when you run at a wall, you should be able to run along the wall or jump straight back and up depending on what angle you approach from.  This is determined by the game.  However, if you don't approach at the correct angle, you many skip off the wall instead of running along it and fall to your death.  This context control scheme does make what looks complicated very simple to perform, but it isn't without it faults.
Likewise the combat is similar.  All you do to attack is hold down one button.  The main character, Turner will then make attacks depending on which direction he is moving in while the attack button is depressed. Same goes for defense.  Just hold down a button.  Now if you time the button press you can do a bit more such as grab and throw an opponent, or catch a weapon.  Despite all of this though, the most effective way to defeat ALL opponents is to simply jump and attack.  I almost never had to use anything else unless I wanted to change things up.  The combat certainly worked well, and it looks quite impressive, it just isn't all neccesary.
My last criticsm is that there wasn't enough to do.  I was able to beat both included campaigns in roughly 3-4 hours.  That's all there was to it.  They still include their sand box levels from the early access version, but they certainly don't have any story or real objectives.  The game also includes workshop content, but the game shouldn't rely entirely on their own community to give their game value.
In conclusion, I DID enjoy playing the game, and despite some flaws it is fun to play, but there just isn't enough here to justify the price they are asking for it.  I would absolutely recommend getting it on sale if it looks like fun to you, but for the full price there just isn't enough here to justify the 9 years or so this game spent in development.

Overall I like this game, it’s definitely not perfect but I like it.
First the pros.
Fairly accurate to the fluff, the orks definitely feel like orks, their plans consist of either bum rushing you while screaming their lungs out; or siting back and firing in your general direction while screaming their lungs out. The space marine feels fairly accurate, super soldiers who butcher their way through the ork ship as fast and efficient as they can and aim for the warboss. however these feel a bit to powerful, especially since they took down a gargant and a whole tyranid swarm on their own, if there were more of them this would be fair a proper tactical squad of five space marines could possibly do this but not just one or two. Also the tyranids feel accurate, one massive swarm that tries to rush down the enemy with their weight of numbers that are controlled by one hive tyrant.
Fairly balanced.
Well balanced, as long as you don't♥♥♥♥♥♥about to much you should be able to beat the game without too much trouble.
Graphics.
they’re not great but I can’t help but like the design of this game; it feels like ork krooser, everything is made of mismatching bits of scrap and looted stuff bolted and welded together into a ramshackle patchwork of machinery that really should not work, but it does... because orks.
Cons.
Controls feel a bit awkward.
Fairly obvious what this means, controls are awkward and it is very obvious that this is made for the Xbox, shooting is odd as is melee.
Camera.
This is the main problem, the camera is just so weird, is can be really annoying when it goes into an odd angle. Not much else to say, the camera is just horrible.
This game is definitely worth picking up if you want a cheap game to play through over a day or two and vent your pent up rage as you gun down waves of orks and tyraninds and chop grots into pieces. however if you want a game that has a lot of replay value and fulfils your bloodlust then get space marine instead, costs more and the extra cost is worth it, better graphics, more accurate to the fluff and has a better combat system in general.

Overfall:
~~~~~~~

After successfully uniting all human tribes and witnessing a glorious victory over the Orcish Emperor, the immortal king of the realm - the one and only “Everking” – summoned two heroes to his citadel! The Everking gave our two incredible heroes a mission to retrieve the “Disc Artefact” from another world, through a particular portal. Day by day, our two heroes venture deep into this strange world and finally obtain the artefact. Upon using the portal to come back and deliver the artefact to the “Everking”, they find out that their beloved king has been missing and the most astonishing aspect of this saga is the fact that they have been gone for over three centuries. . .

Overfall is an RPG/Roguelike/Strategy with turn-based combat game where you take control of two heroes who are searching for their lost king. At the start of the game, you will be choosing what classes your two heroes will be; there are nine classes to choose from but upon your first game, you will automatically be a fighter and a cleric. The other classes will be unlocked throughout the game. Each character has five weapons to choose from (one available and four to unlock) with three special moves, eight skills sets to choose from (again three available and five to unlock) and twenty-five trinklets (abilities, if you like) of which five are granted to choose from on your first game. Then when you are ready, just go through the portal and you will be back in the realm of Dys!
In Dys you will meet your descendant; do not be surprised by his old age when he greets you. After a quick chat and an exchange of family tales (nah . . . just kidding), you will jump on a boat and start exploring the world of Dys. There are plenty of islands to visit and other ships to accost. In the realm, you will notice different types of islands, how they look on the map. That is because you have six races who co-habit this world: Goblins, Dwarves, Elves, Orcs, Hollow and Forsaken. At the start of your game, your reputation will be neutral with all of them. As you go through your journey, you might help the goblins and receive a point towards a better reputation with them, but decrease your reputation points towards other races who are not on friendly terms with the goblins because of that. You can find quests on Island and ships too, and as you successfully achieve your missions, you will receive recognition within the world, which will enable you to unlock a spot to grow your party, and you will be able to recruit another character to join you.
Each time you achieve a positive outcome in a quest you will be rewarded with Frags (the currency), Runes, Dust and/or Food. With frags you can upgrade weapons at bazaars, trade for food with merchants or trade for runes. Runes are sacred stones and are very important in Overfall. When you find and visit an Altar, you can use these stones to either resurrect a fallen character or give protection to several of them, if you carry more than one stone with you. You will also need runes to hire a companion. Dust is a magical ingredient that can be used to learn skills and give a short boost for your ship. As for food, well you have to feed your heroes, my friends, or they will die!
Your heroes can die in combat too; either on a boat or on land. The combat phase is simple and very good. It is a turn based setup but each of your heroes will have three phases per turn - movement, ability and attack. Just a quick word of advice for you - try to get one of your characters to be someone who can heal in battle, or your game will be fairly short. I do like the characters in this game; they have a slightly larger head than their body. I know it is a little thing but it makes it fun!
Graphically, the game looks good. The soundtrack vaguely reminds me of a well-known TV show which is also set in a fantasy world. Good and simple to follow combat system. This game comes with a story builder so you can create your own story for all of us to enjoy!
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	100’s of locations to visits
-	9 classes to choose from
-	Plenty of abilities and characters to unlock
-	Easy to use turn-based combat
-	Interesting story
-	Good replay-ability / Story builder included
-	Achievements and Trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No tutorial (not necessary to have one but it would be nice)
Overfall is a brilliantly combination of RPG/ Strategy/Roguelike with endless replay-ability! A must have!
9/10

This is one of my favourite games of all time, so clearly I am biased towards how much I like it.
Firstly I will state that I have been playing the Elder Scrolls games since Morrowind, the one before Oblivion, and have played Daggerfall and Arena too, but none of those had the same effect Oblivion did, so if you liked them you'll love this.. The main storyline is incredible in depth, and the voice acting is great (got to love Sean Bean!). One of my favourite things about this game is that if you don't like the mission you are doing or don't fancy completing the compaign in one big stint, you can go off and join one of the many guild and try and complete the lengthy compaigns they also have. Fighters Guild is a good one, I must say, but my favourite is The Dark Brotherhood. Sure, they have it in Skyrim, but it's not nearly as good as in this game. Getting creative in killing the target is easy, and the rewards for the extra parts of the missions are awesome. Not to your taste? Speak to the average joe on the street, you can over hear conversations or get mention of missions that  people need doing. The planes of Oblivion are always fun as well, as once you've started there is a lot of locations that they can randomly spawn at (although at certain points during the game the amount of gates will vary). The special items found inside the gates are sweet as well, so its worth having a look just for that. After completing the campaign (or before?) the expansion packs are pretty sweet. Shivering Isles is my personal favourite, and possibly one of my favourite expansions of any game. Sheogorath is just a fantastic character, and the enemies you fight are highly entertaining. Aside from storylines and missions, the way you select your characters traits and abilities is a large improvement on Morrowind, and makes your character more unique. The star signs which give you certain abilities or benefits are very nice, and easily define what kind of play style you go for.
Verdict: I love this game! I would highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys action-RPG's. I find games nowadays are too easy to burn through and complete, but not this one! I have completed most of it on xbox, but I have only just completed the main storyline and The Dark Brotherhood, and my time is nearly 40 hours, and I still have masses left to do. Buy this game!

It's difficult to improve upon what has already been said by others. This is probably the best cRPG since 2000. Everything is incredibly polished, the game is LONG without being boring, and quests make sense in the context of each environment (something sorely missing in, for instance, recent Bethesda games).
The combat system is clearly defined and rewards clever gameplay, while at the same time not giving the computer an unfair advantage. That said, battles will DESTROY you the second you don't take them seriously.
I wasn't really all that impressed by DOS 1, but part of that was that I felt that my characters didn't have much personality, and that made it difficult to immerse myself in the story. The brilliant inclusion of origins characters brings this missing component to the table nicely, and the characters themselves are varied and interesting - they may well put you into dangerous situations, close off quest options, or open doors to new ones.
From a technical standpoint, the voice acting is well above industry standard - I don't believe I've heard an awkward line in 70 hours. The graphics are highly polished, and most abilities and attacks work precisely as expected (a few occasional glitches aside). The story elements are well put together and flow nicely (even the "silly" quests), and include some morally ambiguous situations that you have to actually think about.
Undoubtedly, this is a game that we're going to compare other RPGs against for years to come, a real lesson in maintaining old school mechanics without the old school baggage. A complete masterpiece, and if you don't think so, then cRPGs are probably not for you,

No spoilers review:
Larian has birthed a gust of fresh air into a currently stale RPG-world.
I'll start with the meat and potatoes of the gameplay: combat. It delivers on all promised qualities teased at in the developer updates, beta gameplay, and my own dreams.
The story: it is wonderfully immersive, partially because it is fully voice-acted to the highest of quality. Throughout the main story lies each party member's delightful origin tale that only enhances the experience, something severely lacking in today's games. The only complaint I could find about the plot is the rare loose end here or there: mysteries unsolved one would say (closure is important). Those were from side quests, anyways.

RPG level: DND. The elements that drive home the role-play aspects are innovative and make you feel like your choices aren't just some end-game-mood-changer. Choices in every aspect come with different real-time outcomes.
The graphics for such a detailed game are fantastic, particularly shining in the animations and atmosphere departments.

The difficulty of the game can be underwhelming every so often. Some enemies can be too easy even on the hardest difficulty (not to detract from the insanely hard enemies). With how great Larian is with updates, for example them patching overpowered things already, I wouldn't critique them too hard on this yet.
The direction you take in this game is slightly reminiscent of a sandbox game. You go where you want, when you want, and how you want. Well, for the most part. And sometimes that can confuse people. Generally you can stick to a basic path based on simply reading your ever-updating journal.
The co-op is unprecedented. Why? One reason is the accessibility. You can play split screen, with controllers, keyboards, or with 1-3 other friends across the world. The other reason is the development and design of this game completely took into account that many people would be playing together, thus developed it accordingly. Some companies will just throw in a multiplayer mode, some companies will just allow peope to attach to the host's campaign and feel like they are just a henchman along for the adventure. Larian allows everyone to be the main character. Lastly are the extra modes. Game master: create your own adventure for friends (think DnD). Arena: prove yourself the ultimate combatant against other players (up to four people at a time).

In short:
While the game definitely comes short on a LOT of aspects, the main focus, the combat, is a very strong one that actually outweighs the negatives in my opinion. The game also gives unique experiences you most likely will not have in other (combat) games. Combine this with mods, maps and maybe some friends and you have a very good recipe for repeatable fun.
In less short:
The combat system has had 9 years of development worked into it and it really does show. What the game lacks in story, graphics, polishing, and a bunch more stuff regarding the story, it definitely makes up for in the combat. It really is the heart of the game.
Though it is the heart of the game and easily the best part of it, it's actually very simple! It's a good example of easy to learn, but hard to master (I'm not gonna tell you how it works, this is a review after all).
You'll most likely finish the story pretty soon, and wil probably forget it immediately as well. Yet the game managed to keep pulling me back in thanks to it's well made and extremely fun combat system. Never has a (fighting) game made me go 'OOWWHHH' just because of how painful and hard impacts are, but this game managed to pull it of, and keeps doing it.
The game is however quite pricey, yet I personally don't regret buying it simply because of the experiences this game has given and continues to give me, like what I mentioned before.
In my experience this game is best enjoyed with some replaying, some mods and maps (so, more content), maybe even some friends, but most importantly really understanding the combat system. If you, like many reviewers I've seen, don't fully understand the combat system, the game will be a lot less fun.
So to conclude, I do recommend this game, as long as you're able to look past some bad aspects so you can focus on the main good one.

Is The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion worth playing?
Simply put, yes.
More in-depth, this game is actually better than Skyrim.
Skyrim had it's rich environments that were always hiding at least one little thing, and it's gameplay is admitably smoother. (Mainly because it was designed to be smooth.)
However, where Oblivion downright surpasses Skyrim is in questing. Skyrim's quests were easily forgetable as they weren't themselves rememberable.
In Oblivion, you'll remember having to go swimming for those 10 damn fish that that damn scholar guy wanted and the fisherman couldn't get because he didn't have the balls to go swimming. You'll remember your first time meeting with The Fox, and how you felt actual pressure to compete with the other initiates. You'll remember your first time entering an Oblivion Gate, and running from those god damn Daerdric Maces because you forgot to turn down the difficulty to playable.
Simply put, Oblivion remains replayable while Skyrim just stagnates.

Okay, here's the deal. I love Spore. Like, a LOT. So, when it went on sale a while back, I decided to re-buy it (I owned the disc version, but lost the code, so I basically didn't own it). DLC was only like, $5, and I played Galactic Adventures (I loved it, but that's a review for ANOTHER day). Honestly, it was hardly worth the $5.
So if you don't know, the Creepy & Cute pack adds some new creature parts and patterns, but that's it. The arms and legs are literally all bug parts, so nothing I want to use there, some cool new other bits, though. For patterns, some feel "Creepy" like one pattern that looks kind of like muscles, and not so much cute (though it does add a feather pattern, sort of, which is awesome because I love building birds in this game). It doesn't really add too many parts, and quite a few of them feel like they should be part of the game already.
The other problem is that it only adds CREATURE parts. No new clothes, no building, no new anything. Also, the new animations are only in the test drive mode. They're cool to watch, but would be even cooler to see in game. Oh, and another thing that bothers me (But isn't a deal breaker by any means) is the fact that because of how the expansions worked pre-steam, Steam tracks my hours while playing Creepy & Cute, but not the actual game, which means I have to play without my extra parts if I want steam trading cards.
Overall, don't waste $20 on this expansion. If you have $20 burning a hole in your wallet, and you already own Spore, try out Galactic Adventures. It's pretty awesome, if I do say so myself (owned the Expansion for Disc, so yeah. I plan on getting it on a sale or something).
TL;DR: Doesn't really add a whole lot. Not worth $20, though might be worth it if it's on sale.

I played a little of Dragon Nest waaaay back when (maybe a little of the beta?), and put in maybe ~20 hours or so before I downloaded this on Steam.
Anyhoo- from a gameplay perspective, Dragon Nest resembles Vindictus. You choose a (gender-locked) class, run around a shared town hub and accept quests, then delve into instanced dungeons, slay monsters to transition between areas, and face a boss in the final room.
I'll get a bit more specific...
GAMEPLAY- As outlined above.
You do learn new skills fairly quickly, which are infinitely more entertaining to use than your basic attack combos. There's a level up reward chest you can open every time you level up, as seen in several f2p titles. Dragon Nest has... taken an interesting approach with their iteration; at level 6, you are granted a costume set that- when equipped- grants your character hp and damage far beyond normal means. It will essentially trivialize most content you come across, and is on a 7-day timer. A second identical set is granted at another level, but I forget what it was, exactly...
That being said, it's a lovely little feature if you've played before and want to barrel through story and get into the meatier content. I'm not sure if such a system would be detrimental to a new player's experience- if a time comes when the items expire and that overwhelming power is lost, it may be a bit of a shock having to suddenly rely on player skill and skill synergies... although to be fair, joining parties/guild may help alleviate that issue... I can't assert anything on that issue quite yet.
GRPAHICS- Cute, albeit simplistic aesthetic.
Most things (the older assets for sure) are noticeably low-poly, but it looks like a lot of love went into the textures. The effects on most skills are bright and flashy, and could end up obscuring gameplay in larger groups. But solo, I've had no problem keeping up with things.
Once again comparing this to Vindictus, Dragon Nest is considerably more gentle on my computer's aged hardware. I honestly think a laptop less than 5 years old could handle this pretty well.
STORY- It actually has one, and it's pretty good.
The story arc you experience differs to some degree between each class. Sometimes a lot, sometimes a little. Dialogue is generally pretty funny and light, but there are heavier plot points here and there. Characters are a little... melodramatic, perhaps. But I find I like more characters than I find annoying... so that's nice.
AUDIO/SOUND/MUSIC- Nothing really stands out, but nothing's downright terrible... not even the voice-acting.
Sound effects are loud and bombastic. Music is decent, but the loops are relatively short and can overstay their welcome before too long, so I've disabled it. My biggest complaint is that ambient sounds are directly tied to music, so with that muted, towns and forests sound dead... but still- just queue up your own playlist or internet radio or podcast or whatever. :P
COMMUNITY- Haven't had a lot of dealings with people yet, but things don't seem particularly toxic, at any rate.
There's one server, broken up into channels. I've made a point to select low-pop channels just to avoid crowds, but global chat has stayed relatively quiet. I have no idea if there are just that few people playing, or if more conversations are simply being held in party/guild chat... I certainly hope Dragon Nest isn't "dying", as I do find it rather enjoyable.
CASH SHOP- Doesn't appear to be buy-to-win..?
Basic cosmetics (costumes, and a few exclusive faces and hairstyles for most classes), crafting boosters and whatnot. I have yet to purchase anything, and don't feel like I really have to. I call that a win.
EXTRA- Just some little tidbits I didn't work into the fields above.
-There's a mercenary system that lets any class bring a "combat pet" of sorts into dungeons. It IS stuck behind a few walls; beyond the three starter mercs (which you will be able to choose one upon completing a lvl24 quest), the rare and epic varieties have to either be grinded for, or bought off of the player marketplace. Some of the available mercanaries are npc's from certain class' storylines, so even if you don't really NEED a mercanary, it can be entertaining to battle along side them, and see them toss out a one-liner once a dungeon is cleared... could become more necessary once those super-costume items expire, and you aren't running with a party/guild.
-There's PvP available as early as lvl10, but it's something I've not touched, nor really plan to... like other games, there is a PvP based currency and a variety of items to be bought.
-MOST classes, with the exception of the Lancea, Machina, and two elite classes, will recieve a specialization quest at lvl15, and can subsequently choose one of two secondary classes. This choice grants a second skill tree to develop and populate your hotbar with. The skills from this second tree generally require a certain weapon type be wielded, so bear that in mind when the time comes. For the classes with no specialization choice, your second skill tree simply unlocks when you reach lvl15.
-Building on that, your choice of weapon type affects your basic attacks/combos. You'll begin with a starter weapon of each type, so try them out early on and get a feel for them. ^.^
Think that's it... again, I've yet to experience the full gamut of what Dragon Nest has to offer, so please correct me if I'm wrong about something. o3o

Stalker: CoP is a fantastic game. I play it with the Misery mod, which improves graphics and gunplay, and generally makes the game more difficult. Stalker is definitely the most immersive and atmospheric fps I have ever played, and it probably will be for quite some time until another game can take that title. The thing I love so much about it is that you will find yourself scared out of your wits by completely unscripted events, time and time again. Wandering the Zone in this game is an experience I will never forget, in a good way.
However, I must say that it does have its issues. I'm not sure about playing the game without mods, but with Misery, you WILL suffer frequent frame rate stuttering, which can be quite frustrating until you take the time to research a way to handle it or get used to it. Also, for me, I get a really bad and super noticable fish-eye effect fromt the field of view, at pretty much every setting (which you either have to reinstall or alter game files to change*). It's not so bad when you're outside, but I find it very distracting when I'm in a shop / hub building. Finally, I also get screen tearing all the time, with vertical sync on or off. One final disclaimer, this is very much a trial and error game, especially with the Misery mod. You will encounter enemies who will tear you to shreds the first few times, then badly damage you, and finally you just get to the point where you just re-load the save and do it until you don't get so much as a scratch on you (at least, that was how I ended up playing it).
All that being said, this is still one of my most favorite games I've ever played, and if you can get past the frustrations I mentioned, you will have a lot of fun, if you know what you're doing or not.

This game is horribly frustrating. I feel like I've given it a decent go, but the problem is something most people have noted: the camera angles. You have no control over them, and quite often mean you can't see enemies, or even tell where your character is going. It's not a big issue on the first mission, but as you progress and checkpoints become less frequent, it becomes a major issue.
Added to that is the way that your Space Marine can seem to shoot everything but the enemy. Case in point: a section of one mission requires you to protect a power cell whilst being attacked. Enemies will leap in at you from off-screen, engaging in melee, and trying to fight back against them more often than not leads to your marine blowing up the power cell himself, not the enemy. It's a neat idea, but ruined by the terrible camera and the way that targetting is horrible, really coming down to spray-and-pray. The lack of online co-op is a killer, too, and there's lots of graphical bugs throughout.
I got this as part of a bundle, and I'm glad I didn't pay money specifically for it, or I'd have been left feeling incredibly disappointed. There's some fun ideas, and I like the way you unlock new equipment through killing enemies. I may give it another go at some point, but it's highly unlikely given that there's much better ways to waste my time. As such, I cannot recommend this to anyone but the most hardcore 40k fan.

Pros:
+ Siege windows: Easily my #1 draw. On certain servers, it's only possible to damage buildings between 5pm and midnight. I was a big fan of Reign of Kings and similar survival games but they all suffer from the same massive flaw. You log off, you come back, your stuff is gone. That's not exactly fun or engaging for either party. The gameplay I am after is PVP siege play, defending raids/sieges or raiding/sieging others. I did that once or twice in RoK and it was one of the best gaming experiences I've had in recent memory, but it was the exception and not the rule. In CE it could become the rule.
+Active/listening Devs: I will list some cons coming up but the fact of the matter is that these devs have displayed competency and dedication and for now they have my faith.
+ Decent optimization: For an EA open world game, it is decently optimized. It will only improve.
+ Feels responsive: The basic movement of characters feels pretty good, not all elements but I will cover those below. Running/Jumping/Climbing all look and feel responsive, same with the dodging feature.
+ Progression: So far the methods of progression seem pretty cool. You have stat points and recipe points to spend as you see fit. This encourages teamwork and coordination because you will not be able to learn 100% of the crafting recipes. This allows for individuals to focus and be the guild armorer, blacksmith, builder, slaver, alchemist, engineer, decorator (surprisingly relevant), warrior, archer, tank, and so on.
+ Visuals: The game is visually appealing, and my rig is pretty weak. My settings defaulted to High and I get 50-60 fps with a baby CPU (i3, my bottleneck) and decent GPU (390). The biomes are unique and interesting.
Cons:
- Bows: I've only crafted the bottom tier bow so this could admittedly be updated shortly but the bow range is uncommonly short as a result of intense arrow drop/arc. You will not have played a game with this much arrow drop I can assure you so it will be a little jarring at first. You can, of course, get used to it but it remains to be seen how effective bows will be in PVP if their effective range is so short. This is a large concern for me and something I will be tracking closely.
Mixed:
Melee combat: It's vastly improved from its release iteration but it's not there yet. As of now the only method of blocking is using a shield, I have mixed opinions on that but I will update this review after I've mastered the current combat system. Dodging cancels animations which is cool as I believe blocking (with shield) will stagger you so can cancel out of that. A key piece of info I really should have here is if holding up a block drains stamina (it obviously should), I will edit in a day or two. If this were the resting place of combat I would not be happy but this will only improve as time goes on and it's playable enough now.

An amazingly complex and engrossing game that can make the hours fly by.
Crusader Kings II is difficult to classify. It’s a grand strategy game, a sandbox game, and in some ways a political simulator. It also happens to be one of the best role-playing games I've ever played.  I’m not even sure where to begin describing it, but what I can say without reservation is that it’s extremely immersive and
, which is quite a trick that developer Paradox Interactive pulled off when you consider that the vast majority of the gameplay takes place in menus.
The premise is deceptively simple: you play as a king (hardly a surprise given the game's title), and your number one goal above all else is to have an heir in place who will claim your throne upon your death.  When your character dies, you assume the role of his heir, and so on down the line of succession.  Die without an heir and it's game over.
But of course it’s not quite as simple as that.  As a king, you’re naturally going to want to expand your realm and accumulate wealth and prestige, and this is where you find the meat of the game.  When you start, you can choose to play as anything from a lowly vassal like a duke or a petty king ruling a single province to a monarch of an entire country.  This also serves as a secondary way to adjust the game’s difficulty since a duke or petty king is going to have a harder time of it than the ruler of an entire nation.
And this is where things get interesting.  I call Crusader Kings II a role-playing game because it’s all about navigating the treacherous path of court intrigue and maintaining relationships with the other characters in the game.  Sometimes you might want to have a good relationship with someone, or sometimes you may want them to think very poorly of you, and there are numerous means for doing both, from performing favors, or handing out honorary titles (including Court Jester, which never makes the recipient happy), or even straight-up bribery.  If you have a troublesome vassal, you can try and woo him back into your good graces, throw him in jail, or plot to have him killed.  Any action you choose will always have long-term consequences, for good or ill.  For instance, if you arbitrarily throw someone in jail, or attempt to have them murdered and it’s discovered, you’ll take a relationship hit with other characters almost across the board, and this could be a problem if allies refuse to come to your aid during war, or you end up with a revolt on your hands, or other characters hatch their own plans to kill you or your heir!  It all becomes a delicate balancing act as you try to keep your friends (and enemies) happy while scheming to steal land and titles out from under their noses.
In addition to good old fashioned political intrigue, you will also encounter a number of random story vignettes that present your character with various choices that create a short, branching narrative, the ultimate consequences of which could be positive or negative, depending on your decisions.
When things come to blows, and they inevitably will, it’s time to raise an army and clash steel.  Unfortunately, this is not the most engrossing part of the game.  Your armies march around in multi-unit “blobs” represented by a single soldier sprite with a number indicating the size of the army and a small line representing its morale.  Essentially, if your numbers are higher than an enemy army’s numbers then you’ll (most likely) win the battle.  And that’s pretty much all there is to it: march your “blob” around, defeat other blobs, and lay siege to enemy provinces until your war score reaches 100% and you can force your foe to concede to your demands.  I’m not saying this is necessarily easy, and wars are extremely costly, and sometimes you’ll be thrown an unexpected wrinkle that will turn what you thought was an easy victory into a crushing defeat, but you’re not going to find detailed tactical gameplay here (although full disclosure compels me to mention that I’m not an expert in this game by any stretch, so there may be some nuance here that I’m missing).  At any rate, the simple combat mechanics are adequate because war really isn’t the focus of Crusader Kings II even if it is an important aspect given the setting.
Crusader Kings II plays in real-time, but you can pause at any point if you need breathing room to untangle a particularly difficult political conflict.  You can still interact with the game when it’s paused, but your orders won’t take affect until you start the clock again.  This prevents the game from becoming overwhelming even when things get complicated, which can happen very quickly and often without warning.  Thankfully the interface is very well laid out and places the copious amounts of information you need to manage your empire within easy reach, usually no more than one or two mouse-clicks away.  However, it is a very complex game, and even with over 80-hours under my belt to date, I feel like I’ve still barely scratched the surface.  In order to understand Crusader Kings II, you need to have a basic understanding of Medieval politics and laws, and this isn’t something that most people possess.  For instance, a pop-up will inform you that you have a “Wrong type of holding in demesne”.  What does that even mean, and more importantly, how do you fix it?  Or you might discover that your kingdom is at risk of fragmenting into the hands of multiple petty rulers when your character dies because of a potential succession crisis.  Why is this happening, and what can you do about it?  The game’s manual and tutorial missions do a rather poor job preparing you for your career as a crusader king, so you’ll probably want to find some “Let’s play” videos or a strategy guide or two.  I also suggest keeping a web browser handy while you play because you’ll inevitably have questions throughout the course of the game.
Graphically, Crusader Kings II is probably about as attractive as a game like this can be with the majority of the display occupied by a vast interactive 3D map.  Details are added and subtracted depending on your zoom level, so it’s easy to pull out for a quick overview and then zoom in close enough to see individual cities and holdings dotted across the landscape.  It also runs beautifully in Linux, which always scores extra points in my book.  Sound effects are pretty basic for the most part, but you’ll mostly be listening to the music anyway which is period appropriate orchestral selections.  It can get a little bit repetitive, but there are several music packs available as DLC to expand the score.
Speaking of DLC, if you’re contemplating a purchase of Crusader Kings II, you might be staggered by the fact that there is, at the time of this writing, nearly $250 worth of full-priced DLC currently available, and you may find this off-putting, but consider this: the vanilla game offers a complete experience in and of itself and can give you hours of entertainment.  In fact, I would recommend you play it sans DLC at first to get a feel for the game and to decide which DLC actually appeals to you, because not all of it will (and you should probably wait until it’s on sale anyway to get the most bang for your bucks).  I personally only have around half of the available DLC including several expansions and some of the unit and music packs, but I don’t feel like I’m missing out simply because the other content doesn’t interest me.  I should also note that when Paradox does release a major expansion, it's always accompanied by a patch that adds new features and content to the base game for free.
This review could easily be three times as long, and I still wouldn’t feel like I had given a comprehensive description of Crusader Kings II.  So let’s make this simple: It’s a great game.  Buy it.

I was on the fence before purchasing this game.  I usually play shooters, but I was getting bored with PUBG and CSGO.  I was looking for an RPG, but more of an action RPG title.  I don't usually enjoy turn based RPG's and this game seemed tedious and unapproachable.  I played for 2 hours before I requested a refund, which I wound up cancelling.  This is one of the most immersive games I've ever played.  There are multiple player classes to choose from, and the first few hours of the game will make you feel like you chose poorly.  You didn't.  This game is just hard.  Placement of your characters before and during battles, how you talk to other characters, who you decide to ally with, and how you upgrade your character all make for an immersive and challenging experience.  I ran into two quests which were broken by the end of my 122 hours of gameplay, also the global chat only worked on the first day of gameplay.  There are multiple paths you can play in this game, and each one poses an interesting moral dilemma that makes the game more exciting and rewarding.  If you enjoy engrossing storylines, and big reveals then this story is definitely for you.  I spent my first two hours of gameplay feeling lukewarm about the game, then I couldn't stop playing or talking about it.   I will probably do a second play through soon, as I feel like I learned a little bit about the game playing through and would like to play with either a different solo build, or to try a tankier build since my tank the first play through wound up being my Necro/Pyro mage.  Crazy right?  I know, probably not the best way to do it, but it worked and this game is dope so go play it.

First off, the art style is incredibly unique and charming. I love interacting with whomever my adventurers would cross paths with, and it was neat to discover that the same encounters would play out differently depending on who/what you chose for your adventurers, followers, or conversation arcs.
The writing is also top notch, not every line of dialogue lands, but when they do....it's comedy gold. I don't want to spoil any of it but there is some expertly crafted references to mashup the game universe with our own (if that makes any sense).
Now, don't get the wrong idea about this game. It is most certainly a rogue like game, and a difficult one at that. It took me several playthroughs before I REALLY understood what I needed to do, and if you want to complete the Story successfully, you have to go into this with a plan of what races you're going to befriend, etc. Time is the true enemy in this game, because as time passes more and more of the enemy hordes will begin to populate the game world, causing untold amounts of havoc, and making your task that much harder.
Also, you'll find after several attempts that whether or not you succeed has a whole lot to do with simple dumb luck. For you to gain reputation with any of the 6 different races in the game, you'll have to do things that will earn points with whichever race you are attempting to befriend and eventually ally yourself with to combat the hordes of evil. Well, the way you go about earning said points is by visiting islands that correspond with whichever race you're trying to become BFFs with. Easy right? No. Not when you can visit island after island without getting lucky and getting the random acts that will allow you to gain/lose reputation. I don't really mind it too much myself, but I know that this may be something that could possibly agitate some people.
The trading/upgrade system is fairly simple, almost too simple...but yet I think it fits perfectly here. Each of your two adventurers is allowed 3 Class upgrades that you can purchase from any of the corresponding Class ships (Fighter, Cleric, etc). Class upgrades cost you 5 "Dust" per upgrade, adding up to a grand total of 30 Dust for you to fully upgrade your Class skills. Then you are allowed to visit a Bazaar where you can further upgrade your chosen adventurers with Weapon upgrades. Now this also follows the same rule of 3. Each adventurer can upgrade their Weapon Head, their Weapon Hilt, and then you can roll for a random enchantment to complete the upgrade boogaloo. Now these Weapon upgrades cost "Frags" with each of the Weapon upgrades costing 12 Frags each, and the random enchantment costing 5 Frags per roll. Now BE CAREFUL...Don't be a dummy like I was and roll an awesome enchanment and then forget to apply that awesome enchantment. BE SURE TO CLICK APPLY ENCHANTMENT AS SOON AS YOU FIND ONE THAT YOU WANT. Also, when you're in the screen upgrading Weapons at the Bazaar, you'll have to select which hero you are upgrading by pressing the corresponding button underneath their character portrait. Otherwise you might pimp out one adventurer, while leaving the other one left hanging.
Well...what more can I say...If you like Rogue like games, or games with great art and tremendous dialogue that will at times cause you to roar with laughter then this game is for you...buy it...like now. It's awesome and you'll get an excessive amount of replay value from this game.
If you enjoy games that hold your hand, and wipe your bum, as it compliments you and hands you a "Good Try" Participation Trophy...well this game isn't for you Sparky. Move along.
If you fancy yourself as one of those creative types and would like to make your own story with this games art style...well then you're in luck. I haven't used the Story Builder myself, but I know its an option and I know I'll eventually get around to seeing what I can put together with it...after I play...just one more try
Final Verdict: 5 out of 5 Gibblets

TL:DR - This game is fantasy FTL with turn-based battles.
At first I was dubious about the tactical combat, but I soon realized that it gets quite in-depth. There are a huge number of unlockables and many different party set-ups. You start with 2 characters, but during the game you eventually get two additional companions from a very large selection.
The combat is based largely on conditions and I quickly learned that various combos are incredibly powerful. Vulnerability increases damage taken from each attack by 1, meaning that damage over time effects (bleed, poison, agony, etc.) do 2 instead of 1. Vulnerability + DOT = Awesome!
Tormented is a condition that damages enemies for each tile they move...fear is a condition that forces opponents to move 5 squares at the start of their turn. Add vulnerability to the mix and you have 10 damage before they even start their turn...then if it's a melee unit, it probably won't be able to get back in the fray without dying.
These are just some examples. I'm still learning the intricacies of gameplay. It's very fun, and I highly recommend it!
The only downside I can think of is that most things need to be unlocked before you can use them and that might not be everyone's cup of tea.

Likely the purest implementation of an FPS I've ever played. No introduction, no plot, no explanation, no weapon switching, no cover, no health, no armor, no breaks... no need. Just spawn, kill, learn, die, repeat. A single, simple mechanic that hides significant complexity. Highly addictive. Smooth and responsive controls, excellent sound design. Devil Daggers never feels like it's cheating you out of anything; your successes and (more frequently) your failures are entirely on you.
Good luck.

The story on Overgrowth picks up right after Lugaru, it earns some points with me because I've been dying to know what went on with Turner after Lugaru's ending; to be fair, it sticks to the same story telling of Lugaru, not too much dialog, it's just there to give you a reason to fight, can't really say It's deep or gonna make you cry, but it's there to sustain the constant need to combat or do platform jumping missions. The S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series is one that scratches an itch that many people weren't aware they had, that of a story-based first-person shooter that doesn't skimp on the aspects of character improvement. To be fair, its narrative lacks the strength of an epic such as Half Life, but it makes up for it by presenting a plausible pseudo-scifi flair that doesn't require too much imagination to comprehend. The long and short of it is that, in the area around the Chernobyl catastrophe (known as the "Zone"), radioactive influence has caused the birth of a number of strange anomalies, both helpful and harmful. The former come from 'artifacts', mysterious objects possessing helpful properties like increasing the body's ability to heal, and the latter is in the form of arcane occurrences such as areas where gravity is magnified to a fatal extent, or even things as run-of-the-mill as your typical postapocalyptic creatures seeking to kill you.
What sets the STALKER franchise apart is the emphasis on the balance between the fictional nightmares of the Zone and the interactions with other people just like you -- fortune-seekers trying to locate artifacts for their value in the world at large, while avoiding the pitfalls of anomalies and mutants. While these other Stalkers may not be perfectly represented as flesh-and-blood people, it is entirely possible, within the scope of the games, to make alliances with one faction (say, the Bandits who seek fortune for themselves at the expense of others), which would then make others view you as an enemy.
Call of Pripyat is itself the latest (five years old, mind you) expression of the series, bringing together Shadow of Chernobyl (the first game)'s narrative coherence with Clear Sky (the second, oft-panned game)'s factional warfare and open-ended nature. In CoP, you find yourself in an open world, with 3 main maps available to get your Stalker on. There is a centralized story to follow, involving your character as a special operative for the Russian government attempting to track down the cause of the crashes of an entire squad of other operatives, as if flying over the anomaly-filled Zone wasn't reason enough. But within that overall framework, you are free to either maintain your military nature and focus entirely on the mission, or you can go off and become a Stalker yourself, searching for artifacts and misplaced caches of military gear.
As far as the story goes, it's a pretty linear progression. Each map has a list of things for you to accomplish in the story's progression, and at the end of those things it opens up the way to the next map. It serves a function of allowing you to explore each area, without losing track of the bigger picture always lurking just beneath the surface (unlike other open-world games where you can never complete the 'main quest' and still explore the entirety of the world). This hampers the game somewhat, though, as you as a player may feel railroaded into performing some things just for the sake of progression, even if you want more time to just float around the world.
The real appeal of CoP comes from exploration. Sure, each map is, in the end, just a collection of a dozen or so "points of interest", each of which corresponds to a specific scenario -- here is a building that you can explore, there is a field full of Boiler anomalies that superheat the air, and so forth. But in your first playthrough, at least, exploring each of these locations feels deep enough that it feels like you're really blazing new trails into the mysterious and dangerous Zone.
As far as character progression goes, there aren't any RPG aspects insofar as levels and skills -- no stat distribution screens here. Instead, a fluid progression system emerges from acquiring and upgrading new gear. And while there are certainly high and low ends of the spectrum for both weapons and armor, an interesting upgrade system performed by a mechanic NPC means that even a beginning-of-the-game weapon can perform adequately to let you handle the toughest of mutants and the most heavily-armed NPCs. The real limiting factor is money -- but, as you get more money and/or loot to sell as you do more things in the world, it functions as a sort of experience system, where getting enough money lets you buy a new suit of armor, or perhaps a few upgrades to the suit you already have that increases its survivability in radioactive environments.
Moving on to artifacts: As explained earlier, artifacts are mysterious (there's that word again) objects possessing unique abilities that, more often than not, are helpful to your character. This comes at a cost, though, as many artifacts are still inherently radioactive (represented by a +# representation, based on the radioactivity), and will cause you harm if you use them for too long. Their use is through their placement in an "artifact pouch", wherein their effects -- both positive and negative -- will be able to affect you. Or you can always just carry them in your backpack, where they can't hurt you, but can't help you either. And thus a balance has to be struck between using artifacts that help you in the near future -- mental protection as you're about to fight telepathic mutants, for example -- and either bearing the radioactivity, using your precious anti-rad meds as a stopgap measure, or using one of the slightly-rarer anti-radioactivity artifacts (which have -# in the radioactivity measurement), the lattermost of which can negate the other artifacts, and even give you a baseline radioactivity resistance.
With that, I come to the final point, which is the plethora of in-game stats that the player has to take into effect. There are eight, each with their own means of being inflicted and being protected against or healed. Roughly speaking, these stats and a brief summary are:
1.) Impact -- The effect (damage and flinching) of gravitational effects (anomalies or stuff being thrown at you telekinetically), or being smacked around by mutants with physical attacks
2.) Wounding/Bleeding -- Slow health loss through cuts, bullet wounds, etc.
3.) Explosion -- Self-explanatory
4.) Firearms -- The effect (damage and flinching) of gunfire
5.) Burn -- The damage of thermal effects (fires, thermal anomalies, etc.)
6.) Chemical -- The damage of chemical hazards (typically anomalies)
7.) Electric -- The damage of electrical anomalies
8.) Radiation -- The damage and effect (screen blurring, stamina drain, etc.) of radioactive objects and anomalies
9.) Psy/Mental -- The damage and effect of mental attacks (almost exclusively by psychic mutants)
As you can see, there are many stats to be concerned with, but they fall into two general categories -- combat and environment. For the most part, environmental resistances are only momentary concerns based on the current situation -- no need to worry about Burn resistance unless you're going into a field of hot anomalies -- wheareas the combat stats are all-round necessities. The trick is to balance finding armor with the stats you need (with upgrades providing some measure of balance for stats they lack), artifacts that will resist what you're about to do in the immediate future, and using on-demand items that temporarily boost resistances.
In the end, the Zone is worth at least one solid playthrough, even if in doing so you explore every point of interest, locate one of every artifact, and collect every piece of gear possible. An emergent mod community has also put together mods doing everything from merely adding a handful of gear to be found, to some introducing entire new zones imported from the previous games. In the end, I would conclude that S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat is worth playing, if for no other reason than to demonstrate that an FPS can have a non-setpiece story, and some aspect of RPGs, without losing part of itself in the process.

It breaks my heart.
It breaks my heart since I've waited for this game to come out for so long.
The best word to describe the controls is 'janky'. The main problem is the whole fighting system works well on 1v1, but gets really unreadable with multiple opponents. It realistic in a way, since fighting one against several people is quite hard, but it makes for lousy gameplay.
The problem is that the reaction window is really tight (once again, not a problem in 1v1) but given that melee combat is hard to read with more that one opponent, it quickly gets frustrating.
The problem is that most fight include more than one enemy and it's mindboggling to me that the fighting system wasn't build around that.
Sure, the fighting system is different from everything I've ever played (I won't try to describe here, if you're considering buying, I suggest you do a google search) but it doesn't mean it's better.
The safest bet is to abuse the jump kick. It has a small learning curve, but once you know how to use it, it's the safest way to play along with being stealthy.
Speaking of stealth : It's really barebone. No alarms, no real consequences aside from needing to take down several ennemies at once if one gets spotted. It minimal, but at least it's there.
If you want to describe this game quickly, the right word is barebone.
The plot is paper thin, and really just an excuse for the action.
The fighting system isn't as deep as it seems. Limited moveset, quick attacks, slow movements. It's mostly frustrating.
The stealth system let you move, grab people and stab them once you've donne so. And also, you can drag the corpses. That's all.
And it's really short (main campaign : four hours tops). At least you get Lugaru remastered in the package.
My advice : wait for a discount, maybe the modding will make it worthwhile in time. For now, avoid.

This is one of those games that infuriates me simply because it dares to come close. The gameplay in Kill Team is not bad. Yes, it's a little repetitive, but the upgrade mechanism works well in a world where loot doesn't really make sense. However, the unskippable cutscenes issue simply kills the game utterly. Multi-character replay is not encouraged, as you have to 'learn' the same things you knew before. While I don't have a problem with being unable to skip a cutscene the first time through, let me skip it later. I am aware that these cutscenes may be disguising loading, but in that case the game loads very little information at a time, which is similarly unacceptable. I also have a problem with how far back in a level you are thrown upon death. Certain clear points for a potential 'checkpoint' are not utilised for that, and so you are catapulted back even further, which leaves a sense of futility. While I genuinely enjoy what the game is trying to do, I cannot recommend it.

Warframe is a fantastic free to play co-op third person shooter game developed & published by Digital Extremes in 2013.
[Main Setting] A sci-fi space oppera set in our solar system, rich lore to uncover and many classes and weapons to master. At the time of writing (2017) there are 34 diferent Warframes (classes) and over 300+ weapons.
[Story] Set in the far future, a great empire known as the Orokin had once conquered the system. Fast forward a few years and you, a Tenno, wake up and are thrusted into a world where the Orokin have vanished and different factions are warring for control of the system. You must uncover the truth about the past, about yourself and ultimately forge your own path in this sci fi universe.
[Visuals] Unique artstyle and great effects make Warframe easy on the eyes. Character, weapon, enemy and world design are cohesive and well presented.
[Audio] Nothing ground breaking, but very fitting tracks and nvironmental effects make sure your immersion remains peaked.
[Gameplay] This game is a co-op heavy experience and thus, is recommended to play with friends (or random people) rather than alone. Many people claim Warframe is "grindy" but really, hat depends on how much you want to invest in the game's many choices. Developers keep the game fresh and time sensitive events, missions, raids and new content always provide you with things to do while not penalizing you for playing sparingly.
[Monetization] Platinum, the premium currency in Warframe can be used to buy most things in game, but doing so is a massive waste of resources since most gear and warframes can be built in game. Instead platinum is used to upgrade weapon slots and purchase cosmetics. After all, Fashion Frame is the true endgame. Most importantly: you can obtain platinum by selling rare drops to players in game, so even if you spend 0$ you can enjoy everything the game has to offer.
[Synopsis] If you like games like Borderlands, Destiny and Mass Effect give Warframe a try. It might not be for everyone but you would be surprised about it's quality. Warframe is one of the most well made free to play games out there next to Path of Exile in terms of content and fairness. I have played over 1.000 hours and i regret not a single second of it.

An amazingly complex and engrossing game that can make the hours fly by.
Crusader Kings II is difficult to classify. It’s a grand strategy game, a sandbox game, and in some ways a political simulator. It also happens to be one of the best role-playing games I've ever played.  I’m not even sure where to begin describing it, but what I can say without reservation is that it’s extremely immersive and
, which is quite a trick that developer Paradox Interactive pulled off when you consider that the vast majority of the gameplay takes place in menus.
The premise is deceptively simple: you play as a king (hardly a surprise given the game's title), and your number one goal above all else is to have an heir in place who will claim your throne upon your death.  When your character dies, you assume the role of his heir, and so on down the line of succession.  Die without an heir and it's game over.
But of course it’s not quite as simple as that.  As a king, you’re naturally going to want to expand your realm and accumulate wealth and prestige, and this is where you find the meat of the game.  When you start, you can choose to play as anything from a lowly vassal like a duke or a petty king ruling a single province to a monarch of an entire country.  This also serves as a secondary way to adjust the game’s difficulty since a duke or petty king is going to have a harder time of it than the ruler of an entire nation.
And this is where things get interesting.  I call Crusader Kings II a role-playing game because it’s all about navigating the treacherous path of court intrigue and maintaining relationships with the other characters in the game.  Sometimes you might want to have a good relationship with someone, or sometimes you may want them to think very poorly of you, and there are numerous means for doing both, from performing favors, or handing out honorary titles (including Court Jester, which never makes the recipient happy), or even straight-up bribery.  If you have a troublesome vassal, you can try and woo him back into your good graces, throw him in jail, or plot to have him killed.  Any action you choose will always have long-term consequences, for good or ill.  For instance, if you arbitrarily throw someone in jail, or attempt to have them murdered and it’s discovered, you’ll take a relationship hit with other characters almost across the board, and this could be a problem if allies refuse to come to your aid during war, or you end up with a revolt on your hands, or other characters hatch their own plans to kill you or your heir!  It all becomes a delicate balancing act as you try to keep your friends (and enemies) happy while scheming to steal land and titles out from under their noses.
In addition to good old fashioned political intrigue, you will also encounter a number of random story vignettes that present your character with various choices that create a short, branching narrative, the ultimate consequences of which could be positive or negative, depending on your decisions.
When things come to blows, and they inevitably will, it’s time to raise an army and clash steel.  Unfortunately, this is not the most engrossing part of the game.  Your armies march around in multi-unit “blobs” represented by a single soldier sprite with a number indicating the size of the army and a small line representing its morale.  Essentially, if your numbers are higher than an enemy army’s numbers then you’ll (most likely) win the battle.  And that’s pretty much all there is to it: march your “blob” around, defeat other blobs, and lay siege to enemy provinces until your war score reaches 100% and you can force your foe to concede to your demands.  I’m not saying this is necessarily easy, and wars are extremely costly, and sometimes you’ll be thrown an unexpected wrinkle that will turn what you thought was an easy victory into a crushing defeat, but you’re not going to find detailed tactical gameplay here (although full disclosure compels me to mention that I’m not an expert in this game by any stretch, so there may be some nuance here that I’m missing).  At any rate, the simple combat mechanics are adequate because war really isn’t the focus of Crusader Kings II even if it is an important aspect given the setting.
Crusader Kings II plays in real-time, but you can pause at any point if you need breathing room to untangle a particularly difficult political conflict.  You can still interact with the game when it’s paused, but your orders won’t take affect until you start the clock again.  This prevents the game from becoming overwhelming even when things get complicated, which can happen very quickly and often without warning.  Thankfully the interface is very well laid out and places the copious amounts of information you need to manage your empire within easy reach, usually no more than one or two mouse-clicks away.  However, it is a very complex game, and even with over 80-hours under my belt to date, I feel like I’ve still barely scratched the surface.  In order to understand Crusader Kings II, you need to have a basic understanding of Medieval politics and laws, and this isn’t something that most people possess.  For instance, a pop-up will inform you that you have a “Wrong type of holding in demesne”.  What does that even mean, and more importantly, how do you fix it?  Or you might discover that your kingdom is at risk of fragmenting into the hands of multiple petty rulers when your character dies because of a potential succession crisis.  Why is this happening, and what can you do about it?  The game’s manual and tutorial missions do a rather poor job preparing you for your career as a crusader king, so you’ll probably want to find some “Let’s play” videos or a strategy guide or two.  I also suggest keeping a web browser handy while you play because you’ll inevitably have questions throughout the course of the game.
Graphically, Crusader Kings II is probably about as attractive as a game like this can be with the majority of the display occupied by a vast interactive 3D map.  Details are added and subtracted depending on your zoom level, so it’s easy to pull out for a quick overview and then zoom in close enough to see individual cities and holdings dotted across the landscape.  It also runs beautifully in Linux, which always scores extra points in my book.  Sound effects are pretty basic for the most part, but you’ll mostly be listening to the music anyway which is period appropriate orchestral selections.  It can get a little bit repetitive, but there are several music packs available as DLC to expand the score.
Speaking of DLC, if you’re contemplating a purchase of Crusader Kings II, you might be staggered by the fact that there is, at the time of this writing, nearly $250 worth of full-priced DLC currently available, and you may find this off-putting, but consider this: the vanilla game offers a complete experience in and of itself and can give you hours of entertainment.  In fact, I would recommend you play it sans DLC at first to get a feel for the game and to decide which DLC actually appeals to you, because not all of it will (and you should probably wait until it’s on sale anyway to get the most bang for your bucks).  I personally only have around half of the available DLC including several expansions and some of the unit and music packs, but I don’t feel like I’m missing out simply because the other content doesn’t interest me.  I should also note that when Paradox does release a major expansion, it's always accompanied by a patch that adds new features and content to the base game for free.
This review could easily be three times as long, and I still wouldn’t feel like I had given a comprehensive description of Crusader Kings II.  So let’s make this simple: It’s a great game.  Buy it.

I made a Khajit and he could punch stuff. I leveled up punching stuff, running places, and jumping to their maximum level but when I went to the arena I had trouble. I easily defeated my opponents by punching them until they could no longer stand up, then continuing to punch them as they lay bloody on the arena's dirt floor. I heard the crowd roaring as my fists crashed into the Grey Orc's skull; I felt their love wash over me like a crimson silk gown. Slowly, after the vampire scum gave out his last breath, I walked out of the arena. Not in triumph, not in victory, but in remorse. I had just punched my way through a dozen or more skulls, and for what? In my agony I gloomily set up at the The Bloated Float Inn, located in the Imperial City's Waterfront District. I woke up to the sounds of rustling, was confronted by a clearly beligerant bandit. The man had no idea I was the Arena Champion, he had not heard how I crushed the skulls of countless enemies with my punching, how I jumped clear over them with little effort, or even how I ran circles around the arena dodging every single attack thrown at me before pummeling my opponents into submission. The very idea of the man standing before me, a person unknowing of my athletic prowess, set me in to an uncontrollable rage. I don't recall what happened over then next ten minutes, but my memory picks back up again standing inside of the Inn owner's cabin covered head to toe in blood. I navigated back through the ship, which now more resembled a slaughter house, to try to find someone who could tell me what happened. Located in the messhall I found a naked shivering woman named Selene. I will never forget the look on her face when I approached her, a visage of fear so vivid the viewer can feel it.
It was then I realized what event must had befallen the denizens of The Bloated Float Inn. The ingorance of that would-be bandit set me into a blood fueled rage. I slaughtered every person aboard the ship for his sin, that is, every person save for this trembling woman. I decided then and there to never use my fists again, I set off from the boat, WHICH HADN'T LEFT THE HARBOR, to embark on a pilgrimage. One that would encapsulate all nine divine shrines and eventually lead an unwilling khajit boxer to defeat the ancient Aylied king Umaril using only Talk good skill, run fast skill, and jump high skill. After defeating such an awesome foe I came to the conclusion that one need not fight with his fists to attain his goals. Through the use of hecka convincing words, speedy feet, and super strong legs, anyone can stamp out evil without ever lifting a finger.
Oblivion taught me the greatest lesson of all, that fighting is evil.

Awesomenauts will always be very special to me, played this game over the last 4 years and now I am proud to say I can recommend this game more than ever, with the addition of the Level-Editor.
Before the recent Patch 3.5, Awesomenauts used to just be a great, but also very niche game. Not many players were interested in sticking around with a fun, but casual 2D 3v3 MOBA. And while a much older patch brought us custom matches, you were still very limited to just a MOBA mode & Team Death Match on a semi-custom map.
But now with an awesome Level-Editor, which is easy to get started and has enough complexity to be very creative with, plus additional wacky custom games settings; You can now play Smash-Brothers, Horde Mode, single player maps, or just a custom made map for the default MOBA mode.
Mind you the Level-Editor only has been released a few weeks ago in beta. It has since than been improved and we already saw a wide range of mods, so we will see more and better stuff coming, which is very exciting.
Although the default multiplayer isn't as noob friendly as on launch anymore, it is worth mentioning that this is the only game I know, which is a Plafform MOBA. Since its launch on Steam in 2012, 21 new characters were added to the game (29 total), 9 of them being distributed over 2 DLCs. There is no other pay2win aspect to the game.
Currently 5 maps are in an online rotation, accessible by every player and matches that are 10 to 20 minutes long. It's stillv ery simular to a MOBA, you destroy turrents on 2 lanes and fight for map control. But the fighting dynamic is much more different as it is very easy to escape a fight as it is equally easy to burst down a player, with combined forces. Plattforming feels good, and with various different jumps per naut adds another layer of deapth. However, with not too many people playing, getting into Awesomenauts can be rather frustrating, as most people playing online have at least 100 hours under their belt.
For old players coming back this MOBA mode has been changed a lot over the past years, so here is a quick rundown of all major changes in no particular order:
-> XP system;
-> Galactron matchmaking update;

-> Late- join & Quick-start were removed;
There is no doubt I am very biased at this point, with this many hours, investing in the Kickstarter and sticking with the game for so long. But do consider that these developers, Ronimo, have stuck with the game for nearly 5 years now and that all of these cool features can be yours for $10 or even less. Take care and remember if you ever in need of fun, just call the Awesomenauts. ;)

This game is objectively one of the worst games of all time, and the most overrated by a long shot. The problems start with the first time you launch it--Oblivion was designed around and crippled by its desire to be a SERIOUS CONSOLE TITLE, and you will see this in the insultingly huge billion point font and annoying arrow bar menus everywhere. Yet despite this, there are no gamepad controls at all on the PC. There's a "joystick" option that barely works. This is either intentional, or it's complete incompetence, but that is the kind of thing that characterizes this game as a whole.
Animations are shoddy and choppy. Textures are low res and ugly as hell. Everyone in the game is a carbon copy of each other and there are only about 4 voice actors. There's no sense of place in the game since you can just fast travel anywhere from the start. There's no sense of RPG advancement since everywhere in the game auto-levels and equipment is worthless. Actually, because of auto-levelling, you'd better not run or jump too much or you'll get pulverized by random bandits in full glass armor you can't compete with.
All quest design is of the Fedex variety: take this thingor to the whoozit, kill these whatchits for the thingor, and so on. Every cave is the same. Every dungeon is the same. It is the most sterile open world of all time, with people milling about waiting for you to interact with them in the most shallow way possible. And finally, not even the story in this game is worth playing for. It's absolute dreck. Sean Bean dies. Whoop-de-♥♥♥♥ing-doo.
The whole game is a sandbox the same way your belly button is a sandbox: if you are shallow or stupid enough to be distracted by playing with the bits of detritus that collect there, you will love this game. But you should also probably consider euthanasia.
