I really love this game. It has an intriguing story mode that you could finish in a few hours. The gameplay is adventurous and has a unique storyline about a rabbit named Turner that goes out to save enslaved rabbits from mainly the wolves and the dogs. The music gets really repetitive though and a lot of the characters I tend to forget because they look so similar. A map would be really helpful, or some arrows because it's very easy to lose track of where you are or where you are going. The storyline really could have been longer. Also, there isn't really a couch co-op mode embedded into the game, but there are always ways to add a second player in with mods or other ways. If there's anything that they should add, it should probably be couch or online co-op, a few more side game modes, less time to load between levels, and the ability to change the looks of your rabbit. Adding an editor button into the sandbox mode is key, instead of hitting F1 everytime you want to go to the editor menu (they don't tell you that it F1 in the controls you have to Google it).  I'm not criticizing the game negatively just naming some ways they could improve their game.  Overall, the game is great if you're into fighting with fist, knives, spears, and swords. I feel like the game shouldn't have taken this long to make, but considering it was mainly made by one person it's very good. I would rate it an 8.5/10.

My first impressions of this game were mostly negative, but after playing through it a bit... I actually don't hate it. The game is inoffensive, and as far as casual games go you could do far worse than this.
You play as a boy named Vasja who's climbing a building and causing general mischief with his slingshot, grabbing power-ups and avoiding obstacles along the way. As you approach the top of each building you'll face a boss. Each level basically plays out the same way, adding new characters to the apartment building and increasing the difficulty.
The graphics, music, and gameplay - while nothing to write home about - are acceptable for a game at this price point. There were no discernible bugs that I noticed during gameplay, and the achievement and leaderboard systems are in working order.
A few minor complaints:
- Being hit by enemies reduces your health bar, but running into certain obstacles results in an instant game over. I understand the developer wanted this to be punishing, but I would have preferred if it took away a fixed amount of HP instead.
- Scoring points and recovering HP both appear on-screen in the same shade of blue. It would have been nice if a different color was used to make it easier to distinguish between the two.
- Your character is always on the opposite side of the screen as your aiming reticule. Because of this, dodging obstacles often means you'll be unable to shoot certain targets. It might have been better if you could have controlled the character's position and the aiming reticule separately.
At the end of the day, I can't bring myself to give this game a negative review. If you choose to buy it just know what you're getting into and don't expect anything revolutionary. You get what you pay for, I suppose. Speaking of which, I'd recommend waiting for the game to go on sale or show up in a bundle if you're thinking about purchasing it.

Awesomenauts is a cheap, good value and very enjoyable game. Definitely made for cross platform, playing it in big screen with a controller or with a mouse and keyboard feels just as intuitive, while it is a MOBA (Multiplayer online battle arena) game, a single game session doesn't feel as lengthy as for example DOTA2. I have had both short and long game play sessions. The format of game play is 3 versus 3 of either 'bots' (AI controlled) and humans or all human players.
For any DOTA player's; there is no real jungling or item shop concept; however, ganking and stealthy play or killing an occasional stronger critter for a decent reward is possible on some maps. Players level up automatically by obtaining currency rather then experience and can use said experience to buy 'skills'.
Gameplay feels intuitive, quick to grasp and the game is quick off the bat with some action. It may not always feel perfectly balanced, but if you are playing without friends in random games you may be in a group of hero's that overlap in roles, thus underperforming against well balanced groups. I've never found it really troublesome, you can always switch your hero in the midst of a game if you i.e. need a more damage oriented hero instead of support.
With it's drop in and drop out game play you aren''t a permanent man down like in DOTA 2 when a player leaves, AI will replace a player until a new one joins. From my experience the game's online experience has been stable; however, online play sessions are hosted via another player so if your experiecing lag its a good bet it is on the host's end rather then the game's or the developer's end.
Mix some RPG , action, side scrolling platform elements with moba game play wrapped in a neatly looking 2D graphical engine and you get Awesomenauts, a humor packed arcade-MOBA game.
Try it yourself, definitely worth the 10'er and if you can pick it up on sale, even better.
Lastly I'd like to say it is very doable to play it on split screen at home with a friend if you have multiple controllers to hook up to your PC. Of course; lan and multiplayer works too!

The short of why I don't recommend this game is because it's a bad shmup/bullet hell.
The medium is I literally have the highest score out of anyone who's played it and I still haven't beaten the boss.
The long of it is the how bad the control scheme is, among other problems. The character you control is stuck in the middle of the screen and allowed to move up and down along around the bottom fifth of the screen. That's not the problem though, the problem is that to dodge, you have to move your aiming recticle. Your character will automatically switch the side of the pole so that he's aiming from the far side of the pole. Now that's already annoying enough, but this isn't a horrendous problem with the main part of the game because to hit enemies completely on one side while dodging their attacks makes sense, as enemies will only attack their side. The problem is when there's a boss, who sits on the top of the screen and can move horizontally. This means that depending on on what side you're shot at, you might not be able to hit the boss while dodging, giving free time for more attacks to come at you. It's also much easier to accidentally switch sides while aiming and can get you hit with easily dodgeable shots.
Other problems include: Hitbox is large enough to get hit by items that have already passed you, a single music track that gets tiring after a very short while, bomb item has about a second delay which makes it useless as a panic button, bosses prioritizing your item drops leading to occasions where you can't finish a boss fight, and difficulty is almost entirely increased by increasing enemy damage.
There are a few points that showed the potential of the game, like how the cat attacks is interesting compared to the rest of the enemies, the animations on enemies when you manage to block their attacks, how you actually had to manage your main projectile ammo in addition to your bombs and health, and a developer who actively responds to questions.

Hooligan Vasja is a challenging yet thoroughly enjoyable experience, considering the fact that it’s a decently priced casual game. It relies on both dexterity and pacience which means that quick reflexes alone, won’t help avoiding the constant obstacles within this 2D endless vertical runner. The mouse is the only input method in this game and while the control scheme is both responsive and quick to grasp, you will find yourself button mashing (or clicking in this case) way too often and as far as I’m concerned, this is a weak point. It’s true that especially in the later stages of every level, you have to pay more attention than usual, but the gameplay still puts a lot of stress on the mouse peripheral.  In short-period playthroughs, Hooligan Vasja is a fun distraction and the fact that not many titles on Steam follow its formula, also helps. The presence of a highscore system and a leaderboard, encourages players to some degree. Even if it’s a grinding trial & error experience at first, the game does reward perseverance eventually. Cards and Achievements sweeten an already good deal.
+ Simple yet entertaining gameplay.

This is an incredibly interesting game. It's very similar to Battle Brothers except there is magic and various classes aside from just badass merc character (both are also really good games). In Overfall, you create your own characters (start with 2) and you explore a world that is primarily water with scattered islands throughout (think Wind Waker). On each island you will run into quests, races, aggressive and nonaggressive beings that all seem to offer an interesting little story or quest for you to complete.  Combat is all turn-based in this game and operates similar to games like Heroes of Might and Magic or again, Battle Brothers. However, this game is noticeably different as each combatant has 3 phases to their turn. The movement phase (where they have two moves they can perform but must pick 1), utility phase (3 moves, pick 1) and combat phase (3 moves, pick 1). Skills vary from bleeding effects, AOE effects, skip phase effects or just healing/buff effect. Every fight requires intricate input from the player and even lower level enemies can kick your tail if you're not careful. Also, this game definitely has permadeath and a random map seed every time you play so it's definitely got elements of a Roguelike. Your goal is to make it further each time and try to beat your previous scores.
Aesthetically, this game is great. It's got a strong, adventurous soundtrack that blends seamlessly with the open sea areas but also keeps you invested in the combat. Graphically, the game has a nice artistic style... while nothing especially unique it is definitely a very beautifully designed game.
In summation, this game is looking good for an early access game. While it doesn't feel like it's done anything particularly new, a whole bunch of the quests that are featured in the game are very well woven... for example, the Deceiver's Questline. Really, really enjoyed that one and that alone makes me put this game a head above the other roguelikes I've played lately.

I played this game after playing Baldur's Gate 1 which i enjoyed.
In the first game, you're given a vast open world where you can go where you choose and do what you choose. There are guideposts to the main questline, but how and when you follow them is entirely up to you and your character.
In this game you're railroaded so hard into a single plotline that whatever character you thought you were playing may as well not exist.
This game gives you the option to load your data from a BG1 savegame, which i did. It promptly then deletes all your hard-won items. Then it tells you you did not in fact adventure with the group you thought you adventured with, but with some other people in stead. Then it tells you two of them are dead.
These might be acceptable, as the story can't be written for every possible set of choices in the first game. But as soon as you exist the first dungeon, placed in the centre of a normally-functioning city with exits on all sides, you can go... exactly one place. The others are inaccessible for no apparent reason. You go to this one place and immediately are railroaded into a conversation which you can't get out of and in which no choice you make (especially "i want nothing to do with you, go away") has any effect on the result. You're then teleported to a place you don't want to go with the game telling you that you went there yourself of your own volition, and again no choice you make has any result. You are forced to follow this questline in exactly one way, with no other options.
In the first game there's reason to progress the main questline for pretty much any character. In this game there's no reason to follow this plot with any but one of two characters: a pathetically desperate adventurer who wants to save their friend at all costs, or a foolishly ignorant sociopath who wants revenge and doesn't care about being used. Any other character will not make sense in this game.

Very disappointed with this one. Worse than the first in almost every way. Larian basically took a solid turn-based RPG and made it into a JRPG.
The combat system is broken thanks to the new armor system, which makes characters immune to effects until the armor is completely worn down. This makes battles less fun and less tactical, as the only thing you can do in the first few rounds is chip away at armor.
The AP system has changed as well, instead of the 10-20 APs in the first game now there's only 4-6. The final version also saw some adjustments to abilities and AP costs - while the early access offered some variety (e.g. magic touch attacks compensating for limited range with low AP cost), now almost everything costs 2 AP.  So it's three actions per round and that's basically it, no matter what those actions are. Stats no longer affect the availability of action points, so those super-agile characters will move just as fast the lowliest brutes.
It's nearly impossible to win a fight the first time you attempt it without cheesing it one way or another. But the devs admitted they left the exploits in specifically so players would use them. Yeah, no thanks. Keeping a conversation going while everything around is burning to hell and back is just plain stupid.
Characters and their presentation are so cliched, it's like a 5 year old came up with them. Save for the undead companion, there's no originality whatsoever, nothing you haven't seen before anywhere you look. Walk up to a possible companion to say hi and oh look, you're railroaded into having a knife to your throat in the friggin' dialogue because the character you're talking to is supposed to be badass or something and the only way you can get out is by the equivalent of peeing yourself while reciting bad poetry.
The first D:OS had a lot of cliches, sure, but it thrived on them because it acknowledged them as silly and they became light-hearted fun. This one tries to take itself too seriously and falls flat.
The story is boring. I stopped caring as soon as I left the Fort. Immersion is completely gone. It's what happens when you pair a completely over-the-top combat system with what's supposed to be a serious storyline (yet is so mind-numblingly shallow). They just don't work well together. I can't get invested into the world and the woes of the characters when the next minute I'm fighting boulder-slinging crocs.
Dialogue, while it uses the dialogue interface, is roughly 50% (or what feels like 50%) the narrator intervening with some useless description of what a character is doing, or looks like. The 5 year olds that wrote the script definitely never heard of 'Show, don't tell'.
GM mode had a lot of promise, but it's basically just a limited create-your-own-adventure mode. I was hoping for more control over the main campaign; having something to start from rather than building from scratch wouldn't have been as tedious. The very few assets provided are just that - very few.
Quests are plentiful, but very improperly paced. You'll basically have tens of quests cluttering up the journal before you have a chance to complete one of them. Some quests and encounters are timed, meaning that the NPCs involved either die or move on before you have a chance to interact with them, missing out on precious xp that you have no other way of getting. Because there's no options to grind some xp, even a little, you're forced to minmax and metagame as much as possible to the point where it becomes a chore.
Also on quests, it seems like the game is designed to be played with one character only. Get a quest from an NPC and you can usually progress it only with the same character that initially spoke to the NPC if the quest involves speaking with the same NPC at some point, as having another companion do the talking will get regular greetings as if it's the first time you met the NPC.
Inventory and item management is carried over from the first game and suffers from the same problems. It's tedious, clunky, slow, and frustrating, especially with no way to tell which items you'll need for quests later on and which you can safely lose. If anything, D:OS2 has more items laying about, which wouldn't be a bad thing at all if it didn't mean you have to spend hours just managing your inventory.
The trait system from the first game is gone, replaced by tags. Sure, you can gain a couple of said tags through regular gampley, but it's nowhere as dynamic and rewarding as in D:OS. Tags are now mostly just an extra dialogue option that rarely gives better results than the default ones.
On the upside, the game does look good, equipment is more varied than in its predecessor, the levels are fun to explore, with many secrets and hard-to-spot areas laying about. Combat is fun, only nowhere near as fun as it was in the first game, and there's actually less of it this time around. Having multiple races to play with is definitely interesting, though the elves' corpse eating ability is squandered on meaningless dialogue - while at first it seems like great attention to detail, you'll quickly tire of the endless vague descriptions of past lives of unnamed, irrelevant NPCs. Yeah, I'm so disappointed by this title that even when trying to think of positives I end up discussing the negative aspects of the same mechanic I was trying to praise.
Save your $$$, wait for a sale.

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion was my first introduction to the Elder Scrolls franchise back when it first came out on the Xbox 360. I had more time on this game across the 3 Xbox 360's than almost anything else, and there's a reason for that: this game is fantastic.
I'm a guy that is most at home with RPGs, be it on PC or console and this is truly what I would consider a solid RPG. While it's true the graphics and many of the features are outdated, clunky, and annoying at times, many of these problems have been solved by the Steam and Nexus communities, and even some mods with features you didn't even know you wanted. I bought this with The Elder Scrolls Anthology and didn't play it off of Steam, hence the miniscule playtime, but I assure you, I've played this extensively.
The graphics are old, but they look better on PC than they ever did on console, and with the game's low load on your computer, even mid-tier computers can play it on high settings, and even include mods for more beautiful scenery. While there's not as much "realism" and "grit" put into this game like Skyrim did, I feel that adds to it. Skyrim's aesthetic was simply to look realistic, which seems to take away from how utterly unrealistic the premises of Elder Scrolls games really are. Dwemer Ruins shouldn't look like something out of a hyper-realistic Steampunk gallery, they should look grandiose, colorful, and awe-inspiring for the work that went into them. There's no real aesthetic in Skyrim, but there is in Oblivion. A game has much more lasting power for me if there's a style to it, rather than realism, because realism fades quickly as graphics excel. Oblivion, despite having a very dark storyline and subject matter, was bright, colorful, and vibrant. The faces were much more realistic than most games that followed it for a few years, and even though there was never perfect anything with the graphics, the colors made up for it. Skyrim is so bland and has no real diversity in its fauna and flora. Oblivion's grasses were never the same across every region. The climate changed quickly and realistically when you fast traveled, but it was gradual when you walked through the lands, and you really felt like you were exploring. The map for Cyrodil felt so much larger than Skyrim because there were just so many things to do, places to explore, and quests to do. Sure, there weren't as many mini-quest dungeons and secrets, but I'll be damned if I didn't feel more rewarded when I did finished a Thieves' Guild Quest, or more powerful when I became Arch Mage. They gave you ranks and made you feel important, and the main questline was much more satisfying than Skyrim's. Destroying that last Oblivion Gate made me feel like a God damn champion of Tamriel. I'll admit I felt more important in Skyrim's quest, but it had such an anti-climactic ending, the whole thing just seemed silly. In Oblivion, people would refer to you as the Hero Of Kvatch or any various title you held in relation to them just in casual conversation, when you walked by, or when you interacted with them. It felt like you were recognized for your deeds and not just being some person with special powers. I could keep going about various other things, but for the sake of time, I'll leave it for you to compare and decide.
In short, if you're looking for a true RPG that's both fun and satisfying, and you're willing to sacrifce graphical quality (or if your rig can handle intensive HD graphics and texture mods) then this game is totally up your alley. I'd give the game a solid 8.5/10, so it's definitely worth your time and money. Personally, I'd advise you to go buy The Elder Scrolls Anthology either online or at a local video game store, because you get Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim Steam Codes & data discs, with all the DLC, along with the first 2 Elder Scrolls (Arena and Daggerfall), all for $80. It's totally worth the money in the end, because you can have literally thousands of hours of content to play for $20 more than a brand new game. Or you can pick this up on a Steam Sale, it's up to you. Anyway, have fun with this awesome game!

Is this a "good" game? Absolutely not. The intro video is bright green for myself and many others, the checkpoints are infrequent and dying can take you 10 minutes backwards.
And the camera angles! Imagine Resident Evil 2's stationery perspective, but instead of following you room to room, it stays in one room and your character basically spends 80% of the game off-camera. It is glitchy as hell, I've seen orcs flying around the room like someone taped jetpacks to mosquitoes; they fall through the floor, get stuck in things... The whole game is a mess.
But is the game "good"? Yes, yes it is. It's a lot of fun for a twin-stick shooter. It has a bit of variety in terms of weapons and character selection.
If it had spent another year in development with a competent team who didn't reuse the entire art library from the original DoW, and they implemented proper ideas with a proper checkpoint system and a proper camera, this game would be first class. It's like a TSS version of Space Marine, if Space Marine had only spent 2 months in development.
I would definitely recommend it as fun to play, as long as you can stand the glitchiness of it all. That being said, it's still not as glitchy as a certain French Assassin's Creed title released not too long ago, and that's saying something.

The third and last in the series (both by release date and chronologically), Call of Pripyat is by far the most polished vanilla game in the series. Unlike the prior two, in which a vanilla playthrough of the game was... bearable, while mods made them excellent, Call of Pripyats vanilla playthrough is perfectly fine, although mods still greatly improve the game. The story continues, and although starts a separate storyline (of sorts) it does tie in to Strelok's own storyline, and with that it indirectly ties in to that of Scar's.
Much like the previous two, mods can absolutely change your experience with this game, whether you're just downloading mods to help optimize the game or change it completely, Call of Pripyat has far more complete overhaul style mods than the last two, almost turning it into a different game. Misery, for example, is probably one of if not the most well known of then, which turns Call of Pripyat into a hardcore survival game that will truly test you. This, again, not  only allows for a user to tailor the gameplay to their preference (and its performance to their rig), but also adds a ton of replayability.
Much like the last two in the series it is excellent with tons of replayability and a great story to boot, worth every penny.

I've been following Overgrowth for years and decided to get it as it released. The game is sorely lacking content from the top down. For combat, there's only three kicks (though two of three are dynamically processed to punches or different kicks depending on body positioning) and about 6 weapons which all function as slaps at varying ranges, speed, and strength. Combat ends very quickly, and most of the time, the best option is to just jump kick spam. As far as level design, there's about three pretty good platforming levels built into the base game -- most of the levels feel incomplete artistically. You, as far as I can tell, can't play as any race other than rabbits, which really diminished the content value for me. The storytelling is shallow, and the actual engine for telling stories is limited to triggers into cutscenes, which is behind other high order game editors from a decade ago, like Spore and Warcraft 3.
As far as stability, it usually runs okay. But sudden AI decision making changes (ex.: I kick the guy in the front of the pack, causing the enemy to reorder their positioning while the new front leader wants to attack) causes the game to stutter and freeze for about 2 seconds. Sometimes hit registry also does this, or when I jump into a rope (no idea why there are even ropes, as you can't climb them). Granted, I am running on high graphics with a bottlenecked processor from 2011, but I very rarely stutter in other games.
This game is really geared for people who want to make their own levels or fiddle around with downloading mods. Don't get me wrong, it is a nice platform they've built here. It's just, there's nothing amazing currently running on that platform. If you have a lot of time to spend modding, or you prefer the work of people who are designing games parttime for free (modders) over actual developers, then this game is for you. To me, that's a recipe for low effort, low content material. The price tag as is is way too high for a 3 hour story+gameplay without an ending (literally), and a level editor. I kind of wish I had bought something else instead.

Hooligan Vasja is a slow paced tower climbing action arcade title from Trident Game Studio. The main problem is that the game appears mildly amusing in the trailer, but is actually incredibl boring, tedious, and repetitive, even for something clearly designed more for younger players in mind. The cartoonish artwork reminiscent of the days of The Magic Schoolbus is met with the most basic of stock music with a polka foundation, as well as a slew of typical effects like a brief cat meow before leaping to their death in order to hurt you as you ascend the side of the large apartment complex like Spider-Man.
Use your mouse to aim and fire "bullets" (i.e. rocks) at your enemies as you scale the building, avoiding random pivots in the pipes and other objects that can end your game. If things get tough you can press right mouse button to set off a fire work and kill a bunch of innocent people and animals. Eventually you will reach the levels boss that can range from a giant clown to a giant rat and a few things in between.
The biggest gripe to be had about this title is the lack of a level select. If you die, you go right back to the first level and have to replay the entire thing. This is where the tedious aspect comes into play, as by the third or fourth time through you're just sick of the stock music and nineties children's cartoon aesthetic that is as carboard and generic as everything else about the title.
But if upgrades were added to boost your attack the further along you go, or even the aforementioned ability to bypass playing the same level over and over and over again, there could be a little hope for this game being a quick pick-and-play title, especially for the achievement hunters out there. As you've probably figured out, this game is about driving a truck.  What you might not have figured out is that this game is great for teaching you how to drive.  That's why I bought it, I wanted to learn.  I'm happy to say it's been an excellent teacher and I've learned tons of tips and tricks that are sure to help me get my learner's permit next term.

The game starts you out in someone else's truck which is a very good thing.  By the time I figured out just how long the trailer is I had one or two little mishaps, and to be honest maybe more, that resulted in $6,000 in damages and traffic tickets and I never did get the trailer parked right so it was a good thing that it was someone else's truck.  Also, the game only has a W key (go faster) and an S key (go backwards), just like my mom's PRNDL shifter.  In the game, there's no brake key so you do a tapdance on the S key to slow down and it doesn't wear your brakes.
My dad has always been saying to take it easy on the brakes because they're expensive so I'm taking the lesson that all I need to do is rapidly shift the PRNDL on my mom's car between R and D to slow down and it'll save my dad a ton of money on brakes.  He'll be so pleased that I learned this valuable lesson early.

After the first assignment, you get to choose your next from a list.  I picked one that was a long drive so there'd be more driving, less parking.  I figured it would be easier that way.  I was wrong, but we all have to learn sometime, right?

One of my first lessons during my initial sojourn down the open road is that the road isn't all that open; there just isn't quite enough room between the lines for a truck pulling a trailer that's at least 100 yards long.  Seriously, how can
keep
the wheels in a single lane
the time?  The only conclusion I could come to was that it isn't possible, which means that the reason there's always two lanes on any road is because they're there for me to use them.  Honestly, it works much better taking two lanes at a time, and, this being my second good driving lesson from the game, lead directly to my third, which is that when you center the truck right over the dashed white line then the little cars that used to zip past and then cut in front of you don't do that anymore and the oncoming traffic stops to make it easier for me to get by safely.  It's a great system and I'm sure it will help me when I get out in the real world.

It was soon evening, and then dark, and instead of getting harder because I couldn't see as well, the driving was much easier because there was less traffic.  And there was my next lesson.  Did you know that from about 23:00 to 04:00 you can ignore stop signs and red lights?  Once you think about it, it's only obvious.  Since there's no traffic, there's no reason to waste all that time and gas on unnecessary stopping and what little traffic there is gives you lots of room.

Another lesson was come by with some difficulty.  Did you know you can't pull a longggg trailer through one of those little gas stations when you need gas?  You need a real truck stop.  There's a reason a truck stop has a long easy ramp in and another long easy ramp out.  Remember that, it'll help you when you need gas, both in the game and in real life.

Come dawn the traffic starts to pick up and even taking two lanes at a time doesn't always keep people out of my way.  That's when I discovered my favorite game-changing tip.  Flashers.  Turn on your flashers when you need to merge into traffic and sometimes they'll let you in.  Insist, by merging regardless of traffic, and either you take only insignificant damage or none at all, just so long as your flashers are on.  I started driving with my flashers on all the time and everything got easier with respect to other drivers.  I heartily recommend this tactic, everyone should always drive with their flashers always on and traffic accidents will soon be a thing of the past.  I just know my driver's education teacher next term will give me extra credit just for knowing and consistently using this advanced driving technique.

You'll be happy to know that I only had four major accidents by the time I got the 10,000 mile Steam achievement - the game was teaching me to drive like a pro.  It was soon after that when I accidentally discovered the joy of deliberately annihilating a long line of those plastic 55 gallon drums the highway department marks off construction zones with.  Honestly, it's such a blast it's worth the minor (or sometimes major) damage you get from using your truck to bounce those big orange babies high up in the air and scatter them all over the freeway.  What's also fun is when you catch up to some slow-moving car and you gently tap him from behind at about a 30 MPH difference in speed.  The car spins off into the dirt and you don't take any damage at all!  And then I found something really fun to do.  Did you know you can T-bone a police car right in an intersection and the car will do rolls in the air before it lands well off to the side of the road?  Of course, I'd never do that in real life.  I'm not stupid, after all.
Recommended.  Particularly to teenagers learning to drive.

This game is GOOD. And not just as an opinion. If you enjoyed LoL or dota 2 for it's gameplay you'll love awesomenauts because it follows the same premise. 2 teams of unique characters are pitched against each other, you must destroy each others base to win. Sadly they're turrets in the way that you must destroy. You also have AI teammates to assist you in taking these turrets down but mainly acting as a meatshield so the turrets don't completely destroy you. But what makes awesomenauts better than LoL and dota 2 is because it has a faster gameplay. Which is good in some sense because most of the time dota 2 matches can go on for a while. But don't let that make you think an awesomenaut game will be fast. They  usually take around 10 minutes. Aside from that the game is very solid and the art-style and characters are interesting and unique. The characters each have their own catchy theme that plays as you customize their skills before battle and while you're on a killstreak. And every character is different is their own way. Some more generic than others. But either way not two nauts will offer the same experience. The problem with this concept is that almost always when they add a new character they're broken and op in a few occasions. Lastly, from what I've seen so far: there's no voice chat, which often leads many rage quits and general frustration when I'm teamed with a bunch of brick walls that refuse to listen to my team chat messages. And also it penalizes you for losing by getting de-ranked from your league which puts you with higher skilled players and if you leave in-game you get de-ranked by a large portion. This worked in halo 3 because it didn't have drop in/drop out multiplayer but for awesomenauts it's unacceptable. But ignoring the few flaws with the game it's very fun and is especially worth it's price tag. Awesomenauts gets  7.5/10 for me, while it is still very fun and addicting it's flaws ruin the game and can make it a pain to play. But if you got friends to play with you consider the rating a 8.5 because it demolishes the 2 problems entirely.

The realm of Rivellon feels vibrant and alive. At times sunny and cheerful, with delightfully lighthearted moments, but also deeply disturbing and dark, unafraid of having players face things that can only be described as nightmare fuel. One minute you are talking to a happy bear about honey and the next you are running for your life from a giant spider that wants to feed you to its babies. The balance between those two, the light and the dark, is spot on. The storylines are wonderful and interesting, with tons of variety. Side quests don’t feel like filler content which is a big plus for a game as large and full of things to do as Divinity: Original Sin 2 is.
It's one of the best looking isometric RPG’s ever made. Each of the games four major areas are exquisitely detailed and beautiful in their own unique way. Characters have subtle animations and visual flourishes that really make them stand out. The colour pallet is vibrant, gorgeous and bright with striking blue, green, red and yellow colours. The game does makes sure to contrast that with deep blacks, subtle grays and dark reds when fighting in the darker, more evil infested areas. Everything is visually interesting.
The soundtrack is wonderful. Joyous and fun one moment, tense and foreboding the next. None of the music feels repetitive or overstays its welcome. The sinister transition music that rings out when you enter truly dangerous areas still makes a shiver run up my spine every time I hear it. The fact that every line of dialogue in the game is voice acted is impressive and almost always of impeccable quality. It really helps sells the games more emotional moments.
The turn based combat in Divinity: Original Sin 2 is all about interconnected systems. Fire ignites poison clouds or oil slicks. Rain puts out fire while ice can trip up enemies and allies alike. Necromancy can raise the dead or curse the living but can be countered by healing magic. Everything has a counterpoint of some type and a well coordinated exchange can take advantage of any number of systems to powerful effect. Unlike D&D games where your characters live or die by a lucky or unlucky roll of the dice, Divinity: Original Sin 2 does not make players worship at the alter of the RNG (random number generation) gods quite so much.
The longer you play the more complex the combat interactions. By the time you reach the mid to late game the list of abilities and spells at your disposal is vast. Even though each character chooses a class at the beginning of the game you can place points into whatever skill trees and abilities you want. The game encourages experimentation and since you can respec as much as you want once you leave the games first area there is nothing to stop you from making a character that is exactly what you want it to be.
The early game leans a bit too heavily on basic elemental exchanges like fire and ice, but eventually you’ll spend just as much time raising the dead, summoning demons, blinding your foes or charming people as you will tossing fireballs and ice shards. Because you have so many options when it comes to combat a lot of players have found ways to cheese the system. Some interactions were things the developers intended, but others are clearly breaking the game in ways they never considered. Patches post launch have addressed some of these issues, such as inflicting bleeding damage on an enemy and then transforming them into a chicken that runs itself to death. Or infinite damage loops that result from the interplay between buffs and attacks. That said the game encourages players to find innovative ways to tackle major obstacles. My personal favorite tactic it using teleport to push a tough enemy into the path of another powerful NPC and watch them tear each other to pieces.
Even with the ability to cheese the system at times and the plethora of options at your disposal, playing Divinity: Original Sin 2 on anything above Explorer difficulty can be really, really tough. Especially your first 10 hours with the game as you learn the intricacies of its many systems and options. The AI is smart and deadly and will throw every trick in the book at you. I restarted my campaign a half dozen times and invested almost 20 hours before I found a party composition and set of builds I felt complemented the way I wanted to play the game.
The game features a robust crafting system. Dozens of spells, potions, meals, enchantments and items can be crafted. You can learn recipes from books or experiment on your own to learn new ones. The one area where crafting falls short is weapons and armour.
Freedom and experimentation is at the very heart of what makes Divinity: Original Sin 2 so amazing. It applies not only to combat but how you tackle the games many quests and challenges. Almost everything has multiple avenues of approach and a myriad of solutions. The games main story quests give you a direction to aim yourself at but how you get there is completely up to you.
However this is also where Divinity: Original Sin 2‘s biggest problem rears its head. The game is terrible at informing you if you are on the right track in completing certain quest lines and is often vague, to the point of maddening frustration, when it comes to giving you any sort of hint when it comes to what you should do next. On the one hand it is nice that the game does not hold your hand as if you were a child who never played an RPG before, but on the other it would be nice to know why a quest that seems to be over isn’t. Sometimes you are not sure if you just missed something or if the quest line is just bugged because you approached it in a way the developers never expected or tested for.
This issue becomes more apparent the further along you get in the game. Act 1 is relatively aggravation free when it comes following quest lines or encountering bugs. But by the end of Act 2 you’ll likely pull your hair out over at least a few quests or nonsensical bugs. The game has been out a month now and I’m still locked out of a handful of quest the developers have acknowledged are broken because of the way I triggered them. I was able to get past the major bugs that were in my way but a bunch still remain. The very thing that makes Divinity: Original Sin 2 so amazing is the same thing that has caused issues with progressing further down quest lines or receiving rewards.
It’s by no means a game breaker and given the immense size of Divinity: Original Sin 2 and the sheer scope of what you can choose to do its amazing the game does not have more issues. The quest log definitely needs an overhaul and there are several major bugs that still need addressing but Larian Studios has already dropped a few hotfixes and one very large patch to address players concerns. Given the wonderful support Divinity: Original Sin 1 received I have no doubt that Divinity: Original Sin 2‘s remaining blemishes will be ironed out before too long.

Describtion:
A RNG (random number generator) game, where dice rolls and card builds may be the difference between win or loose. This game is basically like a animated ludo game where you have four different characters with different stats and abilities representing each base or home.
There's a campaign featured  for each standard character in this game as well that has various funny moments due to it's close bonding and dialouge to the different characters. (Not DLC chatacters)

Pros:

+ Events (Holidays and exp + stars drop rate )

* The game is a RNG based game, which means it rely on chance more then most other elements of the game, this may be frustrating to some people.

Summarize:
This game is a great way to spend time with your pals if you'd ever find yourself with nothing to do, It is not really that time consuming and overall it is a great game that you will (admit it or not) find moments of tremendous joy when you just keep rolling those 6's or fall in despair when you only roll 1's.

This game is already showing alot of promise. It's still in early access but there is more than enough content and polish to warrant a purchase at this stage. It's a rogue-like (in its use of permadeath and procedural world generation) with deep tactical combat, nice artwork and tons of replayabilty. But what really sets Overfall apart from the rest is the way it uses story. There is an overarching story that has a sort of timer (invading forces gather strength each day and it's up to you to unite the various races against the looming threat); but there are also self contained narratives delivered via the many small islands of the world. Overfall includes a robust story creator that will teach the player how to put together events or quests that often involve branching choices (it's a really cool feature that allows for alot of creativity, however, story creation is completely optional and the vanilla game would still be great even if this feature wasn't present). The strength of Overfall is that every facet of the game feels well thought out and not watered-down (every part of the game is good enough to stand on its own). Worth mentioning: there are a small amount of bugs still in the game (I haven't encountered any game breaking bugs though) and some of the sound effects are still missing. Also, there is the art style which might turn some people off but I think it looks great. *The price is really good right now and I'm pretty sure it will be cost a few bucks more for the final release. I don't think it'll stay in early access for more than a few months so if you're interested I suggest you buy it while it's still a bit cheaper.

You materialise in front of a shining dagger, the blade hovers in the centre of a platform in an unknown darkness. Accepting the dagger is accepting battle against the devils, demons, and horrors waiting therein. There is little time before more spawn. They keep getting bigger, faster, and stronger. Their growing numbers are a sign of your success, and as they increase, so do your abilities to a degree. Is there an end to this feverish fight? Or is this really hell?
Devil Daggers has an impressive dark/gothic/hellish aesthetic reminiscent of the original Quake and/or Hexen II, laid over top of a rapid and punishing singleplayer arcade/arena "rage" shooter with a one-hit death, and no save features, other than a leaderboard which keeps track of the amount of time you survived, shooting accuracy, and red power-up diamonds collected.
Absolutely fantastic experience which has the player learn the game and necessary skills and techniques by way of trial and error. Also really nice sound design and soundtrack. I love the industrial menu screen track!

I am a fan of Games Workshop, but this was my first venture into their digital realm.  Having played through every mission at least twice now I am very happy with this purchase and what I am seeing in the level of detail and authentic feeling from this studio.  The game runs very smooth and is a joy to play with a dual stick controller.  I did have several glitches with textures, animations, or the camera while playing (tyranids react poorly to the melta gun on the kill cam for some reason), but only once did it feel "broken" with a stuck camera.  On second playthrough at the same point, the game worked fine.  While the unlock system did not make such sense as to why I suddenly got a new weapon or perk, aside from mowing down greenskins, it gave a nice sense of progression and gave reasons for replay as different classes.  The game is SHORT, but I liked that.  It really made it feel like I was a Space Marine on a tactical mission.   If they didn't finish the mission in 5hrs, where is the sense of urgency?  The game plays and sometimes feels like a budget arcade shooter, but the nice polish put on it made me appreciate the work put in.  As an example, shell casings eject from your weapon and bounce across the floor with real physics, and at one particular heavy point in the game I completely covered the entire area in spent rounds.  The physics and detailed character models made this truly feel like something you would expect from Games Workshop.  I would definitely buy a second installment or expansion with more missions.  Time to dust off that copy of Space Marine I have sitting around.

The combat is spectacular. Never, in any game I have played so far, have I seen such a well-thought-out and complete combat system that allows everyone their own style and flair. It might be one of the coolest combat systems in existence. It's grand, and playing with others makes it so much more fun, to chain combos with others. It's not a FPS, its third-person and allows for so much more freedom. And you get to see spells being cast and moves being made, which makes so much cooler.
The monsters are ridiculously easy, but that is overshadowed by the fact that there isn't much grinding in this game. Except for the time I had to wait 10 levels hoping and praying that I would get a wand in a random drop.
This game isn't asking for your money unless you want really fancy mounts or cosmetics or costumes; it provides everything you need for free without grinding, and you get everything you need as you progress through the game.
I will say that there may be too little clothes for comfort. But the character design and story is mindblowing. Serious props to the devs for taking 9 different classes and creating an overarching storyline that differs in litte ways for each class.
And its also not TOO easy -- while leveling up is relatively fast, you need to spend your Skill Points wisely to get new skills and manage your old ones. And the class trees that allow specialization are great, and make the game take on so much more variety. Its great that any two people who start off with the same class will end the game with totally different specializations and playstyles.
Overall, the pro's of this amazing game overshadow any possible cons. Great storyline, amazing combat, smart decision-making, and great design.

Also, I recommend finishing Shadow of Chernobyl before you finish this game, or you will be pretty confused by a certain event that happens near the very end of the game.
Survival Horror at its finest. It controls like any other first person game out there. I had to move some keys around, and I never used the lean keys, but I still appreciate that they've been put in.
Wear some GOOD headphones and crank the volume to 11. It will make you poo your pants with terrified glee, especially if you're a horror buff.
3/5. Playing it through a second time is a bit unnecessary. When you reach the ending, you can choose if you want to continue the free-roam or not. However, it is fun to side with different factions in subsequent playthroughs.
3.5/5. The game is moderately scary. Sure, you'll punch a hole in your roof with frightened♥♥♥♥♥♥when you get jumped by your first few Bloodsuckers or Snorks, but it'll wear off eventually. The enviroment is excellent, though. You'll never know when something will attack you. It's perfectly tense and almost on par with games like Silent Hill 2 and the Resident Evil Remake.
If you're a fan of Survival Horror, Post-Apocalypse, or just atmospheric games in general, I cannot recommend this enough.

LOCAL COOP ON PC!
This is a competent twin-stick shooter set in the Warhammer 40,000 universe, you play as one of four space marine classes as you fight your way through hordes of Orks and Tyranids while unlocking a small amount of gear and upgrades.
You can be a tech marine who has a deployable tarantula turret, a librarian who has a power sword and psychic powers, an assault marine with a jetpack, or a devastator with a heavy weapon. You can also pick from six chapters, Ultramarines, Blood Angels, Blood Ravens, White Scars, Imperial Fists and Salamanders, unfortunately no Black Templars though.
Customization is minimal but fun, as you play you'll unlock three new weapons for each class and modifiers for stats like health, damage, special ability duration, etc.
The graphics are fairly nice and the player models are accurate and finely detailed, with proper chapter heraldry and decorations, which makes the character select menu look awesome.
You'll probably get about 4-6 hours out of the main campaign and there is a score attack horde mode that has a lot of replay value.
My minor complaints are that I think the game could use more chapters (they're just skins), and I would have really liked a terminator as a playable class.
My biggest complaints are that the game has some annoying difficulty spikes, and we encountered a few bugs that required us to reload checkpoints.
The biggest selling point of this game is true local coop on PC, you can connect two controllers and it will let you do couch coop, we hooked my PC up to a 50" TV and played with two 360 controllers in Big Picture, there are so few games on PC that let you do this even though the feature is often present in their console counterparts, and it's a ton of fun.
The game's price is very appropriate, and I got it on sale so I can't fault the game for it's length, if you're looking for a local coop game to play with a friend you'll probably like this.

Friends have described to me how a Kill Team game works in tabletop Warhammer, and I was excited to see this game on sale.  Unfortunately, it is grievously misnamed and has nothing to do with the game mode Kill Team... which is too bad. I was looking forward to tactical, team-based action with very limited manpower and a sharp attention to attrition and strategy.
Instead, I got a very generic 3rd person gauntlet-style shooter.  It's not horrible, but even at the few dollars I spent, I don't feel I got my money's worth.  I can't understand charging $10 for what feels like a mod.  While playing I went from waypoint to waypoint in a completely linear path, shooting orcs on the way.  And that's it.  I got so tired of fighting orks -- there's no strategy to it, and every wave feels the same.  It just went on and on... and nothing really became interesting over time.  Other games have done a much better job at this style of 3rd-person game, including a game I got for free with my graphics card years ago and enjoyed playing all the way through (Space Siege).  This game doesn't bring much to the genre, and feels very samey and tired very quickly.
I'm told this game is Coop, but it doesn't scale the difficulty to meet the extra player.  This is a mistake since the single-player game is overly easy and time consuming already.  I did the first few missions, and finally quit out of boredom.  And disappointment.
Protip: If you're going to sell a glorified game mod (and really, this feels like a mod, not a full release), don't misname it after a far superior (and popular) rules set that doesn't have anything to do with your game!

Talking from 80 patch through 90 patch, some things have changed and somethings have stayed. Sadly though, this game is less about the 89 levels you will achieve now and more about that level 90 since nothing matters untill that point. The game has been like this a little bit but never so hard untill 90 patch.  So for now, I'm going to give a pro and con list on what I think is good about this game and what is not.  I'll also be talking about common problems people say they have with this game and why its true and not true.
Pro:
Good combat, by far it is one of the most fluent and cool looking combat I have ever seen.
Most of the skills you obtain from your class are cool looking.
Leveling up is not so bad.
There are so many nice people that will help you, dont get me wrong there are jerks in this game but people see these people more often because they join parties instantly without any idea of what to do about mechs and what gear to have to do the nest so they get kicked. IF you do not want to be kicked, just create the party and say "Carry pls" or "Practice" since if you join a 90 nest party and people see you do not have the proper gear to contribute, they will kick since they dont want to risks.
The guilds, I feel like people who make guilds in this game are really good at it, the really high level guilds somehow manage to keep the right ranks of each person, make sure everyone gets the help they need, and also make everyone happy and have a fun time with each other.  Smaller guilds are the same thing but more often there are worse guilds; dont get me wrong there are many good small guilds just that some of them are small because they are bad.
Nests and raid 80-90 patch.  I was never really fond of the "Do this little mini-game to get pass this area" type of thing.  The Dragon Nest dev's are deffinitely not good at those things but each boss they make have really good mechanics and fun play against.
The possibility of being able to solo.  Now this topic is really hard to discuss since most of you are probably already saying "If you never get hit in a nest you can solo anything." Or "If you have the proper gear it doesnt matter being able to solo level 90 regular nest, you just do too much damage." what I come in turn of being able to solo is that no matter what gear you have as long as you have level 90 gear that is enhanced even by a little, you are being able to solo a dungeon while being able to take a few hits.  Humans make mistakes, they will get hit, not everyone can do a no hit run.  Just the proper weapon/armor (not even gems/crests) and you can solo the level 90 nests right now but will take a long time.
Now onto the cons, no game is perfect just keep that in mind; I do not want people saying that this game is better than this game for this reason, its just a big mess of crap.  Just see what you like about mmo's and what you hate about them, if any of them are in the list make a chart with those pro and cons, if pro or con outweighs, you choose from there.
Cons:
Jelly's, by how much I will say this game is deffinitely not pay to win, this one part is most likely the most pay to win part.  Jelly's make it so any gear that you want to enhanced that is 6+ wont break, problem with this? You can only pay to gain these or events. No other way.  People also sell these in mp for around 550g-600g for 50 of them, btw it cost 11 to upgrade just epic gear per try.
Lag: Somethings this game lags quite a bit depending on the map; the new nightmare dungeon for me lags more than the main raid with everyone throwing out their abilities with 8 people in raid party vs soloing the nightmare dungeon. I think this is due to the fact with just so many air particles in that dungeon.  What I would like is that if Nexon would turn off air particles so that it makes computer lag less UNLESS if its to fit a important raid like the Desert Dragon.
Obtaining gear: Sometimes obtaining gear is easy, other times it is deffinitely not.  Gear, accessories, dragon gems, and crests can be expensive for newer players.  Some of the best gear (like Nightmare weapons) are also impossible to buy so you have to earn them.  I personally dont see that as a problem but for some of you out there it is.
Mechanics: I know, I said the mechanics on bosses in this game are really good; problem is at first its annoying.  There are party wipe mechanics that are annoying and sometimes hard to time if you did not practice it about 5-6 times. Kind of annoying but not a big problem.
No more practice nests/raids: There used to be a option called "Practice" on nests/raids, this makes it so that you dont lose any durability and or clears while doing that certain dungeon.  It was made to practice it obiovously.  I have no idea why they took this out and I think they should have just implemented this on 90 dungeons.
Levels 1-89 dont matter: Any gear you obtain from level 1-89 wont matter once you reach level 90; no matter how enhanced they are.  It does not matter if their 10+ or even 11+ enhancement they will be useless even if they were level 87. Why? The new dragon gems are super valuable and its out leveled by level 90 gear. Which the gems can be equiped with level 90 epics (blue).
Removed nests/raids/difficulties: I remember when level 16 nest had the abyss difficulty on it, was removed far back since people would spam those dungeons; waste no pwr; and gain hundreds of gold by the gold rabbit with little to no effort.  Now, level 60-70 dungeons dont have abyss difficulty and I find that stupid since its so much harder to level up even though this game its not hard to level up in.  Also the removal of more than HALF of hte nests and raids really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.  They should have just kept the raids/nests if they are reworking them, or even better make new level 90 nests but I guess 1 new level 90 nest is enough like 1 level 80 nest.
Discussion: Now many people I have seen on this review area say this game is PAY TO WIN.  What makes a game pay to win is when you will not reach end game if you do not pay for certain items, when you cant achieve gold without paying, or when you cant even do anything due to the fact of other reasons.  This game is not pay to win because achieving gold is not difficult in this game if your not lazy; do not blame the game if you are lazy that is just you.  Selling nx things like jelly beans is a fast way to obtain gold but reallity, its not worth it unless your a millionair.  Most rich people in dragon nest dont even spend a dime on the game unless they want a costume for one of hteir characters, not to make gold.
Overall: It is a great game for those who want to be in end game content and are willing to spend a lot of time to get there. If you are not dedicated to do so and or are lazy just look away from this game because you will give up when you reach level 90 and get kicked for not thinking or watching video's at least of the mechanics.
If dedicated, 9/10, a game worth your dedication and hard work but will have a few issue's for you but will be worth it.; if you are lazy and not dedicated, 7/10, a game with a couple of flaws and should be played time to time, not worth playing a lot.

The story of Overgrowth was very compelling and a lot of fun! From the platforming segments the the myriad different terrains to fight in, to the advanced weapon combat and new races to fight, I played through it twice the day I got it, once alone, once with my family watching. Of course it's not very long, but I loved it, and even the difficult parts I found myself doing far better at the second time around.
Unfortunately, the main story and the redone Lugaru story is where my enjoyment ended. I've not gone out and seen what other mods have to be offered other than what got me the game, but I feel that some of these should have been simple enough to add without waiting for someone else to make it. The arena, for example, is fun enough for maybe fifteen minutes or so, and the fact that the different arenas seem to work differently is mildly amusing... but why do we never get armor outside of the Lugaru campaign? And why are we allways fighting bunnies instead of Wolves, Dogs, Rats, Cats?
What the Game could REALLY use is a "challenges" Mode like the original Lugaru. Give us an area with those beautifully made terrains, perhaps a weapon or armor, depending on the level, and a group of baddies to fight, so we can sneak, or charge headlong or whatever. I spent HOURS on Lugaru doing those twenty-odd challanges, and it was glorious. I was hoping the "Sandbox" levels might have something like that, but having 1-3 bunnies spread out with no weapons and armor is frankly just insulting.
The combat is definately a little different from Lugaru, it feels like what they took away from it, (reverse somersault away, the bunny run, death from above and weapon sneak attacks) They added in the weapon combat, making using the different weapons far more viable, which I really appreciate. Overall, I enjoyed the game, but if we can just get some of those proper challenges rolling, then that will massively help out it's replayability, and I could spend a lot more time actually playing the game.

I bought the game I think two or three years ago, it was back when the one-on-one fighting thing was introduced. Since then, I've stood behind Wolfire Games and have been anxiously awaiting every update. Now that it is out of beta and we're seeing what kind of game Overgrowth looks like it will become, I can safely say, I'm still just as excited as I was when I first heard of it.
No, it isn't finished by any means, and it's funny because people seem to be reviewing this version as though it is. Though, after nine whole years of development, I feel like they were right to release something for everyone who waited. I can't speak for those who were around in the beginning, but for someone whose seen what the game was, and how it's gone from a simple sandbox combat experience, to this, is nothing if not satisfying.
First of all, the graphics are very impressive. I used to have crazy optimization issues, now I get a cool 60 frames all the time, and I don't even have that great of a PC currently. It's certainly very pretty to look at.
The combat is fun and easy to grasp even when you leave and come back to the game months later (which I have been doing a lot of).  The fighting is as fun as it has always been, with satisfying sound effects and, of course, that blood system. I'm glad they added in difficulty levels, as I was never great at fighting the ai the way it was. Casual is a cakewalk, and the hardest difficulty is way past brutal, I usually stick to the middle one, offers a good challenge and keeps the fights interesting.
The new story...can't say I'm a big fan of it. It's mostly your generic hero comes to new land, kills all the bad guys, frees the innocent, walks away into the sunset in the end kind of story. The main character has more of a personality rather than just being angry and fighty (which he is). He's cocky and cool, not afraid of any fights, just like the player should be. He's honestly the best part of the story for me, other than the range of locations we get. It's a very good example of how big and story driven the final product could be, especially since they have nothing but time to get the story completely right. I don't even think they have to cut anything out for the final version, the game can start where it starts and continue going where it ends, they can just add a bit more in between to give the playtime some more beef.
Maybe the characters could interact a little more like people would. Don't get me wrong, there's certainly a lot of cutscenes where two or more characters talk and you get a feel for who they are and how they feel, I just think we need more of 'who people are' than we do 'what people are doing'. Again, the main character is pretty alright, not much need for changes there.
The story could just use a little more variety to it, it's mostly run around, fight some guys, climb something, fight more guys. For someone like me, who plays this game off and on a lot, that's perfect, but for someone who wants to sit down and get a longer, more interesting experience, it leave much to be desired.
Honestly, I'd say this has definitely been worth my $30. I know it's taken them a long time to get to this point, and all I see is people complaining about how slow they are, and yeah, that's not completely unfair to say. But really, where did everyone's patience go? This is an in-development game after all, I mean, last I checked on their website, Wolfire Games has like 5 people developing this game? So yeah, I don't think anyone should be surprised that the game takes a little longer to get finished than they hoped. if they get some more help and really crack down on making this thing the way it should be made, the way that gets it made as good as it can be, and not the way that gets everything done "now, now, NOW. I WANT IT NOW!" we could be in for the potential I saw when I first signed onto this project. Because really, that's what all the players are at this point, we're all in this fight, ready to see it through to the end.
I'm thoroughly excited to see where Overgrowth goes from here. In its current state, 8/10.

This game is moderately fun as of today, but it does need more content and some mechanical adjustments in order to truly shine.
The combat is oversimplified for how punishing it can be -- one undodged sword swing will end a fight with anything short of a wolf, and wolves can only be beaten in a practical manner by what I consider to be the game's biggest flaw; the drop-kick.
It's not that I don't get the idea conceptually -- rabbits can jump high, they have strong legs, getting drop-kicked by an anthropomorphic rabbit could probably break a neck -- but in gameplay, it feels like you have to purposefully gimp yourself to enjoy the fighting game mechanics since you could very easily lure any enemy into that attack. It's one element of many in the system that makes the difficulty curve a spiky mess, one that is unintuitive at first and upsettingly dull afterwards. Or maybe I'm missing out on something? Some element outside of the usual zoning, right-click dodging and grabs, or the occasional knife throw?
By the way, the game does have some extremely sensitive stealth mechanics, so if that's something you enjoy then you might like some parts of this. There's levels where you sneak along the topography, hiding around buildings or behind dunes or hills, getting ready to rush feverishly towards unsuspecting guards to snag them when their backs are turned. It's pretty cool sometimes.
The only other major issue is that the game has some gorgeous graphics and landscapes, but only a few hours worth of gameplay content in its current package with which to enjoy them. This is supposed to be remedied by the fact that the game has an exhaustive level editor and open-sourced mod support, but that's putting a LOT of weight on to the generosity of strangers. You need a really big and committed community for something like that to work. The developer has spent a long time putting out development videos, seven years at last count, to try and bring such a community together, but I can't help but feel like this game needs more push to get other people interested and working on it. I want to suggest this game to everyone, but I simply CAN NOT suggest this game to people not interested in joining the game's community to help it out, and I furthermore feel that the developer's choice to limit the community forums to those who've bought the game to be a mistake. How can you get people into your community if you won't show that community to people?
Let me be clear -- I think this game could be great, and I want everyone to tell everyone else about it. I just also think that its climbing on a dangerous precipice right now, and that without some strong pushing and pulling, it'll probably just fall by the wayside.

I've played this game for many many hours on my phone before it came to steam.
all in all its fun for a while...  until you hit the enevitable pay wall known as Secret Fight Club (SFC).
The PVP aspect of this game doesnt determine if you have skill, it only calculates your power rating and pits you against 3 players you can beat easily, then places you against a player that has dumped a lot of coin on this game (known as Whales) that you simply cannot compete with.
to reiterate once you make it to SFC and plateau at a rating your win loss cycle will go exactly like this:
win, win, win, loss, loss, win, loss, loss, loss, win.
which after you complete the cycle will place your rating at slightly lower than where you started.
rinse and repeat.
this is exactly what will happen.
When i started playing the game, it seemed to have a very linear, and less pay to win outlook. Card combos were quite finite and gave the impression that in the long run you could obtain all the cards necessary for a very padded deck, just from playing.
But fast foward to about the time that this game made it on to steam, the devs did something to change the dynamic and meta of the game.
They started churning out NEW Legendary and Epics every month, which you need 4 of to max out combos.
And they seem to add 12 to 20 new cards Every month now.
Oh yeah, they also added Pre-Combo'ed Power Cards, which have even higher stats, and are for the most part useless if you only have one of each, you need a dual combo to make them even somewhat relevant.
Sure at low levels these cards are a great boost on their own, but once you make it into SFC, single Legendaries and Power Cards just wont cut it. Quad Fused Epics too are mostly useless once you hit SFC... but unless you dump cash for Legendaries your deck will be mostly comprised of Quad Fused Epics, which work ok until you come across a Whale that has Quad fused Legendary everything.
Add to that the Mythic level cards, which have the highest level stats, which you can buy for literally $200 each (cheap right?), or grind out challenge coins for having a less than .0001% for each super epic pack to produce one. (Seriously knives in CSGO drop more frequently).

That glimmer of having a decently padded deck in due time has now faded, and this game has clearly shown its true nature:
Buy cards and win, or sit and stagnate for months with little to no progression of deck development.
But with the addition of new cards Every month, there is increasing smaller chance to have maxed out legendaries, because the pool of cards is continuing to increase in size. which is really a problem because you simply cannot progress or compete in SFC without having legendaries combo'd to the max.
Unless of course you want to drop $100 each time they whip out a new card pack (2x a month) and even then, there is no guarantee you will get enough good cards to make max combos.
There are literally guys that have spent thousands of dollars building their deck, and those are the whales sitting at the very top of the leaderboards, and you will not even get close to approaching that level unless you too dump thousands of dollars. this is very real, and not an exageration.
The steam version also trims out the "Ad Bonus" that is available to phone users, this adds a multiplier to your winnings in Adventure and Arena modes, which without this multiplier makes the rewards useless.  non-existant on steam Unless you pay $10 per WEEK for just the multiplier bonus.
To further insult to injury, on the mobile version, on occasion you will receive an "Ad Bonus Crate" (completely absent from the Steam version) which is just an on-demand advert, but you get decent *cough* rewards for watching it.
The rewards have 4 tiers, the lowest gives you 500 coins and 5 more adventure energy, the next level 1000 coins and 5 adventure and arena energy, 1500 coins and 10 adventure and 10 arena energy. and the highest 2000 coins, 10 energy to aventure and arena, but also will drop a random card, from rare to legendary.
The added bonus energy points are necessary to compete in any of the weekly competitions in arena, or you get stuck with just minimal points/rewards.
These features are also pay to win, as you are paying your time for their ad revenue profit. the trade off is more adventure and arena time. which translates to more cards and possible competition winnings.
I have regretably dropped around $60 over time on this game, and that has only left me with a mediocre deck with only 8 dual fused legendaries (you need four for max combo) single legendaries are pretty much useless. granted i can do ok at my rank in SFC (stuck at around 1000) but there is no progression, and I actually believe that over time if the current modus operandi of churning out new cards every month continues then you will actually lose rank in SFC unless you start dumping cash on this greed machine.

If you're a fan of games like Fallout, Wasteland 2, DayZ, or Metro, you'll likely love this game.
I recommend going balls-to-the-wall on your first playthrough. Download the Call of Pripyat Complete mod, turn the gamma down a notch or two, and go for the hardest difficulty. I was recommended this on /k/, and I was not disappointed in the slightest. If you want your first time to be completely joyous torture, grab the Misery mod.
Also, if given the option of buying either the Steam or GOG versions of this, go with Steam. It loads much faster (A difference of at least 5 minutes per loading screen. Sometimes even 10-15.) and it plays much smoother. You don't want to be like me, logging 80 hours into Call of Pripyat, over 30% of which was loading time. Thankfully, you can easily transfer your save files from the GOG version to the Steam version.
This was also my first S.T.A.L.K.E.R. game. Sure, I had to look up who
was, but other than that, it was a perfect introduction to the series.
It's a very simple story, but it works well. You're a government agent looking into five helicopter crashes in the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone. If you really power through the story, you can get it done in only a few hours. Also, I recommend finishing Shadow of Chernobyl before you finish this game, or you will be pretty confused by a certain event that happens near the very end of the game.
Survival Horror at its finest. It controls like any other first person game out there. I had to move some keys around, and I never used the lean keys, but I still appreciate that they've been put in.
Wear some GOOD headphones and crank the volume to 11. It will make you poo your pants with terrified glee, especially if you're a horror buff.
3/5. Playing it through a second time is a bit unnecessary. When you reach the ending, you can choose if you want to continue the free-roam or not. However, it is fun to side with different factions in subsequent playthroughs.
3.5/5. The game is moderately scary. Sure, you'll punch a hole in your roof with frightened♥♥♥♥♥♥when you get jumped by your first few Bloodsuckers or Snorks, but it'll wear off eventually. The enviroment is excellent, though. You'll never know when something will attack you. It's perfectly tense and almost on par with games like Silent Hill 2 and the Resident Evil Remake.
If you're a fan of Survival Horror, Post-Apocalypse, or just atmospheric games in general, I cannot recommend this enough.

My first playthrough of Overfall didn't go all that well (as you can see here;

Overfall has a classic RPG feel to it with great elements of fantasy and adventure. You are very much free to choose your own destination and go off on your own adventure.
