Nomad Games pushes out a great addition to the Warhammer 40,000 sage with this rendition of a typical Space Marine mission. Warhammer 40,000: Kill Team is a top down shooter that offers 4-player co-op adventure that’s entertaining to the end.
Your mission begins as you encounter an orc ship on route to invade a sector of the imperium. You are sent on a mission of the upmost importance to disable the invasion ship and figure out the orc plans. As your mission progresses you realize this is an impossible mission and completion requires the top fighters. Luckily you’re a member of the Blood Angles one of the elite fighting forces of the Emperors Space Marines chapters.  It is up to you and your team to defeat the Warboss and protect the galaxy.
The campaign consists of five-levels, which vary in length based on your play style. Each level took me around 30-minutes, with the campaign lasting about 3-4 hours depending on how many times you die. One of the pit falls is that when you die you typically either get warped back a considerable distance or you have to watch a cinematic again. I didn’t find myself dying too much, so it wasn’t too bad but it could get annoying if you happened to die quite a few times. Overall the campaign is typically a run with a varying missions in-between; either surviving waves of enemies in a confined space, running on exploding platforms, planting explosives, fighting epic boss battles, and more.
Overall there are a good variety of enemies which keep the game interesting and offering a nice variety. There are four separate classes two melee and two ranged specialists. The classes form a bell curve of extreme range power to extreme melee power. The weapons and ability power-ups are unlocked randomly throughout the campaign and to achieve the best benefits typically involves switching characters between each map. Each class has a special ability that offers even more diversity between each class. The campaign is a top down shooter where hordes of enemies charge at you and you must fight them off either by slashing them apart, blasting them to shreds, or exploding with bombs.
All and all Warhammer 40,000: Kill Team is a great game. Some of the gameplay elements could use adjusting, but it’s nothing that ruins the game. I personally played the game alone and I had a great time and could only imagine it being better with some friends. The gameplay is relatively straightforward and the difficulty curve is well laid out offering a fun campaign at a good length. I would highly recommend this game if you can get it for a good price (I got it for $1.99 and felt that was just the right price).
Pros:
+Four classes with relatively high diversity making them interesting.
+Buffs and weapons unlocked randomly which cause you to switch classes to take advantage of them.
+Five levels with varying missions, strategies, and battles which offer great dynamics.
+Four player co-operative experience (if you have the friends).
+In mission weapon/buff switch to mix things up if you need to.
Cons:
-Relatively expensive for such a short game, $9.99 is rather high for a 3-hour campaign.
-The checkpoints are few and far between and when you die they cause you to watch cinematics without being able to skip them.
-The camera angles can be a pain every now and then causing you to not see what you’re looking for.
-The melee classes were not designed to solo some of the missions very well.

WH40KKT, or just "KT", is a twin-stick shooter that has you play a Space Marine against the invading Orks. One stick moves, the other stick shoots. There's also some special weapons, and occasional "special moves". Given multiple types of Space Marines (Vanguard, Rearguard, TechMarine, and Librarian) they are armed very differently and they fight very differently. Vanguard is a melee specialist, while rearguard is a shooter. TechMarine is balanced, while librarian is a lot like a wizard with spells.
Ammo's unlimited, and there are weapons "upgrades" that can be unlocked through repeated play. You can also equip up to two perks (a lot like the Halo Spartan twin-stick game) The problem usually is the enemies are just too numerous, even given your powerful weapons, so the game is really meant for co-op. There are many random powerups such as heal, rapid fire, double / triple / quad fire, righteous fury (double melee damage), power shield, and a few others.
The main problem with this game is with its various shifting viewpoints. Generally with a twin-stick shooter the view stays static. However, this game will rotate the camera very often. This is VERY annoying, as the game shifts almost at random from isometric, to sort-of sidescroller, to sort of 2D shooter, to sort of top-down, to behind the shoulder... and more. There's even one where you were looking at the enemy behind you where you need to run forward (i.e. pulling the stick toward yourself).
The difficulty is... high. There are only like 6-7 missions total, but each can be played through by 4 different space marines which would have very different styles. And high scores are recorded separately. I think I died at least once per mission, and while there are many checkpoints, there doesn't seem to be enough in the later missions (or I just suck at these in general). In the end I had to engage Cheat Engine for a little help, but yes, I did finish.
There are 10 collectible "wings" on each mission and collecting all ten gets you a certain bonus achievement. Unfortunately some of those are next to impossible, as they are often in the oddest parts of the level or a part of special sequence that you can't divert from.
For example, one mission had you engaging a small "minelayer". When you shot out one engine, the craft drifting spun around, then crashed toward you. You ran (and if you don't, walkway collapse and you die) and engage more enemies until you reach a section of walkway that is stable. If a wing pops up right then and there, will you be able to grab it before you lose the chance?
There are occasionally other bugs and a few WTF moments. On some levels you *can* fall off the edge of some walkways. There's a common bug on 3rd level where you encounter a "boss" creature who may kill you before you can even start moving. As you can't tap past the cutscenes, this gets very annoying.
All in all, Kill Team is a fun little shooter, but I think the Halo version: Spartan Ops, is better game overall. This game does give you multiple space marines to play with, but it's not balanced quite right, It probably gets better in co-op though. It is rather exciting to play.

I heard good things about Jet Set Radio from back in the day, and got drawn in by the graphical style, killer soundtrack, and simple premise.
I heard many wrong things about Jet Set Radio.
Personally, I was only able to play through about half of the game's campaign before leaving it behind in frustration. The game gives you a simple enough tutorial to get used to the controls; but it's barely enough for the challenges of what you have to do.
The game offers almost no sense of direction; in order to complete each stage there are certain places that you have to tag your mark on, but the game gives you almost no indication as to where these locations are unless you're already looking right at them. Not to mention that in order to tag, you need to make sure you've picked up plenty of spray cans; which you will constantly run out of when some levels require you to make very large tags.
This says nothing about the enemies you'll face; because of course you can't be left alone to paint in peace. From the very first stage outside the tutorial you'll start being pursued by all manner of different officers. Who scale in difficulty and sevarity at an alarming rate [seriously, I was barely halfway through the game and I was being shot at by helicopters, how severe of a crime is tagging in this world?]. Some required tag locations are even located right by enemy spawning locations, meaning that you can be interrupted during a tag, which just burns more time. From all this the enemies aren't so much of an obstacle as they are just flat out annoying.
You know what else is aggravating? The controls. The game does trick you a bit with a fairly straightforward tutorial, not too complex and tells you how every button does with most contexts. Note, I said 'most'. As you progress you'll be challenged to complete a series of tricks to unlock other characters, and these challenges require a mastery of the controls that just isn't feasable; especially with the early character unlocks. Tag locations can be placed in areas that look simple enough to reach, but the way the games controls and physics work, making simple looking jumps can be a major chore. Imprecise with stiff turns, no sense of momentum and weird physics that can lead to weak jumps off ramps while at top speed.
I love what Jet Set Radio looks like, but I simply can't bear how it actually feels firsthand. If you really believe the soundtrack is enough reward to keep you playing, then by all means go ahead. Otherwise, just look to see if you can buy the soundtrack as a standalone to make up for it.

First of all, dont let the hours fool you, I've dumped hundreds of hours into playing an replaying Baldur's Gate II before picking it up on steam.
TLDR: If you like RPG's its criminal to not have this in your library.
This is one of the best RPGs ever made. Want to find out how Bioware developed their reputation for deep, rich storytelling, extremely fleshed out worlds, and great characters? I started with Baldur's Gate and was perfected here in BG2. Everything that was done well in BG was improved for this one.
Characters return from BG, but not in a way that will get confusing for someone who skipped BG1. Romance options were added, though some of them are meh. Characters have their own personalities, motivations, and loyalties so you can have personality conflicts that are often humorous, sometimes deadly.
MASSIVE amount of stuff to do. There are many quests and sidequests and many were added to the EE.
Tactical gameplay is the name of the game here. If youre looking for a run in and hack em up, you're gonna have a bad time. If you enjoyed the tactical camera in Dragon Age Origins, this is that on steroids. You need a balanced party and need to plan engagements to survive. This is not power fantasy like Skyrim, where a high level character is basically a god. There is always something to challenge you. Try to take on the Dragons in this game like you do in Skyrim, you'll be a hero shaped scorch mark pretty quick.
The only Cons I can think of are if you don't like to read, you're just not going to enjor this game. There is voice acting in this game, and it is done well, but you will have to read a lot, as most dialogue is not voiced. I don't really consider it a con, but some might.
Also I've run into some framerate drops which oddly enough were solved by saving my game. Strange.
Highly recommend!!

The premise of the game is pretty simple - you jump out of the portal in a few decades after you'd entered it.
Your king is nowhere to be found and something bad chases you coming from that same portal.
So, you have to find the king while trying desperately not to die from the evil vikings pouring out of portal (the longer you live, the stronger they get).
You'll start with 2 characters - warrior and cleric - and a boat. Then you will sail from island to island in search of your lost king, new unlocks (weapons, trinkets, skills, new classes, etc) for your characters and other general permanent unlocks (e.g. new companions that you can recruit in game).
You will encounter a bunch of races, including dwarves, elves and undeads, which have their own troubles and fights. And you'll be able to interact them based on your reputation with a specific race.
The cool thing is you'll (almost) always have a choice whether to fight, or just ignore the situation in front of you.
The game does includes some amusing writing, so it's pretty cool to read the encounters (well, at least the first time you get into them).
I have not noticed any game-breaking bugs during my playthrough - the game's pretty solid.
The only issue of early access version is essentially limited number of encounters - after some time you'll start getting into same ones again and again.
This is something that can definitely be improved over time by the developers themselves.
The addition of the Story Builder that allows anyone to create their own random encounter using a simple editor and put it into Steam Workshop with one button push will definitely add even more variety to the game later down the line.
If you like the idea of rogue-lite RPG with turn based combat - definitely have a look at Overfall. It's pretty good.
I'd say it's one more example of early access done right. And it's actually pretty cheap for a game of that quality right now (just $10).

is an open world fantasy RPG that was successfully funded on Kickstarter. It has a turn-based combat with a focus on party encounters. The game features over a hundred different locations and dozens of NPCs, party companions and enemies.
The game starts off with a small introduction and after creating your two starting characters you are tossed back into the world. The story is pretty simple, you were sent on a quest to another world by your king and while you were there, centuries passed on your homeworld, while to you it was only a few days. Now, on your return, you find out that your king has gone missing and that your world is in chaos with various factions fighting for control and supremacy.
On your quest you’ll be traveling by boat from island to island and you can board any ship you find at sea, and they will react to you depending on your reputation with said faction. During dialogue you can choose to either trade, attack or persuade the enemy.
Combat will feel pretty familiar to anyone who has played any turn based tactical RPG. However, instead of having a certain number of moves per unit, Overfall arranges the combat in an interesting way. Each turn is divided into different phases: movement, utility and attack. During the Movement phase you can either move your character or use a special move ability such as leaping to get closer to your foes. On the Utility phase you can use abilities that don’t directly damage your enemies but still affect them in some way such as stunning or bleeding. On the last phase you get your chance to use offensive abilities to actually make some real damage to your enemies. I find this combat scheme to work rather well and it opens up many tactical opportunities.
Some characters that you find on islands or ships will let you know about certain events, such as humans that require assistance on an island. Completing tasks such as these will raise or lower your reputation with the various factions. The thing about these random quests is that they are not linear, you can either attack the other party straight up or you can try talking your way out of a fight.
Completing these random events will reward with either reputation or one of the four resources that are in the game. You have Food which is used to heal party members, Dust which is used to upgrade Utility Skills or increase the speed of your ship, Rune that is used to ressurrect or hire new companions and Frag which is the currency in the game. Completing quests is necessary to upgrade your weapons and make your party stronger.
Overfall is a great game and I was really surprised by it. The game by itself has a story mode with random encounters and several different classes and skills to choose from which makes the game perfect for multiple playthroughs. Not only that but the Story Creator only adds up to the replayability, even if you don’t fancy writing your own story to play, you can still check other peoples stories and download them on the Steam workshop. The combat is simple and easy to understand but yet, it requires thinking. Overfall plays great, feels great and runs great! Other than what I mentioned above, I believe I have no other complaints to make at the moment and I highly recommend this game to any fans of turn based combat RPGs or to people who are looking for a very replayable game.

Summary: Pass, unless you want to end up featured in one of those "gamers rage" YouTube compilation videos.
Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is the single most frustrating game that I have ever played.
The premise and execution looked intriguing enough initially; however, once I dove into the game itself I found that this game really punishes you for dying. Not only are you brutally mangled by other players, but the camera forces you to watch your body ragdoll for quite a while before it allows you to look away to "ghost" after other players, while simultaneously showing you just how many times that other player has killed you.
It feels like everything about the death system is about rubbing your nose in it. Unless you're on a kill streak and you're just on fire (proverbially), it's a really unpleasant and enfuriating experience. The Free-For-All gameplay mode is a joke. A surprisingly large number of players rage about "honor" and fighting one-on-one in some of the team-based play modes, but once it becomes a free-for-all, "honor" goes out the window and everyone is running around looking for opportunities to stab- or shoot- someone else in the back.
If I did well in the game, it felt dull, like there was no challenge. If I did poorly, it was infuriating and I felt challenged to continue to play until I was able to do better. Whether I did poorly or well, every time I stopped playing the game, I considered just uninstalling it.
Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is one of the prettiest and most promising failures I've played in some time, but ultimately it is - in my opinion - a complete and utter failure. I never once had a moment in this game where I thought "wow, that was really fun." When I won, I was bored, and when I lost, I was infuriated. I've never experienced that before in a game, and it was a such a bad experience that I'm never going back.

The visuals are fun, and the setting is okay.  The problem I had using the PC version is that the camera was buggy, and it made it unplayable.  It may do better using a gamepad, but for PC using mouse and keyboard, I do not recommend buying it.

The combat seems simple at first, but once you become more familiar with the combat mechanics and unlock new things, you are rewarded with some deep and satisfying gameplay.
If you enjoy turn-based RPGs, definitely give Overfall a try. For 10 bucks, you can't go wrong here.

No longer recommending Dragon Nest after playing Since Aug 2011. I only recently started playing using the Steam engine which is why I only have a few hrs on record.
I usually pick up this game when there's absolutely nothing else to do with my time, but now, I see no reason to even bother logging in. The servers have always lacked stability as far as I can remember. Anyone who's played since 40 cap can tell you how bad it gets. For an MMO, it's not a BAD game, but the server stability is what ruins it for me. (More on that later)
Looking into how bad the server is, sometimes you will disconnect for no apparent reason. It could be right in the middle of a boss battle or raiding. Other times, it could be when you get a good roll on a rare drop and suddenly you get kicked from the server. This has been going on since 40 cap which was already more than 4 years past and Nexon has hardly done anything to manage this problem.
The community is more of the same. You'll meet nice people who just want to play for fun and get by and other times (mainly in PvP) you'll meet a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ elitists who think they're all that. For an MMORPG, it's nothing spectacular.
Class balance will always be an issue in the game. Even before the sub-classes came out in 50 cap, there was still class imbalance mainly in pvp.
Gearing up chars for certain classes will be heavily dependent on how popular that class is. The more "higher" that class, the more expensive and tedious it will be. Again, nothing notable since it's like this in most MMORPGs.
In this game, you'll get 2 nests (or one nest in level 24 and 32) starting at lvl 40 cap for every 10 levels which is like a dungeon but with slightly stronger bosses and mobs with higher rewards. Also starting at level 40 is a Raid which you can team up with 8 players (instead of the usual 4 in dungeons and Nests) with even greater rewards. One issue with this is that the nests/raids will get progressively easier as you level up. A lvl 60 will have no problem doing a level 40 raid, even all by himself.
The focus of the game is to level up your character and get the best gear possible by doing raids or nests. Alternatively, you can gamble by paying real money but you will instead earn "cash-equipment" which is exclusively obtained by spending money, creating an unfair advantage to those who spend money on the game as opposed to those who don't which has always been Nexon's formula. See their pattern now?
Picking up this game was both a blessing and a curse. Having only spend 200 something dollars did NOT detriment my savings but I rather instead spend it elsewhere cause Nexon honestly doesn't deserve your money considering how little they put in to making the game better for everyone. The game leaves a lot to be desired since the popularity is shrinking by the ten-folds and the same content is being recycled, thus making the game dig deeper and deeper into its failing timeline.

Incredible atmosphere, challenging but not artificially difficult, impressive AI, and did I mention the atmosphere?
The base game is great. The "Complete" mod is great for a first time player, and MISERY raises the immersion to levels where you are truly trying your best to survive in the Zone, hunting with your fellow STALKERs at the beginning to make your earnings by selling meat.
There are few moments as memorable in gaming as my first contact with a controller, and this game will forever be remembered as one that did everything right, but appealed to too narrow an audience: players who like to take their time, get sucked into a world, and carefully plan their journey and reap their just rewards.

If you enjoy Super Smash Bros you'll likely dig this title.
EDIT: Having played roughly 200 hours after writing that review I felt I should update it with a list of pros and cons. Here goes:
We'll start pleasantly first..
Pros:
1.  Offers a wide variety between difference in characters and loadouts.
2. Replayability. Rarely gets boring.
3. Growing community of players and new game developments (new characters and versions)
4. Challenging combat. You quickly learn what tactics can and cannot work
Cons:
1.  Game drops. Happens less often now, but still occurs in heat of combat at times.
2. The community, like many multi-player gaming communities, has it's faIr share of bullies.
3.  Having to rely on teammates. This can be both a pro or a con, but considering most casual players just join random games it becomes unfortunate to be brought down by less seasoned teammates.
4. Which leads to my last con. Having played several hundred online games, they're rarely close. Most become quite evident who is in the favor, and it is TOUGH to ever bounce back when the opponent has a commanding lead.
But overall, this is still one of my favorite purchases on Steam and entirely got my moneys worth. Bonus pro, this game is frequently onsale for under $3.00 which IMHO is one of the better deals you can ever find on Steam.

I still recommend this game, as it genuinely is a lot of fun and I have a good feeling that the Steam Workshop will only make this game even more enjoyable than it already is.
However, having said that, this feels unfinished and still too early to leave early access (even after being in 9 years of developent). Levels are short, fighting with weapons can really seem disappointing at times with how quickly they end both against you and the enemy, and way too many loading screens. The game is at it's best when you engage in combat unarmed, the combat requires skill and timing and is ultimately rewarding when done correctly, although when it comes to fighting the stronger enemies with more health, for example the wolves, you just end up throwing that "skill" part of the game out the window and do your jumpy-flying-kicking-move a couple of times until they die, which seems like a massive downgrade from it's precede, Lugaru.
I'm probably only recommending this game for one thing- well, maybe two things, one being that I bought this game in 2013 and still want to support the developers on this game so I might as well give them a thumbs up for this review (even though it did cost me £32 at the time ffs), but the main thing is because of the Steam Workshop. I sense a lot of potential in there, the game is a lot of fun in it's vanilla state, albeit a bit short but still fun, just imaging the extra content that could go into the game through the workshop would be amazing and super beneficial for the overall quality of this "finished game".
Also be sure not make the same mistake I made when I bought this at the time, don't try and play this on a low-to-middle quality laptop, it'll lag and crash and turn your laptop into a portable stove. If you are unsure on thinking if this game can run on your laptop/computer, then if you can try and find a way to test it before purchasing.
All in all I think this is a game worth your time, it's nowhere near perfect and I certainly wouldn't purchase this game for the price that I did back in 2013 at £32, but the price it is at now during the special promotion at the time of writing at £16.09 I think is just about right. Overall, I recommend it ;)

But all in all a remaster that makes BG2 even better game.

I highly recommend Crusaders Kings II, which is truly magnificent achievement from Swedish studio Paradox.

Gameplay is based around a repetitive and linear combat system. It lacks the basic dynamic feeling that gameplay of this sort requires to stay enjoyable.  Unlockables (alt classes/trinkets/weapons) that might add some variation to gameplay are difficult and extremley time consuming to acquire. Character progression is non-existant in any traditional sense. Upgrades are instead purchased or aquired through traits (as often bad as good). Consequently, the steadily increasing difficulty curve gives no heightened sense of achievement, just consternation on the players part. Some classes/races are clearly superior to others, only, you don't have acces to those.
As the end game approaches, players are faced with a need to constantly feed (heal) thier troops, to a point of tedousness and extreme in-game poverty. This is just as well as there arn't many other things to buy. Units do not heal outside of battle, meaning the 'strongest' builds are ones focused around low damage high healing parties, which extends the length of any given combat inordinatly. It seems as though the player is on the wrong end of the developers practical joke--when you manage to recruit a 3rd unit, the enemy has 4. When you manage a 4th they field between 5 or just add additional rounds, between which you are unable to heal.
Eventually you are forced to conclude that combat is a dimintioning return reward system. Random quests which feature no combat often provide greater rewards. Chivalry: Medieval Warfare has a fun atmoshphere with it's menacingly cloudy skies, old looking castles and manly screams.  There is a wide variety of game modes which in turn usually include a series of objectives to complete. Most modes are team based but there are also ones like free for all and duel. You play as one of four customizable classes which you can switch between upon death. Essentially, you have a tank, a swift (and light) dude, a long range decent damage type and an archer. These three work relatively well together, though the long range type is overly popular and one could argue that the archer should be removed as shooting people down from a distance isn't very chivalrous desu.
My favorite part of the game is the atmosphere (which is probably at it's best when storming a rainy castle in one of these team objective modes), but the fighting system is pretty cool too. When it comes to meele weapons, you have three main types of slashes. One is pretty general, one is good for damage, one has nice range. The course of the slashes can be changed my "dragging" one's mouse, which gives a lot of potential for weird and hmm unfair attacks. Slashes can be blocked with a block move. To disrupt an opponent's fighting pattern, one can use a kick move. There are bunch of other moves as well, some of them class specific. All moves cost stamina. It's a pretty skill-based system, so that's big plus.
In Chivalry, one will need to invest a lot of time and practice to get good. Starting out, it's easy to get wrecked all the time, but there is still enjoyment to be found. And the game is about the team objectives too, not just being good at cutting down opponents.
The game can get a bit reperetive and it has some bugs, but overall I've felt mostly nothing but joy from playing this game. I've personally seen nothing like it before, it's definitely something I would recommend.

Gear Up offers fast-paced multiplayer ground-based robot combat with a neat parts-based customization system that allows the player to create an immense variety of shooty zoomies; from the wheels, to the body, to the weapons, there's a lot going on, especially as far as the latter is concerned; there are many weapon types and nearly as many available as secondary weapons to plug into the sides of your turret. As of right now, the game modes are a little predictable; matches are either team deathmatch or "domination" which probably works exactly how you would imagine. I did not, however, find this to be particularly troubling; the game has a BEAUTIFUL art style to accompany its interesting enough level design; at no point have I found the matches to be boring.
There are a handful of games that play exactly the same right now in this genre. I was happy to find that although the games are similar, Gear Up has enough going on for itself in terms of aesthetic and style where it stands on its own as a playable and FUN moon-and-zoom shoot-and-scoot.

Well... after finishing this game, I was taken back to a time when true Roleplaying freedom actually existed, where a developer truly cared about their game and work, back when Bioware were reaching the top of their game. This truly a deep, rich and satisfying RPG, one of the best I've played, even compared to Mass Effect and Witcher.
I was quite used to the isometric style fresh out of playing BG1, Neverwinter Nights, Divinity Original Sin, and Fallout 1/2. As such, I adjusted quickly to the play style and was able to play on Core Rules on my first playthrough, though this proved quite challenging at times.
The gameplay is pretty much the same as BG1, though the expanded level cap and abilities open up new possibilities with how your party can operate. It also makes otherwise weak characters quite potent. Mages are still the most powerful class due to the sheer amount of spells available, and this also makes combat quite dynamic and require preparation and strategy. Perhaps too much, it felt - some abilities are needed, like Breach, Greater Whirlwind, Time Stop, etc... so some research helps with higher difficulties. Pausing is pretty much needed on high difficulties as killing mages is usually a priority, and positioning your tanks appropriately goes a long way to surviving battles.
Sound and voice acting are very good and atmospheric, but was quite subdued for most of the game. However, the amount of character interactions more than make up for it. In BG1 there was barely any, but in this game each character has the amount of dialogue with you that Mass effect did. The romance I had was actually very deep and led to a very satisfying ending for my story, and when I finished the game, I felt genuinely happy with my time with these characters, but also sad as if saying goodbye.
The graphics for the environments look very beautiful with its rich colours appropriate to each setting. The character models are not as sharp, unfortunately, but so long as you don't zoom in too much, its not very noticeable.
The difficulty can be a problem as you go along, however, If you don't follow a walkthrough, chances are you'll miss a really powerful item that turns future encounters easy, rather than frustrating bordering on impossible if you don't have it. That'll be a frustration for anyone who plays the first time through, though perhaps it would be more sensible to play on a lower difficulty first.
All in all, this is one of the RPG experiences that I probably won't forget. It hearkens back to that feeling of being fully immersed in the setting and invested in your character, because you feel like you are the character. It never feels like you're forced into anything... with the exception of one or two dialogue choices. On that note, I also really liked how they handled dragons in this game. Unlike Dragon Age, it never forces dragon slaying down your throat, and the dragons are actually powerful, mystical creatures rather than cannon fodder they are in Dragon Age. The game also lets you spare them even when it's impractical, and I really appreciate that given how many games force you to fight them nowadays.
This game is truly a testament to what RPGs are at their best... but also a sad reminder of how far Bioware has fallen. It seems a symptom of modern day video game industry, and unavoidable. However, I would say support games like this, where the developers show their creativity, care and attention to detail and who deliver rich and satisfying game experiences. This game has what most game nowadays lack: heart.

Jet Set Radio is everything that you would expect from a Japanese game made in the late 90's. Originally on the SEGA Dreamcast, Jet Set Radio is a game where you use magnetic skates to skate around, spray graffiti, and escape a police force that is willing to call in helicopters with missiles just to stop some skating hooligans. It has a very arcade-like feel to it, which definitely suites its gameplay. You go on missions to skate around the city streets to "tag" your graffiti on the walls. Other gangs are trying to steal your turf as well, and sometimes you'll have to duke it out the only way possible... By spraying them with graffiti.
There's a big amount of variety when it comes to movement. You can grind on rails, jump off of walls, do tricks, and skate backwards. A lot of your points are based on how many tricks you can do in a row without touching the ground, which sets an incredibly high skill ceiling, where every time you play, you feel as if you're improving, and getting that combo higher and higher, until you get the highest ranking possible on every single mission.
As much as I want to sit here and boast about how good JSR is, I can't deny its flaws. There are sometimes
spikes in difficulty, where you will sometimes want to scream. It's a matter of trial and error. The camera is also a bit odd. The button used to reset the camera is also the button used to spray graffiti. This normally isn't a problem, but in races when you're trying to tag your enemy, it can become dissorientating as mashing the button will constantly jerk the camera behind you, and button mashing is somewhat required for these missions. You can turn this off in the settings, however that means that there's no longer a way to automatically reset the camera, and you'll have to do it manually. The momentum and physics can also seem a bit slow and floaty sometimes, especially when trying to avoid enemies.
These flaws are not a dealbreaker in any way, as Jet Set Radio boats a very unique style that is hard to ignore. It's very thematically appropriate, and would be hard to imagine looking any other way. Although it looks very polygonal, it doesn't look out of place or ugly because of its iconic stye. Its music is perfectly picked, and there isn't a single track that I dislike. I find myself quite literally "Humming the Bassline" because these tunes are so iconic that they're hard to forget.
Even after you beat the main story, there's still much to do. There's a ton of playable characters, and a handful of secret ones to unlock. Let me be the first to tell you: 100%-ing this game is completely worth it for the characters that it unlocks. 100%-ing is no easy feat however, as there's a ton of hidden graffiti designs to find and unlock (You can also create your own custom graffiti!).
This game definitely has that "Japanese Stank" to it. I can't really describe it. It's just something that when you see it, you'll know what I'm talking about, and it's absolutely amazing.
I've beaten this game countless times, and I'm still constantly replaying it. This is definitely one of my favorite games of all time. I don't see myself stopping any time soon.
This game is a must-have for any fan of platformer/action games. It has everything that you could possibly want, and more.

Of all the RPGs I have played in the previous year, only two from BioWare have taken the epic storyline scale in such a way to warrant a playthrough of 80 hours to come to the end of its journey, the Baldur’s Gate Trilogy (SoD & SoA) and Dragon Age: Inquisition. Even though I am comparing a trilogy of games to one,it’s obvious how much the scope of BG is meant to be examined as a whole, not individually. For example, the beginning of BG2 starts the mid-to-late game of a character’s progression. Anyone in 2017 who wishes to venture into the series should know that is how they should set their expectations for the type of adventure before them.
The journey of that adventure is as important as the camaraderie you forge along the way that has become a staple for modern BioWare, and every game afterwards has been compared to the BG series. Although Baldur's Gate 2 and DAI are separated by nearly twenty years of design philosophies, RPG standards, gamer expectations and opinions on how successful are these games, I found each game’s sense of scale to resonate with one another like brothers long forgotten. While there are inherent differences in the freedom of choices for otherwise linear questlines and stories, the scale of all these linear features offers a sense of non-linearity that is greater than any sandbox hoping to achieve the same effect in the grandness of quantity versus quality.
However, despite the BG series maintaining its quality along with its quantity, BG2 suffers a  problem that I feel is more exasperated in DAI, and that issue is player fatigue with its mechanics.
In my previous review of BG1, I had hoped to learn AD&D someday so well to better appreciate experiences like Durlag’s Tower by mastering the rules themselves. I had considered the pursuit plausible but not worthwhile of my time to beat the rules at their own game. When I choose to take a break after the 40/45 hours of BG1 & SoD, however, I set myself up for disaster; the Chapter 1/Prologue of BG2 only helps you so far before you’re released into the mass of content that is Chapter 2.

What I think is one issue that SoD introduced to the franchise, unintentionally, is that the time it takes to get to BG2 is when the mechanics start to lose their luster. Even without mentioning the expansion for BG1, the expansion Throne of Bhaal eventually bored me from the same problem as I found the repetition of combat without a whole lot of extra complexities or challenges to wear out my patience. Add to the fact that setting the difficulty to anything but Story Mode will also add time because of micromanagement and do overs in combat, and the game begins to show signs that it is overstaying its welcome. That is an issue I think people are going to have to ask themselves whether to keep the challenge to retain your interest in the gameplay or cut-it-out to experience the game faster.
One reason for this feeling of being overwhelmed at the very beginning is how the game acts are structured. Previously, BG1 had you wandering around the woods, funneled by various challenges to guide you to where you needed to go, before giving you a city and the rest of the map to explore. BG2, however, is the exact opposite; you start out in a giant city and world to explore, and as you move on to Chapters 3 – 10, the game gets progressively more linear. Not all the quests must be done before Chapter 3 as you have the chance to continue them, but I think the content would have been better had it not been so cramped at the start and more evened out along the linear parts of the game.
As much as people have given much praise for BG2’s storytelling for BioWare, it’s rather interesting how many people believe the storyline is malleable to player agency when most of it is a guise of choice. However, because of the scale of that journey, the little details like companions forgetting you or coming back to life (Xzar) does not break the immersion. Events play out in a manner that enhances the storyline of the antagonists always being one step ahead of you no matter what you choose, and rather than insulting the player due to the limitations of their decisions or whiplashing the player back on to the linear progression, the story is benefited by this design as it adds character to what many would consider to be the greatest villain of all time, Jon Irenicus.
What also works is that no matter what faction or "good or evil" path you take on repeated
playthroughs there is always something new to experience or a new chain of events that adds value to both the worldbuilding as well as the replayability of BG. This is all before adding difficulty modifiers or handicaps/party-configurations as additional reasons for replaying the game. All of these reasons, and more, are why I believe many feel that BG2 is the pinnacle of RPGs as both a story and a game because both the game-design, gameplay and narrative benefit reopening the book from the start and finding all new details to explore.
And when the Bhaalspawn has undergone all the trials and tribulations, the meanderings of fate and the questions of destiny that plagues every choice, the player reaches its end. Rather than establishing a definitive moral high-ground choice or an absolutely deplorable one, the player is left to make the decision of whether to accept the guidance and struggles of fate to reap the rewards for selfish or alternative reasons in claiming godhood or to renounce everything gained for a quieter life free from immortal concerns and to live out the rest of the days as a mortal with the company discovered along the way.
The finality of this decision cements any lasting concerns or desires to see the storyline to continue from this point onwards and it is why there is no need to make another sequel to extend the continuity any further, a point many series should learn to accept and to move on to greater adventures yet to come.

This is a great game and a pretty good re-release.  There's some expanded content but none of it is really required.  You can also opt into the original UI under betas for the game.
There's an equivalent to Shadowkeeper available as well, so one of the best tools you could get for vanilla BG2 is still basically available.
If you never played this back in the day, it's well worth the asking price to give it a shot.  If you've ever been interested in the Infinity Engine games, this might be the best of the lot.  Although you may want to start with BG1 EE if that's the case.
If you played it back in the day, you'll still enjoy it now.  Difficulty levels can be chosen (PICK CORE RULES if you want the "real deal").  And you can modify them further with a lot of different options.  There's a difficulty for people that want mostly just the story and feel of adventure and there's one for the hardest core players as well as everything in between.
My only two real complaints are the way that the journal has been re-organzied more like a modern quest-list (though you may find this a positive, depending on preference) and that the default AI settings for party members are AWFUL.  Seriously, either turn the party AI OFF or turn most of the contingencies off so they don't waste all their resources constantly.
Overall, it's a great game.  And this re-release mostly just serves to help make it playable on modern machines without the need for lots of mods.

Like EVERY Elder Scrolls game, your character starts off as a prisoner with no backstory or explanation. I get that it's iconic and whatnot, but don't you think it's time for creativity? Is this the best opening they could come up with over YEARS and YEARS of making these games?
Aside from that, I think Oblivion did a really good job executing the plot of the game and the rest of the beginning sequence. However, I would have liked to have seen more of Uriel Septim. When a grand character that just got introduced is murdered, it doesn’t have any emotional impact unless you got to know them. In this case you didn’t. I realize Uriel was part of the older games in the series, but games like that were all about gameplay, rather than character development other than your own person. In the earlier games, Uriel wasn’t that important or developed, other than him being an important but otherwise lifeless and almost nonexistent character in the plot.
I’ll be honest, I played Skyrim before Oblivion, and so I only knew about the Mythic Dawn through that one guy in Dawnstar.  What I didn’t like about that was the fact that Bethesda tried to completely change their backstory. In Skyrim, the cult didn’t mean much to me because I saw it as just another quest. I know the guy was trying to make them sound nobler, but I don’t feel that he was the one who wrongfully portrayed them.
Another thing that I have a problem with is the Frostcrag Spire. You inherit this big ancient tower somewhere along the game from your ancestor. The problem is, that could lead to some severe plot holes. Depending on your selected race, your ancestor probably wouldn’t be a rich mage, due to living conditions, policies and racism. For example, I always play as an argonian. I can’t see an argonian becoming that successful in life during that timeline. If you were an Imperial, for example, the story would make sense. But as a beast race? Not happening.
The graphics were terrible, but it’s an older game so that’s understandable. Now, don’t get me wrong. Graphics don’t mean anything, and they can’t make-or-break a game for me. But this is something I would like to point out. While I do agree that story and gameplay are much more important, the faces in Oblivion are unacceptable. Every human looks like a squash, every khajiit looks like a potato, every orc looks like Shrek...
But onto more important matters. The gameplay. While the combat system isn’t as polished as the system in Skyrim, it is pretty rewarding. But many mechanics are highly lacking. For example, the horrid lockpicking system. It made any quest that involved sneaking into somewhere almost impossible and it was rage inducing to say the least.
Another failure on Bethesda’s part would have to be the leveling system. I would have never figured this one out if I hadn’t gotten advice from a friend. Earning experience alone won’t make you level up. You have to SLEEP to level up, granted if you have enough experience. This is, beyond a doubt, a terrible idea and I sincerely hope to never see it again in any other game. I have no idea what went on in that board meeting.
Now I’ll be talking about the open world, social interactions, and exploring. First off, there are so many places to explore; it’s ridiculous (in a good way). But the thing is, everywhere, at least to me, is very bland and I honestly had no motive to explore more after I completed the main quest. Any pictures or screenshots you see of Oblivion featuring a nice blue lake and green grass, and a beautiful environment are probably modded. Because you won’t see that in the actual game.
Now, the people in Oblivion are...colourful. They’re tons of fun to talk to, since your actions can change what options you have (rather than just provoking nasty comments from people but still being the same personalities in Skyrim). By completing the main quest, it gives pretty much everybody a 100% Like ratio towards you, which is really good. But even overhearing idle chitchat from a distance between two NPCs is fun, albeit repetitive.
What I don’t like is that some characters don’t stay with the continuity. There are two people sparring in the Imperial City, who are training to be combatants in the Gladiator Arena. Alright, so are you. But even when you become the Grand Champion, they’re still training. They were supposed to join roughly when you joined, however, according to their intentions.
I’ll be the first to say it. I like the Adoring Fan. He compliments you and comes with a free torch. But he’s buggy. He runs slower than you do, and if you travel on foot for too long, he won’t catch up to you. He just disappears and randomly comes back a few ingame days later. That really sucks in my opinion.
Going back to gameplay, Oblivion is WAY too dark. Before you tell me to “raise my screens brightness”, do note that the rest of the game is fine and if I raised my brightness, anywhere that isn’t dark would be a lens flare. Every dark building or cave, or even some places outside at night are SO dark that your screen is pitch black. I constantly used the starter heal spell on myself all throughout the game as a temporary light source, because torches die. You have no idea how much magicka was used because of that.
One thing that really sucks is, there is no dual-wielding. That explains itself. But another thing that is terrible in my opinion is the fact that all equipment degrades. This is the worst aspect a game could implement. Sure, you can repair them, but why should you have to? You don’t in Skyrim! Some say it’s to add realism. But it’s just a dumb, primitive mechanic from the days when making a game extremely and unnecessarily difficult was only to prolong gameplay time clocked in.
All in all, I did like Oblivion, but I had no incentive to replay it with another character like I did with Skyrim. If I had to rate Oblivion, I would give it a 6/10. It didn’t get a higher score because of poor lighting, bad gameplay mechanics, the fact that things degrade and an unappealing environment that didn’t make you want to explore it anymore than you needed to. I wouldn’t replay it.

A bit mixed on the game.
On the one hand, it's surprisingly cheap, though it comes up to about the right value once you've played through. It's also got refreshing ideas, new characters, weapons & enemies to play with, and enough things dying or exploding around you to keep you entertained for quite some time. Play difficulty is also somewhat balanced, and the lore is pretty accurate.
On the other hand though, everything sort of just stops short of greatness. The lore doesn't introduce anything new or refreshing, certain weapons are either inaccurate or don't really differ from others (high RoF rocket launcher? Really?), the weapons don't feel as satisfying as in Space Marine, certain missions feel unbalanced or rigged unintentionally against you, music is recycled from DoW2, and most of the animations which make all previous Warhammer 40K games so satisfying and unique are gone in the name of fast, unending action.
I guess that's all because the game is a dual-stick shooter, which has it's uses. But ultimately I think it fails to impress. It just feels bland. Sure hope they start breathing new life into the license, because it's really starting to slow.

- Graphics are fairly solid in all aspects. (Character design is odd yet cute, Skill animations are simple yet satsifying, the background textures are fresh and rich with color)
- Game world is active and extremely dynamic on very rare occasions it can be linear.
- Main story consists of multiple smaller stories that don't occur in a specfic order. The player's choices grant access to certain stories.
- The npcs are most of the time in motion doing their own thing (fighting their own battles, farming resources, sailing, and conquering islands)
- The open world aspect consists of the player sailing across a decently sized map with so many different islands that change depending on which race is the current one that dominated it.
- Perma death is a key part to this game. If you die with both your characters you have to restart but once you restart the world itself is different. Previous perks, characters, events carry over to this new playthrough
- The combat consists of Movement (moving and one ability), utility (which are most cases buffs/de buffs), Attack which is self explanitory.
- There isn't to many skills to choose from before you begin your adventure. There is enough though to form different builds.
- The combat is fairly smooth. It's simple yet complex at the same time. (You can't bring potions into combat, a good amount of the time you are out numbered, In most cases you can out play the enemy if you just adapt)
- There are I guess you can call them "passive effects" that occur are key moments after fighting. Example say you have a character that has been taking a lot of damage throughout the fight and you've been healing him. Once the fight is over he may get an effect that will stick with him for the rest of the current play through. This effect would be something like saying that "He's taken to many blows to the head. Evasion is down by 4, accuracy is down by 2".
- Then there are those same "passive effects" that occur doing certain feats that give you a buff for the rest of this character's life.
- There is a good number of companions to unlock that will aid you on your adventure but they to can suffer from Perma death.
- Once the combat is done your character doesn't heal so you have to eat food. Which heals a small amount, food is rather expensive to get once you first start (Frags are moderately tough to come by at the beginning)
- The game wants you to die so you can expierence more of it's features which is interesting but can be frustrating ( I personally don't mind I've died 17x. Mainly to Vorn hoes -_- (Vikings). But I was able to get new stuff to play with in the next playthrough)
- Encounters with npcs are random in a good way. It could be a combat one, humourous conversation, a game within a game, a few other surprises I won't spoil.
- The choice system is interesting in this game your choices have more instant effects compared to other games. Most of the time you'll see the consequence almost right after making the choice (Whether its positive or negative).
- There is a story builder which you can well... build your own story. I don't know much about this feature since the tut was the only thing available for it.
- You will only run into a few dull characters that lack personality in this game.
- I've run into just half a handful of bugs in the 40 hours i've played this game. I have to say that is pretty impressive.
- Lush yet odd graphics
- Story within a story (Storyception!)
- Dynamic world
- Simple yet tactical combat
- Interesting characters
- There's always something to do
- Expierencing something new after each death (You will die at some point)
- The global passives or traits I guess you can call them that you can obtain
- A decent skill/trait customization system
- Small amount of bugs
- Companions are actually useful
- A great homeage to classic Rogue like games
- Only $9.99 (It's well worth the $9.99)
- Story Builder is fully functional
- Adventuring into vorn (vikings basically) by mistake from the start of the game (Most cases they have 4+ people that will attack you on site)
- Most cases the Vorn will use dust to increase their speed to chase you in the boats.
- Food rationing (Depending on the player) is bad because it heals so little, and is moderately hard to obtain which leaves you vulnerable if you have low healthed heroes.
-Perma Death (That depends on the player). I for one feel that this feature is good and bad since I don't mind restarting the journey with a new twist added but it can also be frustrating.

Overfall is a charming turn based RPG with many roguelike elements and tongue-in-cheek humor mixed that will have you explore a wide-open ocean filled with various factions to befriend, quests to solve and monsters to defeat in glorious battle.
There are over 50 playable classes each with their own spells and abilities, numerous monsters and individuals to fight or chat with, randomized quests that can all be solved in multiple ways as well as plenty of characters, items and spells to unlock for future playthroughs. In short, Overfall has a ton of replayablity and some very nifty features...
Overfall has a rather unique art style that combined with some excellent audio/visual feedback results in a very compelling world to explore and to do battle in. Special mention goes to the character design which combines simple faces with highly detailed armor resulting in memorable and cool looking characters, especially the plate wearers that look like they came straight out of a WoW raid.
The combat in Overfall is done in three phases: the movement phase where you get to move your character and cast movement based abilities such as teleports, the buff/debuff phase where you get to cast non-damage orientated spells such as heals or curses and finally the combat phase where you get to capitalize on all the prep work by smashing enemies over the head.
With each character having 8 spells dived between these three categories you will never be overwhelmed when it comes to combat options but don't make the mistake of thinking the combat in Overfall is simple, or even easy, because if you do you're going to find yourself on the wrong end of an Orc's blade and starting from the very beginning since Overfall has permadeath.
Like all roguelikes out there Overfall features many randomized quests and events, ensuring that each new playthrough doesn't end up feeling the same. Where Overfall differs from the rest is in the fact that seemingly every single encounter has multiple ways of being resolved: either through combat, diplomacy or even character specific abilities such as hypnosis. What this means is that even if you run in to repeat events on your subsequent playthroughs you can get a whole new experience with them by choosing a different path than you did the last time.
But no matter how complex or expansive a roguelike is it will always end up feeling samey if you play it for long periods of time. Luckily, the developers behind Overfall opted to include a fully featured quest/encounter editor that allows you to create your very own stories and share them with other people over Steam Workshop. So if you think, for example, that Overfall is a bit on the easy side you can simply go in to the editor (or the Workshop) and draft yourself some challenging quests and set them to appear only in the areas you feel are lacking.
I cannot overstate how awesome this feature is and how important it will be for Overfall's long term appeal!
Overfall is at its hardest point early on because you can sometimes get locked in to encounters you simply cannot defeat with your two initial heroes which means a trip to the graveyard and a quick restart. On the other hand, once you build up your party and bling out your heroes you are almost indestructible as long as you play it safe and keep those heals rolling.
This is a minor complaint but one that's well worth mentioning. Overfall doesn't explicitly tell you what you need to do in order to unlock new characters and items, instead what you get is a short riddle or poem hinting towards the solution. For the majority of the unlocks this is completely fine but for some of the more complex ones which rely on timing, skill and annoyingly a bit of luck it becomes somewhat of a burden. Again, not much of an issue but if you're a completionist don't hesitate to look up a Wiki if you get stuck on some of the more obscure ones.
If two enemies are standing one above the other its sometimes very hard to know which one you're targeting, especially if the enemies are big fat guys such as trolls. This is once again a minor issue but it will draw out a few curses from you when your execute spell fails because you casted it on a full-health guy standing behind your target.
While the quest editor is an amazing addition to Overfall it isn't without its issues, most notable is the fact that it starts to really, really slow down the game when you're messing around with complex quests filled with branching and interacting choices. It doesn't affect the main game but its still something I would like to see fixed in the near future.
Overfall is an extremely solid blend between turn based strategy and roguelikes that kept me engaged and pushing for more even after hours and hours of play. It does have a few annoying issues but they so easy to overcome when the game itself is this enjoyable.
If you are interested in some stylish turn based combat, slightly cheesy humor and numerous roguelike elements then I fully recommend you give Overfall a try, it has managed to accomplish everything it set out to. And most importantly, it is really fun.

Full review:
Break it down:
The core gameplay loop is interesting and mostly complete (barring balance issues). There are a plethora of encounters that have remained fresh through several (dozen) tries. The game has plenty of unlocks that are persistent even when the actual run at the game fails (much like many rogue lites these days)

Graphically it looks and performs fine, but the options are threadbare (need work for SURE), missing everything but basic sound and resolution options.
BUT the bread and butter will be the story builder, and while the base idea is implemented the story builder is 100% what they need to focus on to build a successful title that will provide the modding scene with the tools to take this game from an interesting FTL-on-a-real-boat into a truly amazing title that will give players many many hours of playtime.

Honestly, I do not see how this game has a 'very positive' review score when compared to similar Free-to-play Action MMORPGs. First of all, the combat is very good. THE BAD:
The UI is clunky and not customizable at all. You can't even see more then one action bar. You can't move UI elements to appease. These are things that should be standard in any MMO since 2003.
You can't keybind more then one action bar full of actions. 1-8 is all you can assign and you have 3 classes worth of skills. This is nonsense.
Loading screens everywhere! Join a dungeon, loading screen. Kill two groups of mobs, loading screen to next area. Kill a group of mobs, go to loading screen to next area. That is INSANE! More loading screens than a PSOne game.
Balance. The game is way, way too easy. From what I read on the forums they nerfed enemy damage and increased EXP multiplier so that you can reach level cap really fast. So people migth think that is a good thing but to me, personally, it is not. Learning the game is half the fun. Do you really want idiots that barely know how to play in PvP and in your Guild because they reached max level cap in less than a week? There is no way they know their class.
Loot at the end of the dungeon/raid is random. So it's very possible that you do a dungeon over  many, many times to get a piece of a equipment that you want. This is crazy. I had to do a dungeon 10 times before I finally got a better weapon.
Cash Shop is full of "7-day" items. You basically pay real money for temporary items. I know it's common in most Korean MMOs but this is complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. All real-money transactions should be permanantly tied to your account.
Another problem is if you go on hiatus for a month they lock your account. Don't be surprised if when you come back from vacation your characters will be gone. You have to contact support and provide detailed information to get it back. This can take up to a week and by then you probably don't want to play anymore.

Wow okay, so where to start?
This is a great game and a pretty good re-release.  There's some expanded content but none of it is really required.  You can also opt into the original UI under betas for the game.
There's an equivalent to Shadowkeeper available as well, so one of the best tools you could get for vanilla BG2 is still basically available.
If you never played this back in the day, it's well worth the asking price to give it a shot.  If you've ever been interested in the Infinity Engine games, this might be the best of the lot.  Although you may want to start with BG1 EE if that's the case.
If you played it back in the day, you'll still enjoy it now.  Difficulty levels can be chosen (PICK CORE RULES if you want the "real deal").  And you can modify them further with a lot of different options.  There's a difficulty for people that want mostly just the story and feel of adventure and there's one for the hardest core players as well as everything in between.
My only two real complaints are the way that the journal has been re-organzied more like a modern quest-list (though you may find this a positive, depending on preference) and that the default AI settings for party members are AWFUL.  Seriously, either turn the party AI OFF or turn most of the contingencies off so they don't waste all their resources constantly.
Overall, it's a great game.  And this re-release mostly just serves to help make it playable on modern machines without the need for lots of mods.

Very short game with a basic story, which is fine for it being a sequel to Lugaru. I enjoyed the campaign but wouldn't recommend it. The meat of the game is combat, and compared to Lugaru it is a disappointing downgrade. I played Lugaru until my fingers were strained, aching and raw from hitting the counter button and my wits stretched as far as I could muster until I beat the game on the hardest difficulty. Where Lugaru was tight, this is as loose as a pillowcase.
Fighting against armed opponents, the controls feel unresponsive and ineffective - I was trying to dodge and I would just turn my back for it to be slashed. Fighting against rats is laughable, while dogs just seem like rabbits with more health. Most disappointingly, wolves are the easiest opponents: you can just jump and leg-cannon them a few times 'til they die. In Lugaru, wolves were amazingly challenging: they would pull you out of the air if you tried to leg-cannon excessively, but it wasn't out of the question to fight them toe-to-toe if you had a knife. Switching weapons is quite unintuitive: If you have a knife sheathed, you can pick up a two-hander, but you cannot pick up anything else if you are holding a two-hander. Similar situation if you are dual-weilding. Some optional, but important, controls (dropping weapons, rolling-pickups of weapons) are not documented within the game, nor are they reasonably intuitive like throat-cutting.
The platforming mechanics have a fluidity to them and it's quite fun, though wallrunning and walljumping is a nightmare to pull off consistently. The final climbing level in the campaign seems to have a marked path that has a wallrun and jump that is impossible to pull off. Knowing how high you can fall from is highly unpredictable, partly due to the death-zones. Also, dying and having to click through dialogue (or mashing enter to skip it all) all the time is stupid for a game in which you die so much.
In short, Lugaru was a much more challenging and fun experience than Overgrowth. The modding tools are excellent from the small amount I've played with, but I have no interest in it when I was looking for tight, challenging combat.

Please disregard the small amount of time that I have clocked in on this game here on Steam. I have the game on my PS Vita (Don't ask why I own one..) and I have to admit that I spent a majority of my time in 2016 dedicated to exploring every nook and cranny that this game has. Jet Set Radio is a really unique game. The cel-shaded graphics make the game pop and look like a comic book, and the music is something you can't find anywhere else. At first glance, you may think this is a super edgy game that involves a street war, gang fights, and an ultimate uprising against a corrupt government. And I'm here to tell you that is exactly correct.
You play as teen (known in the game as Rudies) on the streets of a city Tokyo-To, rollerskating and spraying graffiti all around the area. So what happens when you break the law in this game? The cops try to arrest you!
Your main goal is to tag the town with an amazing selection of assorted and original graffiti, while avoiding the fuzz at all costs. As the game progresses, other people will want to join your gang by either challenging you to a race or they'll just want you to follow thier lead. The characters in this game all stand out individually, even though a majority of the have little to none backstory they still have really cool and creative designs. Even DJ Professor K
is a really likable character.
Overall, this game is superb. But every good game has its flaws. One, the controls are kinda hard to get used to. The game also don't explain everything when it comes to tricks and even performing them at first can be a bit of a hassle, but once you get it down it gets so much easier! Two, the story is kinda..meh. It's nothing extraordinary but it's not bad either. A bit in the middle. Three, it's super easy to take massive amounts of damage. You can still be in a recovery animation after getting shot, and get shot again immediately after. It's a big pain, really. Especially if you have like seven cops attacking and clinging to you at once. Four, in my opinion, the map in the pause menu is hard to use for navigation. The one in JSRF was an improvement!
This game just bleeds creativity. It still reeks of SEGA's whole lolsocoolandxtreme mindset but it's done so well. Extreme sports games were popular at the time so it was pretty appropriate. It's just good to see that the game held up after all these years. The music is something you have to experience for yourself. I've had like, out of body experiences this music is so good. The soundtrack has original songs and songs that were made by underground/unknown bands (minus the US exclusive songs..). Hideki Naganuma (original soundtrack producer) is a music savant, along with the other bands in this game. Guitar Vader, Castle Logical, The Reps (Nobody still has any idea who they were), and my favorite: Deavid Soul.
To rap it all up...I love this game. This game has changed the way I see art, the way I listen to music. The way I see everything. Not to mention that this game was the reason I found out I'm naturally good at live radio and being a DJ. This was the game that changed me as a person, which is kinda weird to say. It may not be the game that changes you, but at least it'll make you feel good.

Warframe is THE free to play game. Solid gameplay, great community, and an amazing dev team that constantly tries to add to their game while keeping the community happy.
You do not need to put any money into this game at all, 100% promise. Spending real money gives you Plat, which you can use to buy warframes, weapons, and cosmetics from the ingame shop, all of which you can earn through normal gameplay at a reasonably fair rate. Plat can also be traded amongst players, meaning you can earn plat just by playing the game and collecting items and parts people are interested in.
The Caveat to all of this quality free to play is that the game does have quite an intensive grind. If you dont like playing repetitive tileset style maps, then the game may not be for you. However, I'd still urge you to give it a shot, the fast paced gameplay and the vast warframe options make the grind not as bad as some might expect.
-------
Gameplay - 8/10 - Parkour space ninja loot grind with magic and guns.
Controls - 8/10 - Controls may be a bit weird at first, but once you start to understand fluid movement within the game, it starts to feel natural. If you still have issues with it after a while, all controls can be rekeybound to your preference.
Difficulty/Balance - 9/10 - Heres where everything comes together, the game, is very easy, and it is also simultaneously very hard. The games weapons are all good, as well as all bad at the same time. Which makes explaining this with text fairly difficult. If you are interested further, I would highly recommend going to the wiki for all of this info (and bookmarking that site if you decide to play). The balancing comes in the form of Mods and in your game knowledge of damage types. Mods are how you enhance your warframe and weapons. With this system, you obviously have meta weapons and frames do well in more situations or that are just innately strong, but you can also make any weapon work in the late game/difficult missions.
Fairness - 8.5/10 - I'm going to break this further down for stages of the game.
A.) Fairness for the New Players - 10/10 - The game is extremely new player friendly. While the tutorial may be confusing and not explain everything it could/should. The progression in the early game is extremely fair. Low level enemies and missions can be beaten with all damage types and frames, regardless of mods. Item progression is decently paced and the game tends to hand you what you need when you need it. The devs also run promotions and special missions that are very helpful to new players, the most recent was a twitchcon event that gave a large quantity of ingame items to all players who watched some streams.
B.) Fairness for the Mid Game - 7/10 - This is where the game hurts people. Its fair, this is a grind game afterall, but theres a lot of moments where you say "Ugh im out of Polymer Bundle again??" and you have to run a mission that you may not enjoy as much, just to get the resources you need. This scenario tends to halt progress, and has turned a lot of people off from the game.
C.) Fairness for the Veterans - 9/10 - This is the people that have everything, that grind everyday. The game doesnt hurt them anymore. You too can get to this point, without putting any money into the game, it just takes time. The fairness issues to vets usually comes in the form of newer weapons, where the devs have no choice but to make newer weapons use a newer or rarer resource (looking at you nitain extract) as a crafting cost. Realistically, its pretty fair, they need to make us play the game too.
Graphics - 8/10 - Graphics can get a little demanding in some more chaotic gameplay moments, but even with all the high paced movement, the game never looks unpleasing or disorienting
Community - 9/10 - Out of all the free to play gaming communities, Warframe puts everyone else to shame. I cant hype this factor enough. If you need help, people will help, if you have questions, people will answer, if you want to play, people will play. And in my 1000+ hours of gameplay, I havent run into anyone that went out of their way to be rude or put someone down. More often than not, you find a random group of strangers that you can sit and chat with in your hour long survival runs, and talk about random nonsense or life.
Story - 6/10 - There IS a story. The way I've always looked at it was that they threw it in so the game had some type of structure to build around. Its not the greatest. But by no means is it bad. It just, doesnt always make sense? Sometimes when you pay attention to it, they have us asking way more questions than the number of answers we are provided. But honestly, its always being updated, this very well could change in the future. They could have a questline in the works that literally ties all the loose ends together.
-------
Come try it out, worst case scenario? You play it as much as we do.

This is a very fun game, and I would reccomend it to any fans of the strategy genre. The game is fun, engaging, interesting and sometimes hilarious, with the occasional occurence that is just messed up. I was once playing as a lustful old guy with a couple lovers. My wife is away at a convent or something, and I decide to see my lover when the event pops up... Little did I know that I would proceed to.... ♥♥♥♥ myself.... And become pregnant.... With my own child....... I think that's definitely a bug, and you can rest assured that the child that was born was disowned and banished.
However, with that aside, I do have one major complaint about this game, namely the DLC. While I understand that Paradox needs to make money and pay its employees, it is utterly ridiculous that a hundred dollars worth of DLC is mostly features that should be in the vanilla game for no extra cost. The Ruler Designer DLC, for example. For five more dollars, you get the ability to customize your character! And that is literally it. For an eighth of the price of the entire game extra, you get the ability to customize the first character of a dynasty. And only the first character.
For the added bonus of being able to play a non-christian ruler, you have to pay more money. Want to have a couple more options for the character customization? Fork out a little extra cash and you can. Want an earlier starting date? Pay Paradox! Twice! Want Genghis Khan to actually look like a Mongol and NOT an Arab? PAY MORE MONEY!
While this is probably the best stategy game I have ever played, it is utterly ridiculous that you have to pay truckloads of money extra to use some features that should be in the CORE GAME. The ability to customize your ruler should NOT be something you pay an extra five dollars for, it should be in the core game for no extra cost. Too large a chunk of the available DLC are simply features that should be in the main game for no extra charge. So while I would recommend this game to fans of the genre, I would NEVER reccomend the DLC, at least not to people who are on a budget. Some of the DLC is worthy of extra cost, most of it is not.
